Chapter IX: 226 Chapter I [p.1]
The Commentary on the Treasury of Abhidharma, the First Chapter of the Treasury.
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
Having paid homage to that Teacher of Reality, who has utterly destroyed all darkness and has lifted the world out of the mire of saṃsāra;
I shall expound the treatise known as the Abhidharmakośa. //1//

Desiring to compose this treatise, [the author] begins with a salutation to his Teacher, preceded by a description of his qualities, in order to make known the greatness of that Teacher. He says "he who" (yaḥ) with reference to the Buddha, the Blessed One. "One who has destroyed darkness" (hatāndhakāraḥ) means one by whom darkness has been destroyed, or one for whom darkness has been destroyed. "One who has destroyed darkness in every way and regarding everything" (sarvathā sarvahatāndhakāraḥ) means one who has destroyed darkness in all manners and in respect to all objects. For ignorance is indeed "darkness" because it obstructs the vision of things as they truly are.

And that [darkness] has been destroyed by the Blessed Buddha through the attainment of the antidote; because it is of a nature never to arise again with respect to all objects of knowledge, in every way and everywhere, he is one who has destroyed darkness in every respect and in its entirety. Although Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas have also indeed destroyed darkness regarding everything—due to the absolute departure of afflicted delusion—they have not done so in every respect.

For indeed, regarding these qualities of a Buddha which are extremely remote in space and time, as well as regarding objects of infinite variety, there exists a non-afflicted ignorance. Having thus praised [the Blessed One] for his perfection in the practice of self-benefit, he praises that same Blessed One again for his perfection in the practice of benefiting others, saying: "He has lifted the world out from the mire of saṃsāra. For saṃsāra is like a mire because it is a place where the world becomes stuck and because it is difficult to cross over.

The Blessed One, feeling compassion for the world submerged therein and without protection, has lifted it up according to its capacity by extending the hand of the teaching of the True Dharma. To him who is thus endowed with the perfection of practice for the benefit of self and others, [the author] says "having paid homage," meaning having prostrated with the head. He is a "Teacher of Reality" (*yathārtha-śāstṛ*) because he teaches according to reality, without error. By this, he reveals his means for practicing the benefit of others.

Because he is a Teacher by virtue of teaching according to reality, he has lifted the world out of the mire of cyclic existence, and not through the power of supernatural feats or the granting of boons. Having paid homage to him, [the author] states what he will do: "I shall expound the treatise. It is called a *śāstra* because it instructs disciples. Which treatise? He says: the *Abhidharmakośa*. What is this that is called Abhidharma?
"Abhidharma is pure wisdom along with its attendants" (2a).

In this context, wisdom (*prajñā*) is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*). "Pure" means untainted (*anāsrava*). "With its attendants" means together with its retinue. Thus, it is stated that Abhidharma consists of the five untainted aggregates (*skandha*). This, first of all, is the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) Abhidharma. As for the conventional (*sāṃketika*) [Abhidharma], it is both that which leads to the attainment of the former and the treatise (*śāstra*) itself. (2b)

Furthermore, that outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsravā prajñā*) consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, as well as that acquired through birth (*upapattipratilambhikā*) along with its attendants, and also the treatise intended for the attainment of this untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*), are called "Abhidharma" because they serve as its equipment (*saṃbhāra*). As for the etymological definition: it is "Dharma" because it maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa-dhāraṇāt*). Thus, it is "Abhidharma" because it is a Dharma directed toward (*abhimukha*) either the ultimate Dharma, which is Nirvana, or the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Abhidharma has been explained. But how is this treatise the *Abhidharmakośa*?
Because one enters into this [treatise] by way of its meaning, and because it is the support for that [Abhidharma], it is called the *Abhidharmakośa*. (2cd)

For that Abhidharma, which is designated as the "treatise" (*śāstra*), is included within this [work] according to its primary meaning; thus, this treatise serves as its "repository" (*kośa*). Alternatively, that Abhidharma is the basis (*āśraya*) for this treatise, since it has been extracted from that. Therefore, because that very Abhidharma is its treasury, this treatise is called the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Furthermore, for what purpose is the teaching of Abhidharma, and by whom was it first taught, such that the Master (Vasubandhu) takes care to speak the *Abhidharmakośa*? To this he says:
Since there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions apart from the discernment of phenomena,
and it is through the afflictions that the world wanders here in the ocean of existence.
For that reason, it is said that this was taught by the Teacher. //3//

Since there is no means for the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*) apart from the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), and since it is the afflictions that cause the world to wander in this great ocean of *saṃsāra*, the Teacher, the Buddha, is said to have taught the Abhidharma for the sake of that discernment of phenomena as its cause; for without the instruction of the Abhidharma, a disciple is not capable of discerning phenomena.

The Vaibhāṣikas say: "That [Abhidharma] was indeed taught by the Blessed One in a scattered manner, but it was compiled and made known by the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and others, just as the Venerable Dharmatrāta composed the Udānavarga. Furthermore, he asks: "Which are those dharmas for the sake of whose discernment the Abhidharma instruction exists? He replies:
"Dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*) and dharmas without outflows (*anāsrava*). (4a)
This is the summary exposition of all phenomena (*dharma*). Regarding that, what are the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena? It is said:
conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), excluding the Path (*mārga*), are contaminated.
With the exception of the truth of the path, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are with-outflows (*sāsrava*). What is the reason?
Because the outflows (*āsrava*) adhere (*samanuśerate*) within them. (Verse 4cd)

Granted that outflows (*āsrava*) do arise even with the truths of cessation and the path as their objects, they do not adhere (*anuśerate*) therein; thus, there is no consequence of those two [truths] being "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). How it is that they do not adhere in this case, we shall explain later in the exposition of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). The "with-outflow" phenomena have been explained. What are the "without-outflow" (*anāsrava*) phenomena?
The truth of the path and the three kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena are without outflows. (5ab)
What are the three kinds?

Space and the two types of cessation. Which two? Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). Thus, these three kinds beginning with space—the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*)—are the untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharmāḥ*). For what reason? Because the outflows (*āsrava*) do not adhere (*anuśerate*) within them.
Regarding these three kinds of unconditioned phenomena that have been indicated, among them, space is non-obstruction. //5d//
Space has the nature of non-obstruction, wherein matter moves.

Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is that which is dissociation (6ab). That dissociation from contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena is cessation through deliberation. Deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā*) is the specific discernment (*prajñāviśeṣa*) regarding the Noble Truths of suffering and so forth; the cessation attained by means of that is cessation through deliberation. This is a compound formed by eliding the middle term, as in the word *goratha* (ox-cart). Now, is there only one single cessation through deliberation for all contaminated phenomena? No, it is said. What then?

For there are as many substances of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-dravya*) as there are substances of conjunction (*saṃyoga-dravya*), each being distinct. Otherwise, it would follow that by realizing the cessation of the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), one would realize the cessation of all afflictions; and if this were so, the cultivation of the remaining antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) would be rendered useless. As for what was stated, "Cessation is without counterpart (*asabhāga*)," what is the meaning of this?

It has no similar cause (sabhāga-hetu), nor is it the [cause] of anything; this is the meaning of that statement, and not that "it has nothing similar to it. Thus has cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) been explained.
The other cessation, which is the absolute obstruction of arising, is [attained] through non-analytical means. 6cd

Apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha (cessation not through deliberation) is that cessation, distinct from disjunction, which acts as an absolute obstacle to the arising of future dharmas. For this [cessation] is not obtained through deliberation; rather, it is due to the deficiency of conditions. For example, when the eye and mind are occupied with a single form, those other forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles pass by; it is impossible for the five groups of consciousness to arise again with those as their objects.

For those [past] truths are not able to take a past object as their support; therefore, their non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is attained due to the deficiency of conditions. In this regard, there is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika): there are those dharmas for which only analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha) is obtained, such as the contaminated (sāsrava) dharmas that are past, present, or destined to arise. There are those for which only non-analytical cessation is obtained, such as the uncontaminated (anāsrava) conditioned dharmas that are destined never to arise.

There are those for whom both [characteristics] exist, namely, those untainted phenomena that are subject to non-arising. There are those for whom neither exists, namely, those untainted phenomena that are past, present, or subject to arising. Thus, the threefold unconditioned has been explained.
As for what was stated—that "conditioned phenomena, excluding the Path, are with-outflows" (*sāsrava*)—which are those conditioned phenomena?
Furthermore, those conditioned phenomena are the five aggregates, beginning with form:

the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*), the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). These are the conditioned phenomena. They are called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) because they are produced by conditions having come together and assembled.

For nothing whatsoever is produced by a single condition; because they belong to that same class, there is no contradiction regarding future [phenomena], just as in the case of milk and fuel. These very [phenomena] are the time-periods (adhvan), the bases of discourse (kathāvastu), those with departure (saniḥsāra), and those with a substantial basis (savastuka). //7cd //

These very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are called "paths" (*adhvan*) because they have gone, are going, or will go; or alternatively, because they are consumed by impermanence. "Speech" (*kathā*) refers to a sentence; its object (*vastu*) is a name (*nāman*). However, because it grasps an object that possesses meaning, the conditioned is called the "basis of discourse" (*kathāvastu*). Otherwise, it would contradict the *Prakaraṇa* treatise, which states: "The bases of discourse are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). "Exit" (*niḥsaraṇa*) means the absence of essence (*niḥsāra*); it is the nirvāṇa of all conditioned things. Since these [conditioned phenomena] possess that [exit], they are "possessing an exit" (*saniḥsāra*).

Because they possess causes, they have a substantial basis (*savastuka*). The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the word *vastu* is indeed a synonym for "cause. Thus, these are synonyms for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Furthermore, those very same conditioned phenomena which are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) are the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*). What is established by this? It follows that while those which are aggregates of clinging are also aggregates, there are aggregates that are not aggregates of clinging—namely, the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) formations (*saṃskāra*). In this context, "clinging" (*upādāna*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*). They are called "aggregates of clinging" because they arise from them, like a fire of grass or chaff; or because they are subject to them, like a king's servant.

Alternatively, they are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*) because clinging arises from them, like a tree that bears flowers and fruit. These same contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are also called "with strife" (*saraṇa*).

Strife (*raṇa*) refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*), because they cause harm to oneself and others. They are "with strife" because they are accompanied by those [afflictions], just as they are "contaminated."
Furthermore:
suffering, the origin, the world, the locus of views, and existence—these are they. (8cd)

It is called *duḥkha* because it is disagreeable to the Noble Ones (*ārya*). It is called *samudaya* because suffering arises from it. It is called *loka* because it disintegrates (*lujyate*). It is called *dṛṣṭisthāna* because views abide within it through latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). It is called *bhava* because it comes into being (*bhavati*). These are the synonymous designations of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena according to their literal meaning.
It has been stated that there are five aggregates (*skandha*), beginning with form (*rūpa*). Among these:
Form consists of the five sense faculties, the five objects, and unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) alone. (9ab)

The five faculties are the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. The five objects are the respective five spheres of those very faculties—the eye and so forth—known as visible form, sound, odor, taste, and the tangible. Together with non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), this constitutes the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Among these, the five objects mentioned, beginning with visible form, are the bases for their respective consciousnesses.
The translucent forms are the eye and the other [senses].

(9cd) Those five translucent forms (*rūpaprasāda*) which constitute the basis for the consciousnesses of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects should be understood, respectively, as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body. As the Blessed One has said: "O monk, the eye is an internal sense-field (*āyatana*), a translucent form derived from the four great elements," and so forth.

Those which were mentioned as the eye and so forth are the translucent forms (*rūpaprasāda*) that serve as the bases for their respective consciousnesses; that is to say, they are the bases for visual consciousness and the others. By defining them in this way, the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise is also followed: "What is the eye? It is the translucent form that is the basis of visual consciousness," and so on in detail. The five sense-faculties have been explained; now the five objects must be explained. Among those, first, visible form (*rūpa*) is of two kinds. (10a)

It consists of color and shape. Among these, color is fourfold, beginning with blue; the others are its subdivisions. Shape is eightfold, beginning with long and ending with irregular. This very same sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) is further said to be twentyfold.

Namely: blue, yellow, red, white, long, short, square, round, high, low, even, uneven, mist, smoke, dust, vapor, shadow, sunlight, light, and darkness. Some recite twenty-one [colors] by adding "the single color of the sky. In this context, *sāta* refers to an even position; *visāta* refers to an uneven position; *mahikā* is frost or mist; *ātapa* is the radiance of the sun.

Light (*āloka*) is the radiance of the moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, and gems. Shadow (*chāyā*) is that wherein forms are visible; darkness (*andhakāra*) is the opposite. The remainder is not elaborated upon because it is easy to understand. There exists a sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) that exists by way of color (*varṇa*) but not by way of shape (*saṃsthāna*); this is what is termed blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, sunlight, light, and darkness. There exists [form] by way of shape but not by way of color; this refers to the spatial extension of length and so forth, which has the nature of bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*). There exists [form] in both ways.

The remainder is the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*). Others maintain that only sunlight and light exist as color (*varṇa*). For the demarcation of blue and so forth as long and so forth is indeed perceived. But how can a single substance exist in two ways? Because both are cognized therein; for this root *vid* has the sense of "cognizing" (*jñāna*), not the sense of "existing" (*sattā*). In that case, the same would apply to bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) as well. Thus has the sphere of visible form been explained.

Sound, however, is of eight kinds. It is first of four types: caused by appropriated great elements (*upātta-mahābhūta*), caused by unappropriated great elements (*anupātta-mahābhūta*), designated as sentient (*sattvākhya*), and designated as non-sentient (*asattvākhya*). This becomes eightfold through the distinction between pleasant and unpleasant. Among these, that caused by appropriated great elements is, for example, the sound of hands or speech. That caused by unappropriated great elements is, for example, the sound of wind, forest trees, or rivers. Sound designated as sentient is vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*); other sound is designated as non-sentient. Others maintain that there is also sound caused by both appropriated and unappropriated great elements.

For example, it is like that which arises from the conjunction of a hand and a drum. However, just as a single color-atom (*varṇaparamāṇu*) is not accepted as being derived from two sets of the four primary elements (*bhūtacatuṣka*), so too this [sound] should not be so accepted. Sound has been explained.
Taste is sixfold (10bc),
due to the division into sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and astringent.

Odor is of four kinds (10c), because of the distinction between pleasant and unpleasant odors, and between those that are balanced and unbalanced. However, in the treatise it is said to be of three kinds: "pleasant odor, unpleasant odor, and balanced odor.
Tangible objects consist of eleven types (10d).
The tangible (*spraṣṭavya*) has the nature of eleven substances:

the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst. Among these, we shall explain the elements later. Smoothness is softness; roughness is coarseness. Heaviness is that by which things are weighed; lightness is its opposite. Cold is that which produces a desire for warmth. Hunger is that which produces a desire for food, through the metaphorical application of the name of the cause to the effect, as in the following example: [the phrase] "he eats the village."
"The arising of Buddhas is happiness; the teaching of the Dharma is happiness;

the harmony of the Saṅgha is happiness; and the ascetic practice of those who are harmonious is happiness. In that realm, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), hunger and thirst do not exist; the rest do. Although garments there are not weighed individually, they are weighed when accumulated. There is no cold that causes harm; it is said, however, that there is cold that is beneficial.

Regarding these various kinds of forms that have been mentioned: sometimes visual consciousness arises from a single substance when there is a discernment of its specific type; sometimes it arises from many substances when there is no such discernment. This is as in the case of one seeing from a distance an array of troops with many colors and shapes, or a cluster of jewels. Visual consciousness and the others should be understood in this same way. However, some maintain that body-consciousness arises at most from five types of tangible objects.

[The tactile consciousness arises] with the four great elements and one [quality], such as smoothness; others say with all eleven. But if this is so, since they would have a composite object, do the five groups of consciousness not result in having general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) as their objects rather than particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)?

There is no fault here, because these are held to have particular characteristics as their objects in relation to the *āyatana*-particular characteristic, not in relation to the substance-particular characteristic (*dravya-svalakṣaṇa*).

This is now investigated: when the objects of the body-faculty and the tongue-faculty are reached simultaneously, which consciousness arises first? That whose object is more intense. However, when the objects are equally reached, the tongue-consciousness arises first, because the continuum is inclined toward the desire to eat. The five sense-faculties and their objects, as well as the manner of their apprehension, have been explained.
Now, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) must be discussed. It is described as follows:
"That continuity, whether wholesome or unwholesome, which persists even in one whose mind is distracted or who is without mind... [p.8]
For that which is derived from the great elements is indeed called non-informative [matter]. //11//
"Of one whose mind is distracted" (*vikṣiptacittaka*) means even of one whose mind is directed toward something else.

"Even of one who is without mind" (*acittaka*) means even of one who has entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). By the word "even," it is understood that this also applies to one whose mind is not distracted and who possesses a mind. "That which is a continuous succession" (*anubandha*) refers to that which is a flow (*pravāha*). "Pure or impure" (*śubhāśubha*) means wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*). Since such a flow exists even for acquisitions (*prāpti*), it is stated—"derived from the primary elements" (*mahābhūtāny upādāya*)—in order to distinguish it [from acquisition]. The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the meaning of "derived from" (*upādāya*) is the sense of "cause" (*hetu*), because [the primary elements] serve as causes for its production and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "it is indeed non-informative" (*avijñapti*), the word "indeed" (*hi*) is for the purpose of making known its designation. Although it has the nature of form and action, it is called "non-informative" because, unlike informative action (*vijñapti*), it does not inform another. The phrase "it is said" indicates the words of the Master [Vasubandhu]. In brief, however, non-informative action is wholesome or unwholesome form produced by informative action or meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
It was stated that it "depends upon the great elements" (*mahābhūtāny upādāya*); which are those? The elements are the earth element, the water, fire, and air elements. (12ab)

Thus, these four are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*); they are called the "four great elements" (*mahābhūta*) because of their magnitude (*mahattva*), due to their grossness in being the support for all other forms of matter. Alternatively, it is because of their vast configuration (*mahāsaṃniveśa*) within the masses of earth, water, fire, and air, wherein their activity is manifest. Furthermore, as to what kind of activity these elements are perfected in and what their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is, he says:
"They are perfected in the activities of supporting and so forth" (12c).

These elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are established respectively in the functions of supporting, cohesion, maturation, and expansion. Expansion, moreover, should be understood as growth and spreading; this is their function. Their intrinsic natures, however, are respectively solidity, moisture, heat, and motion. (12d)

Hardness is the earth element; moisture is the water element; heat is the fire element; and motion is the wind element. Motion (*īraṇā*) is the wind element because by means of it the stream of primary elements is moved toward the production [of its parts] in other locations, like the movement of a flame. Thus it is defined in the *Prakaraṇas* and in the Sūtra: "What is motion? It is lightness and mobility. Furthermore, that lightness is also said in the *Prakaraṇas* to be derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*). Therefore, the nature of wind is that dharma whose intrinsic nature is motion; thus its nature is manifested through its function.
What, then, is the distinction between earth and so forth, and the earth-element and so forth?
Earth is said, according to worldly convention, to be color and shape. (13ab) For when people point out the earth, they point out its color and its shape. As it is with earth, so it is with...
Water and fire are said by worldly convention to be merely color and shape;
wind, however, is the element itself.
That which is the wind element is precisely what is called "wind" in the world; and yet, moreover, //13d//

Just as the earth is called "color" and "shape" by worldly convention, so too is the wind [described] as "a blue whirlwind" or "a circular whirlwind. Why, then, is this aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), ending with non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), so called? Because of its susceptibility to transformation (*rūpaṇāt*). The Blessed One said: "O monks, because it is transformed, it is transformed; therefore it is called the appropriated aggregate of form. By what is it transformed? "Even when touched by the touch of a hand, it is transformed," and so forth in detail. It is transformed in the sense that it is afflicted (*bādhyate*). For thus it is said in the *Arthavargīya*:
If those desires are not fulfilled for that embodied being who longs for them and is filled with craving, he suffers as if pierced by an arrow.

Furthermore, what is the impairment (*bādhana*) of matter (*rūpa*)? It is the production of transformation (*vipariṇāma*). Others say that "matter-ness" (*rūpaṇa*) is resistance (*pratighāta*). In that case, an atom (*paramāṇu*) would not qualify as matter, because it lacks matter-ness. [Response: An atomic matter does not exist as a single, discrete entity; rather, when situated in an aggregate (*saṃghāta*), it certainly possesses matter-ness. [Objection: Then past and future matter would not qualify as matter. [Response: That too is matter, because it has been transformed, will be transformed, and belongs to the same class [as present matter], just like fuel (*indhana*). [Objection: In that case, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) would not qualify as matter.

That informative intimation (*vijñapti*) also becomes "material" (*rūpita*) because of the materiality of its basis, just as a shadow moves when a tree moves; it is not so because of any transformation [in the intimation itself]. Furthermore, upon the cessation of the informative intimation, there would be a cessation of the non-informative (*avijñapti*), just as there is an absence of shadow when the tree is absent. Others say: "[It is material] because its supporting primary elements (*bhūta*) are material. If that were the case, then visual consciousness and the others would also follow as being material, since their bases (the sense organs) are material. This comparison is unequal.

For non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) exists depending upon the primary elements (*bhūta*), just as a shadow depends on a tree or light depends on a gem; however, visual consciousness and the others do not exist by depending on the eye and so forth in that same way. Rather, those [faculties] serve merely as the conditions for the arising of those [consciousnesses]. This view—that a shadow exists depending on a tree and light exists depending on a gem—is at least non-Vaibhāṣika, because it is accepted [by them] that each atom of color, such as a shadow, depends upon its own set of four primary elements.

Furthermore, even though shadow and light are dependent upon their respective supports, it is not tenable that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is likewise dependent in that same way. For it is admitted that even when the great elements (*mahābhūta*) which serve as the support for non-informative matter have ceased, the latter itself does not cease; therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal. Others, however, offer a rebuttal here: the support of visual consciousness and the other [sensory cognitions] is differentiated—some, such as the eye and so forth, are material (*rūpyate*), while others, such as the mind (*manas*), are not material—but non-informative matter is not like that.
Therefore, the consequence is not the same; thus, it is established that "form" (rūpa) is so called because of the deformation of its basis.

Those very things which have been described as having the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)—namely, the sense faculties and their objects—are intended to be the ten bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).

(14ab) In the systematic classification of the bases, there are ten bases: the eye base (*cakṣurāyatana*), the form base (*rūpāyatana*), and so on, up to the body base (*kāyāyatana*) and the tangible base (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*). In the systematic classification of the elements, those same ten are the ten elements: the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*), the form element (*rūpadhātu*), and so on, up to the body element (*kāyadhātu*) and the tangible element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*).

The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and its classification into bases (*āyatana*) have been explained. Now the [remaining aggregates], beginning with sensation (*vedanā*), must be discussed. Among them, sensation is experience (*anubhava*). The aggregate of sensation is a threefold experience: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. When further divided, it consists of the six groups of sensation (*ṣaḍ vedanākāyāḥ*): sensation born of eye-contact, up to sensation born of mind-contact.
Perception has the nature of grasping signs. //14cd//

The apprehension of signs such as blue, yellow, long, short, female, male, friend, enemy, pleasure, pain, and so forth—this is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). When further divided, it consists of the six groups of perception, just like the [six groups of] feeling.
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), however, consists of those [factors] other than the four [aggregates].

(15ab) Other than the four—form, feeling, perception, and consciousness—the formations are the aggregate of formations. However, the Blessed One stated in the Sūtra that "it is the six groups of volition (*cetanā*)," because of its predominance. For that [volition], being the very nature of karma, is primary in the act of conditioning (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*). Therefore, the Blessed One said: "It conditions the conditioned; therefore, it is called the aggregate of clinging to formations (*saṃskāropādānaskandha*)."

For otherwise, because the remaining mental factors (*caitasika*) and the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) would not be included within the aggregates (*skandha*), they would lack the status of being the truths of suffering and its origin; consequently, there would be neither full comprehension (*parijñā*) nor abandonment (*prahāṇa*). And it was said by the Blessed One: "I do not say that there is an end to suffering without having directly known and fully comprehended even a single dharma. Likewise, it was said: "[without] abandoning. Therefore, one must necessarily accept that these are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Furthermore, these three—(15b) [the three roots of unwholesomeness].

The aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations, together with non-informative matter and the unconditioned, are designated as the sphere of phenomena (dharmāyatana) and the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) within the systematic arrangement of the spheres and elements. (15cd)

Thus, these seven substances are designated as the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the individual representation; the representation and apprehension of each respective object is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Furthermore, it consists of the six groups of consciousness, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
This very aggregate of consciousness that was mentioned in the classification of the bases (āyatana) is the mind-base (manāyatana);
and in the classification of the elements (dhātu), it is that same [aggregate].
And seven elements are also recognized:
which seven? The six consciousnesses and, moreover, the mind. (16cd)

The visual consciousness element up to the mental consciousness element, and the mind element. Thus, herein the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements have been explained. The aggregate of form—excluding non-informative matter (avijñapti)—consists of ten bases and ten elements. The three aggregates beginning with feeling, non-informative matter, and the unconditioned phenomena constitute the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana) and the element of mental objects (dharmadhātu). The aggregate of consciousness consists of the mind base (manāyatana), the six consciousness elements, and the mind element.

But has it not been said that the six groups of consciousness constitute the aggregate of consciousness? Then what is this mind-element (*manodhātu*) that is distinct from them? Indeed, it is nothing other than those very [six]. Rather, it is that which is the immediately past consciousness among those six; for that is the mind. (17ab)

Whatever consciousness has ceased immediately prior is called the mind-element (*manodhātu*). Just as the same person who is a son becomes the father of another, or the same thing which is a fruit becomes the seed of another; if this is so, then in terms of substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*), there would be either seventeen elements—due to the mutual inclusion of the six consciousness-elements and the mind-element—or twelve. Why, then, are eighteen established? Even though this is so, the eighteen elements are taught for the sake of establishing a basis for the sixth [consciousness]. (17cd)

The five sense-consciousness elements have the five bases, such as the eye-element and its corresponding sense-fields. For the sixth, the mind-consciousness element, there is no other basis; therefore, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is taught in order to establish its basis. Thus, by way of establishing the sixfold sets of bases, supported [consciousnesses], and objects, there are eighteen elements. [Objection: In that case, the final mind of an Arhat would not be the mind-element, for there is nothing for which it would be the immediately preceding past [condition]. [Response: No.
Because that [consciousness] also exists in the form of the mental faculty (*manas*), the subsequent consciousness does not arise due to the deficiency of other causes.

In this regard, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*); all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) are subsumed under the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*); and all phenomena (*dharma*) are subsumed under the bases (*āyatana*) and the elements (*dhātu*). However, it should be known in brief that the subsumption of everything is achieved by means of one aggregate, one base, and one element. (18abc)

It should be understood that all phenomena are subsumed by the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), and the constituent of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Indeed, wherever this subsumption is mentioned, it should be understood as being by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and not by way of extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*). What is the reason? (Pradhan omits.)
Because of being dissociated from the nature of another. //18d//

For a phenomenon (*dharma*) is indeed dissociated from that which is other than itself; therefore, it is not logical for something to be included by that very thing from which it is dissociated. For example, the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the sense-base and element of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana* and *dhātu*), and the truths of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya-satya*), because it has those as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is not included by other aggregates and so forth, because it is dissociated from their nature.

As for the inclusion of one thing by another that is said to occur—such as the inclusion of assemblies by the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)—that should be understood as merely conventional (*sāṃketika*), since it occurs only occasionally.
But surely there ought to be twenty-one elements, because the eyes are two, as are the ears and the nostrils? It need not be so;
because of the sameness of genus, object, and consciousness, they constitute a single element.

Even though [the two eyes] are distinct, there is a commonality of genus (*jātisāmānya*) because both have the nature of the eye; a commonality of object (*gocarasāmānya*) because both have visible form as their domain; and a commonality of consciousness (*vijñānasāmānya*) because both serve as the basis for the same visual consciousness. Therefore, the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) is indeed one. The same should be applied to the ear and the nose.
However, they arise as a pair for the sake of beauty. (19d)

Even though they constitute a single element (*dhātu*), the occurrence of two each for the eyes and so forth is for the sake of the beauty of the physical basis (*āśraya*). Otherwise, because there would be only one location for the eyes and ears and a single nostril cavity, there would be great deformity. The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) have been explained.
However, this must now be stated: what is the meaning of aggregate, base, and element?
The meanings of aggregate, base, and element are "heap," "gate of arrival," and "lineage" (*gotra*), respectively. (20ab)

Because of the statement in the Sūtra: "Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that, having been gathered together and condensed into one, receives the designation 'form-aggregate' (rūpaskandha)," it is established that the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) is the sense of a "heap" (rāśi).

In this context, past form is that which has ceased through impermanence; the future is that which has not yet arisen; and the present is that which has arisen but not yet ceased. Internal form belongs to one's own continuum, while external form is other than that, or is distinguished by way of its sense bases (*āyatana*). Gross form is that which possesses resistance (*sapratigha*); subtle form is that which lacks resistance (*apratigha*), or is relative. If it is argued that [the distinction between gross and subtle] is unestablished because it is merely relative, we say no, for there is a difference in the basis of comparison. That which is gross in relation to something can never be subtle in relation to that same thing, just like the relationship between a father and a son. Inferior form is that which is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).

The sublime (*praṇīta*) is the undefiled (*akliṣṭa*). The distant (*dūra*) is the past and future; the near (*antika*) is the present. This applies likewise up to consciousness (*vijñāna*). However, this is the distinction: the gross (*audārika*) is that which relies on the five sense-faculties, while the subtle (*sūkṣma*) is that which belongs to the mind (*mānasa*). Or, according to the Vaibhāṣikas, it is distinguished by way of its level (*bhūmi*). The Bhadanta says: "Gross form is that which is grasped by the five sense-faculties; the subtle is other than that. The inferior (*hīna*) is the unpleasant (*amanāpa*); the sublime (*praṇīta*) is the pleasant (*manāpa*). The distant is that which is in an invisible location; the near is that which is in a visible location."

Because the past and so forth are designated by their own specific terms, feeling and the other aggregates should be understood in the same way. Their state of being distant or near, however, is due to the influence of their bases; their coarseness or subtlety is as previously explained.

The meaning of *āyatana* is the sense of being a gateway for the arrival (*āya*) of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). As for its etymological derivation (*nirvacana*), they are called *āyatanas* because they extend (*tanvanti*) the arrival of mind and mental factors; the meaning is that they expand them. The meaning of *dhātu* is the meaning of lineage (*gotra*). Just as in a single mountain there are many lineages of iron, copper, silver, gold, and so forth which are called "elements" (*dhātavaḥ*), so too within a single basis (*āśraya*) or continuum (*santāna*), there are eighteen lineages which are called the eighteen elements. In this context, "lineages" refers to mines.

Of what are these [factors], such as the eye and so forth, the sources (*ākara*)? Of their own kind (*jāti*), because they are homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*). In that case, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) would not be a "realm" (*dhātu*). Others, however, say that this word "realm" denotes the genus (*jāti*) of mind and mental factors; thus, the eighteen realms are the eighteen genera or intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of the eighteen phenomena. If the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) were "heap," it would follow that the aggregates are merely conceptual existents (*prajñaptisat*), because they are collections of multiple substances, like a heap of grain or a person (*pudgala*). This is not so.

Because even a single substantial atom (*dravyaparamāṇu*) constitutes a "skandha," one should not say that the meaning of "skandha" is "heap" (*rāśi*), for a single entity cannot possess the nature of a heap. Others maintain that the meaning of "skandha" is "the bearing of the burden of effects" (*kāryabhārodvahanārtha*), or else "a portion" (*pracchedārtha*); for instance, speakers say, "We shall give what is to be given in three installments (*skandhakaiḥ*). However, this [latter view] deviates from the Sūtra.

For the Sūtra states that the meaning of "aggregate" (*rāśi*) alone is intended: "Whatever form there is—past, future, or present," and so forth. In this passage, it is made known that each instance of past and other forms constitutes an aggregate; that is, all these past and other forms, taken individually, are the "form aggregate. It is not possible to understand it in this way, because of the statement: "having condensed all that into one. Therefore, like a heap, the aggregates exist only as designations (*prajñaptisat*).

In that case, it would follow that even the material sense-bases (*rūpy-āyatana*) are merely conceptual existents (*prajñaptisat*), because they consist of many atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the eye and so forth acting as gateways for the arrival [of objects]. No; because they function as causes either individually when combined or through cooperation with their respective objects, the sense-faculty would not be a separate base. However, it is stated in the *Vibhāṣā*: "If an Abhidharma master considers the conceptual designation of the aggregates (*skandha-prajñapti*), he says: 'An atom is a portion of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). "

Now, if it is argued that [the Buddha] does not take this into account, he says: "An atom is one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*). For indeed, even in the case of a part, there is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) as if it were the whole, just as when one part of a cloth is burned, one says, "The cloth is burned. For what purpose does the Blessed One undertake the threefold teaching by way of the aggregates and so forth? He says: "The three teachings beginning with the aggregates are for the sake of those to be trained, due to the threefold nature of their delusion, faculties, and inclinations. (20cd)

The threefold nature refers to the three categories. It is said that the delusion (*moha*) of sentient beings is of three types: some are deluded regarding mental factors (*caitta*) by grasping at them as a single self; some are deluded regarding form (*rūpa*) alone; and some are deluded regarding both form and mind (*citta*). The faculties (*indriya*) are also of three kinds, because they are sharp, medium, or dull. Inclination (*ruci*) is also of three kinds, because of an inclination toward concise, intermediate, or extensive texts. For these [three types of persons], there are respectively the three teachings on the aggregates (*skandha*), the bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*).

What, then, is the reason that while all other mental factors are placed together within the single aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are made into separate aggregates?

It is said: Because they are the roots of dispute and the causes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), and for the sake of establishing the proper order, feeling and perception are established as separate aggregates from among the mental factors. (21)

There are two roots of dispute: attachment to sensual desires (*kāmadhyavasāna*) and attachment to views (*dṛṣṭyadhyavasāna*). Of these two, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are, respectively, the primary causes. For it is through the power of relishing feeling that one clings to sensual desires, and through the power of distorted perception that one clings to views. These two are also the primary causes of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); for one who is greedy for the relish of feeling and possesses distorted perception wanders in saṃsāra. Furthermore, it should be understood that these two are established as separate aggregates (*skandha*) from the reason for the sequence of the aggregates that will be explained later; we shall establish this point in three ways.

Now, for what reason is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) mentioned among the elements (*dhātu*) and the bases (*āyatana*), but not among the aggregates (*skandha*)? The unconditioned is not mentioned among the aggregates because it does not fit the definition. (22abc) For if it were mentioned among the aggregates, it could not be included within these very ones, because it does not fit the definition. Indeed, it is neither form (*rūpa*) nor, up to, consciousness (*vijñāna*). Nor can it be called a sixth aggregate. Why? Because it does not fit the definition. It has been stated that "the meaning of 'aggregate' is the meaning of 'heap'."

Furthermore, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not differentiated by distinctions such as past and so forth in the manner that form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates are; therefore, it could not be designated as the "unconditioned aggregate" (*asaṃskṛtaskandha*) by being condensed into a single category along with all those [conditioned phenomena]. Indeed, the term "appropriation-aggregates" (*upādānaskandha*) is used for the purpose of making known the basis of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), whereas the term "aggregates" (*skandha*) is used for the purpose of making known the bases of both affliction and purification (*vyavadāna*). Since the unconditioned is neither of these two, it was not established among them due to the lack of logical consistency.

Others maintain that just as the cessation of a jar is not the jar, so too the cessation of the aggregates cannot be the aggregates. For them, this same consequence would apply to the elements and the sense-bases as well. Thus has another classification of the aggregates been explained.
Furthermore, the sequence is according to their coarseness, their defilement, their analogy to a vessel and so forth, and their elements. //22bcd//

For form (*rūpa*) is the most gross of all because it possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*). Among the formless aggregates, feeling (*vedanā*) is gross by way of its manifest activity; for thus do people designate it: "I have a feeling in my hand," or "I have a feeling in my foot. Perception (*saṃjñā*) is grosser than those two. Formations (*saṃskāra*) are grosser than consciousness (*vijñāna*); therefore, that which is grosser is mentioned first. Alternatively, in beginningless saṃsāra, men and women are mutually delighted by forms, and they are further attached to the relish of feelings.

Craving for that [body] arises from a perversion of perception; that perversion arises from the afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), and by those afflictions the mind is defiled—thus the order follows the sequence of defilement. Alternatively, it is according to the analogy of the vessel and so forth: for the aggregates, beginning with form, function as the vessel, the food, the condiment, the cook, and the eater. Or, it is according to the realms (*dhātu*): for the desire realm is characterized by the forms of the objects of sensual pleasure; the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are characterized by feeling; and the three formless realms are characterized by perception.

The peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is manifested solely by formative forces (*saṃskāra*). These very [four] are the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), and consciousness is established within them; thus, the sequence of the aggregates (*skandha*) is intended to demonstrate the relationship between the field and the seed. For this very reason, there are five aggregates—neither fewer nor more. And for this same reason regarding the order, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are made into separate aggregates from among the formative forces.
This is because these two are more gross, are the causes for the sequence of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), serve as the vessel and the condiment, and the two realms (*dhātu*) are manifested by them.

The sequence of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), namely the six beginning with the eye, must be explained. For it is precisely by virtue of that [sequence] that the sequence of their respective consciousnesses is established. Furthermore, among those six, the first five—the eye and so forth—are mentioned first because they have present objects; that is, the five beginning with the eye have present objects. The mind (*manas*), however, has an indefinite object: some have present objects, while others have objects belonging to the three times or even no time at all.

The four [senses] are [so called] because their objects are derived matter (*bhautika*). The word "previously" carries over [from the previous verse]. Furthermore, among the five [senses], four were mentioned earlier because their objects are derived matter. However, the object of the body is indefinite: sometimes it is the primary elements (*bhūta*), sometimes derived matter, and sometimes both.
The others [the remaining senses] function with respect to what is distant or more rapid.

Furthermore, the remaining [faculties] were mentioned first according to their respective functions of operating at a distance or more rapidly. For the eye and the ear have distant objects; therefore, they were mentioned before the other two. Between those two as well, the eye operates at a greater distance, because one may see a river from afar without hearing its sound; thus, the eye was mentioned before it. The nose, however, does not operate at a distance, nor does the tongue.

Between those two, the nose was mentioned first because of its more rapid operation, since it perceives the odor of food even before the tongue has reached it. Alternatively, the order follows the sequence of their positions. (23d)

Alternatively, in this body, the locus of the eye is situated at the top; below that is the locus of the ear; below that is the locus of the nose; below that is the locus of the tongue; and below that is the locus of the body for the most part. The mind, moreover, is dependent upon those very [faculties] and has no fixed location. Thus, their sequence would be according to their positions.

Furthermore, what is the reason that among the ten bases (*āyatana*) subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), only one is called the "base of form" (*rūpāyatana*), and among all things whose nature is phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*), only one is called the "base of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*)? He says:
For the sake of distinction, because of its preeminence, and because it includes many supreme qualities, one base is called "form" (rūpa) and one is called "phenomena" (dharma). //24//

How is it for the sake of specification? It is so that it may be understood that the status of these ten as *āyatanas* is established individually through their relationship as object (*viṣaya*) and subject (*viṣayin*), and not collectively. Furthermore, when specified by the [terms] "eye" and so forth, that which is not designated as "eye" and so on, yet is form (*rūpa*), shall be known as the "form *āyatana*"; thus, no other name is given for it. Alternatively, it is because of the preeminence of the form *āyatana*. For that, due to its resistance (*sapratighatva*), is affected (*rūpyate*) when touched by the contact of hands and so forth.

And because it is visible (*sanidarśana*), it can be specified as "this is here" or "that is there. Furthermore, even in the world, that alone is recognized as "form" (*rūpa*) and not the others. It is precisely for the sake of such specification that only one is called the *dharmāyatana*, and not all of them. Moreover, in this [basis], there is a collection of many phenomena (*dharma*), such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth; therefore, a general designation is made by means of the word "dharma. And it is because the supreme phenomenon, which is *nirvāṇa*, is included here and not in the others.

Others maintain that the single sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) exists because it is coarse due to its twentyfold nature, and because it is the object of the three types of eyes: the fleshly, the divine, and the noble wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*).

Other aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) designated by those names are also found in the Sūtras. Should it be understood that these are included within these [five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements] themselves, or are they distinct from them? They are included within these very ones; they are not distinct. In this regard:

The eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*) which the Sage proclaimed—these are either speech or name; thus, they are included within [the aggregate of] form (*rūpa*) and [the aggregate of] formations (*saṃskāra*). (25)

For those for whom the Buddha’s word has speech as its intrinsic nature, these are subsumed within the aggregate of form; for those for whom it has name as its intrinsic nature, they are subsumed within the aggregate of formations.
Furthermore, what is the measure of a *dharmaskandha*?
Some say it is the measure of the treatise (*śāstra*).
First, some say that the measure of this very Abhidharma treatise known as the *Dharmaskandha* is six thousand *ślokas*. Others, however, say:

The discourse on each of the aggregates and so forth—namely, the discourses on the aggregates, sense bases, elements, dependent origination, truths, nutriments, meditative absorptions, immeasurables, formless attainments, liberations, spheres of mastery, spheres of totality, factors conducive to enlightenment, supernormal powers, analytical knowledges, knowledge resulting from prayer, and the absence of strife—is individually called a "dharma-aggregate. However, it is described that the dharma-aggregate is actually the antidote to specific types of conduct. (26cd)

Thus, they describe eighty thousand types of conduct among sentient beings, distinguished by the variations of conduct such as passion, hatred, delusion, and pride. As an antidote to these, the Blessed One taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*). Just as these eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma are subsumed within these very five aggregates, so too should other aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) be subsumed as appropriate;
having carefully considered their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are to be assigned to those already mentioned. (27)

Furthermore, whatever other aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are mentioned in other sūtras, they too are to be subsumed within these very aggregates and so forth as already described, after having carefully considered their respective individual characteristics as established in this treatise. In that regard, first, among the five aggregates of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*jñānadarśana*), the aggregate of morality is included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); the remaining ones are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

Of the ten *kṛtsnāyatanas*, eight—because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-attachment (*alobha*)—are included in the *dharmāyatana*; however, together with their attendants (*saparivāra*), because they consist of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), they are included in both the *manāyatana* and the *dharmāyatana*. The same applies to the *abhibhvāyatanas*. The four [spheres] beginning with the *ākāśānantyāyatana*—namely, the *ākāśānantyāyatana-kṛtsna* and the *vijñānānantyāyatana-kṛtsna*—because they consist of the four aggregates, are included in the *manāyatana* and the *dharmāyatana*. The five *vimuktyāyatanas*, because their intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*), are included in the *dharmāyatana*.

But together with their retinues, they are included within the spheres of sound, mind, and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Of the two [remaining] spheres, the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) are included within ten spheres, because of the absence of the spheres of odor and taste. Those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatanopaga*) are included within the spheres of mind and mental objects. In this same way, the sixty-two elements (*dhātu*) taught in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra* should also be understood as being subsumed according to their respective natures.

Regarding these six elements mentioned there—the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element—the characteristics of two of them have not been stated. Should one understand that space itself is the space element, and that all consciousness is the consciousness element? No, he says. What then? The cavity in doors, windows, the mouth, the nose, and so forth, is called the "space element.
What is to be understood by this term "cavity"?

It is said that [the space element] consists of light and darkness; for no aperture is perceived apart from light and darkness. Therefore, it is said that the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) should be understood as having light and darkness as its intrinsic nature, and as having night and day as its intrinsic nature. That very same [element] is called "matter adjacent to the impenetrable" (*aghasāmantaka-rūpa*). It is said that "impenetrable" (*agha*) refers to matter existing in a massed state, because of its extreme density (*ghāta*). This [space] is "adjacent" (*sāmantaka*) to that. Others say: it is "impenetrable" (*agha*) because other matter does not offer resistance (*apratighāta*) there, and it is "adjacent" (*sāmantaka*) to other matter.
The consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*) is contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousness. (28cd)
Why are they not said to be untainted? Because these six elements are held to be the supports for birth. (28d)

For these [elements] serve as the support from the mind at rebirth-linking up until the mind at death; however, the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are not like this. This being so, among these [six elements], four are included within the tangible element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*); the fifth is in the form element (*rūpadhātu*); and the sixth is in the seven consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*).

Furthermore, of these eighteen elements that have been mentioned, how many are with demonstration (*sanidarśana*) and how many are without demonstration (*anidarśana*)? Among them, one is with demonstration: form (*rūpa*). (29ab)
For that [visible] can indeed be pointed out as being "here" or "there"; by this it is meant that the remaining [elements] are non-demonstrable (*anidarśana*).
How many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*)? Ten are with resistance; they are the material (*rūpin*) elements. (29bc)

Those ten elements (*dhātu*) mentioned as being comprised within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) are characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*). Resistance means obstruction (*pratighāta*), and it is of three kinds: obstruction as hindrance (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*), obstruction regarding the object-field (*viṣaya-pratighāta*), and obstruction regarding the objective support (*ālambana-pratighāta*). Among these, obstruction as hindrance is the prevention of another's arising in one's own location; for example, a hand is obstructed by a hand or by a stone, and a stone likewise [obstructs] those two. Obstruction regarding the object-field is the [resistance] of the sense-faculties, such as the eye, toward their respective objects, such as visible form.

As it is stated in the *Prajñapti*: "There is an eye that is obstructed by water, not by land—as with fish. There is [an eye] obstructed by land, not by water—as is generally the case for humans. There is [an eye] obstructed by both—as with crocodiles, frogs, piśācas, fishermen, and so forth. There is [an eye] obstructed by neither—setting aside these aforementioned cases. There is an eye that is obstructed at night, not by day—as with the *titīla* bird, owls, and so forth. [There is an eye obstructed] by day, not at night—as is generally the case for humans."

[Resistance] occurs both at night and by day for dogs, jackals, horses, leopards, cats, and so forth; it does not occur in both [cases] for others. Setting aside these forms, this is "resistance regarding the object" (*viṣayapratighāta*). "Resistance regarding the focal point" (*ālambanapratighāta*) refers to the mind and mental factors with respect to their own respective focal points. What, then, is the distinction between the object (*viṣaya*) and the focal point (*ālambana*)? That in which something exercises its activity is its object; that which is grasped by the mind and mental factors is the focal point.

Furthermore, what is it that is obstructed when it operates upon its own object or support? It is said: because it does not operate beyond that [object]. Alternatively, "obstruction" (*pratighāta*) here refers to the very operation within one's own domain. Thus, in this context, the ten [elements] should be understood as having resistance (*sapratighatva*) by way of obstruction as a hindrance (*āvaraṇapratighāta*), due to their mutual exclusion.

Regarding those phenomena that are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) by way of resistance to an object (*viṣayapratighāta*), are they also [resistant] by way of resistance as an obstruction (*āvaraṇapratighāta*)? This constitutes a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*). The first alternative consists of the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and that portion of the phenomenon-element (*dharmadhātu*) which is associated (*saṃprayukta*). The second consists of the five objects (*viṣaya*). The third consists of the five sense-faculties (*indriya*). The fourth consists of the portion of the phenomenon-element excluding that which is associated.

Those dharmas that are "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) by way of resistance to an object (*viṣayapratighāta*) are also [with resistance] by way of resistance to an objective support (*ālambanapratighāta*); this is the "consequent" formulation (*paścātpādaka*). However, those which are [with resistance] by way of resistance to an objective support may or may not be [with resistance] by way of resistance to an object. The five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*) are [with resistance] only by way of resistance to an object, but not by way of resistance to an objective support. That wherein the arising of the mind is capable of being obstructed by others should be known as "with resistance"; the opposite is held to be "without resistance" (*apratigha*).
Thus says the Venerable Kumāralāta. Those that are with resistance and those that are without resistance have been explained.
Among these eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Eight are indeterminate. Which eight? Those ten which were stated to be with resistance (*sapratigha*).
These very [elements] are those that lack form and sound. //29d//

The five faculties, as well as the elements of odor, taste, and tangibles—these eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) because they cannot be defined as being either wholesome or unwholesome. Others say they are indeterminate because they cannot be defined in terms of their maturation (*vipāka*). If that were the case, the same consequence would apply to the untainted (*anāsrava*) factors as well.

The other ten elements are of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral. Among them, the seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) are wholesome when associated with non-greed and so forth; they are unwholesome when associated with greed and so forth; otherwise, they are neutral. The *dharmadhātu* is wholesome when it has the nature of non-greed and so forth, is associated with them, or is produced by them, as well as when it is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*). It is unwholesome when it has the nature of greed and so forth, is associated with them, or is produced by them. Otherwise, it is neutral.

The elements of visible form (*rūpadhātu*) and sound (*śabdadhātu*), when originated by wholesome or unwholesome minds, are themselves wholesome or unwholesome, being comprised within bodily and vocal intimation (*vijñapti*). Those other than these are neutral (*avyākṛta*). Thus has the state of being wholesome and so forth been explained. Among these eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are included in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and how many are included in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?
All are included in the desire realm. (30ab)
"Attained" means they are not dissociated; that is to say, they are associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the form realm (*rūpa*), there are fourteen:
in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are fourteen elements (*dhātu*).
Excluding the elements of odor, taste, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness. //30cd//

For in that realm, odor and taste do not exist; because these two constitute edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), and those who are free from desire for such food are reborn there. Consequently, the consciousnesses of smell and taste also do not exist, due to the absence of their respective objects. If that were the case, it would follow that the element of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) would also be absent there, since it too constitutes edible food. That which does not have the nature of food exists there. This same consequence would apply to odor and taste as well. However, there is no enjoyment of odor and taste without ingestion.

However, there is a function for the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*) insofar as it serves as the basis for the sense faculties, as a support, and as clothing. Therefore, for those who are free from passion for ingestion, odor and taste are useless there, but not so the tangible. Others, however, say: "By means of the support provided by meditative attainment (*dhyānasamāpatti*), visible forms are perceived here and sounds are heard; and the body is sustained by a specific kind of tangible that is accompanied by pliancy (*prasrabdhi*)."

Therefore, it is only these three [tangibles] that are possible in the rebirth-state of the meditative absorptions (dhyānopapatti), but not odor or taste. If this is so, then it follows that the sense-faculties of smell and taste must be absent, since they would serve no purpose. There is indeed a purpose: for without them, there would be no beauty of the physical basis (āśraya-śobhā) nor [the capacity for] conventional usage (vyavahāra). If this is the purpose, let there be only the physical bases for the sake of beauty and speech; let there be no sense-faculty. But it is impossible for a physical base to exist without a sense-faculty.

It is like the physical basis of the male organ; its non-occurrence is logical because it serves no purpose. However, the bases of the nose and tongue do serve a purpose; therefore, their occurrence is logical even without the sense organ itself. Furthermore, the production of a sense organ may occur even when it is purposeless, as in the case of those destined to die in the womb. While it may indeed be purposeless, it is not without a cause. And what is the cause for the arising of the sense organ? It is a specific karma belonging to one who possesses craving for the sense organs.

And since one who is free from craving for an object is necessarily so regarding the sense faculty as well, those who are free from passion for that object should not possess the olfactory and gustatory faculties. Or why would the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) not also be absent? [One might say] because it causes ugliness. But why would the private parts, when enclosed in a sheath, not be beautiful? Furthermore, the arising [of a faculty] does not depend on utility; rather, it depends on a cause. Thus, even that which causes ugliness would certainly arise if the cause were present. [If this is so,] then the Sūtra is contradicted.

"Complete, with unimpaired faculties"—what contradiction is there in saying that they are "complete and with unimpaired faculties" by virtue of whatever faculties exist there? Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the male faculty (purūṣendriya) would also exist [there]. However, they explain it thus: the faculties of smell (ghrāṇa) and taste (jihvā) do indeed exist there, but not their objects, odor (gandha) and flavor (rasa). For the manifestation of craving (tṛṣṇāsamudācāra) regarding the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) occurs by way of the personal existence (ātmabhāva), not by way of the objects; whereas regarding the male faculty, it occurs by way of sexual contact (maithunasparśa). Therefore, it is established that fourteen elements (dhātu) belong to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
The mind-element, the dharma-element, and the mind-consciousness-element belong to the formless realm.

(31ab) Since those who are free from passion for form are born there, the ten elements whose intrinsic nature is form, as well as the five consciousness-elements that have them as their basis and objects, do not exist (or arise) there.

How many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)? These three—the mental faculty element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)—which were mentioned above, are both with and without outflows (31cd).
Those which are included within the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are without outflows; the others are with outflows.
The remaining ones, however, are with outflows.
(31d) The remaining fifteen elements, however, are exclusively with outflows.

How many are with vitarka and with vicāra? How many are without vitarka and with vicāra only? How many are without vitarka and without vicāra? For the five consciousness-elements (vijñānadhātu) possess vitarka and vicāra (32ab);
these elements are always associated with vitarka and vicāra. The word "hi" (for/indeed) has the sense of restriction.

The last three are of three types. (32c) The mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are the last; these three are of three types. Among them, the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the associated portion of the mental-object-element—excluding *vitarka* and *vicāra*—are with *vitarka* and with *vicāra* in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the first dhyāna. In the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), they are without *vitarka* and with *vicāra* only. From the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), they are without *vitarka* and without *vicāra*.

The entire unassociated *dharmadhātu* and *vicāra* in the intermediate dhyāna are also [without vitarka]. However, *vitarka* is always without *vitarka* and consists only of *vicāra*, because of the absence of a second *vitarka* and because of its association with *vicāra*. In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first dhyāna, *vicāra* is not included within these three types; how, then, should it be described? It is "without *vicāra* and consisting only of *vitarka*," because of the absence of a second *vicāra* and because of its association with *vitarka*.

Therefore it is said: "In the stage characterized by both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), there are four types of factors (*dharma*): (1) those associated with both applied and sustained thought, excluding [themselves] from the category of sustained and applied thought; (2) applied thought itself, which is without applied thought but possesses only sustained thought; (3) those dissociated [from mind], which are without applied thought and without sustained thought; and (4) sustained thought itself, which is without sustained thought but possesses only applied thought. The remaining factors are devoid of both. (32d)
The remaining ten material elements are always without vitarka and without vicāra, because they are not associated with them.
If the five groups of consciousness possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), how can they be said to be non-conceptual?
They are non-conceptual by virtue of being free from the conceptualization of investigation (*nirūpaṇa-vikalpa*) and the conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*). (33ab)

It is said that there are three kinds of conceptualization (*vikalpa*): conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*), conceptualization of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*), and conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*). Among these, [the five sensory consciousnesses] possess conceptualization of intrinsic nature, but not the other two; therefore, they are called "non-conceptual" (*avikalpaka*), just as a horse with only one leg is called "legless. In this context, conceptualization of intrinsic nature is *vitarka* (initial mental application), which will be explained later among the mental factors (*caitta*). As for the other two, what is their intrinsic nature? Respectively, they are: distracted wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with the mind, and all mindfulness (*smṛti*) associated with the mind. (33cd)

Wisdom associated with the mental consciousness is called "mental"; when it is not in a state of meditative equipoise, it is called "distracted. For that is the conceptualization of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*). All mindfulness belonging to the mental consciousness—whether in a state of equipoise or not—is the conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).
How many have an object (*sālambana*), and how many are without an object (*anālambana*)? (34ab) The seven mind-elements have objects.

The elements of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness, as well as the mind element—these seven mental elements possess an object (*sālambana*) because they grasp objects. And half of the dharma-element is also with an object; that which has the nature of a mental factor (*caitasika*) is with an object. It is established that the remaining ten material elements and the portion of the dharma-element that is dissociated (*asaṃprayukta*) are without an object. How many are appropriated (*upātta*), and how many are unappropriated (*anupātta*)?
Nine are non-appropriated.
(34c) Which nine? Those seven with objects that were mentioned, together with half of the eighth; these eight and sound. (34c*d)
These nine are non-appropriated: the seven mind-elements, the dharma-element, and the sound-element. The other nine are of two kinds. (34d)

They are both appropriated (*upātta*) and non-appropriated (*anupātta*). Among them, the present eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are appropriated; those of the past and future are non-appropriated. The present elements of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibles are appropriated when they are inseparable from the sense faculties; others are non-appropriated, such as hair, body hair, nails, and teeth—excluding their roots—as well as feces, urine, saliva, nasal mucus, blood, and so forth, and also earth, water, and the like. What is the meaning of "appropriated"?

That which is embraced by mind and mental factors as their basis, because they conform to one another through mutual benefit and injury—that is what is called "sentient" in the world. How many elements have the nature of primary matter (*bhūta*), and how many are derived matter (*bhautika*)?
Tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) are of two kinds.

The primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative matter (*bhautika*). Among these, the primary elements are four; derivative matter consists of seven kinds, such as smoothness and so forth, because it exists within the primary elements.
The remaining nine with form (*rūpin*) are derivative matter:
the five sense-faculty elements and the four objects. These nine elements are exclusively derivative matter.

And a portion of the *dharmadhātu* (35c), designated as *avijñapti*, is derived from the primary elements (*bhautika*). The remaining seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) and the *dharmadhātu*—excluding *avijñapti*—are neither [of these two types]. The Venerable Buddhadeva maintains that "the ten bases (*āyatana*) consist of the primary elements alone.
