But that is not so, because the Sūtra defines the four primary elements by their specific characteristics, such as solidity and so forth; furthermore, these [elements] are objects of touch (*spraṣṭavya*). For hardness and the other [characteristics] are not perceived by the eye and the other [faculties], nor are color and the other [sensory qualities] perceived by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

And it is said in the Sūtra: "O Bhikṣu, the eye is an internal sense-field (āyatana), derived from the four great elements (mahābhūta), a translucent form (rūpaprasāda), material, invisible, and resistant; and so on, up to the body. O Bhikṣu, visible forms are an external sense-field, derived from the four great elements, a translucent form, material, visible, and resistant. O Bhikṣu, sound is an external sense-field, derived from the four great elements, material, invisible, and resistant; and so too are odor and taste."

"O Bhikṣu, tangibles are an external sense-field (*bāhyam āyatana*); they consist of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and that which is derived from the four great elements (*upādāya-rūpa*), being invisible (*anidarśana*) and offering resistance (*sapratigha*). By this, it is clearly demonstrated that because the great elements are included only within one part of the tangible sense-field (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), the remainder [of the sense-fields] are not great elements. As for what was stated in the Sūtra—"that which is hard or of a harsh nature in the lump of flesh (*māṃsapiṇḍa*) that is the eye"—this is a teaching concerning the lump of flesh which exists inseparably [from the great elements].

The statement, "O monk, this person consists of six elements," in the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*, is for the purpose of demonstrating the fundamental substance of a sentient being. Furthermore, because of the subsequent mention of the six bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*), there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence that mental factors (*caitta*) do not exist. Nor is it logical to accept that the mind itself is the mental factors; for it is stated in the Sūtra: "Perception (*saṃjñā*) and volition (*cetanā*)—this dharma is mental, following after the mind, and dependent upon the mind"—and also because of the mention of "mind with passion" (*sarāga-citta*) and so forth.
Therefore, the elements (*dhātu*) possess the nature of both primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*bhautika*), as previously explained.
How many are accumulated and how many are non-accumulated? Ten material [elements] are accumulated. (35d)
The five sense-faculty elements and the five objects are aggregated because they consist of a collection of atoms; it follows, therefore, that the remaining [elements] are not aggregated.
Among the eighteen elements, what cuts, what is cut; what burns, what is burned; what weighs, what is weighed?
It is the four external elements that both cut and are cut. (36ab)

What is this phenomenon called "cutting," which pertains to visible form, odor, taste, and the tangible—designated as axes, wood, and so forth? It is the production of a separation in a stream of composite matter that was previously arising in connection [with its parts]. The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the other faculties are not cut; for even when all limbs are severed, they do not become divided into two, because the faculties themselves do not split. This is because a severed limb is devoid of faculties. Nor do [the faculties] cut, because they are transparent like the luster of a gem.
Thus, it is only the four external elements that both cut and are cut.
It burns and it weighs;
thus, that very same thing burns and that very same thing weighs. It is not the sense organs, because they are translucent like the luster of a gem; nor is it sound, because it is discontinuous.
There is a dispute regarding that which burns and that which weighs. (36d)

Some say that those same four elements are both the burners and the weighed; others say that the fire element alone is the burner, and heaviness alone is what is weighed. How many elements are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), how many are accumulative (*aupacayika*), how many are outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*), how many possess substance (*dravayukta*), and how many are momentary (*kṣaṇika*)? It is said:
"The five internal [elements] are born of maturation and are accumulative" (37ab).

First, regarding the internal [factors], there are five elements, beginning with the eye, which are both born of maturation (*vipākaja*) and accumulative (*aupacayika*). They are not outflowing (*naiṣyandika*), because there is no outflow distinct from those two. Among these, "born of maturation" means produced from a cause of maturation; this is a compound formed by eliding the middle term, as in the word *goratha* (ox-cart). Alternatively, karma that has reached the time of its fruition is called "maturation" (*vipāka*), because it "ripens" (*vipacyate*). That which is born from that [karma] is "born of maturation. Furthermore, the fruit itself is "maturation" because it is the very process of ripening.

Let there be a metaphorical designation of the fruit for the cause, just as there is a metaphorical designation of the cause for the fruit, as in: "These six bases of contact should be understood as past karma. Those [material aggregates] accumulated by means of food, refinement, sleep, and specific meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) are called "accumulated" (*aupacayika*). Some say they are also accumulated through celibacy (*brahmacarya*); however, that [celibacy] would merely prevent harm, not cause accumulation. The stream of accumulation stands as a protection against the stream of maturation (*vipāka*), like a surrounding wall. Sound is both accumulated and outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*); it is not born of maturation (*vipākaja*). (37bc)

What is the reason? Because [the result] proceeds from effort (*īhā*). If that is so, then what about the statement in the *Prajñaptiśāstra*: "Because of the thorough cultivation of abstaining from harsh speech, the mark of a Great Man consisting of a Brahma-like voice (*brahmasvaratā*) is produced"? Some say that this is a third-order succession: for from actions (*karman*) come the primary elements (*bhūta*), and from the primary elements comes sound. Others say it is a fifth-order succession.

For from karma arise the great elements born of maturation (*vipākaja*); from those, the accumulative (*aupacayika*) ones; from those, the outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*) ones; and from those, sound. If that were so, then bodily sensation (*vedanā*) would also not be considered maturation, because it arises from great elements produced by karma—just as with sound. If this were the case, there would be a contradiction with reason. [However,] the eight non-obstructive [elements] are both outflowing and born of maturation. (37cd)

Which eight? The seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). Those that are outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*) are produced by the similar-cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive-cause (*sarvatragahetu*). Those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) are produced by the maturation-cause (*vipākahetu*). There are none that are accumulative (*aupacayika*) among those that are non-obstructive (*apratigha*), because there is no accumulation of them. The others are of three kinds: the other four remaining elements—the form, taste, odor, and tangible-object elements—are born of maturation, accumulative, and outflowing as well.
One is substantial:
for the unconditioned is a substance because of its essential nature; and since that exists within the dharma-sphere, the dharma-sphere alone is endowed with substance. The final three are momentary.
The mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are the last in the order of recitation.

At the very first moment of the outflow-free state—within the complex of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)—these three exist for a single moment as non-outflow-produced (*anaiḥṣyandika*); therefore, they are said to be "momentary. There is no other conditioned phenomenon produced from other causes that is non-outflow-produced. In this context, the mind associated with the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering is both the mind element and the mind-consciousness element; the remaining factors arising simultaneously with it constitute the mental-object element.

This is now investigated: Is one who acquires the possession of the eye-element (cakṣurdhātu) also [simultaneously] acquiring the eye-consciousness-element (cakṣurvijñānadhātu), or is one who acquires the eye-consciousness-element also [simultaneously] acquiring the eye-element? He says:
There may be the acquisition of the eye-element and the eye-consciousness-element either separately or together. (38cd)

First, there may be possession of the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) without the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*): this occurs when one in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) gradually acquires the eye-faculty, or when one dying from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is reborn in the second or higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Conversely, there may be possession of the eye-consciousness-element without the eye-element: this occurs for one born in the second or higher meditative absorptions who brings eye-consciousness into manifestation, or for one dying from those states and being reborn in a lower realm.

One may also acquire possession of both [the eye-element and the eye-consciousness-element] simultaneously when, having passed away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one is reborn either in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or in the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*). One does not possess both [simultaneously] in cases other than these. Regarding the question of whether one who possesses the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) also possesses the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), there are four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*): The first alternative: one born in the second or higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) who is not manifesting eye-consciousness. The second alternative: one in the desire realm who has not yet acquired or has lost the eye.

The third [case] is one who has obtained and not lost the eye in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or one born in the first dhyāna, or one born in the second dhyāna and so forth, while seeing. The fourth is setting aside these modes. In this way, the acquisition (*pratilambha*) and possession (*samanvāgama*) of the eye-element and the form-element, as well as the eye-consciousness-element and the form-element, should be inferred according to the circumstances. The word "also" (*ca*) in the phrase "even together with" (*sahāpi ca*) serves to include this related discussion.
How many elements are internal (*ādhyātmika*)? How many are external (*bāhya*)? Twelve are internal. (39a)

Which are the twelve? Excluding form and the others, the six consciousnesses and their six bases—these twelve elements (*dhātu*) are internal. However, the six objective elements, such as form and so forth, are external. But since a self (*ātman*) does not exist, how can there be "internal" or "external"? Because it is the locus of the conceit of "I," the mind is metaphorically designated as the "self."
It has been said: "For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains heaven. And elsewhere, the Blessed One spoke of the taming of the mind:
"The taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness."

Thus, because they are proximate as the basis for the mind—which is the self—the eye and so forth possess internality; whereas form and so forth possess externality because they exist as objects. If that is the case, then the six consciousness-elements would not qualify as internal, for they do not become the basis of the mind until they have attained the status of the mind-element (*manodhātu*). At that time, they simply become what they already are; thus, they do not transcend their defining characteristic.

Otherwise, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) would exist only in the past, and not in the future or the present; yet it is accepted that the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) belong to all three time periods. Furthermore, if the future and present consciousnesses did not possess the characteristic of the mind-element, then the mind-element could not be established even in the past time-period, for there is no deviation of a characteristic across the time-periods.
How many elements are homogeneous (*sabhāga*), and how many are partially homogeneous (*tatsabhāga*)? First of all, that which is designated as the "dharma" element is exclusively homogeneous. (39bc)

For when a particular object is fixed for a particular consciousness, if that consciousness has arisen with respect to it, or is of a nature to arise, then that object is called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*). And there is no such thing as a dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) where infinite mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has not already arisen or will not arise; for this thought necessarily arises in all noble persons (*āryapudgala*): "All phenomena are without self."

And for that [consciousness], all phenomena—excluding its own nature (*svabhāva*) and its co-existent factors (*sahabhū*)—are the object (*ālambana*). Furthermore, that moment of consciousness is the object of another moment of consciousness; thus, in two moments, all phenomena indeed become objects. Therefore, the *dharmadhātu* is always "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
And the remainder are "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
The word "and" (*ca*) implies "and homogeneous. What is this so-called "partially homogeneous"? [p.28]
He who does not perform his own duty. //39d//

It is said that whatever performs its own function is "partaking" (*sabhāga*). In this context, that eye by which one has seen, sees, or will see forms is called the "partaking eye. The same should be stated for the others up to the mind (*manas*) with respect to their own activity regarding their respective objects. According to the Kaśmīris, the "non-partaking" (*tatsabhāga*) eye is of four kinds: that which has ceased after seeing forms, that which is ceasing, that which will cease, and that which is of a nature not to arise. According to the Westerners (*Pāścāttyas*), however, it is of five kinds.

That very same [element] characterized by non-arising is divided into two types: that which is associated with consciousness and that which is not associated with consciousness. The same should be understood up to the body. As for the mind, it is exclusively of the nature of non-arising and is thus "of its own kind" (tatsabhāga). Regarding visible forms, those which have been seen, are being seen, or will be seen by the eye are "of their own kind" (sabhāga). Those "of their own kind" are of four types: those which, having never been seen, have ceased, are ceasing, or will cease, and those which are of the nature of non-arising. The same applies up to tangible objects.

The [sense organs] are to be understood as "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) or "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) according to the activity of their own respective faculties. That which is the homogeneous eye of one person is the [homogeneous] eye of all; the partially homogeneous is likewise. This applies up to the mind (*manas*). As for visible form (*rūpa*), however, it is homogeneous for one who sees it and partially homogeneous for one who does not see it. What is the reason? For there is the possibility that a visible form seen by one person may be seen by many as well, such as in the case of viewing the moon, a dancer, or a wrestler.

However, it is impossible for two people to see with a single eye; therefore, because this [eye] is not common [to others], its establishment is by way of a single continuum (*santāna*). But because visible form (*rūpa*) is common, its establishment is by way of multiple continua. Just as it is with visible form, so should the elements of sound, odor, taste, and the tangible be understood. Let it be so for sound.

However, those objects such as odors which are perceived by one [person] are not perceived by another, because they must be perceived through direct contact (*prāptagrahaṇāt*); thus, because of their non-commonality (*asādhāraṇatva*), it is logical to extend the same designation to them as to the eyes and other [faculties]. This is indeed so; nevertheless, they do possess commonality with respect to their possibility of occurrence. For there is this possibility: that very same odors and so forth which produce olfactory consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*) and the rest for one person may likewise produce them for others. But the eyes and other [faculties] are not like this. Therefore, they are extended [in their designation] just like visible forms (*rūpa*) and the other [objects].

The eye-consciousness and the others possess the status of being "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) or "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) because they have the nature of either arising or not arising, just like the mind-element (*manodhātu*). What is the meaning of "homogeneous"? "Part" (*bhāga*) refers to the mutual sharing among the sense-faculty, the object, and the consciousness, or the sharing of their activity. That which possesses this [sharing] is "homogeneous. Alternatively, it is so called because they share the same effect, namely contact (*sparśa*). Furthermore, those which are "non-homogeneous" (*asabhāga*) are called "partially homogeneous" because they are homogeneous by virtue of belonging to the same genus as those that are homogeneous. How many elements (*dhātu*) are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), how many are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aheya*)? First, regarding those that possess form:
Ten and five consciousness-elements are to be abandoned by cultivation;
the last three are of three kinds. (40ab)

The mind-element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*): these three elements, being the last in the order of enumeration, are of three types.

The eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), their co-existent factors, their acquisitions (*prāpti*) along with their attendants, are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*). The remaining contaminated (*sāsrava*) factors are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*). The uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) factors are not to be abandoned. But is it not the case that there are other things also to be abandoned by seeing, such as the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) and bodily and vocal actions leading to the miserable realms (*āpāyika*), because they are in opposition to the Noble Path? That is not to be abandoned by seeing. This, then, is the summary.
That which is non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*) is not to be abandoned by vision (*na dṛṣṭiheya*); nor is form (*rūpa*).

There is nothing whatsoever that is non-afflicted and to be abandoned by vision, nor is there form [of such a kind]. Furthermore, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is non-afflicted and neutral (*avyākṛta*), because even those who have severed their roots of virtue (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*) and those who are free from passion (*vītarāga*) still possess it. Form refers to bodily and vocal action; therefore, it is not to be abandoned by vision. Moreover, because there is no misconception regarding the Truths (*satya*), and because it would follow that one would still be an ordinary person at the stage of the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*). Nor is it produced by anything other than the sixth [consciousness] (*nāpy aṣaṣṭhaja*). (40d)

The sixth is said to be the mind-base (*manāyatana*). Therefore, that which arises from elsewhere than that—namely, what is not born from the sixth, as well as what is born from the five sense-faculties—is also not to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*).
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are views (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are not views?
The eye and a portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are views.
(41ab) To the question "What is that [portion]?", he says:

It is eightfold: (41b) the five views beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), worldly right view (*laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi*), the view of one in training (*śaikṣī dṛṣṭi*), and the view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī dṛṣṭi*). This eightfold category of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is "view"; the remainder is not view. Among these, the explanation of the view of a self-identity and the others will be given at the appropriate time in the exposition of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). Furthermore, worldly right view is wholesome, contaminated wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with the mental consciousness. The uncontaminated view of one in training is the view of one in training; that of one beyond training is the view of one beyond training.

The vision of phenomena through afflicted, non-afflicted, mundane, trainee, and non-trainee views is like seeing forms during a cloudy night or a clear day. Now, why is it said that only mundane right view is associated with mental consciousness?
Because wisdom arising simultaneously with the five sensory consciousnesses is not "view," as it does not involve deliberation (atīraṇāt). (41cd)

For a view (*dṛṣṭi*) is investigative (*santīrikā*), because it functions through sustained reflection (*upadhāna*); and wisdom (*prajñā*) co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not like this. Therefore, that [wisdom] is not a view. For this very reason, other wisdom—whether afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*)—is also not a view. [Objection: Now, if the eye does not investigate, how can it be a view? [Response: In the sense that it is the observation of visible forms (*rūpa*). [Objection: Since it is said, "the eye sees visible forms" (42a), if the eye were what sees, then even one who possesses another consciousness would see. [Response: It is certainly not the case that every eye sees. What then?

When it is "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*), that is, when it possesses consciousness, then it sees; at other times it does not. If that is the case, then let it be that the consciousness itself, supported by the eye, is what sees, rather than [the eye] being supported by that [consciousness].
It is impossible to understand that consciousness sees. What is the reason?
Because, it is said, a visible form that is obstructed is not seen. (42cd)

For it is said that form obstructed by walls and the like is not seen. If consciousness were to see, then because it is non-obstructive, there would be no resistance against walls and such; thus, one should see even obstructed form. However, visual consciousness does not arise at all with respect to what is obstructed; how then can that which has not arisen see? Why indeed does it not arise?

However, for one whose eye sees, because the eye is characterized by resistance (*sapratighatva*), it lacks activity toward what is obstructed; thus, the non-arising of consciousness is logical, since [consciousness] functions with the same object as its basis (*āśraya*). But is the eye indeed one that reaches its object like the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), such that it would not see what is covered? [If you say] "because of its resistance," then how is it that an object separated by glass, a film of clouds, crystal, or water is seen? Therefore, it is not because of resistance that the eye does not perceive a form that is obstructed.

What then? Visual consciousness arises precisely where there is no obstruction of light, even when a form is concealed; however, where there is obstruction, it does not arise. Because it does not arise [in that case], one does not see what is concealed. As for what was stated in the Sūtra, "having seen forms with the eye," the intended meaning here is "by means of that basis" (the eye), just as it says, "having cognized phenomena with the mind. And yet, the mind does not cognize phenomena, because it is past. What then?

Mental consciousness is [designated] by way of its basis; or rather, the action of the supported is metaphorically attributed to the support, as in the expression "the beds are crying. And as it is said in the Sūtra: "Forms cognizable by the eye are desirable and lovely. Yet these are not actually cognized by the eye. Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra: "The eye, O Brahmin, is merely a gateway for the seeing of forms. From this it is understood that consciousness sees by means of the eye as a gateway. In that context, the term "gateway" refers to the act of seeing; for it is not logical [to say otherwise].

"The eye is the seeing for the purpose of seeing forms. If it is consciousness that sees, then what is it that cognizes? And what is the distinction between these two? For that which is the cognition of form is itself its seeing. Just as a certain kind of wisdom (*prajñā*) is said both to "see" and to "cognize," so too a certain consciousness is said both to "see" and to "cognize. Others, however, say:

"If the eye sees, one must state what other act of seeing there is for the eye, which has become the agent. This objection is not valid; for if it is accepted that "consciousness cognizes," yet there is no distinction between the agent and the action in that case, so it is here as well. Others, however, say: "Visual consciousness is the seeing; because it is the basis [of that consciousness], it is said that 'the eye sees,' just as a bell is said to 'ring' because it is the basis of the sound."

But if this is so, does it not follow that the eye "cognizes" because it serves as the basis for consciousness? It does not follow; for in common worldly usage, that consciousness is conventionally known as "seeing. Thus, when that [consciousness] has arisen, one says "form is seen," not "it is cognized. It is also stated in the *Vibhāṣā*: "That which is reached by the eye and experienced by visual consciousness is said to be 'seen'. Therefore, it is only said that "the eye sees," not that "it cognizes."

Consciousness, however, is said to "cognize form" by its mere presence, just as the sun is called the "maker of the day. Regarding this, the Sautrāntikas say: "What is this? Is the sky being chewed? For it is in dependence upon the eye and forms that visual consciousness arises. In that process, who sees, or what is seen? This is indeed devoid of activity; it is merely phenomena and merely cause and effect. In this regard, for the sake of conventional usage, metaphorical designations are made according to one's preference."

One should not be dogmatic about the claims that "the eye sees" or "consciousness cognizes. For the Blessed One has said: "One should not be attached to local dialects, nor should one pursue the common designations of the world. However, this is the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas: "The eye sees, the ear hears, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the body touches, and the mind cognizes.
Now, if it is the eye that sees, does one see forms with one eye or with both? There is no fixed rule on this point.

One sees with both eyes because of clear perception. (43ab) The Abhidharmikas maintain that one sees with both eyes; for when both are open, vision is more perfectly pure. Moreover, when one eye is opened and the second is half-closed, there occurs the perception of two moons and so forth, not because of the alteration of either one [of the eyes]. Nor does it follow that consciousness would be subject to division due to the division of its basis, because—unlike material form—consciousness does not abide in a specific location.
If the eye sees, the ear hears, and so on up to the mind cognizes, do these [faculties] have an object that is reached or one that is not reached?
The eye, the ear, and the mind have objects that are not reached. (43cd)

For instance, one sees a form from afar but does not see the collyrium applied to the eye; one hears sound from afar. Furthermore, if the sense organs reached their objects, the divine eye and ear would not arise here for those practicing meditation, just like the nose and other such organs. If the eye perceives objects without reaching them, why does it not see everything that is not reached—namely, what is distant or obstructed? How is it, first of all, that a magnet does not attract every iron that is not reached by it? This same objection applies even if the sense organs do reach their objects.

Why does one not see everything that is reached, such as collyrium or the applicator-stick? Just as for the nose and the other [senses], the object is reached but not everything [is perceived]—because they do not grasp the odor and so forth that coexist with it—so too for the eye, it would be the case that it does not perceive everything even though it is reached. However, because the mind (*manas*) is formless (*arūpin*), it is incapable of reaching [an object] at all. Some, moreover, consider the ear to have both reached and unreached objects, because sound is heard even within the ear canal. As for the remaining three, called the nose, tongue, and body, they are otherwise. (43d)

The meaning is "having reached its object. How is it that the sense of smell reaches its object? Because one who is not breathing does not perceive odors. What is this so-called "reaching"? It is arising without an interval [between the object and the sense organ]. But do atoms touch one another or not? The Kashmiris maintain that they do not touch. For what reason? If they were to touch with their entire substance, the substances would merge; if they were to touch by way of a single part, they would follow as having parts. However, atoms are partless.

How, then, does the production of sound occur? Precisely for this reason: if they were to touch, a hand struck by a hand would stick to it, and a stone [struck] by a stone [would stick]. Why does a mass [of earth] not shatter when struck? Because it is held together by the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). One type of wind element functions to disperse, as during the period of destruction (*saṃvartanī*); another functions to hold together, as during the period of evolution (*vivartanī*). How, then, is it said that the three [senses] have their objects attained through reaching them without obstruction?

Thus, their state of being "without further response" (niruttara) is simply that there is nothing in between them. Moreover, since composite objects possess parts, they do indeed touch; therefore, there is no fault. And by adopting this view, the following passage in the *Vibhāṣā* also becomes logically consistent. After posing the question, "Does that which is touched arise with a cause that is touched, or does it arise with a cause that is not touched? it says: "In regard to the cause, sometimes that which is not touched arises with a cause that is touched, as when [an object] disintegrates."

"Sometimes that which is touched has a cause that is not touched, as when there is an accumulation; sometimes that which is touched has a cause that is touched, as when there is an accumulation of what was already accumulated; and sometimes that which is not touched has a cause that is not touched, as in the case of dust in the atmosphere. The Venerable Vasumitra says: "If atoms were to touch one another, they would persist into a subsequent moment. The Venerable [Dharmatrāta] says: "They do not touch; however, when there is no interval between them, there is the conventional designation 'touched'. And the opinion of the Venerable [Dharmatrāta] is to be accepted.

Otherwise, if atoms were separated by intervals, what would obstruct their movement through those empty spaces, given that they are held to be resistant? Furthermore, since aggregates are not distinct from atoms, it is those very atoms themselves that are touched, just as they are perceived as having form (*rūpyante*). Moreover, if a distinction of spatial parts is imagined for an atom—whether it be touched or untouched—it follows that it must possess constituent parts; if not, then even when touched, it does not follow that it has parts.

Furthermore, do these [faculties], beginning with the eye, grasp an object equal in size to themselves—whereby mountains and the like appear as if they were firebrands whirled in a circle due to rapid movement—or rather do they grasp both objects equal and unequal in size? Regarding those which have been described as having reached their objects, it is held that by these three, beginning with the nose, there is the grasping of an object equal in size. (44ab)

For as many atoms as there are in the sense-faculties, so many atoms of the objects come together to produce consciousness. However, in the case of the eye and the ear, there is no fixed rule: sometimes they are fewer, as when one sees the tip of a hair; sometimes they are equal, as when one sees a jujube fruit; and sometimes they are greater, as when one sees a massive mountain with a mere opening of the eyes. Likewise, it is the same with the ear when perceiving sounds such as those of a mosquito or thunderclouds. But since the mind is indeed formless, its measurement or limitation is not determined.

Furthermore, what is the arrangement of these atoms of the sense-faculties, such as the eye? First, the atoms of the visual faculty are situated within the pupil of the eye like cumin flowers; though covered by a transparent membrane, they do not scatter. Others say they are arranged like a mass, one above the other. And they do not obstruct one another because of their transparency, like crystal. The atoms of the auditory faculty are situated inside the ear-cavity.

The atoms of the olfactory faculty are situated inside the nose like a probe. The first three faculties are arranged like a garland. The atoms of the gustatory faculty are shaped like a half-moon; it is said that an area the size of a hair-tip in the middle of the tongue is not covered by the atoms of the gustatory faculty. The atoms of the tactile faculty are situated according to the shape of the body. The atoms of the female faculty are like the hollow of a drum. The atoms of the male faculty are like a thumb.

In that regard, the atoms of the eye-faculty are sometimes all functioning (sabhāga), sometimes all non-functioning (tatsabhāga), and sometimes some are functioning while others are non-functioning. This remains the case up to the atoms of the tongue-faculty. However, the atoms of the body-faculty are never all functioning; for even in the case of those confined within the blazing hells, immeasurable atoms of the body-faculty remain non-functioning.

It is said that if consciousness were to arise from all [atoms] together, the basis would disintegrate; nor does a single sense-organ atom or a single object atom produce consciousness, because the five groups of consciousness have as their basis and objective support an accumulation [of atoms]. For this very reason, an atom is non-demonstrable, because it is invisible.

Regarding these six consciousness-elements that have been mentioned—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is their support, like their object, present for the first five and of all three times for the last? No, he says. What then?
The support of the last is past; the support of the mind-consciousness-element is the mind that has just ceased immediately prior.
And for the five [faculties], there is also [contact] that is co-nascent with them. //44d//

The word "and" (*ca*) implies "also past. In this regard, the eye is the simultaneous basis (*sahaja-āśraya*) for visual consciousness, and so on up to the body being the basis for tactile consciousness. Furthermore, the mind (*manas*) is their past basis; thus, these five groups of consciousness have two types of faculties as their bases. For this very reason it is said: "That which is the basis of visual consciousness by way of being its basis is also [its basis] by way of being its immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This constitutes a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*). The first alternative is the eye.

The second [alternative] is the mental factor (caitasika) of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) that has just passed away; the third is the mind (manas) that has just passed away; the fourth category consists of those phenomena (dharmas) excluded from what has been mentioned. In this same manner, up to the case of body-consciousness (kāyavijñāna), its own respective faculty (indriya) should be stated. Regarding mental consciousness (manovijñāna), there is the "prior-constituent" (pūrvapādaka): namely, that which is both a basis (āśrayabhāva) and a condition of immediate antecedence (samanantarapratyayabhāva). There may be that which is a condition of immediate antecedence but not a basis: namely, the mental factor of the dharma-realm that has just passed away.

Furthermore, what is the reason that, when consciousness arises from the coming together of both [the sense organ and its object], only the eye and so forth are called the bases (*āśraya*), and not visible form and so forth?
"The bases, such as the eye, are so called because they undergo change according to the changes in those [consciousnesses].

(45ab) This refers to the *dhātus*. For, through the modification of the eye and so forth, there occurs a modification of their respective consciousnesses, because [the consciousnesses] conform to the benefit, injury, acuity, or dullness [of the organs]. However, there is no such modification of them through the modification of visible form and so forth. Therefore, since they are dependent upon those [organs], the eye and so forth alone are the bases, and not visible form and so forth.

What, then, is the reason that form and the other objects are cognized by them [the consciousnesses], yet they are called "eye-consciousness" up to "mind-consciousness," rather than being called "consciousness of form" up to "consciousness of phenomena"? Because these bases—the eye and so forth—are their [respective] supports, consciousness is designated by them due to their uncommon nature. (45cd)

How is it that they are unique? For the eye is not capable of becoming the support for any other consciousness; however, visible form becomes the object of mental consciousness as well as of the visual consciousness of another person. This should be understood in the same way up to the body. Therefore, because of its status as the support and because of its uniqueness, consciousness is designated by that [organ] alone and not by visible forms and so forth, just as one says "the sound of a drum" or "a barley sprout."

Now, regarding the body in which one dwells while seeing forms with the eye: do that body, the eye, the forms, and the visual consciousness belong exclusively to the same level (*ekabhūmika*), or can they also belong to different levels? He replies: there is a distinction among all of them. For one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who sees his own forms with his own eye, everything belongs to his own level. When that same person sees his own forms with the eye of the first dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to his own level, while the consciousness and the eye belong to that [first dhyāna] level.

For one seeing forms belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, all three [the body, the forms, and the consciousness] belong to that same level. For one seeing one's own forms with the eye of the second dhyāna, the body and the forms belong to their own level, the eye belongs to that level [of the second dhyāna], and the consciousness belongs to the level of the first dhyāna. For one seeing forms belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, the consciousness and the forms belong to that level, the body belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), and the eye belongs to the level of the second dhyāna.

For one seeing [forms] belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, the eye and the forms belong to that level, the body belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), and the consciousness belongs to the level of the first dhyāna. In the same way, this should be applied to one seeing forms belonging to their own level or a lower level with an eye belonging to the level of the third or fourth dhyāna. For one born in the first dhyāna who sees his own forms with his own eye, everything belongs to his own level; for one seeing [forms] belonging to his own level or a lower level, three [factors—eye, body, and consciousness—] belong to his own level.

When one sees one's own forms with the eye of the second dhyāna, three factors belong to one's own level: the body and consciousness belong to that [first] level, while the eye belongs to that [second] level. When seeing forms belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the body and consciousness belong to one's own level, the forms are of a lower level, and the eye belongs to that [second] level. When seeing forms belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, the eye and the forms belong to that level, while the rest belong to one's own level. This should be applied analogously for the eye of the third dhyāna.
For one born in the second or higher dhyānas who sees forms of their own or another level with the eyes of their own or another level, it should be applied accordingly as appropriate.
However, this is the fixed rule:

The eye is not lower than the body. For the body, the eye, and visible forms belong to five levels: from those of the desire realm up to those of the fourth dhyāna level. Eye-consciousness belongs to two levels: that of the desire realm and that of the first dhyāna level. In this regard, the eye belongs to the same level as the body, or it may belong to a higher level, but never to a lower level. Visible form is the object of the eye; it may belong to the same level as the eye or to a lower level, but visible form of a higher level is not [perceived] by the eye.
For it is never possible to see a form belonging to a higher level with an eye belonging to a lower level;
and consciousness, like the form, does not exist on a higher level than the eye. [p.36]
But its form consists of both [the body and the mind] throughout the entire body. //46cd//

"For this"—that is, for the visual consciousness just mentioned—visible form (*rūpa*) is its object from all sides: above, below, and in its own level. For the body, both visible form and consciousness exist from all sides.
Just as this eye has been described, so too should the ear be understood in detail.
The ear is not lower than the body, nor is sound higher than the ear;
its consciousness [is higher], but sound [is higher] than the body, and both are present everywhere—
this is to be applied in detail.
But for the three [elements], everything belongs to their own level.

(47ab) For the nose, tongue, and body elements, the body, the object, and the consciousness belong exclusively to their own level. Having thus stated this general rule without distinction, an exception is now undertaken for the sake of specification:
"Body-consciousness belongs to a lower level or its own level" (47cd).

The body, the body-element, and the tangible object always belong exclusively to their own level. However, for some, body-consciousness belongs to its own level—as is the case for those born in the desire realm or the first dhyāna; for others, it belongs to a lower level—as is the case for those born in the second dhyāna and above.
The mind is indeterminate. (47d)

Sometimes the mind belongs to the same level as the body, the mental consciousness, and its objects; sometimes it belongs to a higher or lower level. For even when the body belongs to one of the five levels, the mind and other faculties may belong to any level, as is appropriate at the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or rebirth (*upapatti*). This has been explained in detail in the *Kośasthāna* during the exposition of meditative attainments. However, for the sake of avoiding an excessive burden of text, it will not be explained again here.
Since the purpose is small and the labor great, this incidental discussion is concluded.
This is now investigated: among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), which is to be cognized by which? It is said:
the five external [objects] are cognizable by two.

The elements of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects are experienced respectively by the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, and are subsequently cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Thus, each of these is cognizable by two consciousnesses. It is explained that the remaining thirteen elements, because they are not the objects of the five groups of sensory consciousness, are cognizable by the mental consciousness alone.
Among these eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are permanent and how many are impermanent? Not a single element exists in its entirety as permanent;
rather, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are permanent.
Therefore, one part of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) is permanent, while the remainder are impermanent.
How many are faculties (indriya) and how many are not faculties?
Half of the dharmas and those which are known as the twelve internal [bases] are faculties. (48cd)

Twenty-two faculties (indriya) are taught in the Sūtra: the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the pleasure faculty, the pain faculty, the joy faculty, the displeasure faculty, the equanimity faculty, the faith faculty, the energy faculty, the mindfulness faculty, the concentration faculty, the wisdom faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."

The Abhidharmikas, however, following the established arrangement of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), recite the mind faculty (*manaindriya*) immediately after the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because it possesses an object (*sālambanatva*). In that context, "half of the dharmas" refers to the eleven faculties beginning with the life faculty and a portion of the three [final] faculties, because they are part of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). Among the twelve internal [faculties], the five beginning with the eye are mentioned by their own names. The seven consciousness-elements (*cittadhātu*) constitute the mind faculty; the female and male faculties are a portion of the body-element (*kāyadhātu*), as will be explained later.
It is established that the remaining five elements and a portion of the dharma-element are not faculties.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, titled "Exposition of the Elements" (*Dhātunirdeśa*).
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
This was caused to be written by the illustrious Lāmāvāka.
Chapter II. [p.38]
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the Second Chapter of the Treasury. Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!

The faculties (*indriya*) have been explained. What, then, is the meaning of "faculty"? [The root] *idi* means "supreme sovereignty. They are called faculties because they exercise sovereignty (*indanti*). Therefore, the meaning of "faculty" is the sense of "sovereignty. And over what do these [faculties] exercise sovereignty?
The five [faculties] exercise sovereignty over four objects. (1ab)

First, the eye and the ear each possess sovereignty with respect to four objects: (1) in the beauty of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), because those who are blind or deaf possess an unattractive form; (2) in the maintenance of the personal existence, because by seeing and hearing one avoids dangerous places; (3) in the arising of the visual and auditory consciousnesses along with their associated mental factors; and (4) in being the uncommon cause for the seeing of forms and the hearing of sounds. As for the nose, tongue, and body, [their sovereignty] regarding the beauty of the personal existence is as previously stated.

[The first element] serves for the maintenance of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) through the consumption of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); for the arising of the olfactory and other consciousnesses together with their associated mental factors; and as the specific cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*) for smelling odors, tasting flavors, and touching tangibles. It is said that [the second element] serves two purposes, while [the remaining] four serve four purposes each.

The female, male, life, and mind faculties each exercise sovereignty over two objects. First, regarding the female and male faculties, they exercise sovereignty over the differentiation of sentient beings and their variation. Therein, the differentiation of sentient beings refers to "female" and "male. The variation of sentient beings refers to the differences in physical form, such as breasts and so forth, as well as in voice and behavior. Others say they exercise sovereignty over affliction and purification.

For instance, among those dissociated from that [faculty], namely eunuchs, impotent persons, and those possessing both sets of sexual organs, there is no non-restraint, no commission of the immediate transgressions, and no severance of the roots of wholesome merit; likewise, there is no attainment of restraint, the fruits [of the path], or detachment. Furthermore, the life-faculty functions in the connection and maintenance of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), while the mind-faculty functions in the connection to renewed existence and in the conformity to mastery.

Furthermore, regarding the connection to renewed existence (*bhava*), it is said: "At that time, for the *gandharva*, one or the other of two types of mind becomes manifest—either accompanied by attachment (*anunaya*) or accompanied by aversion (*pratigha*). Regarding the conformity to mastery, it is said: "By the mind this world is led," and so forth. As for the five faculties beginning with pleasure and the eight beginning with faith, these five and eight [faculties] pertain to defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*). (1cd)

Dominance belongs, respectively, to the five [faculties] beginning with pleasure (*sukha*) in regard to defilement (*saṃkleśa*), because passion (*rāga*) and the others adhere to them; and to faith (*śraddhā*) and the others in regard to purification (*vyavadāna*), for by means of them one is purified. Others, however, maintain that pleasure and the others also have dominance in regard to purification, because "the mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," "faith has suffering as its proximate cause," and "the six states of mental joy and so forth are based on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*)," according to the Vaibhāṣikas. Still others, moreover, say:

It is not by means of the eye and the ear that one draws forth the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) through the cognition [of objects], since one avoids danger by means of such cognition; rather, these two exercise sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) over cognition itself. Nor is there any seeing of forms or hearing of sounds other than cognition, by virtue of which their sovereignty would be logically established as distinct due to their being uncommon causes (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*). Therefore, their status as faculties (*indriyatva*) is not in this way. How then?
"Because of their sovereignty in the apprehension of their own respective objects, there are six faculties for everything. (2ab)

The five [faculties], beginning with the eye, possess sovereignty over the apprehension of their respective objects; the mind, moreover, possesses sovereignty over the apprehension of all objects. Therefore, these six are each an *indriya*.
But is it not the case that the objects also possess sovereignty here?

There is no predominance [in the object]. For predominance (*ādhipatya*) is superior sovereignty. The eye has superior mastery over the perception of visible forms, because it is the common cause for the perception of all visible forms, and because perception conforms to its own sharpness, dullness, and so forth; but this is not the case for the visible form. This is because the opposite is true for the form. The same should be applied up to the mind with respect to mental objects (*dharma*). However, the female and male faculties arise from the body due to their predominance over femininity and masculinity. (2cd)

The female and male faculties are established as distinct from the body faculty itself; they are not separate entities. A certain portion of the body faculty, located in the region of the genitals, receives the designation of the female or male faculty, because it exercises sovereignty over femininity and masculinity respectively. In this context, "female nature" refers to the female form, voice, gestures, and intentions; for these constitute the femininity of a woman. "Male nature" refers to the male form, voice, gestures, and intentions; for these constitute the masculinity of a man. [These faculties exercise sovereignty] over the duration of the [homogeneous] group, and over defilement and purification.
Life-force, the five feelings, and those beginning with faith are considered faculties. ||3||

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has sovereignty over the persistence within a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*); the sensations (*vedanā*) have sovereignty over defilement (*saṃkleśa*). For it is said in the Sūtra that passion (*rāga*) underlies pleasant sensation, aversion (*pratigha*) underlies painful sensation, and ignorance (*avidyā*) underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation. The five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) have sovereignty over purification (*vyavadāna*), for by means of them the afflictions are suppressed and the Path is brought forth. Therefore, these too are each accepted as faculties. [Verse 4] Likewise, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) are so designated because they have sovereignty over the successive attainments, such as Nirvāṇa.

The word "likewise" (*tathā*) is used for the purpose of indicating that each faculty [exercises sovereignty] individually. In this regard, the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) has sovereignty over the attainment of the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*); the faculty of "knowing" has sovereignty over the attainment of the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*); and the faculty of "one who has known" has sovereignty over final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*). For there is no final nirvana for one whose mind is not liberated. The word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to indicate other alternative formulations. What is the other formulation? The faculty of "I shall come to know" has sovereignty with respect to the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*).

Regarding the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), there is the faculty of "having known" (*ājñendriya*); regarding dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), there is the faculty of "one who has fully known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). [The opponent argues: "Because they experience the joy and happiness of liberation, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the others should also be included among the faculties on account of their predominance (*ādhipatya*). For ignorance and the others also possess predominance over the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth; therefore, their status as faculties must also be added. Furthermore, speech and the others—namely, speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals—should also be included as faculties because of their predominance in speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and experiencing pleasure, respectively.
Indeed, it need not be added as a supplement, because it is accepted here that the basis of the mind, its transformation,
its duration, and its affliction are [the characteristics of conditioned phenomena].
The equipment and purification—by whatever extent these exist, that much is the faculty. ||5||

In this context, the basis of the mind consists of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*). These six bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute the fundamental substance of a sentient being. The distinction between female and male is established by the female and male faculties (*strī-puruṣendriya*). Persistence is established by the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*). Defilement occurs through the [five] feelings (*vedanā*). The accumulation of purification occurs through the five [faculties] beginning with faith (*śraddhā*); purification itself occurs through three [faculties]. Therefore, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other [links of dependent origination] are not accepted as faculties.

[The fourteen faculties] are for the sake of the basis, the arising, the persistence, and the enjoyment of active existence (*pravṛtti*); likewise, the others are faculties for the sake of cessation (*nivṛtti*). (Verse 6)

The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative opinion. Others, however, say: the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are the basis for active engagement (*pravṛtti*); the female and male faculties are for production, because [beings] are produced from them; the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is for maintenance, because by means of it there is persistence; and experience is through the feelings (*vedanā*). Therefore, these are the fourteen faculties. In that same manner, the others are for cessation (*nivṛtti*); for faith and the rest are the bases for cessation.

The faculty of "I shall come to know" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) is the origin; the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya) is the stability; and the faculty of "one who has known" (ājñātāvīndriya) is the enjoyment. Therefore, there are exactly these many faculties, and for this very reason, they follow this specific order.

Speech, however, is not a sense faculty, because its function of speaking depends upon specific training. Likewise, the hands and feet are not separate faculties from the acts of grasping and moving, for it is those very same organs that, when produced in one way or another place, are called "grasping" and "moving. Furthermore, grasping and moving occur even without hands and feet, as in the case of snakes and other such creatures. Nor is the anus a sense faculty with respect to excretion, because heavy substances fall everywhere in space due to gravity, and because their discharge is impelled by the wind.

Furthermore, the sexual organ (*upastha*) would not possess the status of a faculty (*indriya*), for that pleasure is produced by the male and female faculties. Moreover, the throat, teeth, eyes, eyelids, and joints would also incur the status of faculties, as they function as the instruments for swallowing, chewing, opening and closing the eyes, and contracting and expanding [the limbs]. Or else, if everything that serves as a cause for its own specific action were considered a faculty, then it would be illogical for speech and the other organs to be classified as faculties.

Among those, the exposition of the faculties beginning with the eye and ending with the male faculty has been completed. Because the life-faculty is a dissociated factor (*viprayukta*), its exposition will be made among the dissociated factors themselves. The exposition of faith and the others will be made among the mental factors (*caitta*). The exposition of the [faculties] beginning with pleasure (*sukha*) and the [faculties] beginning with "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) remains to be done; that is now being performed. "The faculty of suffering is bodily feeling that is unpleasant" (7ab).
"Unpleasant" means harmful; that is to say, it is suffering.
Pleasure (*sukha*). Agreeable (*śātā*) bodily sensation is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). "Agreeable" means beneficial; it has the sense of being pleasant (*sukha*).
But in the third dhyāna, that mental [feeling] is the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya). ||7cd||

In the third dhyāna, however, that same pleasant mental feeling is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), for there is no bodily feeling there due to the absence of the five groups of sensory consciousness. Elsewhere—that is, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the first and second dhyānas—this pleasant mental feeling is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*). But in the third dhyāna, because of the absence of passion for rapture (*prīti*), it is exclusively the faculty of pleasure and not the faculty of joy; for rapture is indeed joy.

Furthermore, mental unpleasantness is *daurmanasya* (dejection), while equanimity (*upekṣā*) is that which is intermediate. (8bc) It is neither pleasant nor unpleasant; it is called neutral feeling. That is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). Is it bodily or mental? He says: [it is both].
Regarding both types (8d): what, then, is the reason that these are combined into a single faculty?
Because they are free from conceptual construction (avikalpanāt). [p.42] 8d.

Mental pleasure and pain generally arise from conceptualization (*vikalpa*), whereas physical [pleasure and pain] do not, since they arise even for Arhats due to the power of their objects. Therefore, there is a distinction between those two as faculties (*indriya*). Equanimity (*upekṣā*), however, arises by its own nature even for one who does not conceptualize; thus, whether physical or mental, it is made into a single faculty. Furthermore, physical pleasure benefits in one way, while mental pleasure benefits in another; likewise, physical pain harms in one way, while mental pain harms in another.

However, this discrimination does not exist in equanimity; therefore, there is no distinction [between the types of equanimity], because there is no discrimination regarding the act of being equanimous.
On the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, there are nine and three [types of equanimity] respectively. (9ab)

The faculties of mental pleasure (*manas-sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)—these nine faculties are called three faculties within the three paths. On the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*); on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), it is the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*); and on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), it is the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). What is the reason? For on the path of seeing, one has set out to know what was previously unknown. On the path of cultivation, there is nothing further to be known that was not already known; rather, one knows that very same [truth] for the sake of abandoning the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).

On the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), however, the realization that "it has been known" is *ājñātāvaḥ*. One who possesses this is an *ājñātāvī*; or, one whose nature it is to protect what has been known (*ājñātam avitum*). This is because of the attainment of the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*). The faculty of one who has become such—realizing "Suffering has been fully understood by me; it is not to be fully understood again"—is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).

Having provided the explanation of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the classification of its types must now be stated: how many faculties are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without-outflows (*anāsrava*), and so forth. In that regard, first, these [faculties] just mentioned, beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), are as follows:
The three pure [factors] (amala);
this means they are untainted (anāsrava), because "taints" (mala) is a synonym for "outflows" (āsrava).
The material [faculties], life, and the two types of suffering—

The seven material faculties, the life faculty, and the faculties of pain and mental distress are exclusively with-outflows (*sāsrava*). Furthermore, the seven material [faculties]—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, female, and male faculties—are included within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
Nine are of two kinds. (9d)

The mental faculty (*manas*), pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)—these nine faculties are both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*). Some maintain that the [five] beginning with faith are exclusively without-outflows. For it was said by the Blessed One: "In whomsoever these five faculties are entirely and in every way absent, him I call an outsider, one who stands on the side of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). This, however, is not a definitive proof [that they are exclusively without-outflows], because that statement was made with reference to those [faculties] that are without-outflows.

For it is after establishing the classification of noble persons (āryapudgala) that he says, "for whom these [roots] exist. Or, there are two kinds of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana): the internal one whose roots of merit are not severed, and the external one whose roots of merit are severed. With reference to the latter, he says, "I call him an external person who stands on the side of the ordinary."

And it is said in the Sūtra: "There are beings born in the world and grown up in the world who have sharp faculties, medium faculties, and even dull faculties," even before the Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion. Therefore, faith and the other [faculties] do indeed exist as contaminated (*sāsrava*).

Furthermore, it is said: "As long as I did not understand, as they really are, the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these five faculties, for that long I [did not claim to have awakened] from this world with its devas," and so forth. And this method of examination does not apply to phenomena that are outflows (*āsrava*).
How many faculties are fruition (*vipāka*), and how many are not fruition? First, to speak categorically: the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is exclusively fruition.

Now, as for the fact that an Arhat monk sustains the life-formations (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*), of what is that life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) the maturation? It is said in the Śāstra: "How does he sustain the life-formations? An Arhat monk, possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhimat*) and having attained mastery over the mind (*cetovaśitva*), gives to the Saṅgha or to an individual a bowl, a robe, or any other requisite for the ascetic life; having made a vow regarding that, he enters the fourth dhyāna of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*)."

Emerging from that state, he generates a thought and speaks these words: "May that which was my maturation of wealth become a maturation of life. For him, that which was the maturation of wealth becomes the maturation of life. However, for those who hold the view that it is the remainder of the maturation that ripens, they say: "That [life] is the remainder of the maturation of karma performed in a previous birth; having drawn it forth by the power of cultivation, he experiences it. How does he relinquish the formative forces of life?

In the same way, having given a gift and made a vow, he enters the fourth dhyāna of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*), thinking: "May that which is my maturation of life-span become the maturation of wealth. For him, it becomes so. But the Venerable Ghoṣaka says: "By the power of dhyāna, he brings into manifestation within that very same physical basis (*āśraya*) the great elements (*mahābhūta*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*)—those conducive to life and those antagonistic to it. In this way he sustains the formations of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*), and in this way he relinquishes them. However, it must be understood in this manner.

Such is the power of their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that they cause the momentum of the sense-faculties and the primary elements—which arises from prior karma and determines the duration of their stay—to cease, and they project a new momentum born of concentration. Therefore, that life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*); other than that, however, it is a result of maturation.

From one question, another arises: for what purpose do they sustain the life-formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*)? It is for the sake of the welfare of others, or for the sake of the endurance of the Teaching. For they perceive their own lifespan to be exhausted, and they see no one else capable [of sustaining it]. Then, for what purpose do they relinquish them? They perceive that the welfare of others would be slight while living, and that their own person (*ātmabhāva*) is overcome by disease. As it has been said: "When this holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been well-practiced, and the Path itself has been well-cultivated..."
One becomes joyful at the exhaustion of life,
just as one is upon the departure of a disease.

Thus it is said. Now, where and for whom should this relinquishing (*utsarjana*) or the stabilization (*sthāpana*) of the formative forces of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) be understood? It is among humans alone, in the three continents, by a woman or a man who is an Arhat liberated at all times (*asamayavimukta*) and who has attained the dhyāna of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*). For such a person possesses mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and their continuum (*santati*) is no longer susceptible to the afflictions (*kleśa*). As stated in the Sūtra: "The Blessed One, having sustained the formative forces of vitality (*jīvita-saṃskāra*), relinquished the formative forces of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*). What is the distinction between them?

Some say that there is none at all; for it has been said: "What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)? It is the vitality (*āyus*) belonging to the three realms. Others maintain that the formative forces of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) are the fruit of past karma, while the formative forces of life (*jīvita-saṃskāra*) are the fruit of present karma. Alternatively, those by which one remains within a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) are the formative forces of vitality, whereas those by which one lives for a certain period of time are the formative forces of life. The plural number is used because of the relinquishing and sustaining of many moments of the formative forces of vitality and life.

For there is no relinquishing or sustaining of a single moment. Some say this is for the purpose of showing that life-force (*āyus*) as a substance is not a single entity persisting over a period of time; rather, the designation "life" applies only to a plurality of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*), and there is no such thing as a single substance called life. Others maintain that otherwise [the Buddha] would not have used the term "conditioned factors. For what purpose, then, did the Blessed One relinquish and sustain the conditioned forces of life?

They were relinquished to demonstrate mastery over death, and sustained by empowerment to demonstrate mastery over life. This lasted for exactly three months and no longer, because there was no further work to be done for those to be trained (*vineya*). Furthermore, it was also for the sake of fulfilling that which was vowed: "With these four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) thus cultivated, should I so desire, I could remain for an eon (*kalpa*) or even for the remainder of an eon. According to the Vaibhāṣikas, it was also for the sake of conquering the Māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*) and the Māra of death (*maraṇamāra*), since at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Māra of the afflictions (*kleśamāra*) and the Māra who is the son of a god (*devaputramāra*) had already been conquered. Thus concludes the incidental discussion.
The subject at hand is now commenced:
"Twelve are twofold.
Which are the twelve?

Except for the final eight and from mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*). That is to say, excluding the final eight—the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) and mental dissatisfaction—there are twelve other faculties that are of two kinds: both maturation (*vipāka*) and non-maturation. Among these, the seven beginning with the eye-faculty are accumulative (*aupacayika*) and thus non-maturation; the remaining ones are maturation. The faculties of mind, pain, pleasure, joy, and equanimity are non-maturation when they are wholesome or afflicted, as well as when they belong to the classes of postures (*airyāpathika*), crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and emanations (*nairmāṇika*), according to the case. The rest are maturation.
It is established that, with the exception of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) and the twelve faculties beginning with the eye, the remaining ones are not fruition (*avipāka*).

If the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not fruition, how is the following Sūtra to be interpreted: "There are three types of karma: karma to be experienced as pleasure, karma to be experienced as mental distress, and karma to be experienced as equanimity"? This was stated with reference to being experienced through association (*saṃprayoga-vedanīyatā*). Karma associated with mental distress is "karma to be experienced as mental distress," just as contact associated with pleasure is "to be experienced as pleasure."

In that case, the two types of karma to be experienced as mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) would also be like this. Let it be as you wish. There is no fault in [mental pleasure being] associated [with a root], nor is there any fault in its being a maturation (*vipāka*). For, having no other recourse, one must understand it in this very way. But what is the reasoning here that mental displeasure (*daurmanasya*) is not a maturation? For mental displeasure is produced and ceased by specific conceptual constructions (*parikalpa*), and a maturation is not like that. If that were so, mental pleasure too would not be a maturation.

If, then, mental distress (*daurmanasya*) were a maturation (*vipāka*), the karma of those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) would have already matured, because mental distress arises on account of that [karma]. The same would apply to mental pleasure (*saumanasya*): if mental pleasure were a maturation, the karma of those who perform meritorious deeds would have already matured, because mental pleasure arises on account of that. However, since mental distress is impossible for those free from passion (*vītarāga*), it cannot be a maturation in this way. Furthermore, what kind of maturation could their neutral (*avyākṛta*) mental pleasure be?

"Let it be as it may. However, when there is the possibility [of its occurrence], there is room for mental joy (*saumanasya*) to be a maturation (*vipāka*), but not for mental grief (*daurmanasya*). Because it never manifests in any way, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that mental grief is not a maturation at all. In this regard, the eight faculties beginning with the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are the maturation of wholesome karma in a happy destiny (*sugati*) and of unwholesome karma in a miserable destiny (*durgati*). The mind-faculty (*manaindriya*) is the maturation of both types of karma in both destinies. The faculties of pleasure, mental joy, and equanimity are the maturation of wholesome karma; the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) is the maturation of unwholesome karma.

In the case of a person with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*) in a happy destiny (*sugatī*), the acquisition of that state occurs through unwholesome karma; it does not, however, result from the projection of wholesome karma regarding the faculties. This point has been explained. Now, this must be stated: how many faculties have maturation (*savipāka*), and how many are without maturation (*avipāka*)? That which was just mentioned, namely mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*), is the one [faculty] that has maturation. (10cd)

That one [mental factor] is exclusively with ripening (*savipāka*). The word "but" (*tu*) should be understood as having the sense of "only" (*eva*) and as being displaced in its position. For that [factor] is neither neutral (*avyākṛta*) nor untainted (*anāsrava*), because it is not in a state of meditative concentration (*asamāhita*). Therefore, there is no mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*) that is without ripening. Ten [factors] are of two kinds. (10d)
They are both with outflow (*savipāka*) and without outflow (*avipāka*). Which ten?
The mind, the other sensations, and faith and the rest. (11a)

Because of the mention of "another feeling," a feeling other than mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is understood. Faith and the others—namely, faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—are included. Among those, the mental faculty (*manas*), pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), when unwholesome or wholesome and associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), possess ripening (*savipāka*); when without outflows (*anāsrava*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they do not have ripening. The faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), when wholesome or unwholesome, possesses ripening; when indeterminate, it does not have ripening. Faith and the others, when associated with outflows, possess ripening; when without outflows, they do not have ripening. It is thus established that all others do not have ripening.
How many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate? First of all, eight are exclusively wholesome:
the five beginning with faith, and the three beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
It is of two kinds: mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is both wholesome and unwholesome.
The mind and the other sensations are of three kinds—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate;
the others are of one kind. (11c’d)
Something else: the eye and so forth, with life as the eighth; this is strictly indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Which faculty belongs to which realm among these faculties?

First, it should be understood that the faculties connected with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are those excluding the stainless ones. This is because the triad beginning with the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" faculty (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and thus not connected to any realm at all.

In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the female and male faculties (*strīpuruṣendriya*) are excluded; as well as the two types of suffering (*duḥkha*) and the untainted (*amala*). The term "suffering" here refers to the faculties of physical pain (*duḥkha*) and mental distress (*daurmanasya*). Among these, the female and male faculties do not exist in the realm of form because of the absence of passion for sexual union (*maithunadharma-vairāgya*) and because they would cause a lack of beauty (*aśobhākaratva*). How then are those beings called "men"? Where is this stated?
