In the Sūtra: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a woman should exercise the role of a Brahmā; such a case does not exist. But it is possible that a man [should do so]."

There is another state of masculinity that belongs to males in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The faculty of physical pain (*duḥkhendriya*) does not exist there because the basis (*āśraya*) is translucent and because unwholesome states are absent. The faculty of mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasyendriya*) does not exist because the continuum is moistened by tranquility (*śamatha*) and because objects of malice are absent.
[p.47] That which pertains to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*), as well as the two types of pleasure (*sukha*) and the material faculties, are excluded. (12cd)

The female and male faculties, as well as the faculty of suffering, are excluded from the "pure" [faculties]. What remains? The mind, life, and equanimity faculties, along with the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*). These are associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); no others are.
How many faculties are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)?
The mind and the three feelings are of three kinds. (13a)
What are the three feelings? They are pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Mental distress (*durmanaskatā*) is to be abandoned by two [paths];
that is, mental distress is to be abandoned by both seeing (*darśana*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The governing principle is that nine [faculties] are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The eye and the other [senses], with the life-faculty as the eighth, and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) are exclusively to be abandoned by cultivation.
However, five [of these] may also not be abandoned.
The five faculties beginning with faith are both to be abandoned by cultivation and not to be abandoned, because they are both contaminated and uncontaminated; the three [faculties] are not. (13d)

The triad beginning with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is certainly not to be abandoned, because it is untainted (*anāsrava*); for that which is faultless is not fit for abandonment. The distinction of types has been explained.
Now, the acquisition must be discussed. How many faculties are first acquired as maturation (*vipāka*) in which realm?
In the desire realm, two maturations are first acquired at the outset. (14ab)

The body faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*). These are acquired by those born from eggs, from wombs, and from moisture, but not by those who are spontaneously born (*upapāduka*). Since spontaneous birth is excluded, it should be understood that [these faculties] belong to those born from eggs, from wombs, and from moisture. Why are the mind faculty (*manas*) and the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*) not included? Because at the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*), those two are necessarily defiled (*kliṣṭa*). Now, how many are acquired by those who are spontaneously born?

By them, there are six (14c) if they are without the secondary sexual organs (*avyañjana*), such as those of the first eon (*prāthamakalpika*). Which six? The faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life-force (*jīvitendriya*).
Or seven (14c').

If they possess only one gender, as among the gods and others; or if they possess both genders, there are eight [types]. But do those with both genders also arise through spontaneous birth (*upapāduka*)? They do so in the miserable realms (*apāya*). Such is the case, first of all, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Now, how is it in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)? To this he says:

Regarding the six [objects] in the form realm (rūpa): because desire is predominant, the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is designated as "desires" (kāmāḥ); because form is predominant, the form realm (rūpadhātu) is designated as "forms" (rūpāṇi). It is also stated in the Sūtra: "O monks, those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are formless (ārūpya). In that form realm, six faculties are initially obtained as fruition (vipāka). Those same [faculties] that exist for spontaneously born beings (upapāduka) without sexual organs in the desire realm are increased by one in the higher [realms]. (14d)

The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is superior to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), both because it is higher in terms of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and because it is more preeminent in terms of rebirth (*upapatti*). In that [realm], only the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is initially acquired as a karmic maturation (*vipāka*), and no other. The acquisition has been explained; now the relinquishment must be discussed. When dying in which realm does one cease how many faculties?
One ceases them while passing away: in the formless realm, the life-faculty and the mind-faculty (*manaḥ*).

And equanimity; thus, in the form realm, one dying there ceases eight [faculties]. These consist of those three and the five beginning with the eye. For all beings born by transformation are born and die with their faculties complete. In the desire realm, ten, nine, or eight [are ceased]. (15d)

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one who dies as a hermaphrodite ceases ten faculties: those eight [already mentioned] plus the female and male faculties. One with a single sexual organ ceases nine; one without a sexual organ ceases eight. This is the rule for simultaneous death. However, in the case of gradual death, four [faculties] cease.

One who dies with a wholesome mind (*kuśala-citta*) ceases four faculties: the faculties of body, life, mind, and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). For these do not cease separately. This principle should be understood to apply to death when the mind is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or neutral (*avyākṛta*). However, when one dies while established in a wholesome state of mind, then:
"In every case of the wholesome, there are five. (16b)

One dying with a wholesome mind ceases all the faculties as previously described, plus five additional ones—faith and the others—since these five necessarily exist in a wholesome mind. Thus, one should calculate in detail that in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) one ceases eight faculties, and in the form realms (*rūpa*) thirteen.
In this section on the faculties (*indriya-prakaraṇa*), all the characteristics of the faculties are investigated. Now, which fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇya-phala*) is attained by how many faculties?
The attainment of the two final fruits is by nine. (16c)

The attainment of the two final fruits is by means of nine faculties. Which, then, are the two final ones? They are the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) and arhatship (*arhattva*). Which are the intermediate ones? They are the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*) and the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*). Among these, the fruit of stream-entry is attained by nine: by faith and the others [the five spiritual faculties], excluding the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), together with the faculties of mind (*manas*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*). The faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is to be understood as existing in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

For its attainment is by means of both [the faculties of faith, etc., and the faculty of mind], because they respectively serve as the bringer and the support for the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*). Furthermore, his attainment of Arhatship is by means of nine: the seven beginning with faith (excluding the "I-shall-come-to-know" faculty), the faculty of mind, and whichever one among the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity is applicable.
[Verse 16d: "By seven, eight, or nine, in two cases."

The attainment of the fruits of once-returner and non-returner occurs respectively through seven, eight, or nine faculties. How so? First, regarding the fruit of once-returner: if one attains it by following the gradual path and does so by means of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*), its attainment is by means of seven faculties—namely, the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), along with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) and the faculty of mind (*manaindriya*). Alternatively, if it is attained by means of the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), its attainment is by means of eight faculties.

The faculty of perfect knowledge (*ājñendriya*) becomes the eighth. Now, if one who is already largely free from passion attains it, it is attained by nine [faculties], just as in the case of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*). If one who follows the gradual path attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) by means of a worldly path (*laukikamārga*), its attainment is by seven faculties, just as in the case of the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*). If, however, it is by means of a supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), it is likewise by eight. If one who is already free from passion attains it, it is by nine.

It is as in the case of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*). However, this is the distinction: there is one or another of the faculties of pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*), depending on the specific basis (*niśraya*). Even when this practitioner following the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*) enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) by means of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*) during the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) because of having sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), he still attains the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) by means of eight faculties.

For in that case, if one enters by means of the mundane path, the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) is the eighth in the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), whereas in the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) there is always only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); and its attainment occurs through both of these. Now, if one enters by means of the supramundane path, its attainment occurs through nine faculties; the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*) is the eighth. If so, how is it that the Abhidharma states: "By how many faculties does one attain Arhatship? It says, 'by eleven'?
How then can it be said that it is attained by nine? One attains it by nine alone.
Arhatship is attained through eleven [faculties], though this is stated because of the possibility for one individual.

(17ab) There is the possibility that a single person, falling away again and again, might attain Arhatship by means of pleasure (*sukha*), mental joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); therefore, it is said to be "by eleven. However, there is certainly no possibility for pleasure and the others to exist at one and the same time. Why does this same consequence not apply to the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*)? For he never attains [the fruit] by means of the pleasure faculty when he has fallen away, nor does one who was previously free from passion fall away; this is because his detachment is attained through both paths.
This is now investigated: endowed with which faculty is one necessarily endowed with how many? In this regard:
"One who is joined with equanimity, life, and mind is necessarily possessed of three. (17cd)

Whoever is endowed with any one of these [faculties], such as equanimity (*upekṣā*) and the rest, is necessarily endowed with three faculties—namely, these very ones. For there is no possession of these without their mutual accompaniment. However, regarding the remaining [faculties], there is no fixed rule: one may be endowed with them, or one may not. In that regard, first of all, one born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not endowed with the faculties of eye, ear, nose, or tongue; nor is one endowed with them in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) by those which have not been acquired or which have been lost.

One born in the formless realm (*ārūpya*) is not endowed with the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). One born in the realms of form (*rūpa*) or the formless is not endowed with the female-faculty (*strīndriya*), as is the case in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) for one by whom it has not been acquired or has been lost. The same applies to the male-faculty (*puruṣendriya*). An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm is not endowed with the pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*). One born in the realms of form or the formless is not endowed with the pain-faculty (*duḥkendriya*). One who is free from passion for the desire realm is not endowed with the mental dissatisfaction-faculty (*daurmanasya*). One whose roots of merit have been severed is not endowed with the faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*). Ordinary persons and those established in the fruits [of the path] are not endowed with the faculty of "I shall come to know" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*).

Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) on the paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) are not endowed with the faculty of having known (*ājñendriya*). Ordinary persons and those in training (*śaikṣa*) are not endowed with the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*). In states where it is not explicitly prohibited, it should be understood that one is endowed with the faculties previously mentioned.

Regarding the four [faculties]: whoever is endowed with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is necessarily endowed with four faculties—namely, those three beginning with equanimity (*upekṣā*) and the faculty of pleasure itself. Whoever is endowed with the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) is also endowed with four—the same three and the faculty of the body itself.
One who possesses the eye-faculty and so forth possesses five.

Whoever possesses the eye-faculty necessarily possesses five: the faculties of equanimity, life, mind, and body, as well as that [eye-faculty] itself. It should be understood in the same way for the faculties of the ear, nose, and tongue.
And one who possesses the faculty of mental gladness [also possesses five].

Furthermore, whoever possesses the faculty of mental happiness (*saumanasyendriya*) necessarily possesses five: equanimity, life, mind, physical pleasure (*sukha*), and mental happiness. One born in the second dhyāna who has not yet attained the third dhyāna is endowed with which faculty of pleasure? With the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) pleasure belonging to the level of the third dhyāna. But one who possesses the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhī*) necessarily possesses seven: the body, life, mind, and the four faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*). (18c'd) Whoever possesses the faculty of suffering necessarily possesses these seven.
One who possesses the female faculty and so forth. ||18d||

(19a) By eight: whoever is endowed with the female faculty (*strīndriya*) is necessarily endowed with eight—namely, those seven [mental faculties] and the female faculty. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*), the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasya*), faith (*śraddhā*), and so forth. One who possesses these is also individually endowed with eight: namely, those seven and the eighth, which is the male faculty. It is the same for the faculty of mental distress. But one who possesses faith and the others is endowed with those five, as well as with the faculties of equanimity (*upekṣā*), life (*jīvita*), and mind (*manas*).
However, one who possesses the faculty of "I have known" (*ājñātendriya*) is endowed with eleven. (19a'b)

The faculty of one who has known is the *ājñātendriya*. One who is endowed with the *ājñātendriya* necessarily possesses eleven [faculties]: the faculties of pleasure, mental ease, equanimity, life, mind, faith, and so forth, as well as the *ājñendriya*. The same applies to the *ājñātāvīndriya*; one is endowed with those same ten plus the *ājñātāvīndriya*.
One possessed of the *ājñāsyāmīndriya* is endowed with thirteen. (19cd)
By which thirteen? By the faculties of mind, life, and body; by the four feelings; by faith and the others [up to wisdom]; and by the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."

Now, as for one who is endowed with the very minimum [of faculties], with how many faculties is he endowed? One devoid of merit is endowed with the absolute minimum of eight: namely, the [five] sense-faculties, mind, body, and life. (20abc)

One whose roots of merit are severed is devoid of the wholesome. He is endowed with at least eight faculties: the five feelings (*vedanā*), as well as the body, mind, and life-faculties. For "feeling" (*vit*) is so called because it feels (*vedayate*); or rather, "feeling" (*vedana*) is itself "feeling" (*vit*), just as "attainment" (*sampadana*) is "attainment" (*sampat*).
And just as one devoid of the wholesome is possessed of at least eight faculties, so too is a fool (*bāla*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
"Bāla" (the fool) is a designation for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). By which eight [factors]? By equanimity, life-force, mind, and the wholesome [factors]. (20d)

[They arise] with equanimity, life, mind, and faith and the others. Because they are exclusively wholesome, faith and the others are included by the term "wholesome. [Objection: Does this not entail that the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya) and the others are also included? [Response: No, because of the context of the eight [faculties] and the context of the ordinary person (bāla).
Now, as for one who is endowed with the maximum number of faculties, how many does he possess?
One endowed with the maximum possesses twenty-one, excluding the immaculate ones.
(21ab) That is, excluding the three untainted [faculties]. Furthermore, he...

One with two sexual organs (dviliṅga)—that is, one possessing both sets of marks—who has all faculties complete, is endowed with nineteen [faculties]. And who else? A noble one (ārya) who still possesses attachment (rāgin).
Even a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has not yet abandoned passion is endowed with at most nineteen [faculties], excluding one gender and two of the stains (*amala*). (21c–d)

Excluding one faculty and two untainted faculties, [there are] the faculty of one who has already known and either of the other two. Thus, the detailed classification of the faculties, which arose in the context of the analysis of the elements (*dhātu*), has been explained in full.

This is now investigated: Are these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) such that they possess distinct characteristics and likewise have distinct arisings, or are there some that necessarily arise together? He says: "There are. All these phenomena are fivefold: matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika*), formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Among these, the unconditioned does not arise at all. However, regarding material phenomena, this is the fixed rule:
"In the desire realm, an atom (*paramāṇu*) that lacks sound and lacks sense-faculties consists of eight substances. (22ab)

The most subtle aggregation of matter is called an atom (*paramāṇu*), because it cannot be discerned as having further parts. In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when it is without sound and without sense-faculties, it arises consisting of eight substances (*dravya*). It is never deficient of even one of these. The eight substances are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the four derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*): visible form, odor, taste, and the tangible. However, an atom that possesses a sense-faculty but lacks sound arises with nine substances or ten substances. In that regard, first, an atom possessing the body-faculty consists of nine substances. (22c)

Because the body-faculty (kāyendriya) exists therein, it is called "possessing the body-faculty" (kāyendriyin). In that case, there are nine substances: those eight [previously mentioned] plus the body-faculty.
One possessing another faculty has ten substances. (22d)

In another atom where there is a sense-faculty (*indriya*), there are ten substances: those same nine, plus whichever one among the sense-faculties of the eye, ear, nose, or tongue is present. Furthermore, when these atoms arise accompanied by sound, they arise respectively as consisting of nine, ten, or eleven substances. For there is indeed sound inseparable from the sense-faculties which has its cause in the appropriated great elements (*upātta-mahābhūta*).

How is it that, although the primary elements (bhūtas) here are inseparable, only a certain aggregate arises as solid, while another arises as liquid, hot, or mobile? It is because that which is most intense and predominant in its power is what is perceived there, just like the touch of a bundle of needles or cotton, or like the taste of a powder of parched grain mixed with salt.

But how, then, is the existence of the remaining elements in those [others] understood? It is through their function: by means of cohesion (*saṃgraha*), support (*dhṛti*), ripening (*pakti*), and expansion (*vyūhana*). Furthermore, others maintain that when the necessary conditions are met, solidity and the other qualities undergo transformation into liquidity and so forth; thus, in water, heat is inferred from the intensity of its coldness. However, even in the absence of actual mixture, there can be an intensity of coldness, just as there is an intensity of sound or sensation. Still others hold that these exist within them only as seeds (*bīja*) and not as actual entities (*svarūpa*), because of the scriptural statement: "In this block of wood, there are various elements."

How can there be the existence of color in wind? This matter is to be accepted through faith (*śraddhānīya*), not through inference (*anumānīya*). Because odor is perceived through contact [with wind], and because that [odor] is never found apart from color. It has already been stated that in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) there is an absence of odor and taste; therefore, since the atoms (*paramāṇu*) existing there consist of six, seven, or eight substances according to what was previously described, they are not mentioned again.

Furthermore, in this context, is "substance" (dravya) understood as a single substance-entity, or rather as a sense-sphere (āyatana)? What follows from this? If "substance" is understood as a single substance-entity, then it is stated too little when one says "consisting of eight substances" or "consisting of nine substances. For it must necessarily also include the substance of shape (saṃsthāna), since that too is an accumulation of atoms (paramāṇu). It must also include either heaviness or lightness, and smoothness or roughness; and in some cases, it must also include cold, hunger, and thirst.

Furthermore, if the term "substance" (*dravya*) is taken here to mean "base" (*āyatana*), then this statement that it consists of eight substances is overly extensive; for it should rather be said to consist of four substances, since the primary elements (*bhūta*) are also included within the base of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*). In this context, one kind of "substance" refers to the substance as a causal basis (*āśrayabhūta*), while another kind of "substance" refers to the substance as a dependent entity (*āśritabhūta*) residing within the base. Even so, there would be many more elemental substances, because each derivative form (*upādāyarūpa*) rests upon a set of four primary elements.

In this context, however, "substance" (*dravya*) is understood as referring to the genus (*jāti*), because the various sets of the four primary elements (*bhūtacatuṣka*) do not transcend their own respective genera. But why is it expressed in such a way through this alternative formulation? For the employment of words occurs according to one's preference; rather, the meaning must be examined.
The rule regarding the simultaneous arising (*sahotpāda*) of material things has been stated. That of the remaining factors must now be explained. In that regard, first:
mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) necessarily arise together.
For these are not able to exist without one another.

[The phrase] "necessarily together with all conditioned characteristics" applies here. Whatever arises—whether form, mind, mental factors, or dissociated phenomena—all arise together with the conditioned characteristics.
Or, by means of acquisition (*prāpti*).
The word "or" has the sense of an alternative, meaning that only that which is designated as belonging to sentient beings (*sattvākhya*) arises together with acquisition, and nothing else.
These are called mental factors (*caitta*). What are these mental factors?
Mental factors are fivefold, according to the divisions of the universal ground and so forth. ||23c'd||

There are five types of mental factors (*caitta*): the universal (*mahābhūmika*), the universal wholesome (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), the universal defiled (*kleśamahābhūmika*), the universal unwholesome (*akuśalamahābhūmika*), and the universal minor defilement (*parīttakleśamahābhūmika*). "Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to a sphere of occurrence. That which is the sphere of occurrence for something is called its "ground. In this context, those whose ground is great are the "universal" (*mahābhūmika*) factors—those that arise in every state of mind. Which ones, then, arise in every state of mind? They are:
feeling (*vedanā*), volition (*cetanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), desire (*chanda*), contact (*sparśa*), discernment (*mati*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*).
Attention, resolve, and concentration are present in every state of mind. (24)

It is said that these ten factors are present together in every moment of consciousness. Among them, *vedanā* is the threefold experience: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. *Cetanā* is the mental formation, which is mental action (*manaskarman*). *Saṃjñā* is the act of perceiving; it is the grasping of the signs of an object. *Chanda* is the desire to act. *Sparśa* is the contact born from the coming together of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness. *Mati* is wisdom (*prajñā*), which is the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).

Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetting of the object of focus. Mental attention (*manaskāra*) is the directing of the mind. Resolve (*adhimokṣa*) is conviction. Concentration (*samādhi*) is one-pointedness of the mind. For the distinction between the mind and mental factors is subtle; it is difficult to discern even within their continuous flows, let alone from moment to moment.

Even among certain material plants that possess many flavors, those specific tastes that are perceived by the senses are difficult to discern; how much more so, then, for those phenomena that are formless and grasped only by the intellect? These are the "great wholesome ground-factors" (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), which always arise in a wholesome mind. What are they?
Faith, heedfulness, serenity, equanimity, shame, and dread of blame;
The two roots, non-harming, and vigor are always present in the wholesome. (25)

These ten factors are always present in a wholesome state of mind. Among them, *śraddhā* (faith) is the clarity of the mind; others say it is conviction in the truths, the jewels, and the results of actions (*karmaphala*). *Apramāda* (heedfulness) is the cultivation of wholesome factors. But what is this "cultivation" other than that? It is the state of being attentive toward those [wholesome factors]. Other schools maintain that it is the guarding of the mind; they recite thus in their Sūtra: "It is the guarding of the mind. *Praśrabdhi* (serenity) is the serviceability of the mind. But is not physical serenity (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) also mentioned in the Sūtra? Indeed, it is not that it is not mentioned.

That, however, should be understood as being like bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*). How, then, can it be applied among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)? In that case, bodily pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) should be understood as simply the serviceability of the body (*kāyakarmaṇyatā*). How is it called a factor of enlightenment? Because it is conducive to the factors of enlightenment; for that serviceability of the body brings about the serviceability of the mind (*cittakarmaṇyatā*), which is a factor of enlightenment. Is this seen elsewhere as well? He said: "It is."

For example, the Blessed One has stated that joy (*prīti*) and the factors conducive to joy are the factor of awakening of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*). He has stated that hostility (*pratigha*) and the signs of hostility are the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpādanivaraṇa*). And he has stated that right view, right intention, and right effort constitute the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*). Yet, although intention and effort do not have wisdom as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they receive that designation because they are favorable to it. In the same way, physical pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) also receives the name "factor of awakening" because it is favorable to the factors of awakening.

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the evenness of mind, the state of non-exertion of the mind. How, then, can this be consistent? [The claim that] "in that very same mind there is mental attention (*manaskāra*) consisting of exertion and equanimity consisting of non-exertion. Has it not been said that "the distinction between these is difficult to understand"? Indeed, even that which is difficult to understand is understood; however, this is truly exceedingly difficult to understand: namely, that there is no contradiction despite their being contradictory. For exertion is directed toward one thing, while non-exertion is directed toward another—what contradiction is there in this?

In that case, it would follow that all associated mental factors do not have a single object. Whatever principle applies to other factors of this same category that will arise hereafter should also be understood to apply to this one. *Hrī* (modesty) and *apatrāpya* (shame) will be explained later. The "two roots" are the two wholesome roots: non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*). Non-delusion (*amoha*) also exists, but since its nature is wisdom (*prajñā*), and wisdom is already classified as a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*), it is not mentioned specifically among the wholesome universal factors. Non-violence (*avihiṃsā*) is the absence of cruelty; vigor (*vīrya*) is the mind’s enthusiasm. The wholesome universal factors have been explained.

"Great ground" (*mahābhūmi*) means a vast ground. Those whose ground is the defilements (*kleśa*) are the "great-grounded defilements" (*kleśamahābhūmika*); these are the factors that always exist in a defiled mind. Which ones, then, always exist in a defiled mind?
Delusion (*moha*), negligence (*pramāda*), indolence (*kauśīdya*), lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
[26abc] They are always present in a defiled mind.

In this context, delusion (*moha*) is ignorance (*avidyā*), lack of knowledge, and non-clarity. Heedlessness (*pramāda*) is the non-cultivation of wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*); it is a factor that is the opposite of heedfulness (*apramāda*). Laziness (*kauśīdya*) is the mind’s lack of enthusiasm; it is the opposite of vigor (*vīrya*). Lack of faith (*āśraddhya*) is the mind’s lack of clarity; it is the opposite of faith (*śraddhā*). What is lethargy (*styāna*)? It is heaviness of the body, heaviness of the mind, unserviceability of the body, and unserviceability of the mind. In the *Abhidharma*, it is stated that there is both physical lethargy and mental lethargy.

How can a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) be called "bodily" (*kāyika*)? It is just as in the case of "bodily feeling" (*kāyikī vedanā*). Furthermore, restlessness (*auddhatya*) is the lack of tranquility of the mind. Thus, these six are the great ground factors of affliction (*kleśamahābhūmika*). But are not ten great ground factors of affliction taught in the Abhidharma? Namely: lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kauśīdya*), forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), distraction of the mind (*cetaso vikṣepaḥ*), ignorance (*avidyā*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), improper attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), wrong resolve (*mithyādhi-mokṣa*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and faith (*prasāda*).

The "Beloved of the Gods" (Devānāmpriya) knows the attainment [of the factors], but he does not know the intended meaning (*iṣṭi*). What, then, is the intended meaning here? Because forgetfulness, distraction, lack of clear comprehension, improper mental attention, and false resolve are already included among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), they are not specifically designated as universal afflictive factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*). Just as non-delusion (*amoha*) is not specifically designated as a universal wholesome factor (*kuśalamahābhūmika*) because its intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*), so too, forgetfulness is simply defiled mindfulness (*smṛti*), and distraction is simply defiled concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth.

Therefore it is said: "Those which are universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) are also universal afflictive factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*). This constitutes a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭika*). The first permutation consists of feeling (*vedanā*), volition (*cetanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), desire (*chanda*), and contact (*sparśa*). The second consists of lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kauśīdya*), ignorance (*avidyā*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and negligence (*pramāda*). The third consists of the five afflicted factors as previously stated, beginning with forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*). The fourth consists of excluding these aforementioned forms. Some, however, maintain that distraction (*vikṣepa*) is a mental factor distinct from wrong concentration (*mithyāsamādhi*).

For them, there is otherwise a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika). Furthermore, since *styāna* (sloth) is held to be associated with all afflictions (*kleśa*), what fault is there in its inclusion among the "great ground" afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*)? However, they say this: it ought to have been included, but it was not because it is conducive to concentration (*samādhi*). It is said that one whose temperament is characterized by sloth (*styānacarita*) would more quickly produce concentration than one whose temperament is characterized by restlessness (*auddhatyacarita*). But who is the one characterized by sloth who is not characterized by restlessness, or who is the one characterized by restlessness who is not characterized by sloth?

For these two never abandon their state of coexistence; nevertheless, if one of them is predominant, that person should be known as being characterized by that specific affliction. Therefore, it is established that there are exactly six universal ground-afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*), for these always exist only in a defiled mind and nowhere else.
However, in an unwholesome mind, there are lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). (26cd)

In an unwholesome mind, however, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) are always present; thus, these two factors are called the "great unwholesome ground" (*akuśalamahābhūmika*). Their definitions will be explained later.
Anger, enmity, dissimulation, envy, malice, concealment, avarice, deceit, intoxication, and harmfulness are the factors belonging to the limited ground of affliction (*parittakleśabhūmika*). (27)

This is the stage of limited defilements (*parīttakleśabhūmi*); thus, these are called "factors belonging to the stage of limited defilements" because they are associated solely with ignorance that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) and belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmika*). Their detailed exposition, however, will be given among the secondary defilements (*upakleśa*).

These five types of mental factors (*caitta*) have been explained. There are also others that are indeterminate (*aniyata*), such as initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), and so forth. In this regard, it must be stated how many mental factors necessarily arise in which state of mind (*citta*). First, there are five kinds of minds belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), and [neutral]. Among these, the unwholesome is of two types: that which is independent (*āveṇika*) and that which is associated with other afflictions (*anya-kleśa-saṃprayukta*). The neutral (*avyākṛta*) is also of two types: the obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) and the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Now, first of all, a mind of the desire realm is necessarily accompanied by initial inquiry and sustained investigation; therefore, in this case—

In a wholesome mind of the desire realm, because it is accompanied by both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), twenty-two mental factors (caitasika) necessarily arise: the ten universal factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), as well as applied thought and sustained thought. (28abc)
In some cases, remorse is predominant. ||28d||

For remorse (*kaukṛtya*) does not exist in every wholesome state of mind. However, where it does exist, by adding that very factor, there are twenty-three mental concomitants (*caitta*). What is this so-called "remorse"? Remorse is the state of having done something ill-done (*kukṛta*). But here, moreover, the mental factor that has the ill-done as its object is called "remorse"; it is the regret (*vipratisāra*) of the mind. Just as the door of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) that has emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as its object is called "emptiness," and non-greed (*alobha*) that has the foul (*aśubha*) as its object is called "the foul."

Moreover, in common worldly usage, it is observed that the location is used as a designation for those who occupy it, as in the expressions "the whole village has arrived" or "the whole country has arrived. And remorse (*kaukṛtya*) serves as the locus for regret (*vipratisāra*). Alternatively, this is a metaphorical application of the cause to the effect, just as it was said: "These six bases of contact (*sparśāyatana*) are to be understood as past karma. If that is so, how can there be remorse regarding an object that was not performed? Even with respect to what was not done, the designation "done" occurs, as in: "It was not well done by me that I did not do it."

What is wholesome regret? It is that which one feels remorse for having failed to perform a wholesome deed and for having performed an unwholesome one. By the opposite, unwholesome regret arises. Both of these [types of regret] have both [the wholesome and the unwholesome] as their basis.
However, in the case of the unshared unwholesome [minds] and those associated with views, there are twenty [factors]. (29ab)

In an unwholesome mind that is independent (*āveṇika*), there are twenty mental factors (*caitta*): the ten universal (*mahābhūmika*) factors, the six universal defilements (*kleśamahābhūmika*), the two universal unwholesome factors (*akuśalamahābhūmika*), and applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). An "independent" mind is one in which ignorance (*avidyā*) alone is present, and no other affliction such as attachment (*rāga*) exists. Even in an unwholesome mind associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*), there are the same twenty [factors] as in the independent case. But is it not the case that there would be twenty-one because of the addition of the view? No, they do not.

Because a certain specific type of wisdom belonging to the great elements (mahābhūmika) is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), that which is unwholesome and associated with such a view—wherein there is either false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), or adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—is associated with twenty-one [factors]: the four afflictions beginning with anger (*krodha*), along with remorse (*kaukṛtya*). (29cd)

Furthermore, where an unwholesome mind is associated with four afflictions—either with attachment (*rāga*), or hostility (*pratigha*), or pride (*māna*), or doubt (*vicikitsā*)—there are twenty-one [mental factors]: that affliction and the twenty mentioned in the context of the independent [afflictions]. When the mind is associated with the aforementioned secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) such as anger (*krodha*) and so forth, there are also twenty-one: these twenty and that secondary affliction. There are likewise twenty-one when associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*).

That very remorse (*kaukṛtya*) constitutes the twenty-first [mental factor]. In brief, there are twenty factors in an unwholesome mind that is either independent (*āveṇika*) or associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*). However, when associated with other primary or secondary afflictions (*kleśa-upakleśa*), there are twenty-one. In the obscured [neutral] mind, there are eighteen; the mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) or the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) is the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Therein, there are eighteen mental factors: the ten universal (*mahābhūmika*) factors, the six universal affliction factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*), and both initial inquiry (*vitarka*) and sustained investigation (*vicāra*). The view is exactly as before and does not exceed that number.

Elsewhere, twelve [mental factors] are held to be neutral (*avyākṛta*). (30ab) Neutral means other than the obscured (*nivṛta*); it is the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Therein, twelve mental factors are accepted: the ten universal (*mahābhūmika*) factors, as well as *vitarka* and *vicāra*. The masters of the Outer Regions (*bahirdeśaka*) maintain that regret (*kaukṛtya*) is also neutral; for them, when that is associated with the mind, there are thirteen [factors].
Since sleep (*middha*) is not in contradiction with any [of these], wherever it may occur, it is added on top. (30cd)

Drowsiness (*middha*) is not incompatible with any of these aforementioned mental factors (*caitta*), because it can be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral. Therefore, wherever that [drowsiness] occurs, it should be understood as being added [to the total]. Where there are twenty-two, there are twenty-three; where there are twenty-three, there are twenty-four, and so forth. This is the rule for mental factors in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that has been stated; however, remorse (*kaukṛtya*), drowsiness, and the unwholesome factors do not exist in the first dhyāna. (31ab)

Therefore, in the first dhyāna, as previously stated, there is in no way any unwholesome state such as regret (*kaukṛtya*) or torpor (*middha*). There is also hostility (*pratigha*), and the states beginning with anger (*krodha*), excluding guile (*śāṭhya*), pride (*mada*), and deceit (*māyā*), as well as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). Everything else is exactly as before. Those very same factors that do not exist in the first dhyāna are also absent in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), along with applied thought (*vitarka*); the remainder is exactly as before.
And beyond that, there is also investigation (vicāra). ||31d||

Beyond the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), in the second and subsequent dhyānas as well as in the formless attainments (ārūpya), there is no sustained thought (vicāra), except as previously prohibited; by the word "also" (api), deceit (māyā) and guile (śāṭhya) are likewise excluded. The remainder is exactly as before. For it is taught that guile exists up to the level of Brahmā because of his connection with an assembly, but not above that. Indeed, he was asked a question by the monk Aśvajit in his own assembly: "O Brahmā, where do these four great elements cease without remainder?"

Not understanding this, he made a boastful claim: "I am Brahmā, the Lord, the Maker, the Fashioner, the Creator, the Originator, the Father of all beings. This has been stated regarding whatever mental factors (caitta) exist in whichever stage of existence (bhūmi) and in whichever mind.

Now, the specific distinctions among certain mental factors (*caitta*) as established in the treatise will be explained. What is the distinction between lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*)? Lack of shame is a lack of respect (*agurutā*) toward virtues and those who possess virtues; it is a lack of reverence, a lack of deference, a lack of fear, and a lack of submissiveness. Lack of shame is a factor that is the direct opposite of respect.

Lack of shame (*atrapā*) is the failure to perceive fear regarding what is blameworthy. (32ab) "Blameworthy" refers to that which is censured by the virtuous. The lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) is the state of not perceiving fear with respect to that. Here, "fear" refers to an undesirable result, for one is afraid of it. How is this to be understood: is "perception of fearlessness" (*abhayadarśitā*) the perception of something as fearless, or is it the non-perception of fear? And what follows from this? If it were the perception of something as fearless, it would be understood as wisdom (*prajñā*); if it were the non-perception of fear, it would be understood as ignorance (*avidyā*). However, "perception-ness" (*darśitā*) is neither a perception nor is "non-perception-ness" (*adarśitā*) a non-perception.

What then? It is that secondary affliction which is the cause of those two, and that is *anapatrāpya*. Others, however, say: "Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) is not feeling shame regarding one's faults with respect to oneself; lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) is not feeling shame with respect to others. Even so, how can these two considerations be established simultaneously? Indeed, it is not said that one considers both oneself and others at once; rather, there is sometimes a lack of shame that occurs even when one is considering oneself—that is *āhrīkya*.

That which proceeds by depending on another is *anapatrāpya* (lack of moral dread). Shame (*hrī*) and moral dread (*apatrāpya*) should be understood as the opposite of this. According to the first interpretation, *hrī* is respect and deference, not being under the sway of fear; *apatrāpya* is the failure to see danger in blameworthy things. According to the second interpretation, they are the feelings of shame arising from consideration for oneself and others, respectively. What is the difference between affection (*prema*) and respect (*gaurava*)? Affection is faith (*śraddhā*).

For affection (*prema*) is of two kinds: afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*). Among these, the afflicted is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), such as [the affection] for one's children, wife, and so forth. The unafflicted is faith (*śraddhā*), [directed] toward the Teacher, gurus, and those endowed with virtuous qualities. There may be faith that is not affection: faith that takes suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as its object. There may be affection that is not faith: afflicted affection. There may be both: faith that takes cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as its object. There may be neither: excluding these aforementioned modes.

Regarding persons, however, there is affection (*prema*) but not respect (*gaurava*) toward one's children, wife, co-residents, and disciples; there is respect but not affection toward other teachers; both exist toward one's own teachers; and neither exists apart from these categories. For faith (*śraddhā*) is indeed the estimation of qualities, and affection is the state of being dear preceded by that [faith]; therefore, others maintain that faith itself is not affection. Respect is shame (*hrī*); for respect is indeed the state of having regard [for another], and shame is the sense of modesty preceded by that [respect]; therefore, others maintain that respect itself is not shame.
Furthermore, those [obstacles] exist in the realms of desire and form. (32d)

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), affection (*prema*) and respect (*gaurava*) do not exist. But is it not the case that faith (*śraddhā*) and shame (*hrī*) are also present there, since they belong to the great wholesome ground-factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*)? For faith is of two kinds: toward phenomena (*dharma*) and toward persons (*pudgala*). The same applies to the sense of propriety (*sapratīśatā*). Among these, those instances of faith and shame that have a person as their object do not exist there; and it is these two that are intended here by the terms affection and respect. What is the distinction between applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)? Applied thought and sustained thought are coarseness and subtlety, respectively. (33ab)

Of what? He will state later that it is "of the mind. *Vitarka* is coarseness of mind; *vicāra* is subtlety of mind. But how can these two be conjoined in a single moment of mind? Some say: just as clarified butter dropped into water and struck from above by the rays of the sun neither solidifies too much nor melts away too much, so too, through the conjunction of *vitarka* and *vicāra*, the mind is neither too subtle nor too coarse; thus, both have an operation therein.

If that were so, then applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) would merely be the causes for coarseness and subtlety, just as water and heat are the causes for the solidification and melting of ghee, but they would not themselves possess those natures. Furthermore, since coarseness and subtlety are relative—varying according to the distinctions between levels (*bhūmi*) and types—it would follow that *vitarka* and *vicāra* would exist all the way up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Moreover, it is not logical that there should be a difference in essential nature (*jātibheda*) based on coarseness and subtlety.

Others, however, say: "Vitarka and vicāra are stated in the Sūtra to be the formative forces of speech; having applied vitarka and having applied vicāra, one utters speech, not without applying vitarka and vicāra. In that regard, those which are gross are vitarkas, and those which are subtle are vicāras. And if there is another factor that is gross and another that is subtle within a single state of mind, what contradiction is there here? There would be no contradiction if there were a difference in their intrinsic nature (*jātibheda*), as is the case with feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*)."

In a single category (*jāti*), a mild and an intense degree do not occur simultaneously. Furthermore, there is a distinction between categories. If that is so, then it must be explained; for it is difficult to explain, and thus it is manifested by way of mildness and intensity. But it is not manifested in this manner, because each category possesses its own mildness and intensity. Others say: "Indeed, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) do not exist together in a single moment of mind. [Objection: How is it, then, that the first dhyāna is said to have five factors? [Response: It is said to have five factors in terms of its level (*bhūmi*), not in terms of individual moments (*kṣaṇa*).
What is the difference between pride (*māna*) and arrogance (*mada*)? Pride is haughtiness; arrogance is the total absorption of the mind in one who is attached to his own qualities. (33bcd)

Pride (*māna*) is the inflation of the mind through any conceptualization of superiority over others. Intoxication (*mada*), however, is the total absorption of the mind in one’s own qualities alone. Others say that intoxication is a specific kind of exhilaration born of passion (*rāga*), just as there is exhilaration born of liquor.

Thus have the mental factors (*caitta*) been explained along with the mind according to their types; furthermore, these technical designations for them are now defined, because by means of these terms, correct linguistic usage is maintained in the teaching (*pravacana*).
Mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have the same meaning. (34ab)

It is called *citta* because it accumulates (*cinoti*). It is called *manas* because it cognizes (*manute*). It is called *vijñāna* because it discerns (*vijānāti*). Others say that *citta* is so called because it is built up by pure and impure elements (*dhātu*); that same [entity], when serving as a support (*āśraya*), is *manas*, and when serving as that which is supported (*āśrita*), is *vijñāna*. Just as *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* have one and the same meaning, so too do *citta* and the mental factors (*caitasika*).
They possess a basis (*sāśraya*), an object (*sālambana*), and an aspect (*sākāra*), and they are associated (*saṃprayukta*). (Verse 34bcd)

They have a single meaning. For those very same mind and mental factors (citta-caitta) are said to be "with a basis" because they depend upon the sense faculties; "with an object" because they grasp an object; "with an aspect" because they take on the mode of that very object; and "associated" because they are joined together equally. To the question, "In what manner are they joined equally? he says: "in five ways. (34d)

[They are equal] by way of five types of equality: equality of basis, object, aspect, time, and substance. What is this equality of substance? For just as the mind (*citta*) is one, so too each mental factor (*caitta*) is one. Thus, the minds and mental factors have been explained with their detailed classifications.
However, the formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) are:
acquisition (*prāpti*), non-acquisition (*aprāpti*), and homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*).
The state of non-perception, the two attainments, life-force, and the [four] characteristics. ||35||
And the sets of names and so forth—
these formations are called "dissociated from mind" because they are neither associated with the mind nor are they of the nature of form. Among these, first,
acquisition (*prāpti*) is gain (*lābha*) and possession (*samanvaya*).

For acquisition (*prāpti*) is twofold: the obtaining of what was previously unobtained or lost, and the possession (*samanvāgama*) of what has already been obtained. By contrast, non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) is established as the opposite. But for what things do these acquisitions and non-acquisitions exist? Acquisitions and non-acquisitions pertain to those factors included within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtāna*), not to those included within the continua of others. Indeed, no one is possessed of factors belonging to another; nor do they pertain to those not included in a continuum. For no one possesses factors classified as non-sentient (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*). This, then, is the rule regarding conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena. Regarding unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, however, there are acquisitions and non-acquisitions.
Of the two cessations. ||36d||

All sentient beings are endowed with analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Abhidharma*: "Who is endowed with untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*)? It replies: "All sentient beings. As for analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), all noble ones (*ārya*)—with the exception of those remaining in the first moment of the path who are still bound by all fetters—and certain ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are endowed with it.

But no one is endowed with space; therefore, there is no acquisition (*prāpti*) of it. And for that which has no acquisition, there is also no non-acquisition (*aprāpti*); such is the established tenet. From what [source] is it known that "acquisition" is some distinct entity? It is said: from the Sūtra. For it is stated in the Sūtra: "By the arising, the obtaining, and the possession (*samanvāgama*) of these ten qualities of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one becomes a noble one who has abandoned five factors," and so forth.

In that case, it would follow that there is possession (*samanvāgama*) even of things not belonging to sentient beings (*asattvākhya*), and also of those belonging to other sentient beings. What is the reason? Because of the statement in the Sūtra: "O monks, a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin* rāja) is possessed of seven jewels," and so forth. Here, the word "possession" refers to mastery (*vaśitva*). His mastery over those jewels consists in acting according to his will. Why is it that in this context mastery is "possession," whereas elsewhere it is a distinct substantial entity (*dravyāntara*)? Furthermore, what is the logical inconsistency (*ayoga*) in [accepting] this?

This is untenable because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not perceived, unlike form, sound, and so forth, or like passion, hatred, and so forth; nor does it have a function (*kṛtya*), like the eye, the ear, and so forth. Therefore, since the characteristics of a substantial entity (*dravyadharma*) are impossible, it is untenable. If it is argued that "possession (*prāpti*) is the cause for the arising of dharmas," then [possession] would not exist for unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas. Furthermore, how could there be the arising of those dharmas which have not yet been attained, or those which have been abandoned through changing levels (*bhūmisaṃcāra*) or through detachment (*vairāgya*)? If it is argued that [arising] is caused by innate possession (*sahajaprāpti*), [the same fault remains].

Now, what function would birth (*jāti*) or the birth-of-birth (*jātijāti*) serve? Furthermore, there would be no distinction in the arising of weak, medium, or intense afflictions (*kleśa*) among all those who are bound, because there is no distinction in their possession (*prāpti*). Or rather, let that very distinction from which such a difference arises be the cause of their arising. Therefore, possession is not the cause of arising. And who says that possession is the cause of arising? What then? It is the cause of differentiation (*vyavasthāhetu*).

For if possession (*prāpti*) did not exist, there would be no established distinction among noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) regarding those with worldly minds, such that one could say, "These are noble ones" and "These are ordinary persons. This [distinction] must arise from the difference between having abandoned or not having abandoned the afflictions (*kleśa*). But how will this be possible—that "the afflictions of these have been abandoned" and "the afflictions of these have not been abandoned"—unless possession exists? This is established through the departure or non-departure of that [possession]. This is established through the specific transformation of the basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa*).

For that basis (āśraya) of the noble ones is transformed by the power of the paths of seeing and cultivation in such a way that it is no longer capable of the growth of those afflictions (kleśa) to be abandoned by them. Therefore, when the basis has become seedless regarding the afflictions—like rice seeds burnt by fire—one is said to be "one whose afflictions are abandoned. Alternatively, [the afflictions are abandoned] when their state as seeds is impaired by the mundane path. By the opposite of this, one is "one whose afflictions are not abandoned."

It is designated that one is "endowed" with that which has not been abandoned, and "not endowed" with that which has been abandoned. Wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*) are also of two kinds: those that arise without effort and those that arise through effort; these are called "acquired at birth" (*utpatti-pratilambhika*) and "acquired through application" (*prāyogika*). Among these, one is said to be "endowed" with those that arise without effort because the state of their seeds within the basis (*āśraya*) has not been impaired; conversely, due to impairment, one is said to be "not endowed," as in the case of one whose roots of virtue have been severed (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*).

However, its impairment is to be understood as occurring through wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); it is certainly not the absolute eradication of the seed-state (*bījabhāva*) of wholesome factors (*kuśaladharmāḥ*) from the continuum (*santati*). Furthermore, regarding those factors that arise through effort, when they have arisen, one is said to be "possessed" (*samanvāgata*) of them because the power for their arising is unimpeded in the continuum. Therefore, it is the seed itself—when it is not uprooted, not impaired, and fully nourished—that receives the designation "possession" at the time of mastery; no other substantial entity (*dravya*) does so.

What, then, is this so-called "seed"? It is that *nāmarūpa* which is capable of producing a fruit, either directly or through a succession [of causes], due to a specific transformation of the continuum (*santatipariṇāmaviśeṣa*). What is this so-called "transformation"? It is the alteration of the continuum. And what is this "continuum"? It consists of the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) belonging to the three time periods, existing as cause and effect. As for what was said—that one who is possessed of greed is incapable of cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness—[this refers to the fact that]...

In this context, "possession" (*samanvāgama*) refers to the acquiescence to or the non-removal of greed. For as long as one remains acquiescent to it and does not remove it, one is capable of cultivating those [defilements]. Thus, this possession is in every respect a conventional phenomenon (*prajñaptidharma*) and not a substantial phenomenon (*dravyadharma*); its negation is called "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*). However, the Vaibhāṣikas describe both as being substantially real (*dravya*). Why? Because this is our established tenet (*siddhānta*).
It is said that this "attainment" (*prāpti*) is of three kinds for the factors belonging to the three time periods.
For past dharmas, there is possession (*prāpti*) that is past, as well as future and present; likewise, for future and present dharmas, each has three kinds [of possession].
For those that are wholesome and so forth, the possession is wholesome and so forth:
the possession of the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral is, respectively, wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.

(37c) For those factors belonging to their own realm, the acquisition (*prāpti*) belongs to that same realm. Those factors which belong to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness have acquisitions belonging respectively to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness. For those factors not belonging [to any realm], there are four kinds. (37d)

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas is fourfold: in brief, it belongs to the three realms and is also untainted. Among these, the acquisition of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) belongs to the three realms; the acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) belongs to the realms of form and formlessness and is also untainted; and the acquisition of the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) is exclusively untainted. Thus, taken together, it is fourfold. The acquisition of the dharmas of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is exclusively of those beyond training; the acquisition of the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) is exclusively of those in training. However, there is a distinction regarding the acquisition of dharmas that are neither of those in training nor of those beyond training (*naivaśaikṣānāśaikṣa*). This is explained as being threefold for those that are neither of those in training nor of those beyond training. [p.65] (38a) It is threefold for those that are neither of those in training nor of those beyond training.

The dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner are called the substantial dharmas and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Their acquisition (*prāpti*) is threefold, according to the distinction of learner (*śaikṣa*) and so forth. First, the acquisition of contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas is neither-learner-nor-non-learner. This also applies to the acquisition of non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) when it is acquired by a non-noble person. Furthermore, the acquisition of that very same analytical cessation when it is acquired by the learner-path is learner-acquisition; when acquired by the non-learner-path, it is non-learner-acquisition.

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of those [dharmas] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is, respectively, only that which is to be abandoned by seeing and that which is to be abandoned by cultivation. However, there is a distinction regarding those not to be abandoned (*aheya*); this is now explained: "Those not to be abandoned are considered to be of two kinds" (38b). Dharmas not to be abandoned are the untainted (*anāsrava*) ones. Among them, the acquisition of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is to be abandoned by cultivation. Also, the acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) when it has been attained by a non-noble person (*anārya*) is to be abandoned by cultivation. But the acquisition of that very same [cessation through deliberation] when it has been attained by the noble path (*āryamārga*) is untainted and not to be abandoned, as is the case with the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
Regarding what was stated—that [the acquisition] of dharmas belonging to the three time periods is of three kinds—this is an exception (*apavāda*) to that general rule (*utsarga*):
"The acquisition of the neutral is simultaneous" (38c).

For non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas, the acquisition is only simultaneous; it is neither prior nor subsequent. This is because they are weak. Therefore, for those [dharmas], the acquisition of past ones is only past, up to the point that the acquisition of present ones is only present. Does this apply to every non-obscured neutral dharma? Not to every one.
Except for the *māṇika* [stone], it is not [obtained] through supernatural powers (*abhijñāna*). ||38d||

Excluding the two neutral supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*), for these—because they are powerful and accomplished through a specific application—there is simultaneous acquisition (*sahajā prāpti*) both before and after [the action]. They maintain that this also applies to certain states belonging to the arts (*śailpasthānika*) and to those of deportment (*īryāpathika*) when they have been excessively practiced. One asks: "Is simultaneous acquisition only for the non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*)? He replies:
"And also for obscured form (*nivṛtasya ca rūpasya*). (39a)

Even for informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*) that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), possession (*prāpti*) is only simultaneous, because its weakness is established by the fact that it does not give rise to non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), even when intense.

If this is the distinction regarding the possession of unspecified factors (*avyākṛta-dharma*), is there likewise some distinction in the possession of wholesome (*kuśala*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*) factors? He says: "There is.
[In the realm of] desire, [possession] of matter is not prior. (38b)

For the informative and non-informative matter of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), there is no possession (*prāpti*) that arises prior to it in any way; however, there is possession that arises simultaneously with it and that which arises at a later time.
Is there also a distinction of types for non-possession (*aprāpti*) similar to that of possession? He says: no. What then? Non-possession is undefiled and neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*). (39c)
Non-acquisition is entirely non-obscured and indeterminate. Furthermore, according to the distinction of time periods, that of the past and the unborn is threefold. (39d)
For a present [dharma], there is no non-acquisition that is itself present. However, for past and future [dharmas], it belongs to all three time periods (*traiyadhvika*).

And for those dharmas belonging to the desire realm and so forth, as well as for the untainted (*anāsrava*) ones, it is of three kinds—this is how the text continues. For dharmas belonging to the desire realm, the non-acquisition belongs to the desire, form, and formless realms. The same applies to those belonging to the form and formless realms, and to the untainted ones. There is no such thing as an untainted non-acquisition; for instance:

The non-attainment of the path is intended [as the definition]. (40b) What is the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*)? The text of the treatise states: "The non-acquisition of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). And this so-called "non-acquisition" is indeed non-attainment (*aprāpti*). Furthermore, the state of being a worldling cannot possibly be untainted (*anāsrava*). Of which noble dharmas is there non-acquisition? Of all of them, because it is stated without distinction. However, that [non-acquisition] is the non-acquisition that exists without [prior] acquisition. For otherwise, even a Buddha would be a non-noble one (*anārya*), since he does not possess the lineages (*gotra*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. In that case, the word "only" (*eva*) should have been recited [in the text].

It should not be read [as such]. For even single words can function as exclusives (*avadhāraṇa*), just as in the expressions "one who subsists on water" (*abbhakṣa*) or "one who subsists on air" (*vāyubhakṣa*). Others say: [it refers to] the non-acquisition of the acceptance of the dharma-knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and its co-arising factors. Nor does this entail the consequence of being a non-noble one (*anāryatva*) due to the possession of that [non-acquisition], because that non-acquisition has been utterly destroyed. If so, then since those [acceptances] belong to the three lineages (*trigotra*), of which is there the non-acquisition? Of all of them. If that is the case, then the same fault remains; and the same resolution applies again. In that case, the effort [of the objection] is futile.

However, it is correct in this way, as the Sautrāntikas maintain. And how do the Sautrāntikas [define it]? "Ordinary personhood (*pṛthagjanatva*) is the continuity of the non-arising of noble dharmas. It is abandoned through the acquisition of that [state] and by shifting to another stage (*bhūmi*). (40cd)

Just as the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjanatva*) is the non-acquisition of the noble path, and that [state] is abandoned through the acquisition of that [path] or by changing levels (*bhūmi-saṃcāra*), so it should be applied to other cases as well. "It is abandoned" means that the non-acquisition of that [non-acquisition] arises and its acquisition is severed. But do the possession (*prāpti*) and non-possession (*aprāpti*) of these two also have possession and non-possession? They say that both possess both. [Objection: But in this way, would there not be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā-prasaṅga*) regarding possessions? [Response: There is no consequence of an infinite regress.

Because of their mutual association (*samanvāgama*). For a phenomenon arises as a triad including itself: that phenomenon, its acquisition (*prāpti*), and the acquisition of the acquisition (*prāptiprāpti*). In this regard, through the arising of the acquisition, one becomes possessed of that phenomenon and with the acquisition of the acquisition; furthermore, through the arising of the acquisition of the acquisition, one becomes possessed of the acquisition itself. Therefore, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

And having done so, for a third dharma—whether wholesome or afflicted—that is oneself as the third, three acquisitions (*prāpti*) arise in the second moment; and for those [three], there are again three secondary acquisitions (*anuprāpti*), making six. In the third moment, there are nine acquisitions for the entities produced in the first and second moments, together with their secondary acquisitions, making eighteen.

Thus, through the consequence of ever-increasing growth, these acquisitions (*prāpti*) spread forth; for a single living being, they arise moment by moment as infinite in number, pertaining to all past and future moments of afflictions and secondary afflictions, as well as to innate wholesome moments, together with their associated and co-existent factors, included within the beginningless and endless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Consequently, the moments of personal existence (*ātmabhāva-kṣaṇa*) within each individual continuum of sentient beings consist of infinite entities. Indeed, what a festival this is for the acquisitions!
They are merely non-obstructive, since they find space within space; otherwise, there would be no room even in space for a second living being.

Now, what is this "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*)? Homogeneity is the similarity among sentient beings; it is a substantial entity (*dravya*) called homogeneity, which is the resemblance of sentient beings. In the treatise, its technical designation is "group-homogeneity" (*nikāyasabhāga*). Furthermore, it is both undifferentiated and differentiated. It is undifferentiated as the homogeneity of all sentient beings, because it exists in every single being. It is differentiated, however, as that very same [homogeneity] is restricted to those sentient beings according to the distinctions of realm, stage, destiny, mode of birth, caste, female, male, lay follower, monk, trainee (*śaikṣa*), non-trainee (*aśaikṣa*), and so forth. Moreover, there is "dharma-homogeneity" (*dharmasabhāgatā*) based on the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

If the generic similarity of sentient beings (*sattvasabhāgatā*) were not a distinct entity, there would be no undifferentiated cognition or designation of "sentient being, sentient being" among sentient beings who are distinguished by their mutual differences. The same should be applied to the cognitions and designations of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. There could be one who dies and is reborn, yet is not reborn in that very same place: this refers to the second case, when one enters the state of certainty (*niyama*). For such a person abandons the generic similarity of an ordinary worldling (*pṛthagjana-sabhāgatā*) and acquires the generic similarity of a noble one (*ārya-sabhāgatā*).
The third case occurs through the transition between realms of existence (*gati*). The fourth case is established by excluding these aforementioned modes.

If there exists a substantial entity called "homogeneity of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjanasabhāgatā*), what then is the use of "ordinariness" (*pṛthagjanatva*)? For one does not conceive of "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*) as something other than the "homogeneity of humans. Furthermore, the world does not perceive this homogeneity because it is formless (*arūpin*); nor does it discern it through wisdom (*prajñā*). Yet, people do recognize the non-difference in the species of sentient beings; so even if that homogeneity exists, how could it have any functional activity (*vyāpāra*) in that regard? Moreover, why is a "homogeneity of non-sentient things" (*asattvasabhāgatā*) not also accepted?

Since rice, barley, mung beans, black gram, mangoes, jackfruit, iron, gold, and so forth, possess a similarity within their own respective classes, how can a designation of "homogeneity" (*sabhāgatā*) be applied to those things which are mutually distinct? In doing so, the Vaiśeṣikas would be validated, for they maintain this tenet: there exists a category called "generality" (*sāmānya*), from which the arising of a common cognition occurs even regarding things of dissimilar types. However, this is their specific distinction [from the Buddhist position].

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this homogeneous character (*sabhāgatā*) exists, because it is stated in the Sūtra: "Even though it is one, it subsists in many; whether it is manifested or not manifested. For the Blessed One said: "If he comes to such a state, [he is born] into the homogeneous character of humans. This has indeed been stated, but it was not stated that it is a separate substantial entity (*dravyāntara*). What then is it? It is simply those conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) existing in such a way that the designation "human" and so forth applies to them, just as the term "homogeneity" is applied to rice and other grains.
However, they do not describe it in that way. Now, what is this so-called "state of non-perception" (*āsaṃjñika*)?
The state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) exists among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñin*).
It is the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*).

For those born among the gods who are non-percipient beings, that which is the cessation of mind and mental factors is the substance called "non-perception" (*āsaṃjñika*), by means of which mind and mental factors are completely suppressed for a period of time in the future and do not obtain the opportunity to arise, just like the obstruction of the water of a river. Furthermore, that [substance] is exclusively...
What is the maturation? It is the maturation of the attainment of non-perception. Which are those beings among whom the non-percipient beings reside?
They are the Bṛhatphala [deities]. (41d)

There are the gods named Bṛhatphala, in a portion of whose realm there are certain non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*), just as in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntarika*). But do they ever possess perception? They do so at the time of birth and at the time of death. Having remained for an extremely long period of time, because perception suddenly arises, those beings pass away from that place; such is the reading in the Sūtra. And having passed away from there, like those who have awakened from a long sleep, they are reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and nowhere else.

Due to the exhaustion of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) from previous meditative attainments and the non-accumulation of new ones, beings fall to the earth like arrows whose momentum has been spent once they have been shot. Furthermore, for one who is to be reborn there, there must necessarily exist karma belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), just as those born among the Northern Kurus possess karma to be experienced upon rebirth in the heavens.

Now, regarding what was stated as "the two attainments" (*samāpatti*), which are they? They are the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). What is this attainment of non-perception? Just as it was stated that the "non-percipient state" (*asaṃjñika*) is the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*), so too is the attainment of non-perception.
