It is the attainment of those who are without perception; it is called the "attainment of non-perception" because it is perceived by those without perception. That too is the cessation of mind and mental factors. To this extent, the word "so" (*tathā*) is applied by way of analogy. However, that attainment—
In the final dhyāna—that is, the fourth dhyāna—this [attainment] is included; it does not belong to any other stage. For what purpose do they enter it?
Out of a desire for liberation.

They consider this to be an escape; therefore, out of a desire for liberation, they enter it. It is established that the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*) because it is a maturation (*vipāka*). However, this attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) is exclusively wholesome (*śubha*, *kuśala*). Its maturation consists of the five aggregates among the beings in the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*). Being wholesome, [it is so].

It is exclusively to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedyaiva*). It is not to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*), nor is it indefinite (*aniyata*). Even one who, having produced this [attainment], falls away from it, is said to necessarily produce it again and be reborn among the non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñisattva*). For this very reason, one who has obtained it does not enter the path of certainty (*niyāma*). This is held to belong only to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), not to noble ones (*ārya*).

For the noble ones do not enter the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), viewing it as a place of downfall; rather, they enter it with the perception of it being an escape. Now, do the noble ones, by virtue of attaining the fourth dhyāna, acquire mastery over this [attainment] just as they do over the dhyānas? Others, too, do not acquire such mastery. What is the reason? For although this [attainment] is without thought, it is accomplished through great effort and, being devoid of thought, it is mastered only one at a time.

The meaning is "belonging to a single time. Only that which belongs to the present moment is acquired, just like the *prātimokṣa* restraint. However, once it has been acquired, one remains possessed of it even as a past state during the second and subsequent moments, until it is abandoned. Because it is devoid of mind (*acittaka*), the future state is not cultivated. Now, what is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)? It is called "cessation" in exactly the same way as this [attainment of non-conception].

Just as it is with the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), so too by the word "likewise" (*tathā*) what mode is being grasped? It is the cessation of mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*). However, this is its distinction: they enter into this [attainment] for the sake of dwelling (*vihāra*), through a mental attention preceded by the perception of peaceful dwelling; whereas they enter into that [attainment of non-perception] through a perception preceded by the notion of escape (*niḥsaraṇa*). Furthermore, that [attainment of non-perception] belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna, but this one—
It arises from the peak of existence;
it belongs exclusively to the level of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and it is pure.
It is exclusively wholesome, neither afflicted nor neutral. Being wholesome, it is to be experienced in two ways and is indeterminate:

it is to be experienced in two times, namely, to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) or to be experienced in a subsequent life (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*); and it is also indeterminate with respect to its maturation (*vipāka*), as it may sometimes not mature at all if one attains final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*) here. For its maturation consists of the four aggregates at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). And this [attainment] is exclusively...

It belongs to the noble one (43d'), for ordinary persons are not able to produce the attainment of cessation because they fear annihilation, whereas it is produced by the power of the noble path through their conviction that it is nirvana in this very life. Furthermore, even for the noble one, this is not obtained through the mere attainment of detachment; rather, it is acquired through application (43d'').

This is obtainable only through application (*prayoga*). It is neither obtained as something past, nor is it cultivated as something future, because its cultivation occurs by the power of the mind. Is it also [obtained through application] for the Blessed One? No, he says:
for the Sage, it is obtainable through enlightenment (*bodhi*).

The Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, attain this at the same time as the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*); for the Buddhas there is nothing that is called "attained through preparatory effort" (*prāyogika*). Indeed, the manifestation of the perfection of all their qualities is dependent upon mere wish. Therefore, for them, it is acquired through the attainment of all forms of detachment (*vairāgya*). But how, then, is the Blessed One established as "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) at the moment of the knowledge of destruction, when the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) has not yet been produced? He is so established because he possesses mastery over it, as if it had already been produced.

The Westerners maintain that the Bodhisattva produces that [attainment] even earlier, during the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*). Now, why is this not accepted? And in this way, this guiding principle (*netrīpada*) of the Elder Upagupta would also be authoritative: "Having produced the attainment of cessation, one produces the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*); thus is a Tathāgata described. [The Kashmiris reply: It is not prior; for it is not logical that its production occurs before [the knowledge of destruction]. What is the reason?
Because it is attained in thirty-four moments.

(44b) It is said that a Bodhisattva attains enlightenment through thirty-four mental moments: sixteen during the clear realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), and eighteen during the detachment from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*)—the latter consisting of the arising of nine paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) for the abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions. Thus, these total thirty-four. Since he has already become free from passion regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) upon entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*), the afflictions of the lower stages do not need to be abandoned again.

Therefore, because a dissimilar mind cannot arise during this interval, the attainment of cessation would be impossible. But what would happen if a dissimilar mind were to manifest in the interim? There would be an intention to emerge [from meditative absorption], and Bodhisattvas are characterized by having no intention to emerge. True, they have no intention to emerge; however, is it not the case that they do not emerge from the path of outflows (*āsrava*)?

How then is it that [the Buddha] does not rise from his seat? The outsiders (bahirdeśaka) maintain that because his intention—"I shall not break this cross-legged posture until the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣaya) is attained"—does not waver, he remains on the single path (ekāyana) until the completion of his own goal. However, the Kashmiris explain it as follows: although there are many kinds of distinctions between these two attainments, both have the desire realm and the form realm as their basis (kāmarūpāśraya).

Both of these—the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—will arise in both the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). However, for those who do not accept that the attainment of non-perception occurs in the form realm, this textual passage contradicts their position: "There may be existence in the form realm (*rūpa-bhava*), yet that existence is not one characterized by the five aggregates (*pañca-vyavacara*)."

There may be existence (*bhava*) for beings of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), for gods possessing perception (*saṃjñin*) who abide in a dissimilar state of mind (*visabhāga-citta*), for those who have entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and for gods without perception (*asaṃjñin*) when the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) has been acquired. Therefore, both of these [attainments] have their basis in the desire and form realms. However, there is this distinction:
the one called cessation [occurs] first among humans. (44d)

The attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is first produced among human beings; afterwards, it is produced in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) by those who have previously fallen away from it. Is there, therefore, falling away even from this? He says: "There is. Otherwise, the *Udāyi-sūtra* would be contradicted: "In this world, venerable ones, a monk is endowed with morality, endowed with concentration, and endowed with wisdom."

He repeatedly enters into and emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling, and he understands this state as it truly is: "This is the case. He does not indeed attain full knowledge (*ājñā*) in this very life through practice, nor at the time of death; rather, upon the breaking up of the body, having transcended the gods who subsist on physical food, he is reborn in a certain divine, mind-made body.

Having been reborn there, he repeatedly enters into and emerges from the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāveditanirodha*), and he understands as it truly is: "This state exists. For here, the Blessed One has spoken of a divine, mind-made body belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*). And this meditative attainment belongs to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). How, then, could there be rebirth in the realm of form for one who has not fallen away from that [attainment] and has attained it? Other schools maintain that the attainment of cessation also belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna.

For them, this [attainment] is established even without falling away (*parihāṇi*). However, this very point—that it exists on the level of the fourth dhyāna—is not established. What is the reason? Because of the statement in the Sūtra: "There are nine successive attainments" (*navānupūrvasamāpatti*). If this is a fixed rule, how is it that there are those who possess the attainment by leaping over (*vyutkrāntasamāpatti*)? This rule applies to beginners (*prāthamakalpika*). But those who have attained mastery (*vaśitva*) over their desires enter into attainment even by skipping stages.

Thus, there is a distinction between these two attainments in terms of their level (*bhūmi*), because one belongs to the fourth dhyāna while the other belongs to the highest level (*agrabhūmi*). There is also a distinction in terms of application (*prayoga*), because the former involves an application of mental attention preceded by the perception of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*) and the perception of dwelling (*vihāra*). There is a distinction in terms of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), because they belong to the continua of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*) respectively. There is a distinction in terms of fruit (*phala*), because their fruits are the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). There is a distinction in terms of what is to be experienced (*vedanīya*), because one is necessarily experienced upon rebirth, while the other may be experienced either definitely or not, or both ways. And there is a distinction in terms of initial production, because the former is produced in two realms, whereas the latter is produced among humans.

Why, then, are these two—though their intrinsic nature is the cessation of mind and mental factors—called the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedita-nirodha-samāpatti*)? Because the preparatory practice for those attainments is undertaken in opposition to them. This is like the term "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracitta-jñāna*), even though it also involves knowledge of [their] feelings and so forth. How, then, does mind arise again from a mind that has been ceased for a long time? The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that because the past exists, it can function as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Others, however, say:

How, then, does form arise again for those born in the formless realms even though form has long since ceased? For that [form] arises from mind alone, not from form. Likewise, mind also arises from this very body endowed with sense-faculties, not from mind. For these two—the mind and the body endowed with sense-faculties—are mutual seeds, according to the former teachers.

But the Venerable Vasumitra says in the *Paripṛcchā*: "This fault applies to one for whom the attainment of cessation is without mind (*acittikā*); but for me, the attainment is with mind (*sacittikā*). The Venerable Ghoṣaka says: "This is not tenable. For when consciousness exists, there is the coming together of the three, which is contact (*sparśa*). And it has been stated by the Blessed One that feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) are conditioned by contact. Therefore, there would be no cessation of perception and feeling here either. Now, it might be argued: [p.73]

Just as it has been said that "craving is conditioned by feeling," yet craving does not arise for an Arhat even when feeling is present, so too [one might argue] that feeling and the other factors would not exist even when contact is present. This is not the case, because [contact] was not specified there; for it was stated that "craving arises dependent on feeling born of contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja*)," but in the context of the arising of feeling, contact was not specified. Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is devoid of mind (*acittikā*).

How can these be attainments (*samāpatti*) if they are without mind? Because they bring about the equilibrium of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). And they are called "attainments" because one attains or enters them by means of the mind of attainment (*samāpatticitta*). Furthermore, do these two attainments exist as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*) or as mere designations (*prajñaptitaḥ*)? He says they exist substantially, because they obstruct the arising of the mind. No; for that obstruction is caused by the very mind of attainment itself.

For it is precisely the mind of attainment (*samāpatticitta*) that arises as opposed to other minds, by which there occurs for a period of time the mere non-occurrence of mind. This is because it brings about a basis (*āśraya*) that is opposed [to other mental states]. That which is designated as "attainment" is this mere non-occurrence; it did not exist before, nor does it exist after one has emerged from it. Thus, this attainment is designated as conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Alternatively, attainment is simply the bringing about of the basis itself in such a state.

The same should be understood regarding the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*). It is simply the mind that there acquires a condition opposed to the activity of the mind; and that mere non-activity is designated as "non-perception. They do not describe it in this way. The two attainments have been explained.
What is life? Life is vitality (*āyus*).

For it is stated thus in the Abhidharma: "What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)? It is vitality belonging to the three realms. Yet, this very thing is not understood: what kind of phenomenon is this that is called "vitality"?
For that which is the support of both heat and consciousness—
this was said by the Blessed One: "Life-force, heat, and consciousness— when these abandon the body..."
"Then it lies cast away, like a piece of wood, devoid of consciousness.

Now, that factor which serves as the support for heat and consciousness and is the cause of their persistence is *āyus* (life-force). What, then, is the support for this *āyus*? It is those very same [factors], heat and consciousness. If that is so, since these function in mutual dependence, which of them will cease first, by virtue of which the other two would turn back? This would lead to the undesirable consequence of their never ceasing. Therefore, *āyus* has karma as its support, because it continues for as long as it has been projected by karma.

Why is it not accepted that for heat (*ūṣman*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as well, karma alone serves as the support? [One might argue: "Let it be that not all consciousness is a maturation (*vipāka*) until death. In that case, karma will be the support for heat, and heat will be the support for consciousness. Even so, in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), consciousness would be without a support due to the absence of heat. For that [consciousness], karma will again be the support.

Indeed, it cannot be maintained that there is arbitrary freedom such that in some cases heat alone would be the support of consciousness, while in other cases karma alone would be so. And this has already been stated here. What was stated? That not all consciousness until death is a maturation (*vipāka*). Therefore, life-force (*āyus*) certainly exists as the support for those two. We do not say that it does not exist at all; however, it is not a separate substance (*dravyāntara*). What is it then? It is the projection of the duration of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) by means of karma belonging to the three realms.

For as long as the projection (*āvedha*) of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) has been produced by karma—namely, that "it must remain for this much time"—for that long it remains; this is called "life-span" (*āyus*). It is like the projection of the ripening time of crops, or like the projection of the duration of flight of a discharged arrow. As for one who thinks that a certain specific quality called "impulse" (*saṃskāra*) arises in the arrow, by virtue of which its movement continues until it falls:

Because that [motion] is a single entity and because there is no agent who has undertaken it, the distinctions in the time of arrival—being faster, faster still, or slowest—relative to different locations would be impossible, as would the impossibility of its falling [to rest]. If it is argued that this is due to obstruction by wind, then there would be the consequence of it falling back down, or else it would never fall at all, since the wind remains constant. However, they explain it thus: there exists a distinct substance called *āyus* (life-force).

Now, does death occur only through the exhaustion of the life-span (*āyuḥkṣaya*), or otherwise as well? It is stated in the *Prajñapti* that death occurs from the exhaustion of the life-span, not from the exhaustion of merit (*puṇyakṣaya*). There are four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*): the first alternative is due to the total consumption of karma that has the life-span as its maturation (*vipāka*); the second is due to [the consumption of] karma that has enjoyments as its maturation; the third is due to both; the fourth is due to failing to avoid adverse conditions. One might say it is also "due to the relinquishing of the life-span" (*āyurutsarga*), but this need not be stated. That death occurs only from the exhaustion of the life-span, because it is included within the first alternative.

When the lifespan has been exhausted, there is no capacity for death through the exhaustion of merit alone. Therefore, when both are exhausted, death is said to result from the exhaustion of the lifespan. It is also stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna*: "It should be said that the lifespan proceeds bound to the continuum; it should be said that, having arisen repeatedly, it persists. He asks: "In the case of beings belonging to the desire realm who have entered the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), should it be said that [the lifespan] proceeds bound to the continuum?"

It should be said that for those who have attained meditative absorption (*samāpanna*) and for beings belonging to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpyāvacara*), [the life-force] remains having arisen all at once. What is the meaning of this statement? First, because it is subject to destruction when its basis (*āśraya*) is impaired, as it is dependent upon that continuum (*santati*). Second, because there is no impairment of its basis at all, as it remains just as it arose. The Kashmiris say: "The first is with interruption (*sāntarāya*); the second is without interruption (*nirantarāya*). Therefore, untimely death (*akālamṛtyu*) exists.

The Sūtra states that there are four ways of obtaining a personal existence (*ātmabhāvapratilambha*). There is a way of obtaining a personal existence in which one's own volition (*ātmasaṃcetanā*) operates, but not the volition of another (*parasaṃcetanā*). This is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*). First, only one's own volition operates: this is the case for the gods who are "deluded by play" (*krīḍāpramoṣaka*) and those who are "corrupted in mind" (*manaḥpradūṣaka*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). For these beings, death and departure from that state occur through excessive joy or corruption of the mind, and not otherwise. It should also be said that this applies to the Buddhas as well, because they die by their own will.

For those within the womb or an egg, only the volition of another proceeds. For most of those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), both [types of volition] proceed. For all intermediate state beings (*antarābhava*) and for those of a single class belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), neither proceeds. This is the case for all inhabitants of hell, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, those who have entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the meditative attainment of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samāpatti*), the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*); and for all such as royal sages, messengers of the Victor (*jinadūta*), those commanded by the Victor, Dharmila, Uttara, Gaṅgila, the merchant’s son Yaśas, Kumārajīvaka, and others.

[This applies] to Bodhisattvas in their final existence, to the mother of a Bodhisattva who is pregnant with him, to a Universal Monarch, and to the mother of a Universal Monarch who is pregnant with him. Now, why is it said in the Sūtra: "Venerable Sir, who are those beings for whom neither self-intention nor the intention of others operates? Śāriputra, they are those who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"?

It is said that in other meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*), self-intention (*ātma-saṃcetana*) is the noble path belonging to its own level, while other-intention (*para-saṃcetana*) is the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of a higher level; however, in those [other meditations], both are absent. But would it not follow, in that case, that even there, the noble path belonging to another level constitutes other-intention? In response, it is said: because of the mention of the "limit" (*paryanta*), there is an understanding of the beginning as well. Sometimes there is an understanding of the beginning, and sometimes by means of the beginning, the limit is also understood. As it is said: "For example, the Ābhāsvara gods."

"This is the second birth in happiness. In some cases, the beginning is also understood by means of the end. As it is said: "For example, the Ābhāsvara gods; this is the second birth in happiness. In this context, it is logical that the word *tadyathā* (for example) expresses an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and from this, the understanding of the remainder [of the category] follows. For this is the nature of an illustration: that even if only one member of that class is seen, [the rest is implied]. Since the word *tadyathā* does not exist here [in the case of the third birth], this is not a complete summary.

If this word *tadyathā* were a term expressing an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), it would not apply here in the passage: "There are beings with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans and certain gods. Therefore, it should be understood as serving the purpose of demonstration (*upadarśana*). Enough of this digression. Life-force (*jīvita*) has been explained.
Furthermore, the characteristics are birth, aging, duration, and impermanence. ||45cd||

For these are the four characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Wherever these exist, that phenomenon (*dharma*) is characterized as conditioned; by their absence, it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Among them, arising (*jāti*) brings that phenomenon into being, duration (*sthiti*) stabilizes it, aging (*jarā*) causes it to decay, and impermanence (*anityatā*) destroys it. But has it not been stated in the Sūtra that there are only three characteristics of the conditioned? Should not a fourth also be mentioned elsewhere? What is it that was not mentioned there? He says: duration (*sthiti*).

As for this so-called "alteration of duration" (*sthityanyathātva*), this is a synonym for aging (*jarā*), just as "arising" (*utpāda*) is for birth (*jāti*) and "passing away" (*vyaya*) is for impermanence (*anityatā*). Indeed, those very factors (*dharma*) that function to move conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) from one time-period (*adhvan*) to another are described in the Sūtra as the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of inducing world-weariness. For birth is that which causes conditioned phenomena to transition from the future time-period to the present time-period.

Furthermore, old age and impermanence [are so called] because they weaken the present [condition] and strike it down as it passes into the past. It is said to be like a man who has entered a dense forest and encounters three enemies: one might pull him out of the forest, while the other two would deprive him of his life; such is the case here. Stability (*sthiti*), however, remains embracing those conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) as if desiring that they not be separated from them. For this reason, it is not established as a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, because even the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) exists in its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), others again imagine that the Sūtra stated "alteration of duration" (*sthityanyathātva*) as a single characteristic by combining duration (*sthiti*) and aging (*jarā*). What is the purpose? For this [duration] is a basis for attachment among these [conditioned factors]; therefore, [the Buddha] showed it as being accompanied by the "black ear" (*kālakarṇī*), like prosperity, so that one would not become attached to it. Thus, there are exactly four characteristics of the conditioned.
Since those [characteristics] themselves—such as arising (*jāti*) and so forth—are conditioned, they must also possess other [characteristics] such as arising and so on. Indeed, they do exist.

For each of these [primary characteristics], there are also four secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*): birth-of-birth, stability-of-stability, decay-of-decay, and impermanence-of-impermanence. But does this not result in four characteristics for each single [characteristic], leading to the fault of infinite regress (*aparyavasāna*), because there would be the further necessity of other births and so forth for them? It does not so result, because they function with respect to eight factors as one.

The activity (*vṛtti*) of those [factors], birth and the rest, occurs with respect to eight phenomena. What is this "activity"? It is causal efficiency (*kāritra*), which is human effort (*puruṣakāra*). And how do birth, the "birth-of-birth" (*jātijāti*), and so forth, function with respect to a single phenomenon? By way of this: a phenomenon indeed arises as the ninth, together with the eight characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*). Among these, birth (*jāti*) produces the other eight phenomena, excluding itself; the "birth-of-birth," however, produces that very [primary] birth.

It is said to be just as a certain hen produces many offspring while another produces few; it is the same in this case. Duration (*sthiti*) also establishes the other eight factors, excluding itself, whereas the duration-of-duration (*sthitisthiti*) establishes that very duration alone. In the same way, aging (*jarā*) and impermanence (*anityatā*) should also be applied accordingly. Therefore, there is no consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To this, the Sautrāntikas say: "This is merely splitting the air."

For these factors, such as birth and so forth, do not exist substantially in the manner in which they are manifested. What is the reason? Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). For there is no valid means of cognition—whether perception, inference, or authoritative scripture—to establish their substantial existence, as there is for factors such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest. As for what was stated in the Sūtra: "The arising of the conditioned is discerned, its passing away is discerned, and its alteration while persisting is also discerned."

The "Beloved of the Gods" (the King) knows the letter, but not the meaning; and the Blessed One has stated that the meaning is the refuge. What, then, is its meaning? For fools, blinded by ignorance, are attached to and cling to the stream of conditioned forces (*saṃskāra-pravāha*), conceiving it as a self and as belonging to a self.

In order to turn back that false conviction, the Blessed One—desiring to illuminate the conditioned nature and the dependently originated character of that stream of formations (*saṃskāra-pravāha*)—said this: "There are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. This does not refer to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), for the arising and so forth of a single moment are not perceived. And those which are not perceived cannot properly serve as characteristics.

For this very reason, it is stated in this sūtra that "the arising of the conditioned is also discerned. The term "conditioned" (saṃskṛta) is mentioned again so that it may be understood that these are characteristics *of* the state of being conditioned. Let it not be understood, as in the case of cranes [indicating] water, or the marks of a maiden [indicating] her auspicious or inauspicious nature, that these are characteristics for the existence of a conditioned entity. In this context, the beginning of the continuum is arising (utpāda), its cessation is passing away (vyaya), and that same continuum as it persists is duration (sthiti).

The distinction between its earlier and later states is the alteration of duration (*sthityanyathātva*). Having established it thus, it was said: "Only when they are known do the feelings of the noble son Nanda arise; only when they are known do they persist; only when they are known do they reach their end, exhaustion, and termination. And it is said here: "Birth is the beginning of the stream, cessation is its cutting off, and duration is that [stream] itself; the alteration of duration is simply the state of being distinguished between earlier and later."
Birth is the prior non-existence of an entity; duration is its continuity; destruction is its interruption;
and the alteration of duration is intended as the difference between the earlier and later stages of that continuity.
For indeed, in the case of a momentary phenomenon, there would be destruction without duration.
And yet it does not actually perish by means of that [action]; therefore, the conceptualization of it is in vain.

Therefore, duration (*sthiti*) is simply the stream itself. And by taking it in this way, this explanation from the *Abhidharma* also becomes logical: "What is duration? It is the non-destruction of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) once they have arisen. For there is no non-destruction of a moment that has already arisen. Furthermore, as it is said in the *Jñānaprasthāna*: "In a single moment of mind, what is arising? It is birth (*jāti*). What is passing away? It is death (*maraṇa*). What is the alteration of duration (*sthityanyathātva*)? It is the continuum (*cara*). In that case as well, it is the mind belonging to a homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) that is appropriately applied.

Furthermore, these characteristics of the conditioned are applicable at every moment even without the postulation of them as separate entities. How so? At every moment, arising (*utpāda*) is existence after non-existence; passing away (*vyaya*) is non-existence after having existed; persistence (*sthiti*) is the continuity of each preceding moment with the succeeding one; and the alteration of persistence (*sthity-anyathātva*) is its dissimilarity [to the preceding]. [Objection: But when similar things arise, they would be without distinction. [Reply: How is this known?

Because there is a distinction in the time of falling—whether slow or rapid—for such things as a vajra when thrown by one who is weak versus one who is strong, it is established that there is a specific transformation (*pariṇāma*) of their great elements (*mahābhūta*). However, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), though differentiated by not too many variations, appear to be exactly similar even while undergoing change. In that case, for the final moment of a sound or a flame, and for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) at the time of final nirvana, there is no "change-while-enduring" (*sthity-anyathātva*) because no subsequent moment exists; thus, it follows that the definition [of conditioned phenomena] would be non-pervasive.

Indeed, it is not the mere duration (*sthiti*) of the conditioned that is being described; rather, it is the "alteration of duration" (*sthity-anyathātva*). Therefore, for whatever has duration, there necessarily occurs alteration. Thus, there is no inconsistency in the definition of the characteristics. In brief, the Blessed One has illuminated in this sutra that this is the characteristic of the conditioned: that which, having come into being, exists, and having existed, ceases to be again; and that continuum which is designated as "duration" undergoes alteration.

And it is otherwise as well. What, then, is the use here of separate entities such as "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth? How can that very same phenomenon (*dharma*) which is the object to be characterized (*lakṣya*) be logically applied as its own characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? For instance, how is it that the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*) are not other than the Great Man himself; or that the dewlap, tail, hump, hooves, and horns—which are the characteristics of a cow—are not other than the cow; or that solidity and so forth, which are the characteristics of the earth element and the others, are not other than them?

Just as the nature of smoke is characterized from afar by its upward movement, yet that [movement] is not distinct from it, so too would this logic apply here. However, the conditioned nature (*saṃskṛtatva*) of conditioned phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) is not perceived in that way; for even while grasping their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one does not know their prior non-existence, nor their subsequent state, nor the specific difference in their continuum. Therefore, the nature is not characterized by that very [continuum], nor do categories such as "birth" (*jāti*) exist as separate substances (*dravyāntara*) apart from those [phenomena].

Furthermore, even if birth and the other [characteristics] were indeed distinct entities (*dravyāntara*), what would be incorrect? [One might argue that] a single phenomenon (*dharma*) would be born, endured, decayed, and destroyed at one and the same time, because these [characteristics] exist simultaneously. [This is not so], because there is a difference in the time of their activity (*kāritra*). For birth performs its activity while it is still in the future.

Since that which has not yet been born is not being born, whereas the factors such as the earth-element (*kṣiti*) perform their activity while existing when a dharma has already been born, it is not the case that when it is being born, it simultaneously stands, decays, or perishes. First, this must be investigated here: does the future exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*) or not? Only after that can it be established whether or not it produces [the dharma]. Even if it exists, one must state the definition of the future: how can birth (*jāti*), while performing its activity, be established as being future?

Furthermore, how could [the characteristics] that have arisen and whose activities have ceased bring about the state of being stayed, decayed, and destroyed for a dharma in a single moment? For at the very time that stability (sthiti) stabilizes it, at that same time old age (jarā) causes it to decay and impermanence (anityatā) destroys it. If one were to say that the activities of stability and the others also occur successively, then its momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) would be contradicted.

Moreover, one might say: "This very moment is our [only] moment, insofar as all this is completed. Even so, stability (*sthiti*), having arisen together with those two, would cause them to remain; yet aging (*jarā*) does not cause them to decay, nor does impermanence (*anityatā*) destroy them. Why is this? Because of the superior strength of stability. But by what means is it rendered weak? When impermanence strikes it down along with the dharma itself. Having accomplished its task, it no longer has the power to act further, just like birth (*jāti*). It is logical that the endurer should lack the power [to persist].

For it is not possible to bring back again that which has been brought to the present state by birth and other factors; however, it is indeed possible for duration (*sthiti*) to establish what is to be established, even for an infinite time. Therefore, it is not logical to say that it does not exert its power. What, then, is the obstacle here? It is those very two: aging (*jarā*) and impermanence (*anityatā*). For if those two were more powerful, they would have already acted previously.

Furthermore, when duration has ceased its activity, those two [aging and impermanence] no longer abide, nor does that phenomenon itself. How, then, or where, will they be able to exercise their activity? Or rather, what more is there for them to do? For it was by being sustained by duration that the phenomenon, as soon as it arose, did not perish; but if it is neglected by that [duration], it will certainly not remain—this indeed is its destruction.

Furthermore, let it be granted that for a single dharma that has arisen, non-destruction is "stasis" (*sthiti*) and destruction is "impermanence" (*anityatā*). However, aging (*jarā*), in its true nature, is not like that; for it consists of a difference between the prior and subsequent states and involves transformation. Therefore, when there is such alteration, it is indeed something else. For it has been said: "If it remains as it was, aging is not established; if it becomes otherwise, it is simply another thing. Therefore, aging is not logically possible for a single existing entity."

As for that proponent of another school who says that impermanence destroys [the entity] upon encountering a cause of destruction, it follows for him that a deity causes purging upon encountering a *harītakī* fruit; why then postulate that [impermanence] at all?

Therefore, let destruction arise from a cause of destruction. Furthermore, since it is accepted that mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are momentary, their impermanence does not depend on a cause of destruction; thus, stability (*sthiti*) and impermanence (*anityatā*) would perform their functions at the same time. Consequently, it would follow that a single entity exists and is destroyed simultaneously in one and the same place. Therefore, these characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) are said to refer to the continuum (*pravāha*); in this way, the Sūtra is correctly interpreted.
Moreover, if birth (*jāti*) existing in the future were the producer of that which is to be produced, why do all future things not arise simultaneously? Because:
Birth is the producer of that which is to be produced, yet it does not exist without causes and conditions. //46cd//

For birth (*jāti*) does not become a producer without the totality of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-sāmagrī*). If that is so, then we perceive the efficacy (*sāmarthya*) to belong to the causes and conditions themselves; because [the effect] exists when there is a totality and does not exist when there is none, it is the causes and conditions alone that are the producers, not birth. Furthermore, my friend, is everything that exists perceived? Even subtle natures of phenomena (*dharma-prakṛti*) do exist. However, if birth did not exist, there would be no such expression as "it has been born," nor the use of the genitive case, such as "the conjunction of form" (*rūpasya saṃyogaḥ*).

And how is this genitive case to be understood in the expression "the intrinsic nature of form" (*rūpasya svabhāva*)? Therefore, this is merely a designation (*prajñaptimātra*); it is employed for the purpose of making known the existence of something that did not previously exist, as in "it has arisen. And since this arising, characterized by the coming into being of what was non-existent, possesses many conceptual variations, they employ the genitive case—saying "the arising of form"—for the sake of specification, so that the arising may be understood as belonging specifically to that which is designated "form," and not to anything else.

For example, as with the fragrance and so forth of sandalwood, or the body of a stone statue; in the same way, [the characteristics] such as duration (*sthiti*) and so forth should also be understood according to their respective applications. If something were born without birth (*jāti*), why would unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) such as space (*ākāśa*) and the like not be born? "To be born" means to come into existence after having not existed. And since the unconditioned exists eternally, it is not born. Furthermore, just as by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*) not everything is held to possess birth, so too it must be accepted that not everything is born.

Just as other conditions, despite being equal in their possession of birth (*jāti*), are not capable of producing anything other than themselves, so too all [conditions] would be incapable of producing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). However, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that birth and the other [characteristics] are established as real entities (*dravyabhāva*). For scriptures are not discarded simply because there are critics, nor are barley seeds not sown because there are deer, nor are sweetmeats not eaten because flies alight upon them. Therefore, one must respond to objections while adhering to the established tenets. The characteristics have been explained.

What are the sets of names and so forth? The sets of names and so forth are collections of designations (*saṃjñā*), sentences (*vākya*), and syllables (*akṣara*). (47ab) By the inclusion of "and so forth," the sets of phrases (*pada*) and phonemes (*vyañjana*) are included. Among these, a name is that which effects a designation; for example, "form" (*rūpa*), "sound" (*śabda*), and so on. A sentence is a phrase, which is as much as is required for the completion of a meaning; for example, "Alas, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent," and so on—by means of which the specific relations of action, quality, and time are understood. A phoneme is a syllable; for example, *a*, *ā*, and so on. But are not syllables also the names of the components of writing?

Indeed, syllables were not devised for the purpose of conveying the components of writing; rather, the components of writing were devised for the purpose of conveying the syllables themselves. [The question arises: "How might those [syllables] which are not being heard be understood through writing? Thus, the names of these [components] are not the syllables themselves. And the collections (*samukti*) of these—such as *saṃjñā* and so forth—constitute the groupings of names and so on. They recite the root *uc* in the sense of "collection" (*samavāya*). From that, this form *samukti* arises. The meaning of *samavāya* is the same as the meaning of *samukti*.

In this context, the set of names (*nāmakāya*) refers, for example, to "form," "sound," "odor," "taste," "tangible objects," and so forth. The set of phrases (*padakāya*) refers, for example, to "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," "all phenomena are non-self," "nirvāṇa is peace," and so forth. The set of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) refers, for example, to "ka," "kha," "ga," "gha," "ṅa," and so forth. But since these have speech as their intrinsic nature, they consist of sound and thus possess the intrinsic nature of form (*rūpa*). Why, then, are they said to be dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*)? It is because these do not have speech as their intrinsic nature.

Speech (*vāk*) is indeed sound (*ghoṣa*), yet meanings are not understood by sound alone. What then? Speech operates upon names and illuminates the meaning of the name; speech is not merely sound. Rather, that sound by which a meaning is understood is speech. But by what sound is a meaning understood? By that which has been fixed as a convention (*avadhi*) regarding meanings by speakers. For example, this word "go" (*gauḥ*) has its convention fixed upon nine meanings: "speech, direction, earth, ray, thunderbolt, cattle, eye, heaven, and enemy."

"A wise person should understand the word 'cow' in its nine meanings. For even he who thinks that the name (*nāman*) manifests the object must necessarily admit this, provided that the word has a recognized referent. And since this is established by the mere word itself when its referent is recognized, what is the point of postulating a separate entity called "name"? Furthermore, it is not understood how it operates upon the non-name: does it produce [the cognition], or does it manifest it? If it produces it...

Since speech has the nature of sound, every mere sound will produce a name; or rather, whatever specific sound is intended to be the producer of a name, that alone will be the illuminator of the object. Alternatively, it illuminates: since speech has the nature of sound, every mere sound will illuminate a name; or rather, whatever specific sound is intended to be the illuminator of a name, that alone will be the illuminator of the object.

Furthermore, there is no such thing as a collection of sounds meeting in a single moment, nor is it logical for a single entity to arise in parts; thus, how could speech produce a name? How, then, does the final moment of informative intimation (*vijñapti*), depending on those that have passed, produce non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*)? If that were the case, since the name would be produced by the very last sound alone, even one who hears only that single sound would then understand the meaning.

Furthermore, suppose it were imagined that speech produces the phoneme (*vyañjana*), and the phoneme [in turn] produces the name (*nāman*). Even in this case, the same logical difficulty follows because there is no simultaneous collection (*sāmagrī*) of phonemes. And this same difficulty applies to the claim that speech is the illuminator (*prakāśaka*) of the name. Moreover, even those who are exceptionally wise and possess focused minds are unable to discern a phoneme from its specific characteristics; therefore, it is not tenable that speech is either the producer or the illuminator of the phoneme.

Furthermore, if it is maintained that a name is co-nascent with its object—just like genus (*jāti*) and so forth—then in that case, there would be no present name for an object that is past or future. Since names are assigned to offspring by their parents according to their own wishes, which of these could possibly be co-nascent with the object? Moreover, for unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, with what could a co-nascent name exist? Thus, this [position] is simply unacceptable. As for what was said by the Blessed One:
"Verses depend upon names; the poet is the basis of verses."

In this context, a word (*śabda*) is that which has its limits established regarding meanings; and a "verse" (*gāthā*) is a particular arrangement [of words] by name. Thus, it is dependent upon names. Furthermore, a particular arrangement does not logically constitute a separate substance (*dravyāntara*), just as a row [of ants] or the sequence of moments of consciousness [does not]. Or, even if one were to postulate that the mere phonemes (*vyañjana*) themselves exist as separate substances, the collections thereof would simply be the sets of names and so forth (*nāmakāyādi*); therefore, the conceptual designation (*prajñapti*) of such [separate entities] is useless.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the dissociated formations—the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth—do indeed exist as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*), for not all dharmas are accessible through mere reasoning. Now, it must be stated with what these sets of names and so forth are associated: are they designated as sentient beings (*sattvākhya*) or non-sentient beings (*asattvākhya*); are they born of maturation (*vipākaja*), accumulative (*aupacayika*), or outflowing (*naiṣyandika*); and are they wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or neutral (*avyākṛta*)? He replies: They belong to the realms of desire and form, are designated as sentient beings, and are outflowing and neutral. (47cd)

They belong to the realm of desire and the realm of form. Others say that they also exist in the formless realm, but they are inexpressible there. These are designated as belonging to sentient beings (*sattvākhya*). Furthermore, it is the one who expresses [them] who is endowed with them, not that which is expressed. They are outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*) and non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Just as these sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth are designated as belonging to sentient beings, are outflowing, and are non-obscured indeterminate, so too are the others.
As for homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*), moreover,
it is also a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
It is not only that which is outflowing;
it belongs to the three realms— that is,
it pertains to the spheres of desire, form, and formlessness.
Acquisitions are of two kinds: they are out-flowing and born of maturation;
so too are the [primary] characteristics.
The term "twofold" continues [from the previous rule], as in the case of acquisition (*prāpti*).
The meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and non-possession (*asamanvaya*) are outflows (*niḥṣyanda*). ||48c'd||

The two mindless attainments (*acittasamāpatti*) and non-possession (*asamanvāgama*) are exclusively outflowing (*naiṣyandika*). What remains to be said regarding these has already been stated; we shall not speak again of the remaining two, namely the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*) and the life-faculty (*jīvita*), for they have been explained. How was it stated that acquisition (*prāpti*) and the others pertain to sentient beings? By the mention of "possession" (*samanvāgama*). How was it stated that the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) pertain to both sentient and non-sentient things? Because they are co-existent with all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). The dissociated factors (*viprayukta*) have been explained.
As for what was said—that birth is the producer of that which is to be produced, yet not without causes and conditions—what are these causes and what are the conditions?

The cause is held to be sixfold: the efficient cause (*kāraṇa*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhū*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga*), the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka*), the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga*), and that called the ripening cause (*vipāka*). (Verse 49)

There are these six causes: the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), the associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*), the omnipresent cause (*sarvatragahetu*), and the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*). Among these, all factors other than itself are the efficient cause.

For all phenomena (*dharma*), with the exception of their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), are the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) for the arising of a conditioned phenomenon, because they abide in a state of non-obstruction. But is it not the case that those outflows (*āsrava*) which would have arisen in one who does not know do not arise in one who knows? Thus, knowledge acts as an obstruction to their arising—just as the light of the sun prevents the seeing of the stars. How, then, can all phenomena, excluding their own intrinsic nature, be the efficient cause of a conditioned phenomenon?

It should be understood that this is because [the cause] exists as a non-obstacle to that which is arising. It may well be that those things capable of acting as obstacles to arising function as causes simply by not acting as obstacles; for example, with respect to a ruler who does not oppress, how is he a cause? Or, for instance, in the case of all arisings, such as the arising of *nirvāṇa*, of things whose nature is not to arise, and of hell-beings and so forth, or the arising of the aggregates of beings in the formless realm—even though these do not exist, they would likewise be incapable of creating an obstacle.

For even when a master is incapable, people still speak of him in that way; thus, this very example applies here as a general indication. However, that which is the primary efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is capable even of producing [an effect], such as the eye and visible forms for visual consciousness, food for the body, or seeds and so forth for sprouts and so forth.

But as for one who objects thus: "If all phenomena (*dharma*) are causes by way of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇabhāva*), why does the simultaneous arising of everything not occur? And why, like the killer, do all people not become partakers of the act of taking life?"—this is not a valid objection. For it is asserted that all phenomena are causes by way of non-obstruction, and not by way of being a [specific] causal agent (*kāraṇahetu*). Others maintain that every causal agent possesses the capacity for the arising of everything.

For example, even for *nirvāṇa*, there is visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). How so? Because mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—whether wholesome or unwholesome—arises by taking it as its object; from that, visual consciousness subsequently arises in due order. Thus, through a succession of causes, since it serves as a condition (*pratyaya*) for that [visual consciousness], it possesses efficacy (*sāmarthya*). This should be understood in the same way for other things as well; this is the general direction. The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) has been explained. "Co-existent [causes] are those which are mutual fruits.
(50b) Those phenomena (*dharmas*) which are mutual fruits, either directly or indirectly, are co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) for one another. How is this so?
Like the primary elements, like the mind and its concomitants, and like the characteristics and the characterized. ||50cd||

The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are mutually co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*). Mind is the co-existent cause of mental factors that follow it, and they are also [the co-existent cause] of it. The characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) are the co-existent causes of the characterized (*lakṣya*), and it is also [the co-existent cause] of them. Having established this, all conditioned phenomena are co-existent causes according to their respective application. Furthermore, even in the absence of mutual fruitfulness, it should be added as a supplementary rule: a factor is the co-existent cause of its secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*), but those [secondary characteristics] are not [the co-existent cause] of it.
Which, then, are these factors that conform to the mind?
The mental factors, the two types of restraint, their characteristics, and the characteristics of the mind itself are those that conform to the mind. (50abc)

All [factors] associated with the mind, as well as the dhyāna-restraint and the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara), along with their [respective] characteristics such as birth and so forth, and the mind itself—these factors are said to be "conforming to the mind" (cittānuvartin). How do they conform to the mind? Briefly, by way of time, fruit, and so forth, as well as by way of wholesomeness and so forth. (51cd)

First, in terms of time, they are said to follow the mind because they abide in a state of one-pointedness with it, because they are subject to cessation simultaneously with it, and because they belong to the same temporal period as it. In terms of fruit and so forth, they share the same fruit, maturation, and outflow as it. Furthermore, the first word "one" (*eka*) should be understood in the sense of "together. In terms of purity and so forth, when the mind is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, they are likewise wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral. Thus, for ten reasons, they are called "concomitants of the mind. Among these, even the smallest possible mind is the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) of fifty-eight factors.

Of the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), their forty characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the eight primary and secondary characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-anulakṣaṇa*) [of those ten], there are fifty-four factors that are co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*) for that [mind], excluding its own secondary characteristics. Others say there are fourteen: the ten universal factors and their own characteristics. However, they do not accept this, for it would contradict the *Prakaraṇapāda* treatise.

There may be a truth of suffering that has the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but is not a cause for the view of a self-identity. Excluding the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of the view of a self-identity and of the factors associated with it, whatever other afflicted truth of suffering there is has the view of a self-identity as its cause but is not a cause for the view of a self-identity; and that which was excluded is both a cause for the view of a self-identity and has the view of a self-identity as its cause.

Regarding those who do not recite the phrase "and of the factors associated with that," the Kashmiris maintain that they too must either recite it or understand it by implication as follows: "Whatever is a cause by way of co-existent cause (sahabhūhetu) is also co-existent; however, there may be something that is co-existent but is not a cause by way of co-existent cause—namely, the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇas) of a factor, and those [secondary characteristics] themselves in relation to one another."

The secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇas*) that follow the mind are likewise [not co-existent causes] of one another. Furthermore, derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)—whether it be resistant (*sapratigha*) or some non-resistant (*apratigha*) matter—is not a co-existent cause for one another. All such matter, however, is a co-existent cause for the primary elements (*bhūtas*). Co-nascent acquisitions (*prāptis*) are co-existent with that which is acquired (*prāptimat*), yet they are not its co-existent cause, because they possess multiple fruits, ripenings (*vipāka*), and outflows (*niṣyanda*). Moreover, these acquisitions do not necessarily accompany [the entity] throughout its duration; they may arise before it or even after its production. All of this would indeed be the case.

However, it must be addressed that this principle is not observed in the case of seeds and the like, whose causal relationship as cause and effect is well-established. How, then, can there be a causal relationship between phenomena (*dharma*) that arise simultaneously? For example, in the case of a lamp and its light, or a sprout and its shadow. This must first be carefully considered: is the lamp the cause of the light, or rather, is it the previously arisen complex of conditions (*sāmagrī*) itself that is the cause for the arising of the lamp together with its light and the sprout together with its shadow?

Rather, it is because existence and non-existence belong to them in this way. For logicians declare that this is the definition of cause and effect: when the existence and non-existence of one thing are necessarily accompanied by the existence and non-existence of another, the former is the cause and the latter is the effect. And since among co-existent dharmas, the existence of one entails the existence of all, and the non-existence of one entails the non-existence of all, the relationship of cause and effect is logical. This may well apply to those that arise together; but how can it be so between things that are mutually related?

Therefore, he says: "In that case, this same consequence would apply even to derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) that is inseparable from one another, as well as to [derived matter] together with the primary elements (*bhūta*), and to the secondary characteristics (*anulakṣaṇa*) and so forth of the mind together with the mind and its factors. If it is argued that the state of being cause and effect among co-existent things is established like the mutual support of a tripod, then this must first be examined."

Is their persistence due to the power of simultaneous arising, or does their production occur in that very manner by virtue of a prior causal complex (*sāmagrī*)? Furthermore, is there something else present therein—such as a string, a peg, or the earth—as a supporting factor? Since for these [dharmas] there are also other factors such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and so forth, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is established.
What is the homogeneous cause? The homogeneous cause consists of similar [dharmas]. (52a)

Similar phenomena are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of similar phenomena; for example, the five wholesome aggregates (*skandha*) are [the cause] of wholesome [aggregates] through mutual [relation], the defiled of the defiled, and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) of the indeterminate. Among these, indeterminate form (*rūpa*) is [the cause] of the five [aggregates]. However, others maintain that the four [mental aggregates] are not [the cause] of form, because of its inferiority. Within a single homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*), the *kalala* stage is [the cause] of the ten stages beginning with the *kalala*, the *arbuda* and so forth are [the cause] of the [stages] beginning with the *arbuda*, each being reduced by one at a time.

But among other things of the same class, all ten stages are the [homogeneous cause] of the ten. This should be applied in detail even to external things: for example, barley is the [cause] of barley, and rice is the [cause] of rice. However, for those who do not accept that matter is the homogeneous cause of matter, this textual passage serves to refute their position: "Past great elements are the cause and the dominant condition of future great elements.
But are all similar things the homogeneous cause of similar things? He says: No. What then? Those belonging to their own category and level (*svanikāyabhū*).

Their own category (*nikāya*) and their own level (*bhūmi*) constitute "those belonging to their own category and level" (*svanikāyabhū*). There are five categories: those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*), up to those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*). There are nine levels: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the eight [levels consisting of] the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*). Among these, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, and not for others. Likewise, up to those to be abandoned by cultivation are the homogeneous cause for those to be abandoned by cultivation.

Those belonging to the desire realm [serve as the cause] for those belonging to the desire realm; those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna for those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, and so on up to those belonging to the level of the peak of existence for those belonging to that very same level, but not for others. Furthermore, not all of them [serve as such]; what then?
Those that are previously arisen.

Those that have arisen previously are the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for those that have arisen later, whether they themselves have arisen or not yet arisen. Future factors are never a homogeneous cause. It is the same regarding the past. Why is this so? It is said: from the *Śāstra*. What is the homogeneous cause? Previously arisen roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) are the cause, by way of being a homogeneous cause, for subsequently arisen roots of virtue and for the factors associated with them within their own realm (*svadhātu*). Likewise, past factors are [the cause] for past and present factors.

It should be stated that past and present [dharmas] are causes of future [dharmas]. This treatise also states: "Is there a case where a dharma that is the cause of another dharma is not the cause of that dharma at any time? It says: 'Never. There is no fault here, because this statement was made with the intention of referring specifically to the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).

However, as for one who thinks that even a future phenomenon becomes fixed as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) at the stage of its arising, and that it was said [in the scripture] "it is never not a cause" with reference to that final stage—this is not a valid rebuttal; because that phenomenon, prior to the stage of its arising, was not a homogeneous cause and only becomes so afterwards.

And here too, regarding this question—namely, that a given dharma which is the immediate antecedent (samanantara) of another dharma might at some time not be its immediate antecedent—it would be possible to say, according to this conceptualization, "it is never the case. Why, then, does he say: "if that dharma has not arisen"? This is for the sake of demonstrating both sides; just as it was done there, so should it be done here, and just as it is done here, so should it be done there.

If this were the case, what benefit would be gained? It would only suggest a lack of skill on the part of the author of the treatise. Therefore, the previous resolution alone is correct here. As for that which was stated: "Excluding future *satkāyadṛṣṭi* and the truth of suffering associated with it, whatever other afflicted truth of suffering there is, that has *satkāyadṛṣṭi* as its cause but is not a cause of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*; however, that which was excluded both has *satkāyadṛṣṭi* as its cause and is a cause of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*."

This should be formulated as: "excluding the future truth of suffering associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it should be understood in this sense even according to the meaning [of the text]. How, then, is this statement from the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be interpreted: "All phenomena (*dharmas*) are fixed in four respects; they are fixed in cause, fruit, basis, and object"? Here, "cause" refers to the associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*). "Fruit" refers to the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

It should be understood that the basis (*āśraya*) consists of the eye and so forth, while the object (*ālambana*) consists of visible form and so forth. But if this is the case, does it not follow that the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) becomes a cause only after having previously not been one? This is indeed accepted with respect to its state (*avasthā*), but not with respect to its substance (*dravya*). For it is the causal totality (*sāmagrya*) that results in a change of state, not the substance itself. Furthermore, what would happen if the future homogeneous cause were like the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*)? It would have to be mentioned in the Treatise (*śāstra*).

For that [cause] alone is capable of the activity of grasping and giving a fruit; since it is that very [cause] which is grasped, there is no fault. This is not so. For a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) possesses its fruit by means of a flow-fruit (*niḥṣyanda-phala*). And that is untenable for what is future, because of the absence of priority and posteriority. Nor is it logical for what has arisen to be the flow-fruit of what is future, as is the case with the past being the flow-fruit of the present. Lest the fruit should exist prior to the cause. Furthermore, there is no priority or posteriority within the future time-period (*adhvan*). This is not so.

In the case of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), if there were no temporal sequence of prior and posterior, a similar [dharma] would be the homogeneous cause of a similar [dharma], and because they would thus be mutual causes, it would follow that they are mutual outflows (*niḥṣyanda*). And mutual outflow is not logically tenable. However, in the case of the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), even without a temporal sequence of prior and posterior, it does not follow that there is a state of mutual cause and fruit, because the cause and the fruit have distinct characteristics.

Therefore, while the homogeneous cause is established only as existing in specific stages, the retributive cause is established by its own characteristic; thus, it is not excluded even when it exists in the future.
[AKBh II.52.cd]
As it was stated that a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) belongs to its own level, is this a universal rule? This rule applies to all contaminated (sāsrava) phenomena.
However, the Path (mārga) of the nine levels [acts as a homogeneous cause] for one another. (52cd)

The heading here is "homogeneous cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*). In the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntarika*), the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) is a homogeneous cause for one another. What is the reason? Because this [Truth of the Path] is adventitious to those stages; it does not fall within their realm (*dhātu*) because it is not appropriated by the cravings belonging to those stages. Therefore, it is a homogeneous cause even for that which is of the same kind but belongs to another stage. Furthermore, it [is a homogeneous cause] for what is equal or superior. (AKBh II.52d')

It does not serve as the cause for that which is inferior. For example, the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) is the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) for that very same receptivity when it is future, and for everything superior up to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). This is because the knowledge of non-arising has no other superior [state] for which it could be a cause; it is the cause only for the knowledge of non-arising itself. The paths of seeing (*darśanamārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*) are the causes for three, two, and one [respective categories]. Within those, moreover, the path of one with dull faculties is the cause for the paths of both dull and sharp faculties, whereas the path of one with sharp faculties is the cause only for the path of sharp faculties.

For example, the paths of the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), and the one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) are [the causes] for six, four, and two [types of practitioners] respectively. The paths of the follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and the one liberated without occasion (*asamayavimukta*) are [the causes] for three, two, and one respectively. Furthermore, how can a path belonging to a lower stage be equal to or superior to a path belonging to a higher stage? It is by way of the faculties (*indriya*) and the accumulation of causes (*hetūpacaya*). In that regard, among the paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and so forth, as well as those ranging from the "soft-soft" (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) grade upward, each subsequent one is more accumulated with causes than the preceding.

Even though the paths of the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin) and the follower by dharma (dharmānusārin) cannot both exist within a single continuum, once arisen, it is the cause for that which is yet to come.
But is it only the supramundane path that serves as the homogeneous cause (sabhāgahetu) for what is equal or superior? No, he says; for even mundane [paths] do so.
Those produced by application (*prayogaja*) are homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*) for those very two that are equal or superior, but not for an inferior one. As to which these are, he says:
"those consisting of hearing, reflection, and so forth. (53b)

For these qualities consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation are generally the causes only for those that are equal or superior, not for those that are inferior. For example: those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) consisting of hearing are the causes for those consisting of hearing and reflection; those consisting of reflection are the causes for those consisting of reflection, because there is no [quality] consisting of cultivation there. Those belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) consisting of hearing are the causes for those consisting of hearing and cultivation, because there is no [quality] consisting of reflection there. Those consisting of cultivation are the causes for those consisting of cultivation alone. Those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consisting of cultivation are the causes for those consisting of cultivation alone.

Among these as well, due to the division into nine types, the weak-weak are the cause for all; the weak-medium are the cause for eight; such is the principle. However, all wholesome factors acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*) of the nine types are mutual homogeneous causes (*sabhāgahetu*). Defiled factors are likewise. Unobscured-neutral factors (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), however, are of four kinds: those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*), those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and those arising together with the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*).

These are, respectively, the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for four, three, two, and one [classes of minds]. The mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) is also the fruit of the four dhyānas of the desire realm. In that regard, the fruit of a higher dhyāna is not the similar cause of the fruit of a lower dhyāna; for there is no inferior fruit from a similar cause that is produced through effort (*ābhisaṃskārika*). This is so that effort toward rice, barley, and the like does not become fruitless.

For this very reason, they say: "There may be a case where an arisen untainted (*anāsrava*) state is not the cause of an unarisen [untainted] state; for example, the arisen *duḥkhe dharmajñāna* is not the cause of the unarisen *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣāntis*. Furthermore, everything that is superior is not the cause of what is inferior. There may be a case where an untainted factor belonging to a single continuum, previously acquired, is not the cause of one that arises later."

It may be that future receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣāntayaḥ*) are not the cause of the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*), because there is no fruit that exists prior [to its cause], nor is a future [factor] a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*). It may be that a previously arisen untainted phenomenon (*anāsrava-dharma*) is not the cause of a subsequently arisen untainted phenomenon; for example, a superior [fruit] is not the cause of an inferior one, such as when one who has fallen away from a higher fruit brings a lower fruit into manifestation, or as the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering is not the cause of the acquisitions of the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering arising together with subsequent moments, because they are inferior. The homogeneous cause has been explained.
The associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*), however, consists only of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

If this were the case, it would follow that even those [mental states] arising in different times or different continua would be mutual associated causes. If you say they must have the same aspect (*ākāra*) and the same object (*ālambana*), the same fault follows. If you say they must be simultaneous, then it would follow that even those born in different continua—such as people looking at the new moon and so forth—would be associated causes. Therefore, they must have the same basis (*samāśraya*). (53d')

Those mental states (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*) which have the same basis (*āśraya*) are *saṃprayuktaka-hetu* (associated causes) for one another. "The same" means non-different; for example, that very moment of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) which is the basis of the eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), is the very same [basis] for its associated [factors] such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth, up to the mind (*manas*). That moment of the faculty should be understood as the basis for the mind-consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its associated [factors]. Whatever is an associated cause is also a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Now, in what sense is there the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), and in what sense is there the associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*)? The co-existent cause is so called in the sense of being mutual results, like travelers who travel together by means of their mutual strength. The associated cause is so called in the sense of association through five kinds of equality, like those same travelers engaging in the activity of consuming food, drink, and so forth together. For even if one among them is missing, they do not associate with the whole; such is their nature as a cause. The associated cause has been explained.
What is the omnipresent cause (*sarvatragahetu*)?
The "pervasive" (*sarvatraga*) [cause] consists of the previously arisen pervasive factors within their own level for defiled states.

(54ab) Pervasive factors belonging to their own level that have arisen previously are the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) of subsequent defiled factors.
