We shall explain these further later in the very chapter of the *Abhidharmakośa* that explains the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*). This [pervasive cause] is established separately from the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) because it is the general cause of all defiled factors; for, by virtue of its power, even afflictions belonging to other categories (*nikāya*) arise.

Are the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) dharmas of even a noble person (*āryapudgala*) caused by universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*)? The Kashmiris maintain that all afflicted dharmas have as their cause those factors to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavyahetuka*). Thus it is stated in the *Prakaraṇas*: "Which are the dharmas that have as their cause those to be abandoned by seeing? They are the afflicted dharmas and the maturation (*vipāka*) of those dharmas to be abandoned by seeing. Which are the dharmas that have as their cause the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? They are the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) indeterminate dharmas and the unwholesome (*akuśala*) ones.

The truth of suffering may have the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its cause, but it is not the cause of the view of a self-identity; this is explained in detail up to the point where it says: "excluding the birth, aging, duration, and impermanence of that [view of a self-identity] and of those other phenomena, whatever other afflicted truth of suffering there is. How, then, is this passage from the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be interpreted: "Could there be a phenomenon that is unwholesome and has only an unwholesome cause?"

It may be that an noble person (āryapudgala), while falling away from detachment from the desire realm, first brings into manifestation a defiled volition (kliṣṭā cetanā). This was stated with reference to its cause not yet being abandoned. For its cause—namely, that which is to be abandoned by insight (darśanaprahātavya)—is not mentioned here because it has already been abandoned. The pervasive cause (sarvatragahetu) has been explained. What is the ripening cause (vipākahetu)?
The ripening cause consists of the unwholesome (aśubha) and the wholesome-with-outflows (kuśalāḥ sāsravāḥ). (54cd)

Unwholesome (*akuśala*) dharmas and wholesome-with-outflows (*kuśala-sāsrava*) dharmas are the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), because they possess the nature of being maturation. Why do neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas not produce maturation? Because they are weak, like a rotten seed. Why do those without outflows (*anāsrava*) not [produce it]? Because they are not moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), like a sound seed that has not been moistened. For how could dharmas that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) bring about a maturation associated with any realm? But the remaining ones do bring it about, because they possess both qualities, like a sound seed that has been moistened.

How is this to be understood: is a "maturation cause" (*vipāka-hetu*) the cause of maturation, or is it the cause that is itself maturation? What follows from this? If a maturation cause is the cause of maturation, then the statement "the eye is born of maturation" would not be tenable. If, on the other hand, a maturation cause is the cause that is itself maturation, then the statement "the maturation of karma" would not be tenable. This is not a fault; for it was stated previously that the application [of the term] is valid in both ways. Now, what is the meaning of "maturation" (*vipāka*)?

Vipāka (ripening) is a dissimilar ripening; for other causes, however, the ripening is similar. The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that for one cause (the *vipākahetu*), it is both. But ripening is not at all tenable for those [other causes]. For what is called "ripening" is that which arises from a specific transformation of the continuum (*santatipariṇāmaviśeṣaja*) and culminates in a fruit. Now, there is no fruit arising from a specific transformation of the continuum produced by the co-existent (*sahabhū*) or associated (*saṃprayuktaka*) causes. Nor is there a culmination of fruit for the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the others, because their fruits—such as the wholesome and so forth—recur again and again throughout cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) consisting of one aggregate (*skandha*) has a single fruit: namely, [the primary action] together with its birth-characteristics (*jāti*) and so forth. One consisting of two aggregates has a single fruit: bodily and vocal karma together with their birth-characteristics and so forth. One consisting of four aggregates has a single fruit: informative action (*vijñapti*) in the first dhyāna together with its birth-characteristics and so forth. One consisting of four aggregates has a single fruit: in a wholesome mind that is not in meditative absorption (*asamāhita*). One consisting of five aggregates has a single fruit: in a mind that is in meditative absorption (*samāhita*).

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), a retributive cause (*vipākahetu*) consisting of a single aggregate (*skandha*) has a single fruit: namely, acquisition (*prāpti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), together with their [respective] characteristics such as birth (*jāti*). A [retributive cause] consisting of four aggregates comprises wholesome mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) along with their characteristics such as birth. There is karma for which only a single sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) ripens as its retribution—this refers to that [karma] whose retribution is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). For that [karma] whose retribution is the mind-sphere (*manāyatana*), there are two: the mind-sphere and the sphere of phenomena (*manodharmāyatane*).

Thus, for one whose sense-base is the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) and for whom the body-base (*kāyāyatana*) exists, there are three bases: the body, the tangible, and the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*). Likewise for one whose [bases] are form, odor, and taste. For one whose sense-base is the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*), there are four bases: the eye, the body, the tangible, and the mental-object base. Likewise for one whose [bases] are the ear, nose, and tongue. There is such karma for which five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, or eleven bases ripen as its maturation (*vipāka*).

Because karma has both diverse and non-diverse fruits, like external seeds. For instance, some external seeds have diverse fruits, such as those of the lotus, pomegranate, and banyan tree; others have non-diverse fruits, such as those of barley and wheat. The maturation (*vipāka*) of a single-moment karma ripens over the three times (past, present, and future), but the maturation of a two-time karma does not ripen in a single moment, lest there be an excessive deficiency in the cause. Nor does it ripen immediately after, because the immediately succeeding moment is drawn forth by the *samanantara-pratyaya* (contiguous condition). For the cause of maturation depends upon a continuous stream.

Now, what is the restriction regarding the time periods (*adhvan*) for these causes? Their restriction regarding the time periods has been stated by implication, but not explicitly formulated as a rule (*sūtra*); therefore, it is now formulated:
"The universal (*sarvatraga*) and the similar (*sabhāga*) belong to two time periods" (55ab).
They exist only in the past and the present; they do not exist in the future. And the reason for this has already been stated.

The three [types of causes] belonging to the three time periods are the co-existent, the associated, and the retributive causes; they belong to the three times. As for the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), because no restriction of time is shown, it should be understood as belonging to all time periods and as being dissociated from the mental factors (*citta-viprayukta*). The causes have been explained.

What, then, is that fruit of which these are the causes? [p.91] "Conditioned phenomena, together with dissociation, are the fruit" (55cd). What phenomena are the fruit? The treatise states: "Conditioned phenomena and analytical cessation. If this is so, then because it is a fruit, the unconditioned must have a cause of which it is the fruit; and because it is a cause, it must have a fruit of which it is the cause. However, cause and fruit belong only to conditioned phenomena.
For you, there is no [arising] of the unconditioned. ||55d||

What is the reason? Because of the impossibility of the six kinds of causes and the impossibility of the five kinds of fruits. Why is the path not accepted as the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*)? Because it is established as such by virtue of being a non-obstruction to arising, and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not possess the quality of arising. Whose fruit is it, then, or how is it the fruit of the path? It is because [dissociation] is attained through its power. In that case, attainment (*prāpti*) alone would follow as the fruit of the path, since the path has efficacy only with respect to that [attainment], and not with respect to dissociation itself.

For its capacity regarding attainment is of one kind, while its capacity regarding dissociation is of another. How does it have capacity regarding attainment? By way of production. How regarding dissociation? By way of bringing about [its acquisition]. Therefore, the Path is not in any way the cause of this [dissociation]. And its fruit is dissociation. Now, if there is no dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), how can the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) be a causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*)? It is a causal condition by virtue of being a non-obstruction to arising.

Furthermore, this [unconditioned] has no fruit, because being liberated from the time-periods (adhvan), it lacks the capacity to either receive or bestow a fruit. Indeed, the Blessed One has never stated anywhere that the unconditioned is a cause; however, the Sautrāntikas maintain that it is called a "cause" by way of a figurative designation (paryāya). How has this been stated? [It was said:
"Those causes and those conditions for the arising of form are themselves impermanent.
Since form arises in dependence upon causes and conditions that are indeed impermanent, how could it be permanent?"

"In this way, first of all, [it is said] that consciousness [is conditioned]. If that is so, then it follows that the unconditioned cannot be the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness, because of the restriction [in the sūtra] that "[conditions] are for the sake of arising. It does follow;
for those causes and those conditions which exist for the arising of consciousness, they too are impermanent.

Thus it has been said, but it was not stated that those which are the conditions (*pratyaya*) of consciousness are themselves impermanent. Now, since it is said that whatever causes (*hetu*) exist for the sake of arising are themselves impermanent, there is no prohibition against the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) being a causal cause (*kāraṇahetu*) by virtue of its mere state of non-obstruction. It has been stated in the Sūtra regarding the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), but not as a non-obstructing cause; therefore, the status of the unconditioned as a cause is not established in the Sūtra. Even if it was not explicitly stated, it was not prohibited. Furthermore, since many Sūtras have disappeared, how can it be determined that it was not stated?

Now, what is this so-called "disjunction" (*visaṃyoga*)? Has it not already been stated previously that it is "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*)? In that case, what is cessation through deliberation? It was said to be that which is disjunction; now, what is disjunction? It is said to be that which is cessation through deliberation. Thus, this circular explanation is incapable of illuminating its own essential nature.

Therefore, its intrinsic nature must be stated otherwise. Its intrinsic nature is to be personally realized by the Noble Ones (*ārya*) alone. However, this much can be said: there exists a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*) that is eternal and wholesome; and its dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) is called cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). The Sautrāntikas maintain that all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are without substantial reality (*adravya*). For they do not exist as separate entities like form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth. What then? Space (*ākāśa*) is merely the absence of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*).

For example, just as people say "space" when they find no resistance in the dark; so too, the cessation of arisen latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) and birth through the power of analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), such that others do not arise, is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). That which is non-arising due to the deficiency of conditions even without analytical discernment is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); for example, the remainder of the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) in the case of premature death.

Furthermore, those belonging to other schools say: "The capacity of wisdom (*prajñā*) lies in the non-arising of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); therefore, this is analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). On the other hand, the non-arising of suffering occurs simply due to the deficiency of the latent dispositions—which are the causes of its arising—and thus wisdom has no capacity regarding it; therefore, this is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). However, since even that is not established without analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*), it is indeed analytical cessation."

Others maintain that the very non-existence of what has arisen subsequently is itself *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation), because of its cessation by its own inherent nature (*svarasa-nirodha*). However, according to this conception, *apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* would follow as being impermanent, because it does not exist as long as [the entity] has not yet perished. [Objection: But then *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) would also follow as being impermanent, since it is preceded by deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā*). [Response: Indeed, it is not preceded by deliberation; for deliberation does not first occur and only afterwards the non-arising of things that have not yet arisen. What then? [It is the non-arising itself.]

Their non-arising exists even prior [to the exercise of discernment]. However, those phenomena which would otherwise arise without discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) do not subsequently occur once that discernment has arisen. This is the efficacy of discernment here: namely, the state of being an obstacle to the arising of those things whose arising was previously unobstructed.

If, then, non-arising alone is nirvāṇa, how is this scriptural passage to be interpreted: "These five faculties, when cultivated, developed, and practiced extensively, lead to the abandonment of suffering past, future, and present"? For abandonment is indeed nirvāṇa, and non-arising applies only to the future, not to the past or the present. This is indeed so.

However, the Blessed One has stated that the abandonment of suffering results from the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that take it as their object: "Whatever desire and passion there is for form, abandon that! When desire and passion are abandoned, in this way your form will be abandoned and fully understood," and so on in detail up to consciousness. Thus, the abandonment of suffering belonging to the three time periods is also logical. Furthermore, even if it were said, "for the sake of abandoning past, future, and present afflictions," this same principle applies here as well.

Alternatively, this may be the intended meaning: past affliction refers to that belonging to a previous birth, while present affliction refers to that belonging to the current birth. Just as it is said regarding the eighteen modes of craving (*tṛṣṇā-vicarita*): "The eighteen modes of craving based on the past time," which is spoken with reference to a past birth, and so on up to the present; by means of those two types of affliction, the state of a seed (*bīja-bhāva*) has been deposited in this continuum for the sake of the arising of the future. Through the abandonment of that [affliction], that [seed] also becomes abandoned.

Just as karma becomes exhausted through the exhaustion of its maturation (*vipāka*), so too is there absolute non-arising—which is abandonment—due to the absence of the seed for future suffering or affliction (*kleśa*). Otherwise, what would there be to abandon regarding the past or the present? For effort is not purposeful toward that which has already ceased or is currently ceasing.

If the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not exist at all, then how can that which was said by the Blessed One—"Whatever phenomena there may be, whether conditioned or unconditioned, dispassion (*virāga*) is declared to be the foremost among them"—be possible? For how could that which is non-existent be the foremost among things that are non-existent? We do not say that the unconditioned does not exist at all; rather, we say that it is of such a nature as we have described. It is just as when it is said that there is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of a sound and there is its posterior non-existence (*paścād-abhāva*); yet, furthermore, non-existence is not established as a positive entity (*bhāva*).

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) should also be viewed in this way. Furthermore, even a certain kind of non-existence (*abhāva*) can be most praiseworthy; namely, that which is the absolute absence of all affliction (*upadrava*). It deserves to receive praise as "the foremost" among other things for the purpose of attracting those to be trained (*vineya*) toward it. Even if the unconditioned were a mere non-existence, cessation (*nirodha*) would not be a Noble Truth (*āryasatya*), for it would not exist at all. What, then, is the meaning of "truth" (*satya*)? Is it not rather the meaning of being non-erroneous (*aviparīta*)?

Both of these are seen by the Noble Ones (ārya) without error: namely, that suffering is indeed suffering, and that the absence of suffering is indeed an absence. What contradiction is there in this being a Noble Truth? How could an absence be called a third Noble Truth? It has been stated that because it is seen and taught immediately after the second [truth], it is the third. If the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) were merely a non-existence, then consciousness having space and nirvāṇa as its objects would have a non-existent object.

We shall consider this in the investigation into the existence of the past and the future. Furthermore, if the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) were held to be a substantial entity (*dravya*), what would follow? Moreover, what else would follow? The Vaibhāṣika position would be upheld—provided that they consider it something worthy of being upheld; however, it would then be merely an unreal conceptual construction. Why? Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not perceived, as is the case with form, sensation, and so forth, nor is its function (*karman*) perceived, as is the case with the eye and so forth.

Furthermore, how can the establishment of the genitive case—expressing "this is the cessation of that entity"—be conceived? For there is no connection whatsoever between the two, since a relationship such as that of cause and effect is impossible. What is appropriate, however, is a mere negation, expressed as "the non-existence of that. Even if it were a distinct entity, the cessation which is attained through the severance of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a particular affliction is designated as "belonging to" that affliction. In that case, what is the cause for the restriction of its acquisition?

It is stated in the Sūtra that "a monk has attained Nirvāṇa in this very life. In that case, how could there be the attainment of a non-entity? By means of obtaining the antidote, one attains a basis that is absolutely opposed to the arising of afflictions and future existence; therefore, it is said that Nirvāṇa has been attained. Furthermore, the scripture also indicates mere non-existence. For it says thus:

Indeed, the complete abandonment, relinquishment, disappearance, destruction, fading away, cessation, pacification, and vanishing of this very slight suffering, and the non-reconnection, non-arising, and non-manifestation of further suffering—this is lovely, this is sublime; namely, the relinquishment of all acquisitions (*upadhi*), the destruction of craving, fading away, cessation, which is Nirvana.

Why is it not accepted that "non-arising" (*aprādurbhāva*) means "it does not arise in this"? We see this locative case as being semantically untenable. What is meant [by the objection]? If it is connected with the word "existing" (*satī*), then there would follow the consequence of non-arising being eternal, because Nirvāṇa is eternal. If, on the other hand, it is connected with the word "attained" (*prāpta*), then one should accept the non-arising of suffering precisely when that [Nirvāṇa] has been conceptualized as attained—that is, when it has become manifest or has been reached. And in this way, the example is well-applied.

"His mind is liberated like the extinguishing of a lamp. Just as the extinguishing of a lamp is its non-existence, so too is the liberation of the Blessed One’s mind. It is also stated in the Abhidharma: "Which are the dharmas that lack a substrate (*avastuka*)? They are the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas. By "lacking a substrate," it is meant that they are bodiless and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is not the intended meaning here. What then? There are five kinds of substrate (*vastu*): the substrate of intrinsic nature, as previously described; the substrate acquired, such that one who has attained it is said to be "endowed with that substrate"; and so forth.

The object as a basis (*ālambana-vastu*): as it has been said, "all phenomena are to be known by knowledge according to their actual state. The object as conjunction (*saṃyoga-vastu*): as it has been said, "in whatever object attachment is conjoined with the fetter of attachment, in that very same object there is also the fetter of aversion. The object as cause (*hetu-vastu*): as it has been said, "which are the phenomena that have a basis? They are the conditioned phenomena. The object as appropriation (*parigraha-vastu*): as it has been said, "the object as field, the object as house," and so forth.

Therefore, in this context, the reason is expressed by the word "entity" (*vastu*); thus, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) certainly exists as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*). However, it possesses neither cause nor fruit. This point has been settled for now. Now, among these fruits, which fruit belongs to which cause?
The fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) belongs to the last [cause].

The ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is called "the last" because it is mentioned at the end; its fruit is the ripened fruit (*vipāka-phala*). The dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) belongs to the preceding [cause]. (56b)

The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is "prior" because it was mentioned first. Its fruit is the dominant fruit (*adhipaja-phala*). [Objection: Since it exists merely by way of non-obstruction, what kind of dominance does it possess? [Response: It possesses precisely this. Furthermore, the efficient cause also possesses the status of being a constituent factor (*aṅgībhāva*), as for example, the ten bases (*āyatana*) in relation to the five groups of consciousness, and karma in relation to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). Even the ear and other [senses] possess a dominant influence over the arising of visual consciousness through a mediated succession; for instance, because the desire to see arises after having heard—this and so forth should be applied accordingly. The outflow fruit (*niṣyanda*) belongs to the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). (56cd)
Because these two have similar results, they are outflow-results (*niḥṣyanda-phala*); the result of human effort (*pauruṣa*) belongs to both. [56d']

The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) belongs to the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*). Because it is not distinct from the state of being a person (*puruṣabhāva*), "human effort" (*puruṣakāra*) is simply the person himself; its fruit is "that which pertains to the person" (*pauruṣa*). What is this so-called "human effort"? It is the activity (*kāritra*) of a given dharma. For human effort is like the effort of a person. It is, for example, as with the medicinal plant *kākajaṅghā*, or a "drunken elephant," or a "human. Does the fruit of human effort belong to others as well, or only to these two?

For others as well, there exists [a fruit] other than the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*), because the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) arises either simultaneously with or immediately after [the cause]; however, the fruit of maturation is not like this. For that [fruit of maturation], too, there is a remote fruit of human effort, such as the harvest for farmers; so say others. Now, what is this so-called "fruit of maturation," and what about the others up to the "dominant fruit" (*adhipati-phala*)? Maturation is an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomenon.

For maturation (*vipāka*) is an unobscured-indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomenon; it might also be [classified as] non-sentient (*asattvākhya*), therefore he says: "it is sentient" (*sattvākhya*).
It might also be accumulative (*aupacayika*) or even outflowing (*naiḥsyandika*), therefore he says: [it is neither].

It arises from the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). For that which is wholesome or unwholesome is "determined" (*vyākṛta*) because it is defined in relation to its maturation (*vipāka*). Therefore, that which occurs at a later time—neither simultaneously nor immediately after—is maturation. This is the characteristic of maturation. Consequently, an object not designated as a sentient being (*asattvākhya*) produced by karma is not maturation, because it is common [to others]. For another person is likewise capable of enjoying it in that same way. Maturation, however, is uncommon; for one person does not experience the maturation of karma performed by another.

Why does one experience the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*)? Because it arises from collective karma (*sādhāraṇakarma*). The outflow (*niṣyanda*) is similar to its cause. That phenomenon which is similar to its cause is the outflow fruit; for example, as in the case of the similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*). If the fruit of the pervasive cause is also the same [as that of the similar cause], why is it not accepted as being only the similar cause? Because its similarity consists in its level (*bhūmi*) and its defiled nature (*kliṣṭatā*), but not in its specific mode (*prakāra*). However, that which is similar even in its specific mode is indeed accepted as a similar cause.

For this very reason, a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭika) is established regarding whether that which is a homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) for something is also its pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu): the first alternative is a homogeneous cause that is not pervasive; the second is a pervasive cause belonging to a different category (anya-naikāyika); the third is a pervasive cause belonging to the same category (eka-naikāyika); and the fourth consists of those cases excluding these aforementioned forms. [p.96] Disjunction (visaṃyoga) is the destruction [of defilements] by means of wisdom. (57d)
*Kṣaya* means cessation (*nirodha*). *Dhī* means wisdom (*prajñā*). By this, it is stated that analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) is the fruit of disjunction (*visaṃyogaphala*).

Whatever arises through the power of something, that is the fruit born of human effort (*puruṣakāraja*). For example: a concentration belonging to a higher stage [arising] from a preparatory mind (*prayogacitta*) of a lower stage; the untainted (*anāsrava*) [attainment] arising from a tainted (*sāsrava*) one; a mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) arising from a meditative mind (*dhyānacitta*), and so forth. However, it must be stated that analytical cessation is that which is attained through the power of something.
The unprecedented [result] belongs only to the conditioned;
the conditioned is the dominant fruit. //58cd//

A conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) dharma other than one that has already arisen is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) of every conditioned [dharma]. What is the difference between the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit? The fruit of human effort belongs to the agent; the sovereign fruit belongs even to the non-agent. For example, in the case of an artisan, his craft is both the fruit of human effort and the sovereign fruit; for others, it is only the sovereign fruit. Now, among these causes (*hetu*), which cause grasps or gives its fruit at what time? Five [causes] grasp their fruit when they are present.

The past [dharmas] grasp [their fruits], because they have already been grasped; nor do the future [dharmas], because they lack human effort (*puruṣakāra*). The same applies to the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*). However, it is not mentioned [in this context] because it does not necessarily possess a fruit. Two [causes] bestow [their fruits]. (59b')

The co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*) bestow their fruit while they are present; for the giving and receiving of the fruit by these two occurs at precisely the same time. The other two [causes], being present and past, [bestow their fruit]... (59c)

Regarding the two causes—the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and the pervasive (*sarvatraga*)—which yield a fruit: it is indeed logical that they do so when they are past. But how do they yield a flow-result (*niṣyandaphala*) while they are present? Because they cease immediately [after yielding it]. Once the fruit has been produced, both of them have become past, and the fruit, having already been given, is not given again. There is a fourfold classification regarding whether a wholesome homogeneous cause receives a fruit but does not give one: 1. It receives a fruit but does not give one. 2. It gives a fruit but does not receive one. 3. It both receives and gives a fruit. 4. It neither receives nor gives a fruit.

The first alternative (*koṭi*) consists of those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which one who is severing the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*) abandons last of all. The second consists of those which one who is reconnecting the roots of merit acquires first of all. However, it should be stated as follows: for one reconnecting [the roots], these same [acquisitions] constitute the third alternative; for one whose roots of merit have not been severed, they exist in all remaining states. The fourth alternative is excluding these aforementioned modes. As for the unwholesome (*akuśala*), however, the first alternative is as follows:

The first case concerns those acquisitions (*prāpti*) which one abandons last when attaining detachment from the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). The second case concerns those which one acquires first when falling away from detachment from the realm of desire. However, it should be stated as follows: there may be such [acquisitions] for one who is falling away. The third case concerns the remaining states of one who is already free from passion for the realm of desire. The fourth case is set aside by excluding these aforementioned modes. In the same way, this should be applied accordingly to the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) [mind] based on the attainment of or falling away from Arhatship.

Regarding the unobscured-undefined (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), there is a "subsequent member" [of the tetralemma]: whoever gives, he also receives. However, it may be that one receives but does not give, as in the case of the final aggregates (*skandha*) of an Arhat. But according to the restriction of having an object (*sālambana*), this applies moment by moment. Thus, for a wholesome homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), there is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) regarding whether it receives or gives its fruit. The first alternative is when, immediately after a wholesome mind, one brings forth a defiled or undefined mind. The second is the reverse.

The third [alternative] is that immediately after a wholesome mind, only a wholesome [mind] arises. The fourth is setting aside these aforementioned modes. In the same way, unwholesome minds and so forth should also be applied accordingly. But how is it that the fruit is "received"? Because it has attained the state of being its seed. One [cause], being past, bestows [the fruit]. (59d)

The ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) alone bestows its fruit when it has passed away, because a ripened result does not exist either simultaneously with or immediately after [the cause]. Furthermore, others speak of four kinds of fruits: the fruit of support (*pratiṣṭhā-phala*), such as the water-circle for the wind-circle, up to grass and so forth for the earth; the fruit of application (*prayoga-phala*), such as the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) resulting from [the meditation on] the foul (*aśubhā*); the fruit of the causal complex (*sāmagrī-phala*), such as visual consciousness and so forth resulting from the eye and so forth; and the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*).

Just as there is the emanation of a mind belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), this [emanation] is included within the results of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) and dominance (*adhipati*). The causes and the results have been explained.

Regarding this, he asks: "Which phenomena arise from how many causes? He replies: "In brief, these phenomena are of four kinds, namely: afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭa*), those born of maturation (*vipākaja*), the first untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*), and the remainder besides those. What, then, are the 'remainder'? They are the neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena excluding those born of maturation, and the wholesome (*kuśala*) phenomena excluding the first moment of the untainted. These four kinds of phenomena—afflicted, those born of maturation, the remainder, and the first noble ones—arise respectively [from four, two, three, and four causes].
Excluding the resultants and the universal [factors], the remaining [mental factors] arise together with those two and their own counterparts. (60)

Defiled (*kliṣṭa*) dharmas arise from the remaining five causes, excluding the ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*). Those born of ripening (*vipākaja*) arise from exactly the same five, excluding the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*). Other dharmas arise from the remaining four, excluding those two—the ripening and omnipresent causes. The first pure (*anāsrava*) dharmas arise from the remaining three, excluding those two—the ripening and omnipresent causes—and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). He asks: "Which are these four kinds of dharmas that have been explained? and replies: "Mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). (61a)
Now, as for those factors that are dissociated from thought and those that are material, he asks: "How are they? and replies:
"Likewise, others also [are so], excluding the associated [factors]. (61a'b)

Excluding the single associated cause (*saṃprayuktakahetu*), other factors such as the defiled (*kliṣṭa*) and so forth arise in the same manner as mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*). Among these, the defiled and those born of maturation (*vipākaja*) arise from four causes; the remaining ones from three; and the first pure (*anāsrava*) factors from two. There is no factor that arises from a single cause alone. The detailed exposition of causes is concluded.
What are the conditions (*pratyaya*)? Four conditions have been taught. (61c)

Where are they stated? In the Sūtra: "There are four types of conditionality (pratyayatā): the conditionality of cause, the conditionality of immediate antecedent, the conditionality of object, and the conditionality of dominant influence. Conditionality is the genus of conditions. Among these, that which is called "cause" consists of the five causes. (61d)

Excluding the efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*), the five causes constitute the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*). Mind and mental factors that have arisen, excluding the final ones, are the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). (62ab)

Excluding the final [moments] of an Arhat, the mental states and mental factors that have arisen are the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). It is called the "immediately preceding condition" because it is both equal (*sama*) and immediate (*anantara*). For this very reason, matter (*rūpa*) is not an immediately preceding condition, because its arising is uneven. To explain: immediately after matter belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), there sometimes arises non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*) belonging to both the desire realm and the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), and sometimes [matter] belonging to both the desire realm and the untainted (*anāsrava*) realm; thus, the manifestation of matter is disordered.

The venerable Vasumitra maintains that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is not disordered, because a second [moment of] matter arises within a single, uninterrupted stream of accumulated matter. The Venerable [Ghosaka] holds that it is due to the arising of more or less [matter]; for sometimes a small amount of matter arises from a large amount, as for example ash from a heap of straw; and sometimes a large amount arises from a small amount, as for example a banyan tree with its many branches and descending roots growing gradually from a mere seedling.

But is it not the case that mental factors (*caitta*) also arise in varying degrees—whether in wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral states of mind, or in the three types of concentration such as those with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*)? [The answer is: This variation exists with respect to different classes (*jātyantara*), but not within their own class (*svajāti*). For never does a greater number of sensations (*vedanā*) or perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and so forth arise [simultaneously]. Furthermore, does the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) apply only to its own class? This is not so.

The entire complex [of mental factors] is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for another entire complex; however, it is merely stated here that a large quantity of substance such as feeling does not arise from a small quantity of substance such as feeling. But those who maintain the homogeneity of the continuum (*santāna-sabhāgika*) believe that the immediately preceding condition belongs only to its own kind—for example, mind is [the condition] for mind alone, and feeling for feeling alone, and so forth in detail.

However, when a defiled state arises immediately after an undefiled one, the previously ceased defilement is the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for that [new] defilement; this is just as the mind of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti-citta*) is the condition for the mind of emergence (*vyutthāna-citta*). This [position] will not be accepted, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the first moment of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) could never arise. Furthermore, there are also formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).

For this very reason, because their manifestation is disordered, there is no immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for those [states] not bound to the three realms, since they manifest simultaneously. Why is the future not accepted as an immediately preceding condition? Because the future time is disordered, lacking the sequence of prior and subsequent. How then does the Blessed One know that "immediately after this particular future [state], this other future [state] occurs"? Through inference based on the past and the present.

The Blessed One indeed perceives the past path: that from such a kind of karma, such a kind of ripening arose, or from a dharma, a dharma [arose]; and he also knows that this present karma is of such a kind, and therefore from this as well, such a kind of ripening will arise, or from a dharma, a dharma [will arise]. And yet, this knowledge is not inferential.

Because, by means of inference from the past and the present, the Blessed One perceives scattered future entities directly and knows: "By this person performing such an action, this future fruit has been grasped. If that were so, then the Blessed One would not know the future limit (*aparānta*) without having seen the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). Others, however, say:

There exists, within the continuum of sentient beings, a specific formation (*saṃskāra*) dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) which serves as a sign of the fruit; by observing this, the Blessed One knows the future even without bringing meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) or supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) into manifestation. If this were the case, the Blessed One would be merely a "reader of signs" (*naimittika*), rather than one who possesses direct realization (*sākṣātkārī*). Therefore, the Sautrāntikas maintain that the Blessed One knows everything simply by the mere act of wishing to know.

For it has been said by the Blessed One that "the range of the Buddhas' cognition is indeed inconceivable. Now, if there were no fixed order for the future, why would it be that immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*), only the Receptivity to the Knowledge of Dharma regarding Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises, and no other dharma? And likewise, up until why would it be that immediately after the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama*), only the Knowledge of Destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) arises, and no other dharma? [The answer is: That whose arising is dependent upon another arises immediately after that.

For example, sprouts and so forth arise from seeds and so forth even without an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Why, then, are the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat not an immediately preceding condition? Because they are not connected to another mind. [Objection: But if that were so, since the mind that has just ceased becomes the mind-faculty (*manas*), then because of the absence of a subsequent consciousness, even the final mind would not qualify as the mind-faculty. [Response: The mind-faculty is characterized by its status as a support (*āśraya-bhāva*), not by its functional activity (*kāritra*); thus, its status as a support certainly exists.

However, due to the deficiency of other causes, another consciousness does not arise. But the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is characterized by its functional activity (*kāritra*); therefore, whatever phenomenon has been grasped as a fruit by it cannot be obstructed by any phenomena or by any living beings, such that it would fail to arise. Those phenomena which are immediate to the mind (*citta-samanantara*) are also those that are uninterrupted by the mind (*citta-nirantara*), though this is subject to a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*).

The first category consists of the mind emerging from a mindless attainment (*acittakā samāpatti*) and the moments of the attainment itself from the second moment onward. The second category consists of the birth and other characteristics (*jātyādayaḥ*) of the first moment of the attainment and of the state possessing mind (*sacittakā avasthā*). The third category consists of the first moment of the attainment and the state possessing mind. The fourth category consists of the birth and other characteristics of the second and subsequent moments of the attainment, as well as those of the mind emerging [from it].

Those phenomena that have the mind as their immediate antecedent (samanantara) are also those that are immediately preceded by meditative attainment (samāpatti). This constitutes a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭika): those which are the third and fourth cases should be made the first and second; and those which are the first and second should be made the third and fourth. How then can the emerging consciousness (vyutthānacitta), which is separated by a vast interval, be said to be the immediate antecedent of the consciousness of meditative attainment? Because it is not intervened by any other intervening consciousness. The condition of immediate antecedence (samanantarapratyaya) has been explained.

The objects of focus (*ālambana*) are all phenomena (*sarvadharma*). As appropriate: for visual consciousness together with its associated mental factors, it is visible form (*rūpa*); for auditory consciousness, sound (*śabda*); for olfactory consciousness, odor (*gandha*); for gustatory consciousness, taste (*rasa*); for tactile consciousness, the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*); and for mental consciousness, all phenomena. Whatever phenomenon is the object of focus for a given phenomenon, that phenomenon is never not the object of focus for that [given] phenomenon; even when not being currently apprehended as an object, it remains so by virtue of having such a characteristic.

Just as fuel, such as wood and so forth, is called "fuel" even when not being observed because it possesses that characteristic, so too these factors—the mind and mental states—are restricted to their respective objects by way of the determination of sense-field (*āyatana*), substance (*dravya*), and moment (*kṣaṇa*). Are they also restricted by way of the determination of their basis (*āśraya*)? He replies: "Yes. Those that have arisen are conjoined with their basis; those that have not yet arisen and those that are past are dissociated from their basis. Others say that even past [factors] are conjoined with their basis. The object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) has been explained.
The dominant condition is known as the causal [condition]. ||62d||

That which is the causal condition (*kāraṇahetu*) is itself the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). It is called the "dominant condition" because it is a predominant condition (*adhikaḥ pratyayaḥ*). Since all phenomena (*sarvadharmāḥ*) are both objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*) and dominant conditions, what is its predominance? Coexistent phenomena never become objective conditions, yet they do become dominant conditions; thus, this alone is its predominance. Or, it is the condition for that which is predominant: everything [is the condition] for every conditioned thing (*saṃskṛta*), with the exception of its own self-nature (*svabhāva*).

A phenomenon (*dharma*) may not be a condition for another phenomenon by any of the four conditions. This may be the case for an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) with respect to an intrinsic nature, or for an extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*). It may be the case for the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) with respect to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and for the unconditioned with respect to the unconditioned. Now, when these conditions perform their activity (*kāritra*), in what state of the phenomenon do they perform it? First, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) has been said to be fivefold;
among those, its activity occurs when [the effect] is in the process of ceasing (*nirudhyamāna*).

Two causes exercise their activity upon that which is ceasing—that is, the present—because it is facing cessation. Among these, the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*) exercise their activity; for even though the fruit arises simultaneously with them, the operation of those two occurs [at that time].
Three...
Regarding "that which is being born" (*jāyamāna*) [in verse 63b-c]:

that which is called "being born" is the future [dharma] facing toward its arising. In that state, the similar-cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), the omnipresent-cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and the fruition-cause (*vipāka-hetu*) exercise their activity (*kāritra*). Thus far is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The other two conditions, however, are the reverse of that. [p.101]

By the same logic of activity (*kāritra*) by which cause (*hetu*) and condition (*pratyaya*) were explained as being twofold, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) are to be understood through their opposites. The immediately preceding condition performs its activity while [the mind] is arising, because it provides an opportunity. The object-condition performs its activity while [the mind] is ceasing, because it is grasped by present minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), however, exists in every state by way of non-obstruction; this alone is its activity.
The conditions, together with their functions, have been explained.
Now, which phenomenon arises from how many conditions?
Mental states and mental factors arise from four.

Among these, the causal condition consists of all five causes. The immediately preceding condition consists of preceding mental states and mental factors that are not separated by others. The objective condition consists of the five objects as appropriate, as well as all phenomena. The dominant condition consists of all phenomena, excluding its own nature.

The two attainments [are conditioned] by three [conditions]. (64b) For the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), there is no object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), for these two do not have an object. However, their cause-condition (*hetupratyaya*) consists of two kinds of causes: the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), which includes birth and so forth; and the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), which consists of previously arisen wholesome factors belonging to the same level. The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is the mind of the attainment together with its associated mental factors (*saṃprayoga*). The dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) is as before. Because they are produced from the mental formation (*cittābhisaṃskāra*), these two attainments follow immediately after the mind (*cittasamanantara*).
Because it acts as an obstacle to the arising of the thought [of awakening], it is not the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
However, other [phenomena] arise from two [conditions]. (64c)

Others, however, maintain that dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*) and material factors (*rūpin*) arise from the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), exactly as prescribed. Entities arise from causal conditions; it is not the case, however, that God (*īśvara*), the Primordial Spirit (*puruṣa*), Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), or the like, is the cause of the entire world. What is the reason for this? If you indeed believe that establishment is produced by causes, then does it not follow that this very position refutes the claim that a single cause, such as God and so forth, is the cause of everything?
Furthermore, [the world] does not arise from God and the like due to [the impossibility of] succession and so forth. (64c)

For if God, or some other single cause, were the sole cause, the entire world would have to come into existence simultaneously. Yet, we observe that entities arise in a sequence. In that case, it might be argued that this sequence occurs by the power of God’s will: "Let this be produced now; let this cease; let this arise later. However, because there is a diversity of such wills, it follows that there must be multiple causes. Furthermore, that diversity of will would have to occur simultaneously, since its cause—God—is non-differentiated.

Or, if [the Lord] were to depend upon a distinction among other causes, then the Lord alone would not be the cause. Furthermore, since those [other causes] would also require a distinction among further causes for their sequential production, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Thus, by accepting that this succession of causes, characterized by successive distinctions, is beginningless, this proponent of the Lord as the cause would not have transcended the very logic of the Śākyaputrīyas (Buddhists). Even if [the Lord's] intentions were simultaneous, the world would not be produced simultaneously. If it is argued that [the world arises] according to [the Lord's] intention, [then the problem remains].

No; because there is no distinction among them afterwards. Furthermore, what purpose could there be for the Lord in such an effort toward creation? If it is for the sake of pleasure, then since He is unable to produce that pleasure without a means, He would not be the Lord with respect to that pleasure, and likewise with respect to anything else. And if the Lord takes pleasure in having created beings afflicted by many calamities in hells and other realms, then homage be to such a Lord! And this well-known verse concerning Him is sung: "That which He utterly consumes, that He is sharp, that He is fierce, that He is powerful."
"He who eats flesh, blood, and marrow is therefore called Rudra.

Furthermore, by one who accepts a single cause for the world, the manifest human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of other things would be denied. Moreover, for one who imagines God to be the agent even in conjunction with other causes, it would be a mere expression of devotion; for no activity of anything other than the causes is observed in the production of those effects. And if there were other auxiliary causes, God would not be the sovereign (*īśvara*). Alternatively, if the initial creation were caused by God, then because that too would be independent of anything else, the consequence would follow that it, like God, is beginningless.

The same should be stated, as appropriate, regarding the *pradhāna* as well. Therefore, there is no single cause for the world. It is their own respective karmas that produce them in this or that birth. But wretched people of unrefined intellect, while experiencing their own respective fruits of maturation, falsely imagine another [cause] called Īśvara. This concludes the discussion of what was said [in the verse]: "Others, however, are born from two. Now, how are the primary elements (*bhūta*) the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for the primary elements?
The primary elements are of two kinds as its cause. (65a)

The meaning is "the cause of the primary elements" (*bhūtahetu*). Regarding the derived matter (*bhautika*), however, [the relationship] with the homogeneous (*sabhāga*) and co-existent (*sahabhū*) causes is fivefold.
As for the derived matter, the primary elements (*bhūta*) are its cause in five ways. How so?

Through production, reliance, support, maintenance, and nourishment, this very same efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is further divided into five types: the cause of production, because [the derivative elements] arise from them; the cause of reliance, because once produced they conform to the primary elements, like relying on a teacher and so forth for the sake of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*); the cause of support, because they serve as a basis, like a painting; the cause of maintenance, because they prevent interruption; and likewise, the cause of nourishment. Thus, their nature as the causes of production, transformation, support, persistence, and growth is explained. (65c) The derivative [elements] are threefold with respect to one another.

The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is not always enumerated separately because it functions without distinction [from the other causes]; it is included within the causal, co-existent, homogeneous, and ripening causes. Among these, the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*) consists of bodily and vocal actions that follow the mind, which act mutually upon one another; it does not include other derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*). The homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) consists of all previously arisen [dharmas] for those that are homogeneous. The ripening cause (*vipākahetu*) is that bodily and vocal action of which the eyes and so forth are the ripening; for the primary elements (*bhūta*), that [ripening] occurs in only one way. (65d)

However, for the primary elements (*bhūta*), that derivative form (*bhautika-rūpa*) is exclusively a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*), since the primary elements are the ripening of that bodily and vocal karma.

Mind and mental factors have been stated to be the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) without distinction, but their specific restriction has not been stated—that is, which mind arises immediately after which mind. That must now be explained. In this regard, first of all, there are briefly twelve minds. To the question "For what purpose?", he says: "In the realm of desire, there are wholesome and unwholesome [minds], and the obscured and unobscured mind. (66ab)
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four types of consciousness: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-unspecified, and unobscured-unspecified.

In the form and formless realms, there is no unwholesome [consciousness] other than that; in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), three exist. Likewise in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Thus, these constitute the ten contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousnesses.
The untainted is of two kinds. ||66d||

[These are] the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*) and the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Thus, these constitute twelve minds. Among them, in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), from a wholesome mind (*śubha-citta*), nine minds [arise]. (67ab)

"Immediately after" will be explained later. From whatever wholesome mind exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), nine minds arise immediately thereafter: four belonging to its own level; two belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*)—the wholesome at the time of meditative attainment and the obscured (*nivṛta*) at the time of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*); one belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), which is exclusively the obscured at the time of rebirth-linking—it is not the wholesome because it is too remote; for the formless realms are distant from the desire realm by way of the four kinds of remoteness:
remoteness of basis, aspect, object, and antidote; and finally, the learner’s (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learner’s (*aśaikṣa*) minds.
That arises from exactly eight.

Furthermore, among those, a wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) arises immediately after eight: from the four belonging to its own level, from two of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*)—namely, the wholesome at the time of emergence, and the obscured (*nivṛta*) when one who is oppressed by a defiled attainment (*kliṣṭasamāpatti*) resorts to the wholesome stage of a lower level—and from the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) at the time of emergence. An unwholesome mind [arises] from ten. (67c)

Excluding the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), immediately after all minds of the form and formless realms, an unwholesome mind arises by way of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*).

From that unwholesome mind, four minds arise in immediate succession (*samanantara*); these are exclusively those belonging to its own level. Thus has been explained the case of the unwholesome in the desire realm.
And likewise, the obscured [state]. ||67d||

Immediately after ten [types of mind], and from that [unobscured-neutral mind] again, only four arise. "From five, the unobscured [mind] in the desire realm" is the rule that continues. An unobscured-neutral mind arises immediately after five: from the four belonging to its own level and from the wholesome mind of the form realm, which is the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*).
Therefore, seven minds arise immediately after [the first].

(68b) From the non-obscured-neutral mind of the desire realm, four minds of its own level [arise]; two of the form realm; and the wholesome [mind] arises immediately after the mind of transformation. The defiled [minds] arise at the time of rebirth-linking. Furthermore, the defiled mind of the formless realm arises only at the time of rebirth-linking.
From the wholesome [mind] of the form realm, eleven [minds] arise. (68c)

From a wholesome mind in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), eleven minds arise immediately thereafter—excluding the non-obscured neutral mind belonging to the formless realm (ārūpyāvacara). From nine [minds], that [wholesome mind] arises immediately thereafter. (87d)

However, a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) arises immediately after nine [minds]: excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm and the non-obscured neutral mind of the formless realm. An obscured-neutral mind of the form realm arises from eight [minds]: excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Therefore, immediately after the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), six [minds] arise: the three belonging to its own level and the unobscured-unspecified minds of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), excluding the [obscured-unspecified].
Furthermore, from three [minds], the unobscured-unspecified [mind arises].
The non-obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the form realm arises from only three [causes] belonging to its own level.
From that [state], six [causes] arise:
three belonging to its own level, and two afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) states of the desire realm. Just as the non-obscured-unspecified was explained regarding the form realm, so it is here.
The same principle applies to the formless realm (ārūpya).

Therefore, that [mind] which is non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) also arises from only three [minds] belonging to its own level. And from that [non-obscured-unspecified mind], exactly six arise: the three of its own level and the afflicted (kliṣṭa) minds of the lower realms. Furthermore, from a wholesome (śubha) mind... [69d']
Regarding the nine minds:

from a wholesome mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), nine minds arise—excluding the wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire and form realms.
That [wholesome mind of the formless realm] is the cause of six [minds].
Wholesome [thought] belonging to the formless realm arises from its own three [types], from the wholesome of the form realm, and from the thought of those in training and those beyond training.
From the obscured [neutral], seven arise:
from the obscured of the formless realm, the three of its own level, the wholesome and the obscured of the form realm, and the two afflicted [types] of the desire realm.

Likewise, that [uncontaminated mind] also arises from exactly seven [minds]: excluding the afflicted minds of the desire and form realms, as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training. The mind of one in training arises from four [minds].
From the wholesome [states] of the three realms and from that of the learner (*śaikṣa*).
But from this [state], five arise: those same four and that of the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
But the state of one beyond training [arises] from the fivefold [group]. (70d)
Precisely from that which was just mentioned:
therefore, four minds [arise] from that.

Furthermore, immediately after that mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), four minds arise: the wholesome minds of the three realms and the mind of one beyond training. The twelve minds are thus completed.
Furthermore, these twelve are made into twenty. How so?
The wholesome [mind] is divided into two types in the three realms: that acquired through application and that acquired by birth. (71cd)

In the three realms, the wholesome mind is divided into two types: that which is acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and that which is acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*). The neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind in the desire realm is fourfold: that born of maturation (*vipākaja*), that pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), that pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*), and that pertaining to magical emanations (*nairmāṇika*). (72abc)

The term "dividing" carries over [from the previous verse]. The non-obscured-unspecified (anivṛtāvyākṛta) mind of the desire realm is divided into four types: that born of maturation (vipākaja), that pertaining to postures (airyāpathika), that pertaining to crafts (śailpasthānika), and the mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta).
In the form realm, it is devoid of the craft-mind. (72d)

In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), it is divided into three types, excluding that which pertains to the arts (*śailpasthānika*), because of the absence of such arts there. Thus, these twelve states of mind (*citta*) further become twenty. The wholesome (*kuśala*) is divided into six types, and the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is divided into seven. The states of mind pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*) and so forth do not exist in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) due to the absence of postures and the like. Sound is also an object for that which pertains to the arts, whereas visible forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles are the objects of the others.

These are indeed mental consciousnesses; however, the five groups of consciousness belonging to the postures (*airyāpathika*) and the arts (*śailpasthānika*) are acquired through application (*prāyogika*). Others maintain that there is a mental consciousness produced by the postures which has the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its object.

Furthermore, among these twenty types of consciousness, which arises immediately after which? First, regarding the eight types belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), ten types of consciousness arise immediately after the preparatory (*prāyogika*) [wholesome mind]: seven of its own level (excluding the fruit of superknowledge), the preparatory wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). That [preparatory wholesome mind] in turn arises immediately after eight types of consciousness: from its own wholesome and afflicted [minds], from the preparatory wholesome and afflicted minds of the form realm, and from the minds of those in training and those beyond training.

Immediately after the mind acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*), nine [minds] arise: seven belonging to its own level—excluding the fruit of superknowledge (*abhijñāphala*)—and the two defiled minds (*kliṣṭa*) of the form and formless realms. That [birth-acquired mind], in turn, arises immediately after eleven [minds]: from its own seven as before, and from the two of the form realm—the preparatory (*prāyogika*) and the defiled—as well as from the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Immediately after the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds, seven [minds] arise: their own [seven] as before. These, in turn, arise immediately after fourteen minds.

From its own seven [minds] and from four of the form-sphere minds—excluding the preparatory and the fruit of supernormal knowledge; and from three of the formless-sphere minds—excluding the preparatory—it proceeds. Immediately after the deportment-mind and the mind born of maturation, eight [minds] arise: six belonging to its own level (excluding the preparatory and the fruit of supernormal knowledge), and the two defiled minds of the form and formless spheres. These seven minds, in turn, arise immediately after their own [seven] as previously described. Immediately after the artisan’s mind, six [minds] arise.

Its own [minds] arise from others, excluding the preparatory (*prāyogika*) and the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñāphala*). That [fruit of supernormal knowledge], in turn, arises immediately after seven [minds], from its own [minds] alone, excluding the fruit of supernormal knowledge. Immediately after the fruit of supernormal knowledge, two [minds] arise: its own fruit of supernormal knowledge and the preparatory mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*). That [preparatory mind of the form realm] also arises from these same two.

Now we shall explain the six [minds] belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*). Following a preparatory mind (*prāyogika*), twelve [minds] arise: the two wholesome minds of the desire realm, the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñāphala*), its own six [minds], the preparatory mind of the formless realm, and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). That [preparatory mind of the form realm], moreover, arises immediately after ten minds.

[From the state of] the two [minds] of the desire realm—the preparatory (*prāyogika*) and the fruit of superknowledge (*abhijñāphala*)—there arise eight [minds]: from its own four [minds], excluding the functional (*airyāpathika*) and the fruition-born (*vipākaja*); from the two of the formless realm—the preparatory and the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*); and from the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Immediately after the mind acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*), eight [minds] arise: the two afflicted minds of the desire realm; its own five [minds], excluding the fruit of superknowledge; and the afflicted mind of the formless realm. That [birth-acquired mind], in turn, arises immediately after five [minds]: its own [five], excluding the fruit of superknowledge. Immediately after an afflicted mind, nine [minds] arise.

The four [minds] of the desire realm—namely, the wholesome and the afflicted—follow their own five [minds], excluding the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-phala*). That [fruit of supernormal knowledge], in turn, arises immediately after eleven minds: from the desire-realm [minds] that are innate (*upapatti-pratilambhika*), postural (*airyāpathika*), and resultant (*vipākaja*); from its own five [minds], excluding the fruit of supernormal knowledge; and from three of the formless-realm [minds], excluding the preparatory (*prāyogika*) mind. Immediately after the postural mind, seven [minds] arise.

In the case of a defiled mind of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), five minds arise immediately after it: its own four [minds]—excluding the mind produced by application (*prāyogika*) and the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñāphala*)—and the defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*). Furthermore, that [defiled mind of the formless realm] arises immediately after five minds: only from its own [four], excluding the fruit of supernormal knowledge. The same should be stated for a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*). Immediately after the fruit of supernormal knowledge, two minds arise: only its own [two], namely the mind produced by application and the fruit of supernormal knowledge; and that [fruit of supernormal knowledge] likewise arises only from these two.

Now we shall explain the four [minds] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*). Following a preparatory mind (*prāyogika*), seven [minds] arise: a preparatory mind of the form realm, its own four [minds], and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). That [formless preparatory mind], in turn, follows six minds: from a preparatory mind of the form realm, from its own three [minds]—excluding the mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*)—and from the minds of those in training and those beyond training. Following a mind acquired at birth (*upapattiprātilambhika*), seven [minds] arise: its own four [minds] and the defiled minds (*kliṣṭa*) of the lower stages.

Furthermore, that [resultant consciousness] arises immediately after four of its own [types]. Immediately after a defiled [consciousness], eight arise: its own four, the two preparatory and defiled of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), and the two defiled of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*). That [defiled consciousness], in turn, arises immediately after ten: from its own four, and from the desire and form realms’ [states] acquired at birth (*upapattiprātilambhika*), the postures (*airyāpathika*), and the resultant (*vipākaja*). Immediately after a resultant [consciousness], six arise: its own three—excluding the preparatory—and the three defiled of the lower [realms].

Furthermore, that [state] arises from four [states], namely from its own [category]. Immediately after a state of one in training (*śaikṣa*), six [states] arise: the preparatory states (*prāyogika*) belonging to the three realms, the innate state (*upapattipratilambhika*) of the desire realm, the state of one in training, and the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). That [state of one in training] in turn arises from four: from the three preparatory states and from the state of one in training. Immediately after a state of one beyond training, five [states] arise—just as immediately after a state of one in training, with the exception of the single state of one in training itself. That [state of one beyond training] in turn arises from five: from the three preparatory states and from both the states of one in training and one beyond training.

What, then, is the reason that minds born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), and those pertaining to crafts (*śailpasthānika*) arise immediately after a mind of application (*prāyogika*), but a mind of application does not arise from these? Because they are engaged in the performance of postures and crafts, and because they proceed with difficulty and without effortless spontaneity (*anabhisaṃskāra*), these mental states are not conducive to a mind of application. However, since the mind of departure (*niṣkramaṇacitta*) proceeds effortlessly, its arising immediately after a mind of application is logical.

If that is so, then the *prāyogika* (preparatory) mind would not arise even from defiled minds, because they are incompatible. Nevertheless, for one who is weary of the manifestation of afflictions (*kleśa*), the manifestation of the *prāyogika* is logical due to the thorough knowledge of those afflictions. The [mind] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*) arises immediately after the learner’s (*śaikṣa*) and non-learner’s (*aśaikṣa*) minds, as well as after the preparatory mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because it is sharp. Because it proceeds without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), these [other minds] do not arise from it.

Immediately after a defiled state belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*), a state belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*) that is acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*) arises, because of its clarity. However, immediately after a defiled state belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), a state belonging to the realm of form that is acquired at birth does not arise, because of its lack of clarity.

There are three types of mental attention (*manaskāra*): mental attention to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), such as "form has the characteristic of being subject to transformation," and so forth; mental attention to general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which is associated with the sixteen aspects [of the four noble truths]; and mental attention based on resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), [directed] toward the [meditations on] the foul, the immeasurables, the formless liberations, the bases of mastery, the bases of totality, and so forth.

Immediately after the three kinds of mental attention (*manaskāra*), one brings the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) into manifestation; and from that [Path] as well, one produces precisely those three kinds of mental attention. This being so, it is logical to say: "one cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*) accompanied by the meditation on the foul (*aśubha*). Others, however, maintain that one brings the Noble Path into manifestation immediately after the general mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*). But having first tamed the mind through the meditation on the foul, one brings the Path into manifestation immediately after the general mental attention.

Therefore, with reference to the traditional succession, it was said: "one cultivates the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, accompanied by the perception of the foul. Others, however, maintain that even immediately after the Noble Path, there is only the general mental attention (*sāmānyamanaskāra*). It may well be that when one enters the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*) by relying on the three stages beginning with the *anāgamya*, one would bring into manifestation the desire-realm general mental attention immediately after that path. But what is the case when one enters the path of certainty by relying on the second dhyāna and so forth?

For one belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) is not capable [of this], because it is too remote; nor is that belonging to that level (*tadbhūmika*) attained, except for the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); and a noble one (*ārya*) does not again bring the aids to penetration into manifestation, for it is not fitting for one who has already attained the fruit to manifest its preparatory application (*prayoga*). Thus, another mental attention (*manaskāra*) of a similar kind, which is common to both, undergoes cultivation.

Namely, one will bring face-to-face the realization that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," "all phenomena are non-self," and "nirvana is peace. Regarding this, they do not describe it as follows: for one attaining arhatship by relying on the *anāgamya* stage, the emerging mind (*vyutthānacitta*) belongs either to that same stage or to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*). For one relying on the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it belongs either to that same stage or to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). In the remaining cases, it belongs exclusively to its own respective stage.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are three types of mental attention (*manaskāra*): those consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*), those acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*), and those consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*). There is no [mental attention] consisting of reflection [in this realm]. In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are three: those consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya*), those consisting of cultivation, and those acquired at birth. There is no [mental attention] consisting of reflection; for when they begin to reflect, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) itself arises for them. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are two: those consisting of cultivation and those acquired at birth.
