In that regard, immediately after the fivefold mental application (*manaskāra*), the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) becomes manifest, except for those [mental states] acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*), because [the Noble Path] is dependent upon preparatory effort (*prayoga*). However, immediately after the Path, even the desire-realm (*kāmāvacara*) state acquired at birth becomes manifest, because of its sharpness (*paṭutva*).
Regarding the twelve types of consciousness that have been mentioned, in which consciousness is there the acquisition of how many?
In the defiled [consciousness] of the three realms, there is the acquisition of six, six, and two respectively. (73ab)

When a defiled mind of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) becomes manifest, there is the acquisition of six minds: [the acquisition] of a wholesome mind of the desire realm by one who was previously not endowed with it, due to the reconnection of the roots of virtue through doubt or through returning to that realm; of the unwholesome and the obscured-unspecified minds; of a defiled mind of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), due to returning to that realm or through falling away (*parihāṇi*); of a defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), through falling away; and of the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*). In the case of a defiled mind of the form realm as well, there is the acquisition of six minds.

There is the acquisition of three [types of mind] belonging to the form realm and one unobscured-unspecified [mind] belonging to the desire realm, due to returning to that realm. There is the acquisition of the afflicted [mind] belonging to the formless realm and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), due to falling away. However, regarding the afflicted [mind] belonging to the formless realm, there is the acquisition of two: that very same afflicted [mind] and the mind of one in training, due to falling away.
Regarding the wholesome [mind], there is the acquisition of three when born in the form realm.

In the wholesome [mind] of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), there is the acquisition of three minds: that same wholesome mind itself, and the non-obscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire and form realms. In the learner’s mind (*śaikṣa*), there is the acquisition of four: that same learner’s mind itself, the non-obscured-neutral minds of the desire and form realms, and the wholesome mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*). This occurs through the noble path (*āryamārga*) during the detachment from the desire and form realms.
When that [remainder] remains. ||73d' ||

The remainder has been completed; that which was left over [is now explained]. Where the acquisition (*lābha*) of a mind is not explicitly stated, the acquisition of that very mind itself should be understood there, and not of any other. Others, however, state this without distinction:
"In a defiled mind, the acquisition of nine is said by the wise;
in a wholesome mind, that of six; and indeed, in an indeterminate mind, that of that very one."

In that regard, it should be stated that there are seven [types of mind] in a wholesome state of mind (*kuśala-citta*): because of the reconnection of the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla-pratisandhāna*) through right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), there is the wholesome mind of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*); because of the attainment of detachment (*vairāgya*), there are the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire and form realms; because of the acquisition of meditative concentration (*samādhi-lābha*) as appropriate, there are the wholesome minds of the form and formless realms; and because of the entry into the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānti*) and the attainment of arhatship (*arhattva*), there are the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). The remainder is to be determined from the very same explanation. There is a summary verse (*saṃgraha-śloka*): "In rebirth (*upapatti*), meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and falling away (*parihāṇi*)."
"And in the reconnection of the wholesome, there is indeed the acquisition of a mind not possessed [of it before]. Thus ends the discussion on conditions.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled "Instruction on the Faculties."
The Glorious Māyājāla,
Chapter III [p.111]
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the third treasury-location (*kośasthāna*).
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!

This must now be explained. The exposition of the mind and other factors has been made according to the restriction of the desire, form, and formless realms. In that regard, what are those desire, form, and formless realms? It is said: [4]
Hell-beings, pretas, animals, humans, and the six classes of celestial beings constitute the desire realm (kāmadhātu).

(1abc) There are four destinies (gati) and six classes of gods (*devanikāya*), namely: the Cāturmahārājakāyikas, Trāyastriṃśas, Yāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, and Paranirmitavaśavartins. This is the desire realm together with the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). As for how many locations this consists of, he says: (9)
That [hell] is twentyfold by way of the divisions of hells and continents. //1c'd//

The phrase "locations" (*sthānāni*) is to be understood as completing the sentence. There are eight great hells: Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, Tapana, Pratāpana, and Avīci. There are four continents: Jambūdvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Avaragodānīya, and Uttarakuru. Furthermore, there are the six classes of gods mentioned immediately above, as well as animals and hungry ghosts; these constitute the twenty locations of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

From the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods down to the Avīci hell; however, by including the receptacle world (*sabhājanaloka*), it extends as far as the wind mandala. And above this desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) consisting of seventeen locations.
To the question "How so?", he says:
Each individually:
(18) "Therein, meditation consists of three stages" (2b'c).
(19) The first and second meditations each consist of three stages. (20)
The fourth, however, consists of eight stages.

Among these, the first dhyāna comprises the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā deities; the second, the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara deities; the third, the Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna deities; and the fourth, the Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, Bṛhatphala, Abṛha, Atapa, Sudṛśa, Sudarśana, and Akaniṣṭha deities. These seventeen locations constitute the realm of form (rūpadhātu).

The Kashmiris maintain that there are sixteen [heavens], including the beings who dwell therein. It is said that within the *Brahmapurohita* heavens themselves, a more exalted place for Mahābrahmā has arisen—like a separate assembly hall with a single leader—but it is not a distinct level of existence (*bhūmi*).
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is without location.

For there is no location for phenomena (*dharma*) that are formless. Indeed, it is a fixed principle that past, future, non-informative (*avijñapti*), and formless phenomena do not abide in a specific place. However, that [realm]...

It is fourfold by way of rebirth. (3b) (4) The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is fourfold according to the distinction of rebirth; namely: the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). However, there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority based on location among these, for in whatever place those who have attained those meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) pass away, in that very same place they are reborn. Furthermore, when they pass away from there, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is produced in that very same place. (9)

Just as the continuum of consciousness proceeds for sentient beings possessing form by depending upon form, so too, in the formless realms, depending upon what does it proceed? (10) Here, the continuum of consciousness depends upon the group-homogeneity and the life-faculty. //3cd// (11)

The Abhidharmikas maintain that [the mental continuum] proceeds by depending upon the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). [Objection: Then why does the mental continuum of even material beings not proceed by depending on those two alone? [Reply: Because it is weak. [Question: By what is its strength produced? [Reply: Because it is born from a specific meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). For that attainment is characterized by the disappearance of the perception of form (*vibhūtarūpasaṃjñā*). [Objection: In that case, since it possesses strength precisely because of that, why would it require a further basis (*niśraya*) to proceed?

This also must be explained: just as for sentient beings possessing form, the group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) proceed depending upon form, so too for sentient beings without form, what do these two depend upon to proceed? They depend on each other. If that is so, why do those two not likewise depend on each other for sentient beings possessing form? Because those two are weak. In that case, by what are they strong? Because they are born from a specific meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).

This [dependence] is the same for the mental continuum (*cittasantati*), or for the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Therefore, the Sautrāntikas maintain that for formless beings (*ārūpin-sattva*), there is no mutual dependence between one mental continuum and another. Rather, for whichever mental continuum the cause of its projection (*ākṣepa-hetu*) is not free from craving for form, it arises together with form and thus proceeds depending upon form; whereas for that whose cause is free from craving for form, it proceeds without depending on form, because the cause has become liberated from that [craving].

Now, why are these called the desire, form, and formless realms (*kāma-rūpa-ārūpya-dhātavaḥ*)? A realm (*dhātu*) is so called because it maintains its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). A realm associated with desire is the *kāmadhātu*. A realm associated with form is the *rūpadhātu*; here, the middle term is elided, as in the case of "Vajrabālaka" or "pepper-drink. It is *arūpa* because there is no form (*rūpa*) therein. The state of being *arūpa* is *ārūpya*. Alternatively, that which is susceptible to transformation (*rūpaṇīya*) is *rūpya*; that which is not susceptible to transformation is *arūpya*, and the state of being such is *ārūpya*.

The realm associated with that is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The realm of desires is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); it is so called because it sustains (*dadhāti*) desires. The form and formless realms should be understood in the same way. What is this thing called "desire"? In brief, it is passion (*rāga*) associated with physical food and sexual intercourse.
(2) "Those various things in the world are not desires; rather, a person's desire is the passion of conceptual construction (*saṃkalparāga*).
(3) "The various things remain just as they are in the world; however, the wise subdue desire therein. (4) (5)
Because of the statement in the verse: the Ājīvika replied to the noble Śāriputra:

(6) "Those various beautiful things in the world are not desires; you say that desire here is the passion of conceptualization (*saṃkalpa-rāga*). (7–8) Even a monk might become an enjoyer of sensual pleasures if he conceives unwholesome thoughts."
The noble Śāriputra said:
(9) "If those various things in the world are sensual pleasures (*kāma*), and if it is not the passion of conceptualization (*saṃkalparāga*) that is sensual pleasure for you;
(10) then even your Teacher would be an enjoyer of sensual pleasures, merely upon seeing delightful forms. (11)

Furthermore, are all those phenomena that manifest within the desire, form, and formless realms necessarily associated with the desire, form, and formless realms? No, he says. What then? Those in which the attachments (*rāga*) of the desire, form, and formless realms lie latent (*anuśerate*). But what are these attachments of the desire, form, and formless realms? They are those which lie latent within the desire, form, and formless realms. Now, this is like the case of the horse-tether: "To whom does this horse-tether belong? "To him who owns this horse. "To whom does this horse belong? [The answer would be: "To him to whom the tether belongs. This is the same logic.

Regarding the phrase "the horse-tethering post of this [person]," both [the object and the subject] are unknown. This is not a matter of a horse-tetherer. For the locations in the desire realm have already been specified; the attachment of one who is not free from passion toward those locations is "desire-attachment" (*kāmarāga*). Whatever phenomenon (*dharma*) it underlies is also connected with the desire realm. In the same way, the attachments of the form and formless realms should be understood according to the circumstances for one who is free from passion for the lower [realms]. Alternatively, attachment belonging to the non-concentrated stage is "desire-attachment."

Attachment to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) is attachment to the realms of form and formlessness. (18) How can there be sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) in a mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*)? Because one relishes it after hearing about it or after falling away from it; or because, by the power of emanation, even the mind of the emanator possesses attachment. Or [it is so] because of the emanation of odors and tastes; thus it belongs to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*). This is because those two [odors and tastes] are not emanated by one belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*). Furthermore, is the triple world (*traidhātuka*) only one? There is no end to the triple worlds. As far as space extends, so many are the realms.

For this very reason, there is no manifestation of previously non-existent sentient beings; and even though incalculable sentient beings attain final nirvana with the arising of each Buddha, there is no exhaustion of sentient beings, just like space.

How do the world-systems abide? It is stated in the *Tiryaksūtra* as follows: "Just as when it rains with a downpour like the shafts of a chariot, there is no gap or interval between the streams of water falling from the sky; even so, in the eastern direction, there is no gap or interval between the world-systems as they undergo dissolution and evolution. As it is in the eastern direction, so it is in the southern, western, and northern directions."

However, it was not stated whether "above" or "below. Others say that it means both "above" and "below," because of a different reading in another version of the text: from Akaniṣṭha upwards there is again the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and from the desire realm downwards there are again the Akaniṣṭhas. Furthermore, he who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) with respect to one desire realm is free from passion with respect to all; the same applies to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpya*).

And whoever generates [the mind of awakening] by relying on the first dhyāna, he goes only to the Brahma-world belonging to that very world-system in which he was born when he generated it, and not to another. These three realms that have been mentioned—namely, those called by their own names such as the hells and so forth—are the five destinies within them. (4ab)

Hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, gods, and humans—by their very names, these five destinies (*gati*) are proclaimed among them. In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are four destinies and a portion of the fifth; in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), there is only a portion of the destiny of the gods. Furthermore, are there realms that are excluded from the destinies, such that these [destinies] are said to exist "within the realms"? Yes, there are; for the realms also have as their intrinsic nature the wholesome, the afflicted, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*), and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

As for those which are the five destinies, they are as follows: *(Note: The text fragment provided ends with the phrase "As for those which are the five destinies," indicating that the specific enumeration of the five destinies would follow in the original source.)*
They are exclusively non-afflicted and neutral (*akliṣṭāvyākṛta*), designated as sentient beings (*sattvākhya*), and do not include the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

(4cd) The destinies (*gati*) are exclusively unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); otherwise, there would be a confusion of the destinies. Furthermore, they are designated as sentient beings and do not have the nature of the intermediate state. It is stated in the *Prajñapti*: "The five destinies are subsumed by the four modes of birth (*yoni*), but the four modes of birth are not subsumed by the five destinies. What is not subsumed? The intermediate state. It is also stated in the *Dharmaskandha*: "What is the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?"

Derived from the four great elements, it is that translucent matter which is the eye-faculty, the eye-base, and the eye-element; it belongs to hell-beings, animals, those in the realm of the ancestors, gods, humans, those produced by meditation, and those of the intermediate state. Furthermore, in the Sūtra, the intermediate state is excluded from the [five] destinies. In which Sūtra?

There are seven existences: (18) existence in hell, existence as an animal, existence as a hungry ghost, existence as a god, existence as a human, existence through karma, and intermediate existence. For here [the latter two] are excluded from the five destinies (*gati*). And the Kashmiris recite the Sūtra: the Elder Śāriputra said, "Venerable sir, due to the manifestation of the outflows (*āsrava*) of those in hell, one performs and accumulates karma to be experienced in hell."

Venerable sir, for those who possess crookedness of body, speech, and mind, and who possess the defects and impurities of body, speech, and mind, it is their form, perception, feeling, mental formations, and consciousness that ripen as maturation (*vipāka*) in the hells. Once the maturation has come into being, one comes to be designated as a "hell-being. In this regard, Venerable sir, no hell-being is apprehended apart from those dharmas; therefore, the realms of existence (*gati*) are indeed unobscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).

In that case, the *Prakaraṇa* treatise must be reconciled, for it states: "All latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere within the destinies (*gati*). Since there are five types of rebirth-linking minds (*pratisaṃdhicitta*) belonging to the destinies, there is no fault here because the destinies are understood as including their points of entry (*sapraveśagatigrahaṇāt*), just as the term "village" includes the surrounding vicinity. Others say that even wholesome and afflicted states are included. As for the argument that karma-existence (*karmabhava*) is excluded from those [destinies], a state is not necessarily excluded merely because it is mentioned separately.

For example, among the five corruptions (*kaṣāya*), the corruptions of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*) and views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*) are mentioned separately; yet views are not themselves afflictions. In the same way, even though the existence of karma (*karmabhava*) is itself a destiny (*gati*), it would be mentioned separately for the purpose of making known the cause of that destiny. This same consequence would apply to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as well. But this is not the case, because it is inappropriate. A "destiny" is so called because beings go (*gacchanti*) to it; however, the intermediate state is not something to be gone to, since it arises at the very place of death. Furthermore, the formless realms (*ārūpya*) would also not be destinies.

Because it arises in the very place where death occurs. (8) If that is so, then the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not a "destination" (*gati*) precisely because it is an intermediate state; it is called an intermediate state because it exists in the interval between destinations. For if it were itself a destination, it could not be called an "intermediate state. As for what the Elder Śāriputra said—that once the maturation (*vipāka*) has been produced, one "enters the reckoning" as a hell-being—what he meant by "the maturation has been produced" was not that it is the maturation itself [that is the destination].

As for what was said there—that "O Venerable One, a hell-being is not perceived apart from those phenomena"—this establishes the negation of a *pudgala* substance that goes to a destiny; it does not negate other aggregates, for one says "a hell-being is not perceived apart from the aggregates. Furthermore, the Vaibhāṣikas describe the destinies as being exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Regarding these, some maintain that they have the nature of maturation (*vipāka*) alone, while others hold that they also have the nature of accumulation (*aupacayika*).
In this very context of the three realms containing the five destinies, they should be understood according to their respective order.
Those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions; those with diverse bodies and a single perception;
(16) and by way of reversal, those with a single body and a single perception, and the three formless [beings].
(17) These are the seven stations of consciousness. (6a) (18)

In the Sūtra it is said: "There are beings who possess form, diverse in body and diverse in perception, such as humans and certain gods. This is the first station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Who, then, are those 'certain gods'? They are the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and those belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, excluding those who were first produced [at the beginning of the aeon]. Their bodies are diverse, thus they are 'diverse in body,' because they possess many different colors, marks, and shapes."

(22) There are beings with form who possess diversity of body but unity of perception, namely, the gods of the Brahmakāyika realm who were first produced there. (23) This is the second station of consciousness. For those who were first produced there are all of one perception, thinking: "We have been created by this Brahmā. And it occurs to Brahmā as well: "These were created by me. Thus, because they perceive a non-differentiated cause, they are said to have unity of perception.

(25) However, the height, girth, physical form, mode of speech, and manner of wearing robes of Mahābrahmā are of one kind, while (26) his assembly is of another; thus they are "diverse in body. As it is said in the Sūtra: "It occurs to them: 'We have seen this being who is long-lived and remains for a long duration... Oh, that other beings too might be reborn here in our company! [p.116]

(2) And how did they see that this being had such a mental aspiration, thinking, "May we be reborn here"? Some say they saw him while staying in the Ābhāsvara heaven. But since they have passed away from there, how could they now—having not yet attained the second dhyāna absorption—recollect their former residence belonging to that level? Or, if they had attained it, how could they have become settled in the view of clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśadṛṣṭi*) with Mahābrahmā as its object? Others say they saw him while staying in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Even in that case, it is not possible for them to remain for a long duration because there is no obstruction [to their passing]. (6) How then could it have occurred to them: "We saw this being who was long-lived and remained for a long duration"? (7) Therefore, while remaining right where they were and precisely as they were recollecting his previous history, they saw him staying for a long duration; and having seen him, the thought subsequently arose in them: "We saw him. (8)

There are material beings who are uniform in body but diverse in perception, such as the Ābhāsvara gods. This is the third station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Furthermore, because the term "limit" (*paryanta*) is used here, it should be understood that the entire second dhyāna is intended; otherwise, where would the Parīttābhas and Apramāṇābhas be established among the stations of consciousness? In that [station], they are "uniform in body" because their color, gender-signs, and shape are undifferentiated.

Because they experience pleasure and because they experience neither-pain-nor-pleasure, they possess diverse perceptions (*nānātva-saṃjñin*). It is said that in the fundamental stage (*maulyāṃ bhūmau*), having become weary of the faculty of mental joy (*saumanasyendriya*), they bring forth the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*); and in the preparatory stage, having become weary of the faculty of equanimity, they again bring forth the faculty of mental joy from the fundamental stage.

Just as lords, exhausted by the pleasure of sensual desire (*kāmarati*), experience the pleasure of the Dharma (*dharmarati*), and being exhausted by the pleasure of the Dharma, [experience] the pleasure of sensual desire—does this consequence not also apply to those in the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven]? No, for they have no exhaustion from that bliss. What is the reason? The Sautrāntikas explain that "that bliss is tranquil (*śānta*), whereas mental joy (*saumanasya*) is untranquil because it causes the mind to leap up. As it is stated in the Sūtra, they possess the perception of diversity (*nānātvasaṃjñin*).

In that regard, those beings who have recently been reborn in the Ābhāsvara host of gods—being neither skilled in the dissolution nor skilled in the evolution of this world—become terrified upon seeing that flame; they tremble and fall into a state of agitation, thinking: "This flame, having burned the empty Brahma realm, will come back this way."

In that regard, those beings who have long been reborn in the Ābhāsvara host of gods, and who are skilled in the dissolution and the evolution of this world, reassure those frightened beings: "Do not fear, friends! Do not fear, friends! Previously also, this flame, having burned the empty Brahmā-palace, vanished right here."

Therefore, because they perceive the coming and going of the radiance, and because they perceive fear and the absence of fear, they possess diverse perceptions (*nānātvasaṃjñin*), not because they possess the perception of pleasure or neither-pleasure-nor-pain. There are beings with form who have a uniform body and a uniform perception, such as the Śubhakṛtsna gods. This is the fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). In that state, they have a uniform body because their color, shape, and characteristics are undifferentiated; they have a uniform perception because they possess the perception of pleasure.

In that regard, in the first *dhyāna*, they possess a single perception (*ekatva-saṃjñin*) by means of an afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) perception; in the second, they possess diverse perceptions (*nānātva-saṃjñin*) by means of a wholesome (*kuśala*) perception; in the third, they possess a single perception by means of a perception born of maturation (*vipākaja*). The three formless realms (*ārūpya*) are as described in the Sūtra. These are the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). What here is the station of consciousness? It consists of the five aggregates (*skandha*) associated with those [realms] and four [aggregates] respectively, as appropriate. Why is the remainder not a station of consciousness? Because the remainder is subject to destruction (*paribhedavat*).

What, then, is the remainder? They are the miserable destinies (*durgati*), the fourth dhyāna, and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). For in these places there are disruptions of consciousness; for this very reason, they are not stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). What, then, is this disruption by which consciousness is disrupted? In the miserable destinies, painful sensation (*duḥkhā vedanā*) is the disruption, because it is injurious. In the fourth dhyāna, there are the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*) and the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*). At the peak of existence, there is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), because it cuts off the continuity of the mind. Furthermore, he says:

Where those staying here desire to go, and where those staying there do not desire to depart—that is said to be a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). In the miserable realms (*apāya*), both [of these conditions] are absent. In the fourth dhyāna, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) have minds intent on departing, desiring to enter the state of non-perception (*āsaṃjñika*); noble ones (*ārya*) desire to enter the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*); and because their mental activity is not sharp, they do not desire the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). Thus, these seven stations of consciousness as described, along with the Peak of Existence and the beings in non-perception, are remembered as the nine abodes of beings (*sattvāvāsa*). (Verse 6cd)

For it is in these that sentient beings dwell by their own choice; others do not, because they dwell there against their will. Who, then, are these others? They are the miserable states (*apāya*). For in those places, sentient beings are made to dwell by the *rākṣasa*-demons of karma even though they are unwilling; they do not dwell there by their own choice. Therefore, those [other] abodes of sentient beings are like places of confinement. Elsewhere in another sūtra, seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are taught. Elsewhere...
Furthermore, there are four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

Which four? The station of consciousness associated with form (*rūpopagā*), that associated with feeling (*vedanopagā*), that associated with perception (*saṃjñopagā*), and that associated with mental formations (*saṃskāropagā*). What is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? They are, respectively, the four contaminated aggregates (*sāsravaskandha*).

Furthermore, these [four stations of consciousness] exist only in their own level (*svabhūmi*) and not in another level. What is the reason? For stability (*sthiti*) is indeed a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). And consciousness does not find a firm foundation within the aggregates (*skandha*) belonging to a different level by the power of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Why is consciousness itself not called a "station of consciousness," as it is said that the five aggregates constitute the seven stations of consciousness? Because a station is established by excluding the one who stands; for the one who stands is not himself called the station. Just as the king himself is not called the throne.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that those phenomena (*dharma*) which consciousness mounts and causes to move—according to the analogy of a boat and its helmsman—are called "abodes of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*). However, consciousness does not mount and move upon consciousness itself; therefore, it is not so described. If that is so, how do you explain what was stated in the Sūtra: "In the nutriment of consciousness, there is delight (*nandī*), there is passion (*rāga*); wherever there is delight and passion, there consciousness is established and mounted"? How can this be?

And how is it that the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) are comprised within the five aggregates (*skandha*)? In that case, when consciousness proceeds with attachment toward the aggregates comprised within the spheres of rebirth (*upapattyāyatana*) without distinction, consciousness is a station of consciousness. However, individually, just as form and the other [aggregates] lead to the defilement of consciousness, therefore, among the four stations of consciousness, consciousness alone is not declared to be a station. //7// (7d') (9) Consciousness is not stated to be a station. (8a) (10)

Furthermore, the Blessed One taught the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) as being the nature of a field, and [taught] that consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*) in its entirety is the nature of a seed. He did not, however, establish the seed as the field for the seed; such was the intended meaning he conceived. Those factors that coexist with consciousness are more suitable as its field; therefore, they alone are called its "stations."

Now, how are the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) subsumed within the seven stations of consciousness, or the seven within the four? Indeed, the four are not subsumed by the seven, nor are the seven by the four;
rather, their mutual inclusion is established through four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).

When considering their inclusion [within the aggregates], a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) should be understood: there may be that which is included by the seven [aggregates] but not by the four, and so forth. The first alternative is the consciousness among the seven [aggregates]. The second is the aggregates—excluding consciousness—within the miserable realms (*apāya*), the fourth dhyāna, and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). The third is the four aggregates within the seven [aggregates]. The fourth is setting aside these aforementioned modes.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this triple world (*traidhātuka*), which has been described as divided by distinctions such as the realms of rebirth (*gati*) and so forth, is to be known in this manner.
Therein, there are four modes of birth for sentient beings, beginning with those born from eggs. //8cd// (22)

The egg-born womb, the womb-born womb, the moisture-born womb, and the spontaneously born womb. "Womb" (*yoni*) means birth (*jāti*). It is called a "womb" because beings are born within it and become mixed together due to the commonality of their procreation. What is the egg-born womb? Those beings who are born from eggs, such as geese, cranes, ruddy geese, peacocks, parrots, mynas, and so forth. What is the womb-born womb? Those beings who are born from a placenta (*jarāyu*), such as elephants, horses, cattle, buffaloes, donkeys, pigs, and so forth.

What is the moisture-born (*saṃsvedajā*) womb? It refers to those beings who are born from the moisture of the elements (*bhūta-saṃsveda*), such as worms, insects, moths, mosquitoes, and so forth. What is the spontaneously-born (*upapādukā*) womb? It refers to those beings who are born all at once, complete with no missing parts, with unimpaired faculties, and endowed with all major and minor limbs. Precisely because they perform the act of arising well (*sādhukāritva*) through spontaneous birth (*upapādane*), they are called "spontaneously-born. Such as gods, hell-beings, intermediate state beings (*antarābhavika*), and so forth.
Now, it is asked: how many wombs are found in which realm of existence (*gati*)? He says: humans and animals are of four kinds. (9a) (5)

Humans are of four kinds. First, those born from eggs (*aṇḍaja*), such as the two elders Śaila and Upaśaila who emerged from a *kroñcī* crane, the thirty-two sons of Mṛgāra’s mother, and the five hundred sons of the King of Pañcāla. Second, those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*), such as those at present. Third, those born from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), such as Māndhātṛ, Cāru, Upacāru, Kapotamālinī, Āmrapālī, and others. Fourth, those of miraculous birth (*upapāduka*), such as the beings of the first eon (*prāthamakalpika*). In the same way, animals are also of four kinds; three kinds are indeed seen, while those of miraculous birth include the *nāgas*, *suparṇins*, and so forth.
Hell-beings are of miraculous birth;
(9b) (11) so too are intermediate state beings and gods.
(9c) (12) All hell-beings, intermediate state beings, and gods are exclusively of miraculous birth. (13)
Pretas are also born from a womb (jarāyuja).
By the word "also" (api), it is implied that they are also spontaneously born (upapāduka). A female preta makes this report to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"At night I [give birth to] five sons, and likewise during the day, five others."

I devour them after having produced them, yet even so, there is no satisfaction for me. (17) Which mode of birth (*yoni*) is the most excellent? The apparitional (*upapāduka*). Then, for what purpose does a Bodhisattva in his final existence (*caramabhavika*), despite having attained mastery over rebirth, resort to the womb-born (*jarāyuja*) mode of birth? Because he perceives that by acting in this way, he accomplishes a great purpose.

(19) By virtue of his kinship with the great Śākya clan, it was for the purpose of introducing the Dharma [to them], and for the purpose of winning the respect and devotion of others by showing that he belonged to the lineage of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); (20) and furthermore, it was for the sake of inspiring the trainees (*vineya*) by demonstrating that even those who have become human beings can attain this perfection.

Otherwise, if his family and lineage were unknown, people might speculate that he was some illusory being, thinking, "Is this a god or a *piśāca*?"—just as other heretics falsely claim that at the end of a hundred eons, such a magician appears in the world and devours the world through illusion. But others say:

For the purpose of preserving the bodily relics (*śarīradhātu*) within which humans and other beings, having established their progeny by the thousands, have attained both heaven and liberation (*apavarga*), the bodies of spontaneously born (*upapāduka*) beings do not remain after death; like an oil lamp extinguished at dawn, they vanish. For those who maintain that the Blessed One possesses the power of sustained miraculous transformation (*ādhiṣṭhānikī ṛddhi*), this [previous] explanation is not tenable. From one question, another question arises.

Even though the destruction of the body of spontaneously born beings (*upapāduka*) is not perceived, how is it stated in the Sūtra that "a spontaneously born *suparṇin* seizes a spontaneously born *nāga* for the purpose of eating"? It was not said that he eats it; rather, he seizes it for the purpose of eating out of ignorance, so there is no fault. Or, he may eat it as long as it has not died; however, once it is dead, he does not find satisfaction in it.

Which mode of birth (*yoni*) is the most numerous? Only the spontaneous birth. For it consists of two destinies (*gati*), a portion of three others, and all intermediate state beings (*antarābhavika*).
What is this so-called intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
It is that which exists here between the state of death (*mṛtyubhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*).

That personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) which arises between the state of death and the state of rebirth in order to reach birth in another location is called the "intermediate state," because it exists in the interval between [two] destinies (*gati*). How is it that this is said to be "born" yet not yet "reborn"?
Because it has not yet reached the destination to which it is going, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not "born" (*upapanna*).

(10cd) For one who has arrived (*upagata*)—that is, gone to birth (*upapattigata*)—is said to be "born," since the root *pad* has the meaning of "going. This intermediate state has not reached the destination to which it is going; therefore, it is not "born. What, then, is that destination to be gone to? It is where the projected maturation (*vipāka*) becomes manifest and reaches its completion. Those belonging to other schools maintain that the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) arises from the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*) as something entirely severed [from it]. This is not accepted. What is the reason?
Both by way of reasoning and by way of scripture. First, relying on reasoning, it is said:
(15) "Because of its similarity to the continuity of rice, there is the arising of existence without interruption" (11ab). (16)

For it is observed that phenomena existing in a continuum appear in other locations without interruption, just as in the case of the continuum of a grain of rice. Therefore, this continuum of a sentient being (*sattva-santāna*) will likewise be subject to appearance in other locations without interruption. However, appearance is also observed even when [the continuum] is interrupted, such as the appearance of a reflection from an object in mirrors and the like; in this way, the state of rebirth (*upapatti-bhava*) might arise from the state of death (*maraṇa-bhava*). But a reflection (*pratibimba*) is not a valid example because it is unestablished and because it lacks similarity. (11cd)

It is unproven that what is called a reflection arises as something entirely different with a distinct color; even if it were proven, it would not serve as a valid illustration because of its dissimilarity. How, then, is it unproven?
Because two things cannot exist together in one place.

For in that very same location, both the form of the mirror and the reflection are seen. Yet, it is not possible for two forms to coexist in a single location because their supporting bases (*āśraya*) are distinct. Likewise, due to the arrangement of different directions, reflections of forms situated in locations facing one another are perceived within a single body of water; however, it is not the case that two observers of a single form do not see it simultaneously. Therefore, it is not logical to assume the production of a second form there.

Furthermore, the coexistence of both shadow and sunlight in a single place has never been observed. Yet, a reflection of the sun is perceived in a mirror situated in the shade; therefore, its manifestation there is not logical. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "because two things do not exist together in one place," which two things are meant? They are the surface of the mirror and the reflection of the moon.

(3) For the surface of the mirror exists in one place, while the reflection of the moon is seen within it in another, like water in a well. (4) And that [reflection], being produced there, is not perceived elsewhere; therefore, it does not exist at all. Rather, such is the power of that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that such a perception occurs. For the differentiation of the capacities of phenomena (*dharma*) is indeed inconceivable. Thus, first of all, [the reflection] is unestablished (*asiddha*). How, then, is it not an illustration due to dissimilarity? (7) Because it lacks a continuum (*asantāna*). (8)

For the reflection is not part of the same continuum as the original object, because it is connected to the continuum of the mirror and because it exists simultaneously with it—unlike the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) which follows from the state of death (*maraṇabhava*). Furthermore, the appearance [of a reflection] in different locations is cited as occurring within a continuum through uninterrupted succession, not as something that is not a continuum; thus, the example is not comparable. Moreover, there is a lack of similarity because a reflection arises from two sources [the object and the mirror].

For the arising of a reflection occurs due to two causes: from the object and from the mirror. That which is the cause—the gift—arises depending upon them. However, the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) does not likewise arise from two causes, such as from the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*) and from some other primary cause; therefore, this example is also dissimilar. Furthermore, it is not logical to say that external semen and blood alone are the primary cause of the conscious being.

And where there is the manifestation of spontaneously born beings (*upapāduka*) even in total darkness, what [else] could be postulated there? Thus, first of all, it is not accepted on the basis of reasoning that the manifestation of the birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*) occurs as something severed from the death-existence (*maraṇa-bhava*). Therefore, the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) certainly exists. Furthermore, it exists because it is explicitly stated [in scripture]. It is said in the Sūtra: "There are seven existences: the existence of hell-beings, the existence of animals, the existence of hungry ghosts, the existence of gods, the existence of humans, the existence of karma, and the intermediate existence. This Sūtra is not recited by them. For this reason, therefore—

(12c’) From the *gandharva* (22): the descent of the embryo into the mother’s womb occurs through the presence of three conditions: (23) the mother is healthy and in her fertile period; the parents are in love and have come together; and (24) the *gandharva* is present. Apart from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), what else could this *gandharva* be? Furthermore, they do not even record this [as a *gandharva*]. How then [do they explain it]? They say: "the dissolution of the aggregates (*skandhabheda*) is present."

If this is so, how is the Āśvalāyana-sūtra to be interpreted? You know that this gandharva who has appeared—whether he is a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra; whether he has come from the eastern direction, or from the south, the west, or the north—it is not logical for the breaking up of the aggregates (skandhabheda) to have an arrival. Now, if even this is not recited, then [the answer is given] from the statement of the five [factors] (12d).

The Blessed One said, "There are five non-returners (*pañcānāgāmin*): one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*), one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*), one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyī*), one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyī*), and one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvaṃsrotas*). If there were no intermediate state (*antarābhava*), how could there be one called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state"? Some say that there are gods named "Intermediate" (*antara*). But if that were so, it would follow that those such as "upon rebirth" (*upapadya*) and the others are also gods; therefore, this conception is not correct. Furthermore, [it is known] from the *Gatisūtra*. (12d') [9]

In this sūtra on the "seven destinations of the noble persons" (*sapta satpuruṣagatayaḥ*), three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) are taught, distinguished by differences in time and distance. They are as follows: (1) just as a small spark of fire might go out even as it is being produced, so is the first; (2) just as a spark of iron might go out even as it is flying upward, so is the second; (3) just as a spark of iron might fly up and go out before even falling to the ground, so is the third.

Furthermore, it is not the case that there are such gods called *antarā* who are divided into three types according to the distinctions of time, place, and degree; this is merely a conceptual construction. Others, however, say: "One who abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*) either during the interval of the lifespan or during the interval near the gods is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*). Moreover, he attains parinirvāṇa while still within the realm [of desire], or while within the sphere of perception (*saṃjñā*), or while within the sphere of discursive thought (*vitarka*); thus, he is of three kinds."

The first attains parinirvāṇa after having taken up a communal status (*nikāyasabhāga*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The second does so after experiencing the prosperity of the gods. The third does so after entering into the communal recitation of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃgīti*) among the gods. Furthermore, the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyī*) attains parinirvāṇa after entering a communal recitation that is characterized by excellence, or rather, after having diminished his lifespan significantly rather than immediately upon being reborn; thus, none of these are connected with the analogies of the wood-shavings and so forth.

(19) Because there is no distinction in the movement to a [different] location; furthermore, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*) would also have to be recited among the formless realms (*ārūpya*), since he attains parinirvāṇa within the interval of the lifespan. (20) Yet, he is not so recited. (21) By means of the dhyānas, there are four groups of ten; by means of the formless realms, three groups of seven. (22) Having formed a group of six by means of perception (*saṃjñā*), the aggregate is thus complete. (23)

Thus, in this summary verse (*uddānagāthā*). Therefore, all of this as well is merely conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*). Now, even these sūtras are not recited by them. What can we do now, since the Teacher has passed into final nirvāṇa and this teaching is without a leader, split in many ways, and is even today being divided according to whim both in letter and in meaning? However, for those for whom this scripture (*āgama*) is an authority, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is established even from scripture.

As for what was stated in the Sūtra—that the Māra Dūṣī then fell with his own body into the great Avīci hell—how is that so? For he was embraced by the flames of the hell-dwellers even while still alive; having passed away, he reached Avīci by means of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This is the intended meaning there. Indeed, actions that are extremely intense and fully matured do not wait for the casting off of the body.

Therefore, for this person, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) ripens first, and subsequently karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*). How, then, is the following [scriptural passage] to be interpreted: "Having committed and accumulated the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*), one is reborn in the hells immediately thereafter"? The intended meaning is that one does not go to another realm of existence (*gati*). Thus, the fact that such karma is to be experienced upon rebirth is illuminated therein. Now, if it were interpreted according to the literal wording, it would follow that one must commit all five and not just one.

(9) And [the birth] occurs immediately after the action; it does not occur after living for some other period of time. Who, indeed, would not accept that the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is "in the process of being born" (*upapadyamāna*)? (10) For it is by means of the intermediate state itself that one is reborn in the hells immediately after death, because of its orientation toward that destination. Yet we do not say that one has already "been born" (*upapanna*). How, then, is this verse to be interpreted: (12) "O twice-born one, you have been brought near, afflicted by old age; you have reached the very presence of Death. (13) There is no dwelling place for you in the interval, nor is there any provisions for the journey. (14) [The verse refers to the state of being on the verge of birth.]

The intention here is that even among humans, there is no dwelling whatsoever [for such a being]. Alternatively, it means that even in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there is no dwelling for him, because he proceeds toward and reaches the place of rebirth. As for the question, "What is the basis for saying this is the intended meaning and not that other intended meaning?"—this same inquiry applies equally to you as well. Therefore, since there is no contradiction with the sūtra as stated in either of these two positions, this cannot serve as a proof for the non-existence of the intermediate state.
For indeed, a proof is defined as a resort when there is no other way.

Now, what kind of form does the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) assume for one who is about to go to a particular destiny? (19) Because it is projected by the same [karmic force], it has the form of the future "prior-time existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*). (13ab) (20)

By the very same karma by which a destiny (*gati*) is projected, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is also projected for the sake of reaching it. Therefore, whatever destiny one is destined to go to, the intermediate being has the form of that very destiny’s future "prior-time existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*). If that were so, then since an intermediate being belonging to all five destinies would be produced within the womb of a female dog or similar animal, a hellish intermediate being would burn the womb.

(23) Even in the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*), hell-beings who wander among the secondary hells (*utsada*) are not constantly burning; how much less so those belonging to the intermediate state (*antarābhavika*)? (24) Or, even if they were burning, just as they cannot be seen, they likewise cannot be touched because their physical form (*ātmabhāva*) is transparent (*acchatva*); thus, this is not a point for objection. (25) Furthermore, because intermediate beings do not come into contact with one another within the womb, and because of the obstruction of karma (*karmapratibandha*), there is no burning.

As for the measure of his body, it is like that of a five- or six-year-old boy; however, he possesses mature faculties. In the case of a Bodhisattva, moreover, it is like that of a full-grown youth, complete with the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). For this very reason, while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and entering his mother’s womb, he illuminated a billion four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpika*). As for why, then, the mother saw the Bodhisattva in a dream as a white elephant calf entering her womb: [it was a sign].

That is merely a sign (*nimitta*), because he has long since turned away from rebirth as an animal. For example, King Kṛkī saw ten dreams: (1) an elephant, (2) a well, (3) a clinging [monkey], (4) sandalwood, (5) a young elephant, (6) a grove, (7) likewise the consecration of Kapila, (8) an impure monkey, (9) a cloth, and (10) a quarrel—these are the ten dreams seen by King Kṛkī.

Furthermore, the intermediate state being does not enter the womb by breaking through it; rather, he enters through the mother’s birth canal. For this very reason, between twins, the one who is born later is called the elder (*jyāyān*), and the one who is born first is called the younger (*kanīyān*). How then is the commentary of Dharmasubhūti to be interpreted?
"Having assumed the form of a white elephant, beautiful with six tusks and four feet, the Sage, fully conscious, entered the bed of his mother’s womb as if entering a hermitage. (10–11)

This does not necessarily have to be interpreted [in that way]. For this is neither Sūtra, nor Vinaya, nor Abhidharma; it is poetry (*kāvya*). And in the poetry of poets, certain things are introduced through poetic license (*smāyojanatā*). Alternatively, it must indeed be interpreted [otherwise]: just as his mother saw him entering [her womb] in a dream, so too did he compose the verse. Furthermore, even the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) appears with a fully developed size and clothed.

Because of the predominance of a sense of shame (*apatrāpya*), the Bodhisattva is clothed; and as for the nun Śuklā, by the power of her vow, she was consumed by fire only to the extent that she was wrapped [in her robes]. Others are naked because of the predominance of a lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Now, what is this so-called "existence prior to birth" (*pūrvakālabhava*)? It is that which occurs after death and before the moment of rebirth. (13cd)

Existence (*bhava*), in its general sense, consists of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*). It is divided into four types: (20) *antarābhava* is as previously described; (21) *upapattibhava* is the moment of rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) within the realms of existence (*gati*); and beyond that, excluding the final moment of death, all other existence is (22) *pūrvakālabhava*. The final moment is *maraṇabhava*, after which *antarābhava* arises, provided one is to be reborn among sentient beings possessing form (*rūpin*).
Furthermore, this *antarābhava*: (14ab) is visible to those of the same class and to those with the pure divine eye. (24)

It is seen only by those belonging to the intermediate state who are of the same class; and those whose divine eye is perfectly pure and consists of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) see it. However, it is not seen by the eye of birth (*upapatti-cakṣus*), because of its extreme transparency. A being in the intermediate state of the gods sees all others. According to others, however, those in the intermediate states of humans, hungry ghosts (*preta*), animals, and hell-beings see each in turn, excluding those preceding them. It possesses the impetus of the supernatural power of karma (*karmarddhi-vega*). (14b') (4)

Supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is the ability to travel through space. Supernatural power produced by karma is "karmic supernatural power" (*karmarddhi*). Its "impetus" (*vega*) is its speed; one who possesses this is "one endowed with the impetus of karmic supernatural power. Because of the superior strength of his karma, he cannot be obstructed even by Buddhas. He is "possessed of all faculties," meaning he is complete in all five sense-faculties.

(14c') It is non-obstructive. (10) Obstruction (*pratighāta*) is *pratigha*. That which possesses this is "obstructive" (*pratighavān*); that which lacks obstruction is "non-obstructive" (*apratighavān*). This is because it cannot be hindered even by [substances] such as diamond (*vajra*). For instance, when a glowing iron ball is split open, a worm produced within its core is found to be pierced through. Furthermore, it cannot be turned back in any way from whichever realm of existence (*gati*) it is about to be born into. (14d) (14)

For the intermediate state of a human never ceases to be that and becomes the intermediate state of a deity or another; rather, it is certain that one must be reborn in whichever destiny one has manifested for, and not in another. Furthermore, does the intermediate state belonging to the desire realm also consume solid food? "Yes," he says, "but not coarse [food]. What then? It feeds on odors. (14d')

For this very reason, he is called a *gandharva*; since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the short vowel [in *gandharva*] is like [the shortening in] *śakandhu* and *karkandhu*. However, one designated as having little power (*alpeśākhya*) has a foul-smelling food, while one designated as having great power (*maheśākhya*) has a fragrant food. For how long does he remain? The Venerable One (*bhadanta*) says there is no fixed rule; he remains for as long as he does not obtain the conditions for rebirth, for there is no separate projection of a lifespan for him, because he belongs to the same homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).

Otherwise, death due to the exhaustion of that lifespan would result. If there were a mass of flesh as large as Mount Sumeru, it would all be filled with worms during the rainy season. One must then explain whether their intermediate states (*antarābhava*) had been waiting for that very moment, or from where they came at that time; however, this is not found in the Sūtras or the Śāstras. Rather, it is logical to say this: there is no end to those short-lived creatures who are greedy for odors and tastes.

Having smelled that odor, they become greedy for its scent and taste; as they die, they awaken karma conducive to the state of a worm and, through that craving, are reborn among worms. Alternatively, it is surely only at a time when those specific conditions are abundant that the karmas conducive to such a birth gain the capacity to bring about their maturation, and not otherwise.

(6) For it is thus: when the lifespan of beings is eighty thousand years, or even longer, Cakravartin kings are born; they are not born at any other time. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "The ripening of the karma of sentient beings is inconceivable. (8) The Venerable Vasumitra says that he remains for seven days. If he does not find the necessary conditions within that time, he dies and is reborn right there again. (9) Others say it is for seven weeks.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it is for a short time. For, because he seeks rebirth, having gone through the intermediate state (*saṃdhāva*), he forms the connection (*sandhiṃ badhnāti*). This occurs as long as the conditions (*pratyaya*) are not yet complete. Furthermore, it is certain that he is to be born in that specific place and in that specific birth; at that time, it is the very *karmas* themselves that bring about the completeness of the conditions. However, others hold that if it is not certain, then he is born in another place, in a similar birth.

For example, mating is most prevalent among cattle during the heat of summer, among dogs in autumn, among bears in winter, and among horses in spring; however, for the gayal, the jackal, the donkey, and the hyena, there is no fixed time. Thus, one who would otherwise have been reborn among cattle is reborn among gayals; one who would have been reborn among dogs is reborn among jackals; one who would have been reborn among horses is reborn among donkeys; and one who would have been reborn among bears is reborn among hyenas.

However, it must be stated that its intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) cannot arise in a different group-homogeneity (*nikāyasabhāga*) than the one for which it was projected, because it is projected by a single karma (or projected by desire). Indeed, this intermediate existence, having manifested for the purpose of reaching the destination of its rebirth, goes to that place of rebirth with a perverted mind, out of a desire for pleasure. (15ab)

For with an eye produced by the power of karma, he beholds his own place of rebirth even though it is very far away. There, seeing the sexual union of his mother and father, a male desire for the mother arises in one who is male, and a female desire for the father arises in one who is female. From the reverse [of this], aversion arises. Thus it is recited in the *Prajñapti*:

At that time, one or the other of two types of mind becomes manifest to the gandharva: either a mind accompanied by attachment (*anunaya*) or a mind accompanied by aversion (*pratigha*). Being deluded by these two, through a desire for sexual union, he clings to that place and falsely conceives that state as being himself. Then, when that impurity has reached the location of the womb, he becomes joyful and takes up residence therein.

Then his aggregates (*skandhas*) become solidified and the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) disappear; thus he is said to be "reborn. If he is male, he takes hold of the mother's right flank, sits with his back toward her and his legs drawn up in the fetal position (*utkuṭuka*); if she is female, he takes hold of her left flank, facing her belly. Now, if it is a neuter (*napuṃsaka*), it remains positioned according to whichever passion (*rāga*) it was attached to. Furthermore, there is no intermediate state that exists apart from the elements.

Because it possesses all the sense-faculties (*sakalendriyatva*), it enters [the womb] either as a female or as a male and remains in its respective place; subsequently, as the embryo develops, it becomes a hermaphrodite (*napuṃsaka*). This is now investigated: do the very great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the semen and blood themselves become the basis for the sense-faculties through the power of karma, or rather, are other great elements produced by karma which then serve as the support? Some say: "It is those very [elements of the semen and blood]. Others say: "It is other [elements]."

For the seed and blood, being devoid of sense faculties, cease along with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and that which possesses sense faculties arises; this occurs according to the principle of the cessation of the seed and the arising of the sprout, and is what is designated as the *kalala*. By explaining it in this way, the scriptural passage in the Sūtra—"born from the impurity of the mother and father as the *kalala*"—is well-established. Likewise, [the Sūtra says]: "O monks, for a long time you have increased the cemetery; a drop of blood has been taken up."

Others say that [the embryo] consists of other primary elements (*bhūtāntara*) alone, such as in the case of a leaf-worm. However, because the Sūtra speaks of the embryo’s arising in connection with its dependence on impurity, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra. Thus, first, one enters the egg-born and womb-born modes of birth; in other cases, they say it should be explained according to the circumstances. In this regard, the following principle is observed: "Another [being], desiring odors and a place [to dwell]," (15c) (13)

One entering the moisture-born womb proceeds toward the place of rebirth out of a desire for odors—whether impure or pure—according to one's karma. But one entering the apparitional womb proceeds out of a desire for a location. How can there be a desire for a location in the hells? Because of the perversion of the intellect. For he perceives himself as being tormented by cold winds and rain, and sees fire blazing in the hells; thus, out of a desire for warmth, he runs toward it.

Furthermore, perceiving himself being tormented by the heat of scorching winds, sunlight, and fire, he runs toward the coldness in the hells out of a desire for coolness. The former masters maintain that he runs while perceiving himself and those beings in the state corresponding to the karma he performed that leads to rebirth there. In that regard, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a god moves upward, as if rising from a seat; those of humans, animals, and hungry ghosts move like humans and so forth;
but the hell-being has his feet upward. (15d)
"Indeed, those who revile the seers— those self-controlled ascetics— fall into hell with their feet upward and their faces downward," according to the declaration of this verse. (22–23)

Regarding what was said—that one enters with a perverted mind—is it necessarily the case that every intermediate state (*antarābhava*) descends into the mother’s womb in such a manner? No, he says. What then? Four modes of descent into the womb (*garbhāvakrānti*) are taught in the Sūtra. What are the four? One enters with full awareness (*saṃprajānan*), but either remains or departs without full awareness; (16a) another remains with full awareness but enters and departs without full awareness; another enters and remains with full awareness but departs without full awareness; and another enters, remains, and departs with full awareness. These are the four modes of descent into the womb. Among these, the first three are those who enter with a perverted mind, while the fourth is one who enters with a non-perverted mind. Why is this? Because the intermediate state is like a dream. Just as in a dream one perceives oneself as entering a house, so too does one perceive oneself as entering the mother’s womb. Furthermore, because the intermediate state is similar to the state of consciousness at the moment of death, one enters with a perverted mind. For example, when one dies in the desire realm and is to be reborn in the same realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the desire realm and is to be reborn in the form realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, and odors, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the desire realm and is to be reborn in the formless realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant mental objects (*dharmas*), and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the form realm and is to be reborn in the same realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, and odors, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the form realm and is to be reborn in the formless realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant mental objects, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the formless realm and is to be reborn in the same realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant mental objects, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the formless realm and is to be reborn in the form realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, and odors, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the formless realm and is to be reborn in the desire realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the lower realms and is to be reborn in the higher realms, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the higher realms and is to be reborn in the lower realms, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with unpleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. This is how one enters the womb with a perverted mind. As for the phrase "one remains or departs without full awareness," this refers to the second mode of descent into the womb. As for the phrase "another enters and remains with full awareness but departs without full awareness," this refers to the third mode of descent into the womb. As for the phrase "another enters, remains, and departs with full awareness," this refers to the fourth mode of descent into the womb. Among these, the first three are those who enter with a perverted mind, while the fourth is one who enters with a non-perverted mind. Why is this? Because the intermediate state is like a dream. When one dies in the desire realm and is to be reborn in the formless realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant mental objects, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the formless realm and is to be reborn in the form realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, and odors, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the formless realm and is to be reborn in the desire realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the higher realms and is to be reborn in the lower realms, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with unpleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. This is how one enters the womb with a perverted mind. As for the phrase "one remains or departs without full awareness," this refers to the second mode of descent into the womb. When one dies in the desire realm and is to be reborn in the form realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, and odors, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the desire realm and is to be reborn in the formless realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant mental objects, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the formless realm and is to be reborn in the desire realm, one perceives the place of birth as being filled with pleasant forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and thus one enters with a perverted mind. When one dies in the lower realms and is to be reborn in the higher realms, one perceives the place of
Another also remains (16b);
the phrase "being clearly conscious" carries over [from the previous context]. By the word "also," it is implied that he also enters (16b').
Another [remains]. (16b') (6)
He also emerges with full awareness; he enters, and likewise remains, with full awareness. Another is deluded in all [three stages].

Furthermore, someone else acts entirely without clear comprehension (*asaṃprajānan*); he enters [the womb] without clear comprehension, and likewise remains and even departs [from it]. These four modes of descent into the womb have been taught in reverse order for the sake of conforming to the metrical composition of the verse.
An egg-born being (*aṇḍaja*) is always [thus]. //16d'// (12)

A being born from an egg always acts while entirely deluded. How can one who is already born from an egg enter a womb? Furthermore, even one who is yet to be born is "born from an egg. Alternatively, designations are made by means of future names; for example, as it is said in the Sūtra, "one conditions the conditioned," or in common worldly usage, "he cooks rice" or "he grinds flour. Therefore, this is not a fault.

Furthermore, how does one enter the mother’s womb without clear comprehension (*asaṃprajānan*), and likewise until emerging from it; or how does one do so with clear comprehension (*saṃprajānan*)? First, for a being of little power (*alpeśākhya*), as he enters the mother’s womb, two such perverted perceptions and convictions (*viparītau saṃjñādhimokṣau*) arise: "The wind is blowing" and "the rain is falling."

[Thinking,] "It is cold, it is a foul day, or there is a great clamor from a large crowd; alas, let me enter a thicket of grass (18), or a dense forest, or crawl into a grass hut, or to the foot of a tree, or to the base of a wall," he perceives: "While staying in these, I am staying; while departing from these, I am departing. But for a being of great renown [the thought is]: "Let me enter a grove, or a park, or ascend a palace, or a gabled chamber, or a couch."

"I am thus staying; I am thus departing. In this way, for as long as he enters [the womb] until he departs, he does so without clear comprehension (*asaṃprajānan*). But one with clear comprehension (*saṃprajānan*) correctly understands: "I am entering the mother's womb; I am staying right here; I am departing from right here. In him, no perverted perceptions or convictions (*saṃjñā-adhimokṣa*) arise. Furthermore, it is taught in this regard:
"There are three types of entry into the womb (*garbhāvakrānti*), belonging to the Wheel-turning Kings (*cakravartin*) and the Self-arisen Ones (*svayaṃbhu*). (17ab) (25)

[This applies] to universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), the two types of self-arisen ones (*svayaṃbhū*—namely, *pratyekabuddhas* and *saṃbuddhas*). As he will state at the end, "respectively. Among these, the first [case] concerns the universal monarch: for he enters [the womb] with full awareness (*saṃprajānan*), but neither remains nor departs [with full awareness]. The *pratyekabuddha* also remains [with full awareness]; the Buddha also departs [with full awareness]. Here too, the designation is made by way of their future status. Or rather, it is due to the clarity of their karma, their knowledge, or both, respectively. (17cd)

The first [type of person] consists of those whose actions are pure and who perform noble meritorious deeds; the second consists of those whose knowledge is clear and who have cultivated analytical investigation through extensive learning (*bāhuśrutya*); the third consists of those whose meritorious actions and knowledge are both clear. It is precisely these individuals—such as the universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and others—who are appropriately associated with these [three types] respectively. It follows that for all others, the fourth type applies. At this point, the outsiders (*bāhyaka*), adhering to the doctrine of a self (*ātmavāda*), object: "If it is asserted that a sentient being transmigrates from one world to another, then the self is established. This [position] is now refuted.
There is no self.

Of what kind would such a self be—that which is imagined to cast off these aggregates and link up with other aggregates? Such an internal agent (*antarvyāpārapuruṣa*) does not exist. Thus it was said by the Blessed One: "Action exists and its maturation exists, but an agent is not found—[one] who casts off these aggregates and links up with other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṃketa*)."

In this regard, the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṃketa*) is as follows: namely, "when this exists, that comes to be," and so forth, in detail, [referring to] dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). What kind of self (*ātman*), then, is not denied?

If it is merely the aggregates (*skandhamātra*) that is metaphorically designated as the "self," then that is not denied. If that were the case, however, it would follow that the aggregates themselves migrate to another world; yet it is not the case here that the mere aggregates migrate.
Conditioned by afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, [the continuum] enters the womb through the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), like a lamp.

(18cd) For the aggregates (*skandha*) are momentary; they lack the power to migrate. However, the mere aggregates, permeated by afflictions and karma, enter the mother’s womb by means of a continuity designated as the "intermediate state. Just as a lamp, though momentary, reaches another location by way of its continuity—thus, there is no such fault. (19–20)

Therefore, it is established that even though there is no self (*ātman*), the continuum (*saṃtāna*) of the aggregates (*skandha*), conditioned by afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, enters the mother’s womb. Furthermore, that continuum, having grown gradually according to its projection, goes again to the next world through afflictions and karma. (19abc)

For the projection of the entire continuum of the aggregates (*skandha-santāna*) is not equal, due to the difference in the karma that determines lifespan (*āyuṣya-karman*). Therefore, for whichever [being] there is a projection for a certain duration, for that long its growth occurs gradually. By what sequence? First there is the *kalala*; from the *kalala* the *arbuda* is born;
from the *arbuda* the *peśī* is born; from the *peśī* the *ghana* is born.

From the *ghana* arise the secondary branches (*praśākhā*), as well as the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and so forth; likewise, the material sense-faculties (*indriyāṇi rūpīṇi*) and the minor marks (*vyañjanāni*) appear in succession.

Thus say the Noble Ones (*āryāḥ*). These are the five stages of the embryo (*garbhāvasthā*): the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, *ghana*, and *praśākhā*. Then, after some time, when that thorn of the embryo has reached full maturity, winds born of the ripening of karma (*karmavipākajā vāyavaḥ*) blow within the mother’s womb; these winds turn that thorn of the embryo and position it facing toward the exit-door of the mother’s body.

Like a large wooden log that has been displaced from its position, it turns about in great suffering.
