If, however, at some time due to an improper diet or conduct of the mother, or through the fault of past karma, the fetus meets with destruction while still in the womb, then women skilled in childbirth or nurses for infants—having smeared their hands with lukewarm ghee, oil, well-ground *śālmalī* paste, or another substance—apply a sharp, thin blade there.

Having inserted their hands into that great wound of the channels of desire—which arises from the ripening of past karma, which is covered by a thin skin riddled with holes, which is like a cesspool of excrement, a foul-smelling, dark, and filthy pool, a dwelling for many thousands of swarms of worms, constantly discharging fluids, requiring perpetual treatment, soaked, decomposed, boiled, and slippery with semen, blood, marrow, and impurities; which is most loathsome to behold—they cut off limb after limb and pull them out.

Furthermore, he is led to some state of existence by previous karma to be experienced in a subsequent life. Then, if he is born safely, his mother—desiring a son—or her attendants take hold of the newborn with their hands, which feel like knives or caustic acid to his body that is like a fresh wound; they bathe him and nourish him with breast milk or clarified butter, gradually training him to consume solid food.

(18) Due to the increase of that [defilement] and the maturation of the sense faculties, the afflictions (*kleśa*) manifest once again and karma undergoes accumulation. (19) Through these, after the dissolution of the body, he goes again to the next world by means of the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as before. (20) Thus is the beginningless wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*). //19d// (21)

In this manner, birth has its cause in afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma; from that [birth], there arise again afflictions and karma, and from those, once more birth. Thus, the wheel of existence (*bhavacakra*) should be understood as being without beginning. For if a beginning were postulated, it would follow that it must be without a cause among these [factors]; and if it were without a cause, all of this [existence] would manifest as being without a cause.

The causal efficacy of seeds and other factors in relation to sprouts and so forth is observed, as is the efficacy of fire and other factors in relation to things produced by cooking (*pākaja*), due to the restriction of place and time. Therefore, there is no manifestation that is without a cause. Furthermore, the doctrine asserting the existence of an eternal cause has already been refuted previously. Consequently, there is indeed no beginning to *saṃsāra*. However, an end is logical because of the exhaustion of causes; since birth is dependent upon causes, it is like a sprout [ceasing] upon the exhaustion of the seed.
This very continuum of the aggregates (*skandhasantāna*) has thus been taught as existing through the three stages of birth.
That dependent origination consists of twelve members and three sections.

(20ab) In this context, the twelve members are: ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), existence (*bhava*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). The three sections are the prior limit, the subsequent limit, and the middle—the past, future, and present births. How are the twelve members established within these three sections?
Two each for the prior and subsequent limits, and eight in the middle. (20cd) (9)

Ignorance and the formative forces belong to the prior limit; birth and old age and death belong to the subsequent limit; the remaining eight belong to the middle. But do these eight members exist in every birth? He says: No. Of what [birth], then? Of one that is complete. (20d')

One who possesses completeness (*paripūri*) is called "complete"; this refers here to the person (*pudgala*) who experiences all these intermediate stages, and not to one who dies in the interval itself, nor to one belonging to the realms of form (*rūpāvacara*) or formlessness (*ārūpyāvacara*). For thus, in the *Mahānidānaparyāya*, only a person belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*) is specified, based on the statement: "If, Ānanda, consciousness were not to descend into the mother’s womb..."

(15) However, when dependent origination is said to be twofold—namely, pertaining to the prior limit (*paurvāntika*) and pertaining to the subsequent limit (*aparāntika*)—then seven members constitute that which pertains to the prior limit, ending with sensation (*vedanā*); five [members] constitute that which pertains to the subsequent limit. This is because of the inclusion of the prior and subsequent limits together with their respective fruits and causes. (17) Now, what are these [factors] beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*)? (18) Ignorance is the state of past afflictions (*kleśa*). (21a) (19)

That state of affliction (*kleśa*) in a previous birth is here called "ignorance" (*avidyā*), because of its association with them and because they manifest under its influence—just as when one says "the king is arriving," it is established that his retinue is also arriving. "Formations" (*saṃskāra*) refer to the state of past karma;

the term "ten" [from the previous verse] carries over. That state of meritorious and other types of karma in a previous birth alone, which results in maturation (*vipāka*) here [in this life], is called "formations."
Consciousness, however, consists of the aggregates at the moment of rebirth-linking (21c).
At the moment of linking with the mother’s womb, the five aggregates are consciousness. Name-and-form follows after that (21d).

Prior to the arising of the six sense bases—that is, from the moment after the linking consciousness until the six sense bases have not yet arisen—that state is called "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*). Although one should have said "prior to the arising of the four [mental] sense bases," the term "six sense bases" is used because at that time they are established as such. That [state of name-and-form] precedes the coming together of the triad.
Once the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have arisen, that stage is called "the six sense bases" as long as there is no conjunction of the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness.

(7) Contact (*sparśa*) exists prior to the capacity to discern the causes of pleasure, pain, and so forth. (8) From the conjunction of the three, contact arises; that stage lasts as long as it is not capable of discerning the causes of the three types of feeling. (9) That stage is called "contact. When the capacity for discernment is present, (10) [it is called "feeling"].
Feeling (*vitti*) precedes sexual union;
it is the stage of feeling as long as sexual desire has not yet become active.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) belongs to one who possesses desire for enjoyments and sexual union.

The state in which there is the active manifestation of passion for the qualities of sensual pleasure and sexual intercourse, prior to engaging in the search for those objects, is called *tṛṣṇā* (craving).
(14) However, *upādāna* (clinging) belongs to one who runs about in all directions in order to obtain enjoyments.
(15) That state in which, having entered upon the search to obtain objects, one runs everywhere—that state is called *upādāna*. And while thus running about, (16–17) [one becomes *bhava*].

That karma which produces the fruit of future existence is "existence" (*bhava*). (24ab) As he runs about for the sake of attaining sense objects, he accumulates karma leading to renewed existence; this is his "existence. For by means of that karma, when one has passed away from here, there occurs a rebirth-linking (*pratisaṃdhi*) in the future. That very rebirth-linking is "birth" (*jāti*) once again. (24c) (21)

That which is the factor of consciousness (*vijñāna*) in this very life is itself its birth (*jāti*) in another existence; from that point onward, until the end of knowledge, there is aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). 24d. (23)

From birth onwards, up to the stage of sensation, is old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Those very four members here—name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and sensation (*vedanā*)—are themselves called "old age and death" in another context; thus, these are the twelve members. Furthermore, this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is said to be fourfold: momentary (*kṣaṇika*), prolonged (*prākarṣika*), relational (*sāmbandhika*), and situational (*āvasthika*). How is it momentary? Indeed, even in a single moment, the twelve members exist.

For example, by the power of greed, one might deprive a living being of life. That which is delusion (*moha*) is ignorance (*avidyā*). That which is volition (*cetanā*) is formative action (*saṃskāra*). The specific discernment of objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*). The four aggregates (*skandha*) co-arising with consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). The sense-faculties established within name-and-form are the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The contact of the six sense-bases is contact (*sparśa*). The experience of contact is feeling (*vedanā*). That which is greed is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

The secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) associated with those [aggregates] are *upādāna*. The bodily and vocal actions arising from them are *bhava*. The relinquishing of those factors is *jāti* (birth); their maturation is *jarā* (aging); and their dissolution is *maraṇa* (death). Furthermore, they say: "Momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) and "relational" (*sāmbandhika*) refer to dependent origination as it is taught in the *Prakaraṇapāda*: "What is dependent origination? It is all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). "Staged" (*āvasthika*) refers to the twelve stages consisting of the five aggregates, which are connected across three consecutive births.
That same [dependent origination] is protracted (*prākarṣika*). Among these, which one is intended by the Blessed One?
It is said that this one is intended as situational (*āvasthika*).
If each member [of dependent origination] consists of the five aggregates, for what reason did he proclaim only those factors beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*)?
The mention of the members [of dependent origination] is by way of their predominance.

(25b) One has designated the state in which ignorance is predominant as "ignorance," and the state in which formations are predominant as "formations," continuing thus up to old age and death; therefore, there is no fault. But what is the reason that in the Sūtra twelve members are taught, whereas in the Prakaraṇas it is otherwise? [The question is: "What is dependent origination? It is all conditioned phenomena. The teaching in the Sūtra is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), while the exposition in the Abhidharma is based on the defining characteristics (*lākṣaṇika*).

Furthermore, there is a distinction [of dependent origination] as being situational (*āvasthika*), momentary (*kṣaṇika*), prolonged (*prākarṣika*), relational (*sāṃbandhika*), pertaining to sentient beings (*sattvākhya*), and not pertaining to sentient beings (*asattvākhya*). Why, then, is it taught in the Sūtra as pertaining only to sentient beings?
(25cd) It is for the sake of dispelling delusion regarding the prior, the subsequent, and the intermediate limits.

For this very reason, it consists of three sections (*trikāṇḍa*). Among these, delusion regarding the past (*pūrvāntasaṃmoha*) is that from which arises this doubt: "Did I indeed exist in past time, or did I not exist? Who indeed was I, and how indeed was I? Delusion regarding the future (*aparāntasaṃmoha*) is that from which arises this doubt: "Shall I indeed exist in future time? and so forth. Delusion regarding the middle (*madhyasaṃmoha*) is that from which arises this doubt: "What indeed is this? Who are we? And who shall we become?"

In order to turn back these three kinds of delusion, the *pratītyasamutpāda* consisting of three sections was taught in the Sūtra specifically with reference to those called "beings" (*sattva*), namely, in due order: ignorance (*avidyā*) and the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), and birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), as well as consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to existence (*bhava*).

For it is said in the Sūtra itself: "Monks, when a monk has seen dependent origination and dependently originated phenomena thus as they really are with correct wisdom, he does not resort to the past, thinking, 'Did I indeed exist in the past? and so forth. Others maintain that craving, grasping, and becoming are also mentioned for the purpose of turning back delusion regarding the future.
For these are indeed the causes of that very [suffering]. Furthermore, this twelvefold dependent origination should be understood as having three natures:
afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and bases (*vastu*). Among these, the afflictions consist of three [links].

Three members have affliction as their intrinsic nature: ignorance, craving, and grasping. (8) Two are karma: (26a') (9) two members have karma as their intrinsic nature, namely, formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*). (10)

(26b) (11) Seven bases (*vastu*): the seven members whose intrinsic nature is that of a base are consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death, because they serve as the support for afflictions and karma. And just as the seven members are the bases, so too are they the fruit. (26b') (14)

Only seven members are of the nature of results; the remaining five are of the nature of causes, because they consist of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). What, then, is the reason that cause and result are expanded in the middle [section]? Because the [factors of] the present existence (*vastu*) are divided into five ways, while affliction is divided into two ways. In the future time, the result is condensed because it is divided into only two ways; in the past time, the cause is condensed because the affliction is taught by way of a single aspect.
Thus, there is a condensation of cause and result in the two [extremes], based on inference from the middle. (26cd)

For, by means of the middle [life] alone, the detailed expansion of cause and effect for both the prior limit and the posterior limit can be inferred; thus it was not mentioned [separately], so that one would not have to exert further effort.

If, indeed, dependent origination consists of only twelve members, then, this being the case, because no cause for ignorance is taught, saṃsāra would have a beginning; and because no fruit for old age and death is taught, it would have an end. Or else, another member would have to be added, and yet another for that one as well—thus there would be the consequence of an infinite regress. It need not be added, because it has been shown here by the Blessed One:
"From affliction, affliction and action arise; from those, the basis [of existence] arises; and from that, again..."

Objects and afflictions arise; this is the method of the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*). (27) From affliction arises affliction: from craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises grasping (*upādāna*); from affliction arises karma: from grasping arises becoming (*bhava*), and from ignorance (*avidyā*) arise formative forces (*saṃskāra*). From karma arises the object: from formative forces arises consciousness (*vijñāna*), and from becoming arises birth (*jāti*). From the object arises the object: from consciousness arise name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) up to feeling (*vedanā*) from contact (*sparśa*), and from birth arise aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). From the object arises affliction: from feeling arises craving.

Since this principle regarding the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is thus established, it is thereby made known that ignorance (*avidyā*), which is of the nature of affliction (*kleśa*), arises either from a [prior] entity or from an affliction. Furthermore, because an affliction will arise again from the entity of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) at the conclusion of sensation (*vedanā*), nothing further needs to be added here. This is because of the statement: "In this way, there occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering. For otherwise, what would be the purpose of this [statement]?

In another sutra, it is stated that ignorance has improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) as its cause, and improper mental attention has ignorance as its cause. Others maintain that this [improper mental attention] is also mentioned here because it is included within grasping (*upādāna*). [Question: How is improper mental attention included within grasping? [Answer: If it were by way of association (*saṃprayoga*), then it would follow that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) would also be included therein. Furthermore, even if it were included, how is it made known here that ignorance has improper mental attention as its cause?

If, then, the relationship of cause and effect is understood solely through inclusion, then since craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are also included therein, it would be possible not to treat them as separate members [of dependent origination]. However, another says: "In another sutra, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) is stated to be the cause of ignorance; and that too is specified at the time of contact (*sparśa*), for it is said: 'Depending on the eye and visible forms, there arises a turbid mental attention born of delusion. Furthermore, at the time of feeling (*vedanā*), ignorance must necessarily be present."

(13) From another sutra it is stated: "Craving arises dependent upon feeling born from contact with ignorance. Therefore, (14) improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) existing at the time of contact is established as the condition for the ignorance that co-exists with feeling; (15) thus, ignorance is not without a cause, nor is there a need to add another link [to the chain of dependent origination]. Furthermore, there is no consequence of infinite regress, because that very improper mental attention is said to be born from delusion (*moha*), as it is stated: "Turbid mental attention is born from delusion."

In that case, should this which was stated elsewhere not be stated here? It need not be stated. How is it understood even when not stated? By means of reasoning (*yukti*). By what reasoning? Because for Arhats, faultless sensation does not become a condition for craving, nor does non-perverted contact [become a condition] for afflicted sensation; furthermore, the contact of a faultless Arhat is not perverted. By this reasoning, [the point is established]. [Objection: In that case, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would follow.

(20) As long as something is possible through reasoning, it is understood even if not explicitly stated. Therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal. Rather, this [objection] is simply not to be raised: that because no other members [of dependent origination] are mentioned beyond ignorance and old age and death, it follows that saṃsāra has a beginning and an end; nor is the teaching incomplete. What is the reason?

Because it is intended to explain this much of the subject matter for those disciples who are deluded regarding the process of worldly involvement—namely, how one passes from the next world to this world, and from this world back again to the next world—and because this has already been stated previously:
"For the sake of dispelling delusion regarding the prior, the subsequent, and the intermediate limits. (2)

The Blessed One said: "O monks, I shall teach you dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and dependently originated phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*). Now, what is the distinction between these two? According to the treatise (*śāstra*), there is none at all; for both are defined as all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). How then can future things, which have not yet arisen, be called "dependently originated"? First of all, how can future things, which are as yet unproduced, be called "conditioned"?

Because they are willed by a volition that brings about [the state] (*ābhisāṣkārikā cetanā*). How then are the untainted (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] [willed]? They too are willed by a wholesome volition with respect to their acquisition (*prāpti*). [If you say this,] the same consequence would apply to *nirvāṇa* as well. Because it belongs to the same category, that [definition] is extended (*atideśa*) to that very case; just as it is said, "It is not yet being transformed (*rūpyate*), yet it is called 'form' (*rūpa*) because it belongs to the same category," so there is no fault. However, the intended meaning of the Sūtra is stated as follows: "Here, 'origination' (*samutpāda*) is considered the cause; 'originated' (*samutpanna*) is considered the fruit. (28ab)

A member that functions as a cause is *pratītyasamutpāda*, because [the effect] arises from it; a member that functions as an effect is *pratītyasamutpanna*. In this way, all members are established in both ways, because they possess the nature of both cause and effect. And even though this is so, there is no confusion of the stages, because of the difference in their mutual dependence. That which is depended upon as *pratītyasamutpāda* is not the very same thing that is depended upon as *pratītyasamutpanna*, just like the relationship between cause and effect, or father and son.

The Elder Pūrṇāśa, it is said, maintained that there may be dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that is not dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*) phenomena. This involves four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*). The first alternative consists of future phenomena; the second, the final [moments] of an Arhat; the third, other past and present phenomena; and the fourth, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena. Regarding this, however, the Sautrāntikas clarify: "Are these indeed stated as personal preferences (*iṣṭi*), such that whatever one prefers is accepted, or are they the actual meaning of the Sūtra?"

He says: "This is the meaning of the Sūtra. [The opponent replies: "If this were the meaning of the Sūtra, it would not be the meaning of the Sūtra. Why so? First of all, as for what was said—that this dependent origination is situational (*āvasthika*), consisting of twelve states (*avasthā*) each comprising five aggregates (*pañcaskandhika*) as its twelve members—that contradicts the Sūtra, because it is taught otherwise in the Sūtra. For example: 'What is ignorance (*avidyā*)? It is that lack of knowledge regarding the past,' and so on in detail. Furthermore, that which is of explicit meaning (*nītārtha*) is not to be interpreted further; therefore, this is not the meaning of the Sūtra."

Indeed, not everything is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) merely by way of its exposition; for expositions are made according to what is predominant. For example, in the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*, with reference to the question "What is the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*)?", it says, "Hair, body hair," and so forth, even though other things such as visible form (*rūpa*) also exist there. Likewise, in this case as well, the exposition would be according to what is predominant. This [objection] is not applicable, for in that [sūtra], hair and the rest are not being defined by means of the earth element.

(22) Since their explanation might otherwise appear incomplete, the earth element is explained there by means of hair and so forth alone; yet, because the earth element exists even beyond hair and so forth, its explanation is indeed complete. Likewise here as well, the explanation of ignorance and the other factors is entirely complete and not deficient. [p.137] But is it not the case that the earth element exists even beyond hair and so forth, in tears, mucus, snot, and the like? That too has indeed been included in the explanation.

Or rather, because it is stated that "whatever else in this body is hard or has the nature of hardness" [is included], let there be likewise a remainder of ignorance if it can be demonstrated. But as for another type of ignorance, what basis is there for its inclusion? And even though the five aggregates exist in those states, only that whose presence or absence is invariably determined by the presence or absence of another can be established as a member [of the dependent origination].

Furthermore, even though the five aggregates exist in an Arhat, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) do not have the five aggregates as their cause. What then? They have ignorance (*avidyā*) alone as their cause. Likewise, consciousness that leads to merit, demerit, or imperturbability, as well as craving (*tṭṛṣṇā*) and so forth, are to be understood according to the explanation given in the Sūtra. As for what was said—that "here *samutpāda* is the cause and *samutpanna* is the fruit," up to the fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*)—that too contradicts the Sūtra, because it is explained otherwise in the Sūtra.

What is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? Having explained it in detail as "when this exists, that comes to be," that which here is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthititā*), and so on up to non-perversion—this is called dependent origination. Now, what is called "nature" (*dharmatā*) is the genus of phenomena, the characteristic mode (*śaili*) of phenomena. Therefore, this nature, this fixed rule (*niyama*), is such that only when ignorance (*avidyā*) exists do the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) come to be, and not otherwise.

This dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is not merely a cause. Furthermore, regarding the fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) that was stated: if future phenomena (*anāgata-dharma*) were not dependently originated, it would contradict the Sūtra. [The Sūtra asks: "Which are the dependently originated phenomena? They are ignorance (*avidyā*) up to birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). If one were to maintain that these two [birth and old age and death] are established as belonging to the future time period, the division into three sections (*trikāṇḍa-vyavasthā*) would be undermined. Other schools (*nikāyāntarīya*) hold that dependent origination is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because of the statement, "Whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, this dharmatā remains constant," this very point is established through the force of that intention as being both "thus" and "not thus. In what way, then, is it thus, and in what way is it not thus?

If this is the intended meaning—that whether Tathāgatas arise or do not arise, conditioned phenomena such as the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) always arise in dependence upon [conditions] such as ignorance (*avidyā*), and never arise without depending on conditions or depending on something else, and therefore it is "constant"—then this should be accepted as being so. But if this is the intended meaning—that there exists some distinct entity called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) that is constant—this must be refuted as not being so. Why?

Because arising (*utpāda*) is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṭalaksana*), it is not logical for an eternal, distinct entity to be the characteristic of that which is impermanent. Furthermore, since what is called "arising" belongs to the one who arises, what connection does it have with ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors, such that they are said to be its "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? Moreover, it would follow that the referent of the term is incapable, for it would be both "eternal" and yet "dependent origination."

Now, what is the meaning of the term *pratītyasamutpāda*? The prefix *prati* has the sense of "attaining" (*prāpti*), and the root *i* has the sense of "going" (*gati*). Because the meaning of a verbal root is transformed by the influence of a prefix, the meaning of *pratītya* is "having attained. The root *pad* has the sense of "existence," and when preceded by *sam-ut*, it has the sense of "manifestation. Therefore, *pratītyasamutpāda* means "arising after having attained conditions. This interpretation of the term is not tenable. Why?

For the rule regarding the suffix *ktvā* applies when there are two actions performed by a single agent, [the suffix being used] for the action occurring at the earlier time; for example, "having bathed, he eats" (*snātvā bhuṅkte*). Now, prior to its arising, there is no such thing that exists which, having depended upon something else, arises at a later time. Furthermore, there is no action that is without an agent. Regarding this, it is said: "If it is argued that it does not arise prior to origination because it is non-existent, that is not tenable. If it arises simultaneously, the suffix *ktvā* is not established here, because it is prescribed for an earlier time."

This is not a fault. First, this grammarian should be asked: in what state does a dharma arise—is it present or is it future? And what follows from this? If it arises while being present, how can it be present if it has not yet arisen? Or, if that which has already arisen arises again, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress. If, on the other hand, it arises while being future, how is agency established for that which is non-existent, or how can there be an action without an agent?

(12) Therefore, in whatever state [a thing] arises, in that very same state it undergoes dependence (*pratyeti*). And in what state does it arise? It arises as a future entity oriented toward production. (13) It is said that in that very state it undergoes dependence upon conditions. Furthermore, this grammatical distinction between agent and action is not established; for "to be" (*bhavati*) is the agent, and "becoming" (*bhūti*) is the action. Yet, we do not perceive any action of becoming other than the very fact of the being's existence. (15) Thus, there is no action distinct from the meaning of the being itself.

Therefore, there is no fallacy in conventional usage. This, however, is the meaning of the sentence: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. Whatever is the meaning of this, that is the meaning of *pratītyasamutpāda*. And regarding this, it is said:

"Just as that which is non-existent arises, so too does that which is existent [arise]. If that which has already arisen were to arise again, there would be no end; or else, it would have been non-existent even previously."

Furthermore, the suffix *ktvā* occurs even when there is simultaneity, as in: "Having reached the lamp, the darkness departed" (*dīpaṃ prāpya tamo gataṃ*); and [one] "sleeps with the mouth open" (*āsyaṃ vyādāya śete*). If [the action were] subsequent, why would one not say "when the mouth is closed"? (20–21) Others, however, conceive of this objection differently in order to resolve it: the prefix *prati* has the sense of repetition (*vīpsā*). The root *i* means "to go"; thus, *itayaḥ* refers to things that are non-abiding (*anavasthāyinaḥ*). The root *pad* preceded by *ut* has the sense of manifestation (*prādurbhāva*). Therefore, "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the arising (*utpāda*) through the coming together (*samavāya*) of those non-abiding things with respect to (*prati*) each respective collection of causes (*kāraṇasāmagrīm*). But this interpretation is conceived only in this very context. (22–23)

(24) How is it that here it is said, "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises"? For what purpose, then, did the Blessed One state the two formulations: "When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises"? It is for the sake of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). As he says elsewhere: "When ignorance exists, the formative forces come to be; the formative forces do not exist apart from ignorance. Or, it is to demonstrate the succession of the members (*aṅga*).

"When this factor exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this factor, that arises. (4) Or [it refers to] the succession of births: "When the prior limit exists, the middle limit comes to be; from the arising of the middle limit, the subsequent limit arises. (5) This demonstrates the state of being a condition both directly and through a succession. For sometimes the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) arise immediately after ignorance (*avidyā*), and sometimes they arise through a succession.

Others say that [the phrase] is for the purpose of refuting the doctrines of causelessness (*ahetu*) and eternal causes (*nityahetu*). [They argue: "When there is no cause, an entity does not come to be; nor does anything arise from an unproduced, eternal source such as *prakṛti* or *puruṣa*. However, under this interpretation, the inclusion of the first member [of the formula] would be rendered meaningless, because the refutation of both doctrines is established by the [second member alone]: "From the arising of this, that arises."

There are, however, some who imagine that when a self exists as a supporting basis, the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) and so forth come into being, and that from the arising of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest, those [factors] arise. Therefore, in order to refute that imagination, he established this determination: "From the arising of which very thing another arises, it is only when that very thing exists that the other comes to be, not when something else exists."

Namely: "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces" (12), up to "thus there is the origination of this entire great mass of suffering. The Masters [say] that this is for the purpose of making known their non-abandonment and their arising: "As long as ignorance is not abandoned, the formative forces are not abandoned; from the very arising of that [ignorance], they arise," and so forth in detail. Others say it is for the purpose of demonstrating duration and arising: "As long as the stream of causes exists, the stream of effects exists."

[The opponent argues: "Since the effect arises precisely from the arising of the cause, when 'arising' is the subject under discussion, what occasion is there for mentioning 'abiding'? Furthermore, for what purpose would the Blessed One speak out of order, mentioning abiding first and arising later? Moreover, he said: 'When this exists, that comes to be,' which means that when the effect exists, the destruction of the cause occurs. [The author replies: It might be thought that the effect then arises without a cause; therefore, he says: "It is not without a cause."

Because [it is said]: "From the arising of this, that arises. If this were the meaning of the Sūtra, they would have stated, "When this exists, that does not exist," first; and they would have stated, "When this exists, that does not exist," only after having first explained the arising of the effect. For in this way the sequence would be correct. Otherwise, however, what would be the point of a statement regarding destruction at the beginning of the inquiry, "What is dependent origination? Therefore, this is not the meaning of the Sūtra.
(22) How, then, is it that "conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces," up to "conditioned by birth are aging and death"? We shall demonstrate this merely as a matter of connection. (23)

For the fool, not understanding that this is merely a collection of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) arisen through dependent origination, and being obsessed with the view of self and the conceit "I am," undertakes three kinds of action by means of the body and so forth—either for his own happiness or for what is not happiness. For the sake of future happiness, he performs meritorious action; for the sake of neither-happiness-nor-unhappiness, he performs imperturbable action; and for the sake of happiness in this life, he performs non-meritorious action. With ignorance as its condition, these formations (*saṃskāra*), and by the power of the projection of karma, the continuum of consciousness goes to various states of existence.

Because of the connection with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) through the process of moving like a flame, consciousness has those other formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its condition. This being so, it becomes established that, in the exposition of the limb of consciousness, [the question] "What is consciousness? is answered: "The six groups of consciousness. Furthermore, preceded by consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)—consisting of the five aggregates and encompassing the entirety of birth—is produced in each respective realm of existence. For this is how it is taught in the *Vibhaṅga* and in the *Mahānidānaparyāya*.

(6) Likewise, from the maturation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise in succession; then, when there is the encounter with objects, consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises. (7) The conjunction of these three is contact (*sparśa*), which is to be experienced as pleasure and so forth. From that, the threefold feeling (*vedanā*) arises; from that, craving (*tṛṣṇā*). For one oppressed by suffering, there is craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmatṛṣṇā*) toward pleasant feeling; toward pleasant and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings, there is craving for form (*rūpatṛṣṇā*).

In the state that is neither painful nor pleasant, there is craving for the formless realm (ārūpyatṛṣṇā). From that craving for desirable feelings, the arising of desire (*kāma*) and so forth occurs. Among these, desire consists of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca kāmaguṇāḥ*). Views (*dṛṣṭayaḥ*) number sixty-two, as described in the *Brahmajālasūtra*. Morality (*śīla*) is the abstention from immorality. Vows (*vrata*) include the dog-vow, the cow-vow, and others; for example, as in the case of the Nirgranthas and others, who remain naked and unclothed, and so forth.

Furthermore, there is the undertaking of the staff, antelope skin, ashes, matted hair, triple-staff, tonsure, and so forth, by those such as Brahmins, Pāśupatas, and Parivrājakas. Moreover, "theory of self" (*ātmavāda*) refers to the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*). It is called a "theory of self" because the theory that "this is the self" exists within it. Others say it consists of the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*). How do these two constitute a "theory of self"? Because of the statement "these belong to the self. Since a self does not exist, it is called the "clinging to the theory of self," because one clings to that which is merely a conceptual designation (*prajñaptimātra*).

As it has been said: "O monks, the unlearned ordinary person, following after the designation 'self, self,' does not [perceive] that here there is neither a self nor anything belonging to a self. Grasping (*upādāna*) for those [aggregates] is the desire and lust (*chanda-rāga*) for them. For thus has it been declared by the Blessed One everywhere: "What is grasping? It is the desire and lust herein. Furthermore, conditioned by grasping, karma leading to renewed existence is accumulated; that is *bhava* (becoming).

Furthermore, Ānanda, that karma which brings about renewed existence in the future—this is what is meant here by "existence" (*bhava*) according to the Sūtra. Furthermore, conditioned by existence, there is the descent of consciousness (*vijñāna-avakrānti*). Future birth is "birth" (*jāti*), consisting of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandhika*). When birth exists, there is old age and death (*jarā-maraṇa*), as described in the Sūtra. Thus occurs the origin of this entire great mass of suffering. "Entire" (*kevala*) means devoid of anything belonging to a self (*ātmiya*).

"Of the great mass of suffering" means of the collection of suffering that is without beginning or end. "Arising" means its manifestation. This is precisely the Vaibhāṣika principle that was stated previously. Now, what is the meaning of "ignorance" (*avidyā*)? If it means "that which is not knowledge" (*na vidyā*), then it would follow that the eye and other such faculties are also ignorance. If, on the other hand, it means the absence of knowledge (*vidyāyā abhāvaḥ*), then in that case it would be nothing at all; and this is not tenable. Therefore: Ignorance is a distinct factor (*dharma*) that is the opposite of knowledge, like the word "non-friend" (*amitra*) or "untruth" (*anṛta*). (28cd)

Just as an "enemy" (*amitra*) is someone who is the opposite of a friend (*mitra*)—that is, his adversary—and not merely anyone other than a friend, nor the mere absence of a friend; and just as "truth" (*ṛta*) is said to be "reality" (*satya*), while speech that is its opposite is "untruth" (*anṛta*); and just as "non-dharma," "the non-beneficial," and "the improper" are states that are the direct opposites of "dharma" and so forth—so too, ignorance (*avidyā*) should be understood as a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*) that is the direct opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*). Why is this so? Because it is taught as being a condition (*pratyaya*), and furthermore, because it is spoken of as a "fetter" (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.

In the sūtras, ignorance (*avidyā*) is described as a fetter (*saṃyojana*), a bond (*bandhana*), a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), a flood (*ogha*), and a yoke (*yoga*). It cannot be a mere absence, nor can it be the eye and so forth; therefore, ignorance is indeed a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*). If it is argued that ignorance should be understood in the same way as a "bad wife" is called "no wife" or a "bad son" is called "no son," [we reply: if it were bad wisdom (*kuprajñā*), it would not be [ignorance] because of its being a form of vision (*darśana*). (29b) (12)

For corrupted wisdom (*prajñā*) is indeed contemptible; and since that [corrupted wisdom] has the nature of a view (*dṛṣṭi*), it is not logical for it to be ignorance (*avidyā*). [Objection: Then perhaps that which is not a view will be [ignorance]. [Response: That too cannot be. What is the reason? (14) Because a view is associated with it.
(29c) (15) If ignorance were wisdom, then a view would not be associated with it, because two substances of wisdom do not associate. (16) And for this further reason:

Because of the teaching that wisdom (*prajñā*) is afflicted (*upakleśa*). (29d) It is stated in the Sūtra: "A mind afflicted by passion (*rāga*) is not liberated; wisdom afflicted by ignorance (*avidyā*) is not purified. Yet it is not logical for that very same wisdom to be the affliction of that same wisdom. Just as passion is an affliction of the mind that is of a different nature from it, so too is ignorance [the affliction] of wisdom. Why, then, is this not accepted? [It is because] when wholesome wisdom is intermingled with afflicted wisdom, it is not purified; therefore, that [afflicted wisdom] is the affliction of the former.

Or again, when a mind defiled by passion (*rāga*) is not liberated, does it necessarily mean that it is currently obsessed (*paryavasthita*) by passion? Rather, it is simply impaired by passion such that it is not liberated; however, for one who turns away from that [defiling] cultivation, it becomes liberated. Likewise, we conceive that wisdom (*prajñā*) defiled by ignorance (*avidyā*) is not purified because it is impaired by ignorance. For who can prevent someone from forming such a conception?

However, they describe ignorance (*avidyā*) as being a distinct category altogether. Even for one who maintains that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are ignorance, there is a refutation of that view precisely for this reason: if it were of the nature of all afflictions, it would not be mentioned separately among the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, nor would it be associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, it would have to be stated that the mind is defiled by ignorance alone, because views and the other afflictions do not associate with one another in succession. If it is argued that it was stated in that way for the sake of specification, [the response follows].

(3) Even in the case of wisdom (*prajñā*), a qualification by "ignorance" (*avidyā*) would have to be made. Let ignorance be a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*); but what is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? It is not the non-apprehension (*asaṃprakhyāna*) of the truths, the [four] noble truths, or of karma and its fruits. And this very point is not understood: what is this so-called "non-apprehension"? (5) If it is that which is not apprehension, then even in the case of the mere absence of apprehension, the same fault remains as in the case of ignorance. Or, if it is a distinct entity that is the opposite (*vipakṣa*) of apprehension; (6) [then the question remains: what is its nature?

Thus, it is not known exactly what this is; for such is the manner of explaining phenomena (*dharma*). For example: "What is the eye? It is the translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) which is the basis of visual consciousness. The Venerable Dharmatrāta says: "The notion 'I am' (*asmīti*) is the ignorance of self-identity (*sattvamayatāvidyā*). But what is this *mayatā* other than the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*)?

"Having known thus and seen thus what was spoken in that Sūtra, through the abandoning and full comprehension of all cravings, all views, all *mayatās*, and all underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of attachment to the notions of 'I' (*ahaṃkāra*), 'mine' (*mamakāra*), and the pride of 'I am' (*asmimāna*), one is shadowless and extinguished. [Objection: This *mayatā* exists; but how is it known that this [which is called *avidyā*] is indeed *avidyā*? [Response: Because it cannot be said to be any other affliction (*kleśa*). [Objection: But could it not rather be another form of pride (*māna*) itself?
In this regard, if one were to investigate further, much would have to be said; therefore, let this rest for now.
Now, what is the meaning of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*)? "Form" (*rūpa*) has been explained in detail as previously stated. "Name," however, refers to the formless aggregates (*skandha*).

What is the reason? It is called "name" (*nāma*) because it bends toward objects by the power of the name, the faculties, and the objects. By the power of which name? That which is well-known in the world as the signifier of various objects, such as "cow," "horse," "form," "taste," and so forth. Furthermore, by what is this [designation] a "name"? Because that name bends toward those respective objects. Others say: because when the body has been cast off here, one bends toward another birth, the formless aggregates (*skandhas*) are called "name."
The six sense bases have been explained; contact must now be discussed. There are six types of contact.
"Visual contact," up to "mental contact. Furthermore, these arise from a conjunction (*saṃnipāta*).

They are born from the conjunction of the three: the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness. First, it is logical that there is a conjunction of the five sense faculties with their respective objects and consciousnesses, because they are co-nascent (*sahaja*). But how can there be a conjunction of the mental faculty (*manaindriya*), which has already ceased, with future and present phenomena and mental consciousness? This very relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is their conjunction; or else, the meaning of conjunction is the sense of having a single common effect.

(5) And all three of them are conducive to the arising of contact (*sparśa*). Regarding this point, however, the opinions of the teachers have diverged. (6) For some explain that contact is indeed a simultaneous occurrence (*sakṛn-nipāta*), and they cite a Sūtra as proof for this: "That which is the meeting (*saṃgati*), the coming together (*saṃnipāta*), and the conjunction (*samavāya*) of these three factors—that is contact. (7) Thus they say.

Others, however, explain that *sparśa* (contact) is indeed a distinct mental factor (*dharmāntara*) associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*), and they cite a Sūtra as proof for this: "What is the Dharma-discourse of the Six Sets of Six? They are: the six internal bases (*ādhyātmikāny āyatanāni*), the six external bases (*bāhyāny āyatanāni*), the six groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*), the six groups of contact (*sparśakāya*), the six groups of feeling (*vedanākāya*), and the six groups of craving (*tṛṣṇākāya*). For here, the groups of contact are taught separately from the sense faculties, their objects, and the consciousnesses."

In this regard, those who maintain that contact (*sparśa*) is simply the coming together [of the three] offer this rebuttal: "A distinct entity does not necessarily follow from a separate designation; otherwise, there would be no distinction between feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) from the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). This is not a fault, because the sphere of mental objects exists even apart from those two. However, there is no other triad existing apart from the triad that constitutes contact, such that there could be a remainder to be included here.

For although the sense-faculty and the object might exist without consciousness, consciousness never exists without a sense-faculty and an object. Therefore, when these three have already been specified, the further mention of contact would be redundant. Indeed, not every eye and visible form are the cause of every visual consciousness, nor is every visual consciousness the effect of every eye and visible form.

Therefore, some maintain that those things which stand in a cause-and-effect relationship are established as being of the nature of contact (*sparśa*). However, as for those who claim that contact is something other than the coming together (*saṃnipāta*), how do they resolve this sūtra? [They say: "That which is the meeting, the coming together, and the conjunction of these three is contact. Or else, they do not read it in this way; rather, they read it as "from the meeting, from the coming together, from the conjunction," or they assert that this is a metaphorical designation of the effect for the cause.

This discussion has become far too extensive; enough of this digression. The Abhidharmikas describe contact (*sparśa*) in a different way: of those six types of contact, five are contacts involving resistance (*pratighasaṃsparśa*), while the sixth is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacanāhvaya*). (30cd)

The five contacts of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are called "contacts with resistance" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*), because they have sense-faculties that possess resistance as their basis. The sixth, the contact of the mind (*manaḥ-saṃsparśa*), is called "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*). What is the reason? "Designation" (*adhivacana*) refers to the name (*nāman*). It is said that this [name] is its predominant object (*ālambana*); therefore, it is called "designation-contact."

As it has been said: "The eye-consciousness cognizes blue, but it does not cognize 'blue'; the mental consciousness cognizes blue and also cognizes 'it is blue'. One [type of cognition] is characterized by its basis (*āśraya*), while the second is characterized by its object (*ālambana*). Others, however, say: "The mental consciousness operates upon objects with respect to verbal expression (*adhivacana*), whereas the five [sensory consciousnesses] do not; therefore, that [mental consciousness] alone is 'with verbal expression' (*sādhivacana*)."

The contact associated with that [designation] is "designation-contact" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*); thus, one is characterized by its basis (*āśraya*), while the second is characterized by its association (*saṃprayoga*). Furthermore, those same six contacts become three:

the contacts of knowledge (*vidyā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and the other. These are: contact of knowledge, contact of ignorance, and contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance, which is distinct from those two. Moreover, these should be understood respectively as follows:

Those remaining when the afflicted [contact] has been excluded are as follows: untainted contact (*anāsrava-sparśa*) is "contact associated with knowledge" (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*); afflicted contact is "contact associated with ignorance" (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*), because it is conjoined with both knowledge and ignorance; the remainder is "neither-knowledge-nor-ignorance contact" (*naiva-vidyā-anavidyā-saṃsparśa*), because it is not conjoined with either. What, then, is the remainder? It is wholesome-tainted (*kuśala-sāsrava*) and unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) [contact]. Furthermore, by taking a portion of the contact associated with ignorance that occurs frequently, two types of contact arise:
"contact of aversion" (*vyāpāda-sparśa*) and "contact of attachment" (*anunaya-sparśa*).
Because they are associated with ill-will and attachment; furthermore, by way of a comprehensive summary, there are three [types of feeling], beginning with that to be experienced as pleasant. (31d)

There is contact to be experienced as pleasant (*sukhavedanīya*), contact to be experienced as painful (*duḥkhavedanīya*), and contact to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanīya*). This is because they are conducive to pleasant feeling and so forth. Alternatively, "to be experienced" (*vedanīya*) means that which is experienced or that which is capable of being experienced. What is that? It is what has been felt (*vedita*). Contact in which there is a pleasant feeling to be experienced is "contact to be experienced as pleasant. The same should be applied to contact to be experienced as painful and as neither-painful-nor-pleasant. These constitute the sixteen types of contact. Contact has been explained.
Feeling (*vedanā*) must be explained. In that regard, from the sixfold contact (*sparśa*) previously mentioned, there arise six feelings (*vedanā*):
feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact. Furthermore, of these—
Five are bodily and the other is mental.

(32a'b) The five feelings born from eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact are called bodily feeling because they rely upon the material sense faculties. Furthermore, the feeling born from mind-contact is called mental because it relies solely upon the mind.

Now, does feeling arise after contact, or at the same time? The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it is simultaneous, because they are mutually co-existent causes (*sahabhūhetu*). How is the relationship of producer and produced established between two things that have arisen together? And how is it not established? Because of a lack of capacity; for when a dharma has already arisen, there is no capacity in another dharma [to produce it] that is distinct from the mere proposition [itself].

For that very reason—namely, that there is no relationship of producer and produced between two things that arise simultaneously—is precisely why there is no [causal relationship] of one dharma toward another dharma once it has already arisen. [Objection: In that case, it would follow that they are mutual producers. [Response: This is not a fault, because this is accepted. For it is indeed accepted that simultaneous causes (*sahabhūhetu*) have mutual results. However, while this is accepted [in the Abhidharma], it is not accepted in the Sūtra that contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) have mutual results.

Because it is stated that "conditioned by visual contact, feeling born of visual contact arises," but it is not stated that "conditioned by feeling born of visual contact, visual contact arises. Furthermore, this is untenable because it violates the principle of the producer; for whatever phenomenon is established as the producer of another phenomenon is established as being at a different time from it.

(12) For example: first the seed, later the sprout; first the milk, later the curd; first the impact, later the sound; first the mind, later the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and so forth. Otherwise, because cause and effect are mutually dependent, either everything would arise simultaneously, or nothing would ever arise at all, since there would be no subsequent distinction. Indeed, the temporal sequence of cause and effect is not unestablished; however, their simultaneous existence (*sahabhāva*) is also established.

For example, as in the case of visual consciousness and the others [arising] from the eye, visible form, and so forth—both primary elements (*bhūta*) and derived matter (*bhautika*)—there too, first come the sense faculty and the object, and afterwards the consciousness. If it is accepted that a subsequent [moment] arises from a preceding occurrence of the primary elements and derived matter, what is the objection? The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that just as it is with a shadow and a sprout, so it is with contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*). Others hold that feeling occurs at a time subsequent to contact. For the sense faculty and the object constitute the prior limit, while consciousness [is the intermediate].

Thus, that conjunction of the three is contact (*sparśa*). Following the condition of contact, feeling (*vedanā*) arises in the third moment. If this is the case, then it follows that feeling does not occur in every instance of consciousness, nor is every consciousness accompanied by feeling, nor is all consciousness contact. This is untenable. What is untenable here? Namely, that even when two contacts have different objects, the subsequent feeling is caused by the preceding contact.

How indeed could a feeling (*vedanā*) produced by contact (*sparśa*) having an object (*ālambana*) of one kind have an object of another kind, such that it would have an object different from the mind (*citta*) with which it is associated? Alternatively, let it be that at that time the consciousness (*vijñāna*) constituting contact is devoid of feeling; and let the preceding consciousness which possessed feeling not be contact. If this is so—because of the deficiency of conditions (*pratyaya-vaidhurya*)—what is the fault? [The answer is: The rule regarding the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) is violated.

"In every state of mind, there are ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*). Where is this rule established? In the treatise (*śāstra*). We take the Sūtras as our authority, not the treatises; for the Blessed One said, "One should rely upon the Sūtras. Furthermore, this is not the meaning of "universal" (*mahābhūmika*), namely that ten universal factors occur in every state of mind. What, then, is the meaning of "universal"? There are three levels (*bhūmi*).

The stage with vitarka and vicāra, the stage without vitarka and with vicāra only, and the stage without vitarka and without vicāra. Again, there are three: the wholesome stage, the unwholesome and neutral stage. Again, there are three: the stage of those in training (śaikṣī), the stage of those beyond training (aśaikṣī), and the stage of neither those in training nor those beyond training (naivaśaikṣīnāśaikṣī). Those factors which exist in all these stages are the "great ground" (mahābhūmika) factors. Those which exist only in the wholesome [stage] are the "great wholesome ground" (kuśalamahābhūmika) factors. Those which exist only in the afflicted [stage] are the "great affliction ground" (kleśamahābhūmika) factors.

Furthermore, others maintain that these [mental factors] arise sequentially according to their possibility, and not all of them simultaneously; however, the unwholesome universal mental factors (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*) were not included because they arose in the context of a specific textual recitation (*pāṭha-prasaṅga*), and were not previously recited. If, then, feeling (*vedanā*) occurs at a time subsequent to contact (*sparśa*), the Sūtra would have to be contradicted, for it says: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact; feeling, perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) are co-nascent (*sahajāta*)."

It is said that [consciousness] is "co-arisen," but not "co-arisen with contact"—what is there to be refuted here? Furthermore, this word "together" (*saha*) is seen even in the sense of "immediately following," as in the expression: "one cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness accompanied by loving-kindness. Therefore, this is not a definitive proof. As for what was stated in the Sūtra: "That which is speech, that which is perception, that which is volition, and that which is consciousness—these factors are conjoined, not unconjoined"—from this it follows that there is no consciousness that is not conjoined with feelings.

(16) This must first be considered: what is this meaning of "conjoined" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*)? For in that very Sūtra it is said: "What one feels, that one intends; what one intends, that one discerns; what one discerns, that one cognizes. It is not understood whether this statement refers to a restriction regarding their object (*ālambana-niyama*) or rather a restriction regarding the moment (*kṣaṇa-niyama*). Since the term "conjoined" is used for the coexistence of vitality and heat (*āyur-ūṣman*), the restriction regarding the moment is established.

Furthermore, as it is stated in the Sūtra: "The coming together of the three is contact (*sparśa*). How then could there be consciousness without the coming together of the three, and yet no contact? Therefore, one must necessarily admit that in every instance of consciousness there is contact, and that feeling (*vedanā*) is co-nascent with contact.
Enough of this overly prolix discussion; let us return to the subject at hand. Mental feeling has been explained in brief.
Furthermore, it is of eighteen kinds by way of the mental applications (*manopavicāra*). (32cd)

That same mental feeling (*caitasikī vedanā*) is further divided into eighteen types by way of the establishment of the eighteen mental explorations (*manopavicāra*). Furthermore, a reconnection of the sequence should be observed here. What are the eighteen mental explorations? They are: six explorations of mental joy (*saumanasya*), six explorations of mental grief (*daurmanasya*), and six explorations of equanimity (*upekṣā*). How are these established? If they were established by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be only three: the explorations of joy, grief, and equanimity.

Now, from the perspective of association (*saṃprayoga*), there will be one [type], because all are associated with the mind (*manas*). Now, from the perspective of the object (*ālambana*), there will be six, because they have the six objects—form and so forth—as their objects. (4) By means of all three [criteria], the classification is established: among them, fifteen mental applications (*upavicāra*) regarding form and so forth have unmixed objects, because they have specifically determined objects such as form and so forth. (5) The three mental applications regarding phenomena (*dharma*) are of both kinds. What is the meaning of "mental applications" (*manopavicāra*)?

It is said that these [mental factors], such as mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and so forth, range over objects by depending on the mind (*manaḥ*). Others say that they cause the mind to range over objects; for, under the influence of feeling (*vedanā*), the mind ranges repeatedly over objects. Why is bodily feeling (*kāyikī vedanā*) not considered a mental ranging (*manopavicāra*)? Because it does not depend on the mind alone, nor is it a ranging [mental factor] due to its non-conceptual nature (*avikalpakatva*); thus, it is inappropriate [to include it]. Why is the pleasure of the third dhyāna not included among the mental rangings?

It is said that from the very beginning, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because there is an absence of the faculty of pleasure belonging to the mental level (*manobhūmika*), and because, as its opposite, there is an absence of the mental application (*upavicāra*) of suffering; thus [these applications] belong only to the mental level. If these indeed belong only to the mental level, then how is it that the Sūtra says: "Having seen forms with the eye, one applies oneself to forms that are a basis for joy," and so forth? This was stated with reference to being produced by the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*); for these [applications] actually belong to the mental level.

For example, the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) is produced by visual consciousness and yet belongs to the mental level (*manobhūmikā*). However, because of the statement "having seen" up to "having touched," this is not at all a point for objection. Even those who engage in mental application (*upavicāra*) without seeing, up to without touching, these too are mental applications. Otherwise, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there would be no mental applications of visible forms and so forth that have the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as their object; nor would there be mental applications of odors, tastes, and tangibles in the form realm that have the desire realm as their object.

However, it has been stated in a more explicit manner: even one who, having seen forms, mentally dwells upon sounds—that too is a mental dwelling (*manopavicāra*). Yet, it has been stated in a way that avoids confusion by distinguishing the respective objects of the sense faculties. Is there any form that is exclusively a basis for joy, or even exclusively a basis for equanimity? There is, provided one restricts the reference to a particular mental continuum (*saṃtāna*), but not with respect to the objective support (*ālambana*).

Now, among these mental explorations (*manopavicāra*), how many are associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? And of those, how many have what as their object (*ālambana*)? In this manner, it should be stated up to those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). He says: "In the desire realm, all have themselves as their object.
(33a) All eighteen exist in the desire realm, and that [desire realm] is the object for all of them. Of those very [eighteen], [p.148]...

The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is the object of twelve [mental applications], excluding the six mental applications of odor and taste; this is because those two do not exist there. The higher [realm] is the object of three. (33c)

The term "object" (*gocara*) continues [to apply]. The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is the objective support (*ālambana*) for three mental applications regarding phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*), because of the absence of visible forms and so forth therein. (5) Those associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) have been explained.
(6) Those associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) must now be stated. Among them, first:
(7) In two dhyānas, there are twelve. (33c'd) (8)
Excluding the mental applications of dissatisfaction (*daurmanasyopavicāra*), those twelve (9) are "going to the desire realm" (*kāmagā*).

(10) They are called "going to the desire realm" because they go toward desires; the meaning is that they take the desire realm as their object (*ālambana*). For the use of the verb *gam* is seen in the sense of grasping objects. How is this understood? It is understood in this way. (12)

Its own [realm] is the object of eight. That very same form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is their own; it is the object of eight mental applications (*manopavicāra*), excluding the four applications of odor and taste.
The formless realm (*ārūpya*) is the object of two.
The objects of the two mental explorations of phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) are [the six internal and external bases].
However, in the first two dhyānas, there are six [objects].
In the third and fourth dhyānas, there exist only the six mental explorations of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*) and no others. Furthermore, their objects are—
Sensual pleasures (kāma) are the object of all six [consciousnesses].
(34c) The desire realm (kāmadhātu) is the object of all six as well. (20) One's own [realm] is the object of four. (34c') (21–22)

The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is the object of four [mental applications], because of the absence of odor and taste therein. (23) The other [realm] is the object of one alone. (24) The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is the object of only one mental application, namely that of mental phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*). Those associated with the realm of form have been explained. [p.149]
Now, those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpya*) are discussed.

(2) There are four [mental applications] in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the formless [attainments]. (3) Here, the "preparatory stage of the formless" refers to the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*). In that [stage], there are four mental applications (*upavicāra*) regarding visible forms, sounds, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharma*). (4) And these...

Regarding the form realm (*rūpāvacara*): for those [mental applications] whose object is the fourth dhyāna, it is their specific object (*vyavacchinnālambana*). However, for those whose object is a composite whole (*paripiṇḍitālambana*), there is therein only one mental application to phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) with a mixed object (*saṃbhinnālambana*). One [application] pertains to what is above (*ūrdhvaga*).

In that [formless realm], there is only one mental application regarding phenomena (*dharmopavicāra*) which has the formless realm as its object. (10) One in the fundamental [attainment] (35c). Furthermore, in the fundamental formless attainment, there is only the mental application regarding phenomena; no other exists. And that too— (12)

Their own object (35c') (13) is exclusively the basis of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). For we shall explain later (14) that the fundamental formless attainments do not have a lower realm as their object.
And these are the mental explorations (manopavicāra) (15).

All eighteen [mental applications] are with-outflows (*sāsrava*); there is none that is without-outflow (*anāsrava*). Who is endowed with how many? One born in the desire realm who has not yet attained a wholesome mind of the form realm is endowed with all those belonging to the desire realm, with eight belonging to the stages of the first and second dhyānas, and with four afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) ones belonging to the stages of the third and fourth dhyānas—excluding those having odor and taste as their objects—and with one afflicted mind of the formless realm. One who has not yet abandoned desire for the form realm and has not attained a wholesome mind of the form realm is endowed with all [of these].

[The mind] is associated with ten [mental applications]: the ten belonging to the desire realm and the first dhyāna level. With four afflicted mental applications of joy (*saumanasyopavicāra*), excluding those having odor and taste as objects, and with six mental applications of equanimity (*upekṣopavicāra*) belonging to the stage of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*). With eight belonging to the second dhyāna level. Those belonging to the levels of the third and fourth dhyānas and the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are as previously stated. Following this method, the remainder should be understood.

However, one who has been reborn in the dhyānas should be understood as being endowed with one mental application (*manopavicāra*) of equanimity pertaining to the desire realm—specifically, that which is associated with the consciousness of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*). Another says: "While this is indeed the Vaibhāṣika interpretation of the mental applications, the meaning of the Sūtra appears otherwise. For it is not logical that one who is free from passion for a certain realm would mentally apply himself to an object belonging to that realm. Therefore, not all [mental factors] such as joy (*saumanasya*) and so forth, even if they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), are mental applications."

What then? They are the defiled [mental factors] by which the mind ranges over objects. And how does it range? It is attracted, it is repelled, and it remains indifferent without discernment; these are the opposites of which there are six constant abidings as their antidotes. Having seen forms with the eye, one is neither glad nor sad, but abides in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending; and so on, until having cognized mental phenomena with the mind.

For an Arhat does not lack mundane wholesome mental joy (*saumanasya*) that takes phenomena as its object; rather, it is specifically that which is defiled and constitutes a mental application (*manopavicāra*) that is here prohibited. Furthermore, these same [mental factors] such as joy and so forth constitute thirty-six "Teacher's Words" (*śāstṛpada*), distinguished by whether they are based on worldly attachment (*gardha*) or on renunciation (*naiṣkramya*). This distinction is established by the treatise (*śāstra*); therein, those based on attachment are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), while those based on renunciation are wholesome (*kuśala*).
In this way, this limb of existence called feeling (*vedanā*) should be understood as having many varieties of divisions. As for the remaining limbs, they are not mentioned here. What is the reason?
Because some limbs have already been stated and others will be stated later; among them, consciousness (*vijñāna*) has already been stated.
"Consciousness is the specific cognition [of objects], and it is also the mind-base (*manāyatana*). (15) Furthermore, the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have been described as:
"The translucent material forms, such as the eye and so forth, which are the supports for those consciousnesses. (16–17)

The formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) will be explained in the section on the Treasury of Karma; craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) will be explained in the section on the Treasury of Defilements.
Furthermore, it was previously established that this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), in brief, consists of defilements, karma, and the basis [for them].
However, in this context, the defilement is intended [to be explained].
Like a seed, like a serpent, like a root, like a tree, and likewise like a husk.

(36bcd) What is its similarity to seeds and the rest? Just as sprouts, stalks, leaves, and so forth arise from a seed, in the same way, afflictions, karma, and the bases of existence arise from affliction. Just as a lake presided over by a serpent does not dry up, so too the lake of birth is presided over by the serpent of affliction. And just as trees whose roots have not been pulled out grow again and again even when cut down, so too the realms of existence persist when the roots of affliction have not been extracted.

And just as trees produce flowers and fruits from time to time, so too do the afflictions repeatedly become the cause of afflictions, karma, and the bases [of existence]. And just as rice grains covered by husks are capable of sprouting, whereas they alone are not, so too karma covered by the husks of the acquisition of afflictions is capable of sprouting in another birth, whereas it alone is not. Thus, first of all, the affliction is to be understood as being like the seed and so forth. Karma is like the husked grain, and likewise like the medicinal plant and the flower. (37ab)

That which has husks is called *tuṣī*; thus, the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been described as being like husks. Now, karma—which is like the grain within the husk—is being discussed. There are medicinal herbs that, once their fruit has ripened, cease to produce further results; likewise, karmas, having matured, no longer bring about further maturation. Just as a flower is the proximate cause for the production of fruit, so too should karmas be understood in relation to the production of maturation. The basis [of experience] is like prepared food and drink. (37c) (11)

Just as prepared food and drink are intended solely for consumption and not for further growth, so too is the entity called *vipāka* (maturation). For from one maturation, another maturation does not arise in subsequent births. If it were to arise, there would be no liberation. Indeed, this continuum of birth, arising through dependent origination in this manner, does not transcend the four states of existence; namely, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*), the state of the prior period (*pūrvakālabhava*), and the state of death (*maraṇabhava*). And these have already been explained.

Within those four types of existence, the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is exclusively afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). By which affliction? [It is by all afflictions. (38a) (17) By which affliction? (18)
By all the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to its own level.

Whatever level the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) belongs to, it is connected by all the afflictions belonging to that very level. For there is no affliction by which the connection of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*) is not obstructed; so say the Abhidharmikas. However, it is by the afflictions themselves, and not by the independent outbursts (*paryavasthāna*). Even though that state is weak, whichever affliction one has frequently practiced and is proximate to in that [existence], that very same affliction presents itself at that time due to the force of previous momentum (*pūrvāvedha*).
The linking of rebirth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) should likewise be understood as necessarily afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). (23) "The others are of three kinds" (38c).
(24) The other three states of existence—the intermediate state and so forth—are of three types: wholesome, afflicted, and neutral (*avyākṛta*). [p.152]
Now, among these states of existence (*bhava*), which one is associated with what?

(2) There are three in the formless realm (*ārūpya*) (38c'), excluding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). For the formless realm is not demarcated by a distinct location for the sake of reaching which an intermediate state would be produced. (4) Since the desire and form realms are not specifically enumerated [as excluded], it is thereby admitted that all four states of existence exist therein. (5) Thus has the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of sentient beings been explained in detail. (6)
Now, as to how the subsistence of sentient beings occurs, it is said: (7) "The world subsists on nutriment. (8) 38d.

"There is one dharma which has been declared by the Blessed One, having realized it for himself through direct knowledge: namely, that all sentient beings subsist on nutriment. This is the scriptural passage. What, then, are the nutriments? There are four nutriments. The first is edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), which is both gross and subtle. It is subtle because it is the nutriment of odors for those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); and because there is an absence of excreted waste for gods and for those of the first cosmic age, as [the food] enters their limbs like oil into sand.

Or, for subtle beings such as the moisture-born insects of children, the second [nutriment] is subtle contact (*sparśa*). The third is mental volition (*manaḥsaṃcetanā*). The fourth is consciousness (*vijñāna*) as nutriment. Furthermore, among these, edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but not in the form or formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), because those who are free from passion for it are reborn there. And that [edible food]—
