It consists of three bases.

(39b') All odor, taste, and tangible objects belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are indeed edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), because they are swallowed after being made into mouthfuls; that is, by means of the separation of morsels through the mouth and nose. How can those [objects] existing in shadows, sunlight, flames, and light be considered food? It is said that this definition refers to the majority of cases. However, even those which are not swallowed but nevertheless sustain existence are also subtle food (*sūkṣmāhāra*), like bathing and anointing the body.

Why is the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) not considered nutriment? For that too is swallowed after being made into morsels. (21) The sphere of visible form is not [nutriment] because it does not benefit its own sense organ or those who are liberated. //39cd// (22)

For that which is called "nutriment" is what conduces to the benefit of the sense-faculties and the great elements. However, at the time of ingestion, the visible object (*rūpāyatana*) does not benefit its own sense-faculty or those great elements; how much less so other [faculties], since it is their distinct object? Furthermore, even when a visible object, while being seen, produces pleasure and mental ease, even then it is the contact (*sparśa*) to be experienced as pleasant—which has that [object] as its objective support—that constitutes the nutriment, not the visible form itself. This is because there is no such benefit for liberated ones—Non-returners and Arhats—even when they behold most agreeable food.
Contact, volition, and consciousness—these nutriments are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) in the three realms.

(40ab) Contact is born from the conjunction of the three; volition is mental action; and consciousness—only these, when they are with-outflows, are nutriments. They exist in all three realms. For what reason are those without-outflows (*anāsrava*) not [nutriments]? Because the purpose of a nutriment is for the nourishment of existence (*bhava*), and the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that those [without-outflows] have arisen for the sake of the destruction of existence. Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtra: "These four nutriments are for the stability and maintenance of beings who have come to be, and for the assistance of those seeking rebirth."
And thus, untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena are not nutriments.
For it is known that beings who have already been born are those who have come into existence. Now, who are those seeking rebirth?
(40cd) The mind-made (*manomaya*), the seeker of rebirth, the *gandharva*, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). (41a)

And cessation (*nivṛtti*)—for the Blessed One has spoken of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) by these designations. It is called "mind-made" (*manomaya*) because it is produced from the mind; because it exists without depending on any external [factors] such as semen or blood; because its nature is to seek rebirth, it is "seeking rebirth" (*saṃbhavaiṣin*); because it consumes odors, it is a "gandharva"; and because it is oriented toward birth, it is "arising" (*abhinirvṛtti*). This is based on the scriptural passage: "Having brought about a body subject to affliction, one is born in a world subject to affliction."

Likewise, according to the *Catuṣkoṭika-sūtra*, there is a person for whom the fetter of existence (*abhinirvṛtti-saṃyojana*) is abandoned but not the fetter of rebirth (*upapatti-saṃyojana*). The first alternative refers to the non-returner who has departed upstream (*ūrdhvaṃsrotas*), being free from passion for the two realms [of form and formlessness]. The second refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*). The third refers to those who attain parinirvāṇa upon being born (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*). The fourth consists of excluding these aforementioned cases; it includes those who have already become Arhats, as well as those seeking existence who possess craving.

Now, how many nutriments are for the maintenance of beings, and how many are for the assistance of those seeking rebirth? The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that all of them serve both purposes. For even edible food leads to renewed existence for those who possess craving for it; indeed, the Blessed One said: "These four nutriments are the root of disease, of abscesses, and of arrows, and the condition for old age and death. Furthermore, mental volition is seen here as serving for maintenance; for they explain it thus: [text continues]

It is said that when their father was stricken by famine, he filled a leather bag with ashes, hung it from a peg, and comforted his two sons by telling them it was flour. The two of them remained there for a long time imagining it to be such, but when someone opened it, they fell into despair and perished. Furthermore, men whose ship was wrecked upon the great ocean ran toward a large mass of foam, thinking it was land; but having touched it, they despaired and died.

(2) And it is said in the *Saṃgītiparyāya*: "From the great ocean, coarse creatures emerge from the water onto dry land, lay their eggs on a sandy shore, cover them with sand, and then descend back into the great ocean. Among them, those eggs of the mothers whose mindfulness does not fail with respect to the eggs do not rot; however, those of the mothers whose [mindfulness] fails do rot. The Sautrāntikas do not describe this [as a proof].

Let it not be that [the embryo] is nourished by the food of another. However, they explain it thus: those eggs whose memory of the mother is not lost do not rot; but those whose memory is lost do rot. They remember her at the stage of contact. Now, why are there exactly four nutriments? Is it not the case that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena nourish states of existence (*bhava*)? Although this is indeed so, they are stated here according to their predominance:
"In this context, two are for the sake of nourishing the support and the supported. (Kārikā 6–11)

The dyad is for the purpose of projecting and sustaining another existence, respectively. (41abc) The basis is the body together with its sense faculties; for its nourishment, there is substantial food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*). That which is supported consists of mind and mental factors; for their nourishment, there is contact (*sparśa*). These two, for their part, are predominant in nourishing an existence that has already arisen here; therefore, four [nutriments] have been taught.

For the first two are like nurses, because they nourish what has been born; the latter two are like mothers, because they give birth. Whatever is edible food (*kavaḍīkāra*), all of that is nutriment (*āhāra*). However, there may be that which is edible but not nutriment; this constitutes a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*). The first alternative is that edible food in dependence upon which there is a decline of the sense faculties and a disintegration of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). The second alternative consists of the other three nutriments.

The third [alternative] is that edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) which, being depended upon, results in the nourishment of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and the growth of the great elements (*mahābhūta*). The fourth is setting aside these aforementioned modes. In this way, fourfold alternatives (*catuḥkoṭika*) should also be constructed for contact (*sparśa*) and the others, as appropriate. There may be cases where, depending on contact and so forth, there is the nourishment of the sense-faculties and the growth of the great elements, yet those are not "nutriments" (*āhāra*); such would be the case with those belonging to other levels (*anyabhūmika*) and those that are untainted (*anāsrava*).

For even that which, when consumed, causes affliction to the consumer is indeed food, because it provides benefit at the time of ingestion. (23) For the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that food performs the function of food at two times: while it is being consumed and while it is being digested. (24) Now, in which realm of existence (*gati*) are there how many kinds of food? In all [realms], there are all [four]. Likewise regarding the modes of birth (*yoni*). How can there be solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the hells? [There is] glowing iron balls and molten copper. (25)

If even harmful food were considered nutriment, the fourfold logical alternative (*catuḥkoṭika*) would be contradicted, as well as the *Prakaraṇa* treatise, which asks: "What is edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*)? It is that edible food depending upon which there is the nourishment of the sense-faculties and the growth of the great elements, as well as their maintenance and further sustenance," and so on in detail up to consciousness. There is no contradiction, however, because this was stated with the intention of referring specifically to nutriment that causes nourishment (*upacayāhāra*).

However, because food that causes diminution exists in the hells—since edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) is present there—it is logical that [the category of nutriment] pertains to all five destinies. The Blessed One said: "If one were to feed a hundred external seers who are free from passion for sensual desires, and if another were to feed a single ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) belonging to Jambūṣaṇḍa, this latter gift would yield far greater fruit than that gift. Who, then, is this so-called "ordinary person belonging to Jambūṣaṇḍa"? Some say he is any inhabitant of Jambudvīpa who possesses a physical body.

This is not tenable because of the statement that [the field] is "one. What is the distinction here? It might be argued that if one were to feed many ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), the merit would be greater than if one were to feed a smaller number of those free from passion (*vītarāga*). Others say that a Bodhisattva is proximate [to Buddhahood]. However, they do not describe this [as the intended meaning], for giving to him produces far more merit than giving to millions of Arhats. Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the ordinary person who has attained the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is intended here.

However, this designation is neither etymologically derived nor has it been defined anywhere in the Sūtras or the Śāstras. This notion that one who has reached the Jambūṣaṇḍa grove is a "possessor of the aids to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is merely a fabrication. It is more appropriate to say that it is the Bodhisattva himself who is seated in these Jambudvīpa groves; for he is said to be distinguished from them at that time by virtue of his being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who has attained detachment from the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). Indeed, he is distinguished from them even when compared to those who are infinite in number.

The mention of "one hundred," however, follows from the previous context. This is indeed so, because by excluding [others] in this manner, he specifically distinguished the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala-pratipannaka*) from the outsiders (*bāhyaka*) alone. Otherwise, he would have distinguished him from those belonging to Jambūdvīpa alone. Thus, having explained how the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of sentient beings occurs, their state of existence, and their death through the exhaustion of lifespan and so forth, this must now be stated: in which consciousness (*vijñāna*) being present do death and rebirth occur? To this, he says:
The severance of roots, the reconnection of roots, detachment from the realms and stages, falling away, death, and rebirth—(20) these are held to occur only in the mental consciousness.

(42abc) (21) The severance of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda*), the reconnection of the roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla-pratisaṃdhāna*), detachment from the realms and stages (*dhātu-bhūmi-vairāgya*), falling away (*parihāṇi*), death (*cyuti*), and rebirth (*upapatti*)—these six factors are maintained to exist only in the mental consciousness and not elsewhere. (22) By the mention of "rebirth," it should be understood that the linking of existence in the intermediate state (*antarābhava-pratisaṃdhi*) is also described by this term. However, regarding feeling (*vedanā*)... [p.156]
Death and rebirth occur in the state of equanimity.

(42d) "Death" (*cyuta*) is simply death (*cyuti*); "rebirth" (*udbhava*) is birth (*upapatti*). These two occur within the feeling that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, because that [feeling] is not sharp (*apaṭu*). For the other two feelings are sharp; and death and rebirth are not possible in a sharp consciousness. Furthermore, even in that case, they do not occur in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), nor in one who is one-pointed (*ekāgra*), nor in one who is without mind (*acitta*). (43a)

The phrase "death and rebirth" continues [to apply here]. For one whose mind is in meditative equipoise, there is neither death nor rebirth, because [such a state] belongs to a different level (*visabhāgabhūmika*), is produced by volitional effort (*abhisaṃskārika*), and is supportive (*anugrāhaka*). Nor does it occur for one who is without mind (*acittaka*), for it is not possible to inflict harm upon one who is without mind. When his physical basis (*āśraya*) begins to undergo transformation, then the mind—which is dependent upon that basis—manifests and subsequently passes away; it is not otherwise.

Furthermore, since there is no cause for the interruption of the mind at the moment of rebirth, and since rebirth does not occur without afflictions, it is illogical for one to be without mind [at that time].
(9) It has been stated that the state of existence at death is of three kinds; however, the Arhat attains parinirvāṇa within the two types of neutral states. (43b) (11)

[It occurs] in a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or in a resultant mind (*vipākacitta*). If there is a resultant [feeling] of equanimity (*upekṣā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it occurs there; if not, it occurs only in a mind of deportment. For what reason does it occur only in an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) state and not in another? Because that [indeterminate state], being weak, is conducive to the cutting off of the mind. Now, in which part of the body does consciousness cease for one who is dying? In the case of instantaneous death, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) together with the mental faculty (*samanaska*) disappears all at once. But if one passes away gradually, then in that gradual death, the cessation of the mind occurs in the feet, the navel, or the heart. (Verse 43cd)

Regarding "those who go below, humans, gods, and those who do not return" (adhonṛsuragājānām): they are called *adhogā* because they go downward; they are those who go to the states of woe (*apāya*). They are called *nṛgā* because they go to humans; they are those who go to the human realm. They are called *suragā* because they go to the gods; they are those who go to the celestial realms. For these [three groups], consciousness ceases respectively in the feet, the navel, and the heart. Furthermore, those who are not born again are the *ajā*, the Arhats. For them as well, consciousness ceases in the heart. Others say it ceases in the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*).

Regarding the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), it is excluded from those [parts]. For the body-faculty of one who is dying, like water spat upon a heated stone, undergoes contraction and disappears starting from the feet and so forth. Furthermore, death occurs in this gradual manner; generally, for those struck by the pains of the severing of the vital points (*marmaccheda*), there is the severing of the vital points through the elements such as wind and the rest.

Certain regions of the body, when struck, bring about death; these are called *marmas*. When any one of the elements—water, fire, or wind—becomes excessively aggravated, they are as if cut by the impact of a sharp weapon with intense pains that pierce the vital channels (*nāḍīs*). Yet, they are not actually cut like wood; rather, they are said to be "cut" because, once severed, they no longer function. Why is it not so for the earth element?

Because of the absence of the fourth affliction (*doṣa*). For wind, bile, and phlegm are the three afflictions; these are respectively dominated by the elements of water, fire, and air as appropriate. Others say it is due to the similarity with the destruction of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka-saṃvartanī*). Among the gods, there is no severing of the vital points (*marmaccheda*); however, for a son of the gods subject to falling away (*cyavanadharman*), five preliminary signs appear.

(7) A pleasant sound issues from his garments and ornaments; his natural radiance becomes dimmed. (8) Water droplets remain upon his body after bathing; even though his mind is fickle by nature, it remains fixed on a single object; and the opening and closing of his eyes occur normally. However, these [signs] are subject to deviation. Furthermore, five signs never fail to indicate death.

Their garments become soiled, their garlands wither, sweat is released from their armpits, a foul odor pervades their bodies, and the son of the gods no longer finds delight in his own seat. This world of sentient beings, as it thus arises, persists, and passes away, has been established by the Blessed One within three groups (*rāśi*). What are the three groups? The group fixed in rightness (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), the group fixed in falsity (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), and the undetermined group (*aniyata-rāśi*). Furthermore, among these, those fixed in both rightness and falsity are the noble ones (*ārya*) and those who have committed the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-kārin*). (44cd)

What is rightness (*samyaktva*)? That which is the complete abandonment of attachment, the complete abandonment of hatred, the complete abandonment of delusion, and the complete abandonment of all afflictions (*kleśa*); this is called "rightness" in the Sūtra. Who are the noble ones (*ārya*)? Those in whom the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) has arisen. They are called "noble ones" because they have gone far away from evil states, due to their attainment of the acquisition of ultimate dissociation (*visamyoga*).

For these [persons] are "fixed in rightness" (*samyaktva-niyata*) because they are destined for the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa-kṣaya*); even those who have attained the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) necessarily possess the nature of final nirvāṇa. Why are they not fixed in rightness? Because they might also be fixed in falsity (*mithyātva*). Furthermore, they are not fixed in rightness by way of a temporal limit, as is the case for those such as the "seven-times-at-most" (*saptakṛtvaḥ-parama*) and others. What is falsity? Hells, hungry ghosts, and animals—this is called falsity.

In that regard, those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*) are fixed in falsehood (*mithyātva-niyata*), because they are destined for hell. It is established that those other than those fixed [in either truth or falsehood] are unfixed (*aniyata*). For their status as partaking of both or partaking of neither depends upon conditions (*pratyaya*).

The world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) has been explained; now the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) must be described. Regarding that, they maintain the following arrangement of the receptacle world below:
The wind-circle is sixteen hundred thousand leagues in depth and is incalculable in extent.

[p.158] They maintain that the arrangement of the trichiliocosm is as follows: resting upon space, there arises at the bottom a wind-circle through the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings. Its depth is sixteen hundred thousand *yojanas*, and its circumference is incalculable; it is so firm that even one struck by a thunderbolt cannot break it. Above that—

The water [mandala] is eleven lakhs and twenty thousand [yojanas] in thickness (46ab). The term "mandala" carries over from the previous context. Within that wind mandala, clouds produced by the karma of sentient beings rain down in streams as thick as axles; that constitutes the water mandala. Its measurement is eleven lakhs and twenty thousand yojanas in height and depth. How is it that those waters do not flow sideways? It is through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings.

For just as food and drink that have been eaten and drunk do not enter the receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*) while still undigested—so say some; others belonging to another school maintain that they are held together by the wind according to the analogy of a granary. Furthermore, those waters, being whirled about by winds produced through the power of the karma of sentient beings, become golden on the surface through the process of becoming like the skin of boiled milk. That becomes the circle of water (*apāṃ maṇḍala*).
Later, it remains eight hundred thousand [yojanas] in height, and the remainder becomes gold. (Verse 46cd)

Furthermore, what remains? Three hundred and twenty thousand [yojanas]. That golden earth exists above the waters. (14) Thus has been stated the height of the water and gold mandalas. (15) Horizontally, the water and gold mandala measures twelve hundred thousand [yojanas], plus three thousand, four hundred and fifty. (16–17) //47//

For these two are equal in extent; however, they are threefold all around. When calculated by its total circumference, it becomes threefold: thirty-six hundred thousand, ten thousand, and three hundred and fifty *yojanas*. And that golden mandala of the earth which is situated above the waters—
Therein are Meru, Yugandhara, Īṣādhāra, Khadiraka, and likewise the Sudarśana mountain; Aśvakarṇa, Vinataka, and the Nimindhara mountain. (48bcd–49ab) (2)

Thus, these are the eight great mountains established upon the golden foundation; Sumeru is in the center, while the remaining ones are situated as its surrounding retinue. Of that [world-system] which is encircled by a rampart of the other seven mountains, Nimindhara is the outermost mountain. Beyond that are the continents.
Outside of that are the four continents; furthermore, outside of those is the Cakravāḍa mountain range (49c), by which the system of the four continents is encircled. Now, of these...
The seven [mountains] beginning with Yugandhara are made of gold, while Cakravāḍa is made of iron. Meru consists of the four jewels. (49d–50a)

It consists of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal respectively on its four sides. By the power of whichever side of Sumeru is composed of a particular substance, the sky in that direction appears to be of that same color. They describe the side of Sumeru facing Jambudvīpa as being made of lapis lazuli; because of the reflection of its radiance here, the sky is seen as being made of lapis lazuli.

Now, how does their formation occur? Once again, streams of water fall upon the golden earth. Those waters, containing the seeds of various kinds, being churned by winds distinguished by many types of power, transform them into their respective species. Furthermore, they transform them in such a way that they serve as conditions through the non-coexistence [of heterogeneous elements] when the production of specific effects of different classes occurs; however, this is certainly not a transformation in the manner of a numerical sequence.

And what is the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the Sāṃkhyas? It is the appearance of another property (*dharma*) upon the cessation of another property, while the substance (*dravya*) remains constant. What is the fault here? For that very substratum (*dharmī*) does not exist, which, remaining constant, could be imagined to undergo the transformation of properties. And who says that the substratum is something other than the properties? Transformation is merely the becoming otherwise of that very same substance. Even so, this is incorrect. What is incorrect here?

"This is that very same thing, yet it is not so"—this reasoning of yours regarding the wind is unprecedented. Furthermore, in this manner, gold and the other elements, having come into being, are gathered and heaped together by winds impelled by the power of karma; these become the mountains and the continents. Moreover, those mountains beginning with Sumeru and ending with Cakravāḍa are submerged eighty thousand [yojanas] in the water. (50bc) (3)
Above the golden earth, there are eighty thousand yojanas of water; therein they are submerged.
Rising above the water, Mount Meru is further eighty thousand [yojanas].
Thus, the total height of Meru is one hundred and sixty thousand yojanas.
There is a reduction by half in each of the eight [mountains] (51a).

From the water upwards, Sumeru reaches [its peak]; Yugandhara is half of that, forty thousand *yojanas*. Īṣādhara is half of that; in this way, the reduction by half should be understood for the others as well, until Cakravāḍa, which is half of Nimindhara, measuring three hundred and twelve and a half *yojanas* (51b).
And they are equal in height and thickness.
The meaning is that their height above the water is exactly equal to their thickness or breadth. (12) There are seven cold [seas] as intervals between them. (51c) (13)

Between these mountains, ending with Nimindhara, there are seven intermediate spaces called the Seven Seas, which are filled with water endowed with eight qualities. That water is cool, sweet, light, soft, clear, odorless, and does not irritate the throat when drunk, nor does it cause distress to the stomach once swallowed. Furthermore, of these, the first is eighty thousand [yojanas] deep; the first Sea lies between Sumeru and Yugandhara, and it is eighty thousand yojanas in width.
This is the inner ocean;
for there are two oceans, the inner and the outer. That inner ocean of cool water is three times as large as it is on its sides.

Its width is said to be eighty thousand yojanas; when measured along the shore of Yugandhara, it becomes three times that on its sides, amounting to two hundred and forty thousand [yojanas]. The other Śītā rivers are each half the size of the preceding one. (52c) (2)

The distance between Yugandhara and Īṣādhara is the second cold sea (*śītā*), which is half the size of the first; it is forty thousand *yojanas*. The third is again half of that, and in this manner the subsequent cold seas are each half the size of the preceding one, until the seventh cold sea is twelve hundred and fifty *yojanas*. Their length, however, has not been calculated because they extend and spread out over a vast distance.
The remainder is the outer great ocean (*mahodadhi*). (Verse 52d)

What remains? It is the space between Nimindhara and Cakravāḍa. For that is the outer Great Ocean, full of salt water. It is indeed three hundred twenty-two thousand *yojanas* in extent (53ab). Therein are four continents on the four sides of Sumeru. (10)
In that regard:
Jambudvīpa is two thousand [yojanas] on three sides and has the shape of a wagon.

(53b'cd) Its three sides are each two thousand [yojanas], and its shape is like that of a wagon. In its center, upon the ground made of gold, there is the Diamond Throne (*vajrāsana*) which is perfectly circular; sitting upon it, all Bodhisattvas produce the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*). No other physical basis or location is capable of supporting that [concentration].
One of its sides is three and a half yojanas, and its fourth side is likewise three and a half yojanas; for this very reason, it is shaped like a cart.
Pūrvavideha is like a half-moon.

To the east of here, on the side of Sumeru, is the continent of Pūrvavideha; it is shaped like a half-moon. As for its dimensions, three of its sides are each two thousand yojanas, just as those of Jambūdvīpa.
One side is three hundred and fifty yojanas;
the fourth side is likewise three hundred and fifty yojanas. Godānīya is circular, measuring seven thousand five hundred yojanas. [p.162]

To the west of here, on the side of Mount Sumeru, lies the continent of Aparagodānīya, measuring seven thousand five hundred yojanas in total. It is circular like the full moon; its diameter is two thousand five hundred yojanas, and its middle point lies at two thousand five hundred yojanas from here.

Kuru is eight [thousand] and square, and it is level. (55cd) Here, to the north of Sumeru, is the continent of Uttarakuru. It is eight thousand *yojanas* in total extent and is square, like a gaming board (*kṛtyāpīṭhikā*). On all its sides it is equal; just as one side is two thousand *yojanas*, so too are the others, not exceeding that by even the slightest amount. And whatever the shape of a continent is, such is the shape of the faces of the humans there.

Indeed, in the intervals between those continents, intermediate islands (*antaradvīpa*) have arisen. What are they, and how many are there? He says: (10) Dehas, Videhas, Kurus, Kauravas, Cāmaras, and Avaracāmaras; (11) these eight are the intermediate islands, along with Śāṭhas (Pradhan: Gāṭhas) and Uttaramantriṇas. (12) *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* 3.56.

Among them, Deha and Videha are the satellites of Pūrvavideha; Kuru and Kaurava are those of Uttarakuru; Śāṭha and Uttaramantriṇa are those of Aparagodānīya; and Cāmara and Avara are those of Jambūdvīpa. All are inhabited by humans, though others say one is inhabited by *rākṣasas*. To the north of this [Jambūdvīpa], beyond the nine mountain ranges of Kīṭa, lies the Himavat.

Right here in Jambūdvīpa, to the north of this Jambūdvīpa, there are three Black Mountains; beyond them are another three, and again three more—thus, beyond the nine Insect Mountains (Kīṭaparvata), lies the Himavat mountain. From there: "Five hundred [yojanas] in width and length is the lake situated between [the Himavat and] Gandhamādana. (57b'cd)

Beyond that Himavat mountain and before Gandhamādana lies the lake named Anavatapta, from which four rivers flow: the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, the Śītā, and the Vakṣu. Its width is fifty yojanas and its length is fifty [yojanas]. It is filled with water endowed with the eight qualities. It is inaccessible to humans who lack supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). And in its very vicinity grows the Jambu tree, whose fruits are sweet and delicious.
This continent is known as Jambūdvīpa by virtue of its sovereignty over that tree, or rather, it is called Jambūdvīpa by virtue of its fruit.
In what location are the hells, and what is their extent? Twenty thousand [yojanas] below this [continent], there is Avīci, which is equal in size to it. (58ab) (2)

Twenty thousand *yojanas* beneath this very Jambūdvīpa lies the great hell Avīci, measuring twenty thousand *yojanas* in both height and width; thus its lower surface is forty thousand *yojanas* from here. It is called "Avīci" because suffering is uninterrupted there. In other hells, suffering is intermittent; for example, in Saṃjīva, when the bodies of beings have been cut, pierced, and crushed, cool winds blow and bring those sentient beings back to life once again.

For this very reason, it is called Saṃjīva. Others say it is called Avīci because there is no "wave of pleasure" (*sukhavīci*) in it. (6) Even in other [hells], pleasant feeling as a result of maturation (*vipāka*) does not exist; however, that which is a natural outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*) is not excluded. (7) Above that are seven hells. (58c) (8) Above that Avīci, seven hells are situated one above the other: Pratāpana, Tapana, Mahāraurava, Raurava, (9) Saṃghāta, Kālasūtra, and Saṃjīva. Others say they are on the sides of Avīci. Furthermore, (10) these...
All eight [hells] have sixteen secondary hells (*utsada*).
For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Thus these eight hells are proclaimed, which are difficult to transcend."
They are filled with those of fierce deeds; each has sixteen secondary hells.
(14) They have four walls and four gates, partitioned and measured out in sections. (15) They are surrounded by iron ramparts and enclosed by iron. (16)

And the ground is made of heated iron, blazing and endowed with fiery energy; (17) extending for many hundreds of *yojanas*, it stands ablaze with flames. (18) What are the sixteen secondary hells (*utsada*)? (19)
The Pit of Embers, the Corpse-pile, and then the Razor-path and so forth, as well as the River—these are situated in the four directions of those [hells]. (20–21ab) (59abc) (21)

At each of their gates there are four secondary hells (*utsada*): *Kukūla*, knee-deep, where the skin, flesh, and blood of those beings are dissolved when they step down, yet when they lift their feet, the skin, flesh, and blood grow back again; *Kuṇapa*, a mire of excrement, where creatures called *nyaṅkuṭas*—entirely white with black heads and needle-like mouths—dwell, and which pierce those beings even to the bone.

There is a great road strewn with razor edges, where, as those beings tread upon it, their skin, flesh, and blood are sliced away when they set down a foot, as described previously. There is the Forest of Sword-Leaves (*asipattravana*), where sharp swords fall upon those beings and sever their limbs and members, while brindled dogs devour them. There is the Forest of Iron Silk-Cotton Trees (*ayaḥśālmalīvana*), whose thorns are sharp and sixteen finger-breadths long.

As those beings climb up, the thorns turn downward and pierce their bodies; as they descend, the thorns turn upward. Iron-beaked crows repeatedly pluck out their eyes and devour them. These three—the Path of Razors and the others—are treated as one because of the commonality of being struck by weapons (*śastrābhinipāta-sāmānyāt*).

(6) The fourth protrusion is the river Vaitaraṇī, filled with boiling caustic water. Therein, those beings, being warded off from both banks by men with swords, spears, and javelins in their hands, are steamed and cooked as they go upward; they are steamed and cooked as they go downward or across. It is just like sesame seeds, rice, and so forth, placed in a pot full of water set over a fire.

(9) For that [Great Hell] has arisen like a moat surrounding it; these four secondary hells are called sixteen by way of their division into directions. (10) They are called "secondary" (*utsada*) because they are places of additional torment; for those who have fallen into the primary hells undergo further suffering in these. (11) Others say that after being confined in the primary hells, they sink down into these, hence they are called "secondary" (*utsada*). (12)

From one question, another arises: Are those guardians of hell reckoned as sentient beings, or not? Some say: "No. [Objection: How then do they move about? [Response: By the karma of sentient beings, like the seed-wind at the beginning of a cosmic evolution (*vivartanī*). [Objection: Then what of that which was said by the Venerable Dharmasubhūti:
"Those who are wrathful, performers of cruel deeds, And who delight in evil, And rejoice in the suffering of others— They are born as the rākṣasas of Yama"? // (17) //

Those who, instructed by Yama, cast sentient beings into the hells are called the *yamarākṣasas*; they are not, however, those who inflict the tortures (*kāraṇā*). Some say they are reckoned as sentient beings. Now, where is the ripening (*vipāka*) of that karma? For in those very hells is the space for the ripening of those who have committed the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*); what obstacle is there for them there? Why are they not burned by the fire? Surely because the fire has its limits set by their own karmas, or because of the presence of a particular kind of primary element (*bhūtaviśeṣa*).
These, first of all, are called the eight great hot hells.
(22) The other eight, beginning with Arbuda, are cold.
(23) There are eight other cold hells, namely: Arbuda, Nirarbuda, Aṭaṭa, Hahava, Huhuva, Utpala, Padma, and Mahāpadma. [p.165]

These names correspond to the bodily sounds and transformations of those beings who are afflicted by intense cold. They too are situated horizontally beneath this very Jambūdvīpa, below the great hells. [Objection: How can there be space for the Avīci and other hells beneath such a small Jambūdvīpa? [Response: For the continents are broad at the bottom like a heap of grain; for this very reason, the great ocean slopes gradually downward. Thus, these sixteen hells all arise through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings.

The individual hells, however, are brought about by the respective karmas of many beings, or of two, or even of one. Their differentiation is of many kinds, and their location is not fixed, as they exist in rivers, mountains, desert regions, or elsewhere, and because they occur below [the earth]. Such, then, is the configuration of the receptacle-worlds of the hells. As for animals (*tiryañcaḥ*), they range over land, water, and the air. It is said that their primary location is the great ocean, from which they have spread elsewhere.

Yama is the king of the *pratānas*. His royal capital, which is their primary abode, is located five hundred *yojanas* beneath Jambūdvīpa; from there, others have spread out elsewhere. Some *pretas* possess great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) and bear a splendor like that of the gods. The rest are as described in the *Pretāvadāna*. Now, upon what are these two, the moon and the sun, established? Upon the wind. The winds in the atmosphere, produced by the sovereign power of the collective karma of all sentient beings, revolve around Sumeru like a whirlpool. The movement of the moon, the sun, and the stars is upward.
(12) How far distant from here are the moon and the sun?
(13) The moon and the sun are at half the height of Meru; (60a) they move level with the summit of Mount Yugandhara. What are their dimensions? (15) [They are] respectively—

[The dimensions are] fifty and one *yojana*. (60b) The measure of the lunar disk is fifty *yojanas*; the measure of the solar disk is fifty and one, meaning fifty-one. As for the celestial palaces of the stars, the smallest among them measures one *krośa*. Beneath the solar palace, there is formed externally a crystal disk made of fire-element (*taijasa*), which provides heat and illumination. Beneath the lunar palace, there is a water-element (*āpya*) disk, which is cool and luminous.

For the sake of benefiting or harming the vision, bodies, fruits, flowers, crops, and medicinal herbs of living beings according to their respective karma, one moon and one sun perform their functions throughout the four continents. But does the sun perform its function simultaneously across all four continents? He says: no. What then? "In those [continents], midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise occur at once. (60cd)
When it is midnight in Uttarakuru, then it is sunset in Pūrvavideha, midday in Jambūdvīpa, and sunrise in Godānīya. This should be applied to the others as well.
The increase and decrease of nights and days here occur due to the different movements of the sun. In that regard:
"In the second month of spring, on the ninth day of the latter half, the night begins to grow. (61ab) (2)
In the second month of the rainy season, Bhādrapada, on the ninth day of the second fortnight, the night increases.

(3) But in the fourth month of the winter season, it decreases. (61cd) That same [night] decreases again in the fourth month of the winter season; the phrase "on the final ninth day" carries over [from the previous verse]. This refers to the ninth day of the second fortnight of the month of Phālguna. (5–6)
Due to the reversal of day and night:
when the night increases, the day decreases; when the night decreases, the day increases. By what measure do they increase?
The increase of night and day occurs moment by moment (*lavaśas*).

The night increases by a lava at a time, or the day [increases]; and those respective decreases and increases occur when the sun moves southward or northward. (11) When the sun goes to the southern side of Jambūdvīpa, there is an increase in the night; when it goes to the north, there is an increase in the day. (12–13)
At the beginning of the bright fortnight, the disk of the moon is seen incomplete. What is the cause of this?

When the lunar mansion moves near the solar mansion, it is said that the solar rays fall upon that mansion; consequently, a shadow falling on its opposite side makes the disk appear incomplete—this is the explanation according to the *Prājñapti*. The former masters maintain that the manner of movement is such that sometimes only half of the mansion is visible.

Now, which beings inhabit these celestial palaces (vimānas) of the Sun and others? They are the gods belonging to the Realm of the Four Great Kings (cāturmahārājakāyika). Are these their only abodes? These are the abodes for those who dwell in celestial palaces; however, for those who dwell on the ground, they are the terraces of Mount Sumeru and so forth. How many terraces does it have, and how large are they? It has four terraces, each separated by ten thousand [yojanas]. (63ab)

One [terrace] rises ten thousand yojanas; likewise up to the fourth. By these, half of Sumeru is occupied. And from that, they extend outward respectively by sixteen, eight, four, and two thousand [yojanas]. (63cd) The first terrace extends sixteen thousand yojanas out from Sumeru; the second, eight; the third, four; and the fourth, two. (4)
The Karoṭapāṇis, the Mālādhāras, the Sadāmadas, and the Mahārājika gods [dwell] in them. (64abc) (6)

On the first terrace dwell the yakṣas named Karoṭapāṇis; on the second, the Mālādhāras; and on the third, the Sadāmadās and Sadāmattas. All of these belong to the retinue of the Four Great Kings. On the fourth terrace, however, the Four Great Kings themselves dwell along with their attendants; therefore, that level is called the realm of the Mahārājakāyika gods. Just as the Mahārājakāyika gods reside upon the terraces, so too do they reside upon the seven mountain ranges. (Verse 64d)

On the Yugandhara and other mountains, there are their villages and towns; for this very reason, this class of gods is the most numerous of all. (12) On the summit of Meru dwell the Thirty-three [gods]. (13) Now, how large is the summit of Meru? (14)

And it is eighty thousand [yojanas] on each side, just as it is below. Others, however, say: it is twenty thousand [yojanas] on each side; its four sides are the four directions, each side being twenty thousand yojanas, making eighty thousand in total circumference. And at its intermediate corners (vidikṣu), there are four peaks inhabited by the Vajrapāṇis. (65cd)

The intermediate directions from the summit of Sumeru are its corners. In those [directions], four peaks have risen up, measuring five hundred yojanas, in which yakṣas named Vajrapāṇis dwell. And in the center of that summit of Meru is the city named Sudarśana; it is golden, with a variegated floor, and soft, measuring two thousand five hundred yojanas on each side and one and a half yojanas in height. (66)

In the center of the base of Mount Sumeru is the city named Sudarśana; each of its sides is two thousand five hundred yojanas in length, and it is one and a half yojanas in height. Its walls are made of gold, and its ground is variegated with one hundred and one other minerals. That surface of the ground is soft to the touch like cotton wool, sinking and rising as the feet are set down and lifted; it is the royal capital of Śakra, the lord of the gods. Herein is the Vaijayanta palace, measuring two hundred and fifty yojanas on each side. (67ab) (2)

In the center of the city is the palace of Śakra, the lord of the gods, named Vaijayanta. By its perfection in the arrangement of various jewels and its splendor, it puts to shame the majesty of all other dwellings. It measures two hundred and fifty yojanas on each side. Such, then, is the beauty of the city. Furthermore, as for the exterior:
It is adorned with the Caitraratha, Pāruṣya, Miśra, and Nandana groves. (67b'cd)

For outside that city, on its four sides, there are four gardens and so forth (*udyānādīni*) which are the pleasure grounds of the gods: the Caitraratha garden, the Pāruṣyaka, the Miśrakāvana, and the Nandanavana. By these, that city is adorned on the outside.

(8) On all four sides of these gardens, at intervals of twenty *yojanas*, there are four excellent terrains (*subhūmīni*) which are indeed places of recreation for the gods; they spread their splendor as if in mutual rivalry. (10–11) They are situated right on the outskirts of the city’s side.

In the northeast is the Pārijāta tree, and in the southwest is Sudharmā. (68cd) The tree named Pārijāta is a *kovidāra*; it is the locus for the excellence of sensual delight for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. Its root extends five *yojanas* deep, its height is one hundred *yojanas*, and its branches, leaves, and foliage spread out and remain fifty *yojanas*. When it is in full bloom, its fragrance wafts for one hundred *yojanas* with the wind and fifty *yojanas* against the wind. This much is reasonable regarding the scent carried by the wind.

But how is it [perceived] against the wind? Some say this was said with reference to the tree not being surpassed [by the scent]. For indeed, the wind does not blow against itself; rather, one must acknowledge that the fragrance possesses such a power that even when obstructed by gentle divine breezes, it continues to produce another stream of fragrance.

However, because it begins with a progressively weaker intensity, the continuum is very quickly severed; therefore, it does not extend over such a great distance. Now, does this continuum of the fragrance of flowers proceed as something supported by its own primary elements (*svabhūta*), or is it produced as wind that has been perfumed? There is no fixed rule here, for the Master [Vasubandhu] accepts both possibilities. As for what was said by the Blessed One:
"The fragrance of flowers does not go against the wind, nor does the root-fragrance of *tagara* or *candana*."
"But the fragrance of the virtuous goes against the wind; the good person blows in all directions.

This was said with reference to the fragrance of human flowers, for that is well-known in the world, yet it does not possess such power. However, the Mahīśāsakas recite: "The fragrance wafts a hundred *yojanas* with the wind, and fifty *yojanas* against the wind. The Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods is located in the southwestern quarter, where the gods sit and deliberate upon what ought and ought not to be done.
This, then, is the arrangement of the receptacle world (*bhājana-saṃniveśa*) of the Thirty-three (*tridaśa*). Above that, the gods reside in celestial palaces (*vimāna*).

(69ab) Above the Thirty-three, the gods are established in celestial palaces; they are, moreover, the Yāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, and Paranirmitavaśavartins, as well as the previously mentioned Brahmakāyikas and others included within the sixteen intermediate locations. Thus, these are, in brief, the twenty-two classes of gods for whom a receptacle world is known. (9)
There are six who enjoy sensual pleasures.

Among them, six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) enjoy sensual pleasures, but not the rest. They are as follows: from the Gods of the Four Great Kings (*caturmahārājakāyika*) up to the Gods Who Wield Power over the Creations of Others (*paranirmitavaśavartin*). Furthermore, they engage in sexual union through: (1) pairing, (2) embracing, (3) holding hands, (4) laughing, and (5) gazing. (69cd)

For those dwelling on the earth-bound levels, sexual union occurs through physical coupling (*dvaṃdvana*), just as it does for humans among the Cāturmahārājakāyikas and the Trāyastriṃśas. However, for them, the cessation of feverish passion occurs through the emission of wind, because they lack semen. For the Yāmas, sexual union occurs through embracing; for them, the cessation of feverish passion occurs by mere embracing. For the Tuṣitas, it occurs through the grasping of hands; for the Nirmāṇaratis, through gazing; and for the Paranirmitavaśavartins, [it occurs through the mere touch of the body]. For all those who dwell in their own realms, it occurs through physical coupling.
As for the duration of time, the Vaibhāṣikas state that it has been explained in the *Prajñapti*.

To the extent that the objects [of the senses] become more intense, to that same extent passion also becomes more intense. (18) When a male deity or a female deity is born upon the lap of another deity or a divine maiden, he becomes their son and she their daughter. (19) What is his size at birth? (20) The infant is like one five years old, up to being like one ten years old. (21) He is born among these [deities]. (70abc) (22)
Respectively, among the six classes of gods, they increase very quickly; (23) the gods of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) are born fully formed and clothed.

(70c’d) The gods belonging to the form realm are born with their bodies complete and enveloped in garments. All gods speak the noble language (*āryabhāṣā*). In this regard, it should be understood that [these characteristics apply] within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). (3)

There are three modes of rebirth in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*): the gods of the desire realm together with humans. How so? There are beings for whom sensual pleasures are present; they exercise mastery and control over these present pleasures. These are, namely, humans and certain gods—specifically, the four classes of gods [of the desire realm]. There are also beings for whom sensual pleasures are created; having created these pleasures, they exercise mastery and control over them. These are, namely, the gods who delight in emanations (*nirmāṇarati*).

There are beings who have desires created by others and exercise mastery and control over those desires created by others, such as the gods who are masters of the creations of others (*paranirmitavaśavartin*). These are called the three types of rebirth in the realm of desire because they consist of: (1) enjoying things as they arise; (2) enjoying things created by oneself according to one’s wish; and (3) enjoying things created by others according to one’s wish. However, in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are three types of rebirth in happiness, consisting of the nine levels of the first three dhyānas. (71cd)

The nine stages within the three dhyānas constitute the three types of rebirths in happiness (*sukhopapatti*). For those gods dwell happily for a long duration, abiding in the happiness born of seclusion, the happiness born of meditative concentration, the happiness of joy, and the happiness free from joy; therefore, because they are free from suffering and possess long-lasting happiness, these are called "rebirths in happiness" (*sukhopapatti*). However, regarding rebirth in the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), since the happiness of joy is absent, its status as a "rebirth in happiness" must be examined.

Regarding these twenty-two abodes of the gods that have been mentioned, how far is the distance from each lower one to the next higher? It is not easy to calculate all of this by means of the measurement of *yojanas*. However:
"From each abode, as far as it extends downward, so far does it extend upward from there. (72ab) (18)

Starting from Jambūdvīpa, for every location that lies to the north, there is another location as many leagues above it as there are below it down to Jambūdvīpa. (19) For example, the fourth terrace, which is the primary abode of the Four Great Kings, is forty thousand yojanas from here. (20) As far as Jambūdvīpa is below that [terrace], so many leagues above it is the abode of the Tridaśas.

Therefore, as far as Jambūdvīpa is below, so far above is the abode of the Yāma gods; further still, as far as Jambūdvīpa is below, so far above is the abode of the Tuṣita gods. Thus, following the entire sequence in detail, from the Sudarśana gods down to Jambūdvīpa, so far above is the abode of the Akaniṣṭha gods. Above that, there is no further abode. For this very reason, because they are the most senior (*jyeṣṭha*), they are called Akaniṣṭha.

(24) Others say they are called *aghaniṣṭhā* because "agha" refers to matter (*rūpa*) residing in the mind, and they are the limit (*niṣṭhā*) of that alone. (25) Furthermore, do those born in lower abodes go to the higher celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and see them? There is no vision of what is above for them, except through supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) or by relying on another. [p.171] 72cd (2)

Either by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), they might go from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to the Yāma heaven, or by relying on another; that is, if they were led there by one possessing supernatural power, or by a deity belonging to that [higher] realm. The same applies to the remaining [heavens]. However, one may see someone born in a higher realm who has come here, but not one belonging to a higher world-sphere (*dhātu*) nor a higher level (*bhūmi*). Just as one cannot touch a tangible object [from a distance], because it is not within one's sensory range, for this very reason they do not come with their own physical bodies. Rather, they come by means of a transformation-body (*nirmita-kāya*) belonging to a lower level. According to other schools (*nikāyāntarīya*), one may see them at will as if they were present here.

Now, what is the extent of these [heavens] that know the watches (*yāma*) and so forth? Some say that the measure of the first four is up to the summit of Mount Sumeru; others say it is double each successive one. Others say that the first *dhyāna* is as large as a world-system of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*); the second is as large as a small chiliocosm (*sāhasracūḍika lokadhātu*); the third is as large as a medium dichiliocosm; and the fourth is as large as a great trichiliocosm. Still others say that the first and subsequent [stages] have the dimensions of a small chiliocosm and so forth, while the fourth is immeasurable.
Now, what is this "small thousandfold world-system," and what are the "two-thousandfold" or "three-thousandfold" systems?
A small thousandfold world-system is considered to consist of one thousand sets of four continents, moons, suns, Mount Merus, gods of the desire realm, and Brahma-worlds. (73)

A thousand Jambūdvīpas, a thousand Pūrvavidehas, a thousand Aparagodānīyas, a thousand Uttarakurus; a thousand suns, a thousand moons, a thousand Sumerus; a thousand [realms] of the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods; and a thousand Brahmā-worlds—this is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*). A thousand of those small chiliocosms is a second-order intermediate dichiliocosm (*dvisāhasro madhyamo lokadhātuḥ*). A thousand of those small chiliocosm world-systems is the second-order intermediate dichiliocosm.

A thousand of those [thousandfold world systems] is a trichiliocosm (trisāhasra). A thousand of those two-thousandfold world systems is a great trichiliocosm (trisāhasramahāsāhasra) world system. For this entire [great trichiliocosm] undergoes destruction and origination simultaneously. (74d)
It dissolves equally and evolves equally; for "evolution" (*vivarta*) is indeed "origination" (*saṃbhava*), as will be explained later.

(22) Now, is there indeed a difference in the dimensions of the sentient beings dwelling there, just as there is a difference in the dimensions of the receptacle worlds? (23) He says: "There is. Among them, first: (24) The inhabitants of Jambudvīpa are four and three and a half cubits in height. (75ab) (25)
The humans of Jambūdvīpa measure three and a half cubits, though some are four cubits tall.
By doubling the height successively, those called Pūrva, Godā, and Uttara [are reached]:
the humans of Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru are eight, sixteen, and thirty-two cubits tall, respectively. (75cd) (2–3)
The bodies of the gods who dwell in the desire realm increase by a quarter-krośa (pāda) up to one and a half krośas.

(4) A "quarter" (pāda) is the fourth part of a krośa. The body of the gods of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājakāyika) is that measure; for the Trāyastriṃśa gods it is two quarters; for the Yāma gods, three; for the Tuṣita gods, four; for the Nirmāṇarati gods, five; and for the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods, it is one and a half krośas. (5–7)
But for those with form, at the beginning it is half a *yojana* (76c–d).
For the gods with form, in the first station—the Brahmakāyikas—the body is only half a *yojana* in measure. Beyond that: (76d).

(11) There is an increase by half a *yojana* at each of the three stages: one *yojana* for the Brahmapurohitas, one and a half for Mahābrahmā, and two *yojanas* for the Parīttābhas. (12) Beyond the Parīttābhas, however, the physical support [of the body] increases further. (13)
[The bodies] increase twofold by twofold, except for those from the Anabhrakas upward, which decrease by three *yojanas*.

(77a–b) For the Apramāṇābhas, [the body size] is four *yojanas*; for the Ābhāsvaras, eight. Thus, increasing twofold by twofold up to the Śubhakṛtsnas, it reaches sixty-four. For the Anabhrakas, it is twice that amount minus three *yojanas*, which is one hundred and twenty-five *yojanas*. Beyond that, for the Puṇyaprasavas and so on, the body size doubles again and again until the Akaniṣṭhas, whose bodies are sixteen thousand *yojanas* in height. (77c–d)
Thus, since there is a difference in physical stature, is there also a difference in lifespan? He says: "Yes, there is. In the [northern] Kuru continent, the lifespan is one thousand years.
In two [continents], it is reduced by half and half again.

(78b) Having excluded half of a half from each of the two continents, the lifespan of those in Godānīya is five hundred years; that of those in Pūrvavideha is two hundred and fifty years. Here [in Jambudvīpa], it is indefinite. (78c) (2)
In Jambūdvīpa, there is no fixed limit to the lifespan; sometimes it is longer, and sometimes it is shorter. (3) But at the end, it is ten years.
(78c'd) "Year" (*abda*) means a full year (*saṃvatsara*). At the end, as it decreases, the lifespan becomes ten years. (5)
"At the beginning, it is immeasurable" (78d).

At the beginning, for humans of the first eon (*prāthamakalpika*), the lifespan is immeasurable; it cannot be measured by numbers such as thousands and so forth. It has been stated [regarding] humans; [now] that which pertains to the gods must be explained. Since that can be explained by establishing their day and night (*ahorātra*), that very [measure] is established for them.
Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the inhabitants of the heavens.
(11) Among those in the desire realm, for the lower [gods]...
(79abc) (12) Those which are fifty years for humans are one night and day for the Cāturmahārājakāyika gods, who are the lowest among the deities of the desire realm. (13) (14)
Therefore, their lifespan is five hundred years.
(79c-d) By that [measure], with a day and night being as described, thirty such days making a month, and twelve months making a year, the measure of their lifespan is five hundred divine years.
For those above, both [the length of the day-night cycle and the lifespan] double successively. (80a-b)

For the higher gods, both the day-and-night and the lifespan are each double the preceding ones. How so? One hundred human years constitute one day-and-night for the Trāyastriṃśa gods; with that day-and-night, their divine lifespan is one thousand years. In this same manner, for the Yāma gods and the others, respectively, two, four, eight, and sixteen hundred human years constitute one day-and-night.

By that night and day, the measure of the lifespan is two, four, eight, and sixteen thousand divine years respectively. Above Yugandhara, because of the absence of the sun and moon, how is the establishment of the day and night for the gods, or what serves as the function of light? [It is known] from the closing and opening of flowers, like the friend of the water-lily (*kumuda-bandhu*); from the singing and silence of the birds; and from the departure of torpor. As for the function of light, it occurs through their own radiance. The lifespan of those with sensual desire has been stated. Now, however, [the lifespan] of those with form: (2)
There is no day and night; however, their lifespan is measured in aeons (*kalpa*) corresponding to the size of their own bodies.

(80b–d) For those beings of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) whose body is half a *yojana* in height, their lifespan is half an aeon. For those whose body is one *yojana*, it is one aeon. In this manner, for whichever being the body is so many *yojanas* in height, the lifespan is that many aeons, up until the Akaniṣṭha heaven, where the measure of lifespan is sixteen thousand aeons.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the lifespan increases by twenty thousand aeons at each successive level.

In the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the measure of the lifespan is twenty thousand *kalpas*. (7) In the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), it is more than that by twenty thousand. In the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), it is more than that by twenty thousand. (8) At the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), it is more than that by twenty thousand. Thus, their respective measures of lifespan are twenty, forty, sixty, and eighty thousand *kalpas*. (9–10) Which kind of *kalpa* should be understood here? Is it an intermediate *kalpa* (*antarakalpa*), or a *kalpa* of dissolution (*saṃvartakalpa*), or a *kalpa* of evolution (*vivarttakalpa*), or a great *kalpa* (*mahākalpa*)? (11)

From the Parīttābha [heaven] upwards, the lifespan is a great eon (mahākalpa); below that, it is half [of a great eon]. (81cd) From the very class of the Parīttābhas onwards, the lifespan should be understood as being measured by a great eon. Below that, the lifespans of Mahābrahmā and the others are established by taking half of a great eon and treating it as a full eon. How is this done?

The period during which the world evolves for twenty intermediate aeons (*antarakalpa*), the period during which the evolved world remains for twenty intermediate aeons, and the period during which it dissolves for twenty intermediate aeons—these sixty intermediate aeons are said to constitute one and a half aeons for Mahābrahmā. Having established this, by treating forty intermediate aeons as one [great] aeon, the measure of their lifespan has been stated. Thus, the measure of lifespan in the happy destinies has been explained;
now, that of the miserable destinies must be told. Regarding that, first:
The days and nights in the six [hells] beginning with Saṃjīva are equal, respectively, to the lifespans of the gods of the desire realm.

(19) Just as the lifespans of the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm have been stated, one should understand that the days and nights in the six hells—namely, Saṃjīva, Kālasūtra, Saṃghāta, Raurava, Mahāraurava, and Tapana—are equal to those [lifespans], respectively. (20–22)

Their lifespan is like that of the gods of the desire realm. (82c’d) By means of their own days and nights, their lifespan should be understood to be exactly as it is for the six classes of gods belonging to the desire realm, respectively. How so? For that which is the measure of the lifespan of the gods of the Four Great Kings is one day and night in the Saṃjīva great hell. Calculated by means of twelve-month years, the lifespan there is five hundred years.

That which is the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa gods is one day and night in the Kālasūtra great hell. By that day and night, the measure of lifespan there is one thousand years. In this manner, it should be applied accordingly to the others as well, up until the lifespan of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods; by a day and night equal to that [lifespan], the measure of lifespan in the Tāpana hell is sixteen thousand years. In the Pratāpana hell, it is half an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*); in the Pratāpana great hell, the measure of lifespan is half an intermediate kalpa.
In Avīci, it lasts for an intermediate kalpa; however, for animals, there is no fixed limit,
though at most—

(83c) An eon (*kalpa*) is the maximum lifespan of animals (*tiraścām*). That [maximum] is an intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*), which applies specifically to the *nāgas* such as Nanda, Upananda, Aśvatara, and others. For it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, these eight *nāgas* are great *nāgas*, who endure for an eon and support the earth," and so forth.
(83c'd) For the *pretas*, five hundred years measured by their own days and nights is the maximum lifespan.

That which is one month for humans is a single day and night for the *preta*s. By that measure of days and nights, their lifespan is five hundred years. What is the measure of the lifespan in the cold hells? The lifespan in the *Arbuda* hell is the time it takes to exhaust a *vāha* [measure] of sesame seeds by removing one seed every hundred years;
the lifespans in the subsequent hells increase twentyfold respectively. (84)

The Blessed One has described their lifespan by means of a mere analogy: "Monks, suppose there were here a Magadhan sesame-cart of twenty khārīs, filled to the brim with sesame seeds. If someone were to remove a single sesame seed at the end of every hundred years, monks, this Magadhan sesame-cart of twenty khārīs would more quickly reach exhaustion and depletion by such a process."
But I do not say that there is an end to the lifespan of those born in Arbuda. Monks, just as twenty Arbudas make one Nirarbuda—and so on in detail—just as twenty Padmas make one Mahāpadma;
thus, for these long-lived beings, is there premature death before their lifespan is completed, or not? In all cases, except for [the inhabitants of] Kuru, there is premature death. (85ab)

In Uttarakuru, sentient beings have a fixed lifespan and necessarily live out their entire life; among others, this is not necessarily the case. However, for many individuals—such as a Bodhisattva residing in Tuṣita who is bound to only one more birth, a being in his final existence, one prophesied by a Jina, one who has become a Jina, those who follow through faith or through the Dharma, and the embryos of a Bodhisattva or a Cakravartin king—there is no death in the interim.

The locations and bodies have been described in terms of the *yojana* measure, and the lifespan has been described in terms of the *varṣa* measure; however, the measure of those two [the *yojana* and the *varṣa*] has not yet been stated, so it must be explained. Furthermore, since all things are established by name, the limit of that [name] must also be stated. To provide a uniform explanation for these, the initial sequence is now begun: "Ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), syllables (*akṣara*), and moments (*kṣaṇa*) are the limits of matter (*rūpa*), names (*nāman*), and time (*adhvan*). (85b–c)

The limit of form (*rūpa*) as it is being diminished is the atom (*paramāṇu*). The limit of time is called the moment (*kṣaṇa*); the limit of a name is the syllable (*akṣara*), such as "go" (*gauḥ*). Furthermore, what is the measure of a moment? It is the duration required for a phenomenon (*dharma*) to acquire its own-being when all conditions are complete; or, for a moving phenomenon, the duration required to travel from one atom to the next atom. The Abhidharmikas say that sixty-five moments pass in the mere time it takes for a strong man to snap his fingers. An atom (*paramāṇu*) is the same as a subtle particle (*aṇu*). //85d//

Iron-dust, water-dust, rabbit-hair-dust, sheep-hair-dust, cow-hair-dust, window-dust, nit, and that which arises from it [the louse], as well as the barley-corn and the finger-joint, should be known to increase sevenfold each time. (86) This sequence beginning with the *paramāṇu* (ultimate atom) should be understood as increasing sevenfold at each step: seven *paramāṇus* make one *aṇu*; seven *aṇus* make one iron-dust (*lohareṇu*); seven of those make one water-dust (*abreṇu*); seven of those make one rabbit-hair-dust (*śaśareṇu*); seven of those make one sheep-hair-dust (*eḍakareṇu*); seven of those make one cow-hair-dust (*goraja*); seven of those make one window-dust (*vātāyanacchidrareṇu*); seven of those make one nit (*likṣā*), meaning the louse (*yūka*) that arises from it; and seven lice make one barley-corn (*yava*).

Seven barley grains constitute a finger-joint; it is well known that three joints constitute a finger, so this has not been explicitly stated. When laid side by side, twenty-four fingers make a cubit (*hasta*); four cubits make a bow (*dhanus*). (87abc) (3)
"Vyāma" means "by width" (*vyāsena*). (4) Five hundred of these [bows] constitute a *krośa*, and that is considered a forest (*araṇya*).
(5) Five hundred bows make one *krośa*; and a distance of one *krośa* from a village is intended as the forest (*grāmād araṇyam*). (6)
They say that those eight [yojanas] constitute one *yojana*.
(88a) The measurement of the *yojana* has been explained; now the measurement of time is being stated. (8) Furthermore, one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* [make one lava]. (9)
A *tatkṣaṇa* (88bc):
one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*. Furthermore, sixty of those [make] one *lava* (88c'd).

Sixty *tatkṣaṇas* are called a *lava*. (13) Each subsequent unit is thirty times the length of the preceding one. (14) Three [units] constitute a *muhūrta*, a day-and-night (*ahorātra*), and a month (*māsa*). (89ab) (15)

Thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*; thirty *muhūrtas* constitute one day and night (*ahorātra*). Sometimes the night is longer, sometimes shorter, and sometimes equal [to the day]. Thirty days and nights constitute a month. Twelve months constitute a year, which includes the omitted nights (*ūnarātra*).

There are four months of winter, four of summer, and four of the rainy season; these twelve months, together with the omitted nights (*ūnarātra*), constitute a year. For in one year, six omitted nights are subtracted. How so?
"When one and a half months of winter, summer, and the rainy season have passed, and half a month remains, the omitted night is subtracted by the wise."
The measurement of the years has been stated.
Now, the eon (*kalpa*) must be discussed. (2) The eon is remembered as being of many kinds. (3) 89d.

There are the intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*), the kalpa of dissolution (*saṃvarttakalpa*), the kalpa of evolution (*vivarttakalpa*), and the great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). Among these, first, the kalpa of dissolution is the destruction of the receptacle world (*bhājanakṣaya*) due to the non-existence of hell-beings. (90ab)

Indeed, from the time when beings cease to be reborn in the hells until the destruction of the receptacle world, there are two types of dissolution: the dissolution of the realms of rebirth (*gati-saṃvartanī*) and the dissolution of the elements (*dhātu-saṃvartanī*). Furthermore, there are two other dissolutions: the dissolution of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃvartanī*) and the dissolution of the receptacle world (*bhājana-saṃvartanī*). There comes a time when beings pass away from the hells and are no longer reborn there; that is the beginning of the aeon of dissolution (*saṃvarta-kalpa*).

When this world has remained withdrawn for twenty intermediate kalpas, it should be said that it has emerged [from dissolution]. When it is about to undergo those twenty intermediate kalpas of dissolution, it should be said that it has entered [into dissolution]. When not even a single sentient being remains in the hells, to that extent this world has become dissolved.

(10) That is to say, when the dissolution of the hells occurs, whoever at that time possesses karma that is certain to be experienced in hell is cast into the hells of other world-systems. The same should be stated for the dissolution of the animal realm and the dissolution of the hungry ghost realm. Animals dwelling in the great ocean dissolve first; however, those who live among humans remain together with them.

There is a world where a certain being among humans, having by himself and without a teacher attained the first *dhyāna* through the acquisition of its natural law (*dharmatā*), emerges from that state and utters these words: "O, how blissful is the joy and happiness born of seclusion! O, how peaceful is the joy and happiness born of seclusion! Hearing that sound, other beings also attain [the first *dhyāna*] and, upon passing away, are reborn in the Brahma-world.

When not even a single sentient being remains in Jambudvīpa, to this extent this world has undergone dissolution, namely, by the dissolution of Jambudvīpa. In the same way, the dissolutions of Pūrvavideha, Godānīya, and Uttarakuru are to be described. When not even a single sentient being remains among humans, to this extent this world has undergone dissolution, namely, by the dissolution of the human realm.

But the inhabitants of Uttarakuru, having passed away, are reborn among the gods who dwell in the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*), because there is an absence of detachment (*vairāgya*) there. Likewise, even among the gods of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*), they attain the first dhyāna and are reborn in the Brahma-world. When not even a single sentient being remains there, to this extent this world is said to have been destroyed, namely by the destruction of the realm of the Four Great Kings.

In this manner, the same should be stated up to the destruction of the Paranirmitavaśavartin gods. When not even a single sentient being remains among the gods of the desire realm, to this extent this world is said to be destroyed, namely, by the destruction of the desire realm.

Even in the Brahma-world, a certain being, having attained the second dhyāna—which arises through the very nature of things—emerges from it and utters these words: "O, how blissful is the joy and happiness born of concentration! O, how peaceful is the joy and happiness born of concentration! Hearing that sound, other beings also attain [the second dhyāna], and after passing away, they are reborn among the Ābhāsvara gods.

When not even a single sentient being remains in the Brahma-world, to this extent this world has dissolved, namely by the dissolution of sentient beings (*sattvasaṃvartanī*). Then, when the receptacle world (*bhājana*) is empty and the karma of sentient beings that projected it has been exhausted, seven suns appear from this very vicinity and gradually burn away everything, including the earth and Mount Sumeru, until nothing remains.

Therefore, from that very [fire] thus blazing, a flame cast by the wind goes forth, burning the empty Brahmā-palace. And that flame should be understood as belonging to that same level; for calamities of a different category do not spread. Because it is produced in connection with that [fire], it is said to be "that. For a fire belonging to the desire realm connects with a fire belonging to the form realm. In this way, it should be understood according to the appropriate application in the case of other destructions as well.

This period begins from the time when beings cease to die and be reborn in the hells until the destruction of the receptacle world. (9) The kalpa of evolution lasts from the initial wind until the emergence of the hells. (10) 90cd.

The period from the first wind until the emergence of sentient beings in the hells is called the aeon of evolution (*vivartakalpa*). When the world has thus dissolved, it remains for a long time as nothing but empty space; then, once again, through the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings, very gentle winds begin to stir in the sky as the preliminary signs of the receptacle worlds.

Then, that period during which this world remained dissolved for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*) should be called "elapsed"; that period during which it will evolve for twenty intermediate kalpas should be called "approaching. Thereafter, those winds increasing give rise to the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*) as previously described. From that, gradually and according to the sequence and method already stated, everything arises: the water-circle (*apmaṇḍala*), the great earth consisting of gold (*kāñcanamayī mahāpṛthivī*), the continents (*dvīpa*), Sumeru and the other mountains, and so forth.

First, the Brahma-palace arises; then, up to the Yāma realm, and then the wind-circle and so forth. To this extent, this world is said to have been completed by way of the evolution of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). Then, a certain being, having passed away from the Ābhāsvara heaven, is reborn in the empty Brahma-palace. Other beings also, having passed away from there, are reborn among the Brahmapurohitas, and then among the Brahmakāyikas and the Paranirmitavaśavartins.

Gradually, they are reborn in Uttarakuru, Godānīya, Pūrvavideha, Jambūdvīpa, among the pretas, among animals, and in the hells. For this is the nature of things (*dharmatā*): that which is destroyed last is the first to re-form. When even a single sentient being has appeared in the hells, then the period of twenty intermediate aeons (*antarakalpa*) during which this world re-forms is completed.
When it remains in a state of re-formation for twenty intermediate aeons, that period is reached.
An intermediate kalpa lasts from [the time when the lifespan is] immeasurable down to ten years.

(91ab) While the world is evolving, nineteen intermediate kalpas pass for humans with immeasurable lifespans. [This occurs] as those with immeasurable lifespans decrease until their lifespan becomes ten years. This is the first intermediate kalpa of the world that has evolved and remains.
Thereafter: (4)
There are eighteen other intermediate aeons consisting of increases and decreases.

(91b’cd) Beyond that, there are eighteen further intermediate aeons (*antarakalpa*) consisting of eighteen increases and eighteen decreases. How so? From those beings with a lifespan of ten years, as they undergo increase, their lifespan gradually reaches eighty thousand years; then, as they undergo decrease again, it returns to a lifespan of ten years. This constitutes the second intermediate aeon. In this manner, there are eighteen such [aeons]. There is one final period of increase. (92a) (9)

The twentieth intermediate kalpa is an increase alone, not a decrease. [This refers to] from humans with a lifespan of ten years up to those with a lifespan of eighty thousand years. Now, to what extent do these increases reach?
They reach up to a lifespan of eighty thousand years.

Beyond this they do not increase; for as long as the period of increase and decrease of other intermediate kalpas lasts, so long is the period of decrease of the first, and the period of increase of the last. Thus, all are of equal duration. (13) "Thus this world, having evolved, remains for twenty kalpas" (14). By this principle of intermediate kalpas, this world, having evolved, remains for twenty intermediate kalpas. For as long a time as it remains evolved, (16) for exactly that same length of time (17) [it remains].
It evolves, remains dissolved, and dissolves for an equal duration.

(93ab) It evolves for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), it dissolves for twenty, and it remains dissolved for twenty. Although at that time neither increase nor decrease occurs, the duration is calculated as being equal.
