Among these, by one intermediate kalpa the receptacle worlds (*bhājana*) are formed; by nineteen intermediate kalpas they are inhabited; by one intermediate kalpa the receptacle worlds are destroyed; and by nineteen intermediate kalpas they remain empty.
These twenty sets of four intermediate *kalpas* constitute eighty [intermediate *kalpas*].
These eighty indeed form one great *kalpa* (*mahākalpa*).

This is the measure of a great *kalpa*. What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a *kalpa*? Its intrinsic nature consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). As for the statement that "Buddhahood is attained after three incalculable *kalpas*," which *kalpas* are these? They are precisely those great *kalpas* that have been described.
Buddhahood arises from three incalculable [aeons]. (93d) (4) (94a) (5)

[If it is said that] "by the exhaustion of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons," how can there be a mention of "three" [incalculables] when there is no end to what is incalculable? This should not be understood in that way. What then? A *muktaka-sūtra* recites: "An incalculable consists of sixty numerical places (*sthānāntara*). (7) Which are the sixty? One, being without a second, is the first numerical place. Ten ones are the second. (8) Ten tens are a hundred, the third; ten hundreds are a thousand.

Ten thousands are a *prabheda* (9); ten *prabhedas* are a *lakṣa*; ten *lakṣas* are an *atilakṣa*; ten *atilakṣas* are a *kauṭi* (10); ten *kauṭis* are a *madhya*; ten *madhyas* are an *ayuta*; ten *ayutas* are a *mahāyuta*; ten *mahāyutas* are a *niyuta* (11); ten *niyutas* are a *mahāniyuta*; ten *mahāniyutas* are a *prayuta*; ten *prayutas* are a *mahāprayuta*; ten (12) *mahāprayutas* are a *kaṅkara*; ten *kaṅkaras* are a *mahākaṅkara*.

Ten *mahākaṅkara*s are a *visvara*; ten *visvara*s are a *mahāvisvara*; ten *mahāvisvara*s are an *akṣobhya*; ten *akṣobhya*s are a *mahākṣobhya*; ten *mahākṣobhya*s are a *vivāha*; ten *vivāha*s are a *mahāvivāha*; ten *mahāvivāha*s are an *utsaṅga*; ten *utsaṅga*s are a *mahotsaṅga*; ten *mahotsaṅga*s are a *vāhana*; ten *vāhana*s are a *mahāvāhana*; ten *mahāvāhana*s are a *tiṭibha*; ten *tiṭibha*s are a *mahātiṭibha*.

Ten *mahātiṭibhās* are a *hetu*; ten *hetus* are a *mahāhetu*; ten *mahāhetus* are a *karabha*; ten *karabhas* are a *mahākarabha*; ten *mahākarabhas* are an *indra*; ten *indras* are a *mahendra*; ten *mahendras* are a *samāptam*; ten *samāptas* are a *mahāsamāptam*; ten *mahāsamāptas* are a *gati*; ten *gatīs* are a *mahāgati*; ten *mahāgatīs* are a *nimbaraja*; ten *nimbarajas* are a *mahānimbaraja*.

Ten *mahānimbaraja*s are a *mudrā*; ten *mudrā*s are a *mahāmudrā*; ten *mahāmudrā*s are a *bala*; ten *bala*s are a *mahābala*; ten *mahābala*s are a *saṃjñā*; ten *saṃjñā*s are a *mahāsaṃjñā*; ten *mahāsaṃjñā*s are a *vibhūta*; ten *vibhūta*s are a *mahāvibhūta*; ten *mahāvibhūta*s are a *balākṣa*; ten *balākṣa*s are a *mahābalākṣa*; ten *mahābalākṣa*s are an *asaṃkhya*. Eight [units] from the middle are expanded.

Thus, the eons that have reached the number contained within these sixty places are called "incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*). Having turned back from that point, they are counted again; in this way, three such incalculables are spoken of. It is not, however, that they cannot be calculated at all.

Is it indeed only after a long duration of time that Bodhisattvas who have made their vows awaken to enlightenment? Or will this be so? For Bodhisattvas awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment through a great accumulation of merit and wisdom, by means of the six perfections, through hundreds of thousands of various difficult feats, and over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

Even if there were another way to attain liberation, for what purpose do they undertake such great effort? They undertake such great effort for the sake of others, thinking, "How might I also be able to protect others from the great flood of suffering? What is their own self-interest in this service to others? This very service to others is their self-interest, because it is what they desire. Now, this will be believed.

This is indeed difficult to believe for those who are self-centered and devoid of compassion; yet it is certainly believed by the compassionate. For just as some here, having practiced cruelty, are observed to delight in the misfortunes of others even when their own interests are not at stake, so too it is possible that there exist others who, having practiced compassion, delight in performing deeds for the benefit of others even while their own interests are present. This is not to be doubted.

In the same way, through the power of habituation, those who are ignorant of the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) direct self-attachment toward the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), which are not the self, and consequently undergo sufferings for its sake. Likewise, it is possible that, again through the power of habituation, they turn away self-attachment from those [formative forces], increase their concern for others, and thereby undergo sufferings for the sake of others.

For it is indeed another lineage (*gotrāntara*) that arises in such a manner: one who suffers through the suffering of others and rejoices in their happiness, but not for oneself. Furthermore, they do not perceive any other self-interest. And regarding this, it is said:
"The inferior person seeks by whatever means possible the happiness residing within his own continuum;
the middling person seeks only the cessation of suffering, not happiness, because happiness is the locus of suffering."

"The best [of beings] seeks the happiness of others through the sufferings belonging to his own continuum, as well as the absolute cessation of suffering; for he is one who suffers from their very suffering. (19) Furthermore, do Buddhas arise during the period of increase (*utkarṣa*), or rather during the period of decrease (*apakarṣa*)? (21)

For the decline lasts until the lifespan reaches one hundred years; (94a'b) when the decline has begun among beings whose lifespan is eight thousand years, up until the time when humans have a lifespan of one hundred years—in this interval, Buddhas arise. Why not during the period of increase? Because at that time, sentient beings are difficult to stir with a sense of spiritual urgency (*duḥsamudvejāḥ*). Why not when the lifespan is below one hundred? Because at that time, the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) are excessively prevalent: namely, the corruption of lifespan (*āyuṣkaṣāya*), the corruption of the eon (*kalpakaṣāya*), the corruption of afflictions (*kleśakaṣāya*), the corruption of views (*dṛṣṭikaṣāya*), and the corruption of sentient beings (*sattvakaṣāya*).

Below the period of decline, life-span and the other factors are called "corruptions" (*kaṣāya*) because they have become like dregs due to their inferiority. For by two [of these] there is, respectively, the ruin of life and of the requisites; by two [others], the ruin of the side of wholesome qualities, on account of the pursuit of devotion to sensual pleasure and self-mortification, or else with respect to the sides of householders and renunciants. By one [remaining corruption], there is the ruin of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), due to the loss of stature, beauty, health, strength, growth, mindfulness, vigor, and fortitude.
Now, at what time do Pratyekabuddhas arise? Pratyekabuddhas arise during two [periods]. (94c)

Both during the period of increase and during the period of decrease. For there are two kinds of Pratyekabuddhas: those who move in groups (*vargacārin*) and those who are like the horn of a rhinoceros (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*). Among them, those who move in groups are called Pratyekajinas who were formerly Śrāvakas. Others maintain that there are also those who were formerly ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), namely those who, having produced the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) elsewhere, personally awaken to the Path here in this [degenerate age].

For they recite this ancient account (*pūrvayoga*): it is said that on a mountain, five hundred ascetics were performing painful austerities, until a monkey who had lived with a *pratyekabuddha* arrived and, by demonstrating the latter’s deportment (*īryāpatha*), they realized the enlightenment of a *pratyekabuddha*. Now, those who are noble (*ārya*) would not perform painful austerities; moreover, they dwell alone like the rhinoceros horn. Of those *pratyekabuddhas*, the rhinoceros-like one has been such for a succession of a hundred eons. (94d)

Having practiced for a hundred great aeons (*mahākalpa*) in the accumulations for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*), one becomes like the rhinoceros horn (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*). They are called *pratyekabuddhas* because they have awakened themselves alone without instruction. For they discipline only themselves and no others. What, then, is the reason [for this]? It is not that they are incapable of teaching the Dharma, since they have attained the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); moreover, it is possible for them to teach the Dharma even by recollecting the teachings of former Buddhas.

Nor are they devoid of compassion, for they manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. Nor is it because sentient beings lack the capacity; for there exist those who have attained freedom from passion through the worldly path (*laukikamārga*). What then? Due to the force of their former practice, they possess little zeal and are inclined toward [solitude]; thus, they do not exert themselves to engage others in the grasping of the profound Dharma. For it is difficult to lead people who flow with the current against that current. Furthermore, it is because they fear distraction and social contact, desiring to avoid the consequence of being drawn into leading a community.
Now, when do the Wheel-turning Kings (*cakravartin*) arise?

(2) The arising of a Wheel-turning King does not occur below [an age of] eighty thousand years. (95ab) (3) When the lifespan of humans is immeasurable, up until it reaches eighty thousand years, that is the time for the arising of Wheel-turning Kings, but not below that. This is because those with a lifespan shorter than that are not fit vessels for such abundance of crops. Their nature is to rule a kingdom by means of a wheel; thus they are called "Wheel-turners. Furthermore, they are of four kinds. (5)

Those who possess wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron [are the wheel-turning kings]. (95c) Those who possess wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron—of these, the first is the supreme, the second is nearly supreme, the third is middling, and the fourth is inferior.
They [are ranked] in descending order. (95c’d)

Regarding those who possess wheels of iron, copper, silver, or gold, [it is said]: he whose wheel is made of iron is the sovereign of one continent; he whose is made of copper is the sovereign of two; he whose is made of silver is the sovereign of three; he whose is made of gold is the sovereign of the four continents. This is the explanation according to the *Prajñapti* [treatise]. However, in the Sūtra, because it mentions only the principal [wheel], there is only the single golden wheel.

When, for a consecrated Kṣatriya king, on the fifteenth day of the Poṣadha, having bathed his head and observed the fast, while he is situated upon the upper terrace of his palace surrounded by his assembly of ministers, there appears in the eastern direction a Wheel-Jewel—possessing a thousand spokes, with a hub and a rim, perfect in every aspect, not made by a human artisan, divine, and entirely golden—then that king becomes a Cakravartin.
And in this manner these Cakravartins arise.

And two do not appear simultaneously, as in the case of Buddhas. It is stated in the Sūtra: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, should arise in the world neither before nor after the other; such a thing cannot exist. It is possible that a single Tathāgata [should arise]; and as it is with a Tathāgata, so it is with two Cakravartins. Here, this must be considered: is the "world" intended here the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, or all world systems?

(20) Some maintain that Buddhas do not arise elsewhere [than in Jambudvīpa]. What is the reason? Lest there be an obstruction to the Blessed One’s power (*śakti*). For the Blessed One alone is capable everywhere. If one Buddha were unable to discipline those to be trained (*vineya*) in a certain place, then another would also be unable there. And it is said in the Sūtra: "If... (Pradhan: ...).

"Śāriputra, if someone were to approach you and ask: 'Is there at present any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who is equal to the śramaṇa Gautama, that is to say, in regard to perfect awakening? Being thus asked, how would you answer? If [he were to ask]..."

"Venerable sir, if someone were to approach me and ask this, being thus questioned, I would answer him: 'At present, there is no ascetic or brahmin who is equal to the Blessed One with respect to perfect enlightenment. For what reason?"

"I have heard this directly from the Blessed One and have received it directly from him: it is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Tathāgatas, one before and one after, should arise in the world; such a thing cannot occur. [Objection: But then what of that which was said by the Blessed One in the *Brahmasūtra*, "As far as the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world-system extends, here I hold sway"? [Response: This teaching is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*). What is the intention here? It is because he surveys [the world] up to that extent without any deliberate effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

(5) However, through intentional effort (*abhisaṃskāra*), the range of the Buddhas' vision is infinite. Those belonging to other schools maintain that there are indeed Buddhas in other world-systems. (6) What is the reason? For many are seen to be engaged simultaneously in the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*). And it is not possible for many Buddhas to arise together in one place; yet, since there is no obstacle to their arising, they necessarily arise in other world-systems. (7–8) For many are seen to be proceeding simultaneously in the accumulations, and it is not the case that the simultaneous conjunction of many Buddhas in one [place] is possible; nor is there any impediment to their arising. Thus, they are certainly born in other world-systems.

Regarding "the world-systems in between": even if the Blessed One were to extend his lifespan for an entire eon, he would not be able to act here as he does in other infinite world-systems, let alone within a human lifetime. And how does the Buddha act here?

[He acts] thus: "This person has such a faculty; after such a time, in such a place, by relying on such a person, through the removal of this fault and the application of this factor, by means of this practice, that which has not yet arisen will arise, or that which is incomplete will be brought to fulfillment."

As for this sūtra cited here—“It is impossible, it is out of the question, that two Tathāgatas, neither before nor after the other, should arise simultaneously in one world”—this very point must be considered: was this said with reference to a single world-system, or rather to all [world-systems]? Furthermore, there would be no arising of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) in this world-system [if the restriction applied universally], because their simultaneous arising is prohibited just as it is for Buddhas.

Now, this is accepted: why, however, is this not accepted—that the appearance of Buddhas in the world is a source of merit? (16) If it were to occur for many [Buddhas] in many [worlds], there would be no fault; there would be a connection with the prosperity and the ultimate good of the majority of worlds. (17) But even if it were in a single [world], why do two Tathāgatas not arise simultaneously? Because of the absence of necessity and because of the power of their previous vows.

(18) For in this way Bodhisattvas make their vow: "O, may I arise as a Buddha in a world that is blind and without a guide, as a protector for those who are without a protector. This is for the sake of generating reverence and for the sake of intense aspiration. For when there is only one Buddha, they show greater reverence, thinking, "Another such as this is difficult to find," and they aspire more intensely toward the practice of the teaching, thinking, "Once he has departed or entered final nirvāṇa, we shall not be on this [fortunate] ground. (22)

Now, how do these wheel-turning monarchs (*cakravartin*), conquering the earth with wheels made of gold and other materials, achieve victory? In due order: they conquer by being met in procession, by their own lineage, by conflict, and by weapons. (96cd) (24)

When one possesses a golden wheel, the minor kings go out themselves to meet him, saying: "These territories of Your Majesty are prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many people. May Your Majesty govern them; we shall become Your Majesty’s followers. When one possesses a silver wheel, he himself goes into their presence, and afterwards they bow down before him.

He whose wheel is made of copper goes into their presence and quarrels with them; afterwards, they bow down. (4) He whose wheel is made of iron goes into their presence, they brandish weapons at one another, and afterwards they submit. But all (5) universal monarchs (cakravartins) (6) are non-violent. (7) //96d'// (7)

Even when conquering by means of weapons, no killing occurs; having conquered, they establish sentient beings in the ten wholesome paths of action. For this very reason, they are certain to be reborn among the gods. It is stated in the Sūtra that with the appearance of a universal monarch (cakravartin) in the world, there is the appearance of the seven jewels in the world.

Namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure. How is it that elephants and so forth, which are reckoned as sentient beings, are produced by the karma of another? Indeed, no one is produced by the karma of another; rather, when those [beings] are produced, it is their own karmas—accumulated by whichever sentient being was destined for such a connection—that produce them.

Is this alone the distinction of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) from other kings? There is yet another distinction. Namely, they possess the thirty-two marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*), just like the Buddhas. However, in that regard, the Sage’s marks excel through their [correct] location, brilliance, and completeness.
(97ab) The marks of the Buddhas are more correctly located, more brilliant, and more complete; this is the distinction between them.
Were the humans of the first eon indeed possessed of kings? No, it is said. How then? (18) "In the beginning, beings were like those of the Form Realm" (97c).

(19) The humans of the first eon were like those belonging to the Form Realm (*rūpāvacara*). It is stated in the Sūtra: "They were possessed of form, mind-made, complete with all major and minor limbs, unimpaired, with no deficient faculties, beautiful, abiding in a state of radiant color, self-luminous, moving through the sky, feeding on joy (*prīti*), nourished by joy, long-lived, and remaining for a long duration. (20–22)
Then, gradually, due to attachment to flavors, (97d) and out of laziness, having made provisions for the future, the field-guardian was hired by those who were full of grasping. (98ab)

When they had become thus, the essence of the earth appeared, possessing a flavor as sweet as honey. One being among them, who was by nature greedy, smelled its fragrance, tasted its flavor, and ate it. Other beings likewise did the same. This was the beginning of solid food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*). Through the habitual consumption of that food, coarseness and heaviness entered their bodies, and their [supernatural] powers disappeared.

Then, when darkness had arisen, the sun and moon appeared. As they became greedy for the taste of that essence of the earth (*bhūmirasa*), it gradually disappeared and a crust of earth (*bhūmiparpaṭaka*) appeared. Greedy for that as well, even that disappeared. A forest creeper (*vanalatā*) appeared; greedy for that too, it also disappeared. Unplowed and unsown rice (*śāli*) grew up, and they ate it.

Now, because that [food] was coarse, for the sake of discharging its waste, the urinary and excretory tracts of sentient beings appeared along with the female and male sexual organs, and their physical forms became differentiated. As they gazed at one another and, by the force of past habituation, fell prey to the crocodile of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) surged forth, whereby they engaged in misconduct. This was the beginning of the possession by the demon of desire for those who possess lust.

And indeed, they used to gather that rice in the evening for their evening meal and in the morning for their morning meal. Then, a certain being who was by nature indolent began to store it up; other beings also began to store it up. Once the sense of "mine" had arisen among them regarding that [rice], the rice, though reaped again and again, did not grow back.

Then, having divided the fields and developed an attachment to their own, they began to seize what belonged to others; this was the first beginning of theft. To restrain them, they gathered together and hired a certain distinguished man to protect the fields in exchange for a sixth share of the produce. Because he was the lord (*adhipati*) of the fields (*kṣetra*), the designation "Kṣatriya, Kṣatriya" arose for him.

(15) Because he was highly esteemed by the great body of people and because he gladdened the subjects, the designation "Mahāsaṃmata" (Greatly Esteemed) arose for him as "King. This was the beginning of the royal lineage. Among those there, those whose minds turned away from household life, the designation "Brāhmaṇas" arose for them. Then, due to the greed of a certain king, beings—who were not sharing [the produce]—fell into an abundance of thievery; he approached them with weapons. Thereupon, others began to speak false words, saying, "We are not doers of such things. (19)
Then, due to the increase of the paths of action, there occurs a reduction in the lifespan to ten years.

(98cd) Thus, when the paths of action have increased in this manner, as the human lifespan gradually diminishes, humans with a lifespan of ten years come into being. Therefore, two factors are the root source of this entire flood of misfortune: attachment to savory tastes and laziness. The conclusion of the intermediate kalpa for humans with a ten-year lifespan occurs. To explain how this happens, he says: (23)

The conclusion of the kalpa occurs through weapons, disease, and famine. (99ab) (24) The exit from the intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) takes place by means of weapons, disease, and famine. At the time of the conclusion of the intermediate kalpa, human beings have a lifespan of ten years; they are stained by unrighteous passion, overcome by improper greed, and enveloped by false doctrines. Their malice reaches its peak, and upon seeing one another, a fierce mind of resentment and a murderous intent arise within them.

It is just as when a deer-hunter sees a wild deer in the forest; whatever they seize, whether a piece of wood or a clod of earth, that appears to them as a sharp weapon. They deprive one another of life. Furthermore, at the time of the world's dissolution, when the lifespan of humans is ten years, non-human beings release pestilence because of those very same faults. Incurable diseases and other afflictions appear among them, by which they die.

Furthermore, when the lifespan of humans is ten years, because of those very same faults, the gods do not release rain, whereby famine arises—namely, the *cañcu*, the *śvetāsthi*, and the *śalākāvṛtti*. And how is there the *cañcu*? It is for two reasons: that which is currently called a "collection" (*samavāya*) is then called *cañcu*; and a "winnowing basket" (*samuga*) is also called *cañcu*.

And those humans, overcome by hunger and weakness, gather together and die; they also deposit seeds in jars for the sake of favoring future generations. Therefore, that famine is called *cañcu*. How [is there] "white bones" (*śvetāsthi*)? For two reasons.

For when those whose bodies are withered and parched die, their bones quickly become white; and being struck by hunger, they collect these white bones, boil them, and drink [the broth]. How is there "subsistence by means of a tally" (*śalākāvṛtti*)? It is for two reasons. For those beings distribute food among households by means of a tally-mark, [saying]: "Today the master of the house shall eat; tomorrow the mistress of the house," and so forth.

And having extracted grains from the crevices of grain-stores with a probe, they boil them in abundant water and drink it. They describe it thus: "Whoever has protected the abstention from taking life for even a single day, or has respectfully offered a single myrobalan fruit or a single alms-meal to the Saṅgha, will not be reborn during those intermediate kalpas of weapons, disease, and famine.
Now, for how long a time do these calamities of weapons, disease, and famine persist for those beings?
For seven days, seven months, and seven years, respectively:

(99cd) the slaughter by weapons lasts for seven days; disease lasts for seven months and seven days; and famine lasts for seven years, seven months, and seven days—the word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction. At that time, in two of the continents, there appear their counterparts: malice reaches its peak, as do nakedness, weakness, hunger, and thirst.

As it has been stated, "In this same way, it should be understood that the same applies to the other destructions (*saṃvartanī*) as appropriate. Now, how many are these destructions? Furthermore, there are three destructions: by fire, water, and wind. (100ab) (2)

*Saṃvartanī* means that in this [destruction], sentient beings perish together in a single meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). There is a destruction by fire through seven suns; a destruction by water through rainwater; and a destruction by wind through the agitation of the winds. By these [destructions], not even a subtle part of the receptacle worlds (*bhājanaloka*) remains. However, on this point, certain non-Buddhist teachers (*tīrthaṃkara*) maintain that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal and remain at that time. Why do they maintain this?

Let it not be that the manifestation of gross things occurs without a seed. But has it not been stated that the wind produced by the karma of sentient beings, distinguished by its specific power, is the seed? Or rather, the wind at the summit of the world-system during the period of dissolution (*saṃvartanī*) will be its cause. The Mahīśāsakas recite in their Sūtra: "By means of the wind, seeds are brought from other world-systems. Even so, they do not maintain that sprouts and the like arise from seeds and such. What then?

[They arise] from their own parts, and those [parts] likewise from their own [parts], continuing thus down to the atoms. What is this "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) of seeds and the like toward sprouts and so forth? It is nothing other than the approaching of those atoms. But what is the reason they maintain this? Because it is not logical for something to arise from a heterogeneous cause. Why is it not logical? Because there would be a lack of restriction (*aniyama*). [Objection: This will not be so, because of the restriction of capacity (*śaktiniyama*), just as in the case of the production of sound or qualities produced by heat (*pākaja*).

For the property of a quality (*guṇadharma*) is manifold, but substance (*dravya*) is not so. Indeed, it is observed that substances of the same kind arise only from substances of the same kind; for example, a mat from *vīraṇa* grass, and a cloth from threads. This [argument] is untenable. What is untenable here? That which is unestablished (*asiddha*) is cited as a proof. What is unestablished here? That the mat is something other than the *vīraṇa* grass, and the cloth is something other than the threads.

For those very [parts], being arranged in such-and-such a way, receive their respective designations, just like a row of ants. How is this to be understood? Because a cloth is not perceived when there is a connection with only a single thread. For what obstacle would there be to the perception of a cloth that exists at that time? If it were to exist only partially, then what is present here would be a portion of a cloth, not the cloth itself. Furthermore, the cloth would be merely a collection [of parts]. And what portion of the cloth is there other than the threads?

If one were to depend upon the conjunction with multiple substrata, then the cognition of a cloth would occur only when there is conjunction with its fringe alone, or it might not occur at all, because the middle and further parts would not be in contact with the sense organ. Furthermore, if the conjunction with the parts were successive, there would be no simultaneous cognition of the parts by means of both sight and touch. Therefore, due to successive conjunctions, the determination of a whole arises only with respect to the parts themselves, like the [illusory] perception of a circle of fire from a whirling torch.

Since the color and other qualities of a cloth cannot exist in threads that possess distinct colors, types, and functions, if the cloth were to possess a variegated color and so forth, there would also be the production of heterogeneous effects. Furthermore, on the non-variegated side of the cloth, one would either not see the cloth at all or see it as variegated. It is utterly preposterous to claim that its action is also variegated. Moreover, if there were a difference between heat and light within the radiance of a fire, the color and touch of that radiance would be impossible to establish at its beginning, middle, and end.

Even though atoms are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), they are perceived when in their aggregate state—just as they possess the capacity to initiate effects, and just as those with ophthalmia perceive scattered hairs. For them, a single hair is beyond the senses, just like a single atom. Furthermore, since the designation "atom" is applied only to form and other such qualities (*rūpādi*), the destruction of the atom is established upon the destruction of those qualities.

For if substance (*dravya*) were indeed the atom, and if substance were something other than color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest, then its destruction would not be established upon their destruction. It is illogical for it to be distinct, insofar as it cannot be determined which of these are earth, water, and fire, and which are their respective color-forms and so forth. Furthermore, they are recognized as being graspable by sight and touch; moreover, when wool, cotton, safflower, saffron, and the like are burnt, the cognition of them ceases. Therefore, that cognition occurs only with respect to the specific distinctions of color-form and the rest.

Regarding the recognition of a jar upon the production of its baked state: (7) this occurs because of the similarity of its shape, like a row [of objects], for one who does not see a distinguishing mark lacks recognition. Or rather, what regard can there be for the prattle of fools? (8) So let this non-refutation stand for now.
(9) Now, which is the summit of which dissolution (*saṃvartanī*)?
(10) The three dhyānas, beginning with the second, are their summits respectively. //100cd// (11)

There are three limits of destruction (*saṃvartanī-śīrṣa*). For the destruction by fire, the second dhyāna is the limit; everything below it is consumed by fire. For the destruction by water, the third dhyāna is the limit; everything below it is dissolved by water. For the destruction by wind, the fourth dhyāna is the limit; everything below it is scattered away. That which is above the reach of a particular destruction is called its "limit. But what is the reason that the first, second, and third dhyānas are destroyed by fire, water, and wind respectively?

Because of their similarity to defects (*apakṣāla*): (101a) for in the first *dhyāna*, applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are the defects; and because they burn the mind, they are like fire. In the second [dhyāna], joy (*prīti*) is the defect; and because it makes the basis (*āśraya*) supple through its connection with pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), it is like water. For this very reason, it is stated in the Sūtra that in that [second dhyāna] there is the cessation of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) due to the departure of all bodily harshness. In the third *dhyāna*, inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*) are the defects; and these are indeed wind.

Thus, just as there is a corresponding internal corruption in whichever meditative attainment (*dhyāna-samāpatti*), so too is there a corresponding external [corruption] in that birth in the meditative realm (*dhyānopapatti*). Why does the destruction by earth (*pṛthivī-saṃvartanī*) not occur? For it is the earth itself that is designated as the "receptacle" (*bhājana*); therein, there is conflict with fire, water, and wind, but not with earth. Now, why does the destruction not occur in the fourth dhyāna? Because in the fourth, there is no motion (*aniñjana*).

Because it is free from internal defects, the Blessed One has described the fourth dhyāna as "unshakable" (*āneñja*). Therefore, since external defects do not arise there, there is no destruction (*saṃvartanī*) therein. Others say it is due to the power of the Śuddhāvāsa deities; for they are neither able to enter the formless realms (*ārūpya*) nor to go elsewhere. [Objection: In that case, the receptacle world (*bhājana*) of the fourth dhyāna would have to be eternal. [Response: It is not eternal, because its palaces arise and perish together with the sentient beings [who inhabit them]. (101cd)

For the fourth dhyāna is not connected to a single level; rather, its various locations are separated like stars. Even there, whatever sentient being is born or passes away does so together with his celestial palace (*vimāna*); thus, it possesses no permanence. By what sequence, then, do these destructions (*saṃvartanī*) occur? First, in uninterrupted succession, there are seven destructions by fire. After that—

One [destruction] is by water; (102a') (9) immediately after seven destructions by fire, there occurs a destruction by water. (10) When seven such cycles by water have thus passed, again— (102a''b) (11)
By means of fire, there is a seventh [cycle] (102c).
According to this sequence, when seven cycles of destruction by water have passed, there occurs again a seventh cycle of destruction by fire. After that, there is destruction by wind. (102d)

Afterwards, there occurs one destruction by wind. What is the reason? For just as there is a specific duration of the personal bodies (*ātmabhāva*) of those beings due to the excellence of their meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), so too is there a specific duration of the receptacle worlds (*bhājana*). Thus, there are fifty-six destructions by fire, seven destructions by water, and one destruction by wind.
In this way, the statement in the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* is well-established: "The lifespan of the Śubhakṛtsna gods is sixty-four eons (*kalpa*)."

“Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. Thus ends the *Lokanirdeśa* (Exposition of the World) in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.
The third treasury-location (kośasthāna) is completed.
[This is] the work of the venerable Lāmāvāka.
Whatever merit is herein.
Chapter IV [p.192]
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the Fourth Chapter:
(1) Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!

(2) Now, as for this manifold variety of the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world that has been described, by whom was it created? Indeed, it was not created by anyone preceded by conscious intention. What then? [It was created] by the [karma] of sentient beings. (4)

The variety of the world is born of karma. (1a) If it is born of karma, why is it that by the karma of sentient beings, saffron, sandalwood, and so forth are produced as more delightful than their own bodies? (6) It is precisely the karma of those sentient beings who perform mixed actions that is of such a nature: that their physical bases are born as if they were wounds, while their enjoyments are delightful as a remedy for them. But for the gods, who do not perform mixed actions, both are delightful. What, then, is that karma? He says: (8)

Volition and that which is produced by it. (1b) It is stated in the Sūtra: "There are two types of action: volitional action (*cetanā-karman*) and action after having willed (*cetayitvā*). That which is after having willed is what is produced by volition. These two types of action become three: namely, actions of body, speech, and mind. How are these actions established? Is it by way of their basis (*āśraya*), or by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or by way of their origination (*samutthāna*)? If it were by way of the basis, there would result only one bodily action, because all [actions] are based upon the body.

If [action] is defined by its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then vocal action alone would result, because speech has the intrinsic nature of action. If it is defined by its origination (*samutthāna*), then mental action alone would result, because all [actions] originate from the mind. Thus, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the three [types of action] correspond respectively to the three causes.
Furthermore, in this context: intention (*cetanā*) is mental action. (1c) (15)
It should be understood that volition (*cetanā*) is mental action (*manaskarman*). (16) And the actions of speech and body arise from it.
||1d || It should be understood that those two, the actions of body and speech, are what was referred to as "action after having willed" (*cetayitvā karman*), which is produced by that volition. (18)
But those two, namely the informative and the non-informative, (2a) (19) should be understood as each having the nature of both informative and non-informative action of body and speech.
However, in that regard, (20)
Bodily intimation is accepted as being shape (*saṃsthāna*).

Bodily intimation is the various shapes of the body produced by the power of the mind. Others maintain that it is motion (*gati*), for bodily action belongs to one who is moving, not to one who is not moving.
Regarding these, it is said:
"There is no going, because the conditioned is momentary. (2bc) (2)

What is this so-called "moment" (*kṣaṇa*)? It is the acquisition of self-existence (*ātmalābha*) that perishes immediately thereafter. That which possesses this [nature] is "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*), like one who possesses a staff (*daṇḍika*). For all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) do not exist beyond the acquisition of their own existence; thus, they perish in the very place where they were born. Therefore, it is illogical for them to migrate to another location. Consequently, movement (*gati*) is not bodily action (*kāyakarma*). This would indeed be the case if the momentariness of everything were established. Know that this is already established. Why? Because the conditioned necessarily undergoes cessation. (2d)

For the destruction of entities is indeed spontaneous. What is the reason? For there must be a cause for an effect, yet destruction is non-existence. And what can be done for that which is non-existence? If this spontaneous destruction did not occur to an entity immediately upon its arising, it would not occur later either, because the entity remains the same. If, on the other hand, it has become otherwise, it is not logical for that very same thing to undergo alteration; for it is not possible for that very thing to be characterized differently from itself.

Indeed, the destruction of wood and other substances through contact with fire and so forth is observed. And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) more authoritative than what is observed. Nor is the destruction of everything accidental. How then do you think that you perceive the destruction of wood and other things through contact with fire and so forth? It is simply because they are no longer seen; this matter must first be carefully considered.

Is it that wood and other such things are no longer seen because they have been destroyed by contact with fire, or rather that they have perished of their own accord and others have not arisen in their place, and for that reason they are not seen—just as a lamp [is extinguished] by contact with wind, or the sound of a bell [ceases] by contact with the hand? Therefore, this matter is to be established through inference. What, then, is the inference here? It has already been stated that "non-existence is not an effect. Furthermore: "Nothing could exist without a cause. (3a)

If destruction, like arising, were not causeless for anything because it shares the same nature as its cause, then [the following would be the case]: the destruction of momentary cognitions, sounds, and flames is seen to be spontaneous; thus, this [destruction] does not depend upon a cause. As for the one who thinks that the destruction of a cognition occurs through another cognition, or the destruction of a sound through another sound—that is incorrect, because two cognitions cannot coexist. Indeed, the coexistence of knowledge characterized by doubt and knowledge characterized by certainty is not logical, nor is it logical for pleasure and pain, or for attachment and aversion, to coexist.

And when a weak cognition and sound arise immediately after a sharp cognition and sound, how could a weak phenomenon of the same kind destroy one that is sharper? And how could this occur in the case of the final two? Furthermore, the view that the destruction of flames is due to the absence of a cause for their persistence, or due to the power of merit and demerit (*dharma* and *adharma*), is also incorrect; for non-existence cannot function as a cause.

Furthermore, it is not possible for merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), which are the causes of arising and destruction, to obtain their activity or encounter obstruction moment by moment. Moreover, this conceptualization of a cause could be applied to all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*); therefore, enough with this dispute.

And if the destruction of wood and so forth were caused by conjunction with fire and the like, then in that case, when qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise as more or most cooked, the very cause would be the destroyer. (3b) (4)

Furthermore, the cause itself would be the destroyer. How so? Because when qualities produced by heating (*pākaja*) arise from contact with fire, their destruction occurs either from that very same [cause] or from something similar to it upon the further production of more or most intensely cooked states; thus, the cause itself would be their destroyer, or something indistinguishable from the cause. And it is not logical that their existence should arise from a certain cause or something similar to it, while their non-existence should likewise arise from that very same cause or something similar to it.

(7) They might, at most, postulate a distinction in causes regarding the intervals between flames. But when a specific transformation produced by heating (*pākaja*) arises due to contact with alkali, snow, vinegar, sun, water, and earth, what kind of postulation could they possibly conceive? As for the fact that water diminishes when it is being boiled, what do the conjunctions of fire (*agni-saṃyoga*) accomplish there?

They increase the fire element by its power, through the influence of which the mass of water becomes increasingly diminished until, having reached extreme attenuation, it finally no longer continues its series. This is what the conjunctions with fire do here. Therefore, there is no cause for the destruction of entities; rather, they perish because they are themselves fragile. Perishing as soon as they have arisen, their momentary disintegration (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is established. And because of this momentary disintegration, there is an absence of motion (*gatyabhāva*).

But [the opponent’s] excessive pride [is misplaced], for [the appearance of movement] in other locations occurs through uninterrupted production, like a flame of grass. And since there is no actual motion, it is established that bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) is merely a configuration (*saṃsthāna*).

The Sautrāntikas maintain that configuration does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*). For when a greater amount of color arises in one direction, it is designated as "long" form; in relation to that very same [color], when it is smaller, it is "short. When it is greater in four directions, it is "square"; when it is equal on all sides, it is "round. All cases are to be understood in this way.

For example, when a torch is seen moving rapidly and continuously through various adjacent locations in one direction, it is perceived as "long"; when seen [moving] in all directions, it is perceived as "circular. However, shape is certainly not a separate substance.
For if it were, it would have to be perceivable by two [senses]. (3c)

For if one determines "it is long" after seeing with the eye, and also after touching with the body faculty, it would follow that this [quality] is apprehended by both; yet there is no apprehension of the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) by two [faculties]. Or, just as the apprehension of "long" and so forth occurs in the case of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*), let it be considered the same for color (*varṇa*). In that case, there is merely a recollection (*smṛti*) due to the association with the tangible; however, that arises from association and is not a direct apprehension.

(23) Just as, upon seeing the form of fire, there arises a recollection of its heat, and upon smelling the fragrance of a flower, a recollection of its color; this is logical here because of the invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*). However, one thing cannot be recollected by means of another unless some tangible object is restricted to a particular shape (*saṃsthāna*), such that a recollection of it would necessarily occur therein. Otherwise, even in the absence of a restriction based on constant association (*sāhacarya-niyama*), there would have to be a necessary recollection of the shape.

It would either exist in color, or like color, it would exist in shape without restriction; yet this is not the case. Thus, its recollection from the tangible is illogical. Or, in the case of a multicolored carpet with various colors and shapes, because many [factors] are seen, they would have to occupy the same location, which is also illogical, just as in the case of color. Therefore, shape does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*). Furthermore, whatever form (*rūpa*) exists that is characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*) must necessarily exist in the atom (*paramāṇu*);
yet that [shape] does not exist in the atom.

Furthermore, shape such as length and so forth does not exist within a single atom. Therefore, the designation of "long" and so on applies only when many atoms are arranged in such a manner. Now, if it is thought that atoms of shape themselves, when arranged in such a way, receive the name "long" and so forth—this is merely a partisan bias, because such [atoms of shape] are unestablished. For an aggregation is only logical in the case of those whose own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are established.

Furthermore, since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of shapes and parts is not established in the same way as that of color and so forth, how could there be an accumulation (*saṃcaya*) of them? As for the fact that in the case of clay vessels, the color is seen to be non-different while the shape is seen to be different—has it not already been stated that just as the designation "long" and so forth is applied to color, and just as a distinction such as a "line" or a "circle" is perceived among ants despite their lack of difference, so too it is with shape?

In that case, when people do not see even that color from a distance, yet perceive the length and other qualities of posts and such things, they are actually seeing only the color there in an indistinct manner and then constructing the conceptualization of "long" and so forth—just like the conceptualization of a row or an army. And this is indeed so, because at times a mere aggregate is seen in an indistinct way, with its boundaries undetermined, such that one thinks, "What is this?"

Now, having refuted both the movement and the shape of the body, the Sautrāntikas ask: what do they designate as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)? They designate shape itself as bodily intimation. But is that not [then] substantial (*dravyataḥ*)? And while designating it thus, how do they designate bodily action (*kāyakarma*)? Bodily action is action based upon the body; it is the volition (*cetanā*) that leads the body here and there.

In the same way, the two types of mental action (*manaskarma*) are also to be understood according to their respective applications. As for what was stated—that "action is volition (*cetanā*) and having willed"—first there arises the volition of intention (*saṃkalpa-cetanā*), thinking, "I shall do such and such. Having willed in that manner, there subsequently arises the volition of performance (*kriyā-cetanā*), by which the body is impelled; this is called "action after having willed."

If that were the case, then because of the absence of informative action (*vijñapti*), non-informative action (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm would also not exist; thus, great faults would follow as consequences. Furthermore, there will be counter-consequences to these consequences. If non-informative action were to arise from that very same specific volition designated as bodily action, it would necessarily follow the mind, just like informative action in a state of meditative concentration. But this will not be so, because of the specific projection (*ākṣepa*) resulting from the specific volition. Moreover, even though that informative action exists, it depends upon the power of the volition for its projection, because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*).
The Vaibhāṣikas, however, describe shape as being a real substance; bodily informative action consists of the nature of shape, while vocal informative action is the sound of speech. (3d)

That sound which has speech as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is itself vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*). Non-intimation (*avijñapti*) has already been explained. The Sautrāntikas maintain that it does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*), because it is merely the non-performance [of an action] after having made a commitment; and because it is designated in dependence upon past primary elements (*mahābhūta*), and because those [past elements] lack an existing intrinsic nature and thus lack the characteristic of form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*). The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that it does exist. How is this known? "By the mention of three kinds of form and pure form, by increase, by the path for one who does not act, and so forth. (4ab)

Three kinds of form are taught in the Sūtra: "There are three bases by which the inclusion of form occurs: there is form that is visible and resistant; there is form that is invisible and resistant; and there is form that is invisible and non-resistant."

Furthermore, the Blessed One has spoken of form that is without outflows (*anāsrava*): "What are the phenomena without outflows? That form—past, future, or present—in which neither attachment nor aversion arises, and so on up to consciousness—in which [these do not arise]; these are called the phenomena without outflows. And apart from non-informative form (*avijñapti*), there is no form that is both invisible and non-obstructive, nor is there any such form that is without outflows.

Furthermore, increase has been taught: "For a faithful son or daughter of good family who possesses these seven bases of meritorious action consisting of material things—whether walking, sleeping, standing, or waking—merit constantly and continuously increases and merit is ever produced. The same applies to those [bases] not consisting of material things. And without *avijñapti*, the increase of merit for one whose mind is directed elsewhere would not be logical.

Furthermore, for one who does not act himself but causes others to act, the paths of action would not be established if non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) did not exist. For it is not logical that the informative act of commanding (*ājñāpanavijñapti*) constitutes the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*), because that [actual] action has not been performed. Moreover, even when [the action] has been performed, [the command] remains the same in its essential nature (*svabhāva*).

And it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, the phenomena (*dharma*) are an external sense-field (*bāhyam āyatana*), not included within the other eleven sense-fields, invisible, and non-obstructive. Yet it was not stated that they are formless (*arūpin*). In that case, what would be the purpose if non-informative form (*avijñaptirūpa*), which is included within the sense-field of phenomena, were to be excluded?

Furthermore, the Eightfold Path would not exist without non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), because for one who has entered meditative absorption (*samāpanna*), right speech, right action, and right livelihood would be impossible. If that is so, how do you explain this statement: "For one who thus knows and thus sees, right view reaches fulfillment through cultivation; so too do right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. Moreover, his right speech, right action, and right livelihood have already been purified and cleansed beforehand"?

This was said with reference to the detachment previously achieved through the mundane path (*laukikamārga*). Furthermore, the Prātimokṣa restraint would not exist if non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) did not exist; for after the formal undertaking of the vows, there would be nothing by which one could still be a monk or a nun even when the mind is directed elsewhere.

Moreover, in the Sūtra, abstention is called a "bridge" because it acts as a barrier against immorality. Since that which does not exist cannot serve as a bridge, non-informative matter certainly exists.
On this point, the Sautrāntikas say: "This is much and this is wonderful; however, it is not so. What is the reason?

First, regarding what was stated, 'because of the mention of three kinds of form,' the Yogācāras teach that for those in meditative concentration, a form which is the object of samādhi arises through the power of samādhi. Because it is not an object of the visual faculty, it is non-demonstrable (*anidarśana*); because it does not obstruct space, it is non-obstructive (*apratigha*). Now, if it is asked, 'How then is that form [form]?', this is the same in the case of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)."

As for what was said, "because of the mention of untainted form (*anāsravarūpa*)," the practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*) describe that very form produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as untainted when within an untainted concentration. Others say it refers to the form of an Arhat and external form, because they are not a basis for the outflows (*āsrava*). If so, then what about that which is stated in the Sūtra: "Which are the tainted phenomena (*sāsravā dharmāḥ*)? They are simply the eye, up to and including visible forms," and so forth?

(10) Furthermore, in that context, it is called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*) because it is not an antidote to the outflows. If that were so, then by way of a different perspective (*paryāyeṇa*), that very same thing would be both with outflows and without outflows (*anāsrava*). (11) What would be the consequence? There would be a confusion of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasaṃkara*). For as it is with outflows, so it would never be without outflows. (12) What is the confusion here?

Moreover, if the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth were exclusively with outflows, for what purpose would they be specified in this Sūtra as: "those forms which are with outflows, subject to grasping (*sopādānīya*), and the basis for the barrenness and hypocrisy of the mind," and so forth? (13–14) [End of passage.]

As for what was said, "because of the statement regarding the increase of merit," on that point too the former masters point out: "This is indeed the nature of things (*dharmatā*): just as the gifts of donors are enjoyed, so too, through the excellence of the qualities and the excellence of the favor shown to the recipients, the continuums (*saṃtati*) of the donors—even though their minds are directed elsewhere—become permeated by the volition of giving that had those [recipients] as its object. These continuums attain a subtle, specific transformation (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*), by which they become capable of producing a much greater fruit in the future."

"It is said with this intention: 'Merit indeed increases; merit indeed arises. Now, if it is thought: "How then can a transformation in one continuum be established for another continuum that has a different mind, due to a specific quality in that other continuum? This is the same in the case of non-informative action (*avijñapti*). How then will a distinct factor (*dharmāntara*), namely non-informative action, be established in one continuum due to a specific quality in another continuum? And how will it be in the case of the bases of meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*) that are not connected to material things (*nirupadhika*)?

(21) Because of the repeated practice of volition directed toward that object, those [volitions] continue to follow along even in dreams. However, for those who maintain the doctrine of non-informative action (*avijñapti*), (22) how could there be non-informative action in the case of merit not based on material things (*niraupadhika*), where no informative action (*vijñapti*) exists? Others say that even in the case of merit based on material things (*aupadhika*), it is due to the repeated practice of volition directed toward that object.

As for that which is stated in the Sūtra: "When a monk who is formidable, virtuous, and of excellent character, having consumed alms-food, dwells having personally realized and attained an immeasurable concentration of mind, then on that account an immeasurable outflow of merit, an outflow of the wholesome, a stream of the taste of happiness, is to be expected for the donor, the master of the gift"—in this case, what specific volition (*cetanā*) does the giver possess at that time?
Therefore, it is logical that it is precisely a specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*).

As for what was also asked, "How will the paths of action be established in the case of one who causes another to act?", regarding that they explain as follows: (3) Through the instigation of that [act], due to the specific injury inflicted upon others, a subtle and specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*) arises in the instigator, by virtue of which it becomes capable of producing a much greater fruit in the future, even when [the act] has ceased. (4) And this same principle should be understood to apply to one who acts personally as well, at the completion of the fruit of the action. (5)

This specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtatipariṇāmaviśe�șa*) is designated as "the fruit of action" (*karmaphala*), because the cause is metaphorically attributed to the effect. However, its status as bodily or vocal is due to being the result of those respective actions, just as for those who maintain the existence of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*). The Venerable [Vasumitra] maintains that one is touched by the fault of taking life through volition (*cetanā*) belonging to the three times regarding the appropriated aggregates (*upātta-skandha*), provided that the thought occurs: "I shall kill," "I am killing," or "It has been killed."

However, the path of action is not completed by this much alone; for it must not be the case that those who merely have the conceit of having killed their mother or others—even if they have not actually killed them—would incur an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) karma. Rather, the intended meaning here would be more appropriate if it were that such an extent of mental activity (*cetanā-samudācāra*) occurs in one who kills by his own hand.

What kind of aversion is this, that *avijñapti* is rejected while a specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṇa*) is accepted, even though it is likewise imperceptible? Indeed, there is no aversion at all. Rather, it is because one is not satisfied with the idea that when an action is completed through a bodily application following from the mind, a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*) arises for the agent, separate from those two [the mind and body].

However, satisfaction is attained [by our position] because the completion of an action arises from the application already performed; for it is that very [application] which causes the transformation of the continuum (*saṃtatipariṇāma*) by means of that [action]. Furthermore, the fruit arises in the future from the continuum of mind and mental factors (*cittacaittasaṃtāna*). And regarding this, it has been said: what was said? "Because of the non-existence of informative action (*vijñapti*)," and so forth. Due to the non-existence of that [informative action], there is the non-existence of non-informative action (*avijñapti*).

As for what was said: "(16) 'The fact that the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is formless has not been stated,'" let that very form which was described here as invisible and non-obstructive be what is included within the sphere of phenomena. As for what was said, "'The noble eightfold path would not exist,'" first explain what a "limb" (*aṅga*) is. How do right speech, right action, and right livelihood come to be for one who has entered the path?

Does he speak words, perform actions, or seek robes and so forth? No, it says. What then? He acquires a corresponding type of untainted non-informative action (*avijñapti*), by the acquisition of which, even when he has emerged [from meditative absorption], he no longer engages in wrong speech and the like, but engages in right speech and the like. Therefore, because of the metaphorical application of the name of the effect to the cause, that designation is applied to the non-informative action.

If this is so, why is it not accepted here as well that one who has entered the path acquires a corresponding intention (*āśaya*) and a basis (*āśraya*), even without non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), by the acquisition of which, even after emerging from meditative absorption, one no longer engages in wrong speech and the like, but engages in right speech and the like? Therefore, by applying the designation of the effect to the cause, the eight limbs of the path are established.

But another says: here, mere non-performance would be stated as the constituent factor. That [non-performance] which one obtains through the power of the noble path is a restriction of non-action; and because it is obtained by relying upon the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), it would be untainted (*anāsrava*). For not all factors that exist substantially (*dravyasat*) are enumerated everywhere—for example, the eight worldly dharmas: gain and loss, fame and infamy, blame and praise, pleasure and pain.

Furthermore, there is no such thing as "non-acquisition" of robes and so forth that exists as a distinct substance (*dravyāntara*). There would also be a Prātimokṣa restraint; for by means of a volition (*cetanā*) preceded by a formal rite, one undertakes an engagement that restrains body and speech from prohibited actions. If it is argued that one would not be restrained when possessing a different state of mind, we say: no.

(7) Through the cultivation of that [intention], for one who remembers at the time of action, there arises the presence of that [non-informative form]; thus there would also be the state of a "bridge. (8) Having repeatedly cultivated the vow regarding non-action, one refrains from misconduct out of shame; it is precisely for this purpose that there is the undertaking (*samādāna*) of that [vow]. (9) If, on the other hand, non-informative form alone were to obstruct misconduct, then no one with impaired mindfulness would ever violate the training rules. (10) Enough of this elaboration. The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that non-informative form exists as a distinct substantial entity (*dravyāntara*). (11)

If it exists, it has been stated that it "arises depending upon the great elements. Does, then, the non-informative (avijñapti) arise depending upon those very same great elements of the informative (vijñapti), or does it depend upon others? It arises depending upon other great elements; for it is not logical that the same causal complex should have both a subtle fruit and a coarse fruit. Indeed, does the non-informative exist at the time depending upon those very great elements that exist at the time of the informative?

Almost all derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is thus; however, some present and future [derived matter] arises depending upon past great elements (*mahābhūta*). What, then, is that? (16) After the first moment, non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm arises from past great elements. (4cd) (17)

After the first moment, the non-informative (*avijñapti*) belonging to the desire realm arises depending upon past great elements (*mahābhūta*). These [past elements] serve as its basis (*āśraya*); the present great elements of the body serve as its support (*saṃniśraya*), because they are respectively the causes of its initial activity and its continued persistence, just like the hand that impels and the ground where it rolls for a wheel turning upon the earth. Now, depending upon which great elements does bodily and vocal action arise? To which realm do those [elements] belong?
Bodily and vocal action that is with outflows (*sāsrava*) arises based upon its own primary elements (*mahābhūta*).

(5ab) Bodily and vocal action belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) arises based upon the very primary elements belonging to the desire realm; likewise, up to that which belongs to the level of the fourth dhyāna, it arises based upon the primary elements belonging to that same level. Uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) action arises in whatever place one is born. (5c)

However, it should be understood that untainted (*anāsrava*) bodily and vocal action arises depending upon the primary elements (*bhūta*) belonging to the specific level (*bhūmi*) where one is born and which one produces; this is because untainted factors do not fall within the realms (*dhātu*), because there are no untainted primary elements, and because such action arises through their power.
In this regard, the two types of action known as informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) should be understood. Non-informative action is non-appropriated (*anupāttika*). [Verse 5d]
It is outflowing, designated as sentient,
and furthermore,
it is produced from primary elements that are outflowing and appropriated.

Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises based solely on derivative elements (*bhūta*) that are of the nature of natural outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*), and it also arises based on mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*). This is the mode [of non-informative matter] belonging to the stage of non-concentrated thought (*asamāhitabhūmika*).

(8) [Non-informative matter] born of meditative concentration (*samādhija*) is derived (*aupādayika*), unappropriated (*anupātta*), and produced from undifferentiated elements (*abhinnabhūtajā*). (9) (Verse 6cd) (10)

The non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*) consisting of the meditative and the untainted restraints (*dhyānānāsrava-saṃvara*) arises from concentration (*samādhi*). It arises depending upon the great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are produced by concentration, which are accumulative (*aupacayika*), appropriated (*upātta*), and undifferentiated (*abhinnāni*). Furthermore, depending upon whichever very same elements the abstention from taking life arises, depending upon those very same ones does it arise for everything up to the abstention from frivolous speech. What is the reason? Because, unlike the mind, there is no differentiation among the elements.

In the *prātimokṣa* restraint, however, there are seven non-informative (*avijñapti*) entities based on various distinct great elements (*mahābhūta*). The informative (*vijñapti*), by contrast, is of the nature of outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*). Furthermore, that which belongs to the body is appropriated (*upātta*). Now, when this informative action arises, does it arise by displacing the continuity of the previous shape (*saṃsthāna*), or not? What follows from this? If it arises by displacing it, [then... No.

If the material form (*rūpa*) resulting from maturation (*vipāka*), once severed, were to arise again in a continuous stream, this would result in a position contrary to that of the Vaibhāṣikas. Alternatively, if it were to arise without displacing [the previous matter], how could two distinct shapes (*saṃsthāna*) be established within a single aggregate of primary elements (*bhūtasamghāta*)? At that time, entirely different [matter]—namely, that which is of the nature of outflow (*naiḥṣyandika*)—arises, depending upon which there occurs informative action (*vijñapti*). If that is so, then whichever limb the informative action arises in dependence upon, that very limb ought to become larger.
Because it is pervaded by those great elements; and if it were not pervaded, how could one manifest informative action with the entire body? Since the body is porous, there is space for them.

Indeed, this action (*karman*) is said to be twofold, threefold, and fivefold by way of its classifications: it consists of volition (*cetanā*) and that which is performed after having willed (*cetayitvā*). Furthermore, that which is performed after having willed is twofold: bodily action (*kāyakarman*), vocal action (*vākkarman*), and volition. Bodily action is again twofold: that called informative (*vijñapti*) and that called non-informative (*avijñapti*). Thus, including vocal action and volition, there are five types. Moreover, among these, non-informative action is twofold: wholesome (*kuśala*) and unwholesome (*akuśala*). There is no neutral (*avyākṛta*) non-informative action.

What is the reason? For an indeterminate mind is weak; therefore, it is not capable of projecting a powerful karma that would continue to follow even after that mind has ceased. (27) The other is threefold. Other karma is of three kinds: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate. What is that other? It is informative action (*vijñapti*) and volition (*cetanā*). (3)
Furthermore, regarding the unwholesome:

(4) in the realm of desire, (7bc) (5) it should be understood that unwholesome matter is karma in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and not elsewhere, because the unwholesome roots as well as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) have been abandoned there. However, the wholesome and the neutral exist everywhere, because they are not obstructed. In that regard, (7)

Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) exists even in the realm of form (*rūpa*) (7c). Because of the word "even" (*api*), it exists in the desire realm (*kāma*) as well. It does not exist in the formless realms (*ārūpya*), because of the absence of primary elements (*bhūta*). For where there is the activity of body and speech, there is restraint (*saṃvara*) of body and speech. In that case, would there not be untainted (*anāsrava*) non-informative matter for one who has entered meditative absorption here [in the desire realm], just like informative matter (*vijñapti*)? No; because that [untainted matter] does not fall within the sphere of any realm (*dhātu*). Furthermore, non-informative matter belonging to the formless realm cannot exist by depending upon primary elements of a different category (*visabhāga*). Moreover, because the practitioner of the formless absorption is turned away from all form, he is not capable of producing form.

Because the perception of form has been transcended. Morality (*śīla*) is the antidote to immorality (*dauḥśīlya*); and that immorality belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are distant from the desire realm by way of distance in terms of basis (*āśraya*), aspect (*ākāra*), object (*ālambana*), and antidote (*pratipakṣa*). Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) in these [formless realms].

Informative matter (*vijñapti*) exists in the two levels with discursive thought (*savicāra*). Informative matter, however, exists only in the two stages: in the desire realm and in the first dhyāna, but not above that.

(8a) There is no obscured [unwholesome] [mind] even in the desire realm. However, obscured informative action (*vijñapti*) does not exist even in the desire realm; it exists only in the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*). For it is heard that the bodily action of Mahābrahmā was originated by deceit (*śāṭhya*); indeed, in the midst of his own assembly, he misrepresented himself in order to disparage the Venerable Aśvajit. Above that [level], since vocal informative action is absent, how can there be the sense-sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) there, which has the external great elements as its cause? (20)

Others, however, say: "In the second and subsequent dhyānas as well, there is informative action (*vijñapti*), which is non-obscured and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); it is neither wholesome nor afflicted. What is the reason? For one born in those [higher realms] does not bring into manifestation a mind of that same type belonging to a lower level by which one might produce that informative action, because [such a mind] is inferior and has been abandoned. But they maintain the former [position].
Furthermore, what is the reason that there is no informative action above the Brahma-world, and why is there no obscured-neutral (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) informative action in the desire realm?"

Because its origination is non-existent. (8b) For informative action (*vijñapti*) is originated by a mind accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*); and that [mind] does not exist in the second and higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). Furthermore, it is originated by that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); for that which is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) is inwardly directed. Moreover, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), that which is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) does not exist. (5)

Is it to be understood that the wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of phenomena (*dharma*) is determined solely by way of their origination? No, he says. What then? By four modes: from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), by intrinsic nature (*svabhāvataḥ*), by association (*saṃprayogataḥ*), and by origination (*samutthānataḥ*). Among these, first: liberation is wholesome from the perspective of ultimate reality.
For *nirvāṇa* is the subsiding of all suffering; because it is the supreme security, it is wholesome in the ultimate sense, like health.
The roots of non-shame and non-embarrassment are inherently [unwholesome].

(8d) (10) The three roots of goodness, as well as shame (*hrī*) and embarrassment (*apatrāpya*), are wholesome by their very nature (*svabhāva*), because they do not depend on association with or origination from anything else. (11) They are like salutary medicine.
(12) Those associated with them [are wholesome] through association (*saṃprayoga*). (9a) (13)

Those factors associated with those very same roots of merit, shame, and dread of blame are wholesome by way of association (*saṃprayoga*), because there is an absence of wholesomeness in those not associated with them, like water mixed with medicine. (14) (15) Actions and so forth [are wholesome] by way of origination (*samutthāna*). (9b) (16)

Bodily and vocal actions, as well as the formations dissociated from mind—such as birth and the others, acquisitions (*prāpti*), cessation-attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*)—are wholesome by way of origination (*samutthāna*), because they are produced by those very factors associated with the roots of goodness and so forth. This is like the milk of a wet-nurse produced from the consumption of medicinal herbs and water. However, it must be explained how acquisitions (*prāpti*) that are produced by a mind of a different category (*visabhāga-citta*) can be wholesome.

For example: (19) the reconnection of the roots of merit through doubt, and through returning to or falling away from a realm. And as the wholesome has been explained, (20) the unwholesome is the opposite of that. (9c) (21)

How so? Saṃsāra is unwholesome from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), because its nature consists in the arising of all suffering and it is therefore the supreme lack of security (*paramākṣema*). (22) The roots of the unwholesome, as well as shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), are unwholesome by their very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*). The factors associated with them are unwholesome through association (*saṃprayogataḥ*). Those factors produced by them—namely, bodily and vocal actions, birth, and so forth, as well as acquisitions (*prāpti*)—are unwholesome through origination (*samutthānataḥ*); they are to be compared, for example, to diseases, unwholesome food, and harmful medicines. (23)

If that were so, then nothing would be either tainted (*sāsrava*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*), or wholesome (*kuśala*), because they are all within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). This was stated from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). However, that which is tainted but is not defined in terms of its maturation (*vipāka*) is called "neutral. And that which has a desirable maturation is called "wholesome. But if one seeks what is neutral in the ultimate sense, that is found in: "The two ultimates are neutral and permanent" (9d).

Two unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are, by their very nature, non-obscured and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*): space (*ākāśa*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*).
