This is now investigated: (6) if the wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of bodily and vocal action is due to the power of their origination (*samutthāna*), why is this not the case for the primary elements (*mahābhūta*)? (7) For actions belong to the agent’s intention, not to the primary elements.

In the case of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of one who is in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*), there is no volition (*abhiprāya*), nor is a mind that is not in equipoise its motivator (*samutthāpaka*), because it belongs to a different level (*visabhāgabhūmika*). How, then, can it be wholesome? Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even the divine eye and ear would be wholesome. Effort must be made on this point.

As for what was stated—that a mind to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaprahātavya*) does not originate manifest action (*vijñapti*)—how then is the Blessed One’s teaching to be reconciled? For he said: "From that wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), wrong intention (*mithyāsaṃkalpa*) arises; from [wrong intention], wrong speech (*mithyāvāk*) and wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*) [arise]," and so forth. This is not contradictory. Origination is twofold, known as causal origination and instantaneous origination. (10ab) Origination is of two kinds: causal origination (*hetusamutthāna*) and instantaneous origination (*tatkṣaṇasamutthāna*). Because [the latter] exists at that very moment. (14)

Of these two, the first is the initiator (*pravartaka*), and the second is the follower (*anuvartaka*). (10cd) The causal origination (*hetu-samutthāna*) is the initiator because it projects [the action]; the simultaneous origination (*tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna*) is the follower because it conforms to the time of the activity. (16) What, then, is its efficacy (*sāmarthya*) regarding that specific activity? For without it, even though projected, that [action] would not exist, just as in the case of one who is dead. (17) If that is so, how does it occur when restraint (*saṃvara*) arises for one who is without mind (*acittaka*)? Its efficacy is this: that for one with mind (*sacittaka*), it occurs more clearly. (18) And in that regard: (19)

(11ab) Consciousness to be abandoned by seeing is the initiator. The mind that is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) is the initiator of informative action (*vijñapti*), because it serves as the primary cause for the applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) that give rise to it. However, it is not the follower (*anuvartaka*). This is because when the outward-directed mind is performing its activity, that [mind to be abandoned by seeing] is absent. Furthermore, the form (*rūpa*) produced by that [mind] would have to be something to be abandoned by seeing. What would follow from this? The Abhidharma would be contradicted. Moreover, since there is no contradiction between [the mind to be abandoned by seeing and] knowledge or ignorance, there is no form to be abandoned by seeing.

This position is yet to be proven. In that case, even the primary elements (*bhūta*) would have to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), because they are produced by the same mind. This will not be so, just as [the elements] do not become wholesome or unwholesome. Alternatively, let them be [abandoned by insight]; however, it is not possible in this way. For it is not logical that they are abandoned by insight, nor that they are not to be abandoned at all. What is the reason? Because non-afflicted phenomena (*akliṣṭadharma*) are not in contradiction with either knowledge (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction, because the Sūtra speaks with reference to their arising from causes.
Furthermore, both [types]—
the mental [consciousness] to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya)—
are indeed to be abandoned by cultivation; moreover, this mental consciousness is both the initiator (pravartaka) and the follower (anuvartaka).

The fivefold group, however, is only a follower. (11d) The five bodies of consciousness are exclusively followers. Thus, there are four possibilities: the mind that is to be abandoned by seeing is only an initiator; the five bodies of consciousness are only followers; the mental consciousness to be abandoned by cultivation is both; and the untainted [consciousness] is neither. Now, is it the case that the follower is exactly as the initiator? This is not necessarily so. For when the initiator is wholesome and so forth, the follower may be of all three kinds. (12ab) (13)
When the motivating [mind] is wholesome, the conforming [mind] may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral. The same applies when it is unwholesome or neutral.

(12c) For the Sage, however, the conforming [mind] is equal to the motivating [mind]: when the motivating [mind] is wholesome, the conforming [mind] is wholesome; and when it is neutral, the conforming [mind] is neutral. (17)

The wholesome, up to the point of being virtuous (*kuśala*), may be a follower even when the initiating [mind] is neutral (*avyākṛta*). However, a wholesome initiating [mind] never has a neutral follower. For the teaching of the Buddhas is handed down as such; according to other schools, there is no neutral mind in the Buddhas. For the continuums of the Buddhas are always concentrated (*samāhita*) because they consist solely of the wholesome. As it is said in the Sūtra: "The Nāga is concentrated while walking; the Nāga is concentrated while standing."

"The Nāga is concentrated while sleeping; he is also concentrated while sitting. (23) This was said because the mind does not wander even against its will; it is not, however, that Buddhas lack neutral (*avyākṛta*) minds born of maturation (*vipākaja*), those pertaining to postures (*airyāpathika*), or those of transformation (*nairmāṇika*), according to the Vaibhāṣikas. It has been stated that the mental [consciousness] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) is both the initiator (*pravartaka*) and the follower (*anuvartaka*). (25) All of that—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—should be understood as such. But that which is born of maturation is neither. 12d (2)

But a mind born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is neither an initiator (*pravartaka*) nor a follower (*anuvartaka*), because it proceeds without volitional effort (*nirabhisaṃskāra*). Now, does the informative action (*vijñapti*) correspond to the initiator, or does it correspond to the follower? What follows from this? If it corresponds to the initiator, then here too the informative action would result in being obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*), because it is initiated by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Alternatively, one must state a qualification that not everything to be abandoned by vision (*darśanaprahātavya*) is an initiator.

If it were according to the conforming [mind], then the *prātimokṣa*-informative act (*vijñapti*) of one whose mind is unwholesome or neutral would not be wholesome. It is according to the motivating [mind] that the informative act is so, and not according to whether it is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*); for it is interrupted by that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). If the wholesomeness and so forth of the informative act do not depend on the power of the conforming [mind], then this should not be said: "In the Sūtra, it was stated with reference to causal origination (*hetu-samutthāna*), not momentary origination (*tatkṣaṇa-samutthāna*)."

Therefore, it should be stated that there is no obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) informative action (*vijñapti*) here. This was said with reference to a causal origination (*hetusamutthāna*) that is intervened by something else. The incidental discussion is concluded.

That [non-informative action], however, is what was previously mentioned: "Non-informative action (*avijñapti*) should be known as threefold: restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), and other [neutral] (*itarā*). (13ab) (13)

There is restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*); other than these two is that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint. Restraint is the warding off and the suppression of the outflow of immorality (*dauḥśīlya*). Furthermore, in this regard: Restraint is called *prātimokṣa*, as well as that born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and that which is untainted (*anāsrava*). (13cd) Restraint is threefold: the *prātimokṣa* restraint is the morality (*śīla*) of those belonging to this world, pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*); the restraint of meditative concentration is the morality pertaining to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*); and the untainted restraint is the untainted morality. Furthermore, in this regard:
The so-called *prātimokṣa* is eightfold:

(14a) the restraint of a monk (*bhikṣu-saṃvara*), the restraint of a nun (*bhikṣuṇī-saṃvara*), the restraint of a female trainee (*śikṣamāṇā-saṃvara*), the restraint of a male novice (*śrāmaṇera-saṃvara*), the restraint of a female novice (*śrāmaṇerī-saṃvara*), the restraint of a layman (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), the restraint of a laywoman (*upāsikā-saṃvara*), and the restraint of fasting (*upavāsa-saṃvara*). These eight types of restraint are designated as the *prātimokṣa-saṃvara*. Thus, it is eightfold by name;
however, in terms of substance (*dravyataḥ*), it is fourfold. (14b) (23)

The restraint of a bhikṣu, the restraint of a śrāmaṇera, the restraint of an upāsaka, and the restraint of fasting—thus, this fourfold prātimokṣa restraint exists as distinct entities because their characteristics are specifically determined. The restraint of a bhikṣuṇī is not other than the restraint of a bhikṣu; likewise, the restraints of a śikṣamāṇā and a śrāmaṇerī are not other than the restraint of a śrāmaṇera. The restraint of an upāsikā is not other than the restraint of an upāsaka. How is this known? Because there is a change of name according to gender. (14c) (2)

"Liṅga" is a designation for the sexual organ (*vyañjana*), by which one is characterized as male or female. For it is on account of the sexual organ that the designations "monk" (*bhikṣu*) and "nun" (*bhikṣuṇī*), and so forth, are established. How so? When the sexual organ is transformed, a monk is called a nun, and a nun, in turn, is called a monk. A novice (*śrāmaṇera*) is called a novice nun (*śrāmaṇerī*), and a novice nun, as well as a trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*), is called a novice. A lay follower (*upāsaka*) is called a laywoman (*upāsikā*), and a laywoman, in turn, is called a lay follower.

Furthermore, there is no cause for the abandonment of a previous restraint (*saṃvara*) upon the change of its designation, nor is there any for the acquisition of a restraint not previously possessed. Therefore, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these four restraints is not distinct from the three [preceding ones].

When one undertakes the *śrāmaṇera* restraint from the *upāsaka* restraint, and subsequently the *bhikṣu* restraint from that, are those restraints called "mutually distinct" because they consist of an increase in abstentions—like fifteen, twenty, or a hundred and fifty *dīnāras*? Or do they arise as entirely separate entities? He replied:

(14d) "Distinctly" means that they arise as unmixed and with distinct characteristics. Within the three types of restraint (*saṃvara*), there are three abstinences from taking life, up to the abstinences from drinking intoxicants; the same applies to the remaining [precepts]. What, then, is their distinction? Their distinction arises from the distinction of their causes (*nidāna*). How so?

For as one undertakes more numerous precepts of training, so one turns away from more numerous bases of intoxication and negligence, and turns away from more numerous causes of killing and so forth, while engaging in the causes of abstentions; thus, due to the distinction in their causes, there is a distinction among the abstentions. Furthermore, if this were not the case, one who renounces the monastic restraint (*bhikṣu-saṃvara*) would abandon all three restraints, since the other two are included therein.
But this is not accepted. Therefore, those restraints are indeed distinct.

And these are non-contradictory. (14d') (19) And all three of them coexist; there is no abandonment of the preceding [vow] due to the undertaking of a subsequent vow. Let it not be that one becomes a non-upāsaka simply by abandoning the bhikṣu-vow. (20) And how does one become an upāsaka, how one who abides in the upavāsa, and so on up to a bhikṣu? (21–22)

From the undertaking of abstention from five, eight, ten, and all things to be avoided, there arise the states of being a lay follower (*upāsaka*), one who observes the fast (*upavāsastha*), a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*), and a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) respectively; this should be understood as their sequential designation. By undertaking the vow of abstention from the five things to be avoided—one being the taking of life, the taking of what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants—one becomes established in the restraint of a lay follower (*upāsaka-saṃvara*). By undertaking the vow of abstention from eight things, one is established in the observance of the fast (*upavāsastha*).

By undertaking the abstention from the ten—namely, from taking life, taking what is not given, unchastity, false speech, and the drinking of intoxicants; and from [using] perfumes, garlands, and ointments; from dancing, singing, and instrumental music; from high and large beds; and from eating at improper times—one becomes a *śrāmaṇera*. By adding the acceptance of gold and silver to these very same [precepts], they become ten, since dancing, singing, and instrumental music, as well as perfumes, garlands, and ointments, are here treated as two separate items.

One is called a *bhikṣu* because of undertaking the restraint (*virati-samādāna*) from all bodily and vocal actions that are to be avoided. That very same *prātimokṣa-saṃvara* is called morality (*śīla*), good conduct (*sucarita*), action (*karman*), and restraint (*saṃvara*).
It is "morality" (*śīla*) because of the undertaking of restraint from uneven actions; its etymological derivation (*nirukti*) is "because it is cooling" (*śītalatvāt*).

"The undertaking of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is happiness, for the body is not tormented"—from this statement in the verse [it follows that it is a form of pleasure]. It is called "well-conducted" (*sucarita*) because it is praised by the wise; it is called "action" (*karman*) because its intrinsic nature is activity (*kriyā*). [Objection: But is it not said that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) is "non-activity"? How then can it be an action? [Response: It is called "non-activity" because those possessed of a sense of shame do not commit evil through its undertaking. Nevertheless, it is an action because it is performed by means of informative action (*vijñapti*) and the mind (*citta*). Others say it is an action because it is the cause of action and the fruit of action. It is called "restraint" (*saṃvara*) because of the restraining of body and speech.
Thus, for now, the Prātimokṣa restraint is designated without distinction. Furthermore:
At the first moment, there are both informative and non-informative [acts], which constitute the path of action of the Prātimokṣa. (16bcd)

At the first moment of undertaking the restraint (*saṃvarasamādāna*), the informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) [actions] are called the *prātimokṣa*. This is because, by means of it, one is liberated from or abandons evil; such is the meaning. The augment (*vṛddhi*) is applied for the sake of the word itself, as in the cases of *vaikṛta* and *vaiśasa*. It is also called the *prātimokṣasaṃvara* because it restrains body and speech, and it is called a "path of action" (*karmapatha*) because it is comprised within the fundamental [action]. In the second and subsequent moments, it is only the *prātimokṣasaṃvara*, not the *prātimokṣa*; and the subsequent [action] is not the fundamental path of action.
Now, among these restraints (*saṃvara*), who is endowed with which? (22) Eight are possessed of the Prātimokṣa.

(17a) (23) Eight classes of persons are endowed with the Prātimokṣa restraint: the monk (*bhikṣu*), the nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), and so on, up to the eighth, the one observing the fast (*upavāsastha*). Is it then the case that outsiders (*bāhyaka*) lack the morality of undertaking (*samādāna-śīla*)? They do possess it, but it is not the Prātimokṣa restraint. What is the reason? Because it does not lead to the ultimate liberation from evil; for it is dependent upon cyclic existence (*bhava*). (3)

One who possesses that which is born of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is endowed with it. (17b) That which is born from meditative absorption, or by means of meditative absorption, is "born of meditative absorption. Whoever is possessed of meditative absorption is necessarily possessed of the restraint of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-saṃvara*). Here, even the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) is designated as "meditative absorption," just as the vicinity of a village is also called "the village," as in the expressions: "In this village there is a field of rice" or "there is a field of barley.
Noble beings (*ārya-sattva*) possess the untainted (*anāsrava*) [restraint]. (17c)

Noble persons (*āryapudgala*) are endowed with untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*). Furthermore, they are those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Regarding what was stated concerning the co-existent cause (*sahabhūhetu*), namely that "two types of restraint follow the mind," which two are they? Of these very three, the last two follow the mind. (17d)

[The two types of restraint are] the meditative restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*). They are not the Prātimokṣa restraint. For what reason? Because they continue even for one who possesses a different state of mind or is without mind. Furthermore, those same two—the meditative and untainted restraints—receive the designation "restraint of abandonment" (*prahāṇasaṃvara*). In what state does this occur? He says: "In the *anāgamya* [stage], those two arising from the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*) receive the name 'abandonment'. (18ab) (15)

In the *anāgamya* stage, those two—the meditative (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) restraints—are called "restraints of abandonment" (*prahāṇasaṃvara*) during the nine paths of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), because through them there is the abandonment of immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) and the afflictions (*kleśa*) that originate it. For this very reason, a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is established regarding whether there might be a restraint of meditation that is not a restraint of abandonment: the first alternative consists of the tainted restraint of meditation (*sāsravo dhyānasaṃvaraḥ*), excluding the restraint of the *anāgamya* path of immediate succession.

(18) The second [alternative] is the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) during the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the threshold stage (*anāgamya*). The third is the tainted restraint (*sāsrava-saṃvara*) during the uninterrupted paths of the threshold stage. The fourth is the untainted restraint excluding those of the uninterrupted paths of the threshold stage. In this way, a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) should be understood as applicable: there may be an untainted restraint that is not a restraint of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃvara*). If so, what then of that which was said by the Blessed One: (21) "Restraint of the body is good; restraint of speech is also good; (22) restraint of the mind is good; restraint in all respects is good. (23)

And as for what was said—that one dwells restrained by the restraint of the faculty of sight—what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these two, the restraint of the mind-faculty and the restraint of the mental faculty? Are they both of the nature of non-informative morality (*avijñapti-śīla*)? No; rather: "The restraint of the mind-faculty and the mental faculty are, however, mindfulness and clear comprehension. (18cd) The word "two" is used again in order to indicate that each has a dual nature, so that it is not understood according to their respective order. Thus, the restraint of the mind is also of the nature of mindfulness and clear comprehension, and the restraint of the faculties is likewise.

This is now investigated: who is endowed with which non-informative action (*avijñapti*), and for how long? In this regard: One established in the *prātimokṣa* is always endowed with the present non-informative action, as long as it has not been relinquished. (19abc)

The person who has been described as abiding in the *prātimokṣa* restraint is always endowed with that [non-informative action] (*avijñapti*) while it is present, for as long as he does not abandon it. (9) After the first moment, he is endowed with the past [non-informative action].

(10) After the first moment, he is also endowed with the past [non-informative action]. It should be understood that the phrase "until it is abandoned" applies to all cases. Just as it was stated regarding one abiding in the *prātimokṣa* restraint, (13) so it is here.

In the same way, even one who abides in non-restraint—so long as he does not abandon that non-restraint—is always possessed of a present non-informative [action] (*avijñapti*). After the first moment, he is also possessed of the past [non-informative action].
One who possesses the meditative restraint (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) is always [possessed of it].

One who has acquired the restraint of meditative absorption (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) is always endowed with past and future non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), until it is relinquished. Even in the very first moment [of its acquisition], he obtains the past restraint of meditative absorption that was abandoned in a previous birth.
However, for the Noble One (*ārya*), in the first moment, there is no possession of the past [non-informative matter]. (20cd)

The noble person (*āryapudgala*) likewise possesses [non-informative action] through the untainted (*anāsrava*) [path], but there is this distinction: in the first moment, he is not endowed with the past [non-informative action], because the path has not previously arisen. (21ab) Those two who abide in the concentrated noble path are endowed with the present [non-informative action]. Those two—endowed with the meditative and untainted restraints (*dhyānānāsravasaṃvara*)—who have entered the concentrated noble path, are endowed with the present non-informative action respectively; however, they are not so endowed when they have emerged from it. This is the account, for now, regarding those abiding in restraint and non-restraint. (4)
Now, concerning the neutral person:
(5) "If it exists for the neutral person at the beginning, [it exists] through the intermediate [state].

(21cd) One who abides neither in restraint nor in non-restraint is a neutral person (*madhyastha*). For such a person, non-informative action (*avijñapti*) does not necessarily exist. However, for one who possesses that which is comprised of bad conduct, the factors of morality (*śīlāṅga*), and so forth, he is endowed with the intermediate [non-informative action] at the beginning. This is because present non-informative action lies between the past and the future. (9)
After the first moment, [it is] with two times.

(21d’) After the first moment, [it is] with the past and the present. “Until its relinquishment” is understood [to carry over]. Is one who abides in non-restraint ever endowed with a wholesome informative act (*vijñapti*), or conversely, is one who abides in restraint ever endowed with an unwholesome one? If so, when, and for how long a time? He says: One who abides in non-restraint [is endowed] with the auspicious; one who abides in restraint, with the inauspicious. (14)

One is endowed with non-informative action (*avijñapti*) as long as the force of faith or the force of affliction persists. (22) By whatever force of faith a wholesome non-informative action arises for one who abides in non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), while performing such acts as bowing to a stūpa; and by whatever force of affliction an unwholesome non-informative action arises for one who abides in restraint (*saṃvara*), while performing such acts as killing, binding, or beating—those two non-informative actions persist for as long as those respective forces continue. In the first moment, one is endowed with the non-informative action only as it exists in the present; in subsequent moments, one is also endowed with that which has passed into the past.

(18) The section on non-informative [action] is completed. (19) Regarding informative [action], however, all who are performing it are endowed with it in the present. (23ab) (20) All those abiding in restraint, non-restraint, or the intermediate state, as long as they perform an informative act, are endowed with that which is currently existing. (21)
After the first moment, until it is abandoned, one is endowed with the past informative action.
(23cd) After the first moment, until it is abandoned, one is endowed with the past informative action;
there is no such thing as being endowed with that which is unborn. (23d’) [p.211]
No one is endowed with a future informative act. Furthermore, one is not endowed with past informative acts that are either obscured or unobscured. (24ab)

No one is possessed of past informative acts (*vijñapti*), whether they be obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) or unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). For the acquisition (*prāpti*) of a weak phenomenon is itself weak and does not persist as a continuous succession. What causes its weakness? It is caused by the mind. In that case, let it be that the obscured-unspecified mind also [does not persist]. This is not so; for informative act is insentient (*jaḍa*) and dependent, whereas the mind is not so. Since that informative act is produced by what is weak, it becomes even weaker.

It was stated that one "abides in non-restraint" (*asaṃvara*). What is this so-called non-restraint? Non-restraint, misconduct, immorality, action, and the path of action—these are synonyms for non-restraint. Among these, it is called "non-restraint" because there is no restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*) of body and speech. It is "misconduct" (*duścarita*) because it is censured by the virtuous and because it has undesirable results. It is "immorality" (*dauḥśīlya*) because it is the opposite of morality (*śīla*). It is "action" (*karma*) because it consists of the actions of body and speech. It is the "path of action" (*karmapatha*) because it is comprised within the fundamental [actions]. There is a fourfold logical alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) regarding whether one may be endowed with informative action (*vijñapti*) but not with non-informative action (*avijñapti*). In that regard:
One who is neutral and possesses weak volition is endowed with informative action alone while performing [an act].

(25ab) When one who abides in neither restraint nor non-restraint performs a wholesome or unwholesome act with weak volition, they are endowed only with informative action (*vijñapti*), and not with non-informative action (*avijñapti*); this is even more so in the case of neutral acts, except for the paths of action consisting of the bases of meritorious activity involving material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*).
An noble person (*āryapudgala*) who has abandoned or has not yet produced informative action is endowed with non-informative action. (25cd)

A noble person (*āryapudgala*) is endowed with non-informative action (*avijñapti*) alone, and not with informative action (*vijñapti*), because they have either not yet performed it during the transition to another birth or have lost it. Thus has been explained the establishment of the possession of informative and non-informative action for those who abide in restraint, non-restraint, or the intermediate state.
Now, how are these restraints obtained?
That which is born of meditative absorption (*dhyānaja*) is obtained by the very stage of that meditative absorption. (26ab)

When a contaminated mind belonging to the stage of dhyāna— whether it be of the fundamental (maulīya) or the preparatory (sāmantakīya) level— is attained, then the dhyāna-restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*) also [arises], because it is co-existent with it. When it is uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
it arises through that noble (*āryā*) [path].

When that very same untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative stage is attained, the untainted restraint (*saṃvara*) is obtained. In this regard, there are six untainted meditative stages: the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*antara*); these we shall explain later.
That which is called Prātimokṣa is obtained through the communication of others and so forth. [26c-d] (2)

The Prātimokṣa restraint, however, is obtained through the communication of another; that is, if another informs him, and he [informs] the other. Furthermore, it is from either the Saṃgha or from an individual (pudgala). From the Saṃgha are obtained the restraints of nuns and female trainees (śikṣamāṇā); from an individual are the others. The Vinaya-vibhāṣikas say there are ten kinds of full ordination (upasaṃpad). The word "etc. is used for the purpose of including those [other types]. For Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, it is by means of self-awakening (svayaṃbhū-tva); for the group of five, it is by entering into the state of certainty (niyāma).

For Yaśas and others, it was through the "Come, monk" (*ehibhikṣuka*) formula; for Mahākāśyapa, through his acceptance of the Teacher; for Sodāyin, through the satisfaction of a question; for Mahāprajāpatī, through the acceptance of the eight weighty rules (*gurudharma*); for Dharmadinnā, by means of a messenger;

and for those ordained as the group of sixty auspicious ones (*ṣaṣṭibhadravargapūga*), it was through the threefold refuge formula in the border regions with a quorum of five including a master of discipline (*vinayadhara*), and in the central regions with a quorum of ten. Thus, for these individuals, the Prātimokṣa restraint does not necessarily depend upon formal ritual declaration (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, for how long a period should this Prātimokṣa restraint be undertaken when it is being received?
(10) The undertaking of the restraint lasts for as long as one lives, and for a day and night. (27ab) (11)

The rule is that there is a lifelong undertaking for the Prātimokṣa restraint consisting of the seven classes [of vows], and a day-and-night undertaking for the Upavāsa restraint. What is the reason? Because there are two limits of time: the limit of a day-and-night and the limit of one's life. The fortnights and so forth result from the repetition of days and nights. What kind of phenomenon is this called "time"? It is a designation used to illuminate the conditioned forces (*saṃskāra*).

For in the continents, the state of light is called "day," and the state of darkness is "night. It is indeed reasonable that after one's life has ended, the restraint (*saṃvara*) does not arise even if there is a formal undertaking (*samādāna*), because the physical basis (*āśraya*) is of a different nature and because, due to that, there is no application [of effort] toward it nor any recollection of it. But what obstacle is there to the arising of many fasting restraints (*upavāsa-saṃvara*) beyond a single day and night—for instance, for five nights or ten nights—once the fast has been undertaken?

Thus, there is this restriction: that the Blessed One taught in the Sūtra that the fast (*upavāsa*) lasts for exactly one day and night. This must now be considered: did the Tathāgata teach the day-and-night fast because he saw that restraint (*saṃvara*) does not arise beyond a day and night, or rather because, even for those with weak faculties, there is no logical contradiction in the arising of restraint within a day and night?
Regarding this, the Vaibhāṣikas do not accept that it is not taught for anyone beyond a day and night. Now, what is the temporal limit for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)?
There is no non-restraint for a single day and night (27c).
Non-restraint arises from the lifelong undertaking of evil dharmas (or actions), not for a day and night as is the case with the *upavāsa* fast. What is the reason?
It is said that it is not undertaken in such a manner (27d).

It is said that no one undertakes non-restraint in the same way as they do the fast (*upavāsa*), thinking, "May I be unrestrained for a day and a night," because the action is contemptible. Likewise, no one undertakes it thinking, "May I be unrestrained for as long as I live"; thus, he would not obtain [the discipline] even for the duration of his life.

Even if one does not undertake [the vow] in this manner, nevertheless, by performing that action with an utterly corrupted intention, one acquires non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), but not with an intention that is merely corrupted for a limited period. The fasting restraint (*upavāsasaṃvara*), however, is indeed acquired even when the intention is not ultimate, because it is sustained by the power of formal undertaking (*samādāna*) and because of the desire for restraint. Furthermore, if someone who desires non-restraint were to formally undertake non-restraint for a limited period, he would certainly acquire it.

However, this is not established on the grounds that it has not been observed. The Sautrāntikas maintain that non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), like non-informative action (*avijñapti*), does not exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*). Rather, non-restraint is simply the intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) to commit evil deeds; because it persists as a continuous sequence (*sānubandha*), one is said to possess it even when the mind is virtuous, since that intention has not been discarded. Now, how should the one-day fast (*upavāsa*) be undertaken when it is to be observed for a day and night?
It should be received from another at dawn, while standing in a lower position and repeating what is spoken [by the preceptor].
The fast (*upavāsa*) consists of all its constituent parts; it is observed by one who is without ornaments until the end of the night. (28) (13) First, regarding the morning:

it is at the time of sunrise, because the restraint (*saṃvara*) lasts for a full day and night. However, one who has previously made a formal undertaking (*samādāna*), thinking "I shall observe the fast on the eighth day," may take it even after having eaten. Furthermore, it must be received from another and not by oneself alone, so that even when the conditions [for breaking it] exist, there may be no transgression due to the presence of another witness. One should receive it while standing in a lower position—either squatting or kneeling—and with palms joined in the *kapotaka* gesture, moving from one’s place. (14–16)

For restraint does not arise in one who lacks respect. One should repeat the words of the donor; neither before nor simultaneously [with them]. For in this way, it is properly received from him. Otherwise, the act of giving and receiving would not be accomplished. Furthermore, it must be taken with all its limbs complete—that is, with all eight limbs—and not with any missing limbs. And one should be without ornaments, setting aside habitual adornments. For habitual adornment does not produce excessive intoxication.

And it should be undertaken until the end of the night, as long as the sun does not rise again. For one who undertakes it otherwise, there would be merely good conduct (*sucarita*), but not the restraint of the fast (*upavāsasaṃvara*). By taking it in this way, the efficacy of the day-and-night fast for a butcher or an adulterer is logically established. Others say that it is called a "fast" (*upavāsa*) because by means of it one dwells near (*vasati*) the Arhats, following their example; others say it is so called because by means of it one dwells near the lifelong restraint (*yāvajjīvikasaṃvara*).
(23) Or, it is called *poṣadha* because it nourishes the roots of merit for those whose roots of merit are small;
since it bestows nourishment (*poṣa*) upon the mind that is virtuous, it is said, therefore, by the Blessed One, that this is indeed *poṣadha*. (3)
For what purpose, then, are the eight limbs adopted? Because the limbs of morality, the limb of heedfulness, and the limbs of the vow are, respectively, four, one, and three. (27abc)

First, there are four limbs of ethical discipline (*śīlāṅga*), up to the abstention from false speech, because they consist of the avoidance of natural transgressions (*prakṛtisāvadya*). One limb of heedfulness (*apramādāṅga*) is the abstention from drinking intoxicants; for even one who has undertaken the ethical discipline might become negligent if he is a drinker of intoxicants. There are three limbs of the vow (*vratāṅga*), up to the abstention from eating at improper times, because they are conducive to a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). But what would happen if these limbs of heedfulness and limbs of the vow were not adopted?
By them, there would be the loss of mindfulness and intoxication. (29d)

For one who drinks intoxicants, the very memory of what ought to be done and what ought not to be done would perish. In one who indulges in high beds, luxurious beds, dancing, singing, and so forth, intoxication arises. And for one who is intoxicated, immorality is not far off. On the other hand, for one who eats at the proper time, because he avoids the improper time for meals, mindfulness of the fast and a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) are established. In the absence of that [mindfulness], both of these would not exist.

Some, however, consider the very abstention from eating at improper times to be the *upavāsa* (fast), and hold that the remaining eight limbs belong to it—counting "dance, song, and music" and "perfumes, garlands, and ointments" as two separate items. But if this were the case, the wording of the Sūtra would not be consistent; for after stating the abstention from eating at improper times, it says: "By this eighth limb, I train in accordance with and follow the training of those Noble Arhats."

What, then, is that other fasting (upavāsa) of which these are the limbs? The limbs are the parts of a whole. Just as there are limbs of a chariot, a fourfold army has four limbs, and musical instruments have five limbs, so too should the eight-limbed fast be understood. Abstinence from eating at improper times is the fast itself and also a limb of the fast, just as right view is both the path and a limb of the path.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the factor of enlightenment called investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is enlightenment itself and a limb of enlightenment, and that concentration (*samādhi*) is meditation (*dhyāna*) and a limb of meditation. However, they do not hold that those very same factors, such as right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and so forth, can serve as limbs for one another. If the preceding [moments of] right view and so forth were to be limbs for the subsequent ones, then the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) arising in its first moment would not consist of eight limbs.
Furthermore, is this fasting (*upavāsa*) intended only for a lay follower (*upāsaka*), or is it for others as well?

There is fasting for others as well, but not for one who has not gone for refuge. (30ab) Even for one who is not a lay follower (*anupāsaka*), if he goes for refuge to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha for that day and night and undertakes the fast (*upavāsa*), the restraint of fasting (*upavāsasaṃvara*) arises for him, and not otherwise—except in the case of ignorance. As it is said in the Sūtra: "In this regard, Mahānāman, when a householder, a man clothed in white, endowed with male faculties, goes for refuge to the Buddha, goes for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and utters the words: 'I am a lay follower... [text continues].

"And consider me a lay follower (*upavāsaka*). To this extent, one becomes a lay follower (*upāsaka*). Now, does one become a lay follower merely by going for refuge? According to the outsiders (*bahirdeśaka*), one does. Because it arises from that very [act]—namely, from the undertaking of the status of a lay follower—the restraint [is acquired]. (30cd) (7)

The restraint of a lay follower (*upāsaka-saṃvara*) arises for him precisely from his formal acceptance [of the status]. This occurs when he accepts: "Hold me to be a lay follower from this day forward, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned [taking] life. The phrase "having abandoned life" means "having abandoned [taking] life and so forth," due to the elision of the middle term. Furthermore, although he has already obtained the restraint, the statement of the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) is made just as in the case of a monk, for the purpose of providing instruction. (30d)

Just as a monk, even though he has already obtained the vows (*saṃvara*), is made to take up the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) once again for the sake of thorough instruction—being told, "Your vows consist of this and that"—and just as a novice (*śrāmaṇera*) does likewise, so too is the lay follower (*upāsaka*). However, there is no such thing as a lay follower without the vows;
they are said to be [defined] by the preservation of those [vows]. (31a)

For whoever observes a particular precept (*śikṣāpada*) is said to be a "practitioner" (*tatkārī*) of that [precept]. However, all [lay followers] are equally established in the restraint (*saṃvara*). This [position] deviates from the Sūtra. (18) What here is the deviation from the Sūtra? It is the claim that the acquisition of the restraint occurs simply through the formal acceptance of the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), because [the Sūtra] says, "from abstaining from taking life," and so forth. (19) For the wording of the Sūtra is not stated in this way; rather, the reading is as it appears in the *Mahānāma-sūtra*. Furthermore, the definition of a lay follower is taught only there, and nowhere else. (20) But where this reading occurs:

"For as long as life lasts, having gone for refuge and being full of faith, one is free from [taking] life. In this regard, those who have seen the truths demonstrated their adherence to the true Dharma even at the cost of their lives, following upon their verified faith (*avetyaprasāda*), saying: "We are incapable of abandoning this Dharma even for the sake of our lives. However, this is not the formal instruction on the characteristics of the restraint (*saṃvara*). Furthermore, the phrase "free from [taking] life" (*prāṇāpeta*) is nowhere recited [in the standard texts]. Who would recite such a passage whose meaning is unclear?

However, regarding those who have violated their training by breaking a single rule or the like, it is simply not appropriate to apply the term "lay follower" (*upāsaka*) to them at all. How much less so could there be the renunciation of the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*)? For who, knowing the lay follower's vow (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), would not understand this: that whoever does not break a particular precept (*śikṣāpada*) becomes a practitioner of that very precept? This question, however, is appropriate for those who are ignorant of the full extent of the lay follower's vow and are capable only of observing a limited portion of the training.

"To what extent, Venerable Sir, is a lay follower (*upāsaka*) one who practices a single part, and so on, up to one who practices in full? (5) "If that were so, then there would be lay followers without the vow, or with an incomplete one; likewise, there would also be monks (*bhikṣu*) and novices (*śrāmaṇera*). How, then, is there a fixed determination of the constituent parts for these vows of a lay follower and so forth? It is by virtue of the Teacher’s designation (*śāstṛ-prajñapti*). (7) "Let it be accepted that even the fixed determination of being a lay follower and so forth is by virtue of the Teacher’s designation."

For even without the vow (*saṃvara*), one is designated as a lay follower (*upāsaka*); however, this does not apply to monks (*bhikṣu*) or novices (*śrāmaṇera*). But the Kashmiris do not accept this. The weak, medium, and superior nature of all vows depends upon the mind with which they are undertaken (*samādāna-citta*). This being so, it would follow that an Arhat could possess a weak Prātimokṣa vow, while an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) could possess a superior one. Furthermore, would one become a lay follower merely by taking up the vow, even without going for refuge? No; except in the case of ignorance.

Whoever goes for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—what is it that they go for refuge to? (13) He who goes for the three refuges goes for refuge to the dharmas of one beyond training that constitute the Buddha, to both [types of dharmas] that constitute the Saṅgha, and to Nirvāṇa. (14–15) ||32||

He who goes for refuge to the Buddha goes for refuge to those dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) which constitute a Buddha; primarily because of these, that personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is called "Buddha," or because by the acquisition of these, one becomes a Buddha through the capacity for universal awakening. What, then, are they? They are the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth, together with their attendants. This is because there is no difference in the form-body (*rūpakāya*) before and after [attainment]. Does he go for refuge to all Buddhas or to one? In terms of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), he goes for refuge to all Buddhas.

(18) Because the path has no distinct characteristics. When one goes for refuge to the Saṃgha, one goes to those dharmas—both those of the learners (*śaikṣa*) and the non-learners (*aśaikṣa*)—which constitute the Saṃgha; it is by the acquisition of these that the eight types of persons (*pudgala*) become the Saṃgha. Because they are indivisible. Does this mean going to all Saṃghas or to one? In terms of their defining characteristic, it is to all Saṃghas, because the path has no distinct characteristics. However, as it is said in the Sūtra:

"Whosoever shall be that which is called the Saṅgha in the future time, go for refuge to him as well"—this is said for the purpose of highlighting the nature of the vow (*saṃvara*) that will exist when it becomes manifest. He who goes for refuge to the Dharma goes for refuge to Nirvāṇa, that is, to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it has the single characteristic of being the pacification of the afflictions and of suffering within the continuums of oneself and others.

If the Buddha is only the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), how does shedding the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind constitute an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*)? The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that because the basis (*āśraya*) is destroyed, those [dharmas] are also destroyed. However, the treatise (*śāstra*) does not state that "the Buddha is only the dharmas of one beyond training. What then? It says "those which constitute a Buddha. Therefore, since the Buddhahood of the basis is not denied, this is not a valid objection.

Otherwise, one abiding in a worldly state of mind would not be a Buddha, nor would there be a Saṅgha; and the very morality that constitutes a monk would itself be the monk. But just as one who honors monks honors the morality that makes them monks, so too one who goes for refuge to the Buddha goes for refuge to those dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constitute the Buddha. Others say: "One who goes for refuge to the Buddha goes for refuge to the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*)."

What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the acts of going for refuge? Their intrinsic nature is vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*). Furthermore, what is the meaning of "refuge" (*śaraṇa*)? The meaning of "refuge" is the meaning of protection (*trāṇa*), because by relying upon it, one is completely liberated from all suffering. For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Many people, driven by fear, go for refuge to mountains and forests, to groves, trees, and shrines."
But this refuge is not the best; this refuge is not the supreme.
By resorting to this refuge, one is not liberated from all suffering.
But he who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—
When one perceives with wisdom the four noble truths: suffering, the origin of suffering, the transcendence of suffering, and the noble eightfold path that leads to the security of Nirvana. (15–17)
"For this is the best refuge; this is the supreme refuge.
Having come to this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
(18–19) For this very reason, the goings for refuge serve as the gateway to the undertaking of all vows. (20)

What, then, is the reason that in other vows abstaining from unchastity (*abrahmacarya*) is established as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*), whereas for the lay follower (*upāsaka*) it is from sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*)? Because sexual misconduct is highly censurable, because [abstaining from it] is easy to accomplish, and because one attains the state of non-action [from it]. (III.33ab)

For sexual misconduct is extremely censured in the world because it involves violating the wives of others and because it leads to calamity; unchastity (*abrahmacarya*), however, is not so. Furthermore, for those living in a household, abstaining from sexual misconduct is easy to practice, whereas abstaining from unchastity is difficult; thus, they would not venture to undertake what is difficult. Moreover, the Noble Ones obtain the restraint of non-action (*akaraṇa-saṃvara*) specifically regarding sexual misconduct.

(26) Because one does not transgress [the vow] even in other births, and not because of non-celibacy (*abrahmacarya*), the training rule (*śikṣāpada*) of abstaining from that very [act] was established even for a lay follower (*upāsaka*). This is so that a trainee (*śaikṣa*) who has undergone a change of birth might not remain unrestrained regarding the components of the lay follower’s vows. For the restraint of non-action (*akaraṇasaṃvara*) is indeed a fixed commitment to non-doing. Now, as for those who, being lay followers, take wives—have they obtained restraint with respect to them as well, or not?

[The discipline] has been obtained [in its entirety], so that there may not be the acquisition of a partial restraint. How is it that there is no disturbance of the restraint? Because (4) the acquisition of the restraint is according to the undertaking, not [with respect to] the continuum. (5) 33cd.

For as is their undertaking, so is the acquisition of restraint (*saṃvara*). And how is their undertaking? "I abstain from sexual misconduct. It is not, however, "In this continuum, I shall not practice celibacy (*brahmacarya*). For this very reason, the acquisition of restraint for them arises specifically from the limb of sexual misconduct, and not from unchastity; thus, there is no violation of restraint regarding one who has become a wife.

Now, for what reason is abstinence from false speech alone a training precept (*śikṣāpada*) of the lay follower’s restraint (*upāsaka-saṃvara*), and not abstinence from slander and so forth? It is for these very three reasons:
Because false speech is exceedingly blameworthy, because it is easy [to observe], and because of the attainment of non-action;
and because in the transgression of all other training precepts, there is the consequence of false speech. (34ab) (12)

For in every case, when one is questioned regarding a transgression of the training, this thought arises: "I did not do such a thing. Thus, there is the possibility of false speech; therefore, abstention from false speech is prescribed so that even one who has committed a transgression might reveal himself.

But what is the reason that a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) was not established for him regarding offenses of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*)? [The answer is: It was indeed established from among those very offenses of prohibition. (34cd) (16)

What is the reason that it is from intoxicants alone and not from anything else? (17) For the sake of guarding the others. (34d’) If one drinks intoxicants, the other limbs [of virtue] would remain unguarded. How, then, is the drinking of intoxicants understood to be a fault by prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇasāvadya*)? Because it lacks the characteristic of being a natural fault (*prakṛtisāvadya*). For a natural fault is committed only with a defiled mind (*kliṣṭacitta*). However, it is possible to drink intoxicants with the very intention of remedying [a condition], provided they do not cause intoxication. Yet, that mind which drinks knowing [the substance] to be intoxicating is indeed defiled.

That is not defiled when one drinks having recognized the amount that does not cause intoxication. "Alcohol is a natural offense (*prakṛtisāvadya*)," so say the holders of the Vinaya. "Venerable sir, how should one attend to the sick? "Upāli, with the exception of what is a natural offense," so it was said by the Blessed One. Furthermore, the drinking of alcohol was not permitted even for the Śākyas when they were ill.

And this has been said: "O monks, those who designate me as their Teacher must not drink even as much as a drop on the tip of a blade of kuśa grass. From this, it is known that [the consumption of intoxicants] is a natural transgression (*prakṛtisāvadya*). Furthermore, because the Noble Ones (*ārya*) do not commit it even when they have passed into other births—just like the killing of living beings—and because it is described as a misconduct of the body and leads to rebirth in the miserable destinies (*durgati*). The Abhidharmikas say: "No."

[219] Even though it has been generally prohibited, there is a specific exception for the case of those who are ill regarding this prescribed offense (*prajñaptisāvadya*), in order to avoid an undesirable consequence by restricting the amount of intoxicants. For this very reason, drinking even as much as a drop from the tip of a blade of *kuśa* grass is forbidden. The Noble Ones do not indulge in it because they possess a sense of shame (*hrī*), and because it destroys mindfulness (*smṛti*). One should not drink even a small amount, as there is no fixed limit, just as with poison. It is called a "misconduct" (*duścarita*) because it is a basis for negligence (*pramāda*).

For this very reason, the term "basis for negligence" (*pramādasthāna*) is used here [only for these three], but not for the others, because those are inherently unwholesome (*prakṛtisāvadya*). (5) It is stated that by practicing them excessively, one goes to an evil rebirth (*durgati*); this is because, through addiction to them, there is a continuous flow of unwholesome states, leading to the projection (*ākṣepa*) of karma conducive to the miserable realms (*āpāyika*), or because such karma gains its functional activity (*vṛttilābha*). What is the meaning of "liquor, spirits, and intoxicants that are bases for negligence"? *Surā* is grain-fermented liquor; *maireya* is distilled liquor from decoctions.

Furthermore, since these two [types of intoxicants] may sometimes exist in a state where they have not yet reached or have already passed the stage of intoxication, the term *madya* (intoxicant) is used. Since even betel nuts, *kōdrava* grain, and so forth cause intoxication, the terms *surā* and *maireya* are employed. The expression "basis for negligence" (*pramādasthāna*) is stated to make known the reason why even that which is a transgression by convention (*prajñaptisāvadya*) must be abandoned with diligence; this is because it is the locus of all forms of negligence.

Regarding these three—the Prātimokṣa, Dhyāna, and Anāsrava restraints—is it the case that when one is obtained, the remaining two are also obtained from that same source? He says: No. What then? [The following:]

The [vow] pertaining to the desire realm is acquired from all, both, and those that are present. (35ab) The Prātimokṣa restraint is "pertaining to the desire realm" because it is acquired from the aggregates, bases, and elements that are exclusively present. "From all" means from the fundamental, preparatory, and subsequent [actions]. "From both" means from those designated as sentient beings and non-sentient things, and from natural and proscribed misdeeds. It is acquired only from the aggregates, bases, and elements that are present, because it proceeds with reference to sentient beings; it is not acquired from the past or future, because they are reckoned as non-sentient.
The meditative and uncontaminated restraints [are obtained] from the fundamental [stages] at all times. (35cd) (18)

The meditative (*dhyāna*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) restraints are obtained only from the fundamental paths of action (*karmapatha*), not from the preliminary (*prayoga*) or subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) stages, much less from offenses of conventional designation (*prajñaptisāvadya*). Furthermore, they are obtained from all times—that is, from the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) of the past and the future as well. For this very reason, a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*) is formulated: there are those aggregates, bases, and elements from which only the Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained, and not the meditative or uncontaminated restraints, and so forth.

The first alternative: from present preparatory and consecutive stages (*sāmantaka-pṛṣṭha*) and from transgressions of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). The second: from past and future fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*). The third: from present fundamental paths of action. The fourth: from past and future preparatory and consecutive stages. However, since there are no present paths of action at the time of undertaking the restraint (*saṃvara*), one should say "from those based on present objects."

Restraint is appropriate only for future [actions], not for those that have already passed or are currently occurring. Now, are restraint and non-restraint obtained from all sentient beings, from all components, and by all causes, or is there a distinction? To begin with, restraint is certainly obtained from all sentient beings; however, regarding the components and the causes, there is a variety of cases. (36ab)

Restraint is obtained from all sentient beings, but regarding the [individual] factors, there is diversity. Some obtain it from all [factors], namely the *bhikṣu* restraint; some from four, namely others than that. For the paths of action are the factors (*aṅga*) of restraint. Regarding the causes as well, by one method it is from all, and by another method it is from one. First, by what is it from all? If non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are accepted as the causes. By what is it from one?

If weak, medium, and intense states of mind are accepted as the causes, then, defining it according to the final alternative, it is said: there is one who abides in restraint and is restrained toward all sentient beings, yet not by all factors and not by all causes; namely, one who undertakes the lay follower's (*upāsaka*) or the one-day vow (*upavāsa*) or the novice monk's (*śrāmaṇera*) restraint with a weak, medium, or intense state of mind. There is also one who is restrained toward all sentient beings and by all factors, but not by all causes.

There is one who undertakes the *bhikṣu* restraint with a weak, middling, or superior mind; [this applies] toward all sentient beings, with all factors (*aṅga*), and by all causes (*kāraṇa*). There is one who undertakes the three restraints with the three types of minds; [this applies] toward all sentient beings and by all causes, but not with all factors. There is one who undertakes the lay follower (*upāsaka*), fast-day (*upavāsa*), and novice (*śrāmaṇera*) restraints with weak, middling, and superior [minds]; however, there is no such person who would not [apply it] toward all sentient beings.

Because one who abides in hundreds of virtues that extend toward all sentient beings attains restraint (*saṃvara*), and not otherwise, since the evil intention has not ceased; one attains the Prātimokṣa restraint by making five restrictions (*niyama*). These are: restriction regarding sentient beings, restriction regarding limbs, restriction regarding place, restriction regarding time, and restriction regarding occasion. "I abstain from this particular sentient being" is the restriction regarding sentient beings. "From this particular limb" is the restriction regarding limbs. "In this particular place" is the restriction regarding place. "For as long as a month" is the restriction regarding time.

"Except in battle"—this is the restriction regarding the occasion. However, for one who accepts [the vow] in that manner, there would be merely good conduct (*sucarita*). How is the acquisition of restraint (*saṃvara*) obtained from those [beings] who are impossible [to avoid harming]? Because of the undertaking [of the vow] with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) not to harm the life of any sentient being. If, on the other hand, restraint were obtained only from those who are possible [to avoid harming], it would be subject to increase and decrease, because of the mutual transition between those who are possible and those who are impossible [to harm].

And this being the case, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the acquisition and abandonment of the restraint would occur even without the causes for its acquisition and abandonment. This cannot be so. For just as there is no increase or decrease of the restraint when new grass and such things arise, or when they remain, so too there would be no [increase or decrease] upon the transition between the capable and the incapable; this is because sentient beings exist both before and after, whereas grass and such things do not.

What indeed would be the distinction here, or rather, why would there not be restraint (*saṃvara*) even when grass and such things are non-existent, or why would it be impossible? And since they have completely passed away and no longer exist at all, how could there not be a diminution of restraint? Therefore, this rebuttal is not logical; thus, the former rebuttal alone is sound.

(4) If that were so, since subsequent Buddhas would not obtain the Prātimokṣa restraint from those Buddhas who had previously entered parinirvāṇa, how would it not follow that there is a deficiency in their morality? [It is not so], because they obtain it from all sentient beings. For if those [previous Buddhas] were still present, they would have obtained it from them as well. It has been stated from what [source] restraint is obtained: (7) "But non-restraint is toward all [beings], in all aspects, and not by way of causes. (36cd) (8)

Non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), however, is acquired with respect to all sentient beings and with respect to all paths of action (*karmapatha*). For there is no one who is a non-restrained person by means of a deficient non-restraint. Yet it is not [acquired] through all causes simultaneously, because weak and other grades of mind cannot coexist at once. One who acquires non-restraint with a weak mind, even when depriving a living being of life with an intense mind, remains endowed with that same weak non-restraint, but is endowed with an intense informative act (*vijñapti*) of killing.

In this same way, it should be applied to the medium and superior degrees. Now, these are the persons belonging to the class of those lacking restraint (*asaṃvarika*): namely, sheep-butchers, poultry-slaughterers, pig-butchers, bird-catchers, fishermen, deer-hunters, thieves, executioners, jailers, elephant-trappers, dog-cookers, and netters. Kings, administrators of punishment, and judges are also, in effect, those lacking restraint. They are called *asaṃvarika* because they exist within a state of non-restraint; that is, because non-restraint exists in them by virtue of their abiding therein.

Those who kill sheep are called *aurabhrikas*. In this same way, other [occupations] should also be applied. It is indeed logical that the acquisition of restraint (*saṃvara*) occurs with respect to all sentient beings, because it is undertaken with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the welfare of all sentient beings. But how is it logical that those such as butchers (*aurabhrika*), whose intentions toward their own mother, father, children, wife, and so forth are not corrupted—even though they would not wish to kill them even for the sake of their own lives—possess non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) with respect to all sentient beings? For they might even kill their mother and others if she were to become a sheep.

For surely those who know that "these are indeed those very same individuals" would not kill them. Furthermore, since there is no possibility for those who have become noble (*ārya*) to become animals again, how could non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) exist toward them? Moreover, if one were to be unrestrained toward the present because of a consideration for future states of existence, then they would never kill even sheep and the like once they have become their sons; thus, there would be no non-restraint toward them. For how indeed could there be no non-restraint toward those whom they actually intend to kill?

This is the same regarding those who take only a few precepts and so forth. For how indeed could there be non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) toward those [beings] for those who do not even intend to kill them? (2) Furthermore, consider a thief by birth who, though he takes [what is not given], is content with his own wife and is mute. How could there be non-restraint for him regarding the preliminary factors (*pūrvāṅga*)? Because his intention (*āśaya*) has not been corrupted. Moreover, even a mute person is capable of conveying through the body a meaning that is to be conveyed by speech. (4) What then of one who undertakes two or three training rules (*śikṣāpada*)?

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that there is no such thing as an incomplete, partial, or limited non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). The Sautrāntikas, however, hold that according to one's undertaking, there can be both partial and limited non-restraint as well as restraint (*saṃvara*), with the exception of the eightfold [Prātimokṣa] vows; for by that alone, virtue and misconduct are mutually obstructed. This has been explained regarding those from whom non-restraint is acquired. But it was not stated how it is acquired. Therefore, this is now stated:
"But the acquisition of the remaining non-manifest [karma] (*avijñapti*) is through the field, the undertaking, and earnestness. (37cd)

Or the field (*kṣetra*) may be of such a nature that non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises merely by the gift of a grove and so forth, as in the case of the bases of meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*). Alternatively, one undertakes a formal commitment (*samādāna*), thinking: "I shall not eat without having paid homage to the Buddha," or "I shall always observe the fast-day meals, the monthly meals, or the half-monthly meals," and so forth. With such earnestness, one engages in an action—whether wholesome or unwholesome—of such a kind that non-informative action arises from it.
This has been explained regarding how the acquisition of restraint, non-restraint, and that which is other than these occurs.

The relinquishment [of the vows] must now be explained. In that regard: (17) The relinquishment of the restraint of the Prātimokṣa occurs through the renunciation of the training, through death, (18) through the arising of both sexual organs, through the cutting off of the roots [of merit], and through the passing of the night. ||38|| (19)

"Dama" means that by which one becomes tamed; it refers here to restraint (*saṃvara*), because through it the sense faculties are subdued. The Prātimokṣa restraint is relinquished for four reasons—excluding the fast (*upavāsa*): by renouncing the training rules in the presence of a person capable of understanding them out of sincere intent; by abandoning the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*); by the simultaneous appearance of both sexual organs; and by the total severance of the roots of virtue. However, the fast restraint is relinquished by these four [reasons] as well as by the passing of the night.

These, taken together, constitute the five causes for the relinquishment [of the vows]. But what is the reason that relinquishment occurs through these causes? It is because of the arising of an informative act (*vijñapti*) contrary to the undertaking, the abandonment of the basis (*āśraya*), the transformation of the basis, the cutting off of the cause (*nidāna*), and the exhaustion of the projection (*ākṣepa*) for that duration.
Some say it is also by means of a downfall (*patanīya*).
Others, however, say that the relinquishment of the vows of a monk or a novice occurs through any one of the four downfalls.
Others say [it is due] to the disappearance of the true Dharma;
others say it is because of the disappearance of the true Dharma, since when the true Dharma has disappeared, all training rules, boundaries, and ritual acts are brought to an end.
However, according to the Kaśmīris, for one who has committed an offense, both [the state of being a layperson and the state of being a monk] are accepted as being like wealth and debt.

The Vaibhāṣikas of Kaśmīr, however, maintain this: even for one who has committed a fundamental offense (*maulī āpatti*), there is no loss of the monk’s restraint (*bhikṣusaṃvara*). What is the reason? For it is not logical that the entire restraint should be lost due to the disturbance of a single part. Nor is there a severance of morality (*śīlaccheda*) even for one who has committed another offense. What then? He possesses both: morality and immorality (*dauḥśīlya*). It is just as someone might have both wealth and debt.

Once that offense has been confessed, however, he possesses ethical discipline (*śīlavat*) and is no longer immoral (*duḥśīla*), just as one becomes wealthy after clearing a debt and is no longer a debtor. As for what was said by the Blessed One: "He is a monk who is no longer a *śramaṇa*, no longer a son of the Śākyas; he falls from the state of a monk. His *śrāmaṇya* is destroyed, ruined, fallen, and defeated"—this was said with reference to ultimate (*paramārtha*) monkhood. This [other statement] refers to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

What rashness is there in this? That the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) taught by the Blessed One is again interpreted otherwise, and conditions for immorality and many afflictions are provided. How is this [to be understood as] definitive meaning? For this is the explanation in the Vinaya: "There are four kinds of monks: the monk by designation (*saṃjñā-bhikṣu*), the monk by self-claim (*pratijñā-bhikṣu*), the monk because he begs (*bhikṣate*), and the monk because his afflictions have been shattered (*bhinnakleśatvāt*). But in this context, 'monk' refers to one who has received full ordination through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*jñapticaturthakarman*)."

Furthermore, he was not previously a monk in the ultimate sense such that he would later cease to be a monk. As for what was said regarding "the disturbance of one part," the treatise itself has already provided the rebuttal by employing this analogy: "Just as a palmyra tree cut off at the crown is incapable of sprouting, incapable of attaining growth, increase, or expansion."

(20) What, then, is the meaning of the simile? It is that when even a single part which constitutes the root is severed, the remainder of the restraint (*saṃvara*) is incapable of growing again. (21) And since he, by committing a grave, fundamental offense (*maulāpatti*) that breaches the boundaries of the state of a monk (*bhikṣu*), cuts the root of the restraint due to his association with intense lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*), it is logical that there is a total abandonment of the restraint.

He for whom even the consumption of a single mouthful of food or the use of a space as small as the heel of one foot is not permitted regarding the food and dwellings belonging to the Saṅgha, and who has been excluded from all communal enjoyment with the monks by the Teacher—referring to him it was said:
"Remove the *kāraṇḍavaka* weed; pull out the rotten grass.
Then cast away the scum: the one who is not a monk but claims to be a monk."

"What is the nature of his being a monk? Let it be as it may; there certainly is the state of being a monk. For the Blessed One has said: 'There are four types of ascetics, Cunda; there is no fifth.'"

"The Conqueror of the Path, the Teacher of the Path, he who lives by the Path, and he who defiles the Path"—this has been said. Among sentient beings, one is called a *śramaṇa* because only the outward form remains, like a burnt log, a dried-up pond, a parrot's beak, a rotten seed, a firebrand-circle, or a dead being. For if one were no longer a monk (*bhikṣu*) simply due to immorality (*dauḥśīlya*), there would be no such thing as one who has been granted the training (*śikṣādattaka*). We do not say that everyone becomes guilty of a defeat (*pārājika*) immediately upon committing an offense; however, whoever is defeated is necessarily no longer a monk.

(12) However, the Lord of Dharma has established that someone may not be *pārājika* due to a particularity of their mental continuum (*saṃtāna*), because they did not conceal [the offense] even for a single moment of thought. (13) If, then, one who is *pārājika* is no longer a monk, why is he not ordained again? Because his mental continuum has been ruined by an intense lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*), he is incapable of restraint (*saṃvara*); it is certainly not on account of his status as a monk. For in that case, even one who has renounced the training (*nikṣiptaśikṣa*) is not ordained again.

(15) And what is this persistence in what is meaningless? If he is such [a person], even so, let there be homage to him for that kind of monkhood! (16) However, when the True Dharma has disappeared, because of the absence of formal acts of discipline (*vinayakarma*), there is no acquisition of a new restraint (*saṃvara*); but for that which has been acquired, there is no loss.
(17) Now, how is there a loss of the restraints of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*)?
(18) The wholesome [restraint] attained through meditative absorption is abandoned by changing levels and by falling away. (40ab) (19)

All wholesome states attained through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) are abandoned for two reasons: either by birth, through moving to a higher level, or necessarily by falling away from the attainment, and in some cases, due to the [change of] homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*). Just as wholesome states belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāpta*) are abandoned through moving to another level or through falling away, so too are those belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*); however, noble states (*ārya*) are abandoned through the acquisition of a fruit, through refinement, or through falling away. (40cd)

However, the untainted wholesome [state] is abandoned for three reasons: the previous path is abandoned through the attainment of a fruit; the path of weak faculties is abandoned through the sharpening of the faculties (*indriyottāpana*); and the higher path, whether it be a fruit or a fruit distinguished by excellence, is abandoned through falling away (*parihāṇi*). Thus, first of all, the restraints (*saṃvara*) are relinquished. (41ab) Non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is [abandoned] by the acquisition of restraint, death, and the appearance of both sexual organs. (4)

The abandonment of non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) occurs through three causes: (1) by the attainment of restraint (*saṃvara*); that is, if one undertakes the vows of restraint or acquires the restraint of meditative concentration (*dhyānasaṃvara*). This is because, through the power of causes and conditions, one attains meditative absorption (*samādhi*), whereby non-restraint is severed due to the superior strength of its opposite. (2) By death, through the relinquishing of the physical basis (*āśraya*). (3) By the production of both sexual organs, through the transformation of the physical basis. Furthermore, even when one renounces weapons and nets, [non-restraint is severed] through the intention (*āśaya*) not to act [further]. Without the attainment of restraint, there is no severing of non-restraint.
Just as a disease that has already progressed does not cease even when its causes have been avoided, provided there is no medicine, so too:

(8) When one who is characterized by non-restraint (*asaṃvarika*) undertakes the fast (*upavāsa*), does he return from that restraint (*saṃvara*) back to non-restraint, or rather to neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint? Some say: "To non-restraint," because the intention to abandon [the restraint] is not absolute; they argue that just as a glowing iron ball returns to blackness without being applied [to fire], so it is here. Others say: "To neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint," because the acquisition of that [restraint] depends upon informative action (*vijñapti*). (11)
Now, how is non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that is free from both restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) abandoned?
"But the intermediate [non-informative action] is abandoned through the cutting off of momentum, undertaking, activity, object, life, and roots. (41cd)

For when that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) has been projected by the force of either faith or affliction, it is severed by the cessation of that [force], just like the motion of a potter’s wheel or an arrow. It is also severed by the abandonment of the undertaking (*samādāna*), if one abandons the undertaking, thinking, "Enough with this undertaking. It is also severed by the interruption of the action, as in the case of one who does not perform what was undertaken. It is also severed by the cessation of the object (*artha*). Of what object?

The intermediate non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) is abandoned through these six causes: by the destruction of the objects such as shrines, groves, monasteries, bedding, seats, mechanical devices, nets, and so forth; by the destruction of the life-span; and by the cutting off of the roots of merit (*kuśalamūla*). When one begins to utterly cut off the roots of merit, [the intermediate non-informative matter is abandoned]. Thus, the wholesome non-form [matter] pertaining to the desire realm is abandoned through the cutting off of the roots and through birth in a higher realm. (42ab)

Wholesome states belonging to the desire realm that are immaterial in nature are abandoned for two reasons: either through the total eradication of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-samuccheda*) or through rebirth in the form or formless realms. (22) However, the defiled is abandoned through the arising of the antidote (*pratipakṣodayāt*).
