[Verse 42cd] (p.226) All defiled states that are immaterial in nature are abandoned solely through the arising of the antidote. For whichever type of secondary affliction there is a specific path of abandonment, by that path it is abandoned along with its attendants, and not otherwise. (3)

Now, for which sentient beings is there non-restraint, and for which is there restraint? (4) Non-restraint exists among humans, excluding eunuchs, impotent persons, those of dual gender, (5) and the inhabitants of Kuru. (43abc) (6)

Non-restraint exists only in the human realm and not elsewhere; even there, it excludes the *śaṇḍhas*, *paṇḍakas*, those with both sexual organs, and the inhabitants of Uttarakuru. Restraint is likewise [restricted], as well as that of the gods. (43cd)

Restraint (*saṃvara*) belongs only to humans—as previously stated—and to gods; thus, restraint exists in these two realms of existence. How is it known that eunuchs (*śaṇḍha*) and others lack restraint? It is understood from both the Sūtras and the Vinaya. It is said in the Sūtra: "Mahānāman, when a householder clad in white, a man endowed with male faculties, goes for refuge to the Buddha... and speaks these words: 'Hold me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*)'; by this much one becomes a lay follower."

In the Vinaya as well, it is stated that such a person is to be expelled; what then is the reason that these [beings] lack restraint (*saṃvara*)? It is because their afflictions (*kleśa*) are so intense in both bases [of body and mind], because they are incapable of analytical reflection (*pratisaṃkhyāna*), and because they lack intense shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*). If that is so, why do they not possess non-restraint (*asaṃvara*)? Because their intention (*āśaya*) is unstable even toward evil. Furthermore, where there is restraint, there is also non-restraint, because they exist as opposites (*pratidvaṃdvabhāva*).

Because the inhabitants of Uttarakuru lack both the undertaking [of vows] and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and because they lack the intention to perform unwholesome actions, there is an absence of both restraint (*saṃvara*) and non-restraint (*asaṃvara*). Furthermore, those in the miserable realms (*āpāyika*) lack intense moral shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*vyapatrāpya*); it is through connection with these qualities, and by their impairment, that restraint and non-restraint would otherwise exist.

Moreover, it is indeed their very basis (*āśraya*) that is like a saline field (*ūṣarakṣetra*); for those who are eunuchs (*śaṇḍha*), impotent (*paṇḍaka*), hermaphrodites (*ubhayavyañjana*), inhabitants of Uttarakuru, or those in the miserable destinies (*apāyika*), restraint (*saṃvara*) does not grow in such a basis, nor does non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), just as neither grain nor even weeds grow in a saline field. If that is so, then what about the statement in the Sūtra: "O monks, a serpent born from an egg (*aṇḍaja-nāga*), having emerged on the eighth day of the fortnight, observes the fast (*upavāsa*) endowed with the eight limbs"?
For them, that is merely good conduct (*sucarita*), not restraint (*saṃvara*). Therefore, restraint exists only among humans. Furthermore, among humans, there are three [types of restraint].
(43d) All three restraints—the Prātimokṣa and so forth—are found among humans.
For the gods born in the desire and form realms, [the restraint] is born of meditative concentration (dhyānaja).
(44ab) The restraint of meditative concentration (dhyānasaṃvara) belongs to the gods reborn in the desire and form realms; it does not exist above those.
Furthermore, the untainted (anāsrava) [restraint]— [p.227]
[The untainted restraint] also belongs to those born in the formless realm, excluding those in the intermediate dhyāna and the non-percipient beings.

(2) However, the untainted restraint exists even for those born in the desire and form realms, with the exception of those born in the intermediate dhyāna and the non-percipient beings. (3) Even for those born in the formless realm, it exists for them by way of possession (*samanvāgama*), but not by way of manifest presence (*saṃmukhībhāva*). (4) Beyond this, now, under the heading of the exposition of karma, the exposition of the karmas taught in the Sūtras will begin. There are three karmas: wholesome karma, unwholesome karma, and neutral karma. Regarding these:

Action that is secure, insecure, or other than those two; wholesome, unwholesome, or other than those two—(45ab)—this is the definition of the wholesome and so forth. Wholesome action is secure because it protects one from suffering, having a desirable maturation and leading to the attainment of nirvāṇa. Unwholesome action is insecure, both temporarily and ultimately, by virtue of being the opposite of security, having an undesirable maturation. Action other than these two should be understood as neither secure nor insecure; that is, other than the wholesome and the unwholesome. This means it is "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*). Furthermore, (10)

Meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable; and the triad beginning with that to be experienced as pleasure. (45cd) There are three types of karma: meritorious (*puṇya*), non-meritorious (*apuṇya*), and imperturbable (*āneñja*). Again, there are three: karma to be experienced as pleasure (*sukhavedanīya*), karma to be experienced as suffering (*duḥkhavedanīya*), and karma to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanīya*). Among these, first: In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), wholesome karma is meritorious; that which arises in the higher realms is imperturbable. (14)

"Wholesome" is understood [to carry over]. Wholesome karma belonging to the realms of form and formlessness is "immovable" (*āneñja*). But has it not been stated by the Blessed One that the first three meditations (*dhyāna*) are "shaken" (*señjita*)? For it was said: "Whatever is here thought out (*vitarkita*) and deliberated (*vicārita*), this the Noble Ones call 'shaken' (*iñjita*)," and so forth. This was said with reference to their possession of defects within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). However, they are also called "immovable" in the *Āneñja-sūtra*, starting from the path leading to the attainment of the immovable. What, then, is the reason that what is elsewhere called "shaken" is here called "immovable"?
For in those stages, karma does not waver with respect to its maturation.

(46cd) Indeed, karma belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) wavers with respect to its maturation. How does it waver? Because of its lack of fixed status. For even karma belonging to one destiny (*gati*) may mature in another destiny; and karma belonging to one class of gods may mature in another class of gods. Indeed, that very same karma which is conducive to [specific] dimensions, power, complexion, and the enjoyment of pleasure in other stages, and which would otherwise mature among the gods, may at times—by the force of other conditions—mature among humans, animals, or hungry ghosts (*preta*).

However, karma belonging to the realms of form and formlessness is never able to ripen in a level other than its own; therefore, because its ripening is fixed, it is called "immovable" (*āneñja*). As for non-meritorious karma, it is well known in the world as "unwholesome. Since a meaning that is established by worldly convention is already well known, what need is there for effort regarding it? The explanation of meritorious and other types of karma has been completed. Now, the explanation of those [types of karma] to be experienced as pleasure and so forth must be made; that is now being done: (47ab) That which is wholesome up to the third dhyāna is to be experienced as pleasure.

Wholesome karma to be experienced as pleasure extends up to the third dhyāna; for this is the ground of pleasant feeling, namely, the desire realm and the [first] three dhyānas. Beyond that, however, it is to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.

The term "wholesome" (*śubha*) continues [from the previous context]. Beyond the third dhyāna, wholesome karma is to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, because of the absence of pleasant and painful sensations there. (10) Unwholesome [karma] is to be experienced as pain here. (47d) Unwholesome karma is to be experienced as pain. The inclusion of the word "here" is for the purpose of making known that this occurs only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, sensation alone is not their fruit; what then? It is [the fruit] together with its equipment (*sasaṃbhārā*). (13)
Some say that there is also a middle [type] below;

others, however, say: "This karma which was described as to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant exists even below the fourth dhyāna. For what reason? Because of the maturation of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).

Otherwise, there would be no ripening for the karma of the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), or the intermediate dhyāna itself would not be the ripening of any karma, because of the absence of pleasure and pain therein. Some maintain that for the karma of the intermediate dhyāna, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is the ripening within that very dhyāna; others hold that its ripening is not feeling at all. This [latter view] contradicts the treatise. For it is stated in the treatise: "Could it be that the ripening of a karma ripens as exclusively mental feeling? It could: namely, the ripening of wholesome karma that is without applied thought (*avitarka*)."
For it is maintained that there is a simultaneous ripening (*vipāka*) of these three, being neither prior nor subsequent.

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Śāstra*: "There may be a simultaneous ripening of the three types of karma. There may be [the ripening] of karma to be experienced as pleasure (*sukha-vedanīya*), [namely] matter (*rūpa*]; of karma to be experienced as suffering (*duḥkha-vedanīya*), [namely] mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); and of karma to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanīya*), [namely] factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*). For this reason as well, there exists below [in the desire realm] karma to be experienced as neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. Indeed, nowhere other than in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is there a conjunction of the simultaneous ripening of these three types of karma.

Is that [karma] now wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*)? It is weak. If that is so, then there is a contradiction with the statement: "That which is to be experienced as pleasure (*sukhavedya*) up to the third dhyāna is pure (*śubha*), and the wholesome is that which has a desirable maturation (*iṣṭavipāka*). This teaching should be understood as being based on the majority of cases (*bāhulika*). Furthermore, how can karma, whose intrinsic nature is not feeling (*vedanā*), be said to be "to be experienced as suffering" (*duḥkhādivedanīya*)? That which is beneficial for pleasant feeling is "to be experienced as pleasure" (*sukhavedanīya*), or else it is that for which pleasure is to be experienced. And what is it that is to be experienced?

That which is the maturation (*vipāka*)—for that indeed exists as either "to-be-felt-as-pleasure" (*sukha-vedanīya*), by which one experiences pleasure, like a bathing powder (*snānīyakaṣāya*). In the same way, "to-be-felt-as-pain" (*duḥkha-vedanīya*) and "to-be-felt-as-neither-pain-nor-pleasure" (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanīya*) are to be understood. Furthermore: "By way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*saṃprayoga*), object (*ālambana*), maturation (*vipāka*), and manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*), the state of being felt (*vedanīyatā*) is fivefold. (Verse 49)

The state of being experienced through intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vedanīyatā*) pertains to feelings (*vedanā*), because they are experienced by their very nature. The state of being experienced through association (*saṃprayoga-vedanīyatā*) pertains to contact (*sparśa*), as in the expression "contact to be experienced as pleasant. The state of being experienced through the object (*ālambana-vedanīyatā*) pertains to sense objects (*viṣaya*), as it has been said: "Having seen forms with the eye, one experiences the form, but does not experience passion for the form," and so forth; for it is by means of feeling that one experiences while taking that [object] as an objective support. The state of being experienced as maturation (*vipāka-vedanīyatā*) pertains to karma.

(13) "Karma to be experienced in the present life," and so forth. This refers to experience through manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāvavedanīyatā*). As it has been said: "At the time when a pleasant feeling is occurring, there is no other feeling at that moment; rather, one experiences whichever [feeling] is present. However, because one brings that [feeling] into manifestation, it is said that 'one experiences it. Therefore, because the ripening (*vipāka*) is what is to be experienced, karma is also described as 'to be experienced as pleasure,' and so on. (17) And that is both determinate and indeterminate. (50a) (18)

Furthermore, this threefold karma—namely, that to be experienced as pleasure and so forth—should be understood as being both determinate (*niyata*) and indeterminate (*aniyata*). Indeterminate karma is not necessarily to be experienced. Determinate karma, moreover, is of three kinds, because it is to be experienced in the present life and so forth. (19–21)

Karma that is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*)—these three types of karma are determinate (*niyata*). Together with indeterminate karma (*aniyatavedanīya*), this constitutes four types of karma. Some, however, say there are five types of karma. (50d)

Others, however, maintain that there are five types of karma, having divided the karma of indeterminate experience into two: that which is determinate in its maturation (*vipāka*) and that which is indeterminate. Among these, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) ripens in the very same birth in which it was performed. Karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) ripens in the second birth. Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) ripens after that.

Others maintain that even within the intermediate state (*antara-bhava*), there exists the ripening (*vipāka*) of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*); its designation as such is established by virtue of its commencement. [They argue: "Let it not be that a desirable action has such a very slight ripening. However, the Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this. For there is indeed karma with proximate fruit and none with remote fruit, and the reverse; it is like external seeds.
For example, the *suvarcalā* plant ripens in three fortnights, yielding fruit in three fortnights, whereas barley, wheat, and the like take six months.

Others say there is a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*). However, the Dārṣṭāntikas formulate a fourfold alternative as follows: (1) there is karma that is fixed with respect to its stage but not fixed with respect to its maturation; this is karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) that is indeterminate regarding its maturation. (2) There is karma that is fixed with respect to its maturation but not fixed with respect to its stage; this is karma of indeterminate experience (*aniyatavedanīya*) that is fixed regarding its maturation. (3) There is karma fixed with respect to both; this is karma to be experienced in the present life and so forth that is fixed regarding its maturation. (4) There is karma fixed with respect to neither; this is karma of indeterminate experience that is indeterminate regarding its maturation.

For them, that karma is of eight types: [karma] to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), which is both determinate (*niyata*) and indeterminate (*aniyata*); and so on, up to [karma] to be experienced indeterminately (*aniyatavedanīya*). However, they explain that [the first three]—to be experienced in the present life and so forth—are exclusively determinate, while the fourth is indeterminate. It may be that one projects four kinds of karma in a single moment. This would be the case if, having incited another in three [actions], one were oneself engaged in sexual misconduct, and all of them were completed simultaneously. Furthermore, among these four kinds of karma, the projection of a homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) is by means of three.
For the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) is not projected by karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
In which realm (*dhātu*) and in which destiny (*gati*) is how many kinds of karma projected?
In all cases, there is a projection of four [types of karma]. (51c) (20)

In all three realms and in all states of existence (*gati*), there is the projection of the four types of karma—both wholesome and unwholesome—as the case may be. (21) This is the general rule; the following is its exception: (22) "In hell, the wholesome is of three kinds" (51d). (23) In the hells, there is the projection of the three types of wholesome karma, but not that which is to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), because there is no desirable maturation (*iṣṭavipāka*) therein. (24)

A stable *bāla* who is detached from a certain level does not perform karma to be experienced upon rebirth there. (52ab) Since an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes free from passion regarding a particular level and is stable—meaning he is of a nature not subject to falling away—he does not perform karma to be experienced upon rebirth in that state. What else does he perform? [p.231] A noble one (*ārya*) also does not perform karma to be experienced elsewhere. (52c)

The term "stable" (*sthira*) carries over [from the previous verse]. However, an noble person (*āryapudgala*) who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) and is not subject to falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*) does not perform karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) or in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) in that [attained] state. For such a person is incapable of returning again to a lower plane; yet, having been born there, they may perform indeterminate (*aniyata*) karma or karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Even one who is unstable (*asthira*) does not [perform such karma] in the Desire Realm (*kāma*) or at the Peak of Existence (*agra*). (52d)

However, even an noble person (*āryapudgala*) of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), who is free from passion for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), is incapable of performing karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) or in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*) within those two realms. What is the reason? Because he has fallen away from the fruit; and there is no death for one who has fallen away from the fruit, as we shall explain later. Is there also the projection (*ākṣepa*) of karma in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)? He says: "Yes.
The intermediate state projects twenty-two types [of karma] within the desire realm. (53ab)

The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) projects twenty-two types of karma. How so? There are five stages of the embryo (*garbhāvasthā*): the stages of the *kalala*, *arbuda*, *peśī*, *ghana*, and *praśākhā*. There are five stages after birth: the stages of infancy, childhood, youth, middle age, and old age. In this regard, the intermediate state projects karma to be experienced in the *kalala* stage, both indeterminate (*aniyata*) and determinate (*niyata*). Likewise, it projects [karma] up to that which is to be experienced in the stage of old age, as well as that to be experienced in the intermediate state itself.
And that [karma] has its fruit in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmaphala*).

Furthermore, this karma belonging to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which was stated to be of eleven types and fixed, should be understood as "to be experienced in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). What is the reason? (53d) For it is a single group (*nikāya*).

Indeed, that homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) is one alone, projected by a single karma—namely, the intermediate state and the ten stages that follow it. For this very reason, no other karma to be experienced in the intermediate state has been mentioned, because it is projected by the same [karma] that projects [the karma] to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*).

Furthermore, what kind of action is to be understood as determinate? (21) That which is performed with intense affliction or serene faith, and that which is done continuously; (22) that performed toward a field of qualities is determinate, as is the act of killing one's parents. (54) (23)

For that action which is performed with intense affliction (*kleśa*), that which is performed with intense faith (*prasāda*), and that which is performed continuously or toward a field of qualities (*guṇakṣetra*)—that should be understood as determinate (*niyata*). In this context, the "field of qualities" refers to the Three Jewels, or to a certain distinguished person (*pudgalaviśeṣa*) who has attained a particular fruit or meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). For in those cases, even without intense affliction or faith, or continuity, wholesome or unwholesome action becomes determinate.

Furthermore, "parents" refers to both the mother and the father. Whatever destructive karma (*ghātika-karma*) one commits toward them, in whatever manner it may be, that [karma] necessarily comes to fruition and not otherwise.
Now, what kind of karma should be understood as "to be experienced in this very life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*)? [It is said:
"Karma has its fruit in the present life due to the excellence of the field and the intention. (55ab)

Karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) arises either from a distinction in the field (*kṣetra*), as it is heard that a change of sexual characteristics occurred due to addressing the Saṅgha with the words "women"; or from a distinction in the intention (*āśaya*), as in the case of a eunuch who attained masculinity by liberating bulls from castration; or else, from absolute detachment (*atyantavairāgya*) from that level (*tadbhūmi*).

Alternatively, when one becomes completely detached from the level—whether wholesome or unwholesome—to which that action belongs, that action becomes *karma* to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*). Regarding what kind of action it is for one born on that level, he says:
"That which is fixed with respect to its maturation" (v. 55d).

For this rule applies to that karma which is fixed as to its maturation (*vipāka*), but not fixed as to its timing, nor is it unfixed; however, for that which is fixed to another state, its maturation is certain to occur in that very state, because it is impossible for one who possesses such karma to attain ultimate detachment (*atyanta-vairāgya*). And as for that which is unfixed, there is no maturation at all due to ultimate detachment.

Furthermore, what kind of field (*kṣetra*) is it in which karma necessarily becomes to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-vedanīya*)? It is said: the community of monks headed by the Buddha, and furthermore, five types of persons (*pudgala*).

For those who have emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodha*), from non-contention (*araṇā*), from loving-kindness (*maitrī*), from the vision [of the truths], or from the fruit of arhatship, the fruit of benefit or harm toward them is experienced immediately. (56) One who has emerged from the attainment of cessation attains supreme tranquility of mind, because that attainment resembles nirvāṇa; for he is, as it were, one who has gone to nirvāṇa and returned. The mental continuum of one who has emerged from non-contention proceeds accompanied by an intense cultivation of immeasurable merit, following upon the resolute intention established through the non-contention directed toward immeasurable sentient beings.

The mental continuum of one who has emerged from the meditative state of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) proceeds accompanied by an exceedingly exalted cultivation of immeasurable merit, following from the resolute intention for the happiness of immeasurable sentient beings. The mental continuum of one who has emerged from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) proceeds as stainless due to the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*), because of the abandonment of all that is to be abandoned by seeing. The mental continuum of one who has emerged from the fruit of arhatship proceeds as purified due to the transformation of the basis, because of the abandonment of all that is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Therefore, the fruit of benefits or harms performed toward these [three types of persons] is necessarily obtained in this very life. However, because the remaining path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) has not yet reached its full nature and result, the continuum of those who have emerged from it does not possess such a recent transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparivṛtti*) or a purified intention; thus, they do not constitute a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) in that same way.

Furthermore, ripening (*vipāka*) is primarily characterized by feeling (*vedanā*). This is now being examined: could there be a case where only mental feeling ripens as the result of karma, and not bodily feeling? Or could there be a case where only bodily feeling ripens, and not mental feeling? To this he says: It is held that for wholesome karma that is devoid of discursive thought (*avitarka*), the ripening is considered to be mental feeling alone. (57abc)

Action without applied thought (*avitarka*) exists from the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). The ripening (*vipāka*) of that wholesome action without applied thought is exclusively mental feeling (*caitasikī vedanā*). Why is it not bodily? Because that [bodily feeling] is necessarily accompanied by both applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*). However, for unwholesome action, it is exclusively bodily. (Verse 57d)

The ripening (*vipāka*) of unwholesome (*akuśala*) karma is exclusively bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*). Why is it not mental? For its ripening is painful sensation, and painful mental sensation is mental distress (*daurmanasya*); and it has already been explained that mental distress is not a ripening. If so, when there is a derangement of the mind (*cittakṣepa*) among sentient beings, in which mind does it occur, and by what cause? Derangement of the mind occurs in the mental consciousness (*manaścitta*).
The meaning is *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness). For the mind is not deranged within the five groups of sensory consciousnesses, because they are non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*).
And that [derangement] is born from the maturation of karma (*karmavipākaja*).

And this derangement of the mind in sentient beings is born of their own karma. For those who, by means of substances or the application of mantras, cause the minds of others to be deranged; or who force others to drink poison or intoxicants against their will; or who terrify them; or who set fire to forests during hunts and the like; or who cause them to fall from precipices; or who, by some other means, cause others to lose their mindfulness—their minds will be deranged in the future as the ripening (*vipāka*) of that karma. [It is said: "By fear, injury, imbalance, and grief" (58cd). (22)

First, how is it by way of fear? Non-human beings and others approach humans with hideous forms; the minds of those who are terrified by them become deranged. How is it by way of injury? Enraged non-human beings themselves strike at the vital points (*marmasu*) of humans. How is it by way of an imbalance of the great elements? The wind, bile, and phlegm fall into a state of agitation. How is it by way of grief? As in the case of Vāsiṣṭhī and others.

If the mind is distracted, and mental distraction (*cittakṣepa*) arises from the ripening of karma (*karmavipāka*), how is it that mental feeling (*caitasikī vedanā*) does not also result as ripening? We do not say that the very same mind is the ripening; rather, that which is a disturbance of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is the ripening. What arises from that is therefore "born of ripening" (*vipākaja*). For the mind proceeds in a state of agitation, lacking self-control, and with impaired mindfulness due to an imbalance of the elements produced by karma; thus it is called "distracted."

In this way, this fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is appropriate: "There is a mind that is deranged (kṣipta) but not distracted (vikṣita)," and so forth. First, that which is deranged is not [simply] distracted; it is the afflicted mind of one whose mind is distracted. That which is afflicted is distracted, but not deranged, as in the case of the afflicted mind of one with a healthy mind. Both [are present] in the afflicted mind of one whose mind is deranged. Neither is the case for the non-afflicted mind of one with a healthy mind. Furthermore, of which sentient beings is the mind deranged? [It is deranged] among those in the desire realm, excluding the inhabitants of Kuru. (AKB 2.58d)

[This applies] to the Kurus who possess desire. For even among the gods there are those who are insane, let alone among humans, animals, and hungry ghosts. The denizens of hell, however, are always of deranged mind. For their vital organs are pierced by thousands of various tortures, and being struck by intense pains, they cannot even perceive themselves, much less what should or should not be done. In this regard, the denizen of hell who laments with a distracted mind (*hācittaparidevaka*) should be cited as an example.

Even the minds of the Noble Ones are deranged by an imbalance of the elements, with the exception of the Buddha. It is not through karma, because determinate [karma] has already matured previously, and indeterminate [karma] does not mature [in this life]. It is not through fear, because they have completely transcended the five fears. It is not through injury, because they do not perform anything unpleasing that would cause the provocation of humans. It is not through grief, because they possess direct knowledge of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, three crookednesses (*vaṅka*) are taught in the Sūtra: crookedness of body, crookedness of speech, and crookedness of mind. Three faults (*doṣa*): fault of body, fault of speech, and fault of mind. Three turbidities (*kaṣāya*): turbidity of body, turbidity of speech, and turbidity of mind. In this regard, they should be understood respectively as follows: "The mention of crookedness, fault, and turbidity arises from deceit, hatred, and passion. (59ab)

Bodily action born of deceit is called a "bodily crookedness" (*kāyavaṅka*), because it follows from a crooked disposition. Likewise for the "crookednesses" of speech and mind. Bodily action born of hatred is called a "bodily fault" (*kāyadoṣa*), because it follows from a corruption of the mind. Likewise for the "faults" of speech and mind. Bodily action born of attachment is called a "bodily turbidity" (*kāyakaṣāya*), because it follows from being stained by passion. Likewise for the "turbidities" of speech and mind. Furthermore, action is fourfold according to the distinction between black, white, and so forth. (59cd) [p.235]

There is black karma with black ripening; there is white karma with white ripening; there is black-and-white karma with black-and-white ripening; and there is karma that is neither black nor white, which has no ripening—that karma which leads to the exhaustion of karma. In this regard: Unwholesome [karma], that which belongs to the realm of form and the desire realm, and wholesome [karma] respectively, are black, white, and both; that which is without outflows (anāsrava) leads to their exhaustion. (60)

Unwholesome karma is exclusively black because it is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), and it has a black ripening because its ripening is disagreeable. Wholesome karma pertaining to the realm of form (*rūpāpta*) is exclusively white because it is not intermingled with the unwholesome, and it has a white ripening because its ripening is agreeable. Why is that which pertains to the formless realm (*ārūpyāpta*) not mentioned? It is said that where there are two kinds of ripening—namely, that of the intermediate state (*antarābhavika*) and that of the state of rebirth (*aupapattibhavika*)—and where the three types of action of body, speech, and mind are possible, it is only there that [the classification] is stated.

This too has been stated in another Sūtra: "Wholesome [action] pertaining to the desire realm is black-and-white because it is interspersed with the unwholesome; it has black-and-white ripening because its ripening is interspersed. This is established from the perspective of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), not by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For there is no single karma or ripening of such a kind that could be both black and white, due to their mutual contradiction."

But if this were so, would not unwholesome (*akuśala*) karma also be both black and white, because it is interspersed with the wholesome? (13) It is not necessarily the case that the unwholesome is interspersed with the wholesome, because in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) the unwholesome is powerful. The wholesome, however, (14) is interspersed [with the unwholesome], because it is weak. Untainted (*anāsrava*) karma leads to the exhaustion and abandonment of these three types of karma. (15) For that is neither black—because it is undefiled (*akliṣṭa*)—nor white—because it lacks the whiteness of maturation (*vipāka*).

For this term "non-white" (*aśukla*) is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*). Indeed, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra* with reference to the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): "Ānanda, these dharmas are exclusively wholesome (*ekāntakuśala*) and exclusively irreproachable (*ekāntānavadya*). And in the *Śāstra*: "Which are the white dharmas? They are the unwholesome dharmas and the non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas. [They are] without maturation (*avipāka*) because they do not fall within the realms of existence (*dhātu*), due to the cessation of the process of rebirth (*pravṛtti*).
Furthermore, does all untainted (*anāsrava*) karma lead to the destruction of all three types of karma? It is said: "No. What then?

The twelvefold volition (*cetanā*) that exists during the receptivities to the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), during the state of detachment (*vairāgya*), and during the eight paths of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*), is the karma for the destruction of black karma. (61)

The volition that exists during the four *dharmajñānakṣāntis* on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and during the eight uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*) of detachment from the desire realm—this twelvefold volition is the action for the abandonment of black action. (5) As for the volition in the ninth [uninterrupted path], it is for the destruction of both black and white. (62ab) (6) The volition in the ninth uninterrupted path of detachment from the desire realm is for the abandonment of the ninth category of black-while-white wholesome action and of black unwholesome action. (8)

The volition arising from the final path of immediate succession during the detachment from the meditations of the white [karma]. (62cd) For one who effects detachment from each meditation, the volition that exists in the final ninth path of immediate succession—this fourfold volition is for the abandonment of white karma. But what is the reason that the abandonment of wholesome karma occurs only through the final path of immediate succession and not by any other? It is because there is no abandonment of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); even when abandoned, it can still manifest. What then? It is through the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that have those [wholesome states] as their object.
Therefore, as long as even a single type of affliction having that [object] as its focal point remains, its abandonment is not possible.
Others know that there are two [types of karma]: that to be experienced in hell and that to be experienced in other realms of desire. (63ab)

Other teachers, however, maintain that karma to be experienced in hell and karma to be experienced in other parts of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—other than hell—are respectively black and black-white. For in hell, there is the maturation (*vipāka*) of only unwholesome karma; therefore, karma to be experienced there is called "black. Consequently, in other parts of the desire realm, there is the maturation of both wholesome and unwholesome karma; therefore, karma to be experienced there is said to be "black-white. Others hold that what is to be abandoned by seeing (*dṛgheya*) is black.

Others, however, say: "Karma to be abandoned by vision is black, because it is unmixed with the wholesome. (20) "But other [karma] born of the desire realm is black-and-white" (63c). But what is this other [karma]? It is the karma of the desire realm to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). For that is both wholesome and unwholesome. (22)
It is stated in the Sūtra that there are three forms of silence (*mauneya*): silence of body, silence of speech, and silence of mind. Regarding these:
The actions of body and speech, and the mind itself, of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), are, respectively, the threefold silence. (64abc)

The bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) constitute the silence of body and speech (*kāya-vāṅ-mauneya*). However, the silence of mind (*manomauneya*) is the mind itself of one beyond training, and not mental action (*manaskarma*). What is the reason? For the mind is the ultimate sage (*paramārtha-muni*). It is said that this [sage] is inferred by means of bodily and vocal actions. Furthermore, bodily and vocal actions possess the nature of abstention (*virati*), whereas mental action does not, because there is no non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of the mind. Moreover, "silence" (*mauna*) has the sense of "restraint" (*virama*); therefore, the mind alone when restrained is called "silence."

Why is it that only the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is so designated, and not others? Because the Arhat is a sage (*muni*) in the ultimate sense, due to the cessation of all conceptual proliferation of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Three purities (*śauceya*) are taught in the Sūtra: purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind. All three of these purities consist entirely of the three types of good conduct (*sucarita*). (64cd)

All good conduct of the body is purity of body; all good conduct of speech and mind is purity of speech and mind. This is because it removes the stains of misconduct, either for a limited time or absolutely. Furthermore, this teaching is intended to distinguish those who are devoted to false silence and [false] purity. Three types of misconduct have been mentioned; therein, unwholesome bodily action and so forth are considered the threefold misconduct. (65ab)
Unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are, respectively, misconduct of body, speech, and mind.
However, even that which is not an action—namely covetousness and so forth—is threefold mental misconduct. (65cd)

Even though it does not have the nature of action (*karma*), there exists a threefold misconduct of mind (*manoduścarita*) that is distinct from volition (*cetanā*): covetousness (*abhidhyā*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). The Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that covetousness and the others are themselves mental action (*manaskarma*), because of the statement in the *Saṃcetanīya-sūtra*. However, if this were the case, there would be an identity between action and affliction (*kleśa*). What [harm] would there be if some affliction were also action? This is not so; [otherwise] the Sūtra would be contradicted.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that because volition gives rise to activity through those [three doors], it is by means of them that [volition] manifests itself. Misconduct (*duścarita*) is reprehensible conduct of body, speech, and mind because it has undesirable results;
the opposite is good conduct (*sucarita*).

Desired, wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as non-covetousness, non-malice, and right view, constitute good conduct. [Objection: In the absence of an intention to benefit or harm, how can right view and wrong view be wholesome and unwholesome? [Response: Because they are the roots thereof.
And as for these misdeeds and good deeds that have been mentioned, by way of summarizing those that are gross, ten paths of action are taught, both wholesome and unwholesome, as appropriate. (66bcd)

By way of summarizing those very same good and bad conducts (*sucarita-duścarita*) into their coarse forms, ten paths of action (*karmapatha*) are taught in the Sūtra, as appropriate: the wholesome ones from among the good conducts, and the unwholesome ones from among the bad conducts. What here is not included among the bad conducts? Or what is not included among the good conducts? First, regarding the unwholesome paths of action, a portion of bodily misconduct (*kāya-duścarita*) is not included—namely, that which constitutes the preliminary (*prayoga*) and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*), as well as other afflicted [actions] such as binding and so forth—because these are not excessively coarse.

For that bodily misconduct which deprives others of their life, wealth, or wives is called a path of action (*karmapatha*) for the purpose of distinguishing it from other forms of misconduct. Likewise, among verbal misconduct, only that which is harsh is called a path of action for that same reason. And as for mental misconduct, volition (*cetanā*) is its [path-of-action] portion.

Among wholesome actions, a portion of bodily good conduct consists of the preliminary and concluding stages, abstention from intoxicants and so forth, giving, making offerings, and the like; a portion of verbal good conduct consists of pleasant speech and the like; and a portion of mental good conduct is volition. And regarding these paths of action—

The six unwholesome [paths of action] are non-informative (*avijñapti*). (67a) (15) The six unwholesome paths of action—killing, taking what is not given, false speech, slander, harsh speech, and frivolous chatter—are necessarily of the nature of non-informative action. This is because when one causes another to perform them, there is no primary informative action (*maulavijñapti*) [on the part of the instigator]. (17) One [path of action] is of two kinds. (67b) (18)

Sexual misconduct is always of the nature of both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) action, because it is brought to completion by oneself alone; for one who causes another to perform it does not experience such pleasure. (20) Those [other paths] also [apply] when one performs them oneself. (67b') (21) Those six paths of action, when performed by oneself, are of two kinds—informative and non-informative—if death occurs at that very moment; however, if death occurs later, they are exclusively non-informative. (23)
Furthermore, regarding the wholesome paths of action:
(24) the seven wholesome [paths] are of two kinds.

(67c) (25) The seven material wholesome paths of action are necessarily of two types: informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*). This is because the morality of undertaking (*samādāna-śīla*) is dependent upon the informative act. [p.239]
Non-informative [action] arises from meditative concentration.

(67d) Those comprised within the dhyāna-restraint and the untainted (anāsrava) restraint are said to arise from meditative concentration; for they are exclusively non-informative, because they depend solely upon the mind. However, the preparatory stages (sāmantaka) are informative. (68a)
The preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the paths of action necessarily have informative manifestation (*vijñapti*) as their intrinsic nature;

however, non-informative manifestation (*avijñapti*) may or may not exist. If one undertakes the preliminary effort with intense obsession (*paryavasthāna*) or with a thick essence of faith (*prasāda*), there will be non-informative manifestation; otherwise, it will not exist.

The subsequent actions (*pṛṣṭha*) are the reverse of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*). (68c) The subsequent actions of the paths of action (*karmapatha*) should be understood as being the reverse of their respective preparatory stages. They necessarily have the nature of non-informative action (*avijñapti*). Informative action (*vijñapti*), however, may or may not exist. If, having performed the path of action, one subsequently engages in conduct conforming to it, for him there would be informative action; otherwise, there would not.

Now, from what point until what point is the establishment of these [stages]: the preliminary (*prayoga*), the fundamental (*maula*), and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*)? First, in this case, when someone desiring to kill an animal rises from his bed, takes money, goes [to the market], touches [the animal], buys the animal, brings it back, feeds it, makes it enter [the slaughterhouse], and takes up a weapon to strike it—giving one or two blows but as long as he has not yet deprived it of life—that duration is the preliminary.

However, regarding that blow by which one deprives [a being] of life: the informative action (*vijñapti*) at that moment, or the non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of that same moment, constitutes the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*). For one is touched by the fault of taking life through two causes: through the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) and, once death has occurred, through the fulfillment of the result (*phala-paripūri*). Thereafter, the non-informative actions characterized by their specific marks constitute the subsequent phase (*pṛṣṭha*).

(17) As long as one skins that animal, cleans it, sells it, cooks it, eats it, or speaks of it, (18) so long do even the moments of its manifest action (*vijñapti*) constitute the "consequent" (*pṛṣṭha*). This should be applied similarly to other cases according to what is appropriate. (19) For covetousness and the others, there is neither preliminary application nor a consequent; it becomes a path of action (*karmapatha*) merely by their manifestation. (20)

This must be addressed here: First of all, are the informative and non-informative [actions] belonging to that living being while it is still in the state of death (*maraṇabhava*) considered the path of action (*karmapatha*), or rather when it has died? What follows from this? If they were [the path of action] while it is in the state of death, then even a killer or an instigator who dies simultaneously with the victim would incur the fault of taking life (*prāṇātipāta*); yet this is not the established tenet (*siddhānta*).

Now, regarding what was said concerning death—that the informative act (*vijñapti*) or the non-informative act (*avijñapti*) of that very moment by which one deprives [a being] of life is the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*)—that should not be stated. Furthermore, as it is said in the Treatise (*śāstra*): "Could it be that a living being has been killed, yet the taking of life has not ceased?"

(4) It might be argued that just as when a living being has been deprived of life and the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) has not yet ceased, the term "preliminary effort" is used here to refer to the subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*); however, this contradicts the meaning of the Vaibhāṣikas, because at that time the fundamental [action] (*maula*) itself has not yet ceased. (6) Let it be so formulated in such a way that there is no fault. And how is there no fault? By maintaining that it is the fundamental action itself that is expressed here by the term "preliminary effort. (7) In that case, how can the informative act (*vijñapti*) at that time constitute the fundamental path of action (*karmapatha*)?

And how could it not exist? Because of its lack of efficacy. (8) How, then, does non-informative action (avijñapti) come to be? Therefore, at the time when the fruit of the preliminary effort (prayoga) is perfected, both of those would constitute a path of action (karmapatha). (9) Furthermore, one path of action can also serve as the preliminary effort or the subsequent consequence (pṛṣṭha) for another. For example, all ten paths of action may serve as the preliminary effort for the taking of life.

For example, one might prepare a ritual for the sake of killing an enemy, offering a sacrifice with an animal after making it belong to another, and commit adultery with his wife; one might cause a rift between him and his friends through falsehood, slander, harsh words, and even feigned conciliation—those very things that would otherwise serve as his protection; one might covet his property, harbor ill will toward him, and strengthen wrong views in order to bring about his death.

(13) In the same way, this should be applied accordingly to the other [paths of action] as well. However, covetousness and the others cannot be considered preliminary applications (*prayoga*), for one does not become engaged [in the act] by the mere arising of a thought, since no actual action has been commenced.

(14–15) It is stated in the Sūtra: "Monks, the taking of life is threefold: born of greed, born of hatred, and born of delusion; and so on up to wrong view. In that regard, it must be explained what kind of taking of life is born of greed, and so forth. (16–17) Not all paths of action reach their completion (*niṣṭhā*) through greed and the other [roots];
rather, (18) the preliminary application (*prayoga*) arises from the three roots. (68d) (19)

It is stated thus because of the scriptural teaching on "origination," which says that their preliminary application (*prayoga*) arises from the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*). Among these, killing born of greed (*lobha*) is, for example, when one deprives a living being of life for the sake of its body parts, for the sake of wealth, for the sake of sport, or to protect oneself and one's friends. Killing born of hatred (*dveṣa*) is, for example, for the sake of crushing an enemy. Killing born of delusion (*moha*) is, for example, as practiced by those who sacrifice, who kill with the notion that it is dharma, or by kings who kill based on the authority of dharma-reciters.

It is said that kings who exercise restraint over the wicked partake in merit. (23) And so it is among the Persians; for they say thus: "Parents who are aged or infirm should be killed. Others also say likewise: "Snakes, scorpions, centipedes, and the like, which cause harm and injury to humans, should be killed; and deer, cattle, birds, buffalo, and the like, because they are for the purpose of consumption. And there is the taking of life instigated by false views.

Taking what is not given born of greed is when someone who desires a particular object takes it, either for the sake of further gain, honor, or fame, or for the protection of himself or his friends. That born of hatred is that which is done for the purpose of crushing an enemy. That born of delusion is as in the case of kings, due to their respect for those who recite the Dharma; or for the purpose of suppressing the wicked, as the Brāhmaṇas say: "All this was given by Brahmā to the Brāhmaṇas; it is because of the weakness of the Brāhmaṇas that low-caste men enjoy it."

Therefore, when taking [what belongs to others], a Brahmin takes his own; a Brahmin eats his own, wears his own, and gives his own. Furthermore, they do not have the notion that these things belong to another. And as for sexual misconduct born of greed, which is instigated by false views regarding women and so forth—it is unchastity arising from passion for them, for the sake of gain and honor, or for the protection of oneself and one's friends. That which is born of hatred is for the purpose of inflicting injury upon an enemy.

(8) That born of delusion (*moha*) is, for example, the sexual approach to one’s mother and so forth among the Pārasīkas, and in the *gosava* sacrifice. As it is said: "A Brahmin, having performed the *gosava* sacrifice, observes the cow-vow for a year. He drinks water from the mouth of a cow; he chews grass, approaches his mother, approaches his sister, and approaches a woman of the same clan (*sagotrā*). And those who say: "Women are like mortars, fruits, cooked food, holy fords (*tīrtha*), and roads. False speech (*mṛṣāvāda*) and the others born of greed (*lobha*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) are as previously described.
False speech born of delusion is as it was said: "There is no untruth joined with jesting. (13)
"O King, they say that five kinds of untruths are not sinful: [speaking falsely] regarding women, at the time of marriage, when life is at stake, and when all one's wealth is being seized."

And there is false speech instigated by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). As for malicious speech and the others, when instigated by wrong view, they are born of delusion (*moha*). And as for the prattle of false treatises such as the Vedas, [they are also born of delusion].
How are covetousness and the others born of greed (*lobha*)?
Because they arise immediately after that [greed], covetousness and the others are born of the three roots. (69ab) (20)

Those arising immediately after greed are born of greed; those arising immediately after hatred are born of hatred; those arising immediately after delusion are born of delusion. The unwholesome paths of action have been explained. How are the wholesome ones? He says:
"The wholesome [paths of action], together with their preliminary and concluding phases, are born of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. (69cd)

The wholesome courses of action (*karmapatha*), together with their preliminary applications (*prayoga*) and subsequent consequences (*pṛṣṭha*), arise from non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, because they are originated by a wholesome mind, and because that mind is necessarily associated with non-greed and the other two roots. In this context, the abstention from the preliminary application of an unwholesome course of action is the preliminary application of a wholesome course of action; the abstention from the fundamental act (*maula*) is the fundamental act; and the abstention from the subsequent consequence is the subsequent consequence.

For example, when a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) is being ordained, he enters the separate dwelling, pays homage to the monks, requests a preceptor (*upādhyāya*), and so on, until the first and second formal proclamations (*karmavācanā*) are performed; this is the preliminary action (*prayoga*). At the third formal proclamation, the informative act (*vijñapti*) and the simultaneous non-informative act (*avijñapti*) constitute the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*). Thereafter, as long as the points of dependence (*niśraya*) are announced and one performs the informative act based upon them, and as long as the non-informative act continues, this is the subsequent action (*pṛṣṭha*).
As it was stated that not all courses of action reach their completion through greed and the other [roots], then by which root does each reach its completion?
(70ab) The completion of killing, malice, and harsh speech is through hatred.
(8) The conclusion of these—killing, malice, and harsh speech—is through hatred, because of the manifestation of a mind intent on abandonment and a harsh disposition. (9)
(10) From greed:
the completion of sexual misconduct, covetousness, and taking what is not given.
(11) By means of greed, there is the fulfillment of sexual misconduct, covetousness, and taking what is not given. (12)
But false view is brought to completion through delusion,
for it is when delusion has reached its highest degree that one brings it to its conclusion.
For the remaining [unwholesome roots], it is held that they are completed by all three.
What, then, are the remaining [paths]? They are false speech, slander, and frivolous chatter. The completion (*niṣṭhā*) of these occurs through all three—by greed, by hatred, or by delusion.

Regarding these paths of action which were explained in four sections—three, three, one, and three—their bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*) are, respectively: sentient beings, objects of enjoyment, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and name (*nāman*). (71cd)

Killing and so forth have sentient beings as their basis. Adultery and so forth have objects of enjoyment as their basis. False view has name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as its basis. False speech and so forth have the collection of names (*nāmakāya*) as their basis. (21–22) For one who dies simultaneously or prior [to the victim], there is no fundamental path of action. (72ab) (23) [The verse: "For one who dies simultaneously or prior... Therefore it is said: "There may be one who performs the application and brings the fruit to completion, yet is not touched by the fault of taking life. He asks: "How could this be? It would be as when the victim dies either before or simultaneously with the killer. What, then, is the reason for this? For there is no connection between the killer and the fault of taking life as long as the victim is alive, nor is there such a connection for a killer who has died at the same time [as the victim], because a different basis [of rebirth] has arisen.

The basis by which that preparatory act was performed has been severed, and an entirely different basis, belonging to a distinct *nikāyasabhāga*, has arisen. Since that [new basis] is not the agent, its connection with the path of action (*karmapatha*) is not logical.

Regarding cases such as military expeditions, hunting, or ambushes, where many people unite for the purpose of killing others and one person actually commits the taking of life—by whom is that [act] possessed?
In armies and the like, because they share a single purpose, all are endowed [with the result] just like the agent. (72cd)

For just as the actual perpetrator is, so too are all [the others] fully endowed [with the action], because they share a single purpose. For in effect, they act as mutual instigators of one another. As for one who is led by force, he too becomes fully endowed [with the action], except for one who has made such a resolution: "I will not kill a living being even for the sake of my life," and so on. Furthermore, to what extent does the path of action (*karmapatha*) arise for one who personally commits the taking of life? And to what extent do the paths of action continue up to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)? Their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) must be stated; therefore, they are now explained.

Taking life is the intentional killing of another without error. (73ab) If, with the perception "I shall kill this person," one kills another and kills that very person and no other through confusion, by this much there is taking life. What then of one who kills while in doubt—whether "is this a living being or not a living being? or "is it he or someone else?"—he too necessarily strikes there having gained this certainty: "Let it be whoever it may be. Thus, the intention of relinquishment has indeed been formed by him.

How does the taking of life occur among the momentary aggregates (*skandha*)? That which is called "life-force" (*prāṇa*) is the wind (*vāyu*) that proceeds dependent upon the body and mind. One causes it to fall away, just as one extinguishes a lamp or stops the ringing of a bell or the blowing of a flute. Or, "life-force" refers to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); one causes that to cease. If one creates an obstacle even for a single moment of life as it is arising, one is touched by the fault of taking life; it is not otherwise.

To whom does that life belong, such that in its absence one becomes dead? We shall examine the genitive case "to whom" in the discussion on the person (*pudgala*). However, it was said by the Blessed One:
"When these—vitality, warmth, and consciousness—abandon the body, then it lies cast away, like a senseless log. Thus it is said.

Therefore, it is said that a body with sense-faculties "lives," while one without sense-faculties is "dead. The Nirgranthas maintain that even from the unintentional killing of a living being, demerit accrues to the agent, just as burning results from contact with fire. For them, this same consequence would follow even in the case of looking at another's wife.

Furthermore, [there would be the fault of] plucking out the hair of a Nirgrantha, teaching arduous asceticism to the Teacher, and the death of the donor from cholera caused by that [teaching]; as well as the affliction and death of physicians due to their patients; and the mutual causation of suffering for the mother and the fetus in the womb; and even for the one to be executed, because of his connection with that action, just as fire burns its own substrate. Moreover, there would be no [moral] consequence for the one who causes another to act, because of the lack of such a connection, just as one who causes another to touch fire is not burned by it.

Furthermore, O Householder, it would follow that even insentient things such as wood would incur sin through the killing of living beings; or rather, a proof is not established by a mere example. Thus, the taking of life has been explained.
(73cd) Taking what is not given is the appropriation of another's property by means of force or theft. (73d)

The term "without error" (*abhrāntyā*) continues [to apply here]. If one appropriates another's property by force or by theft, then—provided there is no confusion regarding the object due to a lack of awareness—the act constitutes taking what is not given (*adattādāna*) to that very extent. For one who steals from a *stūpa*, it is taking what is not given from the Buddha; for everything therein was accepted by the Blessed One at the time of his final nirvāṇa. Others, however, hold that it belongs to those [monks] who are responsible for its protection.

For one who extracts a treasure-trove that has no owner, [the offense] is from the lord of the realm; for one who steals a loan, it is from those who have reached the boundary [of the community] if the formal act has been performed, and from all those in training under the Buddhas if it has not been performed. (12) Sexual misconduct, which is intercourse with those who should not be approached, is of four kinds. (74ab) (13)

Sexual misconduct consists of four types of approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyagamana*). One approaches one who should not be approached: either one who is under the protection of another, such as a mother, a daughter, or a female relative by birth on the mother’s or father’s side; or one approaches in a non-genital part, even one's own wife, namely the anus or the mouth; or one approaches in an improper place, such as in public, at a shrine (*caitya*), or in a monastery (*vihāra*); or one approaches at an improper time. What, then, is an improper time? It is when one approaches a woman who is pregnant, one who is nursing, or one who is observing a religious vow (*saniyamā*).

(17) Some say that if one acts with self-restraint by the permission of her husband, there is no offense. The term "without error" continues to apply here. If one were to approach another's wife while perceiving her as his own, it would not constitute a path of action (*karmapatha*). Some say that if one approaches a woman other than [one's own] while perceiving her to be another's wife, there would be an offense because of the application toward another's wife and because of the enjoyment of the object. Others say that because the application is directed elsewhere, there would be no offense, just as in the case of taking life (*prāṇātipāta*). From whom does sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*) arise for one who approaches a nun?

[The offense belongs] to the master of the object; for he must not tolerate it. Furthermore, [it is forbidden] toward one's own wives who are under restraint. However, for one who approaches a maiden, [the offense belongs] to him to whom she has been betrothed; if not, then to him who protects her, and finally to the king. Or, the speech of one who has a different perception [is] a false statement when addressed to one who understands the meaning. (74cd)

If one speaks with a certain intention regarding a particular matter, and the person to whom one speaks understands the meaning of that sentence, then that sentence is false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*). What would it be if the person does not understand? It would be frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). It is called "speech" (*vākya*). Since a sentence sometimes consists of many phonemes (*varṇa*), which among them constitutes the path of action (*karmapatha*)? It is the final one, together with the non-informative (*avijñapti*), at which point the person becomes aware of the meaning.

The preceding syllables constitute the preliminary application (*prayoga*). It is said that one is "one who understands the meaning. Does this refer to a listener for whom the meaning has already been understood, or to one who is capable of understanding? What follows from this? If it refers to one for whom the meaning has already been understood, then because the meaning of a sentence is an object of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and because it would contradict the auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) [if the act occurred simultaneously], only vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) would constitute the path of action (*karmapatha*). However, if it refers to one who is capable of understanding, then no such fault arises.
And how is it that one who is capable of cognizing is able to do so when the state has arisen and auditory consciousness has arisen? Let it be such that there is no fault.

Sixteen modes of legal discourse (*vyavahāra*) are taught in the Sūtra. [The first eight: claiming to have seen what was not seen; claiming to have heard, sensed, or cognized what was not heard, sensed, or cognized; and claiming not to have seen what was seen, up to claiming not to have cognized what was cognized—these are the eight non-noble (*anārya*) modes of discourse. [The latter eight: claiming to have seen what was seen, up to claiming to have cognized what was cognized; and claiming not to have seen what was not seen, up to claiming not to have cognized what was not cognized—these are the eight noble (*ārya*) modes of discourse. In this regard, what is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of these things that are seen, heard, sensed, and cognized?
That which is experienced by the eye, the ear, the mind, and by the [other] three [faculties], is respectively called seen, heard, cognized, and sensed. (75)

That which is experienced by visual consciousness is called "seen"; that which is [experienced] by auditory consciousness is "heard"; that which is [experienced] by mental consciousness is "cognized" (*vijñāta*); and that which is [experienced] by olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses is "sensed" (*mata*). What is the reason? Because odors, tastes, and tangibles are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they are like the dead; therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the term "sensed" applies to these. What is the proof for this? Both scripture (*sūtra*) and reasoning (*yukti*). First, the scripture:

"What do you think, Māhakīmātṛ? Regarding those forms which have not been seen by you with the eye, which were never seen before, which you do not see now, and for which you do not even have the thought, 'May I see them'—do you nevertheless have, on account of them, any desire, passion, affection, attachment, clinging, fixation, or resolve? "No, Venerable Sir."

"Those sounds which have not been heard by you with the ear, nor previously heard, in detail... up to: those mental objects (*dharma*) which have not been cognized by the mind, in detail... [to which Mahakimata replied: 'No, Venerable Sir. And regarding this, it was said to you, Mahakimata: 'In the seen, there shall be only the seen; in the heard, the minded, and the cognized, there shall be only the cognized. Therefore, because the terms 'seen,' 'heard,' and 'cognized' are applied to three objects, it is understood that the term 'minded' (*mata*) refers to odors and so forth."

Therefore, if this were not accepted, there would be no conventional usage regarding odors and so forth, because they would fall outside the categories of the visible and so on; this is the reasoning. As for the Sūtra, however, it does not serve as a proof, because its purpose is different. For in this Sūtra, the Blessed One was not teaching the definition of conventional usages. What then?

In this regard, concerning these six kinds of objects and the four types of conventional usage, there will be for you only the conventional usage of "seen" and so forth, and not the superimposition of signs such as "pleasant" or "unpleasant"—this is seen here to be the meaning of the Sūtra. But what, then, is the "seen," and what is [the "heard,"] up to the "cognized"? Some say: that which is directly perceived by the five sense-faculties is the "seen"; that which is received from another is the "heard"; that which is personally approved through reasoning and inference is the "thought."

That which is presided over by the nature of mental direct perception (*manas-pratyakṣa*) and is to be personally realized (*pratyātmavedya*) is called "cognized" (*vijñāta*). Furthermore, these five objects are conventionally designated as "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*), or alternatively as "heard" (*śruta*), "thought" (*mata*), or "cognized" (*vijñāta*). As for the sixth [object], it is other than what is "seen," and thus there is no consequence of the absence of conventional designation regarding odors and so forth. Therefore, this reasoning also is not a valid argument. The former masters have said this:

(7) That which is seen is what has been directly perceived by the eye; that which is heard is what has been learned from another through the ear; that which is thought is what has been reflected upon by oneself; (8) that which is cognized is what has been personally experienced and realized within, having arisen [in the mind]. (9)

Let us proceed with the treatise by way of a formal inquiry (*prasaṅga*). Could there be lying (*mṛṣāvāda*) for one who brings about a change [in another] by means of the body? It could be so. Therefore it is said: Could there be a case where one does not exert oneself through the body, yet is touched by the fault of taking life? It could be so. Could there be a case where one exerts oneself through speech, yet is touched by the fault of lying? It could be so. Could there be a case where one exerts oneself through the body, yet is touched by the fault of both? It could be so. Could there be a case where one does not exert oneself through the body nor through speech, yet is touched by the fault of both? It could be so.

It may be that the example of the *poṣadha* [confession] was given here because of the mental malice of the sages (13). If, in either case, one does not exert oneself, and there is no non-informative (*avijñapti*) action—specifically no final non-informative action belonging to the desire realm—how can the path of action (*karmapatha*) for those two be established? Effort must be made on this point. False speech has been explained.

(15) Slander (*paiśunya*) is the speech of one with a defiled mind intended to cause division among others. (76ab) (16) That speech of one with a defiled mind which is for the purpose of dividing others and causing dissension is slander. The terms "one who understands the meaning" and "without error" (17) carry over from the previous context. (18)

Harsh speech (*pāruṣya*) is unpleasant (76c) speech. The phrase "of one with a defiled mind" (*kliṣṭacittasya*) continues [from the previous definition]. Also, [it applies] "to one who understands the meaning" and "without error. That unpleasant speech directed at others by one with a defiled mind, which is understood by them and regarding that very thing about which one intends to speak—that is harsh speech. All defiled [speech] is frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). (76c') (22)

The term "speech" (*vākya*) is understood as the governing topic. All afflicted speech is frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*); that itself is the state of being a frivolous chatterer. For it is through association with that [afflicted speech] that one becomes a frivolous chatterer.
Others say: "Afflicted [speech] other than that.
(77a) According to others, frivolous chatter is any afflicted speech other than vocal karma such as lying and so forth. (3)

Like flattery, song, and drama; (4) and like false treatises (77bc). (5) For example, a monk of wrong livelihood engages in flattery; some who are impassioned sing; and others, actors, chatter in drama for the sake of pleasing others. (6) And those with such views also proclaim false treatises. Likewise, lamentation, socializing, and so forth—whatever other afflicted vocal action there is apart from lying and the rest—that is frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*). (7) How is it that during the time of a *cakravartin* there is song, yet no frivolous speech?

For at that time, songs associated with renunciation were sung, not those associated with vulgar pleasures. (9) Others maintain that even then, because expressions such as "marriage" and "wedding" existed, there was frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*), though it did not constitute a path of action (*karmapatha*). (10) However, coveting the property of others is [the path of action of] greed. (77c'd) (11)

"Alas, what belongs to others were mine!"—this improper, unjust longing for the property of others, the desire to appropriate it, whether by force or by some other means, is the path of action known as covetousness (*abhidhyā*). Others maintain that all craving belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is covetousness; for thus it is said in the Sūtra concerning sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) within the section on the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*): "Having abandoned covetousness for the world," and so forth.

Although all covetousness (*abhidhyā*) exists, not all of it constitutes a path of action (*karmapatha*), because [only that which is] coarse is included among the misdeeds (*duścarita*); so say others. This is so that the covetousness of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and the inhabitants of Uttarakuru does not become a path of action.
Malice (*vyāpāda*) is hatred toward sentient beings;
hatred toward sentient beings is malice, which functions in the form of harming others.

The view of non-existence regarding what is wholesome and unwholesome is false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). (78bc) That view which holds that there is no wholesome or unwholesome action is false view. For example: "There is no giving, there is no sacrifice, there is no offering, there is no good conduct, there is no bad conduct," and so forth, up to "there are no Arhats in the world. This constitutes false view in its entirety as the denial of action, fruit, and the noble ones (*ārya*); however, only the beginning has been shown in the verse. [p.248]
These ten paths of action have such characteristics. What is the meaning of "paths of action" (*karmapatha*)? For here, three are paths and seven are both actions and paths. (2) 78c-d (3)

For the three beginning with covetousness (*abhidhyā*) are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*) because they are the paths of action; the volition (*cetanā*) associated with them is carried along by their movement and proceeds by their way, because it performs its formative activity (*abhisaṃskaraṇa*) under their influence. However, the seven beginning with the taking of life (*prāṇātipāta*) are both actions—since they consist of bodily and vocal action—and paths of action, because the volition that originates them proceeds by taking them as its basis.

They are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*) because they are both actions (*karman*) and paths of action; for the grammatical rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one of several identical or similar items) applies even to dissimilar forms. In this way, non-covetousness and the others, as well as abstention from taking life and the others, are to be understood. The preliminary and subsequent actions are not themselves paths of action, because their engagement occurs for the sake of [the primary action] and is rooted in it. Furthermore, as was stated previously, they are included according to what is most prominent.

Furthermore, it is through the increase or decrease of these internal and external entities that the increase or decrease of things occurs in the world. (10) As for those Dārṣṭāntikas who maintain that covetousness and so forth are themselves mental action (*manaskarma*), how can these be "paths of action" (*karmapatha*)? They alone should be questioned on this point. However, it can be said that they are "paths of action" because they are both actions and paths to good and bad destinies. Or else, they are so called because they mutually induce one another.
All these ten unwholesome paths of action are contrary to the manifestation of wholesome dharmas. However, the cutting off of the roots occurs through false view;

specifically, the cutting off of the wholesome roots occurs through a false view that is both excessive and complete. As for what is stated in the treatise: "Which are the excessive unwholesome roots? Those unwholesome roots by which one cuts off the wholesome roots, and which one first eliminates when attaining detachment from the desire realm."

Because wrong view is brought about by the unwholesome roots, this designation of "them" [the roots] is applied to those very views; just as when fire itself burns a village, but because thieves are its instigators, it is said that "the village was burned by thieves.
Of which wholesome roots does the severance occur? It is of those acquired at birth pertaining to the realm of desire.

The wholesome roots belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are severed, because one is no longer possessed of those belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyāvacara*). How, then, is the *Prajñaptibhāṣya* to be interpreted when it says: "By this much, the wholesome roots of this person belonging to the three realms have been severed"? This was said with the intention of referring to the distancing of their acquisition (*prāpti*), because the continuum (*saṃtati*) has been rendered unfit to be a vessel for them. Furthermore, only those [wholesome roots] acquired at birth (*upapattipratilābhika*) are severed, because one has already fallen away from those acquired through application (*prāyogika*) prior to that.
By what kind of object does false view, which denies both cause and fruit, sever [the roots of merit]?
