That which denies the cause, saying "there is no good conduct, there is no bad conduct," and that which denies the fruit, saying "there is no fruition of the results of good and bad deeds"—others maintain that these two correspond respectively to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). [This view] holds that [the false view] has only contaminated (*sāsrava*) objects and not uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects; it has only objects belonging to its own realm (*sabhāga-dhātu*) and not objects belonging to a different realm (*visabhāga-dhātu*). Some say this is because it is weak, as it persists only through association (*saṃprayoga*). However, they explain it thus: [it functions] in every way. (79d) (11)

The nine types of wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) are also severed all at once; some say this is like [the severing of] those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). However, they explain it thus: (11) gradually, (79d') (12) the nine types of wholesome roots are severed by the nine types of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). It is like the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*): (13) up to the point where the extremely intense-very-intense [wrong view] severs the very mild-mild [wholesome roots]. In this way, this textual passage is preserved. What are the "subtle" (*aṇusahagata*) wholesome roots? He says:

By which unwholesome roots the wholesome roots have been severed—(15) he abandons them last of all; when these are scattered, one comes to be designated as "one whose wholesome roots are severed. What, then, is the principle of this passage? Which are the excessive and superlative unwholesome roots? [It refers to] those unwholesome roots by which one severs the wholesome roots. This was stated with reference to their completion [of the severing process], because they are severed without remainder by them.

For even a single type among them, if not severed, would serve as the cause for the re-arising of all of them. Some say that one severs them by means of an "emergence" (*abhyutthāna*), just as in the case of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). However, others describe it as being in both ways: some say that one first abandons the restraint (*saṃvara*) and afterwards severs the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); however, others describe it thus: "The abandonment of that [restraint] occurs through the abandonment of the mind of which that restraint is the fruit.
Where are the roots of goodness severed? Among humans. (79d)

[It occurs] only among humans, not in the miserable realms (*apāya*), because the wisdom (*prajñā*)—whether afflicted or non-afflicted—is not firm there. It does not occur among the gods, because the fruit of karma is directly perceived by them. It occurs in three continents, but not in Uttarakuru, because of the absence of an evil intention (*apāpāśaya*). Others say it occurs only in Jambūdvīpa; however, for them, this textual passage is contradicted: "A person of Jambūdvīpa is endowed with at least eight faculties; likewise one from Pūrvavideha and one from Godānīya. Furthermore, it is a woman or a man who cuts [the roots].

Both a woman and a man cut off [the roots of goodness], because they possess dull desire, energy, and wisdom. Others say it is not a woman who cuts them off; for if that were so, this textual passage would be contradicted: "Whoever is endowed with the female faculty is necessarily endowed with eight faculties. Even among those [who cut off the roots], one whose conduct is driven by craving does not cut them off, because their disposition is fickle. Who then does? One whose conduct is driven by views, because their sinful disposition is firm and hidden. For this very reason, eunuchs and the like do not cut them off, because they belong to the class of those driven by craving, and because they are like those in the miserable states of existence.
What is the intrinsic nature of the severance of the roots of merit?

It is non-possession (*asamanvaya*). For when the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the roots of merit no longer arises and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*) arises, then, upon the arising of that non-possession, the roots of merit are said to be severed.

How is there a reconnection (*pratisaṃdhi*) for those [roots of goodness] that have been severed? (13) Reconnection occurs through doubt and the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*). (14) When either doubt regarding cause and effect arises in him, or the view of existence—that is, right view—arises, then (15) because the attainment (*prāpti*) of those [roots] arises once more, they are said to be "reconnected" roots of goodness. (16) There is a simultaneous reconnection of the nine types [of roots], but their manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*) is gradual, like the recovery of health and the gaining of strength. That, then, is their reconnection. (17)
"Not one who has committed an immediate transgression" (80d).

It would apply to another here, but not to one who has committed an immediate transgression. With reference to such a person, it was said: "This individual is incapable of reconnecting the roots of merit in this very life; he will certainly reconnect the roots of merit either while falling away from the hells or while being reborn [there]."

One who cuts it off while being reborn, while staying in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), or while passing away—that is, facing death—does so by the power of causes (*hetu*). Among these, he who cuts it off [by the power of causes] reconnects it while passing away; he who does so by the power of conditions (*pratyaya*) reconnects it while being reborn. Likewise, it is said that one who does so by his own power or by the power of another [reconnects it in those respective states]. Furthermore, he who cuts it off through a failure of intention (*āśaya*) reconnects it in this very life (*dṛṣṭadharma*); he who does so through a failure of both intention and application (*prayoga*) reconnects it after the breaking up of the body.

Thus, regarding one who has failed in view (*dṛṣṭivipanna*) and one who has failed in both view and conduct (*dṛṣṭi-śīlavipanna*): there may be one whose roots of merit are severed (*samucchinnakuśalamūla*) but who is not fixed in falsehood (*mithyātvaniyata*). There are four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*). The first alternative consists of Pūraṇa and others. The second is Ajātaśatru. The third is Devadatta. The fourth consists of those excluding these aforementioned cases. The maturation (*vipāka*) of the false view that severs the roots of merit occurs in the Avīci hell. However, for those who commit the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), it occurs either there or in another hell.
This discussion continues within the context of the paths of action (*karmapatha*). In this regard, it must be stated with how many paths of action volition (*cetanā*) arises simultaneously.
It arises simultaneously with as many as eight unwholesome [paths of action].
Volition... (81abc).

First, it occurs together with one [path of action]: when covetousness (*abhidhyā*) and so forth become manifest in the absence of another, or when one with an unafflicted mind completes any one of the material paths of action through its preliminary application (*prayoga*). It occurs together with two: when one with a malevolent mind (*vyāpannacitta*) kills a living being, or when one possessed by covetousness commits taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, or frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*), all simultaneously. It occurs together with three: when one with a malevolent mind simultaneously kills and steals the property of another living being belonging to someone else.

In that case, the completion of taking what is not given is not accomplished through greed alone. That rule should be understood to apply when it is brought to conclusion by one whose mind is directed toward nothing else. Furthermore, for one possessed by covetousness and so forth, if the two material [karmapathas] reach completion through its application, they occur with exactly three [mental factors]. It occurs with four [factors] in the case of false speech or harsh speech uttered with the intention to cause division; for in those cases, there is one mental factor and three vocal ones. Or, it occurs for one who has entered into covetousness and so forth.

(16) When, through the performance of that [unwholesome path], one reaches the completion of another of the three forms [of unwholesome action], it should be applied in this way with five, six, or seven [paths]. It occurs together with eight [paths] when, having performed the preliminary effort for six [paths], one personally commits sexual misconduct and they reach completion simultaneously. Thus far regarding the unwholesome [paths].

(19) Regarding the wholesome [paths], up to ten—having established the general rule that volition proceeds together with up to ten wholesome paths of action—he now states the exception: (21) [The exception is as follows:]...

Not with one, eight, or five. (81d’) It does not coexist with one, eight, or five courses of action (*karmapatha*). Among these, it coexists with two in the case of the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) and in the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) during the attainment of the formless realm (*ārūpyasamāpatti*). It coexists with three in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) associated with right view. It coexists with four when one undertakes the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) while possessing an unwholesome or neutral mind. It coexists with six when one undertakes those same vows while in the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses.

With seven [mental factors] in a wholesome mental consciousness when undertaking those very [precepts]; (4) and for one with an unwholesome or neutral mind when undertaking the *bhikṣu* restraint. With nine [mental factors] in the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses; (5) and in the mental consciousness associated with the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*) when undertaking those very [precepts], as well as when that same [consciousness] is included within meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). With ten [mental factors] in a wholesome mental consciousness other than those, specifically when undertaking the *bhikṣu* restraint.

And all volition (cetanā) concomitant with the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara), with the exception of the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) and the knowledge of the meditative absorptions, [is associated with all ten paths of action]. However, with regard to that which is free from restraint (saṃvara-nirmukta), it may be associated even with a single [path of action], when one who possesses a different state of mind undertakes the abstention from one limb. It may also be associated with five or eight [paths of action] simultaneously in a wholesome mental consciousness (manovijñāna) when there is the simultaneous undertaking of two or five limbs. In which realm (gati) are how many unwholesome or wholesome paths of action present, either by way of manifestation (saṃmukhībhāva) or by way of possession (samanvāgama)? In the hells, frivolous speech (saṃbhinnapralāpa), harsh speech (pāruṣya), and malice (vyāpāda) exist in two ways. (82ab)

Thus, these three paths of action exist in hell in two ways: by way of manifestation (*saṃmukhībhāva*) and by way of possession (*samanvāgama*). (13) Because of lamenting, there is idle chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*); because of mutual torment, there is harsh speech (*pāruṣya*); and because of a harsh continuum due to mutual hatred, there is malice (*vyāpāda*). (14) Covetousness and wrong view exist by way of possession. (82cd) (15)

[These do not exist] by way of manifestation, because of the absence of objects that provoke passion and because the fruit of karma is directly perceived. There is no killing because death occurs through the exhaustion of karma. (16) There is no taking what is not given and no sexual misconduct because there is no possession of material goods or women; there is no lying because there is no motive for it. For this same reason, there is no divisive speech, and because [the beings there] are constant, there is no harsh speech. (17–18) In Uttarakuru, there are three. (82d) (19)

The term "by way of possession" (*samanvāgamata*) continues [to apply here]. Covetousness, ill-will, and wrong view do not exist by way of manifest presence (*saṃmukhībhāvataḥ*), because of the absence of the sense of "mine" and of grasping, because the mental continuum is supple, because there is an absence of objects that provoke resentment, and because of the absence of an evil disposition.
The seventh [unwholesome path of action] exists here even by way of its own [manifest presence].

In this realm, frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*) exists even by way of its manifestation; for they, possessing afflicted minds, sometimes sing. However, because they lack evil intentions, there is no killing or other such acts. This is due to their having a fixed lifespan, the absence of possession of property or women, and the absence of any motive [for such acts]. (2) How, then, do they engage in unchaste conduct (*abrahmacarya*)? Indeed, when they desire to dally with a certain woman, they take her by the arm and approach the foot of a tree. (3)
If she is a permissible partner (*gamyā*), the tree covers her and they go to her; if she is not a permissible partner (*agamyā*), it does not cover her and they do not go to her.
Regarding sensual desire, elsewhere there are the ten unwholesome [actions]. (83b) (6)

The phrase "also by oneself" carries over. Apart from the hells and Uttarakuru, in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the ten unwholesome paths of action (*akuśalakarmapatha*) exist even as manifest activities (*saṃmukhībhava*). Among animals, hungry ghosts, and gods, they exist excluding those comprised within non-restraint (*asaṃvara*); among humans, they also include those comprised within non-restraint. Although a god does not kill another god, he may kill one residing in another realm of existence. Others say that even gods die from having their heads or midsections severed. The unwholesome [paths] have been explained. But the three wholesome [paths] exist everywhere, both by way of manifest activity and by way of acquisition. (83cd)
In all five destinies and throughout the three realms, non-covetousness, non-malice, and right view exist both by way of manifestation and by way of possession.
In the formless realm and among the non-percipient beings, seven [wholesome factors] exist by way of possession alone. (84ab)

The seven wholesome [paths of action] pertaining to body and speech exist in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) and among the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) solely by way of possession (*samanvāgama*). This is because noble ones (*ārya*) born in the formless realms possess past and future untainted restraint (*anāsravasaṃvara*), and because non-percipient beings possess dhyāna restraint (*dhyānasaṃvara*). Furthermore, whatever level of basis (*bhūmi*) a path was relied upon when untainted morality (*anāsrava-śīla*) was produced and subsequently ceased, one possesses that [morality] in the formless realms as something past; however, one possesses it as something future based on all five levels. As for the remainder:

And also by way of manifestation, excluding the hells and [the inhabitants of] Uttarakuru. (84bcd) "Remaining" means that which has been left over. Whatever other realm or destiny remains, there these seven wholesome paths of action exist even by way of manifestation, with the exception of the hells and Uttarakuru. Furthermore, among animals and hungry ghosts, they are free from restraint; however, in the form realm, they are comprised within restraint; elsewhere, they exist in both ways. These are the ten unwholesome and wholesome paths of action.
All are considered to yield the fruit of dominance (*adhipatiphala*), the flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), and the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*).

(85ab) First, by practicing, cultivating, and frequently repeating all unwholesome actions, one is reborn in the hells; this is their ripening fruit. If, however, one comes to such a state as a human being, sharing the commonality of humanity: through killing, one becomes short-lived; through taking what is not given, one suffers the loss of wealth; through sexual misconduct, one’s wife is shared with rivals; through false speech, one is frequently slandered; and through malicious speech, one suffers the alienation of friends.

Through harsh speech, one hears unpleasant sounds; through frivolous chatter, one’s words are not taken seriously; through covetousness, there is intense passion; through malice, intense hatred; and through wrong view, intense delusion—this is because of the abundance of delusion. This is their outflow-result (*niṣyanda-phala*). [Objection: A short lifespan among humans is the result of wholesome karma. How, then, can it be the outflow-result of taking life? [Response: It is not said that that very lifespan is its fruit; rather, it is said that by means of it, one becomes short-lived.

Therefore, it should be understood that the taking of life is a cause of obstruction for that lifespan; through the excessive cultivation of the taking of life, external things become diminished in vitality.

Through taking what is not given, [the lands] abound in thunderbolts and dust; through sexual misconduct, they are strewn with dust; (9) through false speech, they have foul odors; through slander, they are uneven with highs and lows; through harsh speech, they are saline, arid, and desolate—wicked lands that are loathed; (10) through frivolous chatter, the seasons change irregularly; through covetousness, the fruits are withered; through malice, the fruits are bitter; through wrong view, the fruits are meager or non-existent. This is their dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).

Is it by that very same karma that one becomes short-lived here in this life, or by another? Some say: "By that very same. [They argue: "That was the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*); this is the outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*). Regarding this, some say: "It is by the preliminary application (*prayoga*) here, not by the fundamental act (*maula*). Others, however, say: "Because the term 'with its retinue' (*saparivāra*) is included, it is stated as being due to the taking of life (*prāṇātipāta*). Furthermore, although this has been called an outflowing fruit, it does not transcend these two: the ripening fruit and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*). It is simply stated in that way because there is no distinction in its nature.

Furthermore, what is the reason that these three kinds of fruit are produced from these paths of action? First, when one commits the taking of life, suffering is produced for the victim being killed, they are slain, and their vitality (*ojas*) is destroyed;
therefore, because of causing suffering, killing, and destroying vitality, there is a threefold fruit. (85cd)

By causing suffering to another, one becomes miserable in hell as the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*). By killing, one becomes short-lived as the flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*). By destroying vitality, external medicinal herbs become weak in potency as the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). This should be applied similarly to other [unwholesome] actions as well. Likewise, the three fruits of the wholesome paths of action should be understood. Through the practice, cultivation, and frequent exercise of abstaining from taking life, one is reborn among the gods.
If one returns to such a state within the common lot of human beings, one becomes long-lived; in this way, everything should be applied by way of the opposite of unwholesome [results].

(23) Regarding that which was spoken of by the Blessed One as wrong speech (*mithyāvāc*), wrong action (*mithyākarmānta*), and wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*): what is this wrong livelihood other than those two? (24) This is not something else.
Rather, bodily and vocal action born of greed is itself wrong livelihood. (86ab) (2)
But the two ends of bodily and vocal action arise from hatred and delusion; and this [third category] is distinguished from those two because it is difficult to purify.

For greed is a pervasive nature; because of the karma arising from it, the mind is not easily purified. Therefore, for the purpose of generating reverence, livelihood is taught separately there [among the five hindrances] with the words, "livelihood is difficult to purify. And it is said here:
"The view of householders is difficult to purify, as they constantly hold various views; But the livelihood of a monk is likewise difficult to purify, as his view is dependent upon others. (9)

If one considers that bodily and vocal action arising solely from greed for the requisites of life constitutes wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) and nothing else— [arguing] that dancing, singing, and so forth, when performed for the sake of one's own pleasure, do not constitute a factor of livelihood— that is not [correct] according to the Sūtra. (86c’d) (10) (11–12) (13)

For in the *Śīlaskandhika*, the Blessed One has classified even such things as watching elephant fights under wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). What is the reason? Because they involve the enjoyment of improper objects. This point is settled. Regarding the five fruits previously mentioned, which action among them is abandoned by how many fruits?
On the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), when it is with outflows (*sāsrava*), action possesses fruit through all five. (87ab)

The path for the sake of abandonment, or that by which the afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned, is the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), namely the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*). Whatever contaminated (*sāsrava*) action exists therein is fruitful by way of five fruits. For its fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is the desirable maturation within its own level (*svabhūmi*). Its fruit of outflow (*niḥṣyandaphala*) consists of subsequent similar states born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Its fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*) is dissociation itself, which is that very abandonment.

The fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) consists of those factors drawn forth by that [action], namely: the path of resolute conviction (*adhimuktimārga*) and its co-arising factors; and that which is cultivated in the future, as well as abandonment (*prahāṇa*). The sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) other than its own nature, excluding those previously arisen.
(22) Regarding the four [fruits] in the stainless (*amala*):
whatever action exists in the untainted (*anāsrava*) path of abandonment, it possesses four fruits, excluding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*). (24)
Furthermore: "Whatever is with-outflow (sāsrava), whether wholesome or unwholesome" (87cd).

Whatever other wholesome karma with-outflow exists apart from the path of abandonment, as well as that which is unwholesome—that too has four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation (visaṃyogaphala). Furthermore, the remainder that is without-outflow (anāsrava), and that which is indeterminate (avyākṛta), have three fruits. (88ab)

Other than the path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*), untainted (*anāsrava*) action and determinate (*vyākṛta*) action [produce results] excluding three fruits—namely, the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visaṃyogaphala*).
(5) Four, two, and likewise three; these are the results for wholesome [action] of the wholesome and so forth.

(6ab) He will explain the sequence later. For wholesome action, wholesome factors are its four fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation. Unwholesome factors are two: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Neutral (*avyākṛta*) factors are three, excluding the fruit of outflow (*niḥṣyandaphala*) and the fruit of disconnection. (8)
For the unwholesome, there are two, three, and four [fruits] starting from the wholesome, respectively.

(89ab) This means "in due order. For unwholesome (*akuśala*) karma, wholesome (*kuśala*) dharmas are its two fruits: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*). For [unwholesome karma], the neutral (*avyākṛta*) views of identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and grasping at extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) are the outflow fruit (*niḥṣyanda-phala*) of the unwholesome universal (*sarvatraga*) dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*). For the neutral, these [wholesome and so forth] are two, three, and three [fruits]. (89cd)

For neutral (*avyākṛta*) karma, wholesome (*kuśala*) dharmas are two fruits: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*). Unwholesome (*akuśala*) dharmas are three [fruits], excluding the fruit of ripening (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visaṃyoga-phala*). This is because unwholesome dharmas, which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) and so forth, are the outflow fruit (*niḥṣyanda-phala*) of the two neutral views. Neutral dharmas are these same three [fruits]. All [dharmas] are four fruits of past [karma]. "All" refers to those belonging to the three time periods. For past karma, dharmas belonging to the three time periods are four fruits, excluding the fruit of disconnection.
For a middle [present] action as well, future dharmas are these same four fruits.
For a present action as well, future dharmas are these same four fruits;
those that are middling [present] are two.
Present dharmas are two fruits of a present [cause]: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
(23) For that which is unborn, there are three fruits when it is future.
[Verse 90c’d] Future [dharmas] are three fruits of a future [cause], excluding the outflow fruit (*niḥṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-phala*). (2)

Dharmas of the same level [as the action] are four fruits of an action belonging to its own level, excluding the fruit of disconnection (*visaṃyogaphala*). Dharmas of another level are three or two fruits.

If the dharmas belonging to other stages (*anyabhūmika*) are untainted (*anāsrava*), they constitute three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of disjunction (*visaṃyogaphala*), because they do not fall within the realms (*dhātu*). If they are tainted (*sāsrava*), they constitute two fruits: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Regarding the learner’s (*śaikṣa*) [karma], there are three [fruits] for learner and other dharmas: for the karma of a learner, learner dharmas constitute three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation and the fruit of disjunction; non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) dharmas are likewise; and dharmas that are neither learner nor non-learner (*naivaśaikṣānāśaikṣa*) also [constitute three fruits], excluding the fruit of maturation and the fruit of outflow (*niḥṣyandaphala*).
But for the action of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):

The factors belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) and so forth are one fruit, three fruits, and two fruits [respectively]. (92ab) For the action of one beyond training, the factors of those in training are one fruit: the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*). The factors of those beyond training are three fruits, excluding the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of disconnection (*visamyogaphala*). The factors that are neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training are two fruits: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the dominant fruit. (14)
For an action other than those two—namely, that which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣānāśaikṣa)—there are two, two, and five fruits for the learner (śaikṣa) and so forth.

(92cd) For an action other than the learner and non-learner—that is, for an action that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner—the learner dharmas are its two fruits: the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) and the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala). Non-learner dharmas are likewise [two fruits]. Neither-learner-nor-non-learner dharmas are its five fruits. (92d–93a) Three, four, and one are the fruits of an action to be abandoned by seeing (dṛgheya), for those [dharmas] beginning with it [the learner]. (93ab)

For karma to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), dharmas to be abandoned by seeing are its three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*). Dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) are its four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation. Dharmas not to be abandoned (*apraheya*) are its one fruit, the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). [The verse states:
"Two, four, and then three are the fruits of karma to be abandoned by cultivation. (93cd)

For karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), dharmas to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) are two fruits: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation are four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*). Non-abandonable (*apraheya*) dharmas are three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the outflow fruit (*niḥṣyandaphala*). For karma that is not to be abandoned, those [dharmas] are respectively one, two, and four fruits. (94ab)

For action that is not to be abandoned (*apraheya*), dharmas to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) constitute one fruit: the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) constitute two fruits: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the sovereign fruit. Dharmas not to be abandoned (*apraheya*) constitute four fruits, with the exception of the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*). Furthermore, the mention of the sequence is for the purpose of indicating that what applies to the beginning and the end also applies to the middle; for this is the rule of ellipsis (*peyāladharma*). In connection with the exposition of action, this is also asked: In the treatises, action is said to be "unrighteously performed" (*ayogavihita*), "righteously performed" (*yogavihita*), "neither righteously nor unrighteously performed," and "neither unrighteously nor righteously performed. What is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of each?

Some say that [action] performed improperly (*ayogavihita*) is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), as is that which deviates from the rule (*vidhibhraṣṭa*). (94cd) According to some, afflicted action is "performed improperly" because it arises from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*). Others say it is also that which deviates from the rule. For example, regarding how one should walk, stand, eat, move about, and so forth—if one performs these in a manner other than prescribed, that is "performed improperly" because of an incorrect performance. Others maintain that wholesome action is "performed properly" (*yogavihita*) and does not deviate from the rule. That which is different from both is neither [of the two].

Neither performed through yoga nor performed without yoga. (10) Does a single action project only a single birth, or does it not even project one? Likewise, does even a single action project a single birth, or many? This is the established doctrine: (12) a single [action] projects a single birth. (95a) (13)

A single action projects only a single birth, not multiple births; this is what is meant by the term *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous group). For when that [group] is obtained, one is said to be "born. As for what was said by the Elder Aniruddha: "As the ripening of that single alms-offering, I was born seven times among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, and finally have now been born here in the foremost Śākya clan"—this is because, having attained such prosperity and being possessed of the memory of his former births (*jātismara*), he performed yet further meritorious deeds.

Then he demonstrated his rising from [the state of] rebirth. Just as a man who has risen from a single *dīnāra* might point to a thousand and say, "By means of that one *dīnāra*, I have attained this sovereignty. Others, however, say: "Taking that alms-food as the basis, a great stream of volitions for giving arose; by some [volition], some fruit was grasped."

Even by many [actions], only one [rebirth] is projected, lest there be a projection of the *nikāyasabhāga* (homogeneous class of beings) in fragments. However, it is held that by a single action, the defiled *nikāyasabhāga* is projected;
multiple actions serve to complete it.

Just as a painter, having sketched a form with a single brush-stroke, completes it with many others, so too, while human birth is equal, one person possesses complete sense-faculties, limbs, and minor parts, shining with the excellence of complexion, shape, stature, and strength, whereas another is deficient in some of these. Furthermore, it is not karma alone that projects birth; what then? Other [factors] that possess ripening also do so. However, in no way do the two mindless attainments (*acittakasamāpatti*) project [birth], nor do the acquisitions (*prāpti*). (95cd)

Even by the two mindless attainments (*acittasamāpatti*), which possess maturation (*savipāka*), the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) is not projected, because they do not coexist with karma. Nor [is it projected] by acquisitions (*prāpti*), because karma has multiple fruits.

The Blessed One has spoken of three obstructions (*āvaraṇa*): the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and the obstruction of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*). What is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
The immediate (*ānantarya*) karmas, intense afflictions, and the miserable destinies (*durgati*).

The Kauravas and the non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñisattva*)—this is considered the threefold obscuration. (8) The five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) constitute the obscuration of karma; namely: killing one’s mother, killing one’s father, killing an Arhat, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, and with a malicious mind, drawing blood from the body of a Tathāgata. (9) Intense affliction (*tīvrakleśatā*) is the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). For affliction is of two kinds: that which is intense (*tīvra*), meaning habitual (*abhīkṣṇika*), and that which is sharp (*tīkṣṇa*), meaning excessive (*adhimātra*). Among these, that which is intense is an obscuration, as in the case of eunuchs (*ṣaṇḍha*) and others. (10–11)

For even a defilement (*kleśa*) that possesses an intense impulse can be destroyed if it is occasional; however, a continuous one cannot be destroyed even if it is weak. When a defilement is continuous, one finds no opportunity for exertion to eradicate it. Depending upon a weak [defilement], a medium one arises; depending upon a medium one, an intense one arises. Therefore, the threefold obstruction consists of the obstructions to the miserable destinies (*durgati*), the obstruction to maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*), and a portion of the obstruction to birth: namely, the inhabitants of Uttarakuru and the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*).

Of what are these obstructions? [They are obstructions] to the Noble Path and to the roots of virtue conducive to the Noble Path. Furthermore, other karmas fixed for the miserable destinies (*apāya*) and so forth, as well as those fixed for birth from an egg, birth from moisture, birth as a woman, and birth as an eighth existence, should also be mentioned.

However, only those [obstructions] which are easily discernible and clearly understood through five causes—namely, by way of their basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), their fruit (*phala*), their destiny (*gati*), their rebirth (*upapatti*), and the person (*pudgala*)—are mentioned, and no others. Furthermore, among these, the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is the most inferior; after that is the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). For the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that one becomes incurable even in a second birth because of the successive bringing forth of these two.

What is the meaning of *ānantarya*? They are called *ānantarya* because they cannot be obstructed (*nāntarāyituṃ śakyāni*) by another karma that has its fruit in a subsequent birth with respect to their own maturation; that is to say, they cannot be set aside. Alternatively, for the person who commits them, there is no interval (*anantara*) after death before proceeding to rebirth in hell; thus he is "one for whom there is no interval" (*anantara*). The state of being such is *ānantarya*. It is that quality through the connection with which one becomes "without interval," just as in the case of the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*).
Now, among these obscurations, which one is to be understood as belonging to which destiny? To begin with, the immediate [karmas] (*ānantarya*) exist exclusively in the three continents;
they do not exist in Uttarakuru, nor in other destinies, much less in another realm (*dhātu*). Even within those [three continents], they belong only to women and men.
But it is not accepted for eunuchs and the like.
What is the reason? That very reason which was indicated for the absence of non-restraint [is applicable here]. Furthermore, it is because they provide little benefit and lack a sense of shame.

Respectively, [this applies] to their mother and father, and to those [beings]. It is said that for these [beings], their mother and father provide little assistance, because they are the dominant cause of an incomplete personal existence (*vikalātma-bhāva*) and because of the smallness of their affection. Furthermore, even for them, no intense sense of shame (*apatrāpya*) is present toward their mother and father, such that by violating it they would be touched by an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*). For this very reason, it is not accepted [that the offense occurs] even in the case of the three types of hungry ghosts (*preta*). The Venerable [Bhadanta] says that it could occur for those with sharp intellects, like a well-bred horse (*aśvājāneya*).
Even for a human being, there would be no immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) for killing non-human parents. (10) The obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) has been explained.
(11) As for the remainder, it exists within all five destinies (*gati*). 97d (12)

What, then, are the remaining two? They are the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscuration of maturation (*vipākāvaraṇa*). Among humans, the obscuration of maturation consists of the inhabitants of the *kaurava* [continent]; among gods, it consists of the non-percipient beings (*asaṃjñisattva*). What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*)? Four are bodily actions; one is vocal action. Three are the taking of life; one is false speech; one is the preparation for the taking of life. For Tathāgatas are by nature incapable of being harmed. Because the fruit is metaphorically designated upon the cause, the schism of the Saṅgha (*saṃghabheda*) is called an immediate transgression. Or rather, it is so called because "by this, [the community] is split. However, the schism of the Saṅgha has the nature of a lack of concord (*asāmagrī*); it is a factor dissociated from thought (*viprayukta*).

(98abc) A dharma that is non-afflicted and neutral (akliṣṭāvyākṛta) is called "schism" (*saṃghabheda*). It is a formation dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) that is unobstructed-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Will that [schism] constitute an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*)? (19) Not at all; the schismatic is not endowed with it. What then?
(20) The Saṃgha is endowed with it. (98d)

The schismatic is possessed of the fault of causing a schism in the Saṃgha. That, moreover, is false speech. Furthermore, it consists of the vocal intimation and non-intimation that arise simultaneously with the schism in the Saṃgha. And the schismatic, being possessed of that fault, is cooked in the Avīci hell for an eon (*kalpa*). He is fully ripened in the great hell of Avīci for an intermediate eon (*anantarakalpa*). But by others [who commit such acts], it is not necessarily in Avīci. Now, if many immediate (*ānantarya*) offenses have been committed by someone, they ripen immediately. What, then, happens to him because of them?
The greater the [offenses], the greater the sufferings.

(99d) For he, by means of more numerous *ānantarya* [sins], obtains in that Avīci hell a body that is denser and more delicate, and the causes [of suffering] are more numerous and more intense, whereby he experiences sensation five, four, three, or two times [more than others]. But who is it that splits the Saṃgha?
A monk who is a practitioner of vision and conduct; he splits it. (100ab) (8)

A monk causes the schism, not a layperson, nor nuns and the like. Furthermore, he is one whose conduct is dominated by views (*dṛṣṭicarita*), not one whose conduct is dominated by craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*). He must be established in proper conduct (*vṛttastha*), not one of broken conduct, because the words of the latter would not be accepted. Where does he cause the schism? Not where the Blessed One is present, but elsewhere;

for it is impossible to cause a schism in the very presence of the Teacher, due to the invincibility (*duṣprasaha*) of the Tathāgatas and the acceptability of their words. Whom does he cause to split?

[He speaks of] fools—namely ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and not noble ones (*ārya*), because the latter have directly realized the Dharma. Others say that even among them, he does not mean those who have attained receptivity (*kṣānti*). To what extent is the Saṅgha split?
It is split when there is receptivity toward another Teacher and another Path. (100cd) (18)

When [the monks] accept a teacher other than the Tathāgata, and a path other than the path taught by him, to that extent the Saṃgha is said to be split. For how long does it remain split? It does not last beyond that very night; for while the schism in the Saṃgha has not yet passed a single night, the Saṃgha is necessarily reunited.

This which is called a schism of the Saṃgha is also considered a schism of the wheel (*cakrabheda*). For at that time, the Wheel of Dharma of the Blessed One becomes split because the progression of the Path is obstructed. For this very reason, it is called both a schism of the wheel and a schism of the Saṃgha. But where does a schism of the wheel occur? [p.262]
In Jambūdvīpa, and not in other continents. By how many monks?
By nine or more.

Having established nine as the minimum, there is no fixed limit beyond that. Eight monks constitute a *saṃgha*; the ninth is the schismatic (*bhedaka*). For a *saṃgha* must necessarily be divided into two factions; in this way, it becomes split. However, there is another kind of schism in the *saṃgha* which arises from a schism in formal acts (*karmabheda*): if they perform formal acts in discord within a single boundary (*ekasīmā*).
This schism in formal acts occurs in the three continents where the Teaching exists. By how many monks?
And it occurs with eight or more [schismatics].
(101d) However, a schism of the Wheel does not occur during six periods. During which ones?
At the beginning, at the end, before the *arbuda* stage, before the pair [of disciples], and when the Sage has passed away. (11–12)
Furthermore, when the boundary has not been established, no schism of the wheel occurs.

(102) [This refers to] at the beginning, when the Wheel of Dharma has recently been set in motion, and at the end, at the time of the Blessed One’s final nirvana; for in these two states, the Saṃgha is of one single flavor. In the interim as well, it is not divided prior to a tumor, so long as neither a tumor of morality nor a tumor of view has arisen within the Teaching. And it is not divided prior to a pair, so long as the foremost pair of disciples has not yet appeared.

Because they have undergone a period of residence under a different rule, and because [the schism] can be reconciled by him; because when the Sage, the Teacher, has passed away and entered final nirvāṇa, there is no adversary; and while the boundary is unbonded—that is, as long as the boundary has not been established—for in a single boundary, a schism in the Saṃgha occurs due to the presence of two factions. During these times, there is no schism of the Wheel (*cakrabheda*). Furthermore, a schism of the Wheel does not occur for all who are bound [by vows], because it depends upon specific karma.
Why is there immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) in cases such as matricide and so forth, but not elsewhere?

Because of the rejection and destruction of those who have been benefactors and fields of virtue. (103ab) First, regarding the killing of mother and father, it is due to the rejection of benefactors. How are they benefactors? Because one's own physical existence originates from them. What is their rejection? It is abandonment. Because they are fields of virtue, the killing of an Arhat constitutes an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*). Furthermore, even if the sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*) of the mother or the father were to change, the transgression would still occur with respect to that same basis (*āśraya*), even though the characteristics have shifted. (103c) (2)

Therefore it is said: "Could it be that one deprives a person of life who is neither his father nor an Arhat, and yet is touched by the fault of an immediate transgression (*ānantarya*)? It could be so, if the mother's sexual characteristics (*vyañjana*) have been transformed. Could it be that one deprives a woman of life who is neither his mother nor an Arhat, and yet is touched by the fault of an immediate transgression? It could be so, if the father's sexual characteristics have been transformed. If the *kalala* of one woman has been discharged and swallowed by another through her womb, which of them is the mother? For whom, if he kills her, would there be an immediate transgression?

"Because she is the one from whose blood he was born. (103d) That woman from whose blood this being (*sattva*) has arisen is his mother; the second [woman] is to be regarded [as such] in all legal matters, for she is the one who carries him in her womb, nourishes him, and brings him up. If, having directed an effort toward the mother, one kills another, there would be no immediate transgression (*ānantarya*). Likewise, if one should kill [the mother] by directing an effort toward someone who is not the mother, there would still be no [immediate transgression]. In this regard, the case of killing a mother who is hidden beneath a bed, and the case of the washerman’s son killing his father by means of an effort directed at a mosquito, should be cited as examples.

When one kills both one's mother and another person with a single blow, there are two non-informative (avijñapti) actions; however, the informative (vijñapti) action is only the immediate transgression (ānantarya), because that karma is more powerful. The Venerable Ghoṣaka maintains that the informative action is also twofold, because it consists of an accumulation of atoms. Even when one kills an Arhat while perceiving him as someone else, the immediate transgression still occurs, because the basis [of the act] is determined by the thought, "I am killing."

If one should harm a father who is an Arhat, he would have only one *ānantarya* [karmic obstruction], because the basis (*āśraya*) is one. How is this *avadāna* to be interpreted: "Go and say to Śikhaṇḍin: 'Two *ānantaryas* have been committed by you—namely, that your father was deprived of life and that an Arhat [was killed]'? It should be said: "By two causes," or "by two aspects. Is it necessarily the case that for a Tathāgata there is an *ānantarya* from the shedding of blood with a malicious mind? It would be so for one who intends to kill him.
Regarding the Buddha, there is no [offense] for one who intends to strike [but does not].

(104a) If one were to form the intention to strike, it would not [constitute an offense against the Buddha]. If one should strike one who is not an Arhat, and that person should become an Arhat after the blow, he is not an Arhat prior to the blow. (104b) He is not an Arhat until after the blow.
The term "immediate transgression" (*ānantarya*) continues to apply here. For he has not performed the preliminary application (*prayoga*) toward that [transgression].

Having performed the application for an immediate transgression, would one fail to attain either detachment (*vairāgya*) or the fruit while it remains unreversed? No; for one who has applied himself to an immediate transgression, the possibility of detachment or its fruit does not exist. (104cd) [p.264]

However, having performed the preliminary application for another course of action, once the Noble Path has arisen, that other course of action does not arise again, because its basis is absolutely opposed to it.
(2) Among these immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*), which one is the most blameworthy?
(3) False speech regarding the schism of the Saṃgha is considered the most blameworthy. (105ab) (4)

That false speech intended for the purpose of causing a schism in the Saṃgha—which, by revealing what is contrary to reality, deceives one who knows the Dharma and non-Dharma—is the most blameworthy among all forms of misconduct. Why is this? Because it strikes at the very body of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, and because it creates an obstacle for the world on the path to heaven and liberation.

For when the Saṃgha is split, the world’s entry into the fixed course of rightness, the attainment of the fruits [of the path], detachment, and the destruction of the outflows are obstructed; even the activities of meditation, study, recitation, and reflection do not proceed, and the world—including gods, nāgas, and humans—remains agitated and dejected until it is reunited again; furthermore, there is maturation [of this act] in Avīci for an eon.

Among the remaining immediate offenses (*ānantarya*), the fifth, third, and first are progressively more serious, while the killing of one’s father is the lightest of all. If that is so, why did the Blessed One state that among the three types of punishment, mental punishment (*manodaṇḍa*) is the most blameworthy, and further declare that wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is the supreme among blameworthy things? And why was schism in the Saṅgha declared the most blameworthy among the immediate offenses? This is because [the statements were made] with specific restrictions: mental punishment was spoken of in reference to the three types of action (*karman*); wrong view was spoken of in reference to views; and schism in the Saṅgha was spoken of as the most blameworthy in reference to the immediate offenses.

Alternatively, with reference to the expansion of the maturation (*vipākavistara*), the killing of many people, and the total severance of the roots of merit (*kuśalamūlasamuccheda*), [the results] are respectively [as follows].

Furthermore, among good conducts (*sucarita*), which one has the greatest fruit? The volition (*cetanā*) regarding the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is the most fruitful among the wholesome in the world. (105cd)

Furthermore, regarding wholesome karma, the volition associated with the supreme stage (*bhavāgra*) is the most productive of great fruit among all [wholesome states]. Its maturation (*vipāka*) is extremely tranquil for eighty thousand eons; and this was said with reference to the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*). However, with reference to the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyogaphala*), the volition associated with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) is the most productive of great fruit among all [states], because its fruit is the total exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*). For this very reason, it is called "the world" (*loka*).

Is it only by means of the immediate (*ānantarya*) offenses that one is necessarily reborn in the hells? One is also necessarily reborn there by means of those similar to the immediate offenses; however, others maintain that this does not occur immediately after death. What are these? He says: Violating an Arhat mother, killing a Bodhisattva established in the certainty [of enlightenment], killing a Śaikṣa, and stealing from the Saṃgha’s means of entry [the monastery gate]. (106) [p.265]

Those similar to the immediate [offenses] (*ānantarya-sabhāga*) are: fifth, the destruction of a stūpa. (107ab) These five are, respectively, similar to the five immediate offenses: if one defiles one’s mother who is an Arhat by engaging in unchaste conduct; if one kills a Bodhisattva who has entered the state of certainty (*niyatipatita*); if one kills a person in training (*śaikṣa*); if one steals what belongs to the mouth and entrance of the Saṅgha; and if one destroys a stūpa. Furthermore, other karma that possesses maturation (*savipāka*) also causes extreme obstruction at three times. At which three?
Karma acts as a supreme obstacle to the attainment of *kṣānti*, the state of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and arhatship.

(107cd) When one passes from the *mūrdhāna* stages into *kṣānti*, karmas leading to the miserable realms (*āpāyika*) stand as obstacles, because one is transcending the level where their maturation occurs. Just as creditors confront a man who is leaving his country, so too do the karmas belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) stand as obstacles for one attaining the fruit of a non-returner—provided that karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) is set aside. Likewise, for one attaining arhatship, the karmas belonging to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*) stand as obstacles in the same manner.
Regarding what was said concerning "the killing of a bodhisattva":
from what point, and starting from what [stage], is one to be called a bodhisattva?
Because he performs the actions that produce the marks.
From the moment he begins to perform the actions that have the marks as their maturation, he indeed becomes one who has entered into certainty. How so? Because from that time onward, he is always:
In a happy destiny, born of noble family, with unimpaired faculties, a male, remembering his births, and irreversible. (108cd)

"Good destination" (*sugati*) means that his destination is praiseworthy because of rebirth among gods and humans. And in that good destination, he is born into a great family of *kṣatriyas*, *brāhmaṇas*, or *gṛhapatis* (*mahāśālakula*), and not into another [inferior] family. "With impaired faculties" (*vyakṣa*) means that his sense-faculties (*akṣa*) are deficient; "not with impaired faculties" (*avyakṣa*) means that his faculties are unimpaired. He is a male (*puruṣa*) indeed, not a woman, much less a eunuch (*śaṇḍha*) or the like. And he is "one who remembers his births" (*jātismara*); "one who turns back" (*nivṛt*) means he returns to every birth; "not one who turns back" (*anivṛt*) means he does not [return].

The meaning is "irreversible. Because they are not wearied by any forms of suffering or by the various forms of misconduct of all sentient beings for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, they are those who are called in the world "slaves not purchased with money. These are the bodhisattvas.

For those great beings, although they have attained the excellence and distinction of all perfections, because they are subject to causeless compassion, they establish themselves among all sentient beings as being like the sons of outcastes through their lack of pride; thus they become endurers of every humiliation from sentient beings and bearers of every toil and restraint.
And as for that which was called "karma ripening into the marks":
[p.266] it is performed only by a male in Jambudvīpa, in the presence [of a Buddha], with his mind directed toward a Buddha. (2)
For when a hundred eons remain, that [karma] consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*) is projected.

(109) It is only in Jambudvīpa that a bodhisattva projects the karma that ripens into the marks; not elsewhere, because the inhabitants of Jambudvīpa possess sharp intelligence. It is only a male, not a female. Only while the Teacher is present does he project that karma consisting of reflection with a volition directed toward the Buddha as its object; it is neither consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya*) nor consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).

When only one hundred kalpas remained, he projected [the remainder of his career] rather than through many more births; however, by means of his blazing vigor, the Blessed One Śākyamuni bypassed nine kalpas, and it was during ninety-one kalpas that he projected [his career]. For this very reason it was said: "O village headman, from ninety-one kalpas ago, I do not recall nor do I perceive even a single family that was harmed or injured for the sake of providing alms-food to a mendicant."

From that time forward, because he possesses the innate recollection of his former births (*jātismara*), the Bodhisattva—who has already emerged from the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*)—turns away from these four continents and acquires two qualities; so say the former teachers (*pūrvācārya*). And of those marks (*lakṣaṇa*), each one arises from a hundred merits (*puṇya*).

What is its measure? Some say it is the amount of the fruit of enjoyment of all sentient beings, excluding those bodhisattvas who are close [to enlightenment]. Others say it is the extent to which the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system is produced through the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings. Still others say that only the Buddhas themselves know its measure.

Now, during his time as a bodhisattva, how many Buddhas did the Blessed One attend upon? In the first incalculable eon (*kalpāsaṃkhyeya*), he attended seventy-five thousand; in the second, seventy-six thousand; and in the third, seventy-seven thousand.
Now, at the end of which incalculable eon was which Buddha? In reverse order, according to the sequence, these were the last-born [Buddhas] of the three incalculable eons.

Vipaśyin, Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaśikhin. (110bcd) During the time of the Perfectly Awakened One Ratnaśikhin, the first incalculable eon was completed; during the Blessed One Dīpaṃkara, the second; and during the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, the third. But Śākyamuni [was prophesied] before all of them. (110d')

The Perfectly Awakened One named Śākyamuni existed previously, at which time the Blessed One, while still a bodhisattva, made his first vow: "May I become a Buddha of exactly this kind. Just as we have appeared in this Kali age, so too did he appear; and like ours, his teaching also lasted for a thousand years. Now, in what state does a bodhisattva fulfill which perfection? By giving everything to everyone out of compassion, there is the fulfillment of the perfection of generosity. (111ab) (5)

When one gives everything to everyone—out of compassion, not out of a desire for a specific worldly success—down to the very marrow of the bones, by this much the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) becomes fulfilled. (6) But through the absence of anger even when one's limbs are being severed, the perfections of patience (*kṣānti*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) [are fulfilled] for one who still possesses passion.

(111cd) When this person, though not yet free from passion, does not feel even the slightest anger while his limbs are being cut off, then his perfections of patience and ethical discipline become fulfilled. (7–10)
Regarding the vigor [displayed] through the *Tiṣya-stotra*:

when the Blessed One was a bodhisattva, seeing that the Tathāgata Tiṣya had entered the fire-element (*tejodhātu*) within a jewel cave, he stood on one foot for seven days and praised him with a single verse:
"Neither in heaven nor on earth, neither in this world nor in the abode of Vaiśravaṇa..."
"Neither in the divine abode of the gods, nor in the cardinal or intermediate directions,
(15) let him wander over the entire, flourishing earth with its mountains and forests,
(16) for where, O Great Śramaṇa, could there be another bull among men equal to you? (16)
At that time, it is said, the perfection of vigor was fulfilled and nine eons were bypassed.

Immediately following wisdom (*dhī*) and concentration (*samādhi*), the perfections of meditation (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) reach fulfillment immediately prior to enlightenment; they are called "perfections" (*pāramitā*) because, in the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), one reaches the further shore of their own excellence.

It is stated in the Sūtra that there are three bases of meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*): the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving, that consisting in ethical discipline, and that consisting in cultivation. How are these three the bases of meritorious action? Merit, action, and their basis—these three are like the paths of action (*karmapatha*). (112cd)

These three are called "bases of meritorious action" (*puṇyakriyāvastu*) because each is, as appropriate, both merit, an action, and a basis. For example, just as those which are both actions and paths are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*), so too are these called bases of meritorious action. Among them, first, in the case of the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving, bodily and vocal action are threefold; the volition that originates them is both merit and action; and the factors co-arising with it are merit alone.

(3) That which consists of morality (*śīlamaya*), however, is exclusively bodily and vocal action, and thus it is threefold. That which consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*) is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); it is both merit (*puṇya*) and the basis for meritorious action (*puṇyakriyāvastu*). Because the volition (*cetanā*) associated with that [loving-kindness] is produced by way of loving-kindness, the volition co-arising with it, as well as morality (*śīla*), is both merit and action. Other factors co-arising with it are merit alone, or rather, they are the cause of merit. Meritorious action (*puṇyakriyā*) is the application of merit; these three are its bases (*vastu*).

"Because one begins the application of merit for the sake of accomplishing these. Others say: "In the ultimate sense, meritorious action is wholesome volition (*kuśalacetanā*); these [three] are its objects. What is this that is called "giving" (*dāna*)? That which is given is giving; however, in this context, that by which something is given is giving.

Giving is also performed out of fear, desire for gain, attachment, and so forth; however, that is not what is intended here. Therefore, for the sake of specification, he says: "Out of a desire for worship and favor" (11). That by which one gives is [the gift] characterized by the desire for the worship and favor of others. But what could that be which is given? (13)
(14) What, then, is that origination of bodily and vocal actions? It is the group [of factors] by which that [action] is originated. And it is said in this regard:
(15–16) "When a person gives his own property with a virtuous mind..."
At that moment, the wholesome aggregates (*skandha*) are designated as "giving" (*dāna*).
(17) And its fruit is great enjoyment.

(113d) This basis of meritorious action consisting of giving has great enjoyment as its fruit. This suffix *-maya* should be understood in the sense of "consisting of" or "having the nature of," just as in the expressions "a house made of grass" (*tṛṇamaya*) or "a vessel made of leaves" (*parṇamaya*). Now, this very giving— (20)
Giving is performed for one’s own benefit, for the benefit of others, for the benefit of both, or for the benefit of neither.

(114ab) In this regard, when a noble one who is free from passion, or an ordinary person who is free from passion, gives a gift to a shrine (*caitya*), that is for their own benefit alone, because there is no benefit to others by means of it. When a noble one who is free from passion gives a gift to other sentient beings—setting aside those gifts to be experienced in the present life—that gift is for the benefit of others, because they are benefited by it; it is not for one's own benefit, because one has completely transcended the level of its maturation (*vipāka*).

When an ordinary person who is not free from passion, or one who is free from passion, gives to other sentient beings, that gift is for the benefit of both. When a noble one who is free from passion gives to a shrine (*caitya*), setting aside that which is to be experienced in the present life, that gift is not for the benefit of both; for it is given solely out of reverence and gratitude.
In general, it has been said that the fruit of giving is great enjoyment;
its specific distinctions, however, arise from the distinctions of the giver, the object, and the field. (114cd)
In that regard, first, the donor is distinguished by faith and so forth:

a donor endowed with qualities such as faith, ethical discipline, and learning becomes distinguished. By virtue of the excellence of the donor, that gift is distinguished with respect to the bestowal of its fruit; and such is that donor.
One gives with respect and so forth. (115b) (11) One gives respectfully, with one's own hand, at the proper time, and without harming others. (12) Therefore: (13)
[The results are] receiving honor, delighting in magnificent enjoyments, obtaining [wealth] at the proper time, and possessing wealth that cannot be taken away.

(115bcd) Therefore, for this donor, having given such a gift, there arise four specific benefits in due order: he becomes one who receives honor; he gains a taste for magnificent enjoyments; he obtains enjoyments at the proper time and not when the time has passed; and he obtains enjoyments that cannot be taken away—his wealth is neither seized by others nor destroyed by fire and the like. Thus it has been explained how the donor is distinguished, and how, through that distinction, the gift itself is distinguished.
Now, how is the object distinguished?

(19) The phrase "the object is distinguished by excellence of color and so forth" carries over [from the previous context]. If that which is given is endowed with even one of the qualities of color, fragrance, taste, or touch, in this way the object is distinguished. What happens after giving such an object? [It results] respectively: (22)
Beauty, renown, (23) popularity, and thereafter limbs that are delicate and pleasant to the touch according to the season.

(24) By giving what is endowed with excellent color, one becomes beautiful. By giving what is endowed with excellent fragrance, one becomes renowned; for fragrance, like renown, is diffused throughout the directions. By giving what is endowed with excellent taste, one becomes popular, being as sweet as flavor itself. By giving what is endowed with excellent touch, one possesses delicate limbs, and one's limbs become pleasant to the touch according to the season, just like those of the "jewel of a woman. (3)

Now, how is the field distinguished? (4) The field is distinguished by way of its [rebirth] destiny, suffering, beneficence, and virtues. (117ab) First, it is distinguished by the distinction of destiny; for thus it was said by the Blessed One: "Having given a gift to one who has gone to the animal realm, a hundredfold maturation is to be expected. Having given a gift to a human being who is immoral, a thousandfold [maturation is to be expected]. (7) It is distinguished by the distinction of suffering; for thus it is said regarding the bases of meritorious action consisting of material things (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*): "A gift to the sick, a gift to the attendant of the sick... (8)

Having spoken of giving during the Śītalikā festival and others, it was said: "For a faithful son of good family or daughter of good family who is endowed with these seven material bases of meritorious action (*aupadhika-puṇyakriyāvastu*), it is not possible to grasp the measure of their merit. This is because there is no difference in the nature of their benefit, as in the case of one's mother and father or other benefactors, according to examples such as the *Ṛkṣamṛga-jātaka* and others.
It is also due to the distinction of qualities, as for instance: "Having given a gift to one possessed of virtue, the maturation [of the fruit] is a hundred-thousandfold," and so forth.
However, among all gifts—

(117c) "The foremost gift is that given by one who is liberated to one who is liberated. (14) It has been said by the Blessed One that this gift of one free from passion to one free from passion is the most excellent among all material gifts. (15) Or [it is the gift] of a Bodhisattva. (117d) (16)

Alternatively, the gift that one gives to a bodhisattva for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings is the foremost kind of taking up [a gift] even by one who is liberated toward one who is not yet liberated. Setting that aside, among the other eight gifts spoken of by the Blessed One, this is the eighth. (117d)

The term "foremost" (*agram*) continues [from the previous context]. Which are the eight? Giving after having approached; giving out of fear; giving because [someone] has given to me; giving with the thought, "I shall give to me"; giving with the thought, "Giving was previously given by me"; giving with the thought, "Giving was given by my fathers and grandfathers"; giving for the sake of heaven; giving for the sake of reputation; giving for the sake of the ornament of the mind; giving for the sake of the refinement of the mind; giving for the sake of the equipment for yoga; and giving for the attainment of the supreme goal.

Regarding that, "giving to those who have approached" refers to giving to those who have come near, according to the ancient teachers. "Giving out of fear" refers to giving when one sees someone facing destruction and thinks, "I shall grant him a boon. The remainder is not analyzed because it is easy to understand. It has been stated in detail in the Sūtra: "Having given a gift to one who is practicing for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāapatti-phala-pratipannaka*), the maturation is immeasurable; even more immeasurable is the gift to a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Furthermore:
"To one's mother, father, the sick, a preacher of the Dharma, and one in their final birth..."
And the gift to a Bodhisattva is immeasurable, even if he is not yet noble.

(118) From these five—though they are still ordinary beings—the gift results in immeasurable fruit. Among them, the Bodhisattva in his final birth is one who is in his last existence. As for the preacher of the Dharma, in which of the four categories of distinguished fields should he be placed? He belongs to the category of benefactors.

(5) For he is a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), the giver of the eye of wisdom to beings blinded by ignorance, the illuminator of what is even and uneven, (6) the bringer about of the untainted *dharmakāya*, and, in brief, the performer of the Buddha’s work. (7) One who wishes to know the gravity or lightness of actions should, in brief, understand six causes. Namely: (8) the subsequent action, the field, the basis, the preliminary application, the volition, and the intention. (9)
Due to the mildness or intensity of these [factors], there is mildness or intensity of the action.

(119) What is called "consequent" (*pṛṣṭha*) is the repeated performance of what has already been done. What is called "field" (*kṣetra*) is that toward which benefit or harm is performed. The "basis" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is the course of action (*karmapatha*). The "preparatory effort" (*prayoga*) is the bodily or vocal action for the sake of that [course]. "Volition" (*cetanā*) is that by which one brings the course of action to completion. "Intention" (*āśaya*) is the very resolve: "I shall do such and such," and "I shall not do such and such. For some, an action becomes grave solely through the inclusion of its consequence.

Because it remains fixed by the necessity of its maturation (*vipāka-naiyamyena*). For some, it is heavy solely by virtue of the field (*kṣetra*); in that very same field, it becomes heavy further by virtue of the basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and not otherwise. For example, [the killing] of one's mother or father is [heavier] than [the killing of others], but it is not so through [the commission of] theft and so forth. The same should be applied to other cases as well. However, for one whose [six factors] are all intense (*adhimātra*), that action should be understood as extremely intense and heavy;
for one whose [factors] are weak (*mṛdu*), it should be understood as extremely weak.

Action is said to be both performed (*kṛta*) and accumulated (*upacita*). How does action become accumulated? By five causes: "Through volition and completion, through the absence of regret and its opposite, through its retinue and through its maturation, action is said to be accumulated. (120)

How is it through intentionality? It is that which is done intentionally, not what is done without prior awareness or impulsively. How is it through completion? (21) Someone goes to the states of woe by means of a single misdeed, while another does so by as many as three; someone by means of a single course of action, while another does so by as many as ten. (22) In this regard, as long as one has not gone [to the state of woe] by means of a certain number [of actions], that karma is "done" but not "accumulated"; however, once it is completed, it is accumulated. How is it through the absence of remorse and its opposite?

And that action is without remorse and without an antidote. How [is it heavy] by way of its retinue? It is unwholesome and has an unwholesome retinue. How [is it heavy] by way of its ripening? It is certain in the granting of its ripening. In this same way, the wholesome should also be applied. Other than this, an action is merely performed, not accumulated.

It has been stated that at a *caitya*, the gift of one who still possesses passion (*sarāga*) is for his own sake. In that case, since there is no recipient, how can merit (*puṇya*) arise? For merit is of two kinds: that which follows from relinquishment (*tyāgānvaya*), which arises from the very act of giving; and that which follows from enjoyment (*paribhogānvaya*), which is produced from the enjoyment of the object given (*deyadharma*).
At a *caitya*, the merit is that which follows from relinquishment.

There is no merit resulting from enjoyment [of a gift]. How, then, can there be merit in that case when no one receives it? Furthermore, what is the reason that merit must exist when there is a recipient, but not when there is none? Because there is an absence of benefit to anyone. This is not a valid reason. For if merit arose only from benefiting others, then it would not exist in the cultivation of the immeasurables such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) or in the cultivation of right view. Therefore, merit must be admitted even in the case of a shrine (*caitya*), just as in the case of loving-kindness and so forth, even though no one receives it.

Just as merit arises from one's own mind even in the absence of a recipient or the actual benefitting of others—such as in the case of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth—likewise, even when a virtuous person has passed away, merit arises from one's own mind produced by devotion to them. [Objection: In that case, the act of giving and honoring would become useless. [Response: No; because the devotion that motivates those actions is more excellent. For example, it is like the bodily and vocal actions motivated by one who intends to kill an enemy.

Even if that person has died, for one who acts with the perception of them as an enemy, a great deal of demerit arises—not by mere intention alone. Likewise, when the Teacher has passed away, for one who performs acts of giving and honor arising from devotion to him, a great deal of merit arises—not by mere devotion alone. If the seed of the act of giving yields a desirable fruit when planted in a good field, will it then yield an undesirable fruit in a bad field? Even in a bad field, there is the production of a desirable fruit, because of the non-inversion of the fruit and the seed. (121cd)

Even in a bad field, it is observed that the fruit does not deviate from its seed: from a grape seed, only a sweet grape fruit arises; from a nimba seed, only a bitter nimba tree. Likewise, even in a bad field, for one who acts with a purified resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), the seed of giving produces only a desirable fruit, never an undesirable one. However, due to the defects of the field, that seed may yield little fruit or no fruit at all. The section on the meritorious action consisting of giving (*dānamaya-puṇyakriyāvastu*), along with its related topics, is concluded.
Now, that which consists of morality (*śīlamaya*) must be explained; thus it is said:
Immorality is unwholesome form; morality is the abstention from it.
(122ab) For unwholesome form is called immorality; therefore, abstention from that is morality. Furthermore, that abstention is twofold. (122b') (7)

That informative act (*vijñapti*) by which one abstains, and that very abstinence which is non-informative (*avijñapti*), constitute morality. Furthermore, morality is not merely the abstention from misconduct (*dauḥśīlya*). What then?

It is also the abstention in two ways from that which has been prohibited by the Buddha—such as eating at improper times—even if it is not inherently misconduct; for one who has undertaken the training, misconduct arises from the transgression of those rules. Thus, morality has been explained in brief.
But the pure [morality] possesses four qualities.
(122d) That morality, however, becomes endowed with four qualities; conversely, it is impure. Now, as to how it possesses four qualities, he says:
It is unassailed by immorality and its causes, and it relies upon their opposites and tranquility. (123ab)

First, it is not impaired by immorality; nor is it impaired by the causes of immorality as previously described, namely, by the afflictions and secondary afflictions such as greed and so forth. It is based on the antidote to immorality because it relies upon the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). It is based on tranquility (*śama*) and does not rely on a particular rebirth, because it is dedicated toward *nirvāṇa*. Others say that it is [distinguished] by five reasons.

(18) It is pure by way of the fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*), pure by way of the preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*), unimpaired by discursive thoughts (*vitarka*), embraced by mindfulness (*smṛti*), and dedicated toward *nirvāṇa*.
