Others say that ethical discipline (*śīla*) is fourfold: (20) discipline out of fear (*bhaya-śīla*), which is observed out of fear for one’s livelihood, ill repute, punishment, or an evil rebirth; (21) discipline born of hope (*āśāsti-śīla*), which is performed out of craving for existence, enjoyments, and honor; and discipline conforming to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga-anuloma-śīla*), which is for the sake of liberation by those possessing right view.
Pure morality is untainted morality because it is stainless. Thus ends the section on morality. (22) But wholesome [states] that are concentrated are cultivation (bhāvanā).
(123cd) What is this so-called "concentrated"? It is that which has concentration as its intrinsic nature and arises simultaneously with it. For what reason is this called "cultivation"? [p.274]
Because of the perfuming of the mind.

(123d’) For that wholesome state of meditative concentration perfumes the mind to an extreme degree, because it causes the continuum [of the mind] to become identical with those qualities, like the cultivation of sesame seeds with flowers. It has already been stated that giving leads to great wealth; how then do ethical discipline (*śīla*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) lead to heaven?
Ethical discipline is primary for [attaining] heaven, while cultivation is for the sake of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*). (124ab)

Generosity also leads to heaven, but ethical discipline (*śīla*) is predominant; ethical discipline also leads to dissociation (*visaṃyoga*), but cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is predominant. As it is said in the Sūtra: "Four types of persons produce Brahma-merit. What is this Brahma-merit? The Vaibhāṣikas say: it is that which was stated in order to indicate the measure of the karma that has the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) as its maturation (*vipāka*). However, the former masters explain:
"The four possess the nature of Brahma-merit because they rejoice in the heavens for an eon (*kalpa*). (124cd)

The amount of merit by which one rejoices in the heavens for an eon is this "Brahma-merit," because the lifespan of the Brahmapurohita deities is one eon. (11) Other schools recite a verse: "One generates Brahma-merit; one rejoices in the heavens for an eon.
(12) The gift of material things has been explained; the gift of the Dharma must now be discussed. That is what is being stated here. (14)

The gift of Dharma is the teaching of the sūtras and so forth, exactly as they are and without affliction. (125ab) The teaching of the sūtras and other scriptures exactly as they are and without affliction is the gift of Dharma. Therefore, those who teach the Dharma erroneously—whether with an afflicted mind or desiring gain, honor, and fame—inflict a great loss upon their own merit. It has been stated that the wholesome is threefold according to the classification of the bases of meritorious action;
furthermore: Wholesome [action] is of three kinds: conducive to merit, conducive to nirvāṇa, and conducive to penetration. (125cd)

That which leads to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*) is that which has a desirable maturation. That which leads to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) is that which, once arisen, makes one destined for final nirvāṇa. When someone, upon hearing a discourse illuminating the defects of cyclic existence, selflessness, and the qualities of nirvāṇa, experiences the bristling of their hair and the shedding of tears, it should be understood that they possess the root of virtue leading to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); just as the presence of seeds in the furrows of a field is inferred from the sprouting of shoots during the rainy season. The fourfold stages leading to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), such as "heat" (*ūṣman*) and so forth, we shall explain later. [p.275]
Regarding that which is called in the world "writing, sealing, calculation, poetry, and arithmetic," what is their intrinsic nature?
Action set in motion by yoga, together with its originator, is threefold;
writing, sealing, calculation, poetry, and arithmetic follow in this order. (126)

"Set in motion by yoga" means set in motion by specific skillful means (*upāya*). "Action is threefold" refers to action of body, speech, and mind. Among these, first, writing and seals are bodily action set in motion by yoga, together with its origination. Calculation and poetry are vocal action. These [four] have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature. Enumeration is mental action, which is the mental synthesis of phenomena (*dharma*).
Now, some synonyms for phenomena are stated: "Faulty, obscured, inferior, and afflicted phenomena" (127ab).
Defiled phenomena have the synonyms "faulty," "obscured," and "inferior. (10) Pure and stainless [phenomena] are (11) sublime. (127bc) (12)

"Exquisite" (*praṇīta*) is a synonym for wholesome and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena. By implication, it is established that those other than the inferior and the exquisite are "intermediate. (127c'd) "Conditioned wholesome phenomena are to be cultivated" (*sevitavya*); this is a synonym for wholesome conditioned phenomena being those which ought to be practiced. It is thereby established that the remaining phenomena are not to be cultivated. Why is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) not to be cultivated? Because it cannot be repeatedly practiced and because it lacks a fruit; for cultivation is undertaken for the sake of a fruit. All other phenomena are "surpassable" (*sottara*).

But liberation is unsurpassed. (127d’) For there is nothing more distinguished than nirvāṇa; and it is distinguished from all [other things] because it is wholesome and eternal. (19) This concludes the "Exposition of Karma" in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*. (20)
The fourth treasury-location (kośasthāna).
[page 276] (no page) CHAPTER V [page 277]
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the Fifth Chapter of the Treasury.
Homage to the Buddha!

It has been stated that "the diversity of the world is born of karma. Those karmas undergo accumulation by virtue of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); without the latent dispositions, they are incapable of bringing about existence (*bhava*). Therefore, it should be understood that the latent dispositions are the root of existence. (1a)

For when a defilement arises, it performs ten functions: it strengthens its root; it establishes a continuity; it prepares the field; it produces an outflow; it brings about the existence of karma; it gathers its own equipment; it causes delusion regarding the object; it bends the stream of consciousness; it diverts one from the side of virtue; and it extends over the sense of bondage by means of not transcending the realm. And how many are these latent dispositions? In brief, there are six.
Which six? They are: attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt. (1bcd)

The inclusion of the word "likewise" (tathā) is for the purpose of making known that others [the secondary afflictions] also adhere to their objects by the power of passion (*rāga*); this we shall explain later. Furthermore, those [secondary afflictions] are... //1d//
The six are said to be seven due to the division of attachment (*rāga*).

These same six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are stated to be seven in the Sūtra by making a twofold division of attachment: the underlying tendency of attachment to sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of attachment to existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*).

How is this to be understood: is the *kāmarāgānuśaya* (latent tendency of sensual desire) simply sensual desire itself as a latent tendency, or is it the latent tendency belonging to sensual desire? And what follows from this? If sensual desire itself were the latent tendency, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra: "In this case, a certain person does not frequently dwell with a mind obsessed by the obsession of sensual desire; he understands, as it truly is, the escape from the arisen obsession of sensual desire."

"His obsession with sensual desire (*kāmarāga-paryavasthāna*), having been thoroughly and completely struck down by its strength, is abandoned along with its latent tendency (*sānuśaya*). If the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) were distinct from sensual desire, it would follow that the latent tendency is a dissociated factor (*viprayukta*), which would contradict the Abhidharma, for it states: "The latent tendency of sensual desire is associated with three faculties. Thus, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the latent tendency is simply the sensual desire itself, and so on up to the point that doubt itself is the latent tendency.

But was it not already stated that this contradicts the Sūtra? There is no contradiction; the meaning is "with latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) and "with continuations" (*sānubandha*). Alternatively, the word "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) in the Sūtra is used figuratively for "possession" (*prāpti*), just as fire is called "suffering. However, in the Abhidharma, the word "latent tendency" is used in its technical sense (*lākṣaṇika*) for the affliction (*kleśa*) itself. Therefore, the latent tendencies are indeed associated (*saṃprayukta*). How is this known? Because [the Sūtra states]: "Because they cause the affliction of the mind, because they are obstructions, and because they are opposed to the wholesome."

Because the mind becomes defiled by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), new wholesome states do not arise, and one falls away from those already arisen; therefore, they are not dissociated (*viprayukta*). Now, if it were the case that this [defilement] occurred through dissociated factors as well, then the wholesome would never be perceived, because those [dissociated factors] are always present. Yet it is indeed perceived. Therefore:
"Because the wholesome is perceived, the latent dispositions here are not dissociated."

This is not a proving argument, because one who maintains that the latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is dissociated from the mind does not accept all of this as being produced by the latent disposition; rather, he accepts it as being produced solely by the affliction (*kleśa*).

But this is correct according to the Sautrāntikas. And how is it for the Sautrāntikas? The latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire is called the "sensual-desire-latent-tendency" (*kāmarāgānuśaya*). Furthermore, the latent tendency is neither associated (*saṃprayukta*) nor dissociated (*viprayukta*), because it is not a separate substantial entity (*adravyāntaratva*). For a defilement (*kleśa*) that is dormant is called a "latent tendency," while one that is awakened is an "outburst" (*paryavasthāna*). What is its dormancy? It is the persistence of the state of being a seed (*bījabhāva*) when it has not become manifest. What is awakening? It is becoming manifest.

What is this so-called "seed-state"? It is the capacity of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) to produce afflictions, born from previous afflictions; just as there is a capacity to produce memory born from the knowledge of experience, and just as sprouts and the like possess a capacity to produce rice-fruits born from rice-fruits. However, for one who postulates a separate, dissociated entity called a "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) as the meaning of the "seed" of the afflictions, it would follow that they must likewise postulate a separate entity as the "seed" of memory.

If, then, in the *Ṣaṭṣaṭkasūtra* it is stated that the affliction (*kleśa*) itself is the latent tendency (*anuśaya*), as in: "In him, there exists a latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) toward pleasant feeling," then by virtue of the word "exists" (*bhavati*), that [feeling] is not itself the latent tendency. When, then, does it exist? When it is dormant (*prasupta*). Or rather, this should be understood as a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) for that [affliction]. Let this digression rest; let the treatise proceed. Regarding this distinction made in the Sūtra between attachment to sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) and attachment to existence (*bhavarāga*), what is this attachment to existence?
Attachment to existence arises from two realms. (2b)
The passion born of the form and formless realms is designated as "passion for existence" (bhavarāga). For what reason is it so designated?
It is so designated because it is inwardly directed, in order to eliminate the notion that it is liberation. //2cd//

For their passion is generally for meditative attainments (*samāpatti-rāga*). Since that passion functions inwardly, it is called "passion for existence" (*bhava-rāga*). It is said that this was taught for those in the two higher realms in order to turn them away from the notion that those states are liberation. Indeed, "existence" (*bhava*) is simply the personal basis (*ātmabhāva*). And those beings, while relishing the attainment along with its support, are actually relishing the personal basis itself; because they are free from passion for the sense-desires (*kāma-vītarāgatva*), that passion is called "passion for existence.

Furthermore, these six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are made ten in the Abhidharma. How so? The views are five: the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, there are ten [factors] consisting of the adherence to views and the adherence to rules and observances. //3//

By dividing the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) into five types of views, they become ten. Five have the nature of views: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of morality and ascetic practices (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Those that do not have the nature of views are attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). Furthermore, these ten underlying tendencies are made into ninety-eight in the Abhidharma: thirty-six belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), twenty-one belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), and thirty-one belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*).

How so? Briefly stated, these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the three realms are to be abandoned either by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) or by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). Among them, first, there are thirty-two belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by vision. Which are they? He says:
"These ten, seven, seven, and eight, excluding three and two views respectively, are abandoned in the desire realm through the vision of suffering and the other [truths]. (4)

Regarding these ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that have been mentioned: in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), all ten exist as being abandonable by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaheya*). From among these very same [ten], seven are abandonable by the vision of origin (*samudayadarśanapraheya*); seven are abandonable by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaheya*), excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the misapprehension of rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Eight are abandonable by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaheya*), excluding the view of a self-identity and the view of grasping at extremes. Thus, these thirty-two underlying tendencies belonging to the sphere of desire are to be abandoned by vision, because they are abandoned merely by the vision of the [four] truths. Four are abandonable by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).

Namely: attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance, because they are abandoned through the subsequent practice of the path once the Truths have been seen. Thus, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) consists of one type and is to be abandoned by seeing suffering. The same applies to the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) consists of four types and is to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. Likewise for the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*). The esteeming of precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists of two types and is to be abandoned by seeing suffering and the path.

Attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance are of five types: those to be abandoned by the vision of the [Four] Truths and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Of what nature are these? Which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, and which up to those to be abandoned by cultivation? Those whose objects are to be abandoned by the vision of a particular [Truth] are themselves to be abandoned by the vision of that [Truth]; those not so distinguished are to be abandoned by cultivation. These same twelve views, four doubts, five attachments, five aversions, five prides, and five ignorances—these constitute the thirty-six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
When these same [tendencies] are again [considered] as being without aversion...

In the form realm (rūpadhātu), having abandoned the five types of resistance (pratigha), those same thirty-one proclivities (anuśaya) belonging to the form realm remain. As it is in the form realm, so it is in the formless realm (ārūpya).
There are thirty-one underlying tendencies; thus, they are considered to be ninety-eight. (5d)
Thus, these six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), through their divisions by way of aspect (*ākāra*), type (*prakāra*), and realm (*dhātu*), are considered by the Abhidharmikas to be ninety-eight.
Regarding those latent dispositions said to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*): are they necessarily abandoned by vision alone? No, he says. What then?
"Those born of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) that are to be destroyed by the receptivities (*kṣānti*) are abandoned only by vision" (6ab).

Those latent dispositions (anuśaya) born of the level of the peak of existence (bhavāgra) that are to be abandoned by the receptivity to subsequent knowledge (anvayajñānakṣānti) are abandoned solely by seeing (darśanaheya) and not by cultivation (bhāvanāheya). Those born of the remaining [levels] are abandoned by both seeing and cultivation. (6bc)

Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in all stages that are to be abandoned by knowledge (*jñāna-vadhya*) are always to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) for both [types of practitioners]. For others maintain that the externalists (*bāhyaka*) do not abandon those [defilements] to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*). Thus, in the *Mahākarmavibhāga-sūtra*, it is stated that there is the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of views—having the realm of desire as their object—even among those who speculate about the past (*pūrvāntakalpaka*), those who hold eternalist views (*śāśvatavādin*), those who hold partial-eternalist views (*ekatya-śāśvatika*), those who hold views of causeless origination (*ahetu-samutpattika*), and even among those free from passion (*vītarāga*).

Furthermore, the defilements belonging to the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) do not have the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as their object, because [those in the realm of form] are free from passion for it. Therefore, those [defilements] that are connected to the desire realm alone remain unabandoned. The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that at the very moment a [wrong] view arises, one falls away from the fruit, just like Devadatta. The five views have been indicated by name, but not by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). What, then, is their intrinsic nature?
They are the views of self and what belongs to self, of permanence and annihilation, and of non-existence, as well as the view of inferiority as superior.
The view of these as being causeless and the view of them as being a path—these are the five views. //7//

The view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) or the view of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*) is the view of a real body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). It is called "real" (*sat*) because it perishes (*sīdati*); "body" (*kāya*) means an accumulation, a collection, or an aggregate (*skandha*). Thus, a "real body" (*satkāya*) is that which is both real and a body; it refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandhāḥ*). This is expressed in this way precisely to cause one to abandon the notion of permanence and the notion of a composite whole. For the grasping at a self with respect to those [aggregates] is preceded by these two notions. A view regarding the real body is the "view of a real body. Indeed, every view that has a contaminated object (*sāsrava-ālambana*) is directed toward the real body.

The view of a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīyadṛṣṭi*) alone is called the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), so that it may be understood: "This view of a real body does not [apply] to a self or to what belongs to a self. As it has been said: "O monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard anything as a self, they all regard these very five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as such. The view of that very object regarded as a self as being either eternal or subject to annihilation is the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), because of grasping at the extremes of permanence and annihilation.

The view that what exists, such as the truth of suffering and so forth, does not exist is false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Indeed, every view that functions with a perverted nature is a false view; however, only one is so designated because it possesses a preeminent quality, like the term "foul-smelling wound. For this one is denigrating (*apavādikā*), whereas the others are superimposing (*samāropikā*). The view that regards the inferior as supreme is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). What is inferior? Everything that is *sāsrava* (subject to outflows), because it has been abandoned by the Noble Ones (*ārya*). To grasp that as supreme is the adherence to views. Although one should have said "adherence to views and so forth" (*dṛṣṭyādi-parāmarśa*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has been omitted.

The view of a cause where there is no cause, and the view of a path where there is no path, is the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). For example, Maheśvara is not the cause of the worlds, yet one views him—or Prajāpati or someone else—as the cause. Furthermore, entering fire or water and so forth are not the cause of heaven, yet one views them as the cause. Merely following rules and observances, as well as the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth, are not the path to liberation, yet one views them as the path. In this case as well, it is said that the word "and so forth" has been omitted; these should be understood as the five [wrong] views.

If the view of a cause in what is not a cause constitutes the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), why is this not to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśanaprahātavya*)? For whoever perceives Īśvara, Prajāpati, or another as the cause, does so by being attached to that [cause] as being eternal, unitary, and a self that is an agent.

Since that [view] proceeds from the misconception (*viparyāsa*) of an eternal self with respect to Īśvara and the like, this attachment to a cause is therefore to be abandoned only through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadṛggheya*). //8//

For it is precisely through the vision of suffering that those two graspings—of permanence and of self—are abandoned with respect to them; therefore, the attachment to a cause produced by them is also abandoned for that very reason.

Furthermore, one who perceives the attainment of heaven through such acts as entering water or fire, or purity through ascetic observances (*śīla-vrata*), must also be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). For this is the scriptural reading: "Those who hold such views and speak thus: 'If this person or individual lives having undertaken the cow-observance, the deer-observance, or the dog-observance, he is purified by that, he is liberated, he transcends pleasure and pain, and he attains the transcendence of pleasure and pain.'"

"One who perceives what is not a cause as a cause is one for whom the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*)," and so forth in detail.

But what is the reason that this [adherence] is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering? Because it is a misconception regarding suffering; because all [afflictions] that have contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*) are misconceptions regarding suffering. Or, what other kind of adherence to rules and rituals is to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*)? That which has as its object what is to be abandoned by the vision of the path is indeed also a misconception regarding suffering.

Furthermore, for one who possesses wrong view or doubt regarding the path as its object—seeing it as "there is no path to liberation" or being in doubt—how could such a person expect purification through that [wrong view or doubt]?

Then, having clung to another path to liberation, one says, "This is not the path to liberation. That person also believes in purification through that other [path] alone, and not through that false view. For him too, this [false view] does not qualify as having as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of the path. Furthermore, why is one who believes in purification through a false view that has as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of origin or cessation not himself to be abandoned by the vision of those [truths]? Therefore, this matter must be examined.

Regarding what was stated, "due to the inversion [of perceiving] a permanent self," are these only two inversions? There are four inversions: [perceiving] the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the impure as pure, and the non-self as self. Now, what is the intrinsic nature of this tetrad of inversions?
The tetrad of inversions [arises] from three views. (9ab)

From the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arises the eternalist view (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), which is the inversion of permanence. From the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) arise the inversions of pleasure and purity. From the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), which is the inversion of self. Others say that [the view of a self-identity] includes everything. How is the view of "mine" (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*) an inversion? And how would it not be an inversion? [It is an inversion] because of the *Viparyāsa-sūtra*. One who perceives the self as the master therein perceives "mine"; thus this is simply the view of a self with two aspects. Otherwise, from the notion "I," there would have to be a distinct view "mine. There would also have to be [the notions] "by me" and "for me."

Why are the other afflictions not considered perversions? Because the establishment of perversions is based on three reasons. Which three? Because they are contrary to reality, because they involve deliberation, and because they involve superimposition. (9bc)

Because it is exclusively inverted, because it determines its object, and because it involves superimposition, the view of annihilationism and false view are not superimposing; this is because they function by way of negation (*abhāvamukha*). The adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not exclusively inverted, because its object is purification through that alone. Other afflictions (*kleśa*) are not investigative; therefore, they are not inversions. As for what was stated in the Sūtra: "Regarding the impermanent as permanent is a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā*), a perversion of mind (*citta*), and a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi*),"—in this context, it is the view itself that constitutes the perversion.
But perception and mind [arise] under its influence. //9//

It is solely by virtue of the perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*) that the associated perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) are called "perversions. Why are feeling (*vedanā*) and the others not also so called? Because of worldly convention (*loka-prasiddhi*). In the world, it is well known that one has a "perverted perception" or a "perverted mind," but not a "perverted feeling. All these perversions are abandoned by the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), because views, along with their associated factors, are to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-praheya*).

There are twelve inversions (*viparyāsa*). Regarding the impermanent as permanent, there are three inversions of perception (*saṃjñā*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), and mind (*citta*). This continues in the same way up to regarding the non-self as self. Among these, eight are to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and four are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). According to other schools (*nikāyāntarīya*), there are also inversions of perception and mind regarding suffering and the impure. Otherwise, how could sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) arise in a noble one (*ārya*) who is not yet free from passion, if it were without the perception of pleasure and purity?

The Vaibhāṣikas do not accept this. For if the two perversions [of permanence and self] are observed in a Noble One because of the occurrence of the perceptions and thoughts of pleasure and purity, why are the other two perversions [of self and permanence] not also accepted as occurring due to the occurrence of the perception and thought of a sentient being? Indeed, sexual desire toward a woman or toward oneself is not logical without the perception of a sentient being. It is also said in the Sūtra: "Insofar as the learned noble disciple understands, as it truly is, that 'this is the Noble Truth of Suffering'..."

"At that time, whatever perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*) he had regarding the impermanent as permanent was abandoned," and so forth in detail. Therefore, it is only perception and mind arising from [wrong] views that are perversions, and not others, because they are merely momentary delusions, like the delusion of a fire-brand wheel or a painted yakṣa. As for what was said by the Elder Ānanda concerning the noble Vāgīśa:
"By a perversion of perceptions, your mind is consumed with fever."
"Therefore, one should avoid that sign which is auspicious and associated with passion.
Thus, others maintain that all eight distortions of perception and mind (*saṃjñā-cittaviparyāsa*) remain unabandoned for a trainee (*śaikṣa*).

These too are abandoned through the thorough knowledge of the noble truths (*āryasatya*) as they truly are; they are not abandoned without that [knowledge]. Since this explains the means [of abandonment], there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.
Now, is this distinction only for the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*) and not for others? It also exists for pride (*māna*). How so? He says: there are seven types of pride:

(1) pride (*māna*), (2) excessive pride (*atimāna*), (3) pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), (4) the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*), (5) overweening pride (*abhimāna*), (6) inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), and (7) false pride (*mithyāmāna*). Pride is said to be the inflation of the mind without further differentiation; it becomes sevenfold through its various modes of operation.

Pride (*māna*) is the inflation of one who thinks, "I am superior to the inferior" or "I am equal to the equal. Excessive pride (*atimāna*) is thinking, "I am superior to the equal. Pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*) is thinking, "I am superior to the superior. The pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*) belongs to one who regards the five aggregates of clinging as self or belonging to a self. Overweening pride (*abhimāna*) is thinking, "I have attained a special realization," when such a realization has not been attained. Inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*) is thinking, "I am only slightly inferior" to one who is vastly superior. False pride (*mithyāmāna*) is thinking, "I possess virtues," when one possesses no virtues.

As for the nine types of conceit (*mānavidhā*) taught in the treatise—"I am superior," "I am equal," "I am inferior"; "there is one superior to me," "there is one equal to me," "there is one inferior to me"; "there is no one superior to me," "there is no one equal to me," "there is no one inferior to me"—these nine types [arise] from these very three conceits. (10ab)

From which three? From pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*). Among these, the first triad consists of the three types of pride based on views: excessive pride, pride, and inferiority pride. The second triad consists of inferiority pride, excessive pride, and pride. The third triad consists of pride, excessive pride, and inferiority pride. It is indeed logical that one who is inferior by a great degree [compared to another] thinks, "I am only slightly inferior," and thus conceives *ūnamāna* (inferiority pride), because this is a basis for arrogance. But in the case of thinking, "There is no one inferior to me," what basis for arrogance could there be?

There exists one who, among the multitude of beings regarded as superior, considers even himself to be inferior; furthermore, there is indeed the rule established in the *Jñānaprasthāna*. However, taking up the exposition from the *Prakaraṇapāda*, there may be pride (*māna*), overweening pride (*atimāna*), or pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*)—the latter three being in relation to those who are inferior, equal, or superior, respectively, based on the thought "I am better. Now, as to whether these seven types of pride are to be abandoned by what, he says:
they are destroyed by vision and cultivation (*dṛgbhāvanākṣayāḥ*). (10b)

Their destruction occurs through vision (*dṛg*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*). What is meant by this is that all [afflictions] are to be abandoned by both vision and cultivation. If an affliction to be abandoned by cultivation has not yet been abandoned, does it necessarily manifest for the Noble Ones (*ārya*)? Not necessarily. For example:
"The outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) such as killing, etc., are to be abandoned by cultivation" (10cd).

That outburst of affliction by which one would intentionally commit the killing of a living being, up to and including false speech—that is to be abandoned by cultivation, because it takes as its object phenomena (*dharma*) that are themselves to be abandoned by cultivation.
Likewise:
(10d) [p.286] the desire for non-existence (*vibhava*),
that is, craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*), is also to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*).
What is this dharma called "non-existence" (*vibhava*)? It is the impermanence of the three realms. Craving for that [non-existence] is craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*).

By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), a portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) is included, such as: "O, would that I were Airāvaṇa, the king of nāgas," and so forth. It has been stated that there are various types of pride (*māna*) that are to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and among them is the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*).
Yet, for a noble one (*ārya*), [this pride does not exist].
The [afflictions] beginning with ignorance arise, but not egoism (asmitā).
By the inclusion of the word "beginning" (ādi), there is the inclusion of everything up to the thirst for existence (vibhavatṛṣṇā). (11abc)

What is the reason that these do not manifest even though they have not been abandoned? Because they are nourished by views: for the various types of pride and the pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*) are nourished by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); thus, because their backs have been broken, they do not venture to rise up again. The obsession with killing and so forth is nourished by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Craving for non-existence (*vibhavatṛṣṇā*) is nourished by the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). A portion of craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) is nourished by the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
Nor is there unwholesome remorse. //11d//
Furthermore, unwholesome regret is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); yet that does not occur for a Noble One (*ārya*), because it is originated from doubt (*vicikitsā*).
Now, among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many are universal (*sarvatraga*) and how many are non-universal?
Those views (*dṛṣṭi*) which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its cause are universal.
Doubt, along with those [ten] and that ignorance which is unique [to the Buddha]. //12//

The views to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as doubt, the ignorance associated with them, and the independent (aveṇikī) ignorance to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin—these eleven underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are universal within their own homogeneous realm (*sabhāgadhātu-sarvatraga*). These consist of seven views, two doubts, and two ignorances, because they take the entirety of their own realm as their object.

Does one take these as objects simultaneously or successively? If successively, the same consequence would apply to other [factors] as well. If simultaneously, who could believe that the entire realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is a means of purification, or that what is not a cause is a cause? It is not said that one takes everything simultaneously as an object; rather, it is all five types [of objects] together that are taken simultaneously. Even so, wherever there is the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), there is craving for self (*ātmatṛṣṇā*); wherever there are the views of excellence and purity (*agra-śuddhi-dṛṣṭī*), there is longing for them, and from that, pride (*māna*). Thus, craving and pride would also result in being universal (*sarvatraga*).

This being the case, since these two have as their objects that which is to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*) and that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), how are they to be abandoned?

They would be abandoned by cultivation because their objects are mixed. Alternatively, however, they are to be abandoned by seeing because they function through the reinforcement of the power of [wrong] views.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that these two are afflictions of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*) and not universal afflictions (*sāmānya-kleśa*); therefore, they are not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*).
Of these eleven underlying tendencies that have been described as universal within their own homogeneous realm, nine have the higher realms as their object, excluding two types of views. (13ab)

Excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the other nine underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are universal within their own dissimilar realms (*visabhāga-dhātu-sarvatraga*). However, they sometimes take one dissimilar realm as their object, and sometimes two. This is because of the statement: "Those underlying tendencies associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that have the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as their object; those associated with the desire realm that have the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as their object; and those associated with the desire realm that have both the form and formless realms as their objects."

When one abiding in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) generates the view of a self-entity (sattvadṛṣṭi) and the view of permanence (nityadṛṣṭi) regarding Brahmā, how is it that the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) do not have a different realm as their object? [The answer is: because there is no grasping [of Brahmā] as "self" or "mine," and because the view of extremes arises from that [view of a self-identity]. What, then, is this view?
"This is not a view; rather, this is false knowledge," so say the Abhidharmikas.
But from what [authority] is it established that one view has that as its object while this other does not?
The established tenet (siddhānta) must be accepted as the proof.
Are only the latent dispositions (anuśaya) universal (sarvatraga)? No, it is said:
"Excluding their acquisition (prāpti), those factors that coexist with them are also universal. (13cd)

Those other dharmas that coexist with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) are also universal. However, their acquisitions (*prāpti*) are not so, because they have multiple fruits. For this very reason, there is a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭika*) regarding whether something may be a universal proclivity but not have a universal cause as its cause: The first permutation consists of future universal proclivities. The second consists of past and present [dharmas] coexisting with them. The third and fourth permutations should be applied accordingly.
Among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many have contaminated objects (*sāsravālambana*) and how many have uncontaminated objects (*anāsravālambana*)?

Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), the ignorance associated with those two, and ignorance alone—these six, which are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, have the uncontaminated as their domain. (14)

There are three latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation: false view, doubt, and ignorance, as well as those associated with them and the independent [ignorance]. These same three are also to be abandoned through the vision of the path. Thus, these six have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object; it is established that the remaining ones have the tainted (*sāsrava*) as their object.
Furthermore, among those, the path is the cessation belonging to its own level.
It pertains to the six stages and the nine stages;
for the path that is the object of those whose range is that [object] is mutually causal. (15)

For those [afflictions] such as wrong view that have cessation as their object, the object is exclusively the cessation of their own level; for those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is exclusively the cessation of the desire realm, and so on up to those belonging to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), for which it is exclusively the cessation of the peak of existence. For those that have the path as their object, all of the path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) across six levels is the object for those belonging to the desire realm. Furthermore, that which is the antidote to the form and formless realms is the nine-level path for those belonging to the eight levels of the form and formless realms.

The entire path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is the object [of the path], because paths serve as mutual causes for one another. Although both dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge are mutual causes, subsequent knowledge is not the antidote to the desire realm; therefore, those [factors] belonging to the desire realm that have the path as their object do not take the factors belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge as their objects. In that case, since dharma-knowledge is the antidote to the form and formless realms, it will be the object of those [factors] belonging to those levels that have the path as their object.

That is not the antidote for all [defilements], because the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) and its origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) are not antidotes for those [defilements of the higher realms]. Nor is it the antidote for all [defilements] of the form and formless realms, because they are not antidotes for those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*). Thus, due to the absence of such [antidotal function], it does not become an object (*ālambana*).

Now, why are attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and the two types of adherence—adherence to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and adherence to rites and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*)—not accepted as having the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object?
[It is because] attachment is not [so accepted] because it is something to be abandoned (*varjyatvāt*). (16a) [p.289]

For passion (*rāga*) is to be abandoned; if it were to have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object, it would not be something to be abandoned, just like the desire for wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-chanda*).

Hatred (*dveṣa*) is not [to be abandoned] because it does not [arise] toward that which causes harm; for hostility (*pratigha*) arises toward an object that causes harm, and neither cessation (*nirodha*) nor the path (*mārga*) are such objects.
There is neither pride nor the two types of grasping, because of its being peaceful, pure, and supreme. //16cd//

Because cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are peaceful, arrogance toward them cannot occur. Because they are pure in their true nature, the grasping at them as pure is not the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Furthermore, these two are supreme; yet, grasping at what is inferior as supreme is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). Therefore, it is illogical for these [two] to have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Among these ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), how many adhere by way of being objects, and how many [adhere] solely by way of association?
The universal underlying tendencies adhere to the entirety [of their respective realms].
The non-universal [mental factors] take their own level as an object and their own category. //17//

Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are universal (*sarvatraga*) adhere (*anuśerate*) to their own entire level (*bhūmi*), comprising all five categories, by way of being its object (*ālambana*). However, those that are not universal adhere to their own category (*nikāya*) alone within their own level by way of being its object, and not to another. For example, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśanaprahātavya*) adhere only to the category to be abandoned by the vision of suffering; likewise, up to those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*), they adhere only to that which is to be abandoned by cultivation, and not to another. Having stated this general rule (*utsarga*), he now states an exception (*apavāda*):
they do not have the untainted (*anāsrava*) or the higher levels as their objects.

Latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object do not increase by way of that object, nor do those that have a higher stage (*ūrdhvabhūmi*) as their object. What is the reason? Because the entity that serves as their object is not appropriated (*asvīkāra*), owing to its being an adversary (*vipakṣa*). (18b)

For when a given thing has been appropriated by the view of self and craving for self, other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are also able to follow along within it, just as dust settles upon a moist cloth. Neither the untainted (*anāsrava*) nor the higher stages are like this; therefore, those [dispositions] do not lie latent with respect to them as their objects. However, one who remains here may still long for that higher stage.

This wholesome desire for the Dharma (dharmacchanda) and the two states of nirvana and the path are the adversaries of the afflictions that take them as their objects; likewise, a higher stage is the adversary of those belonging to lower stages. Therefore, the afflictions do not find a foothold within them, just as footprints cannot leave an impression on a heated stone. Here, the meaning of "latent tendency" (anuśaya) is the sense of being "conducive" (ānuguṇya). Others, however, maintain that they are not conducive to those [wholesome states], like dry food does not adhere to one suffering from flatulence. Thus, it has been explained how they lie latent by way of their objects.
But that which is associated with another is [associated] with it by way of association. //18cd//

The term "they adhere" (*anuśerate*) is understood to carry over. Whatever latent disposition (*anuśaya*) is associated with a particular dharma, it adheres to that dharma by way of association (*saṃprayoga*), provided it has not yet been abandoned; this is the purpose of the word "tu" (but/however). Could there be latent dispositions that have uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) but are not universal (*sarvatraga*) across different realms? And could those latent dispositions adhere by way of association rather than by way of their object? There could be latent dispositions that are universal within a different realm or level (*visabhāga-bhūmi-sarvatraga*). Among these ninety-eight latent dispositions, how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? All those in the higher realms are indeterminate.

First, all [factors] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). What is the reason? Because afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) factors would have suffering as their maturation (*vipāka*), yet that does not exist in those two realms, due to the absence of causes for harming others.
In the desire realm, there is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the delusion (*moha*) associated with these two. (19bcd)

In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), along with the ignorance associated with them, are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). What is the reason? Because they are not in conflict with giving and the other perfections. One gives gifts and observes moral discipline thinking, "I shall become happy after passing away. Even the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) is conducive to liberation. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "This is the foremost among the views of outsiders, namely: 'May I not be, and may nothing be mine; may I not come to be, and may nothing be mine.
Furthermore, because these two views are deluded regarding their own substance and do not function to cause harm to others, they are indeterminate.

The same consequence would apply to the thirst for heaven and the conceit "I am. The innate view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as it exists even among beasts and birds;
however, the former masters maintain that the conceptualized [view of a self-identity] is unwholesome (*akuśala*).
But the remaining ones here are unwholesome. //19d//
The remaining unwholesome latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
How many are roots of the unwholesome (*akuśalamūla*), and how many are not?
In the desire realm, the roots of the unwholesome are attachment (*rāga*), hostility (*pratigha*), and delusion (*mūḍhi*). (20ab)

In the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), all forms of attachment (*rāga*), all forms of hostility (*pratigha*), and all forms of delusion (*moha*)—except for those associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—are, respectively, the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*): greed (*lobha*) as an unwholesome root, hatred (*dveṣa*) as an unwholesome root, and delusion (*moha*) as an unwholesome root. For that which is both unwholesome and the root of the unwholesome is precisely what is intended by the term "unwholesome root. It is established that the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not unwholesome roots.
How many are neutral roots (*avyākṛtamūla*), and how many are not?
"There are three neutral roots" (20c).
By saying "it," he indicates their neutral nature. The Kashmiris maintain: "Whatever craving, ignorance, or wisdom is neutral—even that which is born of maturation—all of this is a neutral root.
Because they function in two ways and toward the higher [realms], there are no others than these. (21a)

It is said that doubt (*vicikitsā*) cannot be a root because its mode of operation is twofold; this is due to its instability. Nor can pride (*māna*) be a root, because its mode of operation is upward, characterized by elevation; this is because it lacks the essential properties of a root. For in the world, roots are observed to be stable and to extend downward.
[p.292] The outsiders (*bāhyaka*) maintain that there are exactly four [unwholesome roots];
the outsiders assert that there are four indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) roots.
He shows that craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and delusion (*moha*)—these are the [unwholesome roots];
however, those [four] are neutral (*avyākṛta*). Craving, views, pride, and ignorance (*avidyā*) are neutral.
For what reason do they maintain that these are neutral roots?
Because there are three types of meditators due to ignorance. //21d//
Because there are three types of meditators—those who meditate on craving, views, and pride—and these arise through the power of ignorance.

Regarding the fourteen indeterminate points (*avyākṛtavastu*) mentioned in the Sūtra, are they so called because they are indeterminate? No, he says. What then? It is said that an indeterminate point is a question to be set aside (*sthāpanīya*). For there are four kinds of questions: those to be answered categorically (*ekāṃśavyākaraṇīya*), those to be answered by analysis (*vibhajyavyākaraṇīya*), those to be answered by counter-question (*paripṛcchyavyākaraṇīya*), and those to be set aside (*sthāpanīya*).
Among these, they should be understood respectively as being answered categorically, by analysis, and by counter-question.
And it is to be established like the distinction between death and rebirth, or the difference between the self and other things. //22//

If one asks, "Will all sentient beings die? it should be answered categorically: "They will die. If one asks, "Will all be born [again]? it should be answered by distinguishing: "Those with afflictions will be born; those without afflictions will not.

If one asks, "Is a human being superior or inferior? it should be answered by asking in return: "In relation to what? If he should say, "In relation to the miserable realms (apāya)," then it should be answered: "He is superior."

Is the sentient being (sattva) other than the aggregates (skandha), or not other? This is to be set aside (sthāpanīya), because of the non-existence of a substantial entity (dravya) called a "sentient being," like the dark or fair complexion of the son of a barren woman.
How, then, is this an explanation?
It is an explanation by way of stating: "This is undeclared (avyākṛta)."

Another says: "This too is a categorical response (ekāṃśavākaraṇa), namely: 'Not all will be born. However, if one were to ask, "Will those who are going to die be born? this would be a question requiring a qualified response (vibhajyavyākaraṇīya). Furthermore, among human beings both inferiority and superiority exist relatively; thus, both should be answered categorically, just as consciousness is both an effect and a cause. But for one who asks with absolute certainty, a qualified response is not appropriate because of the lack of a categorical answer.

That "the sentient being is other than the aggregates" is precisely an undeclared [avyākṛta] matter. And it is not logical that mere non-declaration constitutes a declaration. As for a question that is to be set aside (sthāpanīya), since it is declared by way of being set aside, how is it not declared?
The Abhidharmikas say:

"The Tathāgata is the Blessed One, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha; his Dharma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha of disciples has practiced correctly; form is impermanent, and so on up to consciousness; the designation of suffering, and so on up to the designation of the path—these must be answered categorically because they are connected with the goal."

Analysis by way of division (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*) means that if someone should say, "Speak of the Dharma," one should say to him, "The dharmas are many—past, future, and present; which ones shall I speak of? If he should say, "The past," he should be told, "The past dharmas are also many, from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*). If he should say, "Form," he should be told, "Form is also threefold: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate."

If he says, "It is wholesome," [one should explain: "That too is of seven types, from abstention from taking life up to abstention from frivolous speech. If he says, "Abstention from taking life," [one should explain: "That too is of three types: born of non-greed, born of non-hatred, and born of non-delusion. If he says, "Born of non-greed," [one should explain: "Even that born of non-greed is twofold, through the distinction between informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*"); thus it should be explained by way of such analysis.

And this very case constitutes a "question-and-answer" (paripṛcchya-vyākaraṇa) for one who is deceitful; he should be told, "The dharmas are many," but they should not be analyzed further until he either remains silent or explains it himself. When those two do not ask anything at all but merely request instruction, and nothing is explained to them but they are merely questioned, how can there be a question from these two, or how can there be an answer?
For when someone says, "Tell me the way," has he not asked about the way? Since the answer is given precisely after having asked, how could this not be an answer by way of questioning?

However, that which is to be set aside (*sthāpanīya*) is such as: "Is the world finite, or is it infinite? and so forth. But the definition of the ways of answering questions should be understood from the Sūtras themselves.
The Venerable Mahāsāṃghikas recite the Sūtra:

"Monks, there are these four ways of answering questions. What are the four? Monks, there is a question to be answered categorically; there is one [to be answered] up to [the point of] being set aside. And what, monks, is the question to be answered categorically? 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent'—this, monks, is the question to be answered categorically. And what, monks, is the question to be answered by way of analysis?"

"Having performed an intentional action (*saṃcetanīyaṃ karma*), what does one experience?"—this is a question to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajyavyākaraṇīya*). And what, monks, is a question to be answered by asking for clarification (*paripṛcchyavyākaraṇīya*)? When asked, "Is a person's self identical to their perceptions (*saṃjñā*), or is perception one thing and the self another?", one should ask in return: "But which self, venerable sir, do you maintain? If he should say, "Venerable sir, I indeed maintain a gross self," [then one may explain accordingly].

If this were so, one should say: "The perception is one thing, the self is another. For this is a question that must be answered by way of inquiry (*paripṛcchya-vyākaraṇīya*). And what, monks, is a question to be set aside (*sthāpanīya-praśna*)? It is as follows: "Is the world eternal? Is it non-eternal? Is it both eternal and non-eternal? Is it neither eternal nor non-eternal? Is it finite? Is it infinite? Is it both finite and infinite? Is it neither finite nor infinite?"
"Whether a Tathāgata exists after death, or does not exist after death, up to: whether the soul is one thing and the body another—this, monks, is a question that should be set aside.

However, it must be stated for whichever person whichever latent disposition (anuśaya) lies dormant upon whichever object: "By means of which [disposition] is he associated with which [object], whether past or even present?"

In brief, these afflictions (*kleśa*) are of two kinds: afflictions by their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-kleśa*), namely attachment (*rāga*), hostility (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*); and general afflictions (*sāmānya-kleśa*), namely views (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding those first [the specific-characteristic afflictions]:
through attachment, hostility, and pride that are past or present, one is bound to that object (*vastu*) in which they have arisen and have not been abandoned. (23)

Regarding past and present attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*) that have arisen with respect to a certain object and have not yet been abandoned—one is bound (*saṃyukta*) to that object by them. For these, being afflictions characterized by their own specific marks (*svalakṣaṇakleśa*), do not necessarily arise in everyone toward every object. (24ab) "With all [objects], by these future mental [afflictions]"—the phrase "where they have not been abandoned" carries over. One is bound to every object belonging to the three times by these very same future mental afflictions of attachment, aversion, and pride, because the objects of mental [consciousness] pertain to the three times.

Regarding those belonging to one's own time period (*svādhvika*), one is bound by other [passions], namely future attachment (*rāga*) and hostility (*pratigha*), to a future object itself. Which, then, are the others? They are the attachments and hostilities associated with the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāyika*). And it is only by means of those that possess the nature of arising (*utpattidharma*).
It is by those very ones [that one is bound].
With those that are unborn— namely, those possessing the nature of non-arising— even those belonging to the five groups of consciousness are associated with all objects throughout the three times.
"But by all the remaining ones, one is bound everywhere.

[p.295] What, then, are the "remaining" ones? They are the views (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to the three time periods. By all of these, too, one is bound to every object, because they are universal afflictions (*sāmānyakleśa*). The governing phrase "as long as they have not been abandoned" continues to apply here as well.

Furthermore, does this past and future exist as a substantial entity (*dravyataḥ*), or not? If it exists, then because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) exist at all times, they would follow as being eternal (*śāśvata*). If it does not exist, how can one be joined with or disjoined from it? The Vaibhāṣikas do not assert that conditioned phenomena are eternal, because they possess the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*). Yet, they clearly assert that [phenomena] exist at all times;
what is the reason for this?

Because it has been stated (25a). For it was said by the Blessed One: "Monks, if past form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not have been indifferent toward past form. But because past form does exist, the learned noble disciple is indifferent toward past form. If future form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not have rejoiced in future form. But because future form does exist," and so forth in detail. Because of duality (25b).

It has been stated: "The arising of consciousness occurs in dependence upon a dyad. "What is the dyad? It is the eye and visible forms, up to the mind and mental objects. If the past and future did not exist, then consciousness having them as its object would not arise in dependence upon a dyad. Thus, first of all, the past and future exist according to scripture (*āgama*). They also exist according to reasoning (*yukti*), because there must be an existent object.

Consciousness arises when an object exists, not when it does not exist. If the past and future did not exist, consciousness would have a non-existent object; consequently, consciousness itself could not exist due to the absence of an object.
This is because [consciousness] is the fruit [of its object]. (25b)

If the past did not exist, how could there be a fruit of wholesome or unwholesome karma in the future? For at the time when the fruit arises, the cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) does not exist as something present. Therefore, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the past and the future certainly exist. Indeed, this must necessarily be accepted by one who holds the doctrine of the existence of all things (*sarvāstivāda*); for it is from the assertion of their existence that they are recognized as Sarvāstivādins. (25cd)

Those who assert that everything exists—namely, the past, the future, and the present—are the Sarvāstivādins. However, those who speak by making a distinction, saying that some things exist—namely, the present and that past karma which has not yet yielded its fruit—and that some things do not exist—namely, the past and the future once their fruit has been yielded—are the Vibhajyavādins.
As for how many types of these Sarvāstivādins there are, he says:
they are of four kinds. (25d)
They are designated as those who maintain that there is change in state (*bhāva*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and condition (*avasthā*).

(26ab) The Venerable Dharmatrāta is one who maintains that there is change in state (*bhāvānyathika*). He reportedly says: "When a dharma proceeds through the time-periods (*adhvan*), there is a change in its state, but not a change in its substance (*dravya*). Just as when a golden vessel is broken and made into something else, there is a change in its shape (*saṃsthāna*), but not a change in its color; and just as when milk transforms into curd, it relinquishes its taste, potency, and maturation (*rasavīryavipāka*), but not its color."

In the same way, a dharma, when coming from the future time-period to the present time-period, abandons its future state but not its substantial existence; likewise, when going from the present to the past time-period, it abandons its present state but not its substantial existence.

The Venerable Ghoṣaka is one who maintains that the characteristics [of the time periods] differ. He is said to have stated: "A dharma, as it proceeds through the time periods, when past, is endowed with the characteristic of the past, yet is not dissociated from the characteristics of the future and the present. When future, it is endowed with the characteristic of the future, yet is not dissociated from the past and the present. Likewise, the present is also not dissociated from the past and the future. It is just as, for example, a man who is attached to one woman is not thereby unattached to the others."

The Venerable Vasumitra maintains that change occurs through difference of state (*avasthānyathika*). He says: "A dharma, as it proceeds through the time-periods (*adhvan*), having reached one state after another, is designated as different due to its change of state, not due to a change in its substantial entity (*dravya*). For example, a single counting-stick placed in the units-place is called 'one'; in the hundreds-place, it is called 'one hundred'; and in the thousands-place, it is called 'one thousand'."

The Venerable Buddhadeva is a proponent of "alterity" (anyathānyathika). He is said to have stated: "A dharma, as it proceeds through the time-periods, is called 'other' and 'yet other' in relation to what precedes and follows it; this is not due to a difference in state nor a difference in substance. It is just as a single woman is called either a mother or a daughter.
Thus, these are the four Sarvāstivāda schools.

Among these, however, the first should be placed within the Sāṃkhya position because it asserts transformation (*pariṇāma*). For the second, a confusion of the time-periods (*adhvan*) would result, since everything would be endowed with all characteristics. But in the case of a person, passion for one woman manifests, while for another there is merely its possession (*samanvāgama*); what similarity is there here? Even for the fourth, three time-periods would occur within a single time-period:
in the past time-period, the preceding and succeeding moments would be past and future respectively, and the middle moment would be present; the same would apply to the future as well.
Therefore, among all these [theories], the third is the best— namely,
this one which maintains that change consists in the difference of states. According to him, indeed:
The time periods are established by way of their functional activity. //26cd//

When that dharma does not perform its activity (*kāritra*), it is future; when it performs it, it is present; and when, having performed it, it has ceased, it is past. All of this is well understood. However, this must be addressed: if the past and the future also exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*), why is that called "past" or "future"? Has it not already been stated that the time periods (*adhvan*) are established by way of their activity?
If that is so, what is the activity (*kāritra*) of a present eye that is "of the same class" (*tatsabhāga*)?
It is the giving and receiving of a fruit.

In that case, there would follow the consequence that even past causes—such as the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and others—possess activity because they give a fruit; or else, they would possess only half an activity. Thus, there would be a confusion of definitions (*lakṣaṇasaṃkara*).

And this must be addressed: if a dharma exists by that very same nature and performs its activity eternally, what obstacle is there such that it performs its activity at one time and not at another? If you say it is the incompleteness of conditions (*pratyaya*), we say no; for [you] have admitted its eternal existence. Furthermore, regarding that which is called past, future, and present activity (*kāritra*):

In that case, how is this so? Is there yet another activity (*kāritra*) belonging to activity itself? Or rather, does it neither exist as past, nor as future, nor as present, and yet exist? If so, because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it follows that it exists eternally. Therefore, one should not say that when a dharma does not perform its activity, it is then "future.
This fault would indeed arise if activity were something other than the dharma; however, it is actually [not other].
Since there is nothing other than this, this fault does not arise;
if that is the case, then it is that very same thing.
(27b) The non-connection with the time-periods (*adhvāyoga*).

If the activity (*kāritra*) is indeed the phenomenon (*dharma*) itself, why is that very same phenomenon, existing with that very same nature, sometimes called "past" and sometimes called "future"? Thus, the establishment of the time-periods would not be possible. What is it that is not established here? For that phenomenon which has not yet arisen is the future; that which has arisen but has not yet perished is the present; and that which has perished is the past. This is precisely what must be addressed here: if the past and the future exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*) just as the present exists, then for that [phenomenon],...
Likewise, regarding that which exists:

by what [means] could there be the state of being unborn or destroyed for a dharma that exists by that very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? How can it be established that "this is unborn" or "this is destroyed"? What was previously non-existent for this [dharma], due to the absence of which it is called "unborn"? And what is non-existent afterwards, due to the absence of which it is called "destroyed"? Therefore, the three time periods (*adhvan*) are not established in any way whatsoever here, if one does not accept that "having not been, it comes to be," and "having been, it no longer exists."

As for what was said—that "there is no consequence of eternalism because of the connection with the characteristics of the conditioned"—this is mere words, since production and destruction are impossible [for such a thing]. To say that "that dharma exists eternally by name, yet it is not eternal" is an unprecedented mode of expression. As it has indeed been said:
"The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) exists at all times, yet the entity (bhāva) is not admitted to be eternal;
nor is the entity other than its intrinsic nature—this is clearly the work of Īśvara! [p. 299]

As for what was stated, "because it has been said," we too say that the past and the future exist. However, the past is that which has previously occurred, and the future is that which will occur when the cause is present. It is in this sense that they are said to "exist," but not as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*).
Who says that they exist in the same manner as the present? How else could they exist?

[The opponent asks: "But this [objection] has been raised against you: 'If it exists eternally, how can it be called past or future? Therefore, in order to make known that the cause which previously existed and the fruit which will exist have indeed existed and will exist, and for the purpose of refuting the view that denies cause and fruit, the Blessed One said: "The past exists; the future exists. This is because the word *asti* is an indeclinable (*nipāta*).

Just as people say that a lamp has prior non-existence and subsequent non-existence, and just as they say, "That lamp has ceased, but it was not extinguished by me," so too it is said that the past and future exist. Otherwise, the very existence of the past and future would not be established.

If so, what did the Blessed One mean when he spoke with reference to the *Laguḍaśikhīyaka* wanderers, saying, "That action which is past—exhausted, ceased, vanished, and transformed—that exists"? Did they not accept that the action had previously existed?

Furthermore, in that context, it was said with reference to the capacity to yield a fruit which has been deposited within that continuum. Otherwise, it would not be established that the past exists by way of its own intrinsic nature. And this is exactly as stated by the Blessed One in the *Paramārtha-śūnyatā-sūtra*: "The eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation."

"For thus, monks, the eye, having not been, comes to be; and having been, it passes away. If the future eye were to exist, it would not have been said that "having not been, it comes to be. If you argue that "having not been" means "having not been in the present time," we say no; for the time period is not a different entity from the thing itself. If, on the other hand, it means "having not been in its own self," then it is established that the future eye does not exist.

As for what was said—that "consciousness arises in dependence upon a duality"—this must first be considered here: when mental consciousness arises in dependence upon the mind (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharmas*), are the *dharmas* its generative condition (*janaka-pratyaya*) just as the mind is, or are the *dharmas* merely the objective support (*ālambana-mātra*)?

If, first of all, phenomena (*dharma*) are the productive conditions (*janaka-pratyaya*), how could that which is future—whether it will exist after a thousand eons or not—produce consciousness now? Furthermore, *nirvāṇa* cannot logically be a producer, because it is the cessation of all activity. Alternatively, if phenomena are merely objects of cognition (*ālambana-mātra*), we say that even the past and the future serve as objects.
If they do not exist, how can they be objects?
To this, we now reply: they exist in the very manner in which they are taken as objects.

How was that object [of cognition] in the past, and how will it be in the future? For no one, when recollecting past form or feeling, perceives it as "it exists. What then? They perceive it as "it existed. Indeed, just as present form is experienced, so too is that past form recollected; and just as the future attains the state of being present. Now, if it does not exist, it is established that even a non-existent thing can be an object of cognition.

If it is argued that "that very same thing is merely dispersed," we say no, because what is dispersed is not perceived. Furthermore, if that very same form were simply divided into atoms, then it would follow that atoms are eternal; and in this case, there would be nothing more than the mere aggregation and dispersion of atoms. Consequently, since nothing at all would be produced or ceased, one would be adopting the doctrine of the Ājīvikas.

Furthermore, the Sūtra would be contradicted by the detailed passage: "When the eye arises, it does not come from anywhere," and so forth. How could there be a dispersion of feelings and other mental factors that are not composed of atoms? Moreover, these are remembered exactly as they were experienced when they arose. If they exist in that very same way [as they are remembered], it follows that they are eternal. If, on the other hand, they do not exist [in that way], then it is established that even a non-existent thing can be an object of cognition (*ālambana*). If even a non-existent thing could be an object, then there would have to be a thirteenth sense-field (*āyatana*).
If there is no thirteenth sense-field, then what is the object of this consciousness?

This very name is the object of cognition. If that were so, it would follow that one perceives that the name itself does not exist. And for one who takes the prior non-existence of a sound as an object, what is his object?
The sound itself.

If that were so, then for one who seeks the absence of sound, the sound itself would have to be produced. If you argue that it is in its future state, how can there be the cognition "it does not exist" when it actually exists? If you say it is because the present [sound] does not exist, no; for they are one and the same. Or rather, whatever specific quality it may have, the establishment of its non-existence after having been non-existent [is what is meant]. Therefore, both existence and non-existence are the objective supports (*ālambana*) of consciousness. As for what was said by the Bodhisattva: "That which does not exist in the world, I shall either know or see—that is impossible"—[this refers to the impossibility of perceiving something as a real entity where none exists].

Others, being conceited, perceive even a non-existent appearance as existent; my intention here, however, is that I perceive only what is truly existent as "it exists. Otherwise, if all cognitions always had a real object, from where would this deliberation arise, or what would be the distinction? And this is indeed so, as the Blessed One has stated elsewhere: "Let a monk who is my disciple come; whatever I have taught him in the morning, he shall strive for further distinction by the evening."

"Having been instructed in the evening, he will go forth for further distinction at dawn; he will know the existent as existent and the non-existent as non-existent, the surpassable as surpassable and the unsurpassable as unsurpassable. Therefore, this too is not a valid reason, because consciousness has an existent object.

As for what was said, "from the fruit" (25b): the Sautrāntikas certainly do not describe the arising of a fruit from a past action. What then? [They say it arises] from a specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtānaviśeṣa*) preceded by that [action].
