We shall explain this in detail in the refutation of the theory of a self (*ātmavādapratiṣedha*). For one who holds that the past and future exist as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*), the fruit exists eternally; what, then, is the efficacy of the action in that case? Its efficacy lies in its production [of the fruit].

Thus, it is established that "having not existed, it comes to be. But if everything exists at all times, what now has causal efficacy (*sāmarthya*) toward what? In this way, the doctrine of the Vārṣagaṇyas is illuminated: "That which exists, exists; that which does not exist, does not exist. There is no arising of the non-existent, and there is no destruction of the existent.
In that case, causal efficacy must reside in the act of bringing something into the present.

What is this so-called "making present"? If it means being drawn to another location, then [the dharma] would necessarily be eternal; furthermore, how could that apply to formless dharmas? Moreover, that drawing forth which occurs has come into being after not having existed. If it means a modification of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the fact that it comes into being after not having existed is already established. Therefore, the Sarvāstivāda doctrine—that the past and future exist substantially—is not tenable within the Teaching.

It is correct, however, that one speaks in accordance with what is stated in the Sūtra: "Everything exists. How is it stated in the Sūtra that "everything exists"? It says: "O Brāhmaṇa, 'everything exists' refers precisely to the twelve bases (āyatana), or else to the three time periods. As for how that [everything] exists, it has been explained accordingly. Now, if the past and the future do not exist, how can one be bound by or to them?

One is bound to an object because of the presence of latent dispositions (anuśaya) born from it and caused by it; and because of the presence of the latent dispositions of the afflictions that take that object as their support, one is bound to the thing.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the past and the future certainly exist. Regarding that which cannot be led [into logical consistency], one who desires their own welfare should understand it thus: "Profound indeed is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). (27d)

It is not necessarily the case that [this] is to be established by logical reasoning (*tarka*). There is a way of speaking (*paryāya*) according to which that which arises ceases: form arises, form ceases. There is a way of speaking according to which one thing arises and another ceases: the future arises and the present ceases. Even a time-period (*adhvan*) arises, because that which is arising is included within a time-period. Even from a time-period [something] arises, because the future time-period consists of multiple moments (*kṣaṇika*). This concludes what was introduced as a digression.

Now this is investigated: Is it the case that when an object is abandoned, one is dissociated from that object; or rather, when one is dissociated from something, that object is abandoned for him? First, wherever one is dissociated, that object is abandoned for him. However, there may be abandonment without being dissociated from that [object], as follows:
When what is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering has been abandoned, one remains bound by all the remaining universal [defilements].
And when a category [of defilement] has been previously abandoned, one remains bound by the remaining impurities that have that [category] as their object. (28)

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, the category of afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering is abandoned. When that is abandoned, one remains bound by the universal [afflictions] to be abandoned by the vision of origin which take that [abandoned category] as their object. Regarding the category to be abandoned by cultivation as well, even when a particular type among the nine types has been previously abandoned, it should be understood that one is still associated with the remaining afflictions that take that [category] as their object.

If one were to explain, step by step, how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere to each specific object, it would result in a vast amount that must be said. Therefore, they provide a summary analysis (*piṇḍavibhāṣā*). [The purpose is]: "How may we resolve the great flood of questions with the least possible effort? In brief, these are sixteen factors: those belonging to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, which are of five types, as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*). The minds (*citta*) are also exactly sixteen.
In this regard, having understood which phenomenon is the object of which mind, one should then infer how many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) adhere to that [object].
First, among those [tendencies], there are those born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) which are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, the vision of its cause, and by cultivation.
Their objects are their own three [realms], the one [realm] attained in the form realm, and the pure [unconditioned]. //29//

"Own and those three" (*svakatrayam*) means that which is its own and those three. "One and that belonging to the form realm" (*ekarūpāptam*) means one and that which is attained in the form realm; this is the method of analysis. First, the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), are the objects of five types of consciousness: of the three belonging to its own realm (those same ones), of the one belonging to the higher realm (only that which is to be abandoned by cultivation), and of the untainted (*anāsrava*). "Those born in the form realm are the objects of their own, the three of the lower, the one of the upper, and the pure" (30ab).

Those same three types of dharmas belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) are the objects of eight consciousnesses: of the three belonging to their own realm; of the three belonging to the lower realm; of the one belonging to the higher realm, which is exclusively that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*); and of the untainted (*anāsrava*). Those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyaja*) have as their range the three categories pertaining to the three realms and the untainted. (30cd)

Those same three types of factors belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) are the objects of ten minds: those three types belonging to the three realms, and the untainted (*anāsrava*). Thus, the factors belonging to the three realms that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin, as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation, have been explained.
(31ab) All [factors] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path have their own respective spheres as their domain. [p. 303]

Regarding those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*), their own mind is precisely that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the vision of the path. It should be understood that for such a [mind], those [defilements] are the objects (*ālambana*). How so? For the factors belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation are the objects of six consciousnesses: of the five previously mentioned [consciousnesses] and of that very same [consciousness] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation. The same applies to those to be abandoned by the vision of the path.

[These] are the objects of nine or eleven minds: namely, the five previously mentioned [minds], plus that additional mind to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārgadarśanaprahātavya*). In the same way, those belonging to the realms of form and formlessness [are explained]. A mind to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path is the object of that very [mind] to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, plus an additional mind; thus, they become the objects of nine and eleven minds respectively. The dharmas of the three realms, consisting of five types, have been explained.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) [dharmas] are the objects of the last three [types of minds] of the three realms and of the untainted [minds] themselves. (31cd)

Untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are the objects of ten types of consciousness: those belonging to the three realms that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, and those of each of the three categories [of afflictions], as well as the untainted itself.
Furthermore, this same meaning is summarized in a verse and a half:
"In the three realms, those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its cause, by cultivation, and the stainless ones [are the objects]."

"Those [defilements] abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path have as their objects five, eight, ten, or ten consciousnesses; all of them have as their objects their own [respective category] plus the higher.

Having thus established the sixteen types of mental objects for these sixteen states of mind in various ways, how should the activity of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) be applied? We shall show just a general direction.

When the question arises as to how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere to a consciousness that has the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object, one must investigate as follows: The faculty of pleasure is of seven kinds—the four types belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāprahātavya*), the five types belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), and the untainted (*anāsrava*). In brief, this constitutes the object of a consciousness consisting of twelve factors: namely, the four types belonging to the desire realm, excluding those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśanaheya*).

This is the twelvefold consciousness that has the faculty of pleasure as its object: [consciousness] belonging to the form realm of five types, that belonging to the formless realm of two types—namely, those to be abandoned by seeing the path and by cultivation—and that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).

In this regard, it should be understood that, as the case may be, the four categories belonging to the desire realm, the categories belonging to the form realm that have conditioned phenomena as their objects, the two categories belonging to the formless realm, and the universal latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) all adhere (*anuśerate*) to it.

In a consciousness that has as its object the object of the pleasure faculty (*sukhendriya*), how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhere? Furthermore, that consciousness which has the pleasure faculty as its object is twelvefold; of what consciousness is it the object? It is the object of that very same twelvefold [consciousness], and additionally of two types belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*)—those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and those to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

It should be understood that these fourteen types of consciousness, which take as their object the object of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), have latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) adhering to them—specifically, by adding the two [categories] belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, along with the four groups belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), the four groups belonging to the formless realm, and those belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) that have conditioned phenomena as their objects.
By this method, other cases should also be understood accordingly.

By which latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) a mind is "with latent disposition," those latent dispositions "adhere" (*anuśerate*) to that mind; or they may not adhere. Those latent dispositions which are associated with that mind and have not been abandoned, as well as those whose objects (*ālambana*) have not been abandoned, adhere to it. Those latent dispositions which are associated with that mind but have been abandoned, and whose objects have also been abandoned, do not adhere to it. Having established this, it is said: "A defiled mind is 'with latent disposition' in two ways; a non-defiled [mind] is [so] by means of those that adhere. (32ab)

A defiled mind is "with latent tendencies" (*sānuśaya*) because of the latent tendencies that are active within it—those which are associated with it and have it as their object and have not yet been abandoned—as well as those which are active and have been abandoned but remain associated with it, due to the mind being accompanied by them. A non-defiled mind, however, is "with latent tendencies" only through those latent tendencies that are active and have it as their object and have not yet been abandoned.

Now, how do these ten latent tendencies function? First of all, due to the conjunction with ignorance (*avidyā*), one is deluded regarding the [Four] Truths. Suffering does not appeal to such a person, and so on up to the Path; from that state of delusion arises doubt (*moha-ākāṅkṣā*). (32c)
Having heard both sides, the deluded person gives rise to doubt, thinking, "Is this suffering, or is this not suffering? and so forth. From that arises false view (32bc);
for one who is in doubt, false views proceed from false hearing and reflection, because of the arising of false certainties such as, "There is no suffering," and so on.
From that, the view of a self-identity [arises]. //32d//

It is said that from false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises, because one rejects the aggregates as suffering and instead adheres to them as a self. From that, the grasping at extremes (*antagrāha*) occurs;
from the view of a self-identity, the view of grasping at extremes arises, because one grasps at the extremes of the self being either eternal or annihilated.

Therefore, from the [view of] extremes comes the misapprehension of asceticism and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), because one returns to the notion of purity through that very extreme which one has grasped. From that, [the view of self arises].

The term "clinging" (*āmarśa*) continues [from the previous context]. From the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) proceeds, because one grasps as supreme that by which one believes purification is attained. Following that, there is passion (*rāga*) for one's own view and pride (*māna*), due to attachment to it and the resulting sense of superiority.
Hatred occurs elsewhere [than in one's own view]:

hatred arises toward another’s view which stands in opposition to one’s own view, which has been clung to. Others, however, maintain that hatred occurs even toward one’s own view when it has been abandoned after being previously grasped; for the passion and other afflictions to be abandoned by seeing have as their object the very views belonging to one’s own continuum.
Such is the sequence. (33d)
This is the sequence of the manifestation of these ten afflictions.
When they arise, however, they arise due to three causes:
from the unabandoned latent tendency (*anuśaya*), from the presence of the object (*viṣaya*), and from the [corresponding] attention.

From improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*), affliction arises; that is to say, when the latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*) has not been abandoned and is not fully understood, and phenomena conducive to the outburst of sensual desire (*kāmarāgaparyavasthānīya*) come into range, and there is improper mental attention toward them—in this way, sensual desire arises. These, respectively, are the powers of the cause, the object, and the application. It should be understood that other afflictions as well arise in the same manner when their complete set of causes is present. (34d) [p.306]

It is said that sometimes these arise solely through the power of the object (*viṣaya-bala*) and not through the power of the cause (*hetu-bala*), as in the case of an Arhat subject to regression (*parihāṇa-dharmaka*). These very same latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) were taught by the Blessed One in the Sūtra as the three outflows (*āsrava*): the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). They are also the four floods (*ogha*): the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance. They are likewise the four yokes (*yoga*). Furthermore, they are the four clingings (*upādāna*): clinging to sensual desire, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances (*śīla-vrata-upādāna*), and clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavāda-upādāna*). Regarding these, first:

The outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*) consists of the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) together with the secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), excluding delusion (*moha*). (35abc) Excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), the other afflictions of the desire realm, along with the secondary afflictions, should be understood as the outflow of desire; they consist of forty-one entities: thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—excluding the five types of ignorance—and ten secondary afflictions.
In the realms of form and formlessness, the latent dispositions themselves constitute the outflow of existence (bhavāsrava). //35cd//

The phrase "without delusion" (vinā mohena) carries over [from the previous context]. The outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*) consists of fifty-two entities: the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) belonging to the realms of form and formlessness, excluding ignorance (*avidyā*). Specifically, there are twenty-six latent dispositions belonging to the realm of form, excluding the five types of ignorance; likewise, there are twenty-six belonging to the realm of formlessness.

But is it not the case that even there [in the form and formless realms] there are two types of outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), namely torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*)? And in the *Prakaraṇas* it is said: "What is the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*)? With the exception of ignorance (*avidyā*), those other fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts associated with the form and formless realms. Why, then, are they not included here? The Kashmiris say: "Because they lack independence.
But what is the reason that the latent dispositions belonging to the form and formless realms are stated collectively as a single outflow of existence?
Because they are neutral (*avyākṛta*), inwardly directed, and belong to the stages of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*).

Therefore, they are unified (36abc). For both of these are unified by way of a threefold similarity: they are all neutral (*avyākṛta*), they function inwardly (*antarmukha-pravṛtta*), and they belong to the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmika*). And for the very same reason that "attachment to existence" (*bhavarāga*) was mentioned, for that same reason "the outflow of existence" (*bhavāsrava*) is mentioned; thus it is established that ignorance (*avidyā*) belonging to the three realms is now the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyāsrava*). These consist of fifteen entities.
For what reason is this [ignorance] established separately? Because of all of them... [p.307]
Ignorance is the root; thus, it is a separate outflow (āsrava). //36cd//

Just as these outflows (*āsrava*) have been explained, so too should the floods (*ogha*) and yokes (*yoga*) be understood. However, views (*dṛṣṭi*) are treated separately because of their sharpness. (37ab) The flood of desire (*kāmaugha*) and the yoke of desire (*kāmayoga*) are simply the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*). Likewise, the flood of existence (*bhavaugha*) and the yoke of existence (*bhavayoga*) are simply the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), with the exception of views. It is said that those [views] are established separately within the floods and yokes because of their intensity.
For those who have no companions among the outflows, it is said that there is no conformity with them. //37cd//

The etymological definition of the *āsravas* as "those which cause one to settle" (*āsayanti*) will be explained later. It is said that views (*dṛṣṭi*) alone are not conducive to settling because of their sharpness; therefore, they are not established separately among the *āsravas*. They are established by being mixed together. Thus, the flood of desire (*kāmaugha*) consists of twenty-nine substances: fifteen instances of attachment, hostility, and pride; four instances of doubt; and ten instances of the secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*). The flood of existence (*bhavaugha*) consists of twenty-eight substances: twenty instances of attachment and pride, and eight instances of doubt.
The flood of views consists of thirty-six entities; the flood of ignorance consists of fifteen entities. The yokes should be understood to be like the floods.
As previously stated, that very [flood] together with ignorance is divided into two [yokes] by the separation of views.
The clingings [are as follows]: (38abc)

The *kāmayoga* (the bond of sensual desire), together with ignorance (*avidyā*), constitutes the clinging to sensual desire (*kāmopādāna*), consisting of thirty-four entities: twenty [instances] of attachment (*rāga*), hostility (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance; four instances of doubt (*vicikitsā*); and ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*). The *bhavayoga* (the bond of existence), together with ignorance, constitutes the clinging to the doctrine of self (*ātmavādopādāna*), consisting of thirty-eight entities: thirty [instances] of attachment, pride, and ignorance; eight instances of doubt. Having extracted the precepts and observances (*śīlavrata*) from the bond of views (*dṛṣṭiyoga*), the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*) consists of thirty entities, while the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavratopādāna*) consists of six entities.

Why is it extracted from among the views? Because it is an adversary to the Path and because it deceives both parties. Laypeople are deceived by this through practices such as fasting, under the notion that these constitute the path to heaven; renunciants are likewise deceived by the renunciation of desired objects, under the notion that this leads to the attainment of purity.

For what reason is ignorance not mentioned separately as a "clinging" (*upādāna*), but rather included within clinging? Clingings are so called because they grasp at existence (*bhava*); however, ignorance is not a grasper in that sense, and thus it is mixed in with the others. (38cd) [p. 308]

Because its characteristic is non-apprehension (*asaṃprakhyāna*), ignorance (*avidyā*) is not a grasper due to its dullness; therefore, it is said to be "mixed" [with other defilements]. However, in the Sūtra, the Blessed One said: "What is the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*)? In detail, up to: whatever sensual passion (*kāmarāga*), sensual longing (*kāmacchanda*), sensual affection (*kāmasneha*), sensual love (*kāmaprema*), sensual desire (*kāmecchā*), sensual infatuation (*kāmamūrcchā*), sensual greed (*kāmagṛddha*), intense sensual greed (*kāmaparigarddha*), sensual delight (*kāmanandī*), sensual attachment (*kāmaniyantrī*), and sensual obsession (*kāmādhyavasāna*) he has toward sensual pleasures—that remains, having completely taken possession of his mind."

This is called the bond of sensual desire (*kāmayoga*); likewise, it extends up to the bond of existence (*bhavayoga*). Furthermore, in other sūtras, desire and attachment (*chandarāga*) are stated to be grasping (*upādāna*). Therefore, it is understood that sensual desires and so forth are indeed grasping, because desire and attachment toward sensual desires and the rest constitute grasping. It has been stated in the sūtras that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) themselves are designated as outflows (*āsrava*), floods (*ogha*), bonds (*yoga*), and graspings (*upādāna*). Now, what is the meaning of "latent disposition" (*anuśaya*), and what is the meaning of "grasping" (*upādāna*)?
These are subtle (*aṇu*), they follow along (*anugata*), and they adhere in two ways (*anuśerate*).
And because they bind [the mind], they are therefore known as *anuśayas* (latent tendencies). //39//

In this context, they are called *aṇu* (subtle) because their activity is so minute that they are difficult to discern. They are "concomitant" (*anugata*) because they persist through association and attainment. They "underlie" (*anuśerate*) by way of two modes: by way of the object (*ālambana*) and by way of association (*saṃprayoga*). They "bind" (*anubadhnanti*) because they manifest again and again even when one attempts to prevent them through lack of application. For these reasons, they are termed *anuśayas*. They cause one to dwell (*āsayanti*), they flow (*āsravanti*), they carry away (*haranti*), they leave a residue (*śeṣayanti*), and they seize (*upagṛhṇanti*); such are the etymological definitions of the terms *āsrava* and the others. (Verse 40)

They are called *āsravas* because they cause one to dwell in *saṃsāra* and flow from the peak of existence down as far as the Avīci hell through the six wounds of the sense bases (*āyatana*). They are called *oghas* because they carry one away. They are called *yogas* because they bind one fast. They are called *upādānas* because they seize and grasp.

However, this [explanation] would be more correct: they are called *āsravas* because by means of them the continuum (*saṃtati*) flows toward sense objects. This is in accordance with the statement in the Sūtra: "Venerable ones, for example, a boat is led against the current with great exertions; when those very exertions are relaxed, it is carried along with the current with little difficulty. They are called *oghās* (floods) because of their excessive velocity; thus, one who possesses them is carried away, following after them.

Even when they do not manifest excessively, the applications (*yoga*) are called "graspings" (*upādāna*) because they join one to various sufferings, or because of their constant persistence through the grasping of sense-pleasures and so forth.
Furthermore, they are taught as fivefold according to the distinctions of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the rest.

Those very same latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are further explained by dividing them into five categories: fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts (*paryavasthāna*). Among these, there are nine fetters: the fetters of attachment (*anunaya*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), adherence (*parāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*). Therein, the fetter of attachment is craving belonging to the three realms. The others are to be applied accordingly as appropriate. The fetter of views consists of three views; the fetter of adherence consists of two views.

Therefore it is said: "Could it be that one is bound by the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) to those factors associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta-dharma*), yet not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), and furthermore, that the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*) does not lie dormant therein? He replied: "It could be so. When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, regarding those factors associated with the adherence to views and the adherence to precepts and observances (*dṛṣṭi-śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃprayukta-dharma*) which are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path—one is bound to them by the fetter of attachment, but is not bound by the fetter of views which takes them as its object."

Because the universal [defilements] have been abandoned, and because there is no non-universal fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) that has them as its object or is associated with them, the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*) still adheres to those [objects]. Those two [types of views] are themselves the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) by virtue of their association. But what is the reason that among the fetters, three views are stated separately as the "fetter of views," while two other views are stated separately as the "fetter of grasping"? Because of the commonality of grasping at entities, the two views constitute a distinct fetter. (41cd)

There are eighteen substances and three views; likewise, there are eighteen [substances] for the two views of misapprehension (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*). It is said that because of this commonality of substance, these are established as distinct fetters (*saṃyojana*). Furthermore, since these two have the nature of misapprehension while the others do not, they are also established separately due to this commonality of being misapprehensions, based on the distinction between the object and the subject of grasping. Now, why are envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) stated to be two separate fetters, and no other secondary affliction (*paryavasthāna*)?
Because both are exclusively unwholesome and because both are independent.
Among these, envy and avarice are said to be two distinct fetters. //42//

For there is no other *paryavasthāna* of such a kind in which both these qualities—being exclusively unwholesome (*ekāntākuśalatva*) and being independent (*svatantratva*)—would exist. This might be the case for one who holds that there are eight *paryavasthānas*; however, for one who holds that there are ten, anger (*krodha*) and hypocrisy (*mrakṣa*) are also of both types. Therefore, others say that this is not a valid refutation. Furthermore, elsewhere the Blessed One spoke of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), [stating that] those conducive to the lower realm (*avarabhāgīya*) are fivefold.

Namely: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Why are these called "factors conducive to the lower realm" (*avarabhāgīya*)? Because they are beneficial for the lower realm. For the lower realm is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and these [fetters] are concordant with it. This is because, by means of two [of these], there is no transcendence of the desire realm;
but by means of the other three, there is a return again. (43bc)

Through sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*), one does not transcend the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). Although one may have transcended it by means of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, one returns again, due to their similarity to gatekeepers and attendants. By three [fetters], one does not transcend the inferiority of sentient beings, namely the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*); by two, one does not transcend the inferiority of the realms, namely the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). For this very reason, others maintain that these are called "fettering the lower part" (*avarabhāgīya*).

When, for a stream-enterer, six afflictions have been abandoned through the complete abandonment of the three fetters, for what purpose does [the Buddha] mention only these three—setting aside all views—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)? All of this ought to be stated; however, it is said: "The three are mentioned because they grasp the gateway and the root" (43d).

It is said that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are of three types: those of one type, two types, and four types; their "gate" (*mukha*) is grasped by these three [afflictions]. Furthermore, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is set in motion by the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is set in motion by the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is set in motion by doubt (*vicikitsā*). Therefore, the root is grasped. Others, however, say:
[the obstacles are] the lack of desire to go [to the goal], confusion regarding the path, and doubt about the path.

Thus, because there are obstacles to proceeding toward liberation, there is this teaching of the three [obstacles]. (44) [p. 311] There are three obstacles to traveling to another country: the lack of desire to go, confusion regarding the path due to resorting to another path, and doubt regarding the path. In the same way, these very same three are obstacles to proceeding toward liberation. Among these, for one who has fallen into terror of liberation due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), there is the lack of desire to go. Due to the adherence to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), there is confusion regarding liberation due to resorting to another path. And due to doubt (*vicikitsā*), there is doubt regarding the path.
By indicating the abandonment of these obstacles to proceeding toward liberation, the Blessed One taught the abandonment of the three afflictions (*kleśa*) alone.
Just as the Blessed One has spoken of the fivefold lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), so too, there are likewise fivefold higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
To the question "How so?", he says:
there are two types of attachment, those arising from the form and formless realms;
these two—

“Excitement, pride, and delusion” (45c)—these are the five fetters pertaining to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*). They are as follows: attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), excitement (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*). Because these are not abandoned, one does not transcend the higher realms. The discussion of the fetters is concluded. What are the bonds (*bandhana*)? There are three bonds: all attachment is a bond, all hatred is a bond, and all delusion is a bond. Why did the Blessed One declare that these three alone are the bonds?

The three bonds arise from the power of the [three] feelings. [45d] Due to the power of the three feelings, there are three bonds: for passion (*rāga*) underlies pleasant feeling through both its object and its association; hatred (*dveṣa*) underlies painful feeling; and delusion (*moha*) underlies neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, whereas passion and hatred do not function in that same way. Alternatively, the restriction is based on the fact that they take as their object what belongs to one's own continuum. The underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) have already been explained. The secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) must now be discussed. Among them, those which are primary afflictions (*kleśa*) are also secondary afflictions, because they afflict the mind.

Those other afflicted mental factors included in the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) which are distinct from the primary afflictions are also secondary afflictions (upakleśa), yet they are not designated by the term "affliction" (kleśa). //46//

Furthermore, those other afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) factors, distinct from the primary afflictions (*kleśa*), which are comprised within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) and are mental (*caitasika*), are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). These, moreover, are those recited in the *Kṣudravastuka*; however, here we shall explain only those included among the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), the afflictions, and the stains (*mala*). What, then, are the outbursts? He says: "For an affliction is also an outburst," because of the statement in the Sūtra: "Suffering has the outburst of sensual desire as its condition. But in the *Prakaraṇaśāstra*, it is said:
lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Regret, lethargy, and sleep constitute the eightfold set of envelopments (paryavasthāna). //47//
Furthermore, according to the Vaibhāṣika system, there are ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*): these eight, plus anger (*krodha*) and hypocrisy (*mrakṣa*).

Among these, lack of shame (*ahrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) have already been explained. Envy (*īrṣyā*) is resentment of the mind toward the excellence of others. Avarice (*mātsarya*) is a grasping of the mind that opposes the giving of Dharma, material goods, or skills. Restlessness (*auddhatya*) is the lack of tranquility of the mind. Remorse (*kaukṛtya*) and torpor (*styāna*) have already been explained. Torpor (*middha*) is a contraction of the mind incapable of sustaining the body; however, it is only when afflicted that it constitutes a full-fledged entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), as does remorse. Anger (*krodha*) is a state of hostility toward sentient beings or non-sentient things, excluding malice (*vyāpāda*) and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*).

Concealment (*mrakṣa*) is the hiding of one's faults. Among these ten secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*), lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and stinginess (*matsara*) arise from attachment (*rāga*);
these three secondary afflictions are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of attachment. [p.313]

Regarding concealment (*mrakṣa*), some say it is an outflow (*niḥṣyanda*) of craving; others say it is an outflow of ignorance; others say it is an outflow of both. [This applies] respectively to those who know and those who do not know.
From ignorance arise lethargy, torpor, and lack of shame. (48cd)

These three are the outflows of ignorance (*avidyā-niḥṣyanda*). Regret arises from doubt; anger and envy arise from the sequence of hostility (*pratigha*). These ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are the outflows of the afflictions (*kleśa-niḥṣyanda*). (49ab) They are produced by hostility. Thus, these are the ten secondary afflictions which are the outflows of the afflictions.
And there are six other stains of affliction, namely:
deceit, guile, and likewise arrogance. (49d)

(50ab) "Spite (*pradāśa*), enmity (*upanāha*), and harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*). Among these, *māyā* is the deceiving of others. *Śāṭhya* is crookedness of mind, by which one does not reveal things as they truly are, but evades them or acts in an unclear manner. *Mada* has been explained previously. *Pradāśa* is the stubborn adherence to a blameworthy object, by which one does not accept a reasoned admonition. *Upanāha* is the frequent cultivation of the basis for resentment. *Vihiṃsā* is the act of harming, by which one torments others through blows, harsh words, and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding these six stains of the afflictions (*kleśamala*):
Deceit and arrogance arise from attachment; enmity and harmfulness arise from aversion.
But maliciousness arises from the adherence to views, while guile is produced from views.
This is because of the statement in the verse: "What is crooked? It is evil view. Thus, it is logical that guile is the outflow of views.

Which among these are to be abandoned by what? Regarding those ten envelopments (paryavasthāna) that have been mentioned, among them, lack of shame (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), torpor (styāna), languor (middha), and restlessness (auddhatya) are of two kinds. (51cd)

These five factors are of two kinds—those to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)—because they are associated with both types of afflictions. That which is associated with what is to be abandoned by a particular vision is itself to be abandoned by that vision. Those other than these are to be abandoned by cultivation; the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) comprised within the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), being distinct from them, are exclusively to be abandoned by cultivation. Envy, avarice, regret, anger, and concealment are independent (*svatantra*). These five secondary afflictions are also independent because they are associated solely with ignorance (*avidyā*).
Just as these five secondary afflictions, beginning with envy, are to be abandoned through cultivation and are independent, so too are the stains;
the six stains of affliction are exactly like that.
Furthermore, these aforementioned secondary afflictions are impure in the desire realm; that is, they are unwholesome within the desire realm. Moreover, therein—
Three are of two kinds;
sloth, restlessness, and torpor are unwholesome or neutral; beyond that, they are neutral. (52cd)

Above the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), as far as they may occur. Furthermore, among these, how many are to be understood as belonging to which levels?
Deceit (*māyā*) and guile (*śāṭhya*) exist in the desire realm and the first dhyāna. (53ab)
These two exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and in the first dhyāna. How can there be deceit (*māyā*) in the Brahma-world?
Because it deceives Brahmā.

For there, that Great Brahmā proceeded to deceive the Venerable Aśvajit by presenting a false appearance of himself. Although deceit was already mentioned, it is stated once more as it arises in this context.
Styāna, auddhatya, and mada exist in the three realms;
these three belong to all three dhātus.
The others are born of the kāmadhātu. (53cd)

Subtracting five from the sixteen, the remaining eleven secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) belong exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Thus have the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions been explained.

Now, among these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), how many belong to the level of the mind (*manobhūmika*), and how many belong to the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñānakāyika*)? Briefly stated:
those to be abandoned by insight (*dṛggheya*), together with torpor (*middha*), belong to the level of the mental consciousness (*manovijñānabhūmika*). (54ab)

All those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) belong to the mental level (*manobhūmika*), along with pride (*māna*) and torpor (*middha*), even though these two are also [partly] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). For these are entirely of the mental level. As for the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) that are independent (*svatantra*), whatever secondary afflictions are independent, even while being to be abandoned by cultivation, they should be understood as belonging exclusively to the mental level.
The others have the six consciousnesses as their support. //54d//

Other afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) should be understood as belonging to the level of the six consciousnesses. Which, then, are these others? They are attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), along with the secondary afflictions associated with them: lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*), as well as those mentioned among the great ground of afflictions (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*). Regarding these five faculties, such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, with which faculty is which affliction or secondary affliction associated?
Attachment is indeed associated with the two [faculties of] pleasure. (55ab)
Attachment is associated with pleasure (*sukha*) and mental joy (*saumanasya*);

aversion is the opposite—meaning it is associated with the two types of suffering (*duḥkha*), namely physical pain (*duḥkha*) and mental grief (*daurmanasya*). This is because attachment and aversion function respectively in the modes of elation and dejection, and because they belong to the level of the six consciousnesses.

Delusion (moha) is associated with all five faculties because ignorance (avidyā) is associated with all afflictions. False view (asaddṛṣṭi), however, is associated with the mental faculty and with both suffering and pleasure. (55cd)

Mental suffering is *daurmanasya* (dejection), and mental pleasure is *saumanasya* (contentment). False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is associated with these two respectively for those who perform meritorious deeds and those who perform evil deeds.
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) is associated with dejection;
for one who is uncertain and seeks certainty becomes dejected.

Others with mental pleasure (56ab). Other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are associated exclusively with mental pleasure (*saumanasya*). Which, then, are these others? They are the four views and pride, because they function in the mode of exhilaration. With what are these latent dispositions said to be associated? It is said: born of desire (*kāmajāḥ*). [p.317]
Having thus explained the specific associations, he speaks of them in general: "All [are associated] with equanimity" (56c).

All these latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). It is said that at the time when the continuity of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is severed, equanimity necessarily remains present.
As for how those belonging to the lower stages [are abandoned], he says:
"By their own respective [paths], according to each stage, as with those of the higher stages" (56cd).

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the higher stages are associated with their respective faculties; in whichever stage there are however many faculties, [the dispositions] therein are associated accordingly. Furthermore, those belonging to the four groups of consciousness are associated with those of the four groups of consciousness, and those belonging to the mental level are associated only with those of the mental level, as the case may be. Thus has been explained the association of the afflictions (*kleśa*) with the faculties.
As for the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), moreover:
remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is associated with mental dissatisfaction (*daurmanasya*).
Envy, anger, harmfulness, resentment,
and spite—
these are associated [with the mind] because they function with a form of dejection and because they belong to the level of the mental consciousness. (57abc)
But stinginess is the opposite. //57d//
The meaning is "by way of mental joy" (*saumanasya*), because, being associated with greed (*lobha*), they function in the form of elation.
Deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and torpor (*middha*) belong to both [mental joy and mental grief]. (58ab)

They are associated with both mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) and mental pain (*daurmanasya*). For sometimes one who is joyful deceives another, and sometimes one who is dejected does so; this continues even up to the time of sleep.
Intoxication (*mada*) is associated with the two types of pleasure (*sukha*). (58bc) [p.318]

In the third dhyāna, [the latent dispositions] are associated with pleasure (*sukha*) below and with mental joy (*saumanasya*) above; however, because equanimity (*upekṣā*) is universal, all latent dispositions are associated with it. For there is no restriction on it anywhere, unlike the case of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The other four are associated with five. //58d//

Lack of shame (āhrīkya), lack of dread (anapatrāpya), lethargy (styāna), and restlessness (auddhatya)—these four envelopments (paryavasthāna) are associated with all five faculties, because they belong both to the category of the great unwholesome ground (akuśalamahābhūmika) and the category of the great afflictive ground (kleśamahābhūmika).

Regarding the five hindrances (*nivaraṇa*) mentioned in the Sūtra—sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill-will (*vyāpāda*), sloth-and-torpor (*styānamiddha*), restlessness-and-remorse (*auddhatyakaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—are the sloth, restlessness, and doubt here to be understood as belonging to all three realms (*traidhātukya*), or are they associated only with the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*)? Because the Sūtra states that "this entire, complete mass of unwholesomeness (*akuśalarāśi*) consists of the five hindrances," and because of this declaration of their being exclusively unwholesome, the hindrances belong only to the realm of desire. (59a)

Not in any other realm. But what is the reason that the two—*styāna* and *middha*—are said to be one hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*), and the two—*auddhatya* and *kaukṛtya*—are also one? Because they have the same opposite, the same nourishment, and the same function. Thus, there is a pairing of two into one. (59abc)

The oneness of two is "duality-oneness" (*dvyekatā*). "Antidote" (*vipakṣa*), "counteragent" (*pratipakṣa*), and "non-nutriment" (*anāhāra*) have one and the same meaning. In the Sūtra, there is one nutriment for both sloth and torpor (*styāna-middha*), as well as their non-nutriment. What is the nutriment of the hindrance of sloth and torpor? Five factors: languor, dissatisfaction, yawning, irregularity in eating, and mental depression. And what is the non-nutriment of the hindrance of sloth and torpor? The perception of light (*ālokasaṃjñā*). The function of these two is also one; for both of them cause the mind to sink into lethargy.

[Page 319] Regarding restlessness and remorse as well, one nutriment and one non-nutriment have been taught. What is the nutriment for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse? It consists of four factors: discursive thought concerning relatives, discursive thought concerning the country, discursive thought concerning the immortals (divine beings), and being one who recollects former instances of laughter, play, sport, and enjoyment. And what is the non-nutriment for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse? It is *śamatha* (calm abiding). Furthermore, the function (*kṛtya*) of these two is also one and the same.
For both of these cause the mind to remain unpeaceful; therefore, because they share the same function of providing nourishment for a single adversary, the two are said to be one.
If all afflictions are hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), why are only five mentioned?
"The state of being five is due to their destruction of the aggregates and because of doubt. (59cd)

Through sensual desire and ill-will, there is an impairment of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*). Through lethargy and drowsiness, there is an impairment of the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñāskandha*), and through restlessness and regret, there is an impairment of the aggregate of concentration (*samādhiskandha*). When concentration and wisdom are absent, one becomes doubtful regarding the Truths; therefore, five [hindrances] are taught. However, according to another interpretation, it would follow that the hindrance of restlessness and regret—which opposes the aggregate of concentration—should have been mentioned first.

Therefore, others maintain that by these two [hindrances], the aggregates of concentration and wisdom are respectively impaired: for one engaged in concentration, there is fear of sloth and torpor; for one engaged in the discernment of phenomena, there is fear of restlessness and remorse.

Others, however, describe it differently. How do they describe it? For one who has gone out on a walk, the grasping of signs (*nimittagrāha*) regarding objects that are pleasant or unpleasant causes sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*)—preceded by that grasping—to act as an obstacle at the very beginning of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) when one has returned to one's dwelling. Subsequently, for one who has entered concentration, the failure to apply effort and the lack of cultivation of the specific qualities of calm (*śamatha*) cause torpor-and-drowsiness (*styānamiddha*), restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatyakaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*) to act as obstacles, respectively, to calm and insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Even for one who has emerged [from meditative absorption], doubt creates an obstacle at the time of reflecting on the Dharma; therefore, five hindrances have been taught.

This is now investigated: regarding those universal [defilements] belonging to a different realm (*visabhāga-dhātu*), and those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path (*nirodha-mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) which have contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*), at the time when their object is fully known (*parijñāta*), they are not yet abandoned; and at the time when they are abandoned, their object is no longer fully known. How, then, is their abandonment? The destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*) does not necessarily occur through the full knowledge of the object alone. What then? It occurs through four modes. Which four? First, for those to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*): through the full knowledge of the object and through the destruction of that which takes it as its object.

And through the abandonment of the object (*ālambanaprahāṇāt*)—(60abc)—therein, because of the thorough knowledge of the object, there is the abandonment of those [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin which have their own level as their object and those which have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object; and because of the destruction of that object, there is the abandonment of the universal [defilements] belonging to other realms (*visabhāgadhātu-sarvatraga*), for the universal [defilements] belonging to one's own realm (*sabhāgadhātu-sarvatraga*) have those [other-realm defilements] as their object. When those [other-realm defilements] are abandoned, they too become abandoned. Through the abandonment of the object, there is the abandonment of those to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path which have the tainted (*sāsrava*) as their object, for those [untainted things] are the objects of those [tainted ones].
Therefore, when those [defilements] are abandoned, these [objects] are also abandoned.
Furthermore, for those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation, their destruction occurs through the arising of the antidote. //60d//

For whichever type of affliction (*kleśa*) a path that serves as its antidote (*pratipakṣa*) arises, that [affliction] is abandoned. But what is the antidote for which? We shall explain in detail later that the weakest-weak path is the antidote for the strongest-strong [affliction], and so forth. As for how many kinds of antidotes there are, he says:
they are fourfold, known as abandonment, support, distancing, and revulsion.

The counteractive (pratipakṣa) consists of: (61abc) the counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*), which is the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*); the counteractive of support (*ādhārapratipakṣa*), which is the noble path subsequent to that, by which the abandonment attained by the former is maintained; and the counteractive of distancing (*dūrībhāvapratipakṣa*), which is the path subsequent to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), because it distances the possession (*prāpti*) that has been severed. Others say that the path of liberation is also [the counteractive of distancing], for it too distances that possession. The counteractive of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇāpratipakṣa*) is the path by which one reviles that realm by viewing it as a fault.

Moreover, this sequence of theirs would be correct: the counteragent of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*) is the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) which has suffering and its origin as its object; the counteragent of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*) is the entire path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*); the counteragent of support (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*) is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); and the counteragent of distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*) is the path of distinction (*viśeṣa-mārga*). From where is the affliction being abandoned to be abandoned? It is held that the affliction to be abandoned is [abandoned] from its object (*ālambana*). (VI.61cd)

For a defilement cannot be separated from its association (*saṃprayoga*), but it can be separated from its object (*ālambana*), because it does not arise again by taking that as its object. At least in the case of future [defilements], they could be separated from their objects; but how so in the case of the past? If it is argued that it is to be abandoned through the full comprehension (*parijñāna*) of the object, this is not the meaning here. This too is not definitive. Therefore, this must be stated: To what extent is a defilement said to be abandoned? A defilement belonging to one's own continuum is abandoned through the cutting off of its acquisition (*prāpti*).

However, the afflictions belonging to another's continuum, all form, and non-afflicted phenomena are said to be "distant" because of the abandonment of the afflictions belonging to one's own continuum that take them as objects. How many kinds of distance are there? It is said that distance is fourfold:
due to difference in characteristic, due to being an opposing factor, due to separation of location, and due to time.
Distance exists among beings, moral precepts, locations, and the two time periods, just as it does between physical objects. //62//

Remoteness by way of dissimilarity is, for example, that of the great elements (*mahābhūta*); because they are of different natures, there is remoteness even among those that are co-nascent. Remoteness by way of opposition is, for example, immorality (*dauḥśīlya*) in relation to morality (*śīla*). Remoteness by way of spatial separation is, for example, that of distant places; due to the separation of location, they are like the eastern and western oceans. Remoteness by way of time is, for example, when the past and the future are said to be remote.

From what is it distant? From the present. How can that which has just passed away or is currently arising be distant? It is distant by virtue of being a different time-period (*adhvan*), not because of having long since ceased or being yet to occur. If that were the case, even the present would be considered distant. Then it must be distant because of its lack of activity (*akāritra*). But how is proximity established for the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Because it is attained everywhere. [If so,] the same consequence would apply to the past and the future as well. And how about space (*ākāśa*)?

If that is so, then the past and the future are distant from each other because they are separated by the present; the present is near to both because it is proximate to them; and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is also [near] because it is not separated [from anything]. Even so, since the past and the future are near to the present, both would [absurdly] result in being near. However, this would be logical: the future is distant from the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a phenomenon because it has not yet been reached, and the past is distant because it has already passed away. Does the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*) become more distinguished through progressing to a specific stage of the path? This is not the case, for regarding all afflictions...
The destruction of that which is to be abandoned occurs all at once; by whichever path of abandonment it is abandoned, by that very path its destruction is achieved.
However, the attainment of dissociation from them occurs again and again.
At how many times? He says: at six times—namely, at the arising of the counteragent, the attainment of the fruit, and the increase of the faculties. (63cd)

The "counteragent" (pratipakṣa) intended here is the path of liberation (vimuktimārga). The "fruits" are the four fruits of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala). The "strengthening of the faculties" (indriyavivṛddhi) is the transformation of the faculties (indriyasaṃcāra). At these times, there is the attainment of dissociation from the afflictions (kleśa-visaṃyoga-lābha). This, moreover, should be understood according to the circumstances: for some it occurs at six times, for others as few as two.

That very dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) receives the designation "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*) in various states. For there are two kinds of thorough knowledge: thorough knowledge as cognition (*jñāna-parijñā*) and thorough knowledge as abandonment (*prahāṇa-parijñā*). Among these, thorough knowledge as cognition is contaminated knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*); thorough knowledge as abandonment is abandonment itself, because the cause is metaphorically designated by the name of the fruit. Is there only one such thorough knowledge that constitutes the abandonment of everything? He says: no. What then? There are nine thorough knowledges therein; first, regarding those:
The destruction of the first two types [of defilements] beginning with desire.
(64abc) In the desire realm, the abandonment of the first two types— those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origin— is one thorough knowledge (*parijñā*).
The destruction of two [categories] constitutes those two [parijñās].

(64c) In the desire realm alone, the abandonment of the category to be abandoned by the vision of cessation is one complete knowledge (*parijñā*); that of the category to be abandoned by the vision of the path is another. Just as there are three complete knowledges for the abandonment of those [defilements] belonging to the desire realm to be abandoned by vision, so too, in the higher realms, there are exactly those same three. (64d)

The abandonment of those [defilements] belonging to the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned by seeing likewise constitutes three thorough knowledges (*parijñā*). The abandonment of those to be abandoned by seeing suffering and its origin is one; the abandonment of those to be abandoned by seeing cessation is the second; and the abandonment of those to be abandoned by seeing the path is the third. Thus, the abandonment of all those defilements of the three realms to be abandoned by seeing constitutes six thorough knowledges. The others are the destruction of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), of form, and of all outflows (*āsrava*); these are the three remaining thorough knowledges. (65abc)

The abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) is one full comprehension (*parijñā*). The abandonment of the outflow of form (*rūpāsrava*) is one full comprehension, namely the full comprehension of the destruction of desire for the realm of form (*rūparāgakṣayaparijñā*). The abandonment of all outflows pertaining to the formless realm is one full comprehension, namely the full comprehension of the exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanaparyādānaparijñā*). Why is the abandonment of the defilements of the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) a separate full comprehension, whereas those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) are not? Because the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) for those to be abandoned by cultivation are dissimilar. Thus, there are these nine full comprehensions.
Of these, the first six—the nature of which is the abandonment of what is to be abandoned by seeing—are the fruit of the receptive patiences (*kṣānti*). (65cd)
They are the remnants of knowledge. //65//

The thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) beginning with the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) are the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). How, then, can the patient acceptances (*kṣānti*) be considered fruits of thorough knowledge? Because the patient acceptances have knowledge as their retinue, just as one uses the term "king" for the king's retinue. Furthermore, because they share the same fruit as knowledge. Regarding the fruit of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), all [eight] thorough knowledges are its fruit; or alternatively, five or eight. (66abc)

According to the Vaibhāṣika school, there are five full cognitions (*parijñā*) that are the fruit of the fundamental dhyānas, which have the nature of abandoning the afflictions belonging to the realms of form and formlessness; this is because the abandonment of the afflictions belonging to the desire realm is the fruit of the *anāgamya* stage. According to the opinion of Bhadanta Ghoṣaka, there are eight. For he maintains that even for one who is already free from passion, the abandonment of the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned by seeing is the fruit of the path of seeing, since it involves the acquisition of the untainted attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*). However, the full cognition of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) is indeed the fruit of the *anāgamya* stage alone. The intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) should be regarded as being like the [fundamental] dhyānas. As for the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), however—
One [complete knowledge] belongs to the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*);

specifically, one complete knowledge—the complete knowledge of the destruction of attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*)—is the fruit of the preparatory stage of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-sāmantaka*), as well as that of the three fundamental formless attainments (*maulārūpyatraya*). [66d]
For the three fundamental formless [attainments], there is only one fruit: the thorough knowledge consisting in the total exhaustion of all fetters.
For the noble path, all nine thorough knowledges are the fruit.
Two [parijñās] are the fruit of the mundane path: the two thorough knowledges of the destruction of the lower fetters and of attachment to the realm of form;
and also that of subsequent knowledge.
For subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) as well, two thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) are the result, namely the last two.

However, for dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), there are three; these are indeed the last ones, because it serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to that which is to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) in the three realms.
Six for that side, and five. //67d//

The fruit of the category of dharma-knowledge consists of six thorough knowledges (*parijñā*), which are the same as those of the dharma-patience (*kṣānti*) and dharma-knowledges. The fruit of the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) consists of five, which are the same as those of the subsequent patience and subsequent knowledges. For by the term "category" (*pakṣa*), both the patiences and the knowledges are included. Why is abandonment (*prahāṇa*) not established as a thorough knowledge for each individual [moment]? Because abandonment is established as the fruit of patience:

"Because of the attainment of untainted disjunction (*viyoga*), because of the impairment of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), and because of the uprooting of the two causes, it is a thorough knowledge. (68abc)

Where these three causes are present, that abandonment is called "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*). First, for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), there is neither the untainted attainment of dissociation (*anāsrava-visaṃyoga-prāpti*) nor the impairment of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*); thus, his abandonment does not receive the designation of "thorough knowledge. For a noble one (*ārya*) as well, there is first the abandonment which is the fruit of the receptive patiences (*kṣānti*). In that regard, up until the receptive patience of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna-kṣānti*), although there is the untainted attainment of dissociation, the peak of existence has not yet been impaired.

In the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding suffering, both [the conditions] are present, yet there is no eradication of the two causes, because the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) that is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin has not yet been abandoned. In other subsequent knowledges of phenomena (*dharmānvayajñāna*), all three are present; therefore, in those respective states, abandonment receives the designation of "perfect knowledge" (*parijñā*). Abandonment is the fruit of knowledge, and for these three reasons, as well as the fourth—transcending the realm—it receives the designation of "perfect knowledge. //68d//

When one transcends a realm (*dhātu*), it is due to detachment from that entire realm; others say the fifth cause is the dissociation from both [types of] fetters. This refers to the case where, once a certain category has been abandoned, one becomes dissociated from any other affliction (*kleśa*) that takes that as its object. However, we do not say this is because of the eradication of both causes and the transcendence of the realm.
Who is endowed with how many thorough cognitions (*parijñā*)? One who abides in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is endowed with either one or up to five. (69ab)

First of all, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) is not at all possessed [of these]. Even a noble one (ārya) abiding on the path of seeing (darśanamārga) is not at all possessed [of them] up until the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (samudayadharmajñānakṣānti). At the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (samudaye dharmajñāna), one is possessed of one; at the subsequent knowledge regarding origination (samudaye 'nvayajñāna), of two; at the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (nirodhe dharmajñāna), of three; at the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (nirodhānvayajñāna), of four; and at the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (mārgadharmajñāna), of five.
Furthermore, one abiding in the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is possessed of six, or of one, or of two. (69cd)

Furthermore, a noble person (āryapudgala) abiding on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is endowed with six thorough knowledges (parijñā) at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna), as long as they have not attained detachment from the desire realm (kāmavairāgya). Or, having fallen away from that state, once they have attained detachment from the desire realm—whether previously or subsequently—they are endowed with one thorough knowledge, namely the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters (avarabhāgīyaprahāṇaparijñā). Upon attaining arhatship, they are endowed with only one thorough knowledge, namely the thorough knowledge of the total exhaustion of all fetters (sarvasaṃyojanaparyādānaparijñā). Even if they fall away due to an outburst (paryavasthāna) belonging to the form realm (rūpāvacara), they remain endowed with one thorough knowledge, namely the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters.

One who has attained detachment from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is endowed with two thorough knowledges (*parijñā*): the thorough knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa*) and the thorough knowledge of the destruction of passion for the realm of form (*rūparāga-kṣaya*). Even when one is bound by an active outburst (*paryavasthāna*) belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyāvacara*), it is through these same two that one is liberated. What, then, is the reason that only a single thorough knowledge is established for the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and the arhat, and not more? Because:
"Their consolidation [into a single thorough knowledge] occurs due to detachment from a realm and the attainment of a fruit. (70ab)

The synthesis of the thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) occurs through two causes: by means of detachment from the realms (*dhātu-vairāgya*) and by means of the attainment of a fruit (*phala-prāpti*). Both of these occur in those two states; therefore, all abandonments (*prahāṇa*) are synthesized and designated as a single thorough knowledge. Now, who abandons or acquires how many thorough knowledges?
One, two, five, or six—some abandon or obtain [them]; no one obtains five. (70cd)

One abandons one [complete knowledge] when falling away from arhatship or from detachment from the desire realm. One abandons two complete knowledges when a non-returner who is detached from the form realm falls away from detachment from the desire realm. One abandons five when a person previously detached from the desire realm attains the subsequent knowledge of the path; for upon obtaining the complete knowledge of the abandonment of the lower fetters, he abandons the five previous complete knowledges. One who follows the gradual path abandons six complete knowledges through detachment from the desire realm. The same applies to their acquisition: someone acquires one complete knowledge.

Whoever attains a [result] not previously obtained, someone attains two [results], namely one who falls away from detachment from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) alone; someone attains six, namely one who falls away from the fruit of a non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*). However, no one attains five.
The discussion concerning thorough knowledge (*parijñā*) is concluded.
Thus ends the fifth treasury-location (kośasthāna), titled "Exposition of the Latent Dispositions" (anuśayanirdeśa), in the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.
Whatever merit is here in this [work] of Śīlāmāvāka.
Chapter VI [p. 327]
The sixth treasury-location: The Exposition of the Path and the Persons.
Homage to the Buddha.
It has been explained how abandonment receives the designation of "thorough knowledge" (*parijñā*); and furthermore, that—
The abandonment of the afflictions has been explained as resulting from the vision and cultivation of the truths (1ab).

It has been explained in detail that the afflictions are those to be abandoned by vision and those to be abandoned by cultivation; now it must be stated whether these two—the path of vision and the path of cultivation—are untainted (*anāsrava*) or tainted (*sāsrava*). Therefore, this is said:
"The path of cultivation is twofold, but that called vision is untainted" (1cd).

The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is twofold: mundane (*laukika*) and supramundane (*lokottara*). The path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), however, is exclusively supramundane, because it serves as the antidote to the three realms and because it abandons the nine categories of afflictions to be abandoned by seeing all at once; for the mundane path does not possess this capacity. It was stated [above] that [this occurs] "from the vision of the truths. What are these truths, and how many are there? The truths have been stated to be four.

Where were they taught? In the exposition of contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena: the uncontaminated [phenomena] were taught by their own name as "the truth of the path" (*mārgasatya*); "cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), which is disjunction (*visaṃyoga*)" was taught as the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*); and "suffering, origin, and the world" were taught there as the truths of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) and origin (*samudayasatya*). Is this their only sequence? He says: no. What then? Suffering, and likewise origin;
"Cessation and the path" (2bc):
this is their sequence. The word "thus" (tathā) is for the purpose of demonstrating that their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is exactly as previously stated.
Furthermore, this [is as follows]:
The sequence of these is according to their realization. //2cd//

For that truth whose realization occurs first is taught first; otherwise, there would have been a teaching of the cause first and the result later. For some things, the teaching follows the order of their arising, as in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). For others, the teaching follows the order of their systematic exposition, as in the case of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). Indeed, there is no fixed rule that one must first generate the desire to abandon what has already arisen, and only afterwards [the desire] for the non-arising of what has not yet arisen. However, the teaching of the truths follows the order of their realization (*abhisamaya*).

What, then, is the reason for the realization of these truths in this order? For that to which one is attached, by which one is afflicted, and from which one seeks liberation—that is the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) which is examined first during the stage of analytical investigation. Subsequently, one considers: "What is its cause?"—this is the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*); "What is its cessation?"—this is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*); and "What is the path to it?"—this is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). It is like seeing a disease and then searching for its cause, its elimination, and the medicine.
This very analogy for the truths is also shown in a sutra. In which sutra? In the one that says: "A physician who removes arrows is endowed with four qualities.

And just as there is an examination of the truths during the stage of analytical investigation, so too is there the realization of the truths during the stage of clear realization (*abhisamaya*), due to the momentum of what preceded it, like a horse running unimpeded over ground already seen.

What is the meaning of *abhisamaya*? It means "clear realization" (*abhisaṃbodha*), because the root *iṇ* has the sense of "understanding. Why is it only untainted (*anāsrava*) and not tainted (*sāsrava*)? For it is a correct awakening directed toward *nirvāṇa*. "Correctly" means in accordance with reality (*tattvena*).

In this context, the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) that constitute the fruit are the Truth of Suffering; those that constitute the cause are the Truth of Origination, because [suffering] originates from them. Therefore, because of their relationship as cause and fruit, there is a distinction between these two in terms of name, but not in terms of substance (*dravyataḥ*). However, for Cessation and the Path, there is a distinction even in terms of substance.

"They are called the Noble Truths (*āryasatyāni*) in the Sūtra. What is the meaning of this? It is stated in the Sūtra itself: 'These are the truths of the Noble Ones; therefore they are the Noble Truths. Are these false for others? No; these are truths for everyone because they are non-erroneous. However, the Noble Ones perceive them as they truly are, whereas others do not. Therefore, these are called the truths of the Noble Ones, but not of the non-Noble ones, because the latter possess erroneous views.
As the verse says: 'What the Noble Ones describe as happiness, others know as suffering; what others describe as happiness, the Noble Ones know as suffering.'"
Others say: "Two are truths for the noble ones, and two are both truths and noble.
When only a portion of feeling has the nature of suffering, how can it be said that all contaminated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering? [The answer is:
They are suffering because they are connected with the three types of suffering, without exception, as the case may be.
Those that are agreeable, disagreeable, and others besides these, which are all with outflows (sāsrava). //3//

For there are three types of suffering: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*). By means of these, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) formations (*saṃskāra*) are, as appropriate, entirely suffering.
