Among them, pleasant things are suffering through the suffering of change; unpleasant things are suffering through the suffering of suffering; and those other than these two are suffering through the suffering of conditioned formations.
Which, then, are the pleasant, which are the unpleasant, and which are neither?

There are three feelings in their respective order; by virtue of them, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) such as those to be experienced as pleasant also receive designations such as "agreeable" (*manāpa*).

For pleasant feeling is suffering by way of its transformation (*vipariṇāma*); as it is said in the Sūtra: "Pleasant feeling is pleasant in its arising, pleasant in its staying, and suffering in its transformation. For painful feeling, there is suffering by its very nature of suffering; as it is said in the Sūtra: "Painful feeling is suffering in its arising and suffering in its staying. For neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, there is suffering by way of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) alone, because it is produced by conditions; as it is said: "That which is impermanent is suffering. Like the feelings themselves, the formations that are to be felt should also be understood in this way.
Suffering itself is the nature of suffering; this is the "suffering of suffering. Others maintain that it continues in this way until "conditioned phenomena themselves are the nature of suffering.

(2.2.1b) Because pleasant and unpleasant things are not common to all, the "suffering of change" and the "suffering of suffering" are taught [respectively]. However, all conditioned phenomena are suffering by virtue of the "suffering of conditioned formations" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Only the Noble Ones perceive this. And regarding this, it is said:

"Just as a single eyelash, when resting on the palm of the hand, is not perceived by people, yet that very same lash, when it has entered the eye, produces distress and pain; so too the child, who is like the palm of the hand, does not perceive the eyelash of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), whereas the wise man, who is like the eye, is deeply agitated by that very same thing. For indeed, the perception of suffering does not arise in fools even regarding the aggregates (*skandhas*) of the Avīci hell in the way it arises for the Noble Ones (*ārya*) even regarding those at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
If that is so, then it follows that the Path (*mārga*) would also be the suffering of conditioned existence, because it is conditioned.

Because its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is that which is disagreeable (*pratikūla*), the Path (*mārga*) is not suffering (*duḥkha*). For its arising is not disagreeable to the Noble Ones (*ārya*), since it brings about the destruction of all suffering. Even when they perceive Nirvana as peace (*śāntataḥ*), they perceive the cessation of only that which has been seen as suffering, not the cessation of the Path.
Furthermore, even though there is some happiness (*sukha*) therein, why is it called only the Noble Truth of Suffering?

Some say that because pleasure is so slight, even when mung beans and the like are present, it is designated as a "heap of black gram," just as one might call a small amount of mung beans a "heap of black gram. For what wise person would determine that a boil is "pleasure" merely by following after the pleasure of sprinkling [it with water]?
As it has indeed been said: "Because it is the cause of suffering, and because it is accompanied by no small amount of sufferings..."
"Since suffering exists, because they desire it, they determine that pleasure is suffering.

However, the Noble Ones (āryas) perceive the entirety of existence (bhava), together with pleasure itself, as suffering because it has the single flavor of the suffering of conditioned formations (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā). Therefore, only suffering is established as a Noble Truth (āryasatya), not pleasure.

How then do they perceive a feeling whose intrinsic nature is pleasure as suffering? Because it is disagreeable due to its impermanence (anityatā). Just as they also perceive form (rūpa), perception (saṃjñā), and so forth as suffering, yet these are not suffering in the same way that the feeling of suffering (duḥkhavedanā) is.

But for one who thinks [it is suffering] because it is a cause of suffering, that would be its aspect as origination (*samudaya-ākāra*), not its aspect as suffering (*duḥkha-ākāra*). Furthermore, how could the perception of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃjñā*) arise for the Noble Ones (*ārya*) when they are reborn in the realms of form (*rūpa*) or formlessness (*arūpya*)? For those aggregates (*skandha*) are no longer causes of painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*) for them. Moreover, for what purpose would the "suffering of conditioned forces" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) have been mentioned separately in the Sūtra?

If, then, they see [them] as suffering because of their impermanence, [then] they are suffering because they are disagreeable (*pratikūla*); however, since that which is seen as impermanent becomes disagreeable, the aspect of impermanence (*anitya-ākāra*) draws along with it the aspect of suffering.
Some maintain that there is no such thing as pleasant feeling at all; rather, all feeling is exclusively suffering. How is this understood? Both from scripture (*sūtra*) and from reasoning (*yukti*).

First, how is it understood from scripture? For the Blessed One has said: "Whatever is felt here, that is [included] within suffering"; "Pleasant feeling is to be viewed as suffering"; and "To perceive what is suffering as pleasure is a perversion of perception. Thus, first, it is understood from scripture.

How [is this known] through reasoning? Because of the determination of the causes of pleasure. For whatever things—such as food, drink, cold, or heat—are accepted as causes of pleasure, those very same things, when used in excess or at the wrong time, become causes of suffering. And it is not logical that suffering should arise from an increase in the causes of pleasure, or from them being moderate, at another time; therefore, they are causes of suffering from the very beginning, not of pleasure. It is only at the end that that suffering, having reached an increase, becomes manifest.

The same should be said regarding the conceptualization of postures (*īryāpatha-vikalpa*), as well as the perception of pleasure in the remediation of suffering and in the conceptualization of suffering itself. For nothing at all is experienced as "pleasure" so long as one is not afflicted by another form of suffering arising from hunger, thirst, cold, heat, fatigue, or sensual desire. Therefore, for the ignorant, the perception of pleasure occurs only toward a remedy, not toward actual pleasure. Furthermore, fools produce the perception of pleasure within the conceptualization of suffering, just as when shifting a burden from one shoulder to the other.
Consequently, there is no such thing as pleasure at all.

The Abhidharmikas maintain that it certainly exists, and this is indeed the correct principle. How so? First, this denier of pleasure should be asked: "What is this thing called suffering? If he says it is "that which has the nature of affliction," then he must explain how so. If he says it is "that which is injurious," then it is established that what is beneficial is pleasure (*sukha*). If he says it is "that which is undesirable," then it is established that what is desirable is pleasure.

"For that very thing which is intended becomes unintended for the Noble Ones at the time of their detachment from passion. If it is argued that "therefore, the state of being intended is not established," we say no, because it is otherwise unintended. For whatever feeling is intended by its own characteristic never again becomes unintended by that same characteristic.

For the Noble Ones disparage it through another aspect and perceive it as a ground for negligence, as something to be accomplished through great effort, as subject to transformation, and as impermanent—thereby making it undesirable; yet this is certainly not by way of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If it were desirable by its own nature, no one would ever feel passion toward it, such that they would need to view it as faulty through another mode in order to achieve detachment. Therefore, pleasant feeling (*sukhā vedanā*) does indeed exist by way of its own specific characteristic.

As for that which was said by the Blessed One, "Whatever is felt, all that is here [included] in suffering," this has been explained as of explicit meaning (*nītārtha*) by the Blessed One himself: "Ānanda, it was with reference to the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-anityatā*) and the transformation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-vipariṇāmatā*) that I spoke, saying, 'Whatever is felt, all that is here [included] in suffering. Therefore, it is established that this was not said with reference to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

And if everything that is felt were suffering by its very nature, for what purpose would the noble Ānanda have asked the Blessed One this: "The Blessed One has spoken of these three feelings—the pleasant, the painful, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Yet it was also said by the Blessed One: 'Whatever is felt, that is here [included] in suffering. With what intention, then, did the Blessed One say: 'Whatever is felt, that is here [included] in suffering'?"

For if he had intended this, he would have asked: "With what intention, Blessed One, did you say that there are three feelings? And the Blessed One would have replied: "It was with this intention that I said there are three feelings. But he did not say this. Therefore, the three feelings do indeed exist by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*). However, by saying, "Whatever is felt, that here is [included] in suffering," he demonstrates that this statement is of intentional meaning (*ābhiprāyika*).

As for what was said—that "pleasant feeling is to be viewed as suffering"—both [aspects] exist within it: its state of pleasantness by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) because it is agreeable, and its state of suffering by way of a derivative mode (*paryāya*) because it is subject to change and impermanence. When it is viewed as pleasant, it conduces to liberation through the detachment from it; the Buddhas command that it be viewed in such a way that it conduces to liberation. How is this understood? That it is pleasant by way of intrinsic nature. As it says:
"Having known the impermanence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and likewise their subjectivity to change..."
"Feeling has been declared as suffering by the Perfectly Awakened One who understands," so it is said.

Furthermore, as for the statement, "The perception of pleasure in what is suffering is a perversion of perception (*saṃjñāviparyāsa*)," this teaching is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*). For the world perceives feelings as pleasure, as well as the qualities of sensual desire (*kāmaguṇa*) and rebirth as pleasure. In that regard, there is a perversion for one who views a pleasant feeling—which is in fact suffering by way of its transformation—as being exclusively pleasurable; the same applies to rebirth.
Therefore, the non-existence of pleasant feeling is not established on this basis.

If, however, everything that is felt were suffering by its very nature, what would be the purpose of the statement "there are three kinds of feeling"? If you argue that it was said "in accordance with worldly convention," we say no; for that statement was spoken with the intention (*saṃdhāya*) that all that is felt is suffering, and because it was stated as it truly is (*yathābhūta*).

"Both the faculty of physical pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of mental joy (*saumanasyendriya*) are to be regarded as the feeling of pleasure," having thus spoken in detail, [it continues]: "By whomsoever these five faculties have been seen thus according to reality through right wisdom (*samyakprajñā*), his three fetters (*saṃyojana*) become abandoned," and so forth.

Furthermore, how could the world determine that painful sensation is threefold? If it is argued that the perception of pleasure and so forth occurs respectively toward weak, intense, and middling [pains], this is not so; for since pleasure is also threefold, there would have to be a perception of intense pleasure and so forth even toward weak pains.

And when one experiences pleasure born from a specific odor, taste, or tangible object, what mild suffering could there be at that time for which the perception of pleasure occurs? Furthermore, when that mild suffering has not yet arisen or has already ceased, the perception of pleasure would be even stronger, because of the complete absence of suffering. The same should be said regarding the manifestation of sensual pleasure.
And how indeed could this be logical: that when a mild sensation is felt, a very distinct and intense experience is perceived, while in the case of a moderate one, it is unmanifest?

Furthermore, because "pleasure" is spoken of in the [first] three dhyānas, there would have to be mild suffering; and because "neither-pain-nor-pleasure" is spoken of above those, there would have to be moderate suffering.
Thus, it is not logical to establish the sensations of pleasure and so forth based on mild and other degrees of suffering.
Moreover, it was said by the Blessed One: "If form, Mahānāman, were exclusively suffering, and not pleasure, nor accompanied by pleasure," and so forth. Therefore, some pleasure does indeed exist.

Thus, for now, the non-existence of pleasant feeling is not established by the Sūtra. As for what was said regarding the lack of a fixed cause for pleasure, this is stated because of a failure to fully understand the cause. For an object becomes either a cause of pleasure or a cause of pain only in dependence upon a particular state of the basis (*āśraya*), not as an object alone. When that [object] reaches a certain state of the body and becomes a cause of pleasure, it never fails to be so once that state is reached; thus, the cause of pleasure is indeed fixed.

For example, just as that very same fire, depending on the specific nature of the substance to be cooked, becomes the cause for a delicious cooking, yet that same fire becomes the cause for an unpalatable cooking; however, it is not the case that having reached a certain state of the substance to be cooked and becoming the cause for delicious cooking, it would no longer be the cause upon reaching that same state again—this is the illustration.
And how could the cause of pleasure not be established within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)?

As for what was further stated—that the perception of pleasure is actually the remedy for suffering—the remedy has already been provided [by the teaching itself]. When one experiences pleasure born from specific fragrances and so forth, at that time, toward the remedy for what would the perception of pleasure arise? Furthermore, when that suffering has not yet arisen or has already perished, there should be an even greater perception of pleasure. As for the pleasure born of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), what is it, and of what could it be a remedy? And so on.

Even when shifting a burden, only pleasure arising from a change of state occurs, as long as that particular bodily condition does not disappear; otherwise, there would be an even greater perception of pleasure later on. The same should be understood regarding the various postures of one who is fatigued. If it is asked, "How can there be a perception of suffering at the end if there was no beginning? [the answer is: it is due to a specific transformation of the body, just as wine and other substances turn from sweetness to acidity at the end.

Therefore, it is established that pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) truly exists. Alternatively, all contaminated (*sāsrava*) things are suffering because they are associated with the three types of suffering (*triduḥkhatā*).
As for the claim that "only that which is the truth of origination [is the origin]," this is said to be contrary to the Sūtra. For in the Sūtra, craving alone is mentioned.

It was mentioned in the Sūtra because of its predominance, yet others too are the origin. How is this to be understood? Because elsewhere another is also mentioned. For it was said by the Blessed One:
"Karma, craving, and ignorance are the cause of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) in the future."

Furthermore, it is said: "The five kinds of seeds" is a designation for consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*); "the earth element" is a designation for the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Therefore, the teaching in the Sūtras is intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), whereas that in the Abhidharma is definitive (*lākṣaṇika*).

However, by speaking of the cause of actualization (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*), craving alone was stated as the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*). By speaking of the cause of birth and actualization along with its causes, karma, craving, and ignorance were stated in the verse. This is because it is said in the Sūtra: "Karma is the cause for birth; craving is the cause for actualization," or according to the sequence of the *sahetu-sapratyaya-sanidāna* Sūtra. Furthermore, consciousness and the other factors were also mentioned by one who was elucidating their nature as the seed and the field.

What, then, is birth (*upapatti*), and what is manifestation (*abhinirvṛtti*)? Birth is the production of a personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) through various modes such as realm (*dhātu*), destiny (*gati*), and womb (*yoni*). Manifestation, on the other hand, is the linking of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhāna*) without such distinctions. Of these two, karma and craving for existence (*bhavatṛṣṇā*) are respectively the causes. For example, a seed is the cause for the production of a sprout according to the specific variety of its species, such as rice or barley; water, however, is the cause for the mere growth of all sprouts without distinction—such is the illustration. What is the reasoning here that craving is the cause of manifestation?

Because there is no birth for one who is free from craving (*vītatṛṣṇa*). Both those with craving and those free from craving die; however, it is observed that only those with craving are seen to be born, not those free from craving. Thus, since there is no birth without craving, we recognize craving as the cause for the production of existence (*bhava*). Furthermore, because of the bending of the continuum (*saṃtati*): wherever there is craving, we observe the mental continuum constantly inclining toward that object. Therefore, we conclude that it is the same regarding rebirth (*punarbhava*).

And no other state is so firmly grasped by anything as the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) is by craving, like a limb smeared with a paste of dried lentils used for bathing. Nor is there any other cause so persistently attached as self-love (*ātmasneha*); this is the logical reasoning.

The four truths were also taught by the Blessed One; there are two truths as well: conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). What are the characteristics of these two?
That which, when broken, is no longer perceived as that [object], and that which, when its parts are mentally excluded, is no longer perceived as that, is conventional truth. (2.2.4)
That which is conventionally real is like a jar or water; that which is ultimately real is otherwise. //4//

2.2.4 a) That which, when broken down into its constituent parts, no longer gives rise to the cognition of that [object], is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*), such as a jar. For in that case, when it is broken into shards, the cognition of a "jar" no longer occurs. Furthermore, that for which the cognition of it does not occur when other properties are mentally excluded is also to be understood as conventionally real, such as water. For in that case, when properties such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth are mentally excluded, the cognition of "water" no longer occurs.

However, since the designation "conventional" (saṃvṛti) is applied to those very things, when people say "the jar exists" or "the water exists" by the power of convention, they speak what is true and not false; this is conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).

2.2.4 b) Ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is otherwise than that: where the cognition of a thing persists even when it is broken, and the cognition remains even when other properties are excluded by the intellect, that is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). For example, form (*rūpa*). For in that case, even when the object is broken down into atoms and even when properties such as taste and so forth are excluded by the intellect, the cognition of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form still persists. Feeling (*vedanā*) and the others are to be understood in the same way. Because it exists in an ultimate sense, this is called ultimate truth.

The former masters have stated: "Ultimate truth is that which is apprehended by supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*) or by the mundane knowledge obtained subsequent to it (*tatpṛṣṭhalabdha*); conventional truth is that which is apprehended by other [forms of] knowledge.
Thus the truths have been explained.
(3.1) But how does their vision occur? This must be explained. Therefore, beginning from the initial stage, it is said:
Established in conduct and possessing [the wisdom] of hearing and reflection, one applies oneself to cultivation.

(5ab) One who desires to see the truths here first of all maintains ethical discipline (*śīla*). Thereafter, one acquires the scriptural learning (*śruta*) that is conducive to the vision of the truths, or hears its meaning. Having heard it, one reflects upon it without error; having reflected, one applies oneself to meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for the sake of concentration. Relying on the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*), that consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*) arises; relying on the wisdom consisting of reflection, that consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*) arises. Furthermore, what is the characteristic of these types of wisdom?
The cognitions consisting of hearing and so forth have as their objects both the name and the referent. //5cd//

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*) has names as its object; wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī*) has both names and meanings as its object; and wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*) has only meanings as its object. For the latter proceeds toward the meaning independently of the words. Regarding this, they provide the following analogy: one who has not learned how to swim does not let go of the float at all. One who is somewhat trained might occasionally let it go and occasionally hold onto it. But one who is well-trained crosses over without depending on the float at all. This is the illustration.

3.1.2 However, others maintain that in this conception, the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*) is not established; for that which has names as its object would be [wisdom] consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī*), and that which has meanings as its object would be [wisdom] consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).

But this definition is not faultless. Wisdom consisting of hearing is the certainty produced from the authority of the words of a reliable person (*āptavacana*); wisdom consisting of reflection is that produced from the contemplation of reasoning (*yukti-nidhyāna*); and wisdom consisting of cultivation is that born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is because the suffix *-mayaṭ* is prescribed in the sense of "cause" (*hetu*), as in the examples: "life-breaths consist of food" (*annamayaḥ prāṇāḥ*) and "cows consist of grass" (*tṛṇamayyo gāvaḥ*).
3.2.1 Furthermore, for one thus engaged in cultivation, how is that cultivation accomplished? To this he says:
"For one possessing the two kinds of withdrawal" (6a).
For if one is withdrawn by means of both body and mind, through the removal of social contact and unwholesome thoughts.
3.2.2 Then for whom are those two types of withdrawal easy to accomplish? For one who has few desires and is contented, but not for one who is discontented or has great desires.
(6b) 3.2.2 a1) What, then, is this discontentment, and what is great desire?
Contentment is the absence of further desire for what has been obtained; great desire is the longing for what has not yet been obtained. (6cd)

The Abhidharmikas maintain that "lack of contentment" (*asaṃtuṣṭi*) is the desire for more even when excellent robes and other requisites have already been obtained, whereas "great desire" (*mahecchatā*) is the longing for those things not yet obtained. But one might object: since that desire for more occurs only regarding what has been obtained and not regarding what has not been obtained, what is the distinction between these two? This must be explained. However, it is logical to define them as follows: "contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi*) is the lack of distress regarding what has been obtained when it is neither excellent nor abundant; "great desire" is the longing for what is excellent and abundant, even if it has not been obtained.
3.2.2 b) By way of being the opposites of those [two], their antidotes are to be understood as the reverse of discontent and great desire; namely, contentment and fewness of wishes.
And these two pertain to the three realms and are stainless.

The phrase "their opposites" carries over [from the previous context]. They belong to the three realms and are also unassociated [with the outflows], because they are both with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and without-outflow (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, discontent (*asaṃtuṣṭi*) and great desire (*mahecchatā*) belong exclusively to the realm of desire (*kāmāvacara*).
3.2.2 c) What, then, is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these two—fewness of desires (*alpecchatā*) and contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*)? He says: non-greed (*alobha*). (7c)
For these have non-greed as their intrinsic nature.
3.2.3 And the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*):
the term "non-greed" continues [from the previous context]. Because the noble ones (*ārya*) arise from these, there are four noble lineages; they too have non-greed as their intrinsic nature.
Of these, however, three consist of contentment. (7d)

The first three have contentment as their intrinsic nature: namely, contentment with robes, alms-food, and lodgings. The fourth noble lineage is delighting in abandonment and cultivation. How is it that its intrinsic nature is non-attachment? Because it turns away from craving for existence and sensual desire.
Now, what is shown by the Blessed One through the four noble lineages?
By the last one, [the lineage of delighting in cultivation] is action; by the [first] three, livelihood. (8a)

For the Blessed One, the Lord of Dharma, has prescribed two things—livelihood (*vṛtti*) and activity (*karman*)—to his disciples who have renounced their own worldly occupations and have set out for the sake of liberation. By means of three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), livelihood is prescribed; by the fourth, activity. [He said: "By performing this activity with this livelihood, sirs, you shall before long attain liberation.
But why was such a livelihood and such an activity prescribed?
It is as an antidote to the arising of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Four arisings of craving are taught in the Sūtra: "For the sake of robes, O monk, craving arises, it persists, and it becomes firmly attached; for the sake of alms-food, for the sake of lodgings, and for the sake of existence and non-existence, O monk, craving arises," and so forth in detail. As an antidote to these, the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) have been taught:
"Desire for the objects of 'I' and 'mine' [is abandoned] for the sake of their temporary and ultimate pacification. (8cd)

That same meaning is stated again by way of a synonym: "The objects of the notion of 'mine' (*mamakāra*) are robes and so forth; the object of the notion of 'I' (*ahaṃkāra*) is the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*). Desire therein is craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Among these, there are three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) for the temporary pacification of desire for the objects of 'mine,' and the fourth is for the ultimate pacification of both desires. (3.3) It has been explained how the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*) is accomplished. For one who has thus become a fit vessel (*pātrībhūta*), how does entry into that cultivation occur?
Entry therein occurs through the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) and through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
"Mindfulness" (*smṛta*) means mindfulness itself (*smṛti*).

For whom, then, is it by means of the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*), and for whom by means of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*)? Respectively, for those who have excessive passion and discursive thought (*vitarka*). (9c)

Those for whom passion (*rāga*) and discursive thought (*vitarka*) are predominant are called "those characterized by predominant passion and discursive thought. For one who is intensely prone to passion toward what is nearby, the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) is prescribed; for one who is prone to discursive thought, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is prescribed. Some say that because its object is not manifold, this [mindfulness of breathing] leads to the cutting off of discursive thought, whereas the meditation on the foul brings about discursive thought because its object consists of specific colors and shapes.
Others say it is because it does not look outward: for the meditation on the foul looks outward like visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), due to its close contemplation of external objects.

3.3.1 Furthermore, in that regard, there are four kinds of attachment (*rāga*): attachment to color (*varṇa*), attachment to shape (*saṃsthāna*), attachment to touch (*sparśa*), and attachment to service (*upacāra*). As an antidote to the first, they describe the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) with objects such as the livid corpse (*vinīlaka*); for the second, [the foul] with objects such as the devoured and the scattered; for the third, [the foul] with objects such as the festering, the pus-filled, and the bone; and for the fourth, [the foul] with the object of the motionless dead body.
However, without distinction, the skeleton (*śaṅkalā*) is praised for all those possessed by attachment. (9d)
For within the skeleton, none of these four types of objects of passion exist.

Because it consists of mental attention that is based on resolute conviction and is partial, the meditation on the foul does not result in the abandonment of the afflictions, but only in their suppression.

Furthermore, this practitioner of yoga who cultivates the meditation on the foul is said to be of three kinds: the beginner, the one who has mastered the practice, and the one who has transcended mental attention.

3.3.1 a1) Therein, from the expansion and contraction [of the visualization] of bones as far as the ocean, the beginner— desiring to cultivate the meditation on the foul (*aśubha*)— first fixes the mind on a part of his own body, such as the big toe, the forehead, or wherever he finds delight. There, by means of the progressive process of resolving upon the rotting and putrefaction of the flesh, he purifies the bone and beholds the entire skeleton.

In the same way, he further resolves upon a second [skeleton], and so on, until he resolves upon the entire earth as far as the ocean's edge, filled with skeletons, for the purpose of increasing his resolve (*adhimokṣa*). Then, contracting it again, he resolves upon only his own single skeleton for the purpose of concentrating the mind. It is said that by this much time, the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) becomes perfected. This is the beginner practitioner of yoga (*ādikarmiko yogācāraḥ*).
3.3.1 a2) By discarding the bones from the foot up to half of the skull, one is considered "victorious. (10cd)

Furthermore, for the sake of a specific refinement in the concentration of the mind, he sets aside the bones of the feet within that skeleton and attends to the remainder. In this manner, he proceeds gradually until, having set aside half of the skull, he attends to the other half. This is one who has achieved mastery.
(3.3.1a3) He is "one whose mental application has transcended" because he fixes his mind between the eyebrows.

Having abandoned even that half of the skull, he fixes his mind between the two eyebrows. This, it is said, is the practitioner of yoga who has transcended mental application regarding the meditation on the foul.

3.3.1 a4) There is a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika): it may be limited by way of the limitation of its impure object, but not limited by way of the limitation of mastery. This is because, for those whose mental attention is mastered or unmastered, and for those whose mental attention is unmastered or mastered, [the meditation] takes as its object either one's own body or the far shore of the ocean. 3.3.1 b) Now, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*), how many stages (*bhūmi*) does it comprise, what is its object (*ālambana*), and where does it arise? In due order: Non-greed (*alobha*); ten stages; having the visible objects of the desire realm as its object; born of humans. (11cd)
Its intrinsic nature is non-attachment (*alobha*).

It belongs to ten stages: the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) together with their preliminary stages (*sāmantaka*) and the intermediate meditation (*dhyānāntara*), as well as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Its objective support consists of visible forms belonging to the desire realm. What, then, is the visible? It is color and shape. For this very reason, it is established that its object is the referent (*artha*).
It arises only among human beings, not in any other realm of existence, much less in another world-system (*dhātu*). Even there, it does not arise in Uttarakuru.

That it takes the aspect of the foul (*aśubhākāra*) is established by its very name. Whatever belongs to a particular time-period (*adhvan*), it has that same time-period as its object; however, that which is subject to non-arising (*anutpattidharmin*) has all three time-periods as its object.
Because it consists of attention through resolute belief (*adhimukti-manaskāra*), it is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
It is both acquired through detachment (*vairāgyalābhikī*) and acquired through application (*prāyogikī*), depending on whether it has been previously practiced or not.
Thus, the definition of the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*), along with its classifications, has been explained.

3.3.2 Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). It belongs to the five stages (*pañcabhūmi*) and has wind as its object (*vāyugocarā*). It is based in the realm of desire (*kāmāśrayā*).

(12abc) Inhalation (*ānanam*) is *āna*, which is the breath that enters; exhalation (*apānanam*) is *apāna*, which is the breath that goes out. Mindfulness of these two is mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*).

3.3.2 a) That very [wisdom] has wisdom as its intrinsic nature; however, it is called "mindfulness" because it functions by means of the support of that [wisdom's] power, just like the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

It exists in five stages: in the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because it is associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*). It is said that because it is conducive to applied thought (*vitarka*), it is not associated with pleasure or pain, as they are its opposites; furthermore, pleasure and mental joy (*saumanasya*) are obstacles to concentration (*avadhāna*), whereas this [practice] is to be accomplished through concentration. For those who maintain that equanimity exists even for one who has entered the fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*), it belongs to eight stages, since above that [level], inhalation and exhalation do not exist. Its object is wind, and it is based in the desire realm among gods and humans.
It is both that which is acquired through application and that which is obtained through detachment;
and this is the mental attention to reality regarding these very dharmas.
[It is] not [the knowledge] of outsiders,
because they lack instruction, and because [this knowledge] is the complete awakening to all subtle phenomena.
3.3.2 b) And this [knowledge] is...
It is sixfold, by means of counting and so forth. //12d//

And this [practice] becomes complete when endowed with six causes: counting (*gaṇanā*), following (*anugama*), fixing (*sthāpanā*), observing (*upalakṣaṇā*), transforming (*vivarta*), and purifying (*pariśuddhi*).

3.3.2 b1) Among these, "counting" means that having directed the mind toward the inhalations and exhalations, one counts from one to two up to ten by means of mere mindfulness, while remaining indifferent to the body and mind through non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*). One does not count fewer or more than that, out of fear of mental contraction or distraction.

In that regard, there are three faults: undercounting, if one takes two as one; overcounting, if one takes one as two; and confusion, if one takes an inhalation for an exhalation, or vice versa. Counting correctly is otherwise than these.
Furthermore, if distraction occurs in the interim, one should count again from the beginning until meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is attained.

3.3.2 b2) Following (anugama): This means that one follows the movement of the inhalations and exhalations without deliberate effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), [observing] how far they enter or exit, and whether they pervade the entire body or move only in a single part. One follows them as they enter, in the sequence of entering the throat, heart, navel, hips, thighs, calves, and finally the feet; and as they exit, for the distance of a span (*vitasti*) or a fathom (*vyāma*). Others say this extends as far as the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) and the Vairambha winds.
However, because this involves mental attention to a [conceptualized] reality (*tattva-manasikāra*), it is not tenable.

3.3.2 b3) *Sthāpanā* (establishment) means that one perceives [the winds] as being situated from the tip of the nose down to the big toe, like a thread through a gem. One considers: "Are these beneficial or harmful? Are they cold or hot?

3.3.2 b4) *Upalakṣaṇā* (observation) means that one observes not only these winds alone, but also the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the derived form (*upādāyarūpa*) produced by the great elements, and the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) dependent upon them; thus, one observes the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).

3.3.2 b5) *Vivarta* (transformation) is the turning away of the cognition that takes wind as its object and the application [of the mind] to progressively higher roots of merit, up to the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*).
3.3.2 b6) *Pariśuddhi* (purification) is the entry into the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth.

3.3.2 b7) Others maintain that "transformation" refers to everything from the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), while "purification" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and so forth.
3.3.2 b8) There is a summary verse: "Counting, following, fixing, characterizing, transforming, and purifying— this sixfold mindfulness of breathing is considered [the practice]."
3.3.2 c1) Furthermore, it should be understood that in-breathing and out-breathing belong to the same level as the body;
for whatever level the body belongs to, these two belong to that same level, because they are a part of the body.

3.3.2 c2) Inhalation and exhalation proceed based on specific states of body and mind, because they are absent in those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), in those in the embryonic stage (*kalala*), and in those who have entered the mindless state (*acittaka*) or the fourth dhyāna. Indeed, they proceed only when the body possesses cavities and a mind belonging to the level of inhalation and exhalation is present. They enter [the body] for one being born or emerging from the fourth dhyāna, and they exit for one dying or entering the fourth dhyāna.
3.3.2 c3) And these two, inhalation and exhalation—
They are classified as sentient beings (sattvākhya), not classified as non-sentient; they are unappropriated (anupāttaka). 3.3.2 c4)
Because they are inseparable from the sense faculties.

(3.3.2 c5) They are outflowing (*naiḥṣyandika*), not accumulative (*aupacayika*) or born of maturation (*vipākaja*), because they do not increase with the growth of the body and because they reconnect after being severed; for this is not the case for matter born of maturation.
3.3.2 c6) Nor are those two perceived by a lower mind. //13cd//

The observation of those two [the body and the mind] is performed by a mind belonging to its own level or a higher level, but not by one belonging to a lower level—neither that of deportment (*airyāpathika*) nor that of transformation (*nairmāṇika*).

(3.4) The two gateways for entry have been explained. Having attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through these two, one who has perfected calm abiding (*śamatha*) should practice the cultivation of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
For the sake of accomplishing insight (vipaśyanā).
3.4.1 And how, moreover, should one act?
By examining the two characteristics of the phenomena of poetry, words, and the mind. //14cd//

One examines the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena by way of their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Their specific characteristic is simply their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Their general characteristic, however, is impermanence for conditioned things, suffering for contaminated things, and emptiness and selflessness for all phenomena.
Furthermore, what is the intrinsic nature of the body? It is the state of being the primary elements and their derivatives. Phenomena are those other than the [other] three [foundations].
It is said that for one who is concentrated and perceives the body atom by atom and moment by moment, the application of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) becomes perfected.

3.4.2 a) Now, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)? There are three kinds of application of mindfulness: the application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature, the application of mindfulness by association, and the application of mindfulness by object.
Among these, the application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature is wisdom (*prajñā*).

What kind of wisdom is it? It consists of hearing and so forth—namely, that which consists of hearing, that which consists of reflection, and that which consists of cultivation. The three types of foundations of mindfulness consist of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

Others [say]: "Because of association and because of being the object" (15ab). Other dharmas that coexist with it are the application of mindfulness through association (*saṃsarga-smṛtyupasthāna*); those which have that as their object are the application of mindfulness through the object (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*).

3.4.2 b) Why is it said that "the foundation of mindfulness in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*) is wisdom (*prajñā*)"? Because of the statement: "The foundation of mindfulness is the contemplation of the body within the body. What, then, is this contemplation? It is wisdom; for by means of it, one who possesses it is made a "contemplator" (*anupaśyin*). And because it is said: "He dwells contemplating the body within the body. One who has contemplation (*anupaśyana*), which is vision (*darśana*), is a "contemplator" (*anupaśyin*). One who contemplates the body is a "body-contemplator" (*kāyānupaśyin*). 3.4.3 a) Why was it stated by the Blessed One that wisdom is the foundation of mindfulness?

The Vaibhāṣikas say: "Because of the predominance of mindfulness. The meaning is: "Because it functions through the application of the power of mindfulness," like the wedge that holds together the wood being split.
However, this is more logical: wisdom is the *smṛtyupasthāna* because mindfulness is established by means of it, since [wisdom] expresses what has been seen [by insight].

For it has been said by the Venerable Aniruddha: "As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, mindfulness with the body as its object remains and becomes firmly established," and so forth. And it was also said by the Blessed One: "As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, his mindfulness becomes established and undeluded."

However, where it is said: "O monks, what is the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness? From the arising of nutriment comes the arising of the body; from the cessation of nutriment comes the passing away of the body," here the foundation of mindfulness is stated to be the object itself, on the grounds that mindfulness is established upon it.
And their names are according to their objects. Because they take as their objects the continuums of self, others, or both, each of them is threefold.
3.4.5 a) The sequence:
Regarding the order of their arising (yathotpatti):

why, then, do they arise in this way? Because the coarse [elements] are perceived first. Or, according to the Vaibhāṣikas: because the body is the basis for sensual desire; that [body] arises from the longing for sensation; that [longing] arises from the mind being unsubdued; and that [unsubdued state] arises from the non-abandonment of those afflictions.
But the group of four [is taught] by way of being the antidotes to the perversions. (15cd)
The four foundations of mindfulness are taught as the antidotes, respectively, to the four perversions of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self; they are neither more nor fewer than that.

(3.4.6) Of these, three have unmixed objects of focus (*asaṃbhinnālambana*), while the fourth is of both kinds: if one observes only phenomena (*dharma*), it has an unmixed object; however, if one observes two, three, or all four of the body and so forth together, it has a mixed object (*saṃbhinnālambana*).
(3.5) Having thus practiced the foundations of mindfulness with the body and so forth as their objects,
Abiding in the application of mindfulness to phenomena with all things as its object, he discerns them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. //16//

Abiding in the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) with a combined object, he views all those [objects], beginning with the body, collectively through four aspects: as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self.

3.6.1. From that arises the "Heat" stage (*ūṣmagata*): from that very application of mindfulness to phenomena when practiced in this manner, there sequentially arises the wholesome root named "Heat. It is called "Heat" because it is like heat; for it is the precursor to the fire of the Noble Path which burns the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
That has the four truths as its objective domain; because it is protracted, that "heat" stage has the four truths as its object and possesses sixteen aspects.

One views suffering through four aspects: as impermanent, as suffering, as empty, and as non-self. One views the origin through four aspects: as cause, as origin, as production, and as condition. One views cessation through four aspects: as cessation, as peace, as excellence, and as escape. One views the path through four aspects: as path, as method, as practice, and as leading to liberation. We shall explain the specific distinctions of these later.
3.6.2 a) From the "Heat" [stages], the "Summits" arise. (17cd)
From the "Heat" stages, which have increased through the sequence of weak, medium, and intense, the "Summits" arise;
these too are of the same nature. (17d)

Just as the "heat" (*ūṣman*) has the four truths as its object and possesses sixteen aspects, these [summits] are given a different name because they are more excellent. They are called "summits" (*mūrdhan*) because they are the peak of the unstable roots of merit; for from these, there is either a falling back or a transcending. 3.6.2b) Regarding the "production of both by means of the dharma": furthermore, the production of both these levels—heat and summits—is by means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). What is this "production"? It is the initial arrangement of the aspects (*ākāra*) upon the truths.
But there is also an increase by means of others;

that is, their increase occurs through all four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). For one who is increasing them, there is a non-manifestation of those previously attained because of the presence of great esteem.
From these [foundations], which have increased according to the sequence of weak, medium, and intense, there arises once again [the path of seeing].
From them comes patience (*kṣānti*) (18c), because of the superior endurance of the truths and because there is no falling back. That too is of three kinds: weak, middling, and intense.
3.6.3a) It is likewise twofold (18c).

Just as the summits (mūrdhan) have been described, so too are the weak and medium levels of receptivity (kṣānti), because they are produced in the same manner. However, there is this distinction in their increase: the increase of all receptivity occurs through the Dharma. //18//
It is by means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) alone, and not by any other.

As for the statement, "The highest [stage of] receptivity (*kṣānti*) has as its object the suffering pertaining to the desire realm" (19ab), it follows from the context. Because it is contiguous with the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*), this receptivity has exclusively the suffering of the desire realm as its object. For this very reason, the fact that the levels of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and so forth have the suffering and other aspects of all three realms as their objects is established, since no such restriction was stated.

3.6.3 c) When, by gradually reducing the objects of the aspects of each truth—beginning with the antidotes to the form and formless realms—down to the point where one attends to the suffering belonging solely to the desire realm for two moments, this entire stage is called medium receptivity (*madhyā kṣānti*). When it consists of only a single moment, that is superior receptivity (*adhimātrā*). And it is momentary (*kṣaṇikā*); it is not protracted.

3.6.4. Likewise, the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are just like the highest degree of patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*). They too have the suffering of the desire realm as their object and are momentary. These are called "supreme mundane dharmas" because they are the most excellent of all mundane things; for, even without a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), they draw forth the Path through its own human effort (*puruṣakāra*). 3.6.5.

These [stages], beginning with the "heat" (*ūṣmagata*), are said to be essentially wisdom (*prajñā-ātmaka*), because their intrinsic nature is that of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
However, all five aggregates (19cd),
excluding acquisitions, are included by the inclusion of the "with-possessions" [category]. //19d//

The acquisitions (*prāpti*) are not included within the levels of heat (*ūṣmagata*) and so forth, lest there be the manifestation of the levels of heat and so forth for a noble one (*ārya*) simply through the manifestation of those [acquisitions].

In that regard, when the level of heat is being produced with the three truths as its object, the present application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is active, and the four future ones are cultivated. When the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is the object, that same [application of mindfulness of phenomena] is cultivated in both ways (present and future). In all cases, the aspects (*ākāra*) are homogeneous (*sabhāga*).

In the increase [of the roots] by means of one of the four truths, there is one of the four; the future ones are four. In that same case, when increasing by means of the object of cessation (*nirodha*), the last [present root] is present, and the future ones are four. As for the aspects (*ākāra*), they are all, because the "cows" (the roots) have already been obtained.

3.6.6 b) In the formation of the Summits (*mūrdhan*), even when taking the four truths as objects, and when increasing by means of the object of cessation, the last [present root] is present, and the future ones are four. The aspects are all. When increasing by means of the objects of the three truths, there is one of the four; the future ones are four. The aspects are all.

3.6.6 c) For the *kṣāntis*, the last [member] is present in all cases; four [members] are future. All aspects (*ākāras*) are present. 3.6.6 d) In the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharmas*), the last [member] is present; four [members] are future. There are only four aspects, because of the absence of others and because of their similarity to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
3.6.7 Thus, the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are fourfold. (20ab)

Thus, these four roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are as follows: namely, "heat" (*uṣmagata*), "summits" (*mūrdhan*), "patiences" (*kṣānti*), and "supreme mundane dharmas" (*agradharma*). Among these, the [first] two are weak because they are subject to falling away due to their instability; the "patiences" are middling; and the "supreme mundane dharmas" are superior.

What is the meaning of "conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)? The root *vidh* means "to divide. Penetration (*vedha*) is certain; thus, "penetration" (*nirvedha*) is the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), because by it there is the abandonment of doubt and the discernment of the Truths, [realizing] "this is suffering," up to "this is the path. A "portion" (*bhāga*) of that is a single part of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). They are called "conducive to penetration" because they are beneficial as being the bringers (*āvāhaka*) of that [Path].
And all these four types of factors conducive to penetration consist of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
It is not produced by hearing or reflection.

(3.6.8 b1) It belongs to the stages of the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the four dhyānas; these are its stages because it is subsumed within them. It does not exist in the higher [stages] because it is an accompaniment to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Its absence [in the higher stages] is due to its having the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as its object, and because that [desire realm] must have been previously fully known and abandoned.

3.6.8 b2) For them, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is maturation consisting of the five aggregates; these are only completing [karmas] and not projecting [karmas], because they are averse to existence (bhava).
3.6.8 b3) But two [types of karma] may also exist in the lower realms. //20d//

The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative view. According to the Venerable Ghoṣaka, however, the first two aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) belong to seven levels; they also exist in the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*).
(3.6.8c) But all four of these have their basis in the desire realm. (21a)

Three [of these] arise only among humans, in the three continents; however, for those who have previously produced them, they manifest among the gods. The fourth arises among the gods as well. 3.6.8d) Women obtain the three based on both genders; a woman obtains the supreme dharmas based on two genders. (21ab)

However, regarding the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*), only a woman can attain those based on both genders; a man attains only those based on the male gender, because he has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) of femininity.
3.6.9 a) How are the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) abandoned? "The Noble One abandons them by abandoning the level [of existence]. (21cd)

When an Noble One (*ārya*) abandons a particular stage (*bhūmi*), he also abandons those [attainments] belonging to that stage; it is not otherwise. Furthermore, the abandonment of a stage occurs through the transition to another stage.
But for one who is not a Noble One (*anārya*), [the attainments are lost] through death. (3.6.9b)

An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), however, abandons [the roots] solely by relinquishing the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), whether there is a transition to another stage (*bhūmisaṃcāra*) or not.
The first two [roots] are also abandoned through falling away (*parihāṇi*);

and it is only the ordinary person who abandons them through death. For the noble one (*ārya*), however, there is no falling away from those two. Furthermore, even for the ordinary person, there is no falling away from Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*agradharma*).
3.6.9 c) One who possesses the vision of the truths in that very [life] is one born from the root.

(22b) He who produces the aids to penetration belonging to the level of the root dhyāna necessarily perceives the truths in that very birth, because of the intensity of his spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
3.6.9 d) There is no acquisition of what was not previously obtained when [the roots] have been lost. (22c)

When there is a re-acquisition of those [faculties] that had been lost, then only those not previously acquired are obtained, and not those previously abandoned, because—like the *prātimokṣa* restraint—they must be accomplished through effort rather than being habitually present.
(3.6.9 e) When a teacher who defines the limits is present, one generates them beyond that; when such a teacher is absent, one generates them from the very beginning.
Furthermore, what is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these two: loss (*vihāni*) and falling away (*parihāṇi*)?
There are two types of decline and possession. //22d//

Both of these have the nature of possession (*samanvāgama*). However, falling away (*parihāṇi*) is caused by defects; it is necessarily a falling away, and it is also caused by the excellence of qualities.

3.6.10 a) Even one who has fallen away from the attainment of the "heat" (*ūṣmagata*) stage is necessarily of a nature destined for final nirvāṇa. What is the distinction [of this] from the "aids to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*)? It is the state of being closer to the vision of the truths, provided there is no obstacle.
3.6.10 b) One who has attained the "summits" (*mūrdhan*) does not cut off the roots [of merit]. (23a)

Even if one who has attained the *mūrdhānas* falls away, they do not sever their roots of merit; however, they may go to the miserable realms and even commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*). But one who has attained *kṣānti* does not go to the miserable realms.
Even if that *kṣānti* is lost, one does not again go to the miserable realms, because the karma and afflictions leading to those states have been rendered distant.

Indeed, through the very attainment of patience (*kṣānti*), one acquires the quality of non-arising (*anutpattidharmatā*) for certain destinies, modes of birth, rebirths, physical bases, and afflictions of the eighth existence and beyond: namely, the miserable destinies; the egg-born and moisture-born modes of birth; rebirth among the non-percipient beings, in Uttarakuru, or as a Mahābrahmā; rebirth with a physical basis that is a eunuch, a *paṇḍaka*, or possessing both sexual organs; the eighth existence and those following it; and the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*). This [non-arising] occurs, however, according to the appropriate degree—both in the weak and the intense stages: in the weak stage, there is the non-arising of the miserable destinies, and in the intense stage, of the others.

3.6.11 a) The aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) belong to three lineages (*gotra*), due to the distinction between the lineages of the Śrāvakas and so forth. Among these, having turned away from the lineage of a disciple (*śiṣyagotra*), one may become a Buddha (23cd).

It is possible that one who has produced the stages of *ūṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* from the lineage of a *śrāvaka* might turn back and become a Buddha; however, once *kṣānti* has been attained, such a possibility no longer exists. Why? Because, it is said, the miserable realms (*apāya*) have been turned away from; and while Bodhisattvas plunge even into the miserable realms due to their dependence on performing the welfare of others, for this [śrāvaka] lineage, there is no such possibility because it is irreversible.
The others [the three stages] may also belong to other [lineages]. (23d)

The phrase "it may be by turning back" (*vivartya syāt*) continues [from the previous verse]. All three levels of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) may be turned away from the lineage of the Śrāvakas; "another than a Buddha" means a Pratyekabuddha.
However, those belonging to the Pratyekabuddha lineage cannot be turned away.
For both the Teacher and the Rhinoceros-like [Pratyekabuddha], everything up to enlightenment occurs in a single final dhyāna. (24ab)

The Teacher is the Buddha; the rhinoceros-horn-like one is the Pratyekabuddha. For these two, relying on the very same seat and the fourth dhyāna, because their samādhi is immovable and sharp, there arises everything from the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) up to enlightenment (*bodhi*). We shall establish later that enlightenment consists of the knowledge of destruction and non-arising (*kṣayānutpādajñāna*).
Others say it extends from the meditation on the foul (*aśubhā*) up to enlightenment.
However, for those who hold that there are Pratyekabuddhas other than the rhinoceros-horn-like type, there is no prohibition against the turning away of their lineage (*gotra*).

3.6.12 a) Furthermore, could one who has already perfected the yoga in the very first birth produce the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)? This is not so. For it is necessary that, prior to those [aids to penetration], the aid to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) must first be produced.
3.6.12 b) For even with the minimum of all [possessions], liberation occurs quickly in three existences. //24d//

In one lifetime, one may produce the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); in the second, the factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); and in the third, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). This is like the sequence of sowing a seed, the growth of the crop, and the production of the fruit of supernatural power. For, through this gradual process, entry, maturation, and liberation occur within the continuum of this [being] according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, they describe that which is conducive to liberation as consisting of hearing and reflection, not of cultivation.
3.6.13 b) How many types of action (*karman*) are there?
There are three types of action;

however, mental action (*manaskarma*) is primary. Nevertheless, because it is embraced by that [mental] aspiration, bodily and vocal actions also become conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*). For instance, even by giving a single alms-meal or undertaking a single precept, one projects factors conducive to liberation through the empowerment of the desire for liberation.
3.6.13 c) But this [attainment] is restricted to humans;
it occurs only among men in the three continents, and not elsewhere, because of the absence of wisdom and world-weariness as appropriate to each case.

4. The factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) have been explained as a digression; however, the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) has begun to be taught. Within that, up to the supreme mundane dharmas (*agradharma*) have been stated, and the remainder is yet to be explained.
4.1.1 Therefore, this is said:
from the supreme mundane dharmas...
The receptivity to the dharma is untainted. //25cd //

Immediately after the supreme mundane factors (*laukikāgradharma*), the untainted receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises. Upon what object? Its object is the suffering of the desire realm;

that is, the suffering belonging to the desire realm is its objective support. This is called "receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering. It is qualified by its outflow (*niḥṣyanda*) for the purpose of indicating that it is untainted. It is "receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena" because it is the receptivity for the sake of the knowledge of phenomena, like a tree that bears flowers and fruit.

4.1.1 a) This very [attainment] is called "entry into the determination" (*niyāmāvakrānti*), because of entering the determination of correctness (*samyaktvaniyāma*). In the Sūtra, correctness is said to be Nirvāṇa. In this context, "determination" (*niyama*) or "determination" (*niyāma*) means the state of being fixed (*ekāntībhāva*). "Entry" (*avakramaṇa*) is the approaching of that [state]. 4.1.1 b) And when that [attainment] has arisen, one is called a noble person (*āryapudgala*). By its future [arising], the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is turned back. Only this is accepted as its function while it is still in the future, and nothing else, just like the arising of a lamp.

Others say [the path of seeing arises] through the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). No, because those [supreme mundane dharmas] are of that same nature [as the path of seeing]. There is no fault, because they are in opposition to it, like killing an enemy while mounted upon his shoulders.
Others say it is through both, because of the similarity between the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
4.1.2 Then, right here, there is the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*). (26ab)

Then, immediately after the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), there arises in that very same [category of] suffering belonging to the desire realm the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*dharmajñāna*). That is called "the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering. It should be understood that the context of being untainted (*anāsrava*) applies everywhere.
4.1.3 Just as the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma and the knowledge of the dharma arise regarding the suffering of the desire realm, so too [do they arise] again.
Regarding the remaining suffering, there is the subsequent-knowledge-patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).

(26bcd) Immediately after the dharma-knowledge of suffering, there arises the subsequent-knowledge-patience which has as its object all [the aspects] of suffering belonging to the realms of form and formlessness. This is called the subsequent-knowledge-patience regarding suffering.
4.1.4 Thereafter, subsequent-knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) arises; that is called the subsequent-knowledge regarding suffering.

First, from the knowledge of the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), there arises the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). Following that, subsequently, there is the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) which has suffering as its object, because it follows in the same manner.
4.1.5 Just as these four patiences and knowledges arise regarding the truth of suffering, so too do they arise regarding the [remaining] three truths. 26d.

Immediately after the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*), the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origination regarding the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-samudaye dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises. Following that, there is the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaye dharmajñāna*). In this same manner, through the sequence of immediate succession, there arises the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origination regarding the remaining [realms] (*śeṣe samudaye anvayajñānakṣānti*), followed by the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaye anvayajñāna*); then the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation regarding the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara-duḥkha-nirodhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), followed by the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñāna*); and finally the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation regarding the remaining [realms] (*śeṣe nirodhe anvayajñānakṣānti*), followed by the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe anvayajñāna*).

Regarding the path that is the antidote to the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), there is the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of phenomena regarding the path (*mārge dharmajñāna*); regarding the remaining paths, there is the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārge anvayajñāna*).
Thus, this realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) consists of sixteen moments of mind;
by this sequence, this realization of the truths becomes sixteenfold in terms of consciousness.

4.2.1 As for those belonging to other schools who describe a single realization (*ekābhisamaya*) of the truths, their underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) must be understood as follows: "For realization is said to be threefold, without distinction,
[namely] that called seeing, the object, and the task" (27bc).

Realization through vision (*darśanābhisamaya*) is [the realization] of the truths by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsravā prajñā*). Realization through the object (*ālambanābhisamaya*) is also [realization] by means of the mental factors associated with that [wisdom], such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth. Realization through the task (*kāryābhisamaya*) is also [realization] by means of dissociated factors, such as morality (*śīla*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth. For when suffering (*duḥkha*) is being seen, there is a threefold realization regarding it; whereas for origin (*samudaya*) and the others, there is only realization through the task, because of their [respective] abandonment, realization, and cultivation.

4.2.1 a) If one were to say, regarding the realization of the truths through vision, that there is a single realization [for all of them], one would be speaking incorrectly, because of the difference in their aspects (*ākāra*).

4.2.1 b) Furthermore, if one were to say that there is a vision of all [truths] through the aspect of selflessness (*anātmākāra*), then there would be no vision of the truths as suffering and so forth. And thus, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra, which states: "In this regard, for a noble disciple who attends to suffering as suffering, or the origin as the origin, up to the path as the path, that discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*) which is associated with an outflow-free mental attention (*anāsravamanasikāra*).
If it is argued that this refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), we say no; for cultivation follows the manner in which things were seen.

4.2.1 c) Furthermore, even if one were to speak of a single realization (*ekābhisamaya*) on the grounds that by seeing one [truth], mastery over the remaining ones is obtained, there would be no fault; however, it would remain to be examined whether or not there is an emergence from meditative absorption in the interim. Alternatively, if one were to say: "While fully understanding suffering itself, one abandons origination, realizes cessation, and cultivates the path; therefore, there is a single realization"—even so, there would be no fault, because it is stated that upon the vision of one [truth], there is a realization of the tasks regarding the remaining ones.

4.2.1 d) Regarding the clear realization through vision (*darśanābhisamaya*), however, it appears that in the Sūtra the clear realization of the truths is taught as occurring sequentially. For instance, there are three Sūtras with illustrations in detail, such as: "Householder, for the truths, there is not only a single simultaneous clear realization (*ekābhisamaya*), but also a gradual clear realization (*anupūrvābhisamaya*). If it is argued that there is a single clear realization based on the Sūtra stating, "He who is free from doubt and free from uncertainty regarding suffering is likewise so regarding the Buddha," we say no; for that statement was made with the intention (*abhisandhi*) of referring to the non-manifestation [of defilements] and their necessary abandonment.
4.2.2 This aforementioned clear realization consists of sixteen moments of mind (*ṣoḍaśacittaka*).
It belongs to the same stage as the supreme mundane dharmas. //27d//

These sixteen moments of consciousness belong to the same stage as the supreme mundane dharma (*agradharma*); furthermore, it was stated previously that these [supreme mundane dharmas] belong to six stages.
Why, then, must there necessarily be both patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*)? Because:
Patience and knowledge are, respectively, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). (28ab)

The paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) are the "patiences" (*kṣānti*), because they cannot be interrupted in their function of severing the possession of afflictions (*kleśa-prāpti*). The paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), however, are the "knowledges" (*jñāna*), because they arise simultaneously with the possession of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) once one is liberated from the possession of afflictions. Therefore, both must necessarily exist, like the two actions of expelling a thief and closing the door.

If, on the other hand, the possession of dissociation were to arise together with the second path of uninterrupted transition itself, what would happen? Knowledge that has abandoned doubt would not have arisen with respect to that very object.

If it is argued that this contradicts the treatise which states, "The nine groups of fetters are abandoned through the patiences (*kṣānti*) and are to be destroyed by knowledge (*jñāna*"), it is not so; for the patiences are the retinue of knowledge. This is like the designation "done by the king" applied to what was actually done by the king's retinue.
Furthermore, are all sixteen moments of mind the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) because they consist in the vision of the truths? No, he says. What then?
"Because of seeing what was not previously seen, fifteen moments therein constitute the path of seeing" (28cd).

Beginning from the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñānakṣānti*) up to the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge ’nvayajñānakṣānti*), these fifteen moments constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). What is the reason? Because of the seeing of truths not previously seen. However, in the sixteenth moment, there is nothing further to be seen; therefore, because it is a repetition of what has already been seen, it is indeed the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

4.4.1 a) But does he not also see what was previously unseen by means of the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*)? True; however, the consideration is with respect to the truth (*satya*), not the moment (*kṣaṇa*). For a truth is not considered "unseen" because of a single moment that was unseen, just as a field is not considered "unreaped" because of a single stalk that was unreaped. 4.4.1 b) Because it is a fruit, because it involves the cultivation of the eight knowledges and sixteen aspects, because it abandons the previous path, and because it is continuous, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Its non-retrogression, however, is due to its maintenance of the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*).
4.4.1 c) If it is argued that for this very reason [the first seven moments] constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), we say no, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Why are the [first] seven knowledges (*jñāna*) considered the path of seeing? Because the seeing is not yet complete. For the vision of all the truths has not been finalized; since they occur in the interval before that completion, they too are the path of seeing.

4.5 It has been explained how the path of seeing and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) arise. Now we shall explain the classification of persons (*pudgala*) who have given rise to the noble path (*āryamārga*). Regarding these fifteen moments said to be of the nature of the path of seeing, they should be understood as follows:
Among them, those with dull and sharp faculties are the followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the followers by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).

One who exists among them with dull faculties is called a follower by faith; one with sharp faculties is a follower by dharma. "Following by faith" means following through faith. Because he possesses this, he is a follower by faith; or, because it is his nature to follow by means of faith, he is a follower by faith, since he previously pursued the meaning [of the teachings] based on trust in others. Likewise for the follower by dharma, because he previously pursued the meaning himself by means of the dharmas such as the sūtras.
4.5.1 Furthermore, these two—
Those who have not yet abandoned what is to be abandoned by cultivation are candidates for the first fruit and so forth. //29cd//

The first of the fruits is the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), because it is the first among all attainments of the fruits. If those same two—the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*)—have not previously abandoned the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*) through the worldly path (*laukikamārga*), and are thus bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), they are called candidates for the fruit of stream-entry.

As long as they have destroyed five types [of defilements], if up to five types of the defilements of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned by cultivation have been previously abandoned by means of the worldly path, they are likewise called candidates for the first fruit.
4.5.2. In the second [fruit], up until the destruction of the ninth [category of defilement].

Regarding the second cause, in the second [fruit]: if, beyond that [first fruit], six, seven, or eight categories of those two have already been abandoned, those two are called "candidates for the second fruit. And what is the second? It is the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*). 4.5.3. Those who are detached from the desire realm, or above it, are candidates for the third [fruit]. (30cd)

Furthermore, if through the abandonment of even the ninth category [of afflictions], they become free from passion for the desire realm, or for the higher realms up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*), those two are called "candidates for the third fruit. And what is the third? It is the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).
