"But at the sixteenth [moment], whichever candidate was in which stage, those two become established in that fruit" (31ab).

However, once the sixteenth moment of mind has arisen, those two are no longer called followers by faith or followers by dharma, nor are they called "those who have entered the path. What then? Whichever fruit one was previously entering, at that time one becomes established in that very fruit—whether it be the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning. But it is not possible to attain Arhatship from the very beginning, because the defilements to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) have not yet been abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and because prior detachment from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is impossible.
4.6.1 At that time, those with dull and sharp faculties are respectively called "resolved through faith" (śraddhādhimukta) and "attained through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta). //31cd//

At that time, he who has dull faculties and was previously a follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) is called "one liberated through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*); he who has sharp faculties and was previously a follower of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) is called "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), because they are characterized respectively by the predominance of resolve (*adhimokṣa*) and vision (*dṛṣṭi*) due to the relative excess of faith and wisdom.

But what is the reason that even one who has abandoned five categories [of afflictions] is called only a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) at the sixteenth moment of mind, and not a candidate for the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala-pratipannaka*)?
Because, in a given fruit, there is no attainment of a path superior to that fruit. (4.7)
One who abides in the fruit, if not exerting effort for further distinction, is not a candidate for the next stage. //32//

For when a fruit is being attained, there is this rule: the path distinguished by that fruit is not yet attained. Therefore, as long as one who abides in a fruit does not apply themselves toward a distinction for the sake of attaining another fruit, they are not called a "candidate" (pratipannaka). This should be understood similarly regarding other fruits as well.

However, one who is free from passion for the third dhyāna and enters the path of certainty (*niyāma*) by relying on a lower stage necessarily brings face-to-face the path distinguished by that fruit. Otherwise, having been reborn above that level, they would not be endowed with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).

Thus far, the classification of individuals (*pudgala*) has been established regarding those who have already largely abandoned desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*) upon entering the path of certainty (*niyāma*). Now, however, the gradual progression (*ānupūrvika*) must be explained.

Therefore, this is first established: just as these nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) have been taught in the realm of sensuality, so too are there nine grades of faults in each respective stage (*bhūmi*). (33ab)

This extends up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). Just as there are defects (*doṣa*), so too are there qualities (*guṇa*); their antidotes, known as the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), likewise consist of exactly nine types on each stage (*bhūmi*).
5.1.1 How so? Furthermore, by way of the division of the weak, medium, and intense [faculties] into [further] weak and so forth: //33cd//

There are three basic types: weak, medium, and intense. Since each of these is again threefold—being weak, medium, or intense—nine are established. Namely: the weak-weak type, the weak-medium, the weak-intense; the medium-weak, the medium-medium, the medium-intense; and the intense-weak, the intense-medium, and the intense-intense.

5.1.2 In this regard, by means of the weakest-weak path, there is the abandonment of the strongest-strong affliction; and so on, up to the abandonment of the weakest-weak [affliction] by means of the strongest-strong path. This is because, from the very beginning, a strongest path is impossible, and once a strongest path has arisen, a strongest affliction cannot exist. For coarse impurity is shaken off from a cloth first, and the subtle later; likewise, gross darkness is destroyed by a subtle light, and subtle [darkness] by a strong one—this is the application of the analogy.

For white dharmas are powerful, whereas black ones are weak; because even a momentary, mild Noble Path uproots the afflictions that have been nourished through the succession of beginningless saṃsāra despite being of the highest degree—just as the extraction of *trivṛt* medicine removes long-accumulated defects, or as a small, momentary lamp dispels great darkness.

Thus, regarding all nine grades of afflictions, one who abides in the fruit and has not yet exhausted those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation is "one who will be reborn seven times at most. (34ab)

For one who abides in the fruit [of stream-entry] and has not yet abandoned even a single category of the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation is a *srotāpanna*. He is called "one who acts seven times" (*saptakṛt*) because he undergoes seven births; "the highest" (*paraḥ*) means the very last. For not every [stream-enterer] acts exactly seven times. The reading of the Sūtra is "seven times at most" (*saptakṛtvaḥ-paramaḥ*). The meaning is that his maximum number of births is seven. The word "highest" (*parama*) denotes the limit.
The path is indeed the stream to Nirvāṇa, because one goes there by means of it. One who has entered (*āpanna*), arrived at, or attained that is a *srotāpanna*.

How has he entered [the path]? If it is because of attaining the first path, then even one who is at the eighth stage (*aṣṭamaka*) would be [an enterer]. If it is because of attaining the first fruit, then even one who is already largely free from passion (*bhūyovītarāga*) or entirely free from passion regarding the desire realm (*kāmavītarāga*) would be [an enterer]. This is with reference to one who is attaining all the fruits, because of the attainment of the first fruit. But what is the reason that only this person—and not the one at the eighth stage—is [so designated]? Because at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), he attains both the path of the candidate and the path of the fruit, attains both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, and achieves the complete realization of the stream (*sakalasroto'bhisamaya*).

5.2.3 That very [person] reconnects with seven other rebirth-existences (*upapattibhava*) among humans and seven intermediate existences (*antarābhava*); likewise among the gods, he thus reconnects with twenty-eight existences. However, because of the commonality of the number seven, he is said to be "one who has seven births at most" (*saptakṛtvah-parama*), just as in the cases of "skill in the seven bases" (*saptasthānakauśala*) and the "seven-leafed tree" (*saptaparṇa*); so say the Vaibhāṣikas.

5.2.3 a) As for what was stated in the Sūtra: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should bring about an eighth existence; such a case does not exist"—the intention here is "in a single realm of rebirth" (*ekasyāṃ gatau*). Or, if one were to interpret it according to the literal wording, then even the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) would not exist. Even so, for one who "flows upwards" and has the Peak of Existence as his limit, an eighth birth-existence in a single realm of rebirth would not be possible.
[This objection is answered: there is no fault, because the statement was made with reference to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

5.2.3 b) What is the scriptural authority or reasoning for this? And what is the authority here that it is seven times each among gods and humans, rather than seven times in both combined? For it is recited thus: "Seven times among gods and seven times among humans. One should not be dogmatic on this point.

He who becomes a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) among humans attains parinirvāṇa having returned only to those [human realms]; he who [becomes one] among gods [attains it] having returned only to those [divine realms].
5.2.3 c) Furthermore, what is the reason that he does not produce an eighth existence?

Within that much time, through the necessary ripening of the continuum, the Path arises because it is of such a nature; it is like one bitten by a seven-step venomous snake, or like a quartan fever. Furthermore, it is because seven fetters remain: two belonging to the lower realm and five belonging to the upper realm.
Even while manifesting the Noble Path in the interim, one does not attain final nirvana, because of the sustaining power of karma to be experienced in existence (*bhava*).

5.2.4 When there is no arising of a Buddha, one attains arhatship while still a householder; however, one does not continue to dwell in a household. One acquires the marks of a monk (*bhikṣu-liṅga*) through the attainment of the nature of reality (*dharmatā-pratilambhika*). Others say it is through the marks of another stage of life (*anyāśramika-liṅga*).

5.2.5 Why is one subject to the quality of not falling into the lower realms? Because one does not accumulate karma leading to those states, because there is an incapacity for the maturation of accumulated [karma] to arise, because the continuum is permeated by powerful roots of goodness (*balavat-kuśala-mūla-adhivāsana*), and because of the purity of one's application and intention (*prayoga-āśaya-śuddhi*). However, regarding karma fixed for the miserable destinies (*apāya-niyata*), one would not even produce the stage of receptivity (*kṣānti*) toward it.
And it is said in this regard:
"Having committed even a small evil, the fool goes downward;
having committed even a great [evil], the wise man abandons that misfortune."
For even a small piece of iron sinks in water when it is solid,
yet that very same iron floats when it is fashioned into a vessel, however large.

5.2.6. "He makes an end of suffering"—what is this "end of suffering"? It means that beyond which there is no further suffering; the sense is that he brings about a suffering that is without rebirth (*apratisaṃdhika*). Alternatively, "the end" refers to Nirvana. How does he "make" Nirvana? By removing the obstacles to its attainment. Just as people say, "Make space! or "Bring down the pavilion!
Furthermore, there might be others who are "seven-times-at-most" (*saptakṛtvaḥ-parama*), but because they are not fixed [in their destiny], they are not mentioned here.
5.3. Thus, first of all, one who abides in the fruit and has not yet exhausted the defilements to be abandoned by cultivation becomes one who is "seven-times-at-most."
But one who is freed from three or four types [of defilements] and has two or three births remaining is a *kulaṃkula*. //34cd //

That same stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) becomes a "family-to-family" (*kulankula*) practitioner by virtue of three causes: (1) by the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*), because of having abandoned three or four categories [of them]; (2) by the faculties (*indriya*), because of attaining the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) that are their antidotes; and (3) by birth (*janman*), because only two or three births remain.

In the verse, however, only two [causes] are mentioned because, once the afflictions have been subsequently abandoned by the stream-enterer, the attainment of the untainted faculties that serve as their antidote is established even without being explicitly stated.
As for birth, it might sometimes be fewer [than three], since he may still be capable of further progress; therefore, this [cause of birth] is specifically mentioned here.

5.3.1 b) Why is it that by the abandonment of five types [of defilements], there is not necessarily the abandonment of the sixth upon that abandonment? For a single type of that [sixth category] is not capable of obstructing the fruit, just as in the case of the "one-interval" (ekavīcika), because he has not yet transcended the realm.

5.3.1 c) That same [attainer of the fruit of once-returner] is of two kinds: the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula). The family-to-family among gods is one who, having transmigrated through two or three families among the gods, attains final nirvana there or in another divine assembly. The family-to-family among humans is one who attains final nirvana among humans, either there or in another continent. 5.3.2 Furthermore, that same person established in the fruit [is further distinguished].
One who has destroyed up to the fifth type [of affliction] is a candidate for the second fruit.
It should be understood that when one established in a fruit has abandoned from one type up to the fifth, they are a candidate for the second fruit.
But when the sixth type is exhausted, such a person is a once-returner. (5.3.3)

He attains the second fruit. Having gone to the world of the gods, because he returns to the human world only once more, he is called a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner); this is because there is no further birth beyond that. He is so called also because of the attenuation (*tanutva*) of passion, hatred, and delusion, since only their mild forms remain.

5.4.1 Furthermore, that same person established in the fruit, having destroyed seven or eight portions of the defilements, is one who has only one birth remaining (*ekajanman*) or is separated from nirvana by a single interval (*ekavīcika*).

And the third candidate (36abc) should be understood as that same once-returner who is "separated by one interval" (*ekavīcika*) for three reasons: because of the abandonment of seven or eight categories [of afflictions], because of the acquisition of the untainted faculties that are their antidotes, and because only one birth remains.

How can one category [of affliction] be able to obstruct his fruit? Because of the transcendence of the realm (*dhātu*). For it was stated previously that in three stages, karmas stand as obstructions; and just as with karmas, so too should afflictions be understood, because of the transcendence of the three levels consisting of the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and the fruit of outflow (*niḥṣyanda-phala*).

5.4.1 b) "Vīci" means an interval. Because Nirvana is separated from him by only one birth, or because the fruit of a Non-returner (anāgāmiphala) is separated from him by only one category of affliction (kleśaprakāra), he is called an Ekavīcika—one who has a single interval.
5.4.2 It should be understood that the candidate for the third fruit (the fruit of Arhatship) who is an Ekavīcika is one who has abandoned seven or eight categories [of afflictions].

However, one who has previously abandoned those categories does not become a Kulaṃkula or an Ekavīcika upon attaining the fruit until the path distinguished by that fruit has been brought into manifestation.
5.4.3 Thus, he is a non-returner because of the destruction of the nine [categories of afflictions]. //36d//

Furthermore, that same person, established in the fruit, is taught as a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) due to the abandonment of the nine types [of afflictions] and because of not returning to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It is said, "due to the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)," because of the summation of what has been abandoned; for necessarily two or three [of these] have already been abandoned previously. 5.4.4. [The non-returners are further classified as: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), one who attains parinirvāṇa upon being reborn (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*). (37abc)

"One whose parinirvāṇa occurs in the interval" is an *antarāparinirvṛti*; the same construction applies to "one who has arisen," namely, "by means of effort" (*sasaṃskāra*) or "without effort" (*asaṃskāra*). Furthermore, that very non-returner (*anāgāmin*) is of five types: 5.4.4 a) The *antarāparinirvāyī* is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). The *upapadyaparinirvāyī* is one who, immediately upon being reborn, attains parinirvāṇa before long because his path is both diligent and swift; this is by means of *nirvāṇa with a remainder of substrate* (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

Others say that he also [attains it] by means of *nirvāṇa without a remainder of substrate* (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*). This is not so, because he lacks mastery over the relinquishing of his life-span.

5.4.4 b) It is said that one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyī*) attains parinirvāṇa with exertion because his application is not yet relaxed upon rebirth, owing to the fact that he possesses a path that is both diligent and swift; whereas one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyī*) does so without exertion because he lacks a path that is both diligent and swift. Others say this is because [the former] attains nirvāṇa through a path that takes the conditioned and the unconditioned as its object. But that is not correct, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

5.4.4 c) In the Sūtra, however, the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) is mentioned first. This is indeed logical, because the path that flows outwardly and the path that flows [swiftly] are accomplished respectively by means of non-exertion and exertion, due to being attained without effort and with effort. For the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin), however, the path is more flowing and more intense, while the latent dispositions (anuśaya) are weaker.

5.4.4 d) The "one who flows upwards" (ūrdhvaṃsrotas) is one whose movement is upward; he does not attain parinirvāṇa in the very place where he was reborn. "Flow" (srotas) and "movement" (gati) have the same meaning.
When the meditative absorptions have been intermingled, he goes to Akaniṣṭha. //37d//

The one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*) is of two kinds: by way of cause and by way of fruit. By way of cause, it is because his meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are either mixed or unmixed. By way of fruit, it is because he has either the Akaniṣṭha heaven or the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as his limit.
In this regard, he by whom meditation is mixed goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven and attains final nirvāṇa there;
he is the "leaper" (*pluta*), the "half-leaper" (*ardhapluta*), and the "one who passes away from all [stages]" (*sarvacyuta*). (38ab)
Furthermore, that single type of "one who flows upwards" (*ūrdhvaṃsrotas*), which culminates in Akaniṣṭha, is threefold due to the distinctions of the "leaper" (*pluta*) and so forth.

Among these, the "leaper" is one who, having practiced the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) in this life, falls away from the [higher] three absorptions; having relished the first absorption, he is reborn among the Brahmakāyika gods. Then, by the power of previous practice, he practices the fourth absorption and, passing away from there, is reborn in Akaniṣṭha. He is called a "leaper" because he does not sink into the intermediate realms.
The "Half-Leaper" (ardhapluta) is one who, having been reborn among the Śuddhāvāsa deities, bypasses even a single intermediate station and enters the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
A noble one is not reborn among the Mahābrahmās because that place is a locus for [wrong] views and because there can be only a single leader.
The "All-Descender" (sarvacyuta) is one who, having passed through all the intermediate stations, enters the Akaniṣṭha heaven.

5.4.4 d2) Furthermore, a non-returner never produces a second birth in that very same place of rebirth, because he is one who proceeds toward distinction (*viśeṣagāmin*). In this way, his state of being a non-returner becomes complete, since he does not return at all to the lower realm where he was born, nor to that [upper realm] itself. Thus, first, it should be understood that in the case of mixed meditation (*vyavakīrṇadhyāna*), he goes to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. 5.4.4 e) Thereafter, [he passes away from there].
Another is one who goes to the peak of existence (*bhavāgraga*).

One whose meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are unmixed is an "upward-streamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) who has the peak of existence as his final goal. For he, relishing other attainments (*samāpatti*), is reborn in all the intermediate stages; without entering the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), he proceeds through the successive births in the formless realms (*ārūpya*) until reaching the peak of existence, where he attains parinirvāṇa.
This person is one whose practice is characterized by tranquility (*śamatha*), whereas the former was one whose practice was characterized by insight (*vipaśyanā*).

However, we observe that even for one who "flows upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*), intermediate *parinirvāṇa* is possible; yet, their status as having Akaniṣṭha or the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the limit is due to the absence of any further destination beyond them, just as the status of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) is limited to seven births at most.
These, first of all, are the five types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) who go to the realm of form (*rūpopaga*).
The others, who go to the formless realm (*ārūpyaga*), are of four kinds. (38c)

Another is the non-returner who goes to the formless realm (*ārūpyaga*), who, being free from passion for the form realm, passes away from here and is reborn in the formless realms. He, moreover, is of four kinds due to the distinction between those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth and so forth. These constitute the six types of non-returners. 5.4.4 g) Beyond that, another is one who attains nirvāṇa in this very life (*ihaniḥsṛta*). //38d//
In this very life, another attains final nirvana; he is the seventh, the one who attains final nirvana in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāyī*).
Furthermore, by dividing those three [types] into three kinds each, nine who have reached the realm of form (*rūpopaga*) are taught.
Thus, through the threefold division of the three non-returners (*anāgāmin*), there are nine non-returners who have reached the realm of form.

Of which three? Of the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and the one who goes upstream (*ūrdhvaṃsrotas*). How is there a threefold division? First, regarding the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, it is due to attaining parinirvāṇa quickly, not-so-quickly, or after a long time, according to three similes. Regarding the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, it is due to attaining parinirvāṇa through effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*) or without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*) after being reborn. For all three of these are "those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*) because they attain parinirvāṇa after having been reborn. Regarding the one who goes upstream, it is due to the divisions of the "leaper" (*pluta*) and so forth.
"Or rather, for all three [types of non-returners], there is a threefold distinction based on whether they attain parinirvāṇa quickly, not quickly, or after a long time.
(5.4.5b) Furthermore, their specific differences arise from the distinctions in karma, afflictions, and faculties. (39cd)
Furthermore, among these three and nine types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*), there is a distinction based on the differences in their karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*).

First, regarding the three [types], the distinction arises because they have accumulated karma to be experienced respectively in the intermediate state (*abhinirvṛtti*), upon rebirth (*upapadya*), or in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya*); because their afflictions manifest as weak, medium, or intense respectively; and because their faculties are intense, medium, or weak respectively.

Within each of these groups, there is likewise a distinction according to the circumstances, for the same reasons: for the first two triads, it is due to the difference in afflictions and faculties as before; for the final triad, it is due to the difference in karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
Thus, because of the ninefold nature of their afflictions and faculties, there are nine types of non-returners.
How, then, are seven destinations of the true persons taught in the Sūtra?
The seven good destinations are considered to be established by not differentiating the one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*). (40ab)

One whose nature is to flow upwards is an "upward-streamer" (*ūrdhva-srotas*). Because of the detailed classification of this [type], seven destinations of the noble persons (*satpuruṣagati*) are taught in the Sūtra.
Why, then, are only these considered the destinations of the noble persons, and not other destinations of those in training (*śaikṣagati*)?

For in those who possess these destinations, their activity exists only toward what is true and wholesome, and there is no activity toward what is unwholesome; furthermore, for those who have gone to these destinations, there is no returning again. This [characteristic] as described does not exist elsewhere. Therefore, [only these are so designated].
They [the paths] are so called because of the occurrence or non-occurrence of the existent and the non-existent, and because of having gone without returning. //40cd//
"The paths of the *satpuruṣas* are none other [than those of the noble ones].

As for what was stated in the Sūtra itself: "Who is the *satpuruṣa*? It is the *śaikṣa* endowed with right view," and so forth—others also possess a figurative (*pāryāyika*) status as *satpuruṣas*, because they have obtained the restraint of never again committing the five kinds of evil and have generally abandoned unwholesome states. However, it is those who possess this status non-figuratively (*aniṣparyāyeṇa*) who are the subject here.
5.4.7 a) Furthermore, does this distinction also apply to a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who has undergone a change of birth? No; for it is said:
"A noble one (*ārya*) who has changed births in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) does not go to another realm.

(41ab) A noble one who has completed a further birth within the desire realm does not go to another realm, because having attained the fruit of non-returning, they attain final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*) in that very same birth. However, one who has changed births in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) may sometimes enter the formless realms (*ārūpya*), namely, the one who "flows upwards" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and for whom the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is the limit.

As for what was said by Śakra—"Those gods who are renowned as the Akaniṣṭhas will be my place of rebirth when I finally fall away"—the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that this was because he was ignorant of the Abhidharma; and [they hold] that the Blessed One did not prevent him from saying it because he was to be encouraged. (5.4.7b) And he who is born above possesses neither the transformation of the faculties nor falling away. (41cd)

Furthermore, an Ārya who has undergone a change of birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or one who has been reborn in a higher realm does not transform his faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), nor does he ever fall away from them. What, then, is the reason that for an Ārya who has changed births, the transformation of faculties and falling away are not admitted upon entering the form or formless realms? Because they do not exist [for such a person]. Why do they not exist? Because the faculties have become more fully matured through dwelling in another birth, and because he has obtained a superior basis (*āśraya-viśeṣa*).

5.4.7 c) Now, why does a learner (*śaikṣa*) who is not yet free from passion (*avītarāga*) not become one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*)? The Vaibhāṣikas say: because the path has not been mastered and thus does not manifest, and because the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not extremely weak; furthermore, because the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is difficult to transcend. For much remains to be done by him: the abandonment of unwholesome and neutral afflictions, the attainment of two or three fruits of the religious life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), and the complete transcendence of the three realms. And one situated in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) is not capable of performing these.
5.4.8 a) Regarding what was said: "When meditation (*dhyāna*) has been mixed, one goes to Akaniṣṭha. Now, which meditation is mixed first?
The fourth is mixed first, for it is a concentration (*samādhi*) that is entirely functional (*sarvakarmaṇya*), because it is the foremost among the paths of easy practice (*sukhapratipad*).
5.4.8 a1) Furthermore, it is mixed in this way:

an Arhat or a Non-returner enters the fourth dhyāna, which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and characterized by a continuous flow. Emerging from that, he enters that same [dhyāna] while it is tainted (*sāsrava*) and characterized by a continuous flow, and then again the untainted.
In this manner, by gradually reducing the flow, when—so it is said—he enters two moments of the untainted, two of the tainted, and then again two of the untainted.
This is the application (*prayoga*) of the intermingling (*vyavakiraṇa*).

(5.4.8a2) "Accomplishment" (*niṣpatti*) occurs through the mixing of moments. The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that when one brings a contaminated (*sāsrava*) moment into presence immediately after an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) moment, or an uncontaminated moment immediately after a contaminated one—in this way, because the contaminated moment is mixed with the two uncontaminated ones, the intermingling is accomplished. For two moments resemble the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*), while the third resembles the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
Having thus mixed the fourth dhyāna, by its power the others are also mixed.
(5.4.8 a3) It is first mixed in the desire realm within the three continents, and later, by one who has fallen away from it, in the form realm.
(5.4.8 a4) However, the mixing of moments is impossible except for a Buddha; therefore, we see that it is perfected through entering into three successions of flows according to one's wish.
5.4.8 b) For what purpose, then, is dhyāna mixed?
It is for the sake of rebirth and dwelling [in the form realm], and also out of fear of the afflictions. //42cd//
They intermingle the dhyānas for three reasons:

non-returners with sharp faculties do so for the sake of rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens and for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life; those with dull faculties do so out of fear of the afflictions and for the sake of non-retrogression by distancing themselves from concentration associated with relishing (*āsvādana*).
Arhats with sharp faculties do so for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life; those with dull faculties do so out of fear of the afflictions and for the sake of non-retrogression.

5.4.9 Now, why are there exactly five rebirths among the Pure Abodes? Because that fourth dhyāna which was described as being cultivated through intermingling is of five kinds, there are exactly five rebirths among the Pure Abodes.
For that cultivation through intermingling is of five types, distinguished by the degrees of weak, medium, strong, stronger, and strongest.

In the first [dhyāna], three minds are manifested: the untainted (*anāsrava*), the tainted (*sāsrava*), and again the untainted. In the second, six; in the third, nine; in the fourth, twelve; and in the fifth, fifteen. Correspondingly, the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) are their fruit. One is reborn in those [Abodes] by virtue of that which is tainted therein.
Others say there are five because of the predominance of the faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*).
One who has attained cessation (*nirodha*) is further considered a Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who is a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*). (43cd)

One who has attained cessation is called "an attainer of cessation" (*nirodhalābhī*). For any non-returner (*anāgāmī*) who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is called a "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣī*), because he personally realizes with the body a state that resembles nirvāṇa.
5.4.10 a) But how does he realize it with the body? Because, due to the absence of mind, [that state] arises based upon the body.

It must be understood in this way: for upon emerging from that [attainment], he attains a tranquility of the body accompanied by consciousness which he has never attained before; because of this, it occurs to him: "Truly peaceful is the attainment of cessation! Truly like nirvāṇa is the attainment of cessation! In this manner, its peacefulness is realized by him through the body. For "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*) is indeed the act of making manifest through both attainment and the realization of knowledge.

5.4.10 b) Regarding the sūtra on the eighteen trainees (*śaikṣa*), for what reason is the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) not mentioned? Because there is no [qualifying] reason. What, then, is that reason? The three untainted trainings (*anāsrava-śikṣā*) and their fruit; for it is by way of these distinctions that the trainees are established. Furthermore, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is neither a training nor the fruit of a training.
Therefore, one is not described as a distinct type of trainee on account of possessing that [attainment].
5.4.11 This, then, is the classification of non-returners (*anāgāmin*) according to their coarse divisions. However, when divided subtly, they are distinguished in thousands of ways.

There are three types of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) due to the distinction of weak, medium, and sharp faculties. There are four due to the distinction of levels (*bhūmi*). There are six due to the distinction of lineages (*gotra*), such as those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth. There are sixteen due to the distinction of different locations. There are thirty-six due to the distinction of levels and degrees of detachment (*vairāgya*): ranging from one who is bound by all fetters in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) up to one who is free from passion regarding eight categories [of afflictions] in the fourth dhyāna.

"There are two thousand nine hundred and sixty [types of individuals] due to the distinctions of station (*sthāna*), lineage (*gotra*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and faculty (*indriya*). How is this calculated? In one station there are six lineages. Within each lineage there are nine types of persons, from those bound by all fetters up to those who have abandoned eight categories of passion. From its own station, there are six groups of nine, which makes fifty-four. Sixteen times fifty-four makes eight hundred and sixty-four. When multiplied again by three due to the distinction of faculties, it is thus."

One who is free from passion regarding the nine grades [of afflictions] in the lower dhyāna is said to be "bound by all fetters" with respect to the higher [stages], for the sake of uniform calculation. Just as it is for the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, so it is for all up to the one who flows upwards; thus, when totaled, there are thirteen thousand minus forty non-returners.
One who has destroyed eight parts of the summit of existence is a candidate for arhatship. (44ab)

The term "non-returner" (*anāgāmī*) is understood here as the subject. Indeed, this non-returner, from the point of detachment from the first variety of the first dhyāna up until the abandonment of the eight varieties of the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), is one who has entered the path to arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*).

Even during the ninth uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*)—that is, during the ninth uninterrupted path for the sake of abandoning even the ninth variety belonging to the peak of existence—he is still precisely one who has entered the path to arhatship.
And it is like a diamond. //44d//

And that path of immediate succession is called the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*) because it shatters all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Because they have already been shattered, it does not shatter them again; however, it is capable of shattering all of them, as it is the most supreme among all paths of immediate succession.
6.1.1 a) They describe, moreover, many varieties of diamond-like concentrations.

Those comprised within the *anāgamya* [stage] are: eight associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*) and origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*), having as their objects the suffering and origin belonging to the peak of existence (*bhāvāgrika*); eight associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhadharmajñāna*) and the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*); and four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*), having as their object the cessation of the first dhyāna; and likewise, up to four having as their object the cessation of the peak of existence.

There are four [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), because they take the entire category of subsequent knowledge as their object. These fifty-two diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*) are distinguished by differences in their aspects, modes of cognition, and objects.
Just as those included in the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), so too are those included up to the fourth dhyāna.

Those comprised within the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness are, respectively, twenty-eight, twenty-four, and twenty; this is because among them there is an absence of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) that has the cessation of a lower stage as its object. However, there is subsequent knowledge that has the antidote to a lower stage as its object, because they serve as mutual causes for one another.

6.1.1 b) However, for those who maintain that even the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has as its object the antidote to each individual stage, they add twenty-eight more; thus, there are eighty diamond-like concentrations (*vajropamasamādhi*) included within the *anāgamya* [preliminary] stage. In this same manner, up to those included in the fourth dhyāna, there are forty, thirty-two, and twenty-four respectively in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and so forth.
Furthermore, they become even more numerous due to the distinctions of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*).
6.2.1 As for that ninth category belonging to the peak of existence (*bhāvāgrika*) which was mentioned, and whose abandonment is effected by the diamond-like concentration—
Through the attainment of the destruction of that [defilement], there is the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*).

Furthermore, simultaneously with the attainment of the destruction of that ninth category, the knowledge of destruction arises. It is the final path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) immediately following the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*). For this very reason, that knowledge of destruction is primary, because it is co-nascent with the attainment of the destruction of all outflows (*āsrava*).
At that time, he is an Arhat beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Furthermore, when the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) has arisen, that one who was previously practicing for arhatship becomes a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*), having attained the fruit of arhatship. Because there is no further training to be undertaken regarding another fruit, he is a non-learner. For this very reason, he is called an "arhat" because he is worthy (*arhat*) of performing the welfare of others and because he is worthy of the veneration of all those still possessed of passion. Thus it is established that the other seven types of persons mentioned previously are learners (*śaikṣas*).

6.2.3 By what [reason] are they called "those in training" (*śaikṣa*)? Because they have the habit of constantly training for the sake of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) in the three trainings—namely, higher ethics (*adhiśīla*), higher mind (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhiprajña*). Furthermore, these consist of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Does it not follow that even an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would be a learner (*śaikṣa*)? No, because they do not understand the truths as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*), and because they may again fail to train. For this very reason, it is stated twice in the Sūtra: "O Śivaka, he trains in the training, he trains in the training; therefore he is called a learner (*śaikṣa*). This is so that the restriction may be understood: one who only trains and does not fail to train is a learner.

How can a noble one (*ārya*) who remains in their natural state (*prakṛtistha*) be characterized by the habit of training? [He is so] by way of intention (*āśaya*), like a traveler who has paused on the road, and by way of the persistence of the attainment (*prāpti*) of the three trainings.

6.2.4 What, then, are the dharmas of one in training (*śaikṣa*)? They are the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas of one in training. What are the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)? They are the untainted dharmas of one beyond training. Why is *nirvāṇa* not considered "of one in training"? Because it is possessed by both those beyond training and by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). Why is it not considered "of one beyond training"? Because it is possessed by both those in training and by ordinary worldlings.

6.2.5 These are all eight noble persons (*āryapudgala*): four who are practicing the path (*pratipannaka*) and four who are established in the fruit (*phale sthita*). That is to say: one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) and the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*); and likewise, up to one who is practicing for the realization of the fruit of arhatship and the arhat (*arhan*). By name there are these eight, but in terms of substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*), there are five.

The first candidate for the fruit and the four who abide in the fruits [are distinct]; the remaining candidates are not separate from those abiding in the three fruits, because they are included therein. This is said with reference to the gradual path. However, those who have already largely abandoned desire or are free from desire may be candidates for the fruits of Once-returner and Non-returner while on the path of seeing, yet they are not yet Stream-enterers or Once-returners.

(6.3) For the path of cultivation is said to be of two kinds: mundane and supramundane. By what means does this trainee attain detachment, and from what? Detachment from the Peak of Existence is attained by the supramundane [path]. (45cd)

Not by means of the mundane [path]. What is the reason? Because there is no mundane [path] above that level, and because that which belongs to its own level is not an antidote. Why is it not an antidote? Because the afflictions of that level are latent there. For an object upon which an affliction is latent does not lead to the abandonment of that affliction; and where something is an antidote, that affliction does not lie latent therein. From another perspective, it is twofold. (45d)
From all stages other than the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there is detachment both by means of the mundane path and by means of the supramundane path.
Furthermore, in that regard, when an Ārya attains detachment through the mundane path, the acquisitions of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) are of two kinds. (VI.46ab)
For one who attains noble detachment by means of the mundane path, two kinds of acquisitions of dissociation arise: mundane and supramundane.
6.3.1a) Some say that this is also the case for the supramundane path; others say it is likewise for the supramundane. What is the reason?
When [the path] is abandoned, [the abandonment] is not possessed because of the non-possession of the afflictions. //46d//

For if the worldly acquisition of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) were not to arise for one attaining detachment by means of the noble path (*āryamārga*), then it would follow that an Āryan who has become detached from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) by means of the noble path and subsequently transforms his faculties (*indriya-saṃcara*) by relying on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), would—due to the total abandonment of the previous path and the acquisition of only the path of the fruit—not possess dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the higher stages. And once that [dissociation] is abandoned, he would again come to possess those afflictions.
[The verse states: "But there is non-possession [of the afflictions], like one half-liberated from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) or one born in a higher stage. (47ab)

However, even in the absence of a worldly attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*), there would be no possession (*samanvāgama*) of those [defilements]. For example, in the case of one who is half-liberated from the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), even though there is no worldly attainment of dissociation from them—and even when the supramundane attainment has been relinquished through the transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*)—there is no further possession of those afflictions (*kleśa*).

And just as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) born above the level of the first dhyāna does not again possess the afflictions of the desire realm due to the relinquishment of the attainment of dissociation from them, this [example] is not a proof [for your position].
6.3.2 Furthermore, by means of which stage does detachment from what occur?
Detachment from all [stages] occurs through the untainted [path] of the *anāgamya* [preparatory stage]. (47cd)
Up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra).

6.3.2a) Now, regarding one who attains detachment from a lower stage by relying on a preparatory concentration (sāmantaka), do all their paths of liberation (vimuktimārga) arise from that preparatory concentration, just like their uninterrupted paths (ānantaryamārga)? No, he says. What then?
"In the conquest of the three stages, the final path of liberation arises either from the dhyāna or from the preparatory concentration" (48ab).

For there are nine planes of rebirth: the entire realm of desire and the eight [levels of] meditative absorption and formless attainments. Among these, mastery over the three planes consists in the detachment from the second dhyāna. In that case, the final path of liberation arises either from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) or from the fundamental dhyāna itself.
6.3.2b) Not above, from the preparatory stage.

Above the conquest of the three stages, [the final path of liberation] arises from the fundamental absorption (*maula*) itself and not from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*), because of the commonality of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). For in the first three dhyānas, due to the difference between the faculties of the preparatory and fundamental stages, some are unable to enter the fundamental dhyāna because the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*) is difficult to accomplish. Therefore, upon detachment from the three stages, the final path of liberation arises even from the preparatory stage of dhyāna.

(6.3.2 c) It has been stated that detachment occurs through the untainted (*anāsrava*) [path] by means of the *anāgamya* [attainment] in all cases, but this was not stated regarding the others. Hence, it is said:
By means of the eight noble [paths], there is victory over one's own and higher realms. //48cd//

Through the eight untainted [attainments]—the dhyānas, the intermediate dhyāna, and the formless attainments—one achieves detachment from one’s own level and from the levels above it, but not from lower levels, because one is already free from passion regarding them.

In this regard, it is established that the supramundane paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) proceed with the aspects (*ākāra*) of the truths, since they have the truths as their object.
However, the mundane paths of liberation and uninterrupted transition proceed respectively [with the aspects of calmness and coarseness].
The paths of liberation have the aspects of "peaceful" and so forth, while the uninterrupted paths have the aspects of "gross" and so forth; these, moreover, follow their respective order. (49abc)
They have the upper and lower realms as their sphere of activity. //49d//

The paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) take the higher stage as their object through the aspects of being peaceful (*śānta*), excellent (*praṇīta*), and a state of escape (*niḥsaraṇa*), as far as possible. The paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) take the lower stage as their object through the aspects of being gross (*audārika*), painful (*duḥkhila*), and like a thick wall (*sthūlabhittika*). It is "gross" because it is not peaceful; it is "more laborious" due to requiring greater effort. It is "painful" because it is not excellent, being more disagreeable due to its greater degree of functional rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*). It is "like a thick wall" because one cannot escape from that stage, just as one cannot escape through a wall. The aspects of peace, excellence, and escape are the opposites of these.
6.4 The incidental discussion is concluded; however, this must now be stated:
what arises immediately after the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*)?
If one is not detached, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) arises after the knowledge of destruction. (50ab)
If he is an Arhat of immovable nature, then immediately after the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) arises for him;
if not, [there arises] either the knowledge of destruction or the vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣī dṛṣṭi). (50bcd)

If one is not of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), then from the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) there arises either the knowledge of destruction itself or the right view of a trainee (*śaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi*), but not the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), because of the possibility of falling away. But does that [knowledge of non-arising] never arise for one of immovable nature? It arises for every Arhat. (50d)

Even for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), following the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), sometimes only the knowledge of non-arising arises, and sometimes the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣī samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Regarding these four fruits that have been mentioned, whose fruits are they? They are the fruits of recluseship (*śrāmaṇyaphala*). What is this so-called "recluseship" (*śrāmaṇya*)?
Recluseship is the stainless path (*amalo mārgaḥ*).

The untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is asceticism (*śrāmaṇya*), for by means of it one becomes an ascetic (*śramaṇa*) through the pacification of the afflictions (*kleśa*). As it is stated in the Sūtra: "By this [path], various kinds of evil and unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*)—extensively, up to those leading to old age and death—are pacified; therefore, one is called an 'ascetic'. Because they have not attained ultimate pacification, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) are not ascetics in the ultimate sense.
Furthermore, the fruit of that asceticism is both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Indeed, the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), are further stated in the Sūtra to be four;
moreover,
they are eighty-nine in number.
What, then, are those?
They are the paths of liberation together with the cessations. //51d//

For the abandonment of those [defilements] to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), there are eight paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*). For the abandonment of those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), in each of the nine stages, for the abandonment of the nine grades of defilements, there are exactly that many paths of uninterrupted transition and paths of liberation. Among these, the paths of uninterrupted transition constitute the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*), while the paths of liberation are the conditioned fruits of recluseship (*saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Thus, there are eighty-nine [moments].

6.5.2 a) If that is so, then it follows that an addition must be made for the Buddha. It need not be made; for although there are many fruits, the establishment of four fruits is due to the presence of five causes.
(52ab) For it is said that the Blessed One established a fruit in whichever stage of the path of abandonment those five causes are present.
6.5.2 b) What are the five? They are:
the abandonment of the former [path], the attainment of another path, the summation of destruction, and [the realization] in the fruit. //52cd//
The attainment of the eight knowledges; then the cultivation of the sixteen aspects;

the abandonment of the previous path and the acquisition of the previous path, due to the abandonment and acquisition of the paths of the candidate and the fruit; the summation of abandonments, due to the acquisition of a single possession (*prāpti*) of all [abandonments]; and the simultaneous attainment of the eight knowledges, namely the fourfold dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges. The cultivation of the sixteen aspects refers to the aspects beginning with "impermanent" and so forth. Indeed, these five causes occur for each and every fruit.

If the untainted (*anāsrava*) path constitutes the state of a recluse (*śrāmaṇya*), how can it be logical that the two fruits obtained by means of the worldly path (*laukikamārga*) are also considered fruits of the recluse?
But that which is attained through worldly [paths] is a fruit because it is mixed and because it is maintained by the attainment of the untainted. //53cd//

For in that case, the abandonment resulting from the mundane path alone does not constitute the fruit of once-returning or the fruit of non-returning. What then? The abandonment resulting from the path of seeing is also mixed therein, because one attains a single acquisition of disjunction that subsumes all those fruits.

For this very reason it is said in the Sūtra: "What is the fruit of the once-returner? It is the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion. What is the fruit of the non-returner? It is the abandonment of the five lower fetters. That abandonment is maintained by means of the attainment of dissociation (*visaṃyoga-prāpti*) which is untainted (*anāsrava*); by its power, one does not die having fallen away from it. For this reason also, its status as a fruit of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphalatva*) is logical.
6.5.4 a) And that which has been called "asceticism" (*śrāmaṇya*) is precisely this...
It is that very thing which is Brahminhood and the Wheel of Brahmā.
It is Brahminhood because it carries away the afflictions; as for the Wheel of Brahmā:

Because he practices the way of Brahmā (*brahmavartanāt*), and because he is endowed with unsurpassed Brahminhood (*anuttarabrāhmaṇya*), the Blessed One is "Brahmā. For there is a Sūtra which says: "This Blessed One is indeed Brahmā; he is called 'the Peaceful' and also 'the Cooled'. This wheel belongs to him, thus it is the "Wheel of Brahmā" (*brahmacakra*), because it was set in motion by him.
6.5.4 b) But the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*) is the Path of Seeing (*dṛṅmārga*).
Because it moves, it is a wheel (*cakra*); by virtue of its similarity to that, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*).
How is there this similarity?
Through [qualities] such as rapid movement and through the spokes and so forth. (54d)

Because of its swift movement, its progressive abandonment, its victory over the unconquered and its dwelling in what has been conquered, and because of its rising and falling—thus, by way of these qualities such as swift movement and so forth, and due to its similarity with the spokes and other parts, the Noble Eightfold Path is called a "wheel" (*cakra*), according to the Venerable Ghoṣaka. For right view, intention, effort, and mindfulness correspond to the spokes; right speech, action, and livelihood correspond to the hub; and concentration corresponds to the rim.

From where is it known that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is the Wheel of Dharma? From the scriptural statement that upon its arising in the noble Kauṇḍinya, [the Buddha] declared: "The Wheel of Dharma has been set in motion."
6.5.4 c1) How is it that [the Wheel of Dharma] has three turnings and twelve aspects?

"This is the noble truth of suffering," "That indeed must be fully known," and "That indeed has been fully known"—these are the three turnings. And in each turning, "Vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, and awakening arose"—these are the twelve aspects. These occur for each truth; however, because of the commonality of the triad and the dodecad, it is described as having three turnings and twelve aspects, just as in the teaching on skill in the two and the seven bases.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that by these revolutions, the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning are shown respectively. [Objection: If this is so, then the path of seeing alone does not possess three revolutions and twelve aspects; how, then, is it established as the Wheel of Dharma? Therefore, it is logical that this very discourse on the Dharma (*dharmaparyāya*) is the Wheel of Dharma, characterized by three revolutions and twelve aspects.

6.5.4 c3) Furthermore, how is it "three turnings"? Because the [four] truths are turned three times. How is it "twelve aspects"? Because the four truths are treated in three ways: as suffering, origin, cessation, and path; as that which is to be fully known, abandoned, realized, and cultivated; and as that which has been fully known, abandoned, realized, and cultivated. 6.5.4 c4) Moreover, its "setting in motion" is its proceeding into the mental continuum of another by means of making the meaning known.

Alternatively, the entire Noble Path is the Wheel of Dharma because it proceeds through the mental continua of those to be trained (*vineya*). However, because it begins to turn by producing the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the continuum of another, it is called "set in motion" (*pravartita*).
6.5.5 Now, in which realm (*dhātu*) are how many fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) obtained? [The answer is: three are obtained in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). (55a)
The attainment of three fruits of asceticism occurs only in the desire realm and not elsewhere; the last fruit of asceticism, which is arhatship, is attained in all three realms.
(55ab) The last fruit of asceticism is arhatship; its attainment occurs in the three realms.

6.5.5 a) First, since the two fruits are attainable by those who have not yet abandoned desire (*avītarāga*), it is logical that they are not attained in the higher realms; however, why is the third fruit not attained there?
For "the path of seeing does not exist above" (55b).

Indeed, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) does not exist above the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). And without that [path], there is no attainment of the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) for one who has abandoned desire; this is the reason.

6.5.5 b) But what is the reason that the path of seeing does not exist there? First, in the formless realms (ārūpya), it is because of the absence of hearing [the Dharma] and because they do not take the lower realms as their object. In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), however, it is because of the lack of spiritual urgency (asaṃvega) and because of the scriptural authority stating: "What is practiced here is brought to completion there" (i.e., in the formless realms). //55cd//

For ordinary beings in the realm of form (*rūpāvacara*) do not experience spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), because they are attached to the bliss of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-sukha*) and because of the absence of painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*). And without spiritual urgency, the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) cannot be attained. This, first of all, is the reasoning. There is also this scriptural authority (*āgama*): "Of the five types of persons (*pudgala*), here is the preparation (*vidhā*) and there is the culmination (*niṣṭhā*," ranging from the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) up to the one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*). For "preparation" (*vidhā*) refers to the commencement of the path, as it is the means to nirvāṇa."

6.6.1 This was stated: "If one is unshakable (*akopya*), from the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) there arises the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). In that regard, is there also a distinction among Arhats? It is said that there is. Six types of Arhats are recognized;

it is stated in the Sūtra: "There are six Arhats: the one of a nature prone to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), the one of a nature intent on volition (*cetanādharman*), the one of a nature prone to guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the one who remains steadfast (*sthitākampya*), the one capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*), and the one of an unshakable nature (*akopyadharman*)."
6.6.1 a) Among them, five are those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimuktika*).
Excluding those of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), the other five are those previously [described] as being resolved through faith;
their liberation is occasional (*sāmayikī*). (56abc)

And it should be understood that for these five, there is a temporary and pleasant liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*), because it must be constantly guarded. For this very reason, they are called "those liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*). They are "liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*) because they are both dependent on the occasion (*samaya*) and liberated (*vimukta*); this is a compound formed by eliding the middle term, like the expression "a jar of ghee" (*ghṛtaghaṭa*). For their manifestation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is dependent on the occasion, as it depends upon specific requisites, health, and particular locations.
[6.6.1 b1] ... [the one who is] immovable, possessing an immovable nature. (V.56d)
But for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), liberation is unshakable (*akopyā*), because it cannot be shaken due to the absence of falling away.
Therefore, he is "liberated at any time" (*asamayamukta*);

for this very reason, he is called "liberated independent of time" (*asamayavimukta*). Indeed, he is liberated regardless of time, and because he so desires, he brings about the manifestation of meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

6.6.1 b2) Alternatively, the distinction between those of "shakable" and "unshakable" nature is based on liberation that is temporary versus ultimate; and their state of being liberated "by occasion" or "not by occasion" is due to the possibility or impossibility of falling away [from that state].
6.6.1 b3) And he is of the lineage of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*);
it should be understood that this person of unshakable nature was previously one who had attained vision.
6.6.2 Furthermore, do these six types of Arhats belong to that lineage from the very beginning, or do they become so later?
Some belong to that lineage from the beginning; others have attained it through refinement. (57cd)

Some belong from the very beginning to the lineage of those characterized by volition (*cetanādharmagotra*); others, however, having previously been of the lineage of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharma*), reach the state of being characterized by volition through the refinement of their faculties (*indriyottāpanā*). In this same manner, it should be understood that they may likewise reach the state of being unshakable (*akopyadharma*).

6.6.2 a) Among these, one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) is one who is liable to fall away, but not one of the nature of volition and so forth. One of the nature of volition (*cetanādharman*) is one who is liable to will [the end]. One of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*) is one who is liable to guard [the attainment]. One who is stable and unshakable (*sthitākampya*) is one who, in the absence of a powerful condition for falling away, is liable to remain even without guarding it; he is neither liable to lose it nor, without exertion, liable to increase it. One capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*) is one who, being unshakable, is liable to penetrate [the higher stages].
One of the nature of being unshakable (*akopyadharman*) is one who is simply not liable to fall away.

6.6.2 b) The first two [types of arhats] were previously already lacking in both constant application (*sātatyaprayoga*) and respectful application (*satkṛtyaprayoga*) while in the stage of a trainee (*śaikṣa*). The third is one who practices with constant application; the fourth is one who practices with respectful application; the fifth is one who practices in both ways but has dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*); and the sixth is one who practices in both ways and has sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*).

6.6.2 c) Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) actually falls away, nor that one capable of penetration (*prativedhanābhavya*) actually penetrates. However, this is stated in reference to the possibility (*saṃbhava*). Having established this, the six types of arhats are applicable even within the three realms (*dhātutraya*).

However, for those who necessarily fall away until they again penetrate [the truth], there are six types in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*) there are the "steadfast" (*sthitākampya*) and the "unshakable" (*akopyadharman*). This is because in those two realms, there is an absence of falling away, the volition [to die], and the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).
Furthermore, from what do these fall away: from the fruit (*phala*) or from the lineage (*gotra*)? There is falling away from the lineage for four, and from the fruit for five. (58ab)

For the four beginning with those of the nature of volition (*cetanā-dharma*), there is falling away from their lineage (*gotra*). Indeed, one who is of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇa-dharma*) does not fall away again from his own lineage. For the five beginning with those of the nature of falling away, there is falling away from the fruit.
Furthermore, even for them, it is not from the previous [fruit]. (58b)

Whichever is one's first lineage (*gotra*), from that one does not fall away, because it has been made firm by both the paths of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). However, a person in training (*śaikṣa*) does not fall away from their own lineage because it has been made firm by both the mundane and supramundane paths. But from that which was later acquired through refinement (*uttāpanā*), one may fall away. Furthermore, whichever is one's first fruit (*phala*), from that one does not fall away; one falls away from the remaining fruits. For this very reason, there is no falling away from the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*).

6.6.3 b) And having established this, there are three types for one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*): attaining parinirvāṇa while remaining in that state, the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*), or falling away from the state of a trainee (*śaikṣatva*). For one of the nature of volition (*cetanādharman*), there are four: these same three, plus returning to the lineage of the nature of falling away. In the same way, for the other three, it should be understood that there are five, six, and seven types respectively, by adding one type to each in successive order.

6.6.3 c) Furthermore, whichever was one's original lineage (*gotra*), having fallen away [from a higher state] and become a learner (*śaikṣa*), one remains in that very same lineage and not in another. For otherwise, by obtaining a superior distinction of that lineage, there would be only progress for such a person, not falling away.
6.6.4 What, then, is the reason why there is no falling away from the first [noble states]?

6.6.4 a) Because those things to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*) lack a real objective basis (*avastuka*). For these [defilements] function with the self as their foundation, since they are rooted in the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); and yet, that self does not exist.
In that case, it would follow that [the afflictions] have non-existent objects.
They do not have non-existent objects, because they have existent things as their objects; however, they have false objects. And what affliction is there that does not function in this way?

This is the distinction. For the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) superimposes a false selfhood upon the entity consisting of form and so forth, by way of [the entity] being an agent, an experiencer, or having mastery; and since the views of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and so on follow as based upon that, they are said to be "without a real object" (*avastuka*). However, those [defilements] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*)—namely, attachment, hostility, pride, and ignorance—operate toward the entity of form and so forth merely through the modes of clinging, aversion, arrogance, and lack of clear comprehension; thus, they are said to be "with a real object" (*savastuka*). And there exists that mere "pleasantness" and so on upon which their activities occur, yet not even a trace of a self or the like.

6.6.4 b) For indeed, for those [afflictions] to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), there exists a specific object characterized as pleasant or unpleasant; however, for those to be abandoned by seeing (*darśanaheya*), there is no such object characterized as a self (*ātman*) and so forth. For this reason also, they are said to be "without a real basis" (*avastuka*).

6.6.4 c) Furthermore, an affliction arises for a noble one (*ārya*) when not attending closely (*anupanidhyāyataḥ*) due to a lapse of mindfulness (*smṛtisaṃpramoṣāt*), but not when attending closely—just as the perception of a snake in a rope does not arise for one who is attending closely. Moreover, it is not logical for views such as the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) to arise for one who is not attending closely, because [such views] are investigative in nature (*santīrakatvāt*).
Thus, there is no falling away (*parihāṇi*) from the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing.

6.6.5 The Sautrāntikas maintain that there is no falling away even from arhatship, and this alone is the correct principle. How is this known? From scripture and from reasoning. How from scripture? [It is said: "Monks, that which is abandoned by noble wisdom is truly abandoned. Furthermore, the attainment of the first and last fruits occurs only through noble wisdom. And it is said: "Regarding what must be done with heedfulness, I say that for one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) there is something to be done with heedfulness," but not for an arhat.

In this sūtra, it is stated: "Ānanda, I declare that even for an Arhat, gain and honor are obstacles," whereby falling away from merely the pleasant dwelling in the present life is mentioned; yet it is also said: "But as for the unshakable liberation of mind (akopyā cetovimuktiḥ) which has been realized by him with his body, I do not say that there is falling away from that in any way whatsoever."

6.6.5a1) If it is argued that there is [liberation] which is occasional (*sāmayikī*), we also say this; however, that must be examined: is it the state of an Arhat (*arhattva*) or the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)? For the fundamental meditative concentration (*maulo dhyānasamādhiḥ*) is called "occasional liberation" because it manifests at a specific time. And it is called "delightful" (*kāntā*) because it is to be sought again and again for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*).

Others say it is because it is to be relished (*āsvādanīya*). But liberation as the state of an Arhat is not appropriately called "occasional," because it is constantly present; nor is it "delightful," because it is not to be sought after again.

6.6.5 a2) Furthermore, if falling away from arhatship were possible, for what reason would the Blessed One have spoken only of falling away from the pleasant dwellings in the present life that consist in higher mental states?
6.6.5 a3) Therefore, it is understood that the liberation of every arhat is unshakable.

However, regarding the pleasant dwellings in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), some who possess dull faculties fall away due to the fault of distraction caused by gain and honor, because they have lost their mastery; others who possess sharp faculties do not fall away. Among them, he who falls away is one of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*); he who does not fall away is one of the nature of not falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*). The same should be applied to those of the nature of volition (*cetanādharman*) and the others.
What is the distinction between those of the nature of non-falling away (*aparihāṇadharman*), those who are steadfast (*sthitākampya*), and those of the unshakable nature (*akopyadharman*)?

One of the nature of non-retrogression has not reached refinement through heating (*uttāpanā*), whereas one of the immovable nature has reached refinement through heating. For these two, whichever specific meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) they produce, they do not fall away from it.

However, one who is stable and unshakable merely does not fall away from whatever quality he is established in; he does not produce another [quality], or if he does produce it, he may waver from it. This distinction is observed.

6.6.5 a) The venerable Gautika, having become a learner (*śaikṣa*), repeatedly fell away from his occasional liberation (*sāmayikī vimukti*) due to excessive relishing and because of his dull faculties. Becoming despondent, he took up a weapon; and because he was indifferent toward both body and life, he attained arhatship at the very moment of death and entered final nirvana (*parinirvṛta*). Therefore, even he did not fall away from arhatship. 6.6.5 b) Furthermore, it is stated in the *Daśottara-sūtra*: "One dharma is to be produced: occasional liberation of mind (*sāmayikī antā cetovimukti*). One dharma is to be realized: unshakable liberation of mind (*akopyā cetovimukti*)."

Furthermore, if arhatship were the occasional and pleasant liberation of mind (*sāmayikī kāntā cetovimukti*), for what purpose would it have been mentioned twice in that very same decalogue (*daśaka*)? Moreover, nowhere is it said that arhatship is "to be produced" (*utpādayitavya*); rather, it is "to be realized" (*sākṣātkartavya*).

6.6.5 b1) It must be explained whether Arhatship is comprised within those of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*). What is indicated by this? If it means that it can be produced, then other [liberations] can also be produced. If it means that it deserves to be produced, then others deserve it all the more. Therefore, occasional liberation (*sāmayikī vimukti*) is not Arhatship.

6.6.5 b2) How, then, is one called an "Arhat liberated by occasion" (*samayavimukta*)? It is because, due to having dull faculties, the manifestation of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) depends upon the right occasion. By contrast, one who is the opposite is "liberated without regard for occasion" (*asamayavimukta*).

6.6.5 c) It is also stated in the Abhidharma: "The latent tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) arises through three conditions: the latent tendency of sensual desire is not abandoned and not fully understood; phenomena conducive to the outburst of sensual desire appear before one; and there is improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) toward them. If it is argued that arising occurs only when [these conditions] are complete, then how could there be the arising of anything whose causes are incomplete? Thus, first of all, it is established by scripture (*āgama*).

6.6.5 d) How [is it] by way of reasoning? If, first of all, such an antidote has arisen in an Arhat that the afflictions have attained the state of being absolutely non-arising, how then could he fall away? Or, if it has not arisen, how can he be one whose outflows are exhausted when the nature of those seeds has not been absolutely uprooted; or conversely, how can one whose outflows are not exhausted be an Arhat?
Thus [it is] by way of reasoning.

In that case, the *Aṅgārakarṣūpama-sūtra* must be explained away, wherein it is said: "Indeed, for that learned noble disciple who thus conducts himself and thus dwells, occasionally and at some time, due to a lapse of mindfulness, evil and unwholesome thoughts arise. For in that passage, he is indicated to be an Arhat, because of the statement: "For a long time his mind has been inclined toward seclusion... [and so on]... leaning toward Nirvāṇa. Indeed, this power is stated elsewhere to belong specifically to an Arhat.

Because it is stated that [the Arhat] has become cooled and has vomited out [all defilements] with respect to all phenomena conducive to the outflows (*āsrava*), this is indeed so; however, as long as his conduct (*cāra*) has not been thoroughly penetrated, there remains the possibility of the arising of afflictions even for a trainee (*śaikṣa*) practicing in such a manner. Since this statement refers specifically to the stage of a trainee, there is no fault.
Nevertheless, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that there is falling away (*parihāṇi*) even from the state of Arhatship.
Furthermore, do only these Arhats possess the six lineages (*ṣaḍgotra*), or do others also possess the six lineages?
Learners (*śaikṣa*) and non-noble ones (*anārya*) also possess the six lineages;
learners and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) likewise possess the six lineages, for the lineages of Arhats are preceded by those very [lineages].
Moreover, there is no transition in the act of seeing. //58d//

The transformation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) occurs elsewhere than on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because such application is impossible on the path of seeing; some transform their faculties while in the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and some do so while in the state of one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).
