Regarding what is stated in this Sūtra: "As for those four higher mental states of abiding in happiness in the present life which have been attained by him, I declare that he may fall away from one or another of them; however, as for the unshakable liberation of mind which has been realized by him alone through his own body, I do not declare that he can fall away from it in any way whatsoever. How, then, can there be a falling away from the abidings in happiness in the present life for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*)?
Falling away is to be known as threefold: by way of what has been attained, what has not yet been attained, and enjoyment.

Loss of what has been attained (*prāptaparihāṇi*) occurs if one falls away from a quality already acquired. Loss of what has not been attained (*aprāptaparihāṇi*) occurs if one does not attain a quality that is to be attained. Loss of enjoyment (*upabhogaparihāṇi*) occurs if one does not manifest a quality already attained.
Furthermore, among these types of loss:
the last [type] belongs to the Teacher (the Buddha), who is unshakable; the middle [type] belongs to others; but for [others], there are all three kinds. (59cd)

For a Buddha, there is only the loss of enjoyment (*upabhogaparihāṇi*) and no other; for one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), there is both that [loss of enjoyment] and the loss of what has not yet been attained (*aprāptaparihāṇi*), because he has not attained the qualities of a superior person (*pudgalaviśeṣadharma*). For another Arhat, there is also the loss of what has already been attained (*prāptaparihāṇi*).
Therefore, by speaking of the "loss of enjoyment," there is no contradiction with the Sūtra regarding one of immovable nature.

(6.6.7 b) The liberation (*vimukti*) of everyone is immovable (*akopyā*). However, the formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*) of one of immovable nature is as has been explained. Therefore, the proponent of non-retrogression (*aparihāṇivādin*) maintains that this [objection] is not to be raised.
6.6.8 a) Now, if one who has fallen away from the fruit of arhatship is born again, that is not the case. Why? Because "one who has fallen from the fruit does not die.

Indeed, no one who has fallen away from the fruit passes away; for it is said in the Sūtra: "O monks, the lapse of mindfulness of a noble disciple is slow, and yet his fault quickly reaches its end and perishes immediately. Otherwise, the holy life would be without security.
6.6.8 b) Furthermore, regarding the fruit from which one falls away: one who has fallen away does not perform that improper act which was performed by one established in that fruit.
Even though he has fallen away, he does not perform an action contrary to that fruit, just as a hero may stumble but does not fall.
6.6.9 a) Now, for those who are transitioning between the faculties (*indriya*), how many paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are there?
Regarding the verse: "In the case of the unshakable (*akopya*), there are nine paths of liberation and paths of uninterrupted transition" (60cd).

When the lineage of the unshakable (*akopya-gotra*) is being penetrated by one capable of penetration (*prativedhanā-bhavya*), there are nine paths of uninterrupted transition and nine paths of liberation, just as when one attains arhatship.
What is the reason? Because of the excessive cultivation of that lineage of dull faculties. //60d//

"Because that lineage of dull faculties has been intensely cultivated, it cannot be turned back by slight effort, since it has been made firm by both the path of training and the path beyond training.

6.6.9 b) Regarding the attainment of vision (*dṛṣṭyāptatā*): when the state of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) is being realized, there is exactly one path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
The path of preparation, however, is in every case only one. Furthermore, all those paths of uninterrupted transition and paths of liberation are untainted (*anāsrava*).
For the Noble Ones do not undergo the transformation of the faculties by means of a path that is still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*).
Where, then, are the faculties increased?
They are increased among humans.

The transformation of the faculties occurs only among humans and not elsewhere, because [in other realms] falling away is impossible. (6.6.9 e1) Furthermore, relying on which stage does one transform the faculties?
One who is beyond training (aśaikṣa) relies on nine stages. (61cd)
The preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
As for the learner (*śaikṣa*), however, there are six, excluding the formless [attainments]. What is the reason?
"Having abandoned the fruit along with its distinction, he attains the fruit by increasing [the faculties].

(62ab) For when transitioning the faculties, having abandoned the path of dull faculties—which is the fruit distinguished from the fruit—he acquires only the path of the fruit belonging to the lineage of sharp faculties; and this is the reason why there is no fruit of a Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) comprised within the formless realm (*ārūpyabhūmi*). These Arhats are all of nine types, due to the difference in their faculties. How so?
These nine—the two types of Buddhas and the seven types of Śrāvakas—are those with ninefold faculties. //62cd//

Which are the seven types of śrāvakas? They are the five beginning with those subject to retrogression (parihāṇadharman), and the two types of those of immovable nature (akopyadharman): one who has attained through refinement (uttāpanāgata) and one who belongs to that lineage from the beginning (āditaḥ tadgotra). Within the very category of the immovable, there are two types of Buddhas: the pratyekabuddha and the [perfect] Buddha. Thus, these constitute nine persons based on the distinctions of the nine grades of faculties, such as the "soft-soft" (mṛdu-mṛdu) and so forth. However, all noble persons (āryapudgala) are indeed sevenfold: the follower by faith (śraddhānusārin), the follower by dharma (dharmānusārin), the one resolved through faith (śraddhādhimukta), the one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), the body-witness (kāyasākṣin), the one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta), and the one liberated in both ways (ubhayatovimukta). Furthermore, these—

The seven types of persons are established by way of application (*prayoga*), faculties (*indriya*), meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), liberation (*vimukti*), and both [liberation and attainment] (63abc). By way of application: the followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the followers by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), because they previously applied themselves to the meanings through reliance on others and through following the dharma, respectively. By way of faculties: those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), due to having dull or sharp faculties, and because of the predominance of resolution through faith or of wisdom (*prajñā*), respectively. By way of attainment: the bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*), because of the direct realization of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). By way of liberation: the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*). By way of both attainment and liberation: the one liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
7.1.1 By name, these are seven persons;
however, by way of substance, these are six.
Because there are two [moments] for each of the three paths. //63d//

For on the path of seeing, there are two types of persons, the follower by faith and the follower by dharma; these same two become the one liberated by faith and the one attained through vision on the path of cultivation; and these two, in turn, become the one liberated by occasion and the one liberated irrespective of occasion on the path of no-more-learning.

In this regard, there are three types by way of faculty (*indriya*): the followers by faith (*śraddhānusārin*). There are five by way of lineage (*gotra*). There are fifteen by way of the path (*mārga*), consisting of those established in the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the seven knowledges (*jñāna*). There are seventy-three by way of detachment (*vairāgya*): nine for one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) through detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and likewise up to nine for detachment from the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). There are nine by way of basis (*āśraya*), being born in the three continents and the six classes of gods.
When combined by way of faculty, lineage, path, detachment, and basis, they total one hundred forty-seven thousand eight hundred and twenty-five.
In this way, other types of persons (*pudgala*) may also be enumerated according to their possible existence.
7.2: Who is called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), and who is "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*)?
One who has attained cessation (*nirodha*) is liberated in both ways; the other is liberated by wisdom. (64ab)

One who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), because they are liberated from both the obscurations of the afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obscurations to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*) through the powers of wisdom (*prajñā*) and concentration (*samādhi*). The other is "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*), because they are liberated solely from the obscurations of the afflictions through the power of wisdom.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "But he who, having abandoned the five afflictions in this very world... (7.3)
"One whose qualities are unassailable is a perfected trainee" (ahāryadharmā paripūrṇaḥ śaikṣaḥ).
To what extent is a trainee considered perfected?
One who is complete in terms of meditative attainments, faculties, and fruits is designated as a learner (śaikṣa). //64cd//

The perfection of one in training (*śaikṣa*) is threefold: by way of fruit (*phala*), by way of faculties (*indriya*), and by way of attainments (*samāpatti*). There is perfection by way of fruit alone for the non-returner (*anāgāmin*) who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and is not a bodily witness (*akāyasākṣin*). There is perfection by way of faculties alone for the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) but is not yet free from passion (*avītarāga*). There is perfection by way of both fruit and faculties for the non-returner who has attained vision but is not a bodily witness. There is perfection by way of fruit and attainment for the one liberated through faith who is a bodily witness. There is no perfection by way of attainment or faculties alone without [the presence of] the fruit.
The perfection of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is twofold: (65ab) [by way of fruit and by way of faculties].

[This distinction is made] by way of faculties (*indriya*) and by way of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). However, since one who is incomplete in terms of the fruit does not possess the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣatva*) at all, his completeness or incompleteness is not further established by way of the fruit. [The classification is as follows: by way of faculties alone, there is the one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) who is liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*); by way of attainment alone, there is the one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) who is liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*); and by way of both faculties and attainment, there is the one liberated at any time who is liberated in both ways.

8. These many different types of paths have been taught: the mundane and supramundane paths of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*); as well as the paths of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), uninterruptedness (*ānantarya-mārga*), liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), and excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*). In brief, how many kinds of path are there?
In brief, the path is fourfold, known as the paths of excellence, liberation, uninterruptedness, and preparation. (65bcd)

The path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) is that from which the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) arises immediately after; the path of uninterrupted transition is that by which one abandons the hindrances; the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is that which first arises as being liberated from those very hindrances to be abandoned; and the path of distinction (*viśeṣamārga*) is any path other than these. Why is it called a "path" (*mārga*)? Because this is the road to nirvāṇa, since one goes to it by means of it, or because they seek nirvāṇa by means of it.

How do the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the path of excellence (*viśeṣa-mārga*) possess the nature of a "path"? Because they are of the same kind [as the path of seeing] yet more intense, because they lead to ever higher stages, or because they lead to entry into the state without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*). Furthermore, the path itself is called the "way" (*pratipad*) because it brings about the attainment of *nirvāṇa*. There are four ways: there is a way that is painful with slow direct knowledge; there is one that is painful with quick direct knowledge; likewise, there is also a pleasant way of two kinds. 8.1.1 In this regard:
In the dhyānas, the path is the easy practice (66ab).
In the four dhyānas, the path is the easy practice because it proceeds without effort due to the possession of the [dhyāna] factors and the equilibrium of calm abiding and insight.
In other stages, it is difficult (66b).

In other stages—the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the formless realms (*ārūpya*)—the path is a difficult practice (*duḥkhā pratipad*) because it is not supported by the [meditative] factors, because there is a deficiency in either calm (*śamatha*) or insight (*vipaśyanā*), and because it must be cultivated with effort. For indeed, in the preparatory stage and the intermediate dhyāna, calm is deficient; in the formless realms, insight is deficient.
(8.1.2) Furthermore, both of these paths are of two kinds: slow superknowledge (*dhandhābhijñā*) for one of dull intellect, but quick superknowledge (*kṣiprābhijñā*) for the other. (66cd)

For one of dull faculties, whether the path is pleasant or painful, it is slow direct knowledge; for one of sharp faculties, it is swift direct knowledge. Regarding this path of slow direct knowledge, it is called "slow direct knowledge. Likewise for swift direct knowledge. Or, because this belongs to a person who is slow, it is called "slow direct knowledge."

Furthermore, this path also receives the designation "factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣya*). There are thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven limbs of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path.
In that regard, enlightenment (*bodhi*) consists of the knowledge of non-arising and the knowledge of exhaustion (67ab).

The knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are called the three types of awakening (*bodhi*) according to the distinction of individuals: the awakening of the disciples (*śrāvakabodhi*), the awakening of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabodhi*), and the unsurpassed perfect awakening (*anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi*). This is because, through these two [knowledges], there is the abandonment of ignorance without remainder, and because one awakens to the fact that one's own welfare has been accomplished as it truly is and that there is nothing further to be done. Because they are conducive to that [awakening], there are thirty-seven factors belonging to its side (67bc).
Because they are in conformity with enlightenment, they are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
All factors conducive to awakening consist of ten substances. Which ten?
Faith, vigor, mindfulness, wisdom, concentration, joy, equanimity, pliancy, morality, and intention. (68abc)
Thus, these are the ten substances.
How so?
For wisdom (*prajñā*) is indeed the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthiti*). (VI.8d)
Vigor is called the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are concentrations (*samādhi*).

For the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right abandonments, and the bases of psychic power have the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of wisdom (*prajñā*), vigor (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*) respectively. Therefore, first of all, the faculties (*indriya*) and the powers (*bala*) consist of five substances (*dravya*) designated by their names: faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. The foundations of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasambodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) are wisdom alone. The right abandonments, the factor of enlightenment that is vigor (*vīryasambodhyaṅga*), and right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*) are vigor alone.

The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the factor of enlightenment that is concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) are simply concentration itself. The factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*) and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) are simply mindfulness itself. What remains? The factors of enlightenment consisting of joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*prasrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*), as well as right intention (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) and the factors of ethical discipline (*śīlāṅga*). These constitute five entities (*dravya*). Thus, these factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*) consist of ten entities.
According to the Vaibhāṣikas, there are eleven; because bodily and vocal actions are not conflated, the factors of ethical discipline are considered two distinct entities.

Regarding what was stated—that "the applications of mindfulness and so forth have wisdom, vigor, and concentration as their intrinsic nature"—it should be understood here that this is a mention of the primary factors; however, all those qualities are indeed produced through application. (69cd)

This was stated by mentioning only the primary [factors]. However, all the qualities resulting from application (*prāyogika*) consist of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Why is vigor (*vīrya*) called "right effort" (*samyakpradhāna*)? Because by means of it, body, speech, and mind are rightly exerted (*pradhīyante*). Why is concentration (*samādhi*) called a "base of psychic power"? Because the perfection of all qualities is established upon it.

However, for those who say, "Concentration itself is the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), and the bases [of power] are desire and so forth," it follows that there would be thirteen factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*) in substance due to the addition of desire and mind. Furthermore, this contradicts the Sūtra: "Monks, I will show you supernormal power and the bases of supernormal power... What is supernormal power? Here, monks, a monk experiences various kinds of supernormal domains: having been one, he becomes many," and so forth in detail.

8.2.2 c) Why are the faculties (*indriya*) themselves called powers (*bala*)? Because of the distinction between weak and intense [degrees], and because of being susceptible or not susceptible to being crushed. 8.2.2 d) What is the sequence of the faculties? For one who has faith undertakes vigor for the sake of the fruit. For one who has undertaken vigor, mindfulness is established. For one whose mindfulness is established, the mind becomes concentrated due to the absence of distraction. One whose mind is concentrated understands things as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*). 8.2.3 a) In which state are which of those factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*) manifested?
In the stages of the beginner and the levels conducive to penetration, seven groups are manifested respectively in the realms of existence and in vision. //70//

In the stage of a beginner, there are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) for the purpose of observing the body and so forth. In the "heat" (*ūṣmagata*) stage, there are the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) because of the increase of vigor through the attainment of distinction. In the "summits" (*mūrdhan*) stage, there are the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) because of entering into roots of merit that do not lead to decline. In the "patiences" (*kṣānti*) stage, there are the faculties (*indriya*) because of attaining sovereignty through non-retrogression. In the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*agradharma*) stage, there are the powers (*bala*) because they cannot be crushed by the afflictions, or alternatively, because they cannot be crushed by other mundane dharmas.

Because they are close to enlightenment, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); because it is characterized by movement, the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) belong to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), since that [path] proceeds swiftly. However, for the sake of establishing their numerical order, seven were mentioned first and eight later.

Regarding this, the Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is both enlightenment (*bodhi*) and a factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) is both the path (*mārga*) and a factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
8.2.3 b) Others, moreover, describe the sequence of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣya*) without breaking the order at all:

first of all, there are the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) for the purpose of restraining cognitions that scatter by being dispersed among various objects. This is because of the statement in the Sūtra: "The mind is fixed [on the body] precisely for the sake of dispelling memories and intentions based on sensual desire.
By the power of that, one rightly exerts the mind to accomplish the fourfold task through the intensification of vigor; thus, there are the right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*).

Then, from the purification of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there arise the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Based upon meditative concentration, there are the faculties (*indriya*), such as faith and the rest, which become predominant over supramundane phenomena (*lokottaradharma*). These same [faculties], when the activity of their opposites has been conquered, are the powers (*bala*).
On the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), because for the first time one perceives the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*).

The factors of the path belong to both [the truths]. For it has been said: "When the Noble Eightfold Path reaches the fulfillment of cultivation, the four foundations of mindfulness reach the fulfillment of cultivation, up to the seven factors of enlightenment. Furthermore, it has been said: "'Proclaiming speech as it truly is,' monks, is a designation for the Four Noble Truths; 'proceeding by the path as it was attained,' monks, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path.
Therefore, the Noble Eightfold Path must be accepted as belonging to both.

8.2.4 The sequence is established. However, this must be stated: how many factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are with outflows (*sāsrava*), and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are without outflows, because they are established as such on the paths of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and seeing (*darśanamārga*). For there are indeed mundane [factors] such as right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and so forth, but they do not receive the designation "Noble Path" (*āryamārga*).
The others are of two kinds. (71b) The other factors conducive to enlightenment are both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
8.2.5 On which stage (*bhūmi*) are how many factors conducive to enlightenment present?
All [thirty-seven factors] are present in the first dhyāna;
that is, all thirty-seven are found in the first dhyāna.
In the preparatory stage (anāgamya), they are present with the exception of joy (prīti).

Why is there an absence of joy (*prīti*) in the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*)? Because the threshold concentrations must be carried by effort (*balavāhanīya*), and because they involve apprehension regarding the lower stage.

In the second [dhyāna], elsewhere than in the case of right resolve (*samyaksaṃkalpa*), there are exactly thirty-six [factors], because of the absence of applied thought (*vitarka*) therein; in the two [lower dhyānas],
those two are excluded.
In the third and fourth dhyānas, there are thirty-five [mental factors], being devoid of joy (*prīti*) and initial application (*vitarka*).
In the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), there are likewise exactly thirty-five, being devoid of those same two.
By means of the factors of morality and those two [meditations], there is [attainment] in the three formless realms. //72cd//

The term "excluded" (*varjitā*) carries over [from the previous context]. In the formless realms (*ārūpya*), thirty-two [factors] are excluded: by way of right speech, right action, right livelihood, joy, and right intention.
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), the factors of enlightenment and the limbs of the path are excluded;
thus there are twenty-two factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*) in those two [realms], because of the absence of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) therein.
8.3 In which state should it be understood that one who abides in the factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣya) attains verified clarity (avetyaprasāda)?
[It is attained] upon the vision of the three truths, regarding both ethical discipline and the Dharma. (73cd)
There is also the acquisition [of faith] regarding the Buddha and his Saṅgha at the moment of the clear realization of the Path.

(74ab) When one clearly realizes the truths of suffering, its origin, and its cessation, one acquires verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) toward the Dharma and the virtues dear to the Noble Ones (*āryakāntāni śīlāni*). When one clearly realizes the truth of the Path, one acquires verified clarity toward the Buddha and his Śrāvaka-Saṅgha. For that clarity toward those two is, in fact, clarity toward the qualities that constitute a Buddha which are still in training (*śaikṣa*), and toward the qualities that constitute the Saṅgha which are both in training and beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). By the word "also," it is indicated that one also acquires verified clarity toward the Dharma and verified clarity toward the virtues.
What is intended here by the term "dharma"?
Dharma refers to the three truths for both Bodhisattvas and Pratyekabuddhas. //74cd //

And because the path [is included] therein, one attains verified clarity regarding the Dharma through the clear realization of all four truths. 8.3.1 a) These are called the four verified clarities by name, according to the distinctions of their bases of faith.
Substantially, however, there are two: faith and ethical discipline (74ab).

The verified clarity regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha has faith as its intrinsic nature, and the ethical discipline beloved by the Noble Ones is ethical discipline; thus, these constitute two substantial entities.
8.3.1 b) Are these, moreover, with outflows or without outflows? They are exclusively verified clarity.
They are stainless.
(75b) 8.3.1 c) What is the meaning of "verified clarity" (*avetyaprasāda*)? Verified clarity is the firm conviction that arises from understanding the truths as they truly are.

8.3.2 And just as one who has emerged from meditative absorption brings them to mind, so is their sequence. How does one who has emerged bring them to mind? "The Blessed One is indeed a perfectly awakened Buddha; his Dharma and Vinaya are well-proclaimed; his Saṅgha of disciples is practicing rightly"—this is because they function as the physician, the medicine, and the attendant. Furthermore, the clarity of ethical discipline (*śīlaprasāda*) is said to be produced by the clarity of the mind, and thus it is mentioned last. For one who is thus clear in faith, this is the practice, either because it functions as health, or like a guide, a path, a caravan leader, and a vehicle.

8.4.1 It is stated in the Sūtra: "The learner (*śaikṣa*) is endowed with eight factors; the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) is endowed with ten factors. Why are right liberation (*samyagvimukti*) and right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) not mentioned for the learner? Liberation is not stated to be a factor of the learner because he is still bound. For the learner is even now bound by the fetters of the afflictions (*kleśa*). How could liberation be established for one who is still bound? Indeed, one who is liberated from only a portion of his bonds is not called "liberated. Furthermore, in the absence of liberation, how could the knowledge of liberation (*vimuktijñāna*) be established?

The one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), however, is characterized by liberation and the personal knowledge thereof, because of his absolute release from the bonds of all afflictions; therefore, it is only for him that such a designation is appropriate. What is this so-called "liberation"?
Furthermore, it is twofold. (75d)
It is both conditioned and unconditioned. In this regard:
"The unconditioned is the abandonment of the afflictions, while resolve is conditioned" (76ab).
The abandonment of the afflictions is unconditioned liberation; the resolve of one beyond training is conditioned liberation.
That very same conditioned liberation is said to be the limb of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because the limbs are conditioned. That very same liberation is two [types].

That very [state] when cultivated is liberation; two types of liberation are mentioned in the Sūtra: liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*) and liberation by wisdom (*prajñāvimukti*). The aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*) should also be understood as being that same thing.

If that is so, then what about the statement in the Sūtra: "And what, O Vyāghrabodhyāyana, is the preeminent factor for the purification of liberation? Here, a monk’s mind becomes detached from passion and liberated; his mind becomes detached from hatred and delusion and liberated. Thus, for the fulfillment of the aggregate of liberation that is not yet fulfilled, or for the maintenance of that which is already fulfilled, there is desire and vigor," and so forth? Therefore, resolve alone is not liberation. What then? Others maintain that liberation is the stainlessness of the mind when passion and the other afflictions have been removed by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Right liberation has been explained. But what is right knowledge, which is distinct from right view?
Knowledge is awakening (bodhi), as previously described. (76d)

For that which was previously called "awakening" (bodhi) should be understood here as "right knowledge" (samyagjñāna), namely, the knowledge of destruction (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Furthermore, what kind of mind is liberated—is it the past, the future, or the present?
"The mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is liberated from obscuration as it arises. (77ab)

"The future mind, as it arises, is liberated from the obscurations for one in training (*śaikṣa*)," so says the text of the treatise. But what is its obscuration? It is the possession of the afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*), because that constitutes an obstruction to its arising. For in the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*), that possession is abandoned, and thus that mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) has arisen and is liberated. If so, then what of the mundane mind that is not currently arising? That too is liberated. However, only that which is certain to arise was mentioned [in the text]. From what is the mundane mind liberated? Precisely from that same obscuration to its arising.

But surely, even for a learner (śaikṣa) who is not yet liberated, worldly [knowledge] arises? That is not of such a kind. Of what nature is it? It is accompanied by the possession (prāpti) of the afflictions (kleśa).
At what stage does the path abandon the obstruction to its arising?
"The path, while in the process of ceasing, abandons that obscuration. (77cd)
The meaning is "present.

Now, regarding that which is called unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛtā vimukti*) and those three elements (*dhātu*) that are spoken of—the element of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*), the element of dispassion (*virāgadhātu*), and the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*)—what is the distinction between them?
It is simply that the unconditioned itself is designated by the name "element" (*dhātu*).
That very unconditioned liberation consists of three realms. Furthermore, among them, detachment (*virāga*) is the exhaustion of passion (*rāga*);
the abandonment of passion is the realm of detachment (*virāga-dhātu*).

"The element of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*) is the complete destruction of others" (78c)—the phrase "is the complete destruction" carries over [from the previous verse]. The abandonment of afflictions other than attachment is the element of abandonment.
However, that which is called cessation (*nirodha*) is the [destruction] of the objective entity itself. (78d)

The term "complete exhaustion" (*saṃkṣaya*) continues to apply here. The abandonment of a thing that is free from afflictions is the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*). Regarding the question of whether one becomes weary of a certain thing and also becomes dispassionate toward that same thing, there are four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*). How so?
One becomes weary through the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding suffering and its cause. (79ab)
One becomes weary through the patiences and knowledges of the origin of suffering alone, and not through others;
one becomes detached through all [patiences and knowledges], and abandons [the defilements] through those by which [detachment occurs]. (79bc)
One becomes detached by means of all the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, through which one abandons the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Thus, there is the occurrence of four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭika*). //79d//
Thus, a fourfold alternative (catuṣkoṭika) is established:

one becomes weary (*nirvidyate*) through the patiences and knowledges regarding suffering and its origin, yet does not abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*), because they take objects that are grounds for weariness as their focus; one becomes detached (*virajyate*) through the patiences and knowledges regarding cessation and the path, while abandoning the afflictions, because they take objects that are grounds for joy as their focus; both [weariness and detachment] occur through the former [patiences and knowledges] while abandoning the afflictions; and neither occurs through the latter [patiences and knowledges] when not abandoning the afflictions.

In that regard, one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) does not abandon the afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of the receptivities to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) while perceiving the truths; nor does he abandon them by means of the knowledges (*jñāna*) comprised within the paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*), liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and excellence (*viśeṣamārga*).

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, titled "The Exposition of the Path and the Persons" (*mārgapudgalanirdeśa*). Whatever merit there is herein belongs to the venerable Lāmāvāka.
CHAPTER VII:
THE SEVENTH STOREHOUSE OF ABHIDHARMA-KOŚA [p.391]
Homage to the Buddha.

The *kṣāntis* are said to be both knowledges (*jñāna*) and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), as well as right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). But then, are the *kṣāntis* not knowledge and not view? The pure (*anāsrava*) *kṣāntis* are not knowledge because the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*), which is to be abandoned by them, has not yet been abandoned. However, they are views because their nature consists of investigative discernment (*santīraṇa*). And just as the *kṣāntis* are views but not knowledge, so it is again:
The cognitions of destruction and non-arising are not views.

(1b) The knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not views because they lack investigative judgment, searching, and the underlying intention [to seek].
Noble cognition other than those two is both. (1c)
Wisdom (*prajñā*) other than the knowledges of receptivity (*kṣānti*), destruction (*kṣaya*), and non-arising (*anutpāda*) is both vision (*dṛṣṭi*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
Other [wisdom] is knowledge; all mundane wisdom (*laukikī prajñā*) is exclusively knowledge.
And there are six types of vision. //1d//

The five views and worldly right view—this sixfold wisdom is worldly view; other [wisdom] is not view. However, both this and other [wisdom] are knowledge (*jñāna*). By how much is there a summary of all knowledge? By ten knowledges. But in brief, knowledge is with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and without-outflow (*anāsrava*);
furthermore, of these two:
The first is that which makes known conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).

That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), because it generally grasps conventionalities such as pots, cloths, women, and men; others say it is so called because it is obscured by ignorance (*ajñāna*).
The untainted (*anāsrava*) is of two kinds: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) alone. (2cd)

Untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is divided into two types: knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). Thus, these two knowledges become three when conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is added—namely, conventional knowledge, knowledge of phenomena, and subsequent knowledge. Among these, conventional knowledge has everything as its object; all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena can potentially serve as the cognitive objects (*ālambana*) of conventional knowledge.
The object of the [knowledge] called dharma (dharmākhyam) has as its domain the suffering and so forth belonging to the desire realm;
it takes as its objective support the suffering of the desire realm, as well as its origin, its cessation, and their respective antidotes. (3bc) It is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
Subsequent knowledge, however, has as its object the suffering and so forth of the higher realms.
(3cd) The object of subsequent knowledge consists of the suffering belonging to the form and formless realms, as well as their origins, cessations, and antidotes.
These very same [objects], distinguished by way of the truths, constitute the four [subsequent knowledges]. (4ab)

These very same dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), when distinguished by way of the [four] truths, further become four knowledges: the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. This is because they have those as their objects.
These two types of knowledge—the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna) and the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)—are of four kinds. (4bc)

These same fourfold dharma-knowledges and subsequent knowledges (*dharmajñāna* and *anvayajñāna*), when they do not have the nature of [wrong] views, are called the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Furthermore, those two arise first as the subsequent knowledges of suffering and its cause (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna* and *hetu-anvayajñāna*).

However, when the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) first arise, they take the aggregates of the peak of existence as their object through the aspects of suffering and its origin, because they are subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) regarding suffering and its origin. Indeed, does the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) also have the same object as those two? If it has suffering and its origin as its object, then it shares the same object; but if it has cessation or the path as its object, it does not share the same object. [The knowledge] of others' minds arises from four [knowledges]. (5b)

*Vid* means "he knows"; thus, *vit* is knowledge (*jñāna*). Knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) should be understood as consisting of four types of knowledge: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Furthermore, this is its specific restriction:
it does not know that which transcends [its own] level (*bhūmi*), faculty (*akṣa*), or person (*pudgala*), nor that which is past (*naṣṭa*) or unborn (*ajāta*). (5cd)

Regarding the statement "it does not know that which transcends its level": one who belongs to a lower dhyāna stage does not know that which belongs to a higher dhyāna stage because it transcends the faculties. One does not know the path of a person who has attained through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) or who is liberated irrespective of time (*asamayavimukta*), because it transcends the person [of the former], such as by means of the path of one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*). Among the paths of the non-returner (*anāgāmin*), arhat, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and Buddha, one does not know the higher by means of the lower, nor does one know what is lost or yet to arise, because [the knowledge of others' minds] has as its object the present mind and mental factors of another. Furthermore, those belonging to the categories of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) do not know each other. (6ab)

The knowledge of others' minds belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge does not know a mind belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), nor does that belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge know one belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge. This is because those two have as their objects the antidotes to the desire realm and the higher realms, respectively. There is no knowledge of others' minds within the path of seeing (darśana-mārga); however, there is [knowledge of others' minds] that takes that path as its object. In that regard, one who desires to know the path of seeing through the knowledge of others' minds applies effort and perceives the first two moments of seeing.
A Śrāvaka knows [two moments], a Pratyekabuddha (Khaḍga) knows three, and a Buddha knows all [moments] through such application. (Verse 6bcd)

A Śrāvaka, by means of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), knows two moments following the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*): the receptivity to the knowledge of dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) and the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*). This is because the objective support belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) must be accomplished through a separate application (*prayoga*). By the time he initiates that application, the other [the Śrāvaka] has already reached the sixteenth moment of mind; thus, he does not know [the intervening moments]. A Pratyekabuddha knows three moments.

The first two [moments] and the eighth, which is the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvayajñāna*), are characterized by weak application because they involve the initial practice; others say these are the first, second, and fifteenth moments. However, the Buddha knows all the moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) without any application of effort.
Now, what is the distinction between the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)?
For the knowledge of destruction is the certainty regarding the truths that they have been fully known and so forth.
The cognition that "there is nothing to be fully known," and so forth, is considered the wisdom of non-arising. //7//

What is the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*)? One knows: "Suffering has been fully understood by me"; one knows: "The origin has been abandoned, cessation has been realized, and the path has been cultivated. Based on that, whatever is knowledge, vision, non-delusion, intelligence, awakening, wisdom, light, and clear realization—this is called the knowledge of destruction. What is the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*)? One knows: "Suffering has been fully understood by me; it is not to be fully understood again," and so on, up to: "The path has been cultivated; it is not to be cultivated again. Based on that, as explained at length in the treatise.

How does one know in this way by means of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*)? One knows in this way precisely while emerged from that state by means of the subsequently attained knowledge (*tatpṛṣṭhalabdha*). Therefore, the distinction between those two [knowledges] is due to the distinction between them; thus it is indicated in the Treatise (*śāstra*), say the Kaśmīris. Others maintain that one knows in this way even by means of the untainted [knowledge]. However, the use of the term "seeing" (*darśana*) is either in consideration of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) or because it functions as direct perception (*pratyakṣa-vṛtti*).

Therefore it has been said: "As far as there is knowledge, so far is there vision. Thus, these are the ten knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Among these, conventional knowledge is one knowledge and a portion of one [other knowledge]. The knowledge of phenomena is one knowledge and a portion of seven [others].

[The knowledge of] suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the knowledges of destruction, non-arising, and the minds of others [are included]. Likewise for subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). The knowledge of suffering is one knowledge and a portion of four: namely, the knowledges of dharma, subsequent, destruction, and non-arising. Likewise, the knowledges of origin and cessation are portions of four. The knowledge of the path is one knowledge and a portion of five: namely, the four just mentioned and the knowledge of the minds of others.

The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is one knowledge and a portion of four: namely, the knowledges of phenomena (*dharma*), subsequent (*anvaya*), path (*mārga*), and conventional (*saṃvṛti*). The knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) is one knowledge and a portion of six: namely, the knowledges of phenomena, subsequent, suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and path. The same applies to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Why, then, are these three established as ten?
Because of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), and by way of their aspects (*ākāra*), the aspects of those aspects, and their objects (*gocara*).
There are ten [stages] due to the accumulation of causes consisting in the completion of the preparatory practice. //8//

It is said that the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) are established by way of seven reasons: 1. By way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), because it is not ultimate knowledge (*paramārthajñāna*). 2. By way of antidote (*pratipakṣa*), there are the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), because they are the antidotes to the desire realm and the higher realms, respectively. 3. By way of aspect (*ākāra*), there are the knowledges of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and origin (*samudayajñāna*), because there is no difference in their aspects. 4. By way of aspect and object (*ālambana*), there are the knowledges of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the path (*mārgajñāna*), because there is a difference in both their aspects and their objects. 5. By way of application (*prayoga*), there is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*); for it is not the case that mental factors (*caitta*) are not known by it.

However, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is mentioned because it is accomplished by one who is engaged for the sake of knowing the minds [of others]. The knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) arises from having completed what was to be done, because it arises within a continuum that has fulfilled its task. The knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) arises first through the accumulation of causes, because it has all untainted (*anāsrava*) states as its cause.

Because the whole serves as the antidote to the whole, it is said that the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is the antidote to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Furthermore, regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), whether it concerns cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*), it is the knowledge of phenomena.
That [knowledge] is the antidote to the three realms;
(9abc) the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, when comprised within the path of cultivation, are the antidotes to the three realms.
However, the subsequent knowledge is not [the antidote] to the desire realm. (9d)
Subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), however, is in no way an antidote to the desire realm.
Among these ten knowledges,
the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge possess sixteen aspects (10ab).
We shall explain those [factors] later;
otherwise, it is likewise conventional. (10bc)

Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) has sixteen aspects as well as other aspects, because it grasps the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and so forth of all phenomena.
[Verse 10cd: "The four [knowledges] by means of their respective aspects of the truths.
The knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path proceed by means of their respective aspects of the truths; thus, each one possesses four aspects.

Likewise, the supreme, pure, stainless knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is exactly like that; because it takes the aspects of its own [noble] truths, it has four aspects due to being a knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*). However, when it is with stains (*samala*), it is as follows:

The knowledge of others' minds with outflows (sāsrava-paracittajñāna) has the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) of the objects of knowledge as its aspect (ākāra). It takes as its aspect that which is the specific characteristic of the minds and mental factors (citta-caitta) that are the objects of knowledge, because it apprehends specific characteristics. However, both [types of this knowledge] have each individual substance (dravya) as their object. (11d)
When one grasps the mind, at that time one does not grasp the mental factors; when one grasps feeling, at that time one does not grasp perception, and so forth.
If that is so, then what of that which was said by the Blessed One: "One understands a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust,' according to reality," and so on?

There is no simultaneous apprehension of those two, just as there is no simultaneous apprehension of a garment and its stain. "A mind with lust" (*sarāga-citta*) refers to a twofold state of having lust: the state of being mixed with lust (*saṃsṛṣṭa-sarāgatā*) and the state of being associated with lust (*saṃyoga-sarāgatā*). Among these, a mind associated with lust is "with lust" in both ways; other contaminated (*sāsrava*) minds are "with lust" by virtue of the state of being associated with lust. However, according to some, in this Sūtra, "with lust" means associated with lust, while "free from lust" (*vigatarāga*) means the antidote to lust.
For if a mind not associated with lust were "free from lust," then even a mind associated with other afflictions would have to be so.

If that were so, then a non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*) contaminated mind (*sāsrava-citta*) that is not the antidote to that [passion] would be neither "with passion" (*sarāga*) nor "free from passion" (*vigatarāga*), and so forth. Therefore, others maintain that a mind should be understood here as "with passion" precisely because of its association (*saṃprayoga*) with passion; and in this same way, up to "with delusion" (*samoha*) and "free from delusion" (*vigatamoha*), it should be understood. The Westerners (*Pāścāttyāḥ*) hold that a wholesome mind is "contracted" (*saṃkṣipta*) due to the contraction of its object; a defiled mind is "distracted" (*vikṣipta*) due to its association with distraction (*vikṣepa*). Furthermore, they say that a mind associated with torpor (*middha*) is contracted, while other defiled minds are distracted.

They do not describe it in this way; for that very same mind would then be both concentrated and distracted due to its association with afflicted torpor (*kliṣṭamiddha*). Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with the Treatise (*śāstra*), which states: "One knows the concentrated mind as it truly is. That knowledge consists of four knowledges: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)."

A sunken mind is afflicted because it is associated with laziness; an uplifted mind is wholesome because it is associated with vigor. A limited mind is afflicted because it is practiced by those who are limited in purification; a vast mind is wholesome because it is the opposite of that. Furthermore, this is due to the abundance or scarcity of roots, value, retinues, attendants, and power: an afflicted mind has its root in two unwholesome roots, whereas a wholesome mind has its root in three wholesome roots. An afflicted mind is of little value because it is accomplished without effort.

The wholesome is of great value because it is accomplished through great effort. The afflicted, however, does not have a large retinue because there is no cultivation of future states of that same kind; it is accompanied by three aggregates. The wholesome, on the other hand, has a large retinue and is accompanied by four aggregates. Furthermore, the afflicted is indeed weak in power while the wholesome is powerful in power; for by a single receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are utterly eradicated.

Therefore, the defiled is limited, while the wholesome is extensive. The agitated is defiled because it is associated with agitation; the non-agitated is wholesome because it is its antidote. Likewise, there is the uncalmed and the calmed. The unconcentrated is defiled because it is associated with distraction; the concentrated is wholesome because it is its antidote. The uncultivated is defiled because it has not been cultivated through either cultivation by acquisition or cultivation by practice; the cultivated is wholesome because it has been cultivated by those two.

The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the defiled is "unliberated" because it is not liberated by way of intrinsic nature or by way of the continuum, whereas the wholesome is "liberated" because it is liberated from those two.

However, in this way, the Sūtra is not followed, nor is the specific meaning of these terms explained. How is the Sūtra not followed? It is stated in the Sūtra: "How is the mind internally contracted? It is when the mind is accompanied by sloth and torpor, internally accompanied by suppression, but not endowed with insight (*vipaśyanā*). How is it externally distracted? It is when the mind is distracted after following after and being dispersed among the five strands of sensual pleasure."* *Note: This passage is from the *Śrāvakabhūmi*, which defines the states of mental contraction and distraction.*
But was it not said that the very same mind could be both concentrated (*saṃkṣipta*) and distracted (*vikṣipta*)?
This has been said, but it is incorrect, because it is not admitted that a defiled mind accompanied by torpor (*middha*) is distracted.
But was it not also said that this would contradict the treatise (*śāstra*)?
It is better to contradict the *śāstra* than to contradict the *sūtra*.

How so? Because no distinction in meaning has been stated for these terms: since the characteristics of distracted, sunken, excited, unpacified, unconcentrated, uncultivated, and unliberated minds are described as non-different [from others], and the same applies to the contracted, uplifted, and so forth.

It is certainly not the case that a specific meaning for these terms has not been stated; for even regarding the general category of the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), their specific defects are demonstrated in the detailed explanation: "this mind is afflicted, distracted, or sluggish," and so forth. Likewise, by demonstrating the specific qualities of the wholesome (*kuśala*), a specific meaning is indeed stated. However, since the contradiction with the Sūtra remains unresolved, this cannot be the meaning of these terms.

Furthermore, if that very same sluggish mind were intended to be that very same excited mind in the Sūtra, this would not have been stated: "At whatever time the mind is sluggish, or at whatever time there is apprehension of sluggishness, that is the improper time for the cultivation of the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

At whatever time the mind is excited, or at whatever time there is apprehension of excitement, that is the improper time for the cultivation of the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy."

Furthermore, what is meant by the "separate cultivation" of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)? It is held that their cultivation consists in mental attention (*manasikāra*), not in a state of confusion; thus, there is no fault here. In this context, a mind with an excess of laziness is called "sunk" (*līna*), while one with an excess of restlessness is called "agitated" (*uddhata*); hence there is no contradiction. Because these two coexist, we say that the very same mind is both sunk and agitated. We do not deny that such an intentional statement (*abhiprāyika*) may be made; however, we maintain that this was not the intended meaning in the Sūtra.

As for what was said—that "every mind associated with attachment (*rāga*) is 'with attachment' (*sarāga*)"—which mind is associated with attachment? If it means "accompanied by the possession (*prāpti*) of attachment," then the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind of a trainee (*śaikṣa*) would follow as being "with attachment. If it means "having attachment as its object (*ālambana*)," then even the contaminated mind of an Arhat would have to be grasped as "with attachment," because it has attachment as its object. Or else, how is that [Arhat’s mind] contaminated? If you say it is because it has the general afflictions (*sāmānyakleśa*) as its object, [the same objection applies].

Even so, one might [wrongly] grasp it as being "with delusion" because its object is delusion; yet, the knowledge of another's mind does not have attainment (*prāpti*) as its object, nor does it have that [other person's] mind as its object in the way that greed has its object. Therefore, a mind is not intended here to be "with greed" merely through association with greed. What then? The intention of the Sūtra is seen to be this: a mind associated with greed is "with greed," while one not associated with it is "free from greed."

As for what was said—“That mind of his becomes free from passion, free from hatred, free from delusion, and of a nature not to return to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm”—that was stated with reference to the cessation of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of those [defilements]. But was it not also said: “Even a mind associated with other afflictions would be ‘free from passion’ because of its dissociation from passion”? There is no fault here, provided one understands this underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*). However, it is not understood as being “free from passion” in that sense. What then?
"With hatred," "with delusion," and so forth. Enough of this digression; let the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) be described.
Does the knowledge of another's mind (*paracittajñāna*) grasp the aspect (*ākāra*) or the object (*ālambana*) of that other mind?

It does not grasp them. For, independent of both aspect and object, one knows, "This mind is lustful," but one does not know, "It is lustful toward this specific form. Otherwise, that [knowledge] would also have form as its object, and for one who grasps another's mind while having that [form] as its object, it would follow that there is a grasping of the [other mind's] own nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, all knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) has as its object the substantial unique characteristics (*dravyasvalakṣaṇa*) of present minds and mental factors belonging to the continua of others, whether associated with the desire realm or the form realm, or dissociated from them; it is excluded from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and is found on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). It should be understood that it is dissociated from the concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*), is not included within the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and is excluded from the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*). Knowledge of others' minds has been explained.
(12ab) Regarding the remaining [knowledges], they possess fourteen aspects, excluding emptiness and selflessness. (12ab)

The remaining two, the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), possess fourteen aspects (*ākāra*), excluding the aspects of emptiness (*śūnya*) and selflessness (*anātman*). This is because, although they are ultimate (*pāramārthika*), they still rely upon conventional designations (*saṃvṛti*); for instance, through the subsequent discourse (*anuvyavahāra*) based on their power, one says: "Birth is exhausted for me; I know there is no further existence beyond this.

Is there, then, an untainted (*anāsrava*) aspect that possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), or not? According to the Kaśmīris, first of all: "There is no pure aspect other than the sixteen" (12cd).
There is no untainted aspect apart from the sixteen aspects;
according to the treatise, there are others. //12d//

Others, however, the outsiders (Bahirdeśakas), say that it exists. How is this known? For the Śāstra says thus: "It may be that one cognizes factors associated with the desire realm with a mind not associated [with them], by way of the impermanent, the suffering, the empty, and the non-self; by way of cause, origin, production, and condition. One should cognize this through reasoned application (yogavihitata), thinking: 'This possibility exists; this fact exists.'"

This is not the meaning of this [sūtra]: that one should understand it thus, "this possibility exists, this thing exists. Rather, [the meaning is] that there exists this possibility, there exists this thing, such that one might understand [it] as impermanent and so forth. [To this we reply: No, because it is not stated elsewhere. If this were the intended meaning of the treatise, then why is it recited: "Could one understand the factors associated with the desire realm by means of a mind to be abandoned by seeing? He replies: One could understand them.

"From [the view of] self, from what belongs to self, from annihilationism, from eternalism, from causelessness, from [denying] action, from deprecation, from superiority, from excellence, from preeminence, from purity, from liberation, from deliverance, from doubt, from perplexity, and from uncertainty—one might become attached, feel aversion, conceive pride, or be deluded; one might understand [things] as improperly established. Here too, the reading would have been: "This possibility exists, this fact exists," but it is not read in that way. Therefore, this is not its meaning.

Furthermore, do these sixteen aspects exist nominally or substantially? Some say they are seven substantially and sixteen nominally; for there are four aspects of suffering, while the aspects of origin, cessation, and the path each constitute a single substance. However, they explain it thus:
the sixteen aspects exist substantially.

It is impermanent because it is dependent upon conditions; it is suffering because its nature is affliction; it is empty as the antidote to the view of "mine-ness"; and it is non-self as the antidote to the view of a self. It is a cause by way of possessing the nature of a seed; it is an origin by way of manifestation; it is a source by way of continuity; and it is a condition in the sense of bringing something into existence—just as, for example, a jar is brought into existence through the conjunction of a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, a string, and water, so too is this. It is cessation because of the stopping of the aggregates.

It is "peaceful" because the fire has been extinguished; it is "sublime" because it is free from affliction; and it is "deliverance" because it is liberated from all defects. It is a "path" in the sense of going; it is "right method" because it is endowed with yoga; it is a "practice" in the sense of correct proceeding; and it is "leading to liberation" because it completely transcends [suffering].

Alternatively, it is impermanent because it is not ultimate; it is suffering because it is not a state of repose; it is empty because it is devoid of an internally active person; and it is non-self because it cannot act according to one's will. It is a cause (*hetu*) by way of arrival; an origin (*samudaya*) by way of emergence; a source (*prabhava*) by way of expansion; and a condition (*pratyaya*) in the sense of being a support. It is cessation (*nirodha*) because it is the end of connection and is disconnected; it is peaceful (*śānta*) because it is free from the three characteristics of the conditioned; and it is sublime (*praṇīta*) because it is wholesome.

Because it is the supreme consolation, it is "deliverance" (*niḥsaraṇa*). It is the "path" (*mārga*) as the antidote to wrong paths; it is "reasoning" (*nyāya*) as the antidote to what is irrational; it is the "practice" (*pratipad*) in the sense of not being obstructed by the city of Nirvāṇa; and it is "leading to liberation" (*nairyāṇika*) because it is the counteragent to all existence (*bhava*). This is one way of explaining these terms; we shall now explain them according to our own intention.

It is impermanent because it arises and passes away; it is suffering because its nature is contrary [to what is desired]; it is empty because it is devoid of a self; and it is non-self because it is itself without a self. As for its being a cause, an origin, a source, and a condition, this is exactly what was stated in the Sūtra: "These five aggregates of clinging have desire as their root, desire as their origin, desire as their class, and desire as their source. In the treatise (*śāstra*), the word "source" (*prabhava*) alone should be recited last. What, then, is the distinction between these terms?

For desire (*cchanda*) is fourfold: first, the desire for self-existence (*ātmabhāva-cchanda*), which is undifferentiated by the thought "I am"; second, the desire for renewed existence (*punarbhava-cchanda*), which is undifferentiated by the thought "May I be"; third, the desire for renewed existence as differentiated by the thought "May I be thus"; and fourth, the desire for the connection of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha-cchanda*), or alternatively, the desire for the formative activity of karma (*karmābhisaṃskāra-cchanda*). Among these, the first is the root cause because it is the primary cause of suffering, like a seed is to a fruit. The second is the origin (*samudaya*), because through it that [suffering] arises, like the production of a sprout and so forth from a fruit.

The third is the condition for that kind of suffering, just as the field, water, manure, and so forth are for a fruit; for it is by virtue of the field and other factors that differences in the fragrance, taste, potency, maturation, and power of the fruit arise. The fourth is the source, because from that alone it originates, just as the end of the flower is for the fruit.

Alternatively: among the discursive tendencies of craving (*tṛṣṇā-vicarita*), there are two groups of five, two groups of four, and four types of desire. "O monks, when 'I am' exists, there occurs the thought 'I am thus,' there occurs the thought 'I am in this way,' there occurs the thought 'I am otherwise,' there occurs the thought 'I am existent,' and there occurs the thought 'I am non-existent. There occurs to him the thought 'I shall be,' 'I shall not be,' 'I shall be thus,' 'I shall be in this way,' or 'I shall be otherwise.'"

The thought "May I be" occurs to him; [furthermore,] the thoughts "May I be thus," "May I be so," "May I be otherwise," "May I indeed be," "May I be not thus," "May I be not so," and "May I be not otherwise" occur to him. It is cessation because of the stopping of the process of becoming (*pravṛtti*). It is peace (*śānta*) because of the absence of suffering, according to the statement: "For in this way, monks, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering; Nirvana is peace. It is sublime (*praṇīta*) because there is nothing superior to it. It is the escape (*niḥsaraṇa*) because there is no returning again. It is the path (*mārga*) because it serves as the way.
It is called "reasoning" (*nyāya*) because it proceeds in accordance with reality; it is called "the path" (*pratipat*) because it is specifically determined. As it has been said:
"This is indeed the path; there is no other for the purification of vision.
It is called "leading to liberation" (*nairyāṇika*) because it results in ultimate deliverance.

Alternatively, the aspects of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self serve as the antidotes for those whose conduct is dominated by the views of permanence, pleasure, selfhood, and what belongs to a self. The aspects of cause, origin, production, and condition serve as the antidotes for those whose conduct is dominated by the views that things arise without a cause, from a single cause, through transformation, or by prior intelligence. The aspect of cessation serves as the antidote for those whose conduct is dominated by the view that there is no liberation. The aspect of peace serves as the antidote for those whose conduct is dominated by the view that liberation is suffering. The aspect of excellence serves as the antidote for those whose conduct is dominated by the view that the bliss of meditative absorption is the highest good.

Because liberation is not ultimate due to repeated falling away, this is the aspect of departure for those whose conduct is dominated by views. Because there is no path, this other path is a false path and a path that leads back again, these are the aspects of the path, the method, the practice, and the departure for those whose conduct is dominated by views.
What is this dharma called "aspect" (*ākāra*)? It is wisdom (*prajñā*).

If that were so, then wisdom (*prajñā*) would not possess an aspect (*sākāra*), because it would not be conjoined with another wisdom. However, this would be logical: the "aspect" is the mode of grasping the object (*ālambana*) by all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Now, does wisdom alone produce the aspect? No, he says. What then? Together with it;
those possessing an object (*sālambana*) produce the aspect. (13bc) [p.402]
Wisdom and all other dharmas that possess an object take on mental aspects; however, everything that exists is taken as an object. (13d)

Whatever exists, all of it is taken as an aspect (*ākāryate*). This being so, it is established that wisdom (*prajñā*) both takes an aspect and is itself taken as an aspect; other [mental states] that possess an object (*sālambana*) both take an aspect and are themselves taken as an aspect, whereas those that are objects (*ālambana*) are only taken as an aspects.
Beyond this, we shall explain the distinctions of these cognitions, such as whether they are wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth:
"The first is of three kinds; the others are wholesome. (14a)

Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is the first because it occurs at the beginning of the verse; it is of three types: unwholesome, wholesome, and neutral. The other nine knowledges are exclusively wholesome.
The first [conventional knowledge] exists in all stages, from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

That which is called dharma-knowledge exists in six [stages]: in the four dhyānas, the preparatory stage (anāgamya), and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara). That which is called subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), however, exists in nine [stages]. (14d–14cd)
Subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) exists in those same six stages as well as in the three formless realms;
likewise, it consists of six [aspects]. (14d)

The knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, the path, destruction, and non-arising also exist without distinction in these same nine stages. However, when distinguished, those comprised within the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) are in six stages, while those comprised within subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are in nine.

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), which is the knowledge of another's mind within the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), it exists only in the four dhyānas and nowhere else.
And that has its basis in the desire and form realms;
for that knowledge of others' minds is manifested in the desire and form realms. However, the one called the knowledge of phenomena has its basis only in the desire realm.
Dharma-knowledge, however, has its basis exclusively in the desire realm; it is not manifested in the form or formless realms. The other [knowledges] have all three realms as their basis. (15d)

What else? Knowledge of others' minds, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). The explanation of the levels and bases has been completed; now the inclusion within the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) must be stated. This is what is said:
"The wisdom regarding cessation is one application of mindfulness" (16ab).
*Dhī*, *prajñā*, and *jñāna* are synonyms.
The knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) is one [aspect] of the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittadhī*) [is another].
Three [of the applications of mindfulness]—
namely, the knowledge of others' minds— are the three applications of mindfulness regarding feelings, mind, and phenomena; the remaining four are all four.
The knowledges other than the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of others' minds are the four foundations of mindfulness.
Of which knowledge are how many knowledges the object? The sphere of the knowledge of phenomena consists of nine [knowledges]. (16d)
The objects of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) are nine knowledges, excluding subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).

(17a) For the two knowledges of the path (*mārgānvayadhi*), that is, for subsequent knowledge as well, the objects are nine knowledges, excluding dharma-knowledge. For path-knowledge (*mārgajñāna*) as well, the objects are nine knowledges, excluding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).

The two [knowledges] of suffering and its cause have two as their objects; (17b) for the knowledges of suffering and origin, conventional knowledge and knowledge of others' minds are the objects. For four [knowledges], there are ten. (17c)
The ten knowledges are the objects of the conventional knowledge, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of destruction, and the knowledge of non-arising; however,
they are not the object of even one [of these], namely, the knowledge of cessation, for which no knowledge whatsoever serves as an object.
Furthermore, ten factors are to be applied. //17//
Which are the ten?
"The dharmas of the three realms and the immaculate ones, the unconditioned, and [the conditioned] divided into two and two" (18ab).

Conditioned dharmas are divided into eight types: by way of the distinction between the associated and dissociated factors belonging to the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as those that are untainted (*anāsrava*). Unconditioned dharmas are divided into two types: by way of the distinction between the wholesome and the indeterminate. How are these ten dharmas to be applied? How many are the objects of which knowledge?

In that regard, all ten phenomena are the objects of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). For the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there are five: the four untainted (*anāsrava*) states belonging to the desire realm and the wholesome unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
For the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), there are seven: the six untainted states belonging to the fine-material and immaterial realms and the wholesome unconditioned.
For the knowledges of suffering and its origin, there are six: those belonging to the desire, fine-material, and immaterial realms.
The knowledge of cessation has one [object]: the unconditioned that is exclusively wholesome. The knowledge of the path has two [objects]: the untainted [factors].
The knowledge of others' minds has three [objects].

The associated [dharmas] belonging to the realms of desire and form, as well as those that are untainted (*anāsrava*), are the objects of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). These consist of nine categories of dharmas, excluding the neutral (*avyākṛta*) unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Could one know all dharmas through a single knowledge? No, one could not. However, [p.
405] conventional knowledge (*sāṃvṛtajñāna*) may know everything other than its own group as being selfless (*anātman*). (Verse 18)

Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) should know all phenomena other than its own group as being selfless, thinking, "All phenomena are selfless. Its own group consists of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the phenomena co-arising with it. These are not apprehended [by that knowledge] because of the distinction between object and subject, because they share a single objective support (*ekālambana*), and because of extreme proximity.
