Furthermore, that [conventional knowledge] belongs to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) when it is produced by hearing or reflection (*śrutacintāmaya*), and to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) when it is produced by hearing or cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*). This is because its objective support is restricted to a specific level (*bhūmi*); otherwise, there would be simultaneous detachment from all realms. This point is established.

This, however, must be stated: who is endowed with how many knowledges (*jñāna*)? First, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is endowed with one: conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). One who is free from passion, however, is also endowed with the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). Furthermore, a noble one (*ārya*) who still possesses passion is endowed with a single knowledge at the first moment of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state:

(19ab) "One who has not yet abandoned passion for the desire realm is endowed with only conventional knowledge during the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*)."
In the second [moment], there are three: (19c) in the dharma-knowledge of suffering, there are the three consisting of conventional knowledge, dharma-knowledge, and the knowledge of suffering.
But in the four [moments] above that, each has one additional [knowledge]. (19cd)

Beyond this, in the four moments [of the path of seeing], one should understand that there is an increase of one knowledge at each stage: in the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding suffering, the subsequent knowledge increases; in the dharma-knowledges regarding origin, cessation, and the path, the knowledges of origin, cessation, and the path increase respectively. Thus, in the dharma-knowledge of the path, one becomes endowed with seven knowledges. However, one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) should be known to be endowed everywhere with the additional knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). Now, in which state are how many knowledges cultivated?

Just as they arise, the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated during the path of seeing. Regarding the future [states] (20abc): whatever patience or knowledge arises within the path of seeing, that which is of the same kind becomes cultivated in the future; it consists of exactly those four aspects (*ākāra*). Why is there cultivation only of the aspects of homogeneous knowledge on the path of seeing? Because the lineages (*gotra*) have not yet been attained.
In that very same [context], there is also the conventional [knowledge] in the three subsequent [knowledges]. //20cd//

In that very path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is also cultivated during the three subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) of suffering, origin, and cessation. It is not cultivated during the dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*), because the realization of the truths is not yet complete.
Therefore, it is called "at the end of the realization" (*abhisamayāntya*);

for this very reason, it is designated as "conventional knowledge at the end of the realization" (*ābhisamayāntika-saṃvṛtijñāna*), since it is cultivated at the conclusion of the realization of each individual truth. Why is it not cultivated during the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*)? Because the truth of the path has not previously been realized by a worldly path, and because its realization is not yet complete.

For while the entirety of suffering can be fully known (*parijñā*), its origin (*samudaya*) abandoned, and its cessation (*nirodha*) realized, the path (*mārga*) cannot be cultivated in its entirety; thus, because there is no conclusion to the realization (*abhisamayānta*) regarding it, the "conclusive-of-realization" (*ābhisamayāntika*) state is not cultivated therein. Furthermore, at that time, the origin has not yet been entirely abandoned, so it would not be "conclusive-of-realization. It is not the case that everything to be abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) has been abandoned.

The path that serves as the antidote to what is to be abandoned by seeing cannot be cultivated in its entirety, because there are many lineages (*gotra*); thus, there is a great distinction. Others say it is because it is an attendant of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). However, this [reason] is not a proof, as it is yet to be established. Furthermore, is that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) pertaining to the limit of reality (*ābhismayāntika*) ever brought into manifestation? Never; for it is exclusively of a nature that does not arise (*anutpattidharmaka*).
How, then, can it be said to be "cultivated"?
Because it is the attainment of what was previously unattained.
How, then, is it attained now if it cannot be brought into manifestation?
By way of acquisition (*prāpti*).

"To say that 'it is obtained because it was obtained' is an unprecedented manner of explanation; therefore, cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not established in this way. However, it is established in the manner that the Former Teachers (*Pūrvācāryāḥ*) have stated. And how do the Former Teachers state it? Through the power of the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated, such that one who has emerged from meditative absorption brings forth a more distinguished knowledge having the truths as its object. And its very acquisition (*lābha*) consists in obtaining a basis (*āśraya*) capable of bringing that [knowledge] into manifestation."
For when the lineage (*gotra*) is obtained, that which belongs to the lineage is obtained; however, the Vaibhāṣikas do not accept it in this way.
Furthermore, of how many stages is that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) cultivated? It is of its own stage and the lower stages of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

When cessation (*nirodha*) is realized, that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is the final application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), namely the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). By this specific enumeration of one, it is established that the remainder consists of all four applications of mindfulness. Furthermore, this conventional knowledge at the conclusion of the realization (*ābhisamayāntika*) possesses the aspects (*ākāra*) of its own respective truth; whatever truth is realized, it takes on the very aspect of that truth. By stating its aspects, it is implied that its object (*ālambana*) is that same truth. Moreover, it is so called because it is obtained through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
That which is produced through effort. //21d//

The meaning is "pertaining to the preparatory stage" (*prayogika*). Because the inclusion of the retinue is specified, these consist of the four or five aggregates belonging to the desire and form realms.

Regarding the six for one who still possesses passion (*sarāga*) at the sixteenth moment—the phrase "are cultivated" (*bhāvyante*) carries over from the previous context—at the sixteenth moment, which is the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), two knowledges are present: the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*). Six future [knowledges] are cultivated: the knowledges of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), origin (*samudayajñāna*), cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the path (*mārgajñāna*).
But for one who is free from passion, there are seven.
(22b) For one who is free from passion, the knowledge of others' minds is cultivated as the seventh.
On the path of cultivation when still possessing passion, and beyond that, there is the cultivation of seven. //22cd//

After the sixteenth moment, as long as one has not yet become free from passion on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), seven knowledges are cultivated throughout all the paths of preparation (*prayoga*), uninterrupted (*ānantarya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and excellence (*viśeṣa*). These are: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the conventional (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. If the path of cultivation is worldly (*laukika*), the conventional knowledge is present; if it is supramundane (*lokottara*), any one of the four knowledges of phenomena is present.

[These seven knowledges are cultivated] during the victory over the seven stages, during the acquisition of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), during the attainment of the unshakable state (*akopya*), and during the mixed cultivation (*ākīrṇabhāvita*);
furthermore, they are cultivated in the paths of uninterrupted transition and in the eight paths of liberation that follow. (Verse 23)

The phrase "seven knowledges are cultivated" continues [from the previous context]. The seven stages are the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*). Mastery over these is detachment (*vairāgya*). In that detachment from the seven stages, in the five superknowledges (*abhijñā*), in the penetration of the unshakable state (*akopyaprativedha*), and in the mixed cultivation of the meditative absorptions—whichever paths of uninterrupted activity (*ānantaryamārga*) exist for a learner (*śaikṣa*) in all those cases, those same seven knowledges are cultivated. If the path of cultivation is mundane (*laukika*), then conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is present.

If it is supramundane, it is any one of the four subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) or the two dharma-knowledges (*dharma-jñāna*). However, regarding the penetration of the remaining [realms], conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is not cultivated, because it is not an antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). In that case, the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) should be understood as the seventh. Furthermore, even after the detachment from the seven stages, during the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) in the detachment from the peak of existence, only seven knowledges are cultivated: the knowledges of dharma, subsequent, suffering, origin, cessation, path, and others' minds.

Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is not cultivated [in that state], because it is not an antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). However, as for the present [knowledge], it is one or another of the four subsequent knowledges (*anvayajñāna*) or the two dharma-knowledges (*dharmajñāna*).
Or, in the liberation through the removal of the learner’s qualities (*śaikṣottāpana*), there is the cultivation of six or seven knowledges. (24ab)

In the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) during the sharpening of the faculties (*indriyottāpanā*) by a trainee (*śaikṣa*), one who is still subject to passion (*sarāga*) cultivates six knowledges: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. One who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) cultivates seven, by adding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). According to some, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is also cultivated by both. In this context, the word "or" (*vā*) is used to indicate a difference of opinion. However, in the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), both cultivate conventional knowledge as well. In the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryapatha*), there is the cultivation of six. (24c)

For a trainee (śaikṣa), whether free from passion or not yet free from passion, during the path of uninterrupted activity (ānantaryamārga) for the sharpening of the faculties (indriyottāpanā), there is the cultivation of six [knowledges] as previously stated. There is no cultivation of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), because it resembles the path of seeing (darśanamārga). There is no cultivation of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), because it is excluded from all paths of uninterrupted activity. Why is it excluded in this case? Because it is not an antidote (apratipakṣatvāt).
It is likewise in the conquest of the peak of existence (bhavāgra). (24d)
Even in the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) during the detachment from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), there is likewise the cultivation of six knowledges.

However, regarding the nine [knowledges], at the moment of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*)—which is the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) during the detachment from the peak of existence—the knowledge of destruction is cultivated; therein, there is the cultivation of nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
For one of immovable nature, there is the cultivation of ten [knowledges].

(25b) But for one who is of an immovable nature, there is the cultivation of the ten knowledges, because of the attainment of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). [This occurs] upon that transition and at final liberation. (25c)

Even for one who proceeds toward immovability (*akopyatā*), there is the cultivation of ten [faculties] in the final path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*); in the remaining cases mentioned, there is the cultivation of eight. //25//

What, then, remains? [The remaining cases are: the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) in the detachment from the desire realm; the paths of liberation during the detachment from the seven stages, the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), and the mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇabhāvanā*); the eight paths of liberation in the penetration of the immovable state (*akopyaprativedha*); and all paths of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and special paths (*viśeṣamārga*) of one who is already free from passion (*vītarāga*). In all of these, eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated through future cultivation, excluding the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Such is the case for the learner (*śaikṣa*).

Furthermore, for one who has not trained in the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there are nine or ten knowledges (*jñāna*) in the paths of preparation, liberation, and excellence; however, in the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberation paths when the supernormal powers are cultivated in an interspersed manner, there are eight or nine. But because the two liberation paths of the supernormal powers are neutral (*avyākṛta*), nothing is cultivated as future [knowledge] therein.

For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), however, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is cultivated as a future state in the final paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) during the detachment from the desire realm and the first three dhyānas; and it is cultivated in the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the cultivation of qualities such as the dhyāna levels, the three supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the paths of liberation, and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is cultivated in these cases, except for the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). For in those [aids to penetration], the knowledge of others' minds is not cultivated, because they are attendants of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). In other instances, when there is the acquisition of a path not previously attained, only conventional knowledge is cultivated as a future state.

Now, on which path is how many levels of knowledge cultivated? First, regarding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*): it is cultivated as future [knowledge] belonging to the same level as the path itself, and also to whichever level is first attained. However, as for untainted knowledge (*anāsrava*), it is not only that which belongs to the level of the path; what then?
It is cultivated at the level for which there is detachment, at the level of its attainment, and also below that. (26ab)

For indeed, the twofold path—the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*) and so forth—exists for the sake of detachment from a particular level; and when one attains a certain level through detachment, the untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledges belonging to that level as well as those belonging to lower levels undergo cultivation, as do the tainted (*sāsrava*) ones at the moment of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*).

However, at the moment of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), even those impure qualities belonging to all stages that are acquired through the attainment of the knowledge of destruction undergo cultivation—such as the meditation on the foul, mindfulness of breathing, the foundations of mindfulness, the immeasurables, the liberations, and so forth. This is like the swelling of a sack when its cord is cut. For one who has attained sovereignty over his own mind, all wholesome dharmas come forward to meet him by means of their acquisitions (*prāpti*), just as subjects come forward to meet a king upon his accession to the throne with tribute. Whatever is obtained is cultivated;
whatever is obtained for the first time is cultivated.
That which has been previously attained is not cultivated. //25d//

That which was lost and is obtained again is not cultivated (*bhāvyate*), because it has already been cultivated and then relinquished. Is cultivation (*bhāvanā*) indeed nothing other than acquisition (*pratilambha*)? It is said: no; for cultivation is fourfold: cultivation as acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), cultivation as practice (*niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā*), cultivation as counteraction (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), and cultivation as removal (*vinirdhāvana-bhāvanā*). Among these, the two called cultivation as acquisition and cultivation as practice pertain to the cultivation of wholesome conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding the cultivation of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) and expulsion (*vinirdhāva*), these pertain to the contaminated (*sāsrava*).

However, regarding the cultivation of acquisition (*pratilambha*) and practice (*niṣevaṇa*), there is one for future wholesome conditioned phenomena (*kuśala-saṃskṛta-dharma*) and both for those that are present. The cultivation of antidotes and expulsion pertains to contaminated phenomena. Thus, there are four types of cultivation for wholesome contaminated phenomena; two for the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); and [two] for the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and the neutral (*avyākṛta*).

According to the outsiders and the Abhidharmikas, there are six types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*): these four [previously mentioned], plus the cultivation of restraint (*saṃvara-bhāvanā*) and the cultivation of elimination (*vibhāvanā-bhāvanā*). The former pertains to the sense faculties (*indriya*), and the latter to the body. As it is said: "These six faculties, when well-tamed... up to... well-cultivated," and likewise: "In this body there are head-hairs," and so forth in detail. However, the Kashmiris maintain that these two are included within the cultivation of the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) and the cultivation of expulsion (*nirdhāva*). In general, for all individuals (*pudgala*), the cultivation of qualities is said to occur at the moment of the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*). The eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), such as the powers (*bala*) and so on, are as follows: (28ab)

Those which reach cultivation only in the Buddha, the Blessed One’s, knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), and not in that of anyone else—what are these eighteen? They are the ten powers (*bala*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). For that which is not shared [with others] is called "unique" (*āveṇika*). Among them, regarding the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthānajñānabala*): there are ten knowledges in the knowledge of what is possible and impossible.

Regarding the fruit of karma (28d), the power of knowledge of the ripening of karma consists of eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path; [in the case of the power of knowledge of the faculties], there are nine. //28d//

Regarding the meditations (*dhyāna*), the faculties (*indriya*), the inclinations (*adhimokṣa*), and the realms (*dhātu*)—(29ab)—the power of knowledge concerning the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments consists of nine knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*). In the same way, the power of knowledge concerning the superior and inferior faculties, the power of knowledge concerning various inclinations, and the power of knowledge concerning various realms are to be understood.
However, regarding the paths (*pratipat*)—[p.412]—(29b) [the power of knowledge concerning the paths consists of ten knowledges].

The word "or" (*vā*) is used for the purpose of indicating an alternative view, namely that there are either ten or nine [knowledges]. If the path together with its fruit is included, the power of knowledge regarding the path leading everywhere consists of ten knowledges; if it is not, there are nine, excluding the knowledge of cessation.
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) pertains to two [of these]. (29ab)
The power of the knowledge of recollecting former abodes and the power of the knowledge of death and rebirth are conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
At the moment of destruction [of the outflows], there are either six or ten [knowledges]. (29d)

The power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*) consists of six knowledges: the knowledges of phenomena (*dharma*), subsequent realization (*anvaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), destruction (*kṣaya*), non-arising (*anutpāda*), and conventional (*saṃvṛti*). If the knowledge of cessation itself is the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows, then [it consists of those six]; however, if the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows is the knowledge within the continuum of one whose outflows are exhausted, then it consists of ten knowledges.
The intrinsic nature has been explained; now the stages (*bhūmi*) are stated:
"The powers of recollection of former abodes and of death and rebirth reside in the dhyānas" (30ab).
"Death" (*cyuta*) is simply "passing away" (*cyuti*). The power of the knowledge of former abodes, death, and rebirth has the four dhyānas as its stage.
The remainder [of the powers] exists on all stages. (30bc)

The remaining power is comprised of all stages (*bhūmi*). Those stages, moreover, are eleven: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the [four] dhyānas, and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*). All [these powers] have their basis in the men of Jambudvīpa, except when no Buddha has arisen [there]. This tenfold knowledge is not called a "power" for anyone other than a Buddha; it is the power of the Buddha alone. By what means is his power unimpeded? //30cd//

Because his knowledge operates unimpeded regarding all that is to be known (*jñeya*), it is called a "power" (*bala*); however, the knowledge of others is obstructed, for even when they desire to know something, their cognition does not proceed. Therefore, it does not deserve the name of "power. An example here is the Elder Śāriputra’s refusal of a man seeking ordination, and his lack of knowledge regarding the birth and subsequent limits of a bird afflicted by a hawk. Thus, because their knowledge is unobstructed, the mental power of the Buddhas is infinite, just like the objects of knowledge;
furthermore, there is the Nārāyaṇa strength in their bodies.
Furthermore, regarding the body of the Buddha, some describe it as having the strength of Nārāyaṇa;

others say that in each and every joint there is the strength of Nārāyaṇa. The Venerable [Bhadanta] says that his bodily strength, like his mental strength, is infinite, for otherwise he would not be able to sustain the power of infinite knowledge. Furthermore, the joints of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Cakravartin kings are like the knots of a serpent, a bamboo joint, and a *śaku* [reed], respectively.
Furthermore, what is the measure of the strength of Nārāyaṇa? It is ten times greater than the strength of the sevenfold series beginning with the elephant (31bc).

The strength of ten ordinary elephants is equal to that of one scent-elephant (*gandhahastin*). In this manner, a tenfold increase should be stated for the Mahānagna, Praskandin, Varāṅga, Cānūra, and Nārāyaṇa. Others say that by a tenfold increase starting from the ordinary elephant, the scent-elephant, and the Mahānagna and Praskandin, the strength of an Ardhanaurāyaṇa is reached, and double that is a Nārāyaṇa. However, the former [calculation] is more appropriate. And that is the sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*). (31d)

And what is this physical power? It is of the nature of the entire sphere of the tangible (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), being simply a particular state of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*). Others maintain that derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is something distinct from the seven [bases]. The powers have been explained.
As for the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), they are fourfold, just as stated in the Sūtra. Furthermore, these four fearlessnesses—

Just as in the first and tenth powers, and likewise in the second and seventh—just as the power of knowing what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), so should this fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) be understood: "Alas, while I am one who has attained perfect enlightenment. Just as the power of knowing the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*), so is this fearlessness: "Alas, while I am one whose outflows are destroyed. Just as the power of knowing that karma is one's own (*karmasvaka-jñānabala*), so is this fearlessness: "Furthermore, those things which have been declared by me to be obstructive for my disciples."

Just as the power of the knowledge of the path leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*) is, so too should this fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*) be understood: "Furthermore, the path that has been proclaimed by me for the deliverance of the disciples. How is it that knowledge itself is fearlessness? For fearlessness is the state of being without fear (*nirbhayatā*), and one becomes fearless through these [knowledges]. It is logical that fearlessness is produced by knowledge; it is not knowledge itself. There are three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) according to the distinctions among the assemblies, as stated in the Sūtra. But this is as follows:
The triad consists of mindfulness and wisdom. //32d//

These three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have the nature of mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*saṃprajñāna*). When even a disciple (*śrāvaka*) feels neither joy nor malice toward those who wish to listen, those who do not wish to listen, or both, why are these called the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*)? Because he has abandoned [these defilements] along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanaprahāṇāt*). Alternatively, for one who has disciples, there is an opportunity for mental pleasure and so forth toward those who wish to listen, those who do not, or both; such is not the case for anyone else. Since it is only for him that this non-arising occurs, it is established as a marvel, and not for anyone else.
Now, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) must be explained. It is stated as follows:
"Great pity is conventional cognition" (33a).

Great compassion has the nature of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*). Otherwise, it would not be established as having all sentient beings as its object, nor would it have the three types of suffering as its aspect, just like ordinary compassion.
Why is this called "great compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*)? Because of its equipment (*saṃbhāra*), its aspects (*ākāra*), and its objective sphere (*gocara*);
because of its equality (*samatva*) and its intensity (*ādhimātrya*). (33bc)

By way of its equipment, because it is the full realization of the great equipment of merit and wisdom; by way of its aspect, because it takes the three types of suffering as its aspect; by way of its object, because it has the three realms as its object; by way of its equality, because it functions equally toward all sentient beings; and by way of its intensity, because there is nothing more intense than it. What is the difference between compassion (*karuṇā*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)? The difference is eightfold. (33d)

By way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because they have the nature of hatred and delusion; by way of aspect (*ākāra*), because they have the aspects of one and three types of suffering; by way of object (*ālambana*), because they have as their objects one and three realms (*dhātu*); by way of level (*bhūmi*), because they belong to the levels of the four dhyānas and the fourth dhyāna;

by way of continuum (*saṃtāna*), because they are born from the continua of Śrāvakas and so forth, up to Buddhas; by way of attainment (*lābha*), because they are attainable through detachment from the desire realm and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*); and by way of non-protection and protection, because of their practice of incomparable and comparable compassion. Furthermore, are all Buddhas identical in every respect? He says: No.
All Buddhas are equal by virtue of their equipment, their Dharma-body, and their conduct for the benefit of the world; they are not equal in terms of lifespan, caste, or physical stature. //34//

All Buddhas are equal for three reasons: because of their attainment of the complete equipment of all merit and gnosis (*puṇyajñānasaṃbhāra*); because of the perfection of the *dharmakāya*; and because of their conduct for the benefit of the world. However, there is a distinction made on account of lifespan, caste, lineage, and physical stature; that is, according to the time, due to differences in living for a long or short duration, differences in caste as Kṣatriya or Brāhmaṇa, differences in lineage such as Kāśyapa or Gautama, and differences in small or large physical stature.

And by reflecting upon these very three kinds of perfection—a wise person is able to generate intense love and reverence toward the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; namely, the perfection of cause, the perfection of fruit, and the perfection of benefit.

In this regard, the perfection of cause is fourfold: the cultivation of the entire equipment of merit and knowledge, cultivation over a long period of time, uninterrupted cultivation, and respectful cultivation. The perfection of fruit is fourfold: the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of power, and the perfection of the form body.

The perfection of the fourfold benefit consists in the perfection of the ultimate liberation from the suffering of the three miserable realms and of cyclic existence, or alternatively, the perfection of establishing beings in the three vehicles and the happy destinies. Furthermore, the perfection of knowledge is fourfold: untaught knowledge, omniscience, knowledge in every respect, and effortless knowledge. The perfection of abandonment is also fourfold: the abandonment of all afflictions, their ultimate abandonment, their abandonment along with their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and the abandonment of all obstructions to meditative concentrations and attainments (*samādhi-samāpatti*).

The perfection of power is fourfold: the perfection of mastery over the transformation, conversion, and sustenance of external objects; the perfection of mastery over the relinquishment and sustenance of life-span; the perfection of mastery over passing through obstructions, traveling swiftly to distant places in space, and entering into small and large spaces; and the perfection of various innate and marvelous qualities. The perfection of the form-body is fourfold: the perfection of the primary marks, the perfection of the secondary characteristics, the perfection of strength, and the perfection of bones as solid as adamant. This is the summary of the majesty of the Buddhas.

When divided, however, it becomes of infinite variety; and only the Buddhas are capable of knowing and explaining it all, even if they were to sustain their life for many incalculable eons. Thus, the Tathāgatas are great jewel-mines of benefit, possessing infinite, marvelous qualities, knowledge, and power.

Moreover, fools—whose resolve is destroyed by the poverty of their own virtues—even though they hear of such an abundance of qualities, do not honor the Buddha nor his Dharma; the wise, however, take refuge in that Blessed One and his Dharma even with their very marrow.

For even those who possess only a mere measure of faith, having become single-mindedly devoted, overcome heaps of evil whose maturation is not yet fixed, and surpassing both divine and human prosperity, they turn toward Nirvana as their ultimate goal. For this very reason, the Tathāgatas are called the unsurpassed field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), because their desired, excellent, swift, and final fruits are never in vain.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "Those who shall perform even slight services for the Victor, the Guide..."
Having gone to a wondrous heaven, they will obtain the state of the deceased;
these, for now, are called the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas.
Other qualities are shared with disciples; however, other qualities of the Buddhas are shared with Śrāvakas, and some are even shared with ordinary worldlings. (35ab)

What, then, are these? They are, as appropriate, the qualities of *araṇā* (non-conflict), *praṇidhijñāna* (knowledge resulting from resolve), the *pratisaṃvids* (analytical knowledges), and so forth (35cd).

These include *araṇā*, *praṇidhijñāna*, the *pratisaṃvids*, the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and others. In this context, *araṇā* refers to a certain Arhat who, having understood that the suffering of sentient beings arises from afflictions (*kleśa*) and recognizing himself as a preeminent object of offerings (*dakṣiṇīya*), desires to prevent the arising of afflictions in others directed toward him. He generates such a knowledge by which he does not cause conflict (*raṇa*) to arise in others in any way whatsoever.

No passion, hatred, or pride arises in anyone with that as its object; because this practice does not cause anyone to conflict, it is called "non-conflict" (*araṇā*). Furthermore, this non-conflict is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
This is its intrinsic nature:
it belongs to the level of the final dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, because it is the foremost among the easy paths of practice.

It belongs to one of immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), and not to any other Arhat; for another [Arhat] is sometimes unable to ward off the battle of the afflictions even from within his own continuum.
It is born of humans (*nṛja*).
They arise only among humans in the three continents;
they have as their object the defilements belonging to the desire realm that have not yet arisen and which possess a real basis. (36cd)

The future afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) that have a real basis (*savastuka*) are the objective support (*ālambana*) for this [knowledge], because it functions in such a way that "no other affliction shall arise.
However, afflictions without a real basis (*avastuka*) cannot be avoided, because universal (*sarvatraga*) afflictions take the entirety of their own level as their objective support.
And as it has been stated by Āraṇa:

In the same way, the knowledge resulting from resolution (*praṇidhijñāna*) is also conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*); it belongs to one of unshakable nature (*akopyadharmā*) in the final dhyāna, has a human basis,
and yet it has everything as its object.

The distinction is simply that the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) has all phenomena as its object. However, the formless realms (*ārūpya*) are not known directly by the knowledge resulting from aspiration; rather, they are known through the excellence of one's perfected conduct. Regarding this, the Vaibhāṣikas provide the illustration of a "rough" [or "hard"] example. Knowledge preceded by an aspiration is "knowledge resulting from aspiration"; for when one makes an aspiration and enters the fourth meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*), thinking, "May I know this," one knows it as it truly is. Everything is the object of that concentration, and thus it is so.
And [he possesses] the clear comprehension of phenomena, their meaning, their etymological definitions, and eloquence. //37bcd//

There are four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). These—namely, the analytical knowledges of phenomena, meaning, language, and eloquence—are in the same manner as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*). Why are they the same? Because, like the absence of conflict, they are based upon persons who possess the quality of being unshakable (*akopyadharman*). However, their specific distinctions regarding their objects (*ālambana*), levels (*bhūmi*), and intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are stated separately: "Three are, respectively, the irreversible knowledge of names, meanings, and speech. (38ab)

The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) regarding phenomena, meaning, and etymological expression consist respectively in the non-retrogressive knowledge that expresses the meaning within the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes.
The fourth [analytical knowledge] pertains to mastery over appropriate and fluent speech and over the path. (38cd)

The term "irreversible knowledge" carries over [from the previous context]. Irreversible knowledge regarding the state of speaking with what is logical and well-spoken, as well as the clear manifestation through mastery of meditative concentration, is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-saṃvit*).
Furthermore, this has both speech and the path as its objects; that is, both speech and the path are its objective supports (*ālambana*).
The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) has nine knowledges as its intrinsic nature, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*);
it belongs to all stages.
And this [analytical knowledge] belongs to all stages, from the desire realm up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), because it takes as its object either speech or the path.

Regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthasaṃvit*) and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānasaṃvit*): if "meanings" refers to all phenomena (*dharmas*), there are ten knowledges; if "meaning" refers to *nirvāṇa*, there are six knowledges—the knowledges of dharma, subsequent knowledge, the knowledge of cessation, the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and conventional knowledge.

That [analytical knowledge] is present everywhere; moreover, this analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) belongs to all stages (*sarvabhūmikā*), whereas the others belong to the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). //39d'//

Others, however, maintain that the two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) concerning phenomena (*dharma*) and etymology (*nirukti*) have conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as their intrinsic nature, because their nature consists in taking the sets of names (*nāmakāya*) and so forth, as well as speech, as their objects.

Regarding the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), it exists in five levels— comprising the desire realm and the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*)— because above those [levels], the sets of names do not exist.

Regarding speech, [this applies] to the first dhyāna and the desire realm (kāmadhātu). "Speech" and "etymological explanation" (nirukti) have the same meaning. The analytical knowledge of etymology (nirukti-pratisaṃvid) belongs to the levels of the desire realm and the first dhyāna, because there is an absence of applied thought (vitarka) above that. However, in the *Prajñapti*, there is an exposition specifically of the analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid): "The irreversible knowledge regarding words and phonemes, their respective meanings, the designations for those [meanings] as singular, dual, plural, feminine, masculine, and so forth, and the lack of attachment toward them, is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid). For this very reason, the sequence of these [analytical knowledges] is established.

It is said that the preliminary practices (*pūrvaprayoga*) for the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are, respectively, grammar (*nirvacana*), mathematics, the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*), the science of language (*śabdavidyā*), and the science of logic (*hetuvidyā*). Furthermore, one who has not cultivated skill in these cannot produce them. However, they describe the word of the Buddha alone as the practice for all of them. And for whomsoever there is even one, there must necessarily be all four analytical knowledges;
one does not possess them if they are incomplete, for one does not become a possessor of the analytical knowledges through those that are deficient.
And these qualities that have been taught, beginning with *araṇā*, are six in number and belong to the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*). //40d//
The acquisition of these occurs through the power of the *prāntakoṭika* (ultimate-limit) dhyāna.

That [dhyāna] is of six kinds; furthermore, that *prāntakoṭika* fourth dhyāna consists of eight aspects (*aṣṭātmaka*). [These are: *araṇā*, the knowledge resulting from prayer (*praṇidhijñāna*), the three analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and that very same *prāntakoṭika* [dhyāna]. Regarding the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), its acquisition is by means of that power, but it does not itself belong to the level of the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, what is this so-called "ultimate limit" (*prāntakoṭika*)?
It is the final dhyāna, namely, the fourth dhyāna.

It is conformed to all stages and has reached the pinnacle of development. (41bc) How is it conformed to all stages? From a mind belonging to the desire realm, one enters the first dhyāna; from there, the second; and so on in sequence up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Then, in reverse order, one returns down to a mind of the desire realm; from there, again in forward order, one proceeds up to the fourth dhyāna. In this way, it is conformed to all stages. How has it reached the pinnacle of development? Having cultivated it in that manner, one enters the medium degree from the weak, and the superior degree from the medium.

For the culmination of increase is the limit of increase (*vṛddhikāṣṭhā*). This is "reaching the extreme limit" (*prāntakoṭika*) because its limit (*koṭi*) has reached the end (*anta*). Furthermore, here "limit" (*koṭi*) means either increase or a type, as in the case of the "fourfold limit" (*catuṣkoṭika*).
Moreover, these qualities of a Buddha—[p.421] those other than a Buddha's, which are born of application (*prayogaja*). //41d//

For anyone other than a Buddha, these [supernormal powers] are acquired through application (*prāyogika*) and are not obtained through detachment (*vairāgyalābhika*). For a Buddha, there is nothing that is acquired through application; because he is the sovereign of all phenomena (*sarvadharmeśvara*), the manifestation of the perfection of all qualities is dependent solely upon his will. These, beginning with the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), are qualities shared with the disciples (*śrāvaka*); they are also possessed by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). What is this so-called "supernormal power"? It consists of:

psychic power (*ṛddhi*), the divine ear (*śrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*manaḥparyāya*), recollection of former births (*pūrvajanma*), knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyudaya*), and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*kṣaya*).

The superknowledges (*abhijñā*) consisting in the realization through knowledge are sixfold: (42abc) the superknowledge consisting in the realization through knowledge regarding the domain of supernormal power; the superknowledge consisting in the realization through knowledge of the divine ear, of the thoughts of others, of the recollection of former abodes, of death and rebirth, and of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). These are the six superknowledges. Among these, five are shared with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*);
however, all of them—
The wisdom regarding the path to liberation. //42d//
They have the nature of the wisdom of the path of liberation, like the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).

There are four conventional knowledges (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), excluding the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the knowledge of others' minds (*cetaḥparyāya*) and the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Regarding the mind, there is a fivefold knowledge:
(43b) the supernormal knowledge of the modes of others' minds consists of the five [knowledges]—dharma, subsequent, path, conventional, and knowledge of others' minds.
The supernormal knowledge of destruction is like the power. (43c)

Just as the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñānabala) has been described, so too should it be understood: it consists of six or ten knowledges. It should likewise be known to belong to all stages (sarvabhūmika). As for the remaining [powers], however:
Five [are present] in the four dhyānas. (43d)

The five supernormal knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) belong to the level of the fourth dhyāna. Why do they not exist on the levels of the formless realm (*ārūpyabhūmi*)? First, three of them do not exist because they have form as their object (*rūpālambanatvāt*). The supernormal knowledge of the mental states of others (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*) also does not exist there, because it must be accomplished by means of a physical basis (*rūpatīrthyābhiniṣpādyatvāt*). The supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsasmṛti*) also does not exist there, because it is accomplished through the successive stages of death and because it has as its objects [details such as] place, lineage, and so forth. For one who wishes to know the mind of another first grasps the signs (*nimitta*) of both his own body and mind.

"Whatever kind of body I have, what kind of mind does it possess?"—by thus directing his attention toward others as well, there arises the knowledge of their minds. Once this supernormal power (*abhijñā*) is perfected, he knows without depending on visible form (*rūpa*). Desiring to recollect his former lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), he grasps the sign (*nimitta*) of the mental consciousness that has just ceased; then, by proceeding in reverse order from that immediately preceding moment, he attends to the various successive states until he reaches the mind of rebirth-linking (*saṃdhicitta*).

Then, even at death, it becomes perfected in a single moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). In this way, one also remembers another's [mind]. Once fully perfected, there is also remembering by skipping over [intervals]. There is remembering only of what has been previously experienced. How is there remembering of the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*)? Because they have been experienced through hearing. For one who has passed away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn here, [the supernormal powers] are produced by means of presiding over the mental continuum (*saṃtati*) of another; for others, they are produced by means of presiding over their own mental continuum. However, the preliminary application (*prayoga*) for the supernormal powers such as miraculous power (*ṛddhi*) consists of mental attention (*manasikāra*) to lightness, sound, and light. Furthermore, these are the five supernormal knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
(44a) Having their objects within their own lower levels:

whichever level the supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhyabhijñā*) belongs to, one travels to that level by means of it, or creates emanations (*nirmāṇa*) on that level, but not on a higher one. Likewise, by the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotrābhijñā*), one hears sounds belonging only to one’s own level or to a lower level, but not to a higher level. By the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*), one does not know a mind belonging to a higher level. By the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), one does not recollect [lives] of a higher level. By the supernormal power of death and rebirth (*cyutopapādābhijñā*), one does not see [beings] in a higher level.

For this very reason, a mind belonging to the formless realm is not apprehended by the supernormal knowledges of the penetration of others' minds and the recollection of former existences, because it belongs to a higher level.
How are these [supernormal knowledges] obtained? Those not previously cultivated are obtained through application; those already cultivated are obtained through detachment. (44ab)

The superknowledges (*abhijñā*) practiced in previous lives are obtained through detachment (*vairāgya*), while the specific ones are obtained through application (*prayoga*). However, the production of all of them occurs through application.

Regarding the third, there are three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): the superknowledge of the mental states of others (*cetaḥparyāyābhijñā*) consists of the three applications of mindfulness—feeling, mind, and phenomena—because it has the mind and its mental factors as its object.
The first [supernormal power] resides in the ear, the [divine] eye, and the [divine] ear-faculty. //44d//

The term "higher knowledge" (abhijñā) continues [from the previous context]. The higher knowledges of supernormal power, the divine ear, and the divine eye are the first foundation of mindfulness; this is the meaning, because they have form as their object. Supernormal power has the four external sense-bases as its objects, with the exception of sound. The higher knowledges of the divine ear and the divine eye have the sense-bases of sound and form as their respective objects.

How then is it that one knows through the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) such things as, "These venerable beings are possessed of misconduct of body," and so forth? One does not know those things by means of that [knowledge] itself. Rather, another knowledge that accompanies the supernormal power (*abhijñāparivārajñāna*) arises for the noble ones (*ārya*), by which they know in this way. Since there is no specific restriction [to a single application], it is established that the remaining two have the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the two supernormal powers of the ear and the eye, they are neutral (*avyākṛta*); the others are wholesome (*śubha*). (45ab)

The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of the divine eye and divine ear are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); they are, moreover, wisdom (*prajñā*) associated with visual and auditory consciousness. How, then, are they established as belonging to the levels of the four dhyānas? Because their level is designated by virtue of their basis (*āśraya*); for the eyes and ears that serve as their bases belong to the levels of the four dhyānas. Or [they are so designated] by virtue of the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*). The other four [supernormal powers] are wholesome (*kuśala*). As for what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*: "What is supernormal power? It is wholesome wisdom," this is a description based on predominance or based on the majority of cases. Among these supernormal powers, three are the three types of knowledge (*vidyā*).

The three realizations—the knowledge of former abodes, the knowledge of death and rebirth, and the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows—are called the "vidyās" (clear knowledges) of one beyond training. Why are only these and no others so designated?
Because they turn back ignorance regarding the past limit and the other [limits]. (47cd)
For these [three knowledges], in their respective order, dispel delusion regarding the past, the future, and the middle [present]. Among them, in the ultimate sense,
the final one belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)— the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*)— is itself the *vidyā* of one beyond training.

The two [knowledges] so named are called "learner" because they arise from the continuum of a learner; the other two are called "non-learner" because they are produced from the continuum of a non-learner. However, those two are neither learner nor non-learner. Why, then, are these two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) not said to belong to a learner? Why are they not called "learners' sciences" (*vidyā*)? It is because although they are accepted as belonging to a learner, they are not called "sciences" due to their association with a continuum that still possesses ignorance (*sāvidya-saṃtati*). (46cd)

For it is not logical to establish the presence of knowledge (*vidyā*) within a continuum that is still possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*), because ignorance would once again overcome it. Furthermore, among these supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the first, the third, and the sixth are the miracles (*prātihārya*). (47ab)

The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) of psychic power (*ṛddhi*), knowledge of others' minds (*cetaḥparyāya*), and the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) are, respectively, the three miracles (*prātihārya*): the miracle of psychic power, the miracle of instruction, and the miracle of admonition. They are called "miracles" because they initially and exceedingly captivate the minds of those to be trained; for the prefixes *prāti-* and *ati-* signify "initial action" and "intensity," respectively. Alternatively, they are called "miracles" because by means of these, they win over the minds of those who are hostile or indifferent. Furthermore, among these, the miracle of admonition is the foremost. (47bc) The miracle of admonition is the supreme miracle.
Because it is non-deviant and because it connects one with the desired fruit of welfare. //47cd//

For supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) and the power of instruction (*ādeśana*) are transformed by means of spells (*vidyā*). There exists, for instance, a spell called *Gāndhārī*, by which one travels through the air; and there is also a spell called *Īkṣaṇikā*, by which one knows the minds of others. However, instruction according to reality (*yathābhūtānuśāsana*) cannot be made otherwise, because of its non-erroneous nature. While those two [spells] primarily serve merely to attract [others], through the miracle of instruction (*anuśāsanapratihārya*), there occurs a connection with beneficial and desired results due to the teaching of the means (*upāya*); thus it is necessarily called "supernormal power. What is this supernormal power? According to the system of the Vaibhāṣikas:

Supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is meditative concentration (*samādhi*); it should be understood as such because one succeeds by means of it. What is accomplished by that? It is movement and creation; from that [arise these two]. (48ab)
In that regard, movement is threefold: movement by carrying the body, movement through resolute intention, and movement with the speed of mind. Among these, movement is [the first].

The Teacher’s [movement] is "mind-swift" (*manojavā*); because its speed is like that of the mind, it is called mind-swift. This movement belongs only to the Buddha and no one else, because he can reach even an extremely distant location in the time it takes for a thought to arise. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "The domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable. As for the other two movements, they are established for the Buddha even without being explicitly mentioned. For others, however, there is also the movement consisting of resolve (*ādhimokṣikī*), as well as the movement by means of transport (*vāhinī*). (48cd)

The movement of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is "bodily" because they travel by carrying their bodies step by step like birds; it is also "resolute" because they travel swiftly by resolving that what is distant be near. Furthermore, emanation (*nirmāṇa*) is of two kinds: belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) and belonging to the form realm (*rūpāvacara*).
Among these, first, the external emanation belongs to the desire realm.

The emanation belonging to the desire realm consists of four sense bases (caturāyatana); its intrinsic nature is the sense bases of form, taste, odor, and the tangible. Furthermore, that is of two kinds. (49b)
It is connected with one's own body or another's body. Regarding the form realm (*rūpāpta*), there are two:

the emanation belonging to the form realm consists of the two spheres of visible form and tangible objects (*rūpa-spraṣṭavyāyatana*), because odor and taste are absent there. That [emanation] is likewise of two kinds [in both realms]. Thus, this fourfold emanation exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and similarly in the form realm; in brief, emanation is of eight kinds. How is it that for one born in the form realm, there is no possession (*samanvāgama*) of odor and taste when manifesting an emanation belonging to the desire realm? It is not a possession, like [the possession of] clothing or ornaments. Others say that he manifests two spheres [of odor and taste].

Is it the case that only through supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) is an emanation (*nirmāṇa*) created? No, it is said. What then? It is by means of the fruits of supernormal knowledge. Respective to their order, there are two up to five fruits of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

(50ab) The fruit of the first meditative absorption consists of two emanation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*): those belonging to the level of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the first meditative absorption. The fruit of the second meditative absorption consists of three: those belonging to the levels of the desire realm, the first, and the second meditative absorptions. In this way, four and five [emanation-minds] should be applied respectively for the levels of the third and fourth meditative absorptions. It should be understood that an emanation-mind which is the fruit of meditative absorption belongs either to its own level or to a lower level.
Above:

(50b) There exists a transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to a higher level that is the fruit of a lower meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). A transformation [body] belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), which is the fruit of the second or higher absorptions, is superior in terms of its range of movement (*gati*) to that which belongs to the level of the first absorption.
Its acquisition is like that of the absorptions themselves. (50c)

And the acquisition of those emanation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) is like that of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*). But is emergence [from the absorption] indeed from the emanation-mind itself? This is not so. Why? Because it arises:
"From the pure [meditation], and from that itself" (50cd).
An emanation-mind arises at the end from a pure meditation (*śuddhakadhyāna*), or from an emanation-mind, but not from anything else.
And from that too, they [arise]. //50d//

From a mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*), both a pure (*śuddhaka*) dhyāna and another mind of emanation arise, but nothing else. For one who abides in the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is no emergence from it without first re-entering that concentration. Furthermore, regarding all emanations, the emanation belongs to its own level;
an emanation belonging to another level is not produced by a mind of emanation belonging to a different level.
"And speech is [produced] by one of a lower level" (51b).

The word "and" (ca) implies that it is also produced by a mind belonging to its own level. For a created being (*nirmita*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the first dhyāna speaks by means of a mind belonging to its own level; however, one belonging to a higher level speaks by means of a mind belonging to the first dhyāna, because above that there is no originator of informative action (*vijñapti*). As for the speaking of many created beings, it occurs together with the creator alone, except in the case of the Teacher (the Buddha). (51c)
The emanation of anyone other than a Buddha speaks together with its creator. And when many emanations exist, they speak simultaneously.
As the verse says: "When one speaks, the emanations speak together;
when one becomes silent, they all become silent."

The emanations created by a Buddha speak according to his will, whether before or after him. When there is the mind of speaking, at that time there is an absence of the emanation-mind; and since there is an absence of the emanation-mind, there is an absence of the emanation. How, then, do they speak through this? By means of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the subsequent engagement of another [mind]. Having empowered the emanation with the desire for it to remain, they set speech in motion by means of another mental state. Does this empowerment continue only as long as one is alive, or does it persist even after death?
Even for one who has died, there is empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*),
because through the empowerment of the noble Mahākāśyapa, that collection of bones remained for a long time; however, that [empowerment] does not occur for one who is not firm.
However, for an unstable entity, there is no empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because the noble Kāśyapa did not empower his flesh and so forth.
Others, however, say no;
others further say that there is no empowerment for one who is dead, but the persistence of the skeletal frame is due to the power of the deities.
Does one create only a single emanation with a single mind?
At first, one creates many with one; but once mastery is attained, it is the reverse. (52cd)

At first, one creates a single emanation by means of multiple emanation-minds; however, once supernormal power has been mastered, one creates many [emanations] with a single mind, as many as one desires to create.
Now, is every emanation-mind neutral (*avyākṛta*)? It is neutral when born of cultivation (*bhāvanāja*).
That which is the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*) is necessarily neutral (*avyākṛta*).
However, that which is born of rebirth (*upapattija*) is of three kinds.

The mind acquired at birth (*upapattipratilambhika*), such as the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*) belonging to gods, *nāgas*, *piśācas*, and so forth, may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral. And the transformation of one’s own or another’s body produced by that [mind] consists of nine bases (*navāyatanika*), because it lacks the base of sound and the base of form, and because it is not dissociated from the sense faculties. Yet, a sense faculty itself is not transformed. Are these two types of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*)—that consisting of cultivation and that acquired through rebirth—the only ones?
And this [supernormal power] is of two kinds; furthermore, including that produced by spells, medicinal herbs, and karma, it is fivefold. (53)

In brief, they describe five kinds of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*): that which is the fruit of cultivation, that acquired at birth, that born of mantras, that born of medicinal herbs, and that born of ritual action—as in the case of Māndhātṛ and those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Regarding what has been called the divine ear and the divine eye: are these truly divine, or are they "divine-like," as in the case of the divine ears and eyes of Bodhisattvas, Cakravartins, and Householder-treasures? [54a]
The two translucent forms (*rūpaprasāda*) belonging to the stage of meditative absorption (*dhyānabhūmika*) arise from you [the elements].

(54ab) For one who has entered meditative absorption, through the application of attention to sound and light, the two translucent forms—the eye and the ear—arise based upon the primary elements belonging to the stage of meditative absorption; they serve as the causes for seeing and hearing visible forms and sounds in their vicinity. Because they belong to the stage of meditative absorption, these two, the divine eye and the divine ear, are indeed "divine. Furthermore, those two...
It is always homogeneous and unimpaired, and its range consists of objects that are distant, subtle, and so forth. //54cd//

The divine eye and ear are not "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga), because they are always accompanied by consciousness; nor are they deficient, as there is no absence of blindness or distortion, just like the beings of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*). Forms and sounds that are distant, subtle, or obstructed are also the objects of these two. As it is said in this regard:
"One does not see what is distant, obstructed, or subtle, nor [what is] on all sides."
Since the fleshly eye perceives only form, the divine eye is therefore held to be superior.

Furthermore, to what distance does one see with the divine eye? It depends on the kind of eye one possesses. However, the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas, without deliberate effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*), see respectively a thousand, two thousand, and three thousand world-systems. But with deliberate effort: "Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Teachers see two, three, and incalculable [thousand-world systems]. (55ab)

With all deliberate effort (*sarvābhisaṃskāreṇa*), even a Śrāvaka sees a two-thousandfold world system with the divine eye; one who is like a rhinoceros horn (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*) sees a three-thousandfold world system; but the Blessed Buddha sees as many incalculable world systems as he wishes.
Is it only supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) that is acquired at birth, or is there something else as well?
There is indeed something else acquired at birth.

The fourfold set beginning with the divine ear is also acquired through birth; however, nothing acquired through birth receives the designation of "higher knowledge" (*abhijñā*). As for the divine eye acquired through birth, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not visible to it. (55d)

For the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is seen only by the eye of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñācakṣus*), not by that acquired through birth. However, regarding that [knowledge of others' minds], it continues [to be said] that it is of three kinds when acquired through birth; but the knowledge of others' minds acquired through birth should be understood as being of three types: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
And that [knowledge] is produced by logic (*tarka*) and by spells (*vidyā*).

Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds belonging to logicians (*tārkika*), as well as that which is produced by spells for those who practice divination (*naimittika*), should also be understood as being of three kinds; it is not exclusively wholesome like the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*). However, at the beginning, hell-beings know through the two [knowledges] acquired at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika*): the knowledge of others' minds and the recollection of former existences (*pūrva-nivāsa-anusmṛti*).
As long as they are not overwhelmed by painful sensations, those dwelling in other realms always know [the thoughts of others]; for humans, however, this knowledge is not innate. //56d//

Among humans, these aforementioned qualities such as supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth do not exist as innate (*upapatti-prātilambhika*). As for the fact that some are naturally able to remember their past lives (*jātismara*), this arises from a specific type of karma (*karma-viśeṣaja*). For the recollection of former abodes (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti*) is of three kinds: the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*), that obtained through birth (*upapatti-labdha*), and that born of karma (*karma-ja*).
//* // The Seventh Chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled "Exposition of Knowledge" //* //
Whatever merit is herein from the Elder Śrīlāta.
Chapter VIII [p. 432]
In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, the eighth chapter: Exposition of Meditative Attainments (*Samāpatti-nirdeśa*).
Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!

Under the heading of knowledge (*jñāna*), the description of qualities consisting of knowledge has been provided. Now, however, the description of its essential natures (*svabhāva*) must be made; therefore, the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are commenced from the very beginning, because they are the basis for all qualities.
Meditative absorptions are of two kinds:
briefly, there are two types of meditative absorptions due to the distinction between those of rebirth (*upapatti*) and those of attainment (*samāpatti*). Furthermore, these—
There are four [meditative absorptions],

from the first dhyāna up to the fourth. Furthermore, the rebirths within those dhyānas need not be stated here, for those rebirths have already been explained in the section of the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* that provides an exposition of the world (*Lokanirdeśa*).
How are they described?
"There, each meditation consists of three stages; however, the fourth consists of eight stages."
Now, the meditative absorption (*samāpatti-dhyāna*) must be explained. Therefore it is said:
"Absorption is pure one-pointedness" (1c);
that is, without distinction, meditation (*dhyāna*) is the one-pointedness of a wholesome mind, because its intrinsic nature is concentration (*samādhi*).
But the five aggregates, together with their attendants. //1d//

It should be understood that, together with its attendants, it has the five aggregates as its intrinsic nature. What is this so-called "one-pointedness"? It is the state of having a single object. If that is the case, then it follows that concentration (*samādhi*) would be merely those moments of mind having a single object at one time, rather than being a distinct mental factor (*caitasika dharma*). It is not the minds themselves that are concentration; rather, that factor by which those minds proceed in a one-pointed manner is concentration. And that is precisely what is meant by "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*).

If it is argued that because of momentariness, every state of mind is one-pointed (*ekāgra*) and therefore there is no distraction (*avikṣepa*) from a second [object], then concentration (*samādhi*) would be redundant when [the mind] is associated [with another mental factor]. Furthermore, why is it not accepted that the single-objectedness of minds arises from that very same [factor] as concentration? Moreover, since concentration is a universal mental factor (*mahābhūmika*), it would follow that all states of mind are one-pointed. [This is not so] because concentration is weak; rather, concentration is simply the states of mind themselves being one-pointed. For others hold that the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*) and the primary purification of mind mentioned in the Sūtra refer to the four dhyānas.

What is the meaning of *dhyāna*? It means "they meditate by means of this," which is to say, "they discern clearly. This is because one whose mind is concentrated possesses discernment (*prajñā*) of things as they truly are. For this verbal root has the sense of "thinking," and it is an established tenet that thinking is discernment (*prajñā*). If that is so, then it would follow that all concentrations (*samādhi*) are meditation (*dhyāna*). No; for that name is applied only to that which is characterized by excellence, just like the word "sun" (*bhāskara*). And what is characterized by excellence? That concentration which is endowed with the [meditative] factors (*aṅga*).

For that [state] is called an "abiding in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) because it proceeds with calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) joined together like a pair of oxen yoked to a cart, and it is called an "easy path" (*sukhā pratipad*); therefore, one meditates (*dhyāyati*) by means of it all the more intensely. How can that which is afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) be considered meditation (*dhyāna*)? Because it is a false concentration (*mithyopanidhyāna*). [If so,] there would be an over-extension of the term. No; for the designation is applied only to what resembles it, just as one speaks of "rotten seeds. Furthermore, the Blessed One has even spoken of "unwholesome meditations" (*akuśala-dhyāna*). What kind of wholesome one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*) is the first meditation, and what kind are those up to the fourth? First, regarding the first:
(2a) Possessing investigation (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*):

that wholesome one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*) associated with investigation, joy, and bliss is the first *dhyāna*. By the mention of "investigation," "applied thought" (*vitarka*) is also implied, because they are concomitant, like smoke and fire; for there is no investigation accompanied by joy and bliss without applied thought. Furthermore, the remaining three *dhyānas* are devoid of each preceding factor. (2b)

The term "pure one-pointedness" (*śubhaikāgrya*) continues to apply here. The second is devoid of investigation (*vicāra*) and possesses joy and bliss (*prītisukha*); the third is devoid of investigation and joy; and the fourth is devoid of investigation, joy, and bliss. Just as with the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), so too are the formless attainments (*ārūpya*). In what manner? For these also are twofold, by way of rebirth (*upapatti*) and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). Their four rebirths have already been explained. However, the formless attainments, without distinction, have the nature of wholesome one-pointedness; in this manner, they are accompanied by their retinues (*saparivāra*).
They consist of four aggregates because of the absence of accompanying form; they are born from seclusion from the lower stages. (2cd)

The sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) is born from seclusion from the fourth dhyāna; the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) is born from seclusion from that; the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is born from seclusion from that; and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is born from seclusion from that—thus are the four formless [attainments].
What is this so-called "seclusion"? It is the path by which one is liberated from below, through the attainment of dispassion (*vairāgya*).
And these very same [states] are the formless [attainments].
Those known as "having transcended the perception of form" are [the three] together with their preliminary stages (sāmantaka).

The preliminary stage of the sphere of infinite space does not receive the designation "having transcended the perception of form" because it takes the fourth dhyāna as its object; for in that case, the perception of form has not been transcended—that is, it has not departed.

As for what was stated—that "the four aggregates [exist]"—this is first of all a point to be proven: that there is no form (*rūpa*) in the formless realms (*ārūpya*). For if form were present there, how could they be called "formless"? [They would be so called] only because of the presence of a slight amount of form, like something slightly tawny (*āpiṅgala*).

What kind of "slight form" (*īṣadrūpa*) is intended there? If it is merely the restraint of body and speech, how can those two restraints exist in the absence of that [form]? Nor is it logical for derived matter (*bhautika*) to exist when the primary elements (*bhūta*) are absent. If it is argued that this is like the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), [we reply] no, because the tainted primary elements do exist [there]. Furthermore, the negation of that [form] has already been stated regarding meditative attainment (*samāpatti*). If, on the other hand, the body exists there as well as the material sense-faculties, how can they be considered "slight forms"? If it is because their dimensions are minute, [then...]

There would be the same logical consequence for minute beings whose forms are invisible. If you argue that this is because they are transparent (*acchatva*), then the same consequence would apply to those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the form realm (*rūpāvacara*), since nothing is more transparent than they are; otherwise, only the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) would be formless (*ārūpya*). Furthermore, just as with meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), there is a distinction in their rebirths;
yet, since the form of the rebirth in the dhyānas is also not perceived by the sense faculties of a lower level, what difference is there between them?

If it is argued that the designations for these two [realms] are literal, but not so for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), what is the reasoning here? If you say: "Because of the statement that vitality (*āyus*) and heat (*uṣman*) are conjoined; because of the statement that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are mutually dependent like two bundles of reeds; because of the statement 'name-and-form have consciousness as their condition' (*vijñānapratyayaṃ nāmarūpam*); and because, apart from form up to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the coming and going of consciousness is denied in the formless realms—therefore, the existence of form in the formless realms is established," we say: No.

This must first be considered: regarding this statement that life-force (*āyus*) and heat (*uṣman*) are conjoined, was this said with reference to the life-force of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*), or rather to all [life-forces]? And regarding the statement that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are mutually dependent, was this said with reference to the name-and-form of the desire and form realms, or rather to all [name-and-form]? Furthermore, regarding the statement that name-and-form have consciousness (*vijñāna*) as their condition, was it stated here that all consciousness is the condition for name-and-form, or that all name-and-form has consciousness as its condition?

Furthermore, regarding the denial of the coming and going of consciousness apart from form and the other [aggregates], does this denial apply only when all of them are absent, or even when just one is absent? If it is argued that no distinction need be made because the statement is made without qualification, then there would be an over-extension of the principle. For then it would follow that external heat could not exist without life-force (*āyus*), and that external form also would have to be dependent upon name (*nāman*), since the statement is likewise made without qualification.
