If it is argued that, just as there are four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), because of the mention of the fourfold food (*āhāra*), it would follow that even the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*); [we reply: there is likewise no such consequence for matter (*rūpa*) in the formless realms. This is because of the scriptural statements: "The formless [attainments] are the escape from forms"; "Those peaceful liberations which, having transcended forms, are the formless"; and "There are beings without form, through the complete transcendence of perceptions of form."

For if form existed, they would necessarily perceive their own form. If it is argued that this was said with reference to the coarse form belonging to the lower stages, then the same applies to edible food (*kavaḍīkāra*). Furthermore, since the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) also involve an escape from the lower stages, it would follow that they too are "formless" (*ārūpya*). Why, then, are they not described as an escape from feeling and so forth? [The answer is: because they are an escape from the feelings of the lower stages. However, they have transcended the entire category of form, but not the categories of feeling and so forth; therefore, they are described as an escape from forms.

The statement that existence is not an escape from existence is because one cannot escape from that very same existence, and because it is neither a complete nor a final escape. Furthermore, regarding the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the Blessed One said: "Whatever there is therein, whether belonging to the category of form (*rūpagata*) or up to the category of consciousness (*vijñānagata*).

If there were a presence of form within those [formless states], why would he not have said "or belonging to the category of form"? Therefore, there is no existence of form in the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
How, then, can there be the arising of form again for those who have fallen from it after form has been interrupted for many eons?
The arising of form, however, is from the mind. (3d)
The arising of form occurs from mind alone, having acquired its activity through being permeated by the cause of its maturation (*vipāka-hetu*).
How does the mind function without depending on form?
Why should it not so function?
Because it is not observed here in this way:

even without other types of physical food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), beings in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) do not fail to subsist. What is the reason? Because it is not observed here in this way; and it has already been explained previously how they do subsist. This point is settled. Now this must be addressed: Is it because space and so forth are the very objects of perception (*ālambana*) for these [meditative attainments], such as the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), that they are designated in this manner? No, it is not so. How then? First, there are three...

Those termed "infinite space," "infinite consciousness," and "nothingness" apply these names because of their respective applications: by attending to the thought "space is infinite," "consciousness is infinite," and "there is nothing at all," they apply themselves to those [attainments] in that order; therefore, these are their designations.
But due to dullness, one who lacks even perception is called "non-percipient" (asaṃjñaka). //4cd//

However, because perception (*saṃjñā*) is subtle, it is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). For that perception is not sharp, yet it is not entirely without perception either. Even though there they apply such expressions as, "Perception is a disease, perception is an abscess, perception is a thorn; non-perception is delusion; this is peaceful, this is sublime, namely, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception," one must necessarily explain why they grasp it in such a way. It is precisely for this reason—that perceptions are subtle—that it has been so stated.
Thus, the fundamental substance of attainment is of eight kinds (5ab).
These are the eight fundamental substances of attainment, namely: the four meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*). Furthermore, these are of three types.
Seven (5bc):
the seven [realms] other than the peak of existence are of three kinds;
they are associated with tasting, pure, and untainted (5cd).
They are associated with relishing, pure, and untainted;
the eighth is of two kinds. (5d)

The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) and is also pure (*śuddhaka*); it is not untainted (*anāsrava*). Furthermore, therein, that which is associated with relishing is accompanied by craving (*satṛṣṇa*), for craving is indeed relishing.

Worldly wholesome [states] are pure (*śuddhaka*). A worldly wholesome substance of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-dravya*) is called "pure" because it is associated with pure factors (*śuddha-dharma*) such as non-greed (*alobha*). Furthermore, what is it that is relished by that [attainment] which is not associated with tasting (*āsvādana*)?

That [attainment] is to be tasted; that pure substance of attainment is tasted by it immediately after it has passed away. One has emerged from that which one tastes, and one has entered into that by means of which one tastes. It is supramundane and untainted. (6cd–6d)

That substance of meditative attainment which is supramundane is untainted (*anāsrava*). Among these substances of meditative attainment, only the *dhyānas* exist, not the formless attainments (*ārūpyas*). In that regard, there are five factors in the first part of the first [dhyāna].
And applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), as well as joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and concentration (*samādhi*).

(7ab) Applied thought, sustained thought, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*): these five factors (*pañcāṅga*) constitute the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). It is said that concentration is both a factor and the absorption itself; the remaining ones are merely factors. Just as there is an army with four divisions, so too is the meditative absorption fivefold. [p.438]
In the second [dhyāna], there are four factors: joy and the others, as well as serenity. (7cd)
In the second dhyāna there are four factors: internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).

In the third, however, there are five: equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), discernment (*prajñā*), bliss (*sukha*), and stability (*sthiti*). (8ab) In the third dhyāna, however, there are five factors: equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension (*saṃprajñāna*), bliss, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). For "stability" is a synonym for meditative absorption, as it is stated in the Sūtra: "What is right concentration? It is the stability of the mind."
The four [dhyānas] at the end consist of equanimity, mindfulness, and concentration, which are neither painful nor pleasant. //8cd//

The fourth dhyāna is the last. It has four factors: neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, purity of equanimity, purity of mindfulness, and concentration. Thus, these constitute eighteen dhyāna-factors, because the first and third [dhyānas] have five factors each, while the second and fourth have four factors each. This is so by way of name; by way of substance, however, there are ten and one.

In substance, these constitute eleven factors: five belong to the first dhyāna; in the second, internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) increases; in the third, equanimity (*upekṣā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), clear comprehension (*saṃprajñāna*), and bliss (*sukha*); and in the fourth, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*). Therefore it is said that "those factors which are in the first dhyāna are also in the second" constitutes a fourfold alternative (*catuṣkoṭika*). The first alternative consists of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); the second is internal serenity; the third is joy (*prīti*), bliss, and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).

The fourth category consists of those factors excluded from what has been mentioned. In this manner, all the members of the meditative absorptions (*dhyānāṅga*) are to be applied to one another. Why is bliss (*sukha*) said to be a distinct entity (*dravyāntara*) in the third absorption? Because that is the bliss of feeling (*vedanāsukha*), whereas in the first two absorptions it is the bliss of pliancy (*prasrabdhisukha*).

It has been stated that in the first and second dhyānas there is the pleasure of pliancy (*prasrabdhi-sukha*). Why is it that here [in the third dhyāna] it is the pleasure of sensation (*vedanā-sukha*), whereas in those [two] it is the pleasure of pliancy? Because the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is not associated with the two meditative attainments (*dhyāna-samāpatti*). For it is not logical that it be bodily in those two, because for one who has attained them, the groups of consciousness (*vijñānakāya*) are absent. Nor is it mental, because of the mention of "joy" (*prīti*); for joy is mental well-being (*saumanasya*). And there is no simultaneous occurrence of pleasure and mental well-being. Furthermore, it is not logical for the two to occur alternately within the dhyāna, because of the statement that it possesses five factors (*pañcāṅga*). [p.439]

Others, however, say: "There is no mental faculty of pleasure at all in any of the three dhyānas; rather, it is established that only bodily pleasure constitutes a factor [of the dhyāna]. If so, then as for what is stated in the Sūtra: "What is the faculty of pleasure? That which arises when one is touched by a contact to be experienced as pleasant—whether it be bodily or mental, agreeable, felt, and belonging to sensation—this is called the faculty of pleasure. This reading is an interpolation.

Because in all other schools (*nikāya*) the reading is simply "bodily" (*kāyika*), and because it is stated in its own words: "and he experiences pleasure with the body. If you argue that it means "with the mind-body" (*manaskāyena*), what benefit is gained by saying this? Furthermore, even though there is an abundance of pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) in the fourth dhyāna, pleasure (*sukha*) is not mentioned there. If you argue that pliancy conducive to the feeling of pleasure is what is called "pleasure," then why is pliancy-pleasure not mentioned in the third dhyāna? If you say it is because it is impaired by equanimity (*upekṣā*), that is not so.

Its increase occurs through equanimity alone, because it is distinct from the previous [stages]. In the Sūtra which states, "At whatever time the noble disciple, having realized with his own body the joy born of seclusion, dwells having attained it," pleasure is not identical to pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), because pliancy and pleasure are mentioned separately. If it is asked how there can be bodily consciousness for one who has entered meditative absorption, [the answer is: because the body is pervaded by a wind produced by a specific concentration, designated as "pliancy," which is to be experienced as pleasure.

If it is argued that there is a lapse from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) due to external distraction, we say no; for the bodily pleasure produced within the body by means of concentration is conducive to concentration itself. If it is argued that at the time of the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), one must have emerged from concentration, we say no; for precisely because of this, a body-consciousness of the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) does not arise through a body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*). If it is argued that [the body-consciousness] would not arise, we say no; for the consciousness of pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) arises. Furthermore, both the tangible object and the body-consciousness could even be untainted (*anāsrava*).

If it is argued that no part [of the body] should be both with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and without-outflow (*anāsrava*), [we reply] because of the mention of the factor of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) of physical pliancy (*kāyikaprasrabdhi*). If it is argued that this is accepted because it is conducive to the factors of enlightenment, then being without-outflow would also be established in this way. If it is argued that this contradicts the Sūtra which says, "Which are the dharmas with-outflow? They are the eye, up to and including the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*)," we say no; for that statement was made with the intention of referring to other tangibles and body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).

If it is argued that within the untainted (anāsrava) state, one part could not be tainted (sāsrava) and another part untainted, we reply: what fault is there, since they do not occur simultaneously? If it is argued that because pleasure (*sukha*) and joy (*prīti*) cannot coexist, it would not possess five factors (*pañcāṅga*), we say no; for the teaching is given with respect to their possible occurrence, just as in the case of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). If it is argued that this remains to be proven, we say it is already established, because grossness (*audārikatā*) and subtlety (*sūkṣmatā*) of the mind are mutually exclusive, and because no fault has been stated [to the contrary].

Therefore, the establishment of the second and subsequent dhyānas occurs through the removal of two, three, or four of those very five factors that exist in the first dhyāna. For this very reason, it is said that there are five factors as "factors" (*aṅga*) in the first dhyāna, because the higher dhyānas are established by the removal of those [factors]. However, perception (*saṃjñā*) and the others are not stated to be factors. Or, if it is asked why only five are stated to be factors, and if you say it is because they are beneficial (*upakāraka*), that is not so.

Because mindfulness and wisdom are more beneficial than applied thought and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), there is this doctrine held by some. However, the former teachers did not explain it in this way for all the factors ending with wisdom; therefore, this matter requires investigation. What is this factor called "inner serenity" (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*)? Inner serenity is the tranquil flow of the mental continuum due to its freedom from the agitation of applied and sustained thought.

For the mental continuum, agitated by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), proceeds without clarity, like a river with waves. If that [serenity] is therefore not a distinct substance, how can there be eleven factors in substance? Therefore, faith is serenity (*prasāda*). (9c)

For upon attaining the second dhyāna, a conviction arises regarding the emergence from the state of meditative concentration; this is what is meant here by "inner serenity" (*adhyātma-saṃprasāda*). Others, however, maintain that neither applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), nor concentration (*samādhi*), nor even inner serenity, are distinct substantial entities. [The opponent asks: If they are not distinct substantial entities, how is their status as mental factors (*caitasika*) established? [The response is: A particular state of the mind is indeed called a mental factor. However, this is not the established tenet of the treatise.

As it was said: "Joy (*prīti*) is indeed mental pleasure (*saumanasya*). How is this understood? Could it be otherwise? As those belonging to other schools maintain: that joy is a distinct mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*), whereas mental pleasure (*saumanasya*) is the bliss (*sukha*) in all three dhyānas. But it is certainly not logical that bliss in the dhyānas is mental pleasure; rather, joy is mental pleasure because of two scriptural authorities. (9cd)

For it was said by the Blessed One in the *Aviparītaka-sūtra*, after describing the third dhyāna: "Herein, the faculty of mental pleasure (*saumanasyendriya*) that has arisen ceases without remainder; and in the fourth dhyāna, the faculty of physical pleasure (*sukhendriya*) ceases. Furthermore, it was said: "Through the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and through the previous disappearance of mental pleasure and mental pain (*daurmanasya*). For this reason also, the faculty of mental pleasure does not exist in the third dhyāna. Therefore, joy (*prīti*) alone is mental pleasure, not physical pleasure.
Furthermore, do the factors exist in the defiled meditative absorptions exactly as they have been prescribed? No, they do not. What is it that is absent in those defiled states?
In the defiled [absorptions], joy, bliss, clarity, discernment, mindfulness, equanimity, and the purity of mindfulness are absent. (10abc)

In the first dhyāna, there is no joy and happiness born of seclusion, because it is not yet secluded from the afflictions (*kleśa*). In the second dhyāna, there is no internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), because it is turbid with afflictions. In the third, there is no mindfulness and clear comprehension (*smṛtisamprajanya*), because one is distracted by defiled happiness. In the fourth, there is no purity of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣāsmṛtipariśuddhi*), because it is stained by afflictions. Thus say some. Others [say] that [there is no] pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣaṇa*) [in the first two]. (10d)

Furthermore, some maintain that in the first and second [dhyānas], when they are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*), there is no pliancy (*prasrabdhi*); and in the third and fourth, there is no equanimity (*upekṣā*), because these two are factors of the wholesome universal ground (*kuśalamahābhūmika*). Moreover, the Blessed One has stated that the first three dhyānas are "shaken" (*señjita*) because they possess defects (*sāpakṣāla*). Because it is said to be free from the eight defects, the fourth is "unshaken" (*āniñja*). What, then, are those defects?
Applied thought and sustained thought, the two breaths, and the fourfold [set] beginning with pleasure. //11cd//

Initial thought and sustained thought, pleasure and pain, mental joy and dejection, and inhalation and exhalation—among these eight, not even one of these defects exists in the fourth [dhyāna]; therefore, it is called "unshakable" (*āneñjya*). Others say that the fourth dhyāna is unshakable because it cannot be moved by initial thought, sustained thought, joy, or pleasure, as illustrated in the Sūtra by the simile of a lamp in a windless place.

In the first two dhyānas, mental joy (*saumanasya*) is mentioned by virtue of the term "rapture" (*prīti*); in the third, pleasure (*sukha*); and in the fourth, equanimity (*upekṣā*). Now, are the feelings (*vedanā*) that exist in the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the dhyānas the same as those in the rebirths (*upapatti*) within those dhyānas? No, he says. What then? Mental joy, pleasure, and equanimity; equanimity and mental joy; pleasure and equanimity; and equanimity alone—these are known to exist in the rebirths of the dhyānas. (12)

Upon birth in the first dhyāna, there are three feelings: pleasure associated with the three groups of consciousness, mental joy belonging to the level of the mind, and equanimity associated with the four groups of consciousness. Upon birth in the second dhyāna, there are two feelings—mental joy and equanimity—both belonging to the level of the mind; there is no [bodily] pleasure because of the absence of those groups of consciousness. Upon birth in the third dhyāna, there are two feelings: pleasure and equanimity, both belonging to the level of the mind. Upon birth in the fourth dhyāna, there is only equanimity.

If the three groups of consciousness and applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) do not exist in the second and higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), how is it that those [beings] see, and so forth, up to touching, and how do they produce non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)? It is certainly not the case that visual consciousness and the others do not exist for those born there; however, they do not belong to their own level. What then? The consciousnesses of body, eye, and ear, as well as that which originates informative matter (*vijñapti*), belong to the first [level] in the second [dhyāna] and above. (13abc)

Beings in the second and higher meditative absorptions (dhyāna) manifest the visual, auditory, and tactile consciousnesses, as well as the consciousness that originates informative action (vijñapti), belonging to the level of the first dhyāna. This is like a mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta), by means of which they see and so forth, up to originating informative action.
Furthermore, that [consciousness] is non-defiled and neutral (akliṣṭāvyākṛta). //13d//

That consciousness belonging to the level of the first dhyāna which they bring into manifestation should be understood as unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*); it is not afflicted because they are free from passion, nor is it wholesome because it is inferior. The discussion on the function of dhyāna is concluded. Now, how is the acquisition of the pure (*śuddhaka*) and other dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*)?
One who does not yet possess them acquires the pure [dhyāna] through detachment (*vairāgya*) or through rebirth (*upapatti*). (14ab)

One who is not already endowed with it attains either a pure (*śuddhaka*) dhyāna or an immaterial attainment (*ārūpya*) through detachment from a lower stage, or through rebirth in a lower stage—with the exception of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), for there is no attainment of it through rebirth there. Why is one said to be "endowed" with that which one does not possess? One attains a pure *nirvedhabhāgīya* through application, or a *hānabhāgīya* through falling away from a pure state.

Therefore it is said: "There may be pure (*śuddhaka*) dhyāna that one acquires through detachment (*vairāgya*) and abandons through detachment; likewise through falling away (*parihāṇi*) and through rebirth (*upapatti*). There may be the first dhyāna belonging to the category of falling away (*dhānabhāgīya*); for that is acquired through detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and abandoned through detachment from the Brahma-world (*brahmaloka*). It is acquired through falling away from detachment from the Brahma-world and abandoned through the loss of detachment from the desire realm. One who is being reborn above [the Brahma-world] acquires it; one who is being reborn again from there into the desire realm abandons it."
"But the untainted [attainment] is obtained through detachment" (14d).

The phrase "one who does not possess it obtains it" carries over. However, one who already possesses it obtains the *aśaikṣa* [attainment] even from the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*), and obtains both the *śaikṣa* and *aśaikṣa* [attainments] through the transformation of the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).

But is it not the case that one who has entered the path of certainty (*niyāmāvakrānta*) also obtains the untainted [attainment] for the first time? Not necessarily; this is because it is not obtained by one who follows the gradual sequence (*ānupūrvika*). It has been explained according to how it is necessarily obtained.
The defiled [mind] arises through decline or rebirth. //14d//

The phrase "one who does not possess that attains it" continues to apply here. [One attains it] through falling away, if one falls away from the detachment regarding that [level]; or through rebirth, if one is reborn from a higher plane into a lower one.

Immediately after which substance of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-dravya*) do how many arise? Immediately after the untainted (*anāsrava*) first dhyāna, six arise: the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted of its own level, and those belonging to the levels of the second and third dhyānas. Immediately after the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), seven arise: the pure and the untainted of its own level, and those belonging to the level of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). [The sphere of] the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) arises only as pure, because the untainted does not exist there. Immediately after the second dhyāna, eight arise.

[The mind] belonging to its own level—both the pure (*śuddhaka*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*)—and those belonging to the levels of the third, fourth, and first dhyānas. Immediately after the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), nine [minds] arise: two belonging to its own level, four belonging to the levels of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the fourth dhyāna, and three belonging to the levels of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). In this same manner, ten substances should be applied immediately after the other dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*). This, however, is the summary:
From the third [dhyāna] up to the upper and lower [levels], the wholesome arises immediately after the untainted. (15abc) [p.444]

By the term "pure" (*śubha*), both the pure (*śuddha*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*) are included because the untainted substance of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-dravya*) is wholesome (*kuśala*). Immediately after that, both the pure and the untainted states belonging to its own level arise; furthermore, those belonging to higher and lower levels arise up to the third [level]. For those who practice the "leap-over" attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) do not venture to skip beyond the third. Furthermore, they enter the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) immediately after subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), but not immediately after dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), because the latter has a lower basis and object. This should be understood as being the same as what was stated regarding what arises immediately after the untainted.
Likewise, [the mind] takes as its object the pure and the afflicted [dharmas] belonging to its own level. //15cd//

Immediately after the pure [attainment], there additionally arises the defiled [attainment] belonging to its own level. The remainder is exactly as in the case of the uncontaminated [attainment]. For indeed, there is no arising of a defiled state immediately after an uncontaminated one.
From a defiled [attainment], there arise its own pure and defiled states;
that is, immediately after a defiled substance of meditative attainment, the pure and defiled states belonging to its own level arise.
And thus is the pure [attainment] of a lower level.

For one oppressed by afflictions values even a pure attainment of a lower level highly. If, having discerned it as afflicted, one descends to a lower level, one has descended from the wholesome, not from the afflicted.

Now, how does one transition without having delimited [the stage]? It is due to a previous impulse (*pūrvāvedha*). For previously, he has had such a desire: "It is better to have a pure [state] below than a defiled one above. And the continuum of sentient beings follows their prior intention, just as one who has fallen asleep after making a resolve wakes up at the intended time. However, the untainted (*anāsrava*) never arises immediately after a defiled state in any way whatsoever. This was said with reference to the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*);
for immediately after a pure or a defiled state, only a defiled state of its own level arises, not one of another level.
Regarding death, however, from the pure [attainment], the defiled arises in its entirety.
(16cd) At the time of death, immediately after the pure attainment acquired at birth, a defiled state belonging to any level arises. But from the defiled, nothing higher arises. (16d) [p.445]

However, immediately after a defiled *dhyāna* or *ārūpya* at the time of death (*cyuti*), a defiled state belonging to its own level or a lower level arises; one from a higher level does not. Furthermore, an untainted (*anāsrava*) meditative attainment (*samāpatti-dravya*) does not arise from every pure (*śuddhaka*) attainment. What then? The pure [attainment] is fourfold, beginning with that conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*). (17ab) The pure [attainment] is of four types: conducive to decline, conducive to distinction (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), conducive to stability (*sthitibhāgīya*), and conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). However, the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is of three types, excluding that conducive to distinction.
What is its characteristic?
It is, respectively:
conducive to the arising of afflictions, to one’s own level, to higher levels, and to the outflow-free state. (17bcd)

That which is conducive to the arising of afflictions is conducive to decline (*hānabhāgīya*); that which is conducive to its own level is conducive to maintenance (*sthitibhāgīya*); that which is conducive to a higher level is conducive to distinction (*viśeṣabhāgīya*); and that which is conducive to the untainted (*anāsrava*) is conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). From that [last one], the untainted arises. Now, among these four, how many arise immediately after which?
Two, three, three, and one arise respectively after decline and the others. (18ab)

That which pertains to decline (*hānabhāgīya*) is the part belonging to decline; immediately after it, two arise: that which pertains to decline and that which pertains to stability (*sthitibhāgīya*). Immediately after that which pertains to stability, three arise, excluding that which pertains to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Immediately after that which pertains to distinction (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), three arise, excluding that which pertains to decline. Immediately after that which pertains to penetration, only one arises. How is the meditative attainment of leaping (*vyutkrāntakasamāpatti*) produced?
"Having gone and returned, in two ways, through the eight [levels], the defiled ones are skipped by one. (16cd)

The leaping meditative attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*) proceeds to the third level of a different nature. (19ab) "Having gone" means having entered them in forward order; "having come" means having entered them in reverse order. "In two ways" refers to the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) levels. "Eight" refers to the meditative attainments of the dhyānas and the formless realms (*ārūpya*). "Defiled" means in successive order. "Skipped by one" means having passed over one by one. Having mastered the eight contaminated levels through entry in both forward and reverse order, as well as the seven uncontaminated ones, one subsequently enters the contaminated third dhyāna from the contaminated first dhyāna.

From that, one enters the sphere of infinite space; from that, the sphere of nothingness. Having thus mastered them again in reverse order, one also enters the untainted states by skipping one, both in direct and reverse order. This is the preliminary practice for the "leaping" meditative attainment (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*). When, however, one enters from the first tainted dhyāna into the third untainted dhyāna, from that into the tainted sphere of infinite space, and from that into the untainted sphere of nothingness—and likewise again in reverse order—[this constitutes the actual attainment].

At that time, it becomes fully accomplished by proceeding through a third substance of a different category (*visabhāga*). Because it is extremely remote, one does not enter the fourth [attainment]. And only an Arhat who is liberated at all times (*asamayavimukta*) produces this in the three continents, because he is free from defilements and possesses mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Although one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) possesses mastery over concentration due to having sharp faculties, he is not free from defilements. Although one who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) is free from defilements, he lacks mastery over concentration. By means of which basis (*āśraya*) are how many dhyānas and formless attainments (*ārūpya*) manifested?
They have as their basis only their own lower stage;
they have as their basis only the meditative absorptions, namely the dhyānas and the formless attainments.

The peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is manifested both at the peak of existence and below, down to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The remaining [attainments] are manifested in their own level and below. For what reason does one born in a higher [level] not manifest an attainment of a lower level? Therefore, for such a person, the lower is useless. (19d)

For there is no purpose served for him by a lower substance of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-dravya*), because it is inferior. Having stated this general rule (*utsarga*), he now provides an exception (*apavāda*): "Through the manifestation of the Noble Nothingness (*āryākiṃcanya*), however, there is the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) at the Peak of Existence" (20ab). For one born at the Peak of Existence, the destruction of the outflows occurs through the manifestation of the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of nothingness. How does that manifestation occur for one born there? Because of the absence of [the sphere of nothingness] belonging to that level itself, and because of the prior cultivation (*abhyāsa*) of that [untainted state].

Now, what is the object (*ālambana*) of these meditations (*dhyāna*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya*)? "Those associated with craving have their own existence as their object" (20c). Those associated with relishing (*āsvādana*) take as their object the existence belonging to their own level. By the term "existence" (*bhava*), contaminated (*sāsrava*) entities are understood. They do not take a lower level as an object because they are free from passion (*vītarāga*) toward it; nor do they take a higher level as an object because the levels are delimited by craving; nor do they take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena as objects, for that would entail [the states being] wholesome (*kuśala*).
Meditative absorption has a real object and is virtuous. //20d//
Wholesome dhyāna is both pure (*śubha*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). It has everything as its object, whatever exists, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The fundamental wholesome formless attainments (*ārūpya*) do not have the tainted lower realms as their sphere of activity. (21ab)

For the fundamental wholesome formless attainments (*ārūpya*), a contaminated (*sāsrava*) entity belonging to a lower level is not an object, because they take as their objects only their own or higher levels; however, an uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) entity is an object. [In this regard], everything belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) is an object, but nothing belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) nor the cessation (*nirodha*) of a lower level is. However, for the preparatory (*sāmantaka*) and uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) paths, the lower level is indeed an object. Furthermore, regarding these three types of meditative absorptions—the form and formless ones—it is by means of the uncontaminated that the afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned. (21cd)

It is not by means of the pure [attainment], much less by the defiled; because of being free from passion, it is not from below; because that [pure attainment] is not its antidote, it is not in its own stage; and because it is more distinguished, it is not from above.
And also by means of the preparatory stage (sāmantaka). //21d//

The afflictions are abandoned by means of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the meditations and the formless attainments, even by those that are merely pure (*śuddhaka*), because they serve as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to the lower levels. Furthermore, how many preparatory stages are there? There are eight preparatory stages, one for each [dhyāna], by which one enters them. Are these also of three types [pure, undefiled, and defiled] in the same way, and is the feeling (*vedanā*) within them likewise? It is said: no.

For they are pure, neither-painful-nor-pleasant, and indeed "pure" (*śuddhaka*). They are associated with the faculty of equanimity because they must be brought about through effort, because the agitation regarding the lower stages has not yet departed, and because they constitute the path to detachment; thus, they are not associated with relishing (*āsvādana*).
And the first is noble (*ārya*).

The first preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) is the "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*); it is both pure (*śuddhaka*) and untainted (*anāsrava*). Although the connection of rebirth (*pratisaṃdhibandha*) by means of a preparatory mind is defiled (*kliṣṭa*), defilement is excluded for that which is in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*). Some maintain that it is of three kinds; others, however, assert that the "not-yet-arrived," the preparatory stage, and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*) are also called [preparatory stages] even when associated with relishing (*āsvādana*). Is this [term] synonymous, or do they have different meanings? For the preparatory stage is the path of detachment (*vairāgyamārga*).
The intermediate meditation is without applied thought. //22d//

Indeed, that very dhyāna which is dissociated from applied thought (*vitarka*) is the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), because it is a specific variety of dhyāna. For this very reason, it is not established within the second and subsequent dhyānas, as there is no such distinction [in them]. Furthermore, that intermediate dhyāna is threefold:
associated with tasting (*āsvādana*), pure (*śuddhaka*), and untainted (*anāsrava*).

And that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukha*); the meaning is that because there is neither pleasure nor pain here, it is associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). It is not associated with joy (*prīti*) because it proceeds with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*). For this very reason, it is a difficult path (*duḥkhā pratipad*). What, then, is the specific fruit of that intermediate dhyāna?
Its fruit is that of Mahābrahmā.

For by cultivating that intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntarika*), one becomes a Mahābrahmā. Furthermore, having summarized all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), three types of samādhi are taught in the Sūtra: samādhi with applied thought (*savitarka*) and sustained thought (*savicāra*); samādhi without applied thought and with sustained thought only (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ*); and samādhi without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarko 'vicāra*).

Among these, it is indicated that the intermediate dhyāna is first the samādhi without applied thought and with sustained thought only, because there is no negation of applied thought alone. Therefore, the lower samādhi is "with applied thought and sustained thought" (23cd).
Therefore, the concentration below that intermediate dhyāna is with vitarka and with vicāra—namely, the first dhyāna and the anāgamya;
beyond that, it is without both. //23d//

Because there is no duality here, it is "non-dual" (*advaya*). Furthermore, beyond the intermediate dhyāna, there is a concentration that is without applied thought (*avitarka*) and without sustained thought (*avicāra*), extending from the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of the second dhyāna up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).

Again, three concentrations are taught: the emptiness concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and the signless (*ānimitta*). Among these, emptiness [is so called] because of the emptiness of self and phenomena.
The concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) proceeds conjoined with the two aspects of selflessness and emptiness; it thus possesses two aspects.
The wishless (*apraṇihita*) [concentration] consists of the remaining aspects of the truths. (24cd)

Concentration associated with the remaining aspects of the truths is the wishless (*apraṇihita*) concentration, which has ten aspects. Because of the agitation caused by impermanence, suffering, and their causes, and because the path must necessarily be abandoned due to its resemblance to a raft, the concentration having those aspects is wishless. However, there is no agitation regarding emptiness and selflessness, because they are common to nirvāṇa; this is because it is oriented toward transcending that [samsāra]. These three concentrations are of two kinds: pure (*śuddha*) and stainless (*amala*).
They are both pure and untainted (*anāsrava*), because they are mundane and supramundane. They are mundane in the eleven stages; they are supramundane where the Path exists.

But those stainless ones are the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*). (25ab) These three untainted concentrations are called the three gates of liberation: emptiness as a gate of liberation, the wishless, and the signless as a gate of liberation, because they are doors to liberation.
Furthermore, it is said: there are three other concentrations known as the emptiness of emptiness and so forth. //25cd//

The emptiness-of-emptiness, the wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and the signlessness-of-signlessness [are so called] because they have emptiness and the others as their objects; thus they receive those names.
Furthermore, regarding those [three], two take the state beyond training (aśaikṣa) as their object, both through the aspect of emptiness and through the aspect of impermanence. (26ab)

Two other concentrations take the concentration of one beyond training as their object: the emptiness-of-emptiness takes the emptiness-concentration of one beyond training as its object by way of the aspect of emptiness; the wishlessness-of-wishlessness likewise takes the wishlessness-concentration of one beyond training as its object by way of the aspect of impermanence—not by way of suffering or cause and so forth, because that which is untainted does not possess those characteristics, nor by way of the aspects of the path, because it is to be rejected. However, the signless-of-signless [takes] the cessation [of the signless] as its object by way of peace, through non-analytical cessation. (26cd)

The signless-signless concentration (*ānimittānimitta-samādhi*), however, takes as its object the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the signless state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). It does so by way of the aspect of "peaceful" (*śānta*), because there is no analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) for that which is untainted (*anāsrava*). It does not take it by way of the aspects of "cessation," "excellent," or "escape," because [non-analytical cessation] is common to the cessation of impermanence, is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and is not a disjunction (*avisaṃyoga*). Furthermore, these other concentrations are exclusively tainted (*sāsrava*).
Because they are hostile toward the noble path, for [those views] are not thus without outflows (*anāsrava*). Where do they arise?
Only among humans (*manuṣya*), not among gods. For whom do they arise?
It belongs to the Immovable Arhat and not to any other; it pertains to how many stages?
To all except the seven preparatory stages.

Excluding the seven preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), there are four cultivations of concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*) in the other eleven stages: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the threshold meditation (*anāgamya*), the intermediate meditation (*dhyānāntara*), the [four] meditations (*dhyāna*), and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*). Furthermore, it is said: "There is a cultivation of concentration which, when practiced, developed, and cultivated frequently, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life," and so forth. In that regard: The first pure meditation is indeed for the sake of happiness. (27cd)

The cultivation of concentration for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life consists of the first *kuśala* [state], whether it be pure (*śuddhaka*) or untainted (*anāsrava*). Because it is the primary one, others should also be understood accordingly. It is not necessarily for the sake of dwelling in happiness in future lives, because that is absent for those who have not fallen away, those born in higher realms, and those who have attained parinirvāṇa.
The divine eye supernormal power (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*) is held to be for the sake of seeing; it is the cultivation of concentration for the sake of the vision of knowledge (*jñānadarśana*).
Those born of application are for the differentiation of wisdom.
(28b) All qualities born of application—whether belonging to the three realms or untainted—are the cultivation of meditative concentration for the sake of the differentiation of wisdom.
That which is like a diamond, occurring in the final dhyāna, is the cultivation for the destruction of the outflows. (28cd) [p.452]

The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) in the fourth dhyāna is the cultivation of concentration for the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*). It is said that this teaching of the Dharma by the Blessed One is directed toward himself; therefore, he spoke only of these four. The exposition of the concentrations according to their sequence has been completed. Now is the time for the exposition of the qualities dependent upon concentration; thus they are explained: the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

They are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). They are called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) because they take immeasurable sentient beings as their object. Why are there exactly four?
Because they are the antidotes to ill-will and so forth.
For those who abound in ill-will, harmfulness, discontent, and sensual desire and ill-will, there are four [immeasurables] respectively for the sake of abandoning them.

What is the distinction between the meditation on the foul (*aśubha*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) in their function as antidotes to sensual desire (*kāmarāga*)? The Vaibhāṣikas maintain that the meditation on the foul is for desire regarding physical beauty (*varṇarāga*), while equanimity is for desire regarding sexual intercourse (*maithunarāga*). However, it is more logical to hold that the meditation on the foul is for desire regarding sexual intercourse, whereas equanimity is for desire regarding one’s mother, father, children, and kinsmen. In this context, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is non-hatred (*adveṣa*);
that is, its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is non-hatred.
Compassion is likewise [the absence of aversion]; sympathetic joy is mental gladness. //29d//

Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) has the nature of mental gladness (*saumanasya*). Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is non-attachment (*alobha*); equanimity consists of the essence of non-attachment. How is it the antidote to ill-will (*vyāpāda*)? Because that [ill-will] is drawn forth by attachment. However, it is more appropriate for this [equanimity] to have both natures. Now, regarding these [immeasurables], such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the rest, [p. 453]...
The aspects are: “May beings indeed be happy,” “Alas, they are suffering,” and “May they rejoice” (30abc).

By attending to the thought, “May beings indeed be happy,” one enters into the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). By [attending to] “Alas, beings are suffering,” one enters into compassion (*karuṇā*); by “May beings indeed rejoice,” one enters into sympathetic joy (*muditā*); and by attending simply to “beings,” one enters into equanimity (*upekṣā*), because of neutrality. [Objection: Since there is the resolve for happiness in those who do not possess it, how is this not a perversion? [Response: Because the intention is that they *do* exist [in that state], or because the perception of the resolve is not perverted due to the purity of the underlying disposition (*āśaya*).

Alternatively, what fault is there in such a state of being contrary? If it is argued that it would be unwholesome (*akuśala*), we say no; for it has roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*) and serves as an antidote to malice (*vyāpāda*) and the like. Their mental aspect (*ākāra*) has already been explained. As for their object (*gocara*), it is sentient beings of the desire realm (*kāmasattva*). //30d//

Beings of the desire realm (*kāmāvacara*) are the objects of these [immeasurables], because they serve as the antidotes to ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and so forth that take those beings as their objects. As for what was said, "I resolve upon one direction," this indicates by means of the container (*bhājana*) that which is contained within the container.
To how many stages (*bhūmi*) do these belong?
Joy (*muditā*) belongs to the two dhyānas.
Sympathetic joy (*muditā*) exists in the first and second dhyānas because it is of the nature of mental gladness (*saumanasya*).

As for the others: "the other three immeasurables exist in six levels" (31ab); that is, they exist in the six levels—the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), and the [four] dhyānas—since this includes both the preliminary applications (*prayoga*) and the fundamental states (*maula*).
Some, however, [place them] in five;

others, excluding the *anāgamya*, maintain that these exist in five; still others say they exist in ten, by including the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), and by taking both the concentrated and non-concentrated, as well as the fundamental and the preliminary stages. As for what was said, "Because they are the opposites of ill-will and so forth" (29b), does the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) also occur through the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*)?
No, there is no abandonment by means of them. (31c) [p.454]

Because they belong to the levels of the fundamental dhyānas, because they consist of mental attention through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-manasikāra*), and because they have sentient beings as their object, they are said to be the antidotes to ill-will and so forth; for by means of their preliminary practice (*prayoga*), ill-will and the like are suppressed, and because [the defilements] are rendered distant through abandonment. Indeed, there exist forms of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other immeasurables belonging to the Desire Realm and the stage of "not-yet-attained" (*anāgamya*), which resemble the fundamental immeasurables. Having suppressed those [defilements] by means of them, one abandons them through the paths of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*). Thereafter, in the state of being free from passion (*vītarāga-avasthā*), because of the attainment of the fundamental immeasurables, one becomes invincible even when encountering powerful conditions, owing to the power of those [immeasurables].

How, then, does a beginner apply himself to loving-kindness (*maitrī*)? Just as he considers himself happy, or hears of others—namely, the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble Śrāvakas—he resolves that beings likewise possess that happiness, thinking, "O, may beings be happy! If he is unable to do so because the activity of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is predominant, he divides the category of friends into three parts and first resolves upon that happiness for the superior friend; then for the middling, and finally for the inferior.

If he attains equal loving-kindness toward them, then [he directs it] toward the side of neutral persons. Then, having divided the side of enemies into three categories, he resolves upon that happiness for the mild [enemy]. Then for the middling, and then for the intense. If his resolution of happiness toward the side of friends does not waver even as much as it did for the intense [enemy], then he gradually extends his resolution of happiness to the village and the kingdom, until he pervades one direction and finally the entire world with loving-kindness.

But he who perceives all virtues quickly generates loving-kindness (*maitrī*). For it is possible to perceive virtues even in one whose roots of merit are severed, and to perceive faults even in a Pratyekabuddha, by first observing the fruits of merit and demerit. In the same way, one applies oneself to compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*), resolving: "May these beings, though submerged in a flood of manifold calamities, be thus liberated from suffering; may they thus rejoice exceedingly. However, one begins equanimity (*upekṣā*) from the side of neutrality. And these immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are produced only among humans. (31cd)
They arise among humans and nowhere else.
Furthermore, is one who is endowed with a single immeasurable necessarily endowed with all of them? Rather, one is certainly endowed with three. (31d)

One born in the third or fourth dhyāna is not endowed with sympathetic joy (*muditā*); however, one who has attained the [other] three immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) is always endowed with them. The eight liberations (*vimokṣa*): "Possessing form, one sees forms"—this is the first liberation. "Not perceiving internal forms, one sees external forms"—this is the second. "Having personally realized the beautiful liberation with the body, one dwells having attained it"—this is the third. There are the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*). And the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāveditanirodha*) is the eighth. Of these:

The first two liberations are impure (32ab). The first two liberations have impurity as their intrinsic nature, because they consist of the aspects of the livid corpse and so forth. Therefore, the method for these two should be understood as being the same as that for the meditation on impurity. And these two [exist] in the first two dhyānas (32b).

They belong to the first and second dhyānas, and not to any other stage; they serve respectively as the antidotes to the passion for color and the passion for beauty belonging to the desire realm and the stage of the first dhyāna. The third, the beautiful liberation, is in the last, that is, in the fourth dhyāna.

And that [liberation] is non-attachment (alobha); it has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature, but not impurity as its intrinsic nature, because it has the aspect of the beautiful. Together with their attendants, however, these have the five aggregates as their intrinsic nature. As for the formless liberations, they are the beautiful formless states in meditative equipoise. (32d)

Only those that are wholesome (*kuśala*) and concentrated (*samāhita*) receive the designation "formless liberation" (*ārūpyavimokṣa*), neither the afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) nor those that are unconcentrated, such as at the time of death. Others maintain that there are also unconcentrated states at other times. Furthermore, the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) also receive the designation "liberation," but not the uninterrupted paths (*ānantaryamārga*), because they have a lower realm as their object; for the meaning of "liberation" (*vimokṣa*) is the sense of turning away (*vaimukhya*). However, the cessation-attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*)— [Page 456, 33a]

The eighth liberation, however, is the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāveditanirodha*), which is the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). This has already been explained previously, as it involves turning away from perception and feeling, or from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Others say it is called a "liberation" because it liberates one from the obstacles to meditative attainment. They enter that attainment immediately after the "subtle-subtle" state. For perception at the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*) is subtle; having made that even more subtle, they enter cessation. But for those who have entered [this attainment]:
Then, emergence from that [meditative state] occurs by means of a mind that is either one's own pure [state] or an inferior noble [state]. //33cd//

Emergence from that occurs either by means of a pure mind belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) or by means of a contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind belonging to the level of the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Thus, while the mind of attainment for that [liberation] is contaminated, the mind of emergence is immediately preceded by a contaminated state. Regarding these liberations (*vimokṣa*), it is said: "The first have as their object the visible forms pertaining to the desire realm" (34ab).
For these, the objective support (*ālambana*) is the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) of the desire realm, being either unpleasant or pleasant according to the case.
But those which are formless have as their objects the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), the higher realms, and the suffering and so forth of their own level. (34bcd)

The objects of the formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*) are the suffering belonging to their own level and higher levels, as well as its cause and cessation; the entire path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*) should also be mentioned, as well as space for one [liberation]. Why is there no liberation in the third dhyāna? Because of the absence of attachment to the color-form (*varṇarāga*) belonging to the level of the second dhyāna, and because it is agitated by the essence of pleasure (*sukhamaṇḍa*). Therefore, one produces the beautiful liberation (*śubhavimokṣa*).

[One practices] in order to gladden a mental continuum that has become sluggish through the meditation on the foul, or for the sake of inquiry: "Are the two liberations based on the foul perfected? Furthermore, those two are considered perfected when no affliction arises even while one attends to the object as beautiful. For there are two reasons why practitioners produce the liberations and so forth: for the purpose of distancing themselves from afflictions, and for the purpose of attaining mastery over meditative attainments. [They are also practiced] for the production of qualities such as the absence of strife (*araṇā*), and for noble supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
This latter [power], moreover, is that by which transformations of objects, empowerments, the relinquishing of the life-span, and so forth, are performed.

Why is direct realization (*sākṣātkaraṇa*) stated only for the third and eighth [liberations] and not for the others? Because they are primary and because they abide at the limits of the realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*).
There are eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Perceiving forms internally, one sees external forms that are limited, beautiful or ugly; having mastered those forms, one knows them and sees them, and being thus percipient, this is the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*). The same applies to extensive [forms]. Likewise for the internal non-perception of form. Thus there are these four. Furthermore, with internal non-perception of form, one sees blue, yellow, red, and white; thus there are eight. Of these, two are like the first liberation (*vimokṣa*).
Just as with the first liberation, so it is with the first and second bases of mastery;
two are like the second [liberation].
Just as with the second liberation, so it is with the third and fourth bases of mastery.

The others, moreover, are like the pure liberation (śubha-vimokṣa). Just as it is with the pure liberation, so it is with the other four. However, this is the distinction: by those [liberations], there is merely the removal of aversion; but by these [masteries], there is mastery over the object at will, because they are not [mere] liberations and because afflictions do not arise. There are ten total masteries (kṛtsnāyatana).

There are ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), so called because they pervade everything without interval: the totalities of earth, water, fire, air, blue, yellow, red, and white; and the totalities of the spheres of infinite space and infinite consciousness.
Among these, eight—the first eight—are of the nature of non-attachment (*alobha*).
In the final dhyāna— that is,
in the fourth dhyāna alone— its range of activity, moreover, is as follows:
The objects of desire (kāmāḥ) are the sphere of visible forms (rūpāyatana) of the desire realm; some say they are the sphere of tangible objects (spraṣṭavyāyatana) of wind.
There are two pure formless [attainments] (śuddhakārūpya).
The last two totalities have the nature of the pure formless [attainments] and have their own four aggregates as their object. //36d//

The four aggregates belonging to their own level are the objects of these two [the first two liberations]. The spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are the introductory stages to the liberations (*vimokṣa*); the totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are the introductory stages to the spheres of mastery, because each subsequent one is more distinguished than the preceding. All these [meditative attainments], beginning with the liberations, exist within the mental continuums of both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*), with the exception of the liberation of cessation (*nirodhavimokṣa*).
Regarding cessation:
the liberation of cessation has already been explained in all its aspects.
But that which is obtained through the practice of detachment is the remainder.

(37ab) The [attainments] other than cessation—the liberations and so forth—are both acquired through detachment and acquired through application, depending on whether they have been previously practiced or not. They have their basis in all three realms, while those designated as "formless" and the remainder are born among humans. (37cd)

The formless liberations (*ārūpyavimokṣa*) and the formless totalities (*ārūpyakṛtsna*) have their basis (*āśraya*) in all three realms; the remainder have their basis exclusively in the human realm, because they are produced through the power of instruction (*upadeśa*). How is it that the specific formless attainments and meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are produced in the form and formless realms? The production of the meditative absorptions and formless attainments occurs by way of three causes: the powers of cause (*hetu*), karma (*karman*), and the nature of things (*dharmatā*). Among these, the production of the formless [attainments] in both realms occurs through the power of cause and the power of karma. (38ab) [p.459]

In the two realms—the form and formless realms—the production of the formless attainments occurs through the power of causes, namely from recent or habitual practice, and through the power of karma, because the maturation of karma belonging to a higher plane that is to be experienced in a subsequent life has become present. For it is not possible for one who is not free from passion for a lower level to be born in a higher one.
However, in the case of the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) within the form realm, [their production occurs] through those two [causes] and also by the very nature of things (*dharmatā*). (38cd)

The production of dhyāna in the realm of form occurs through these two powers—causal power and karmic power—and by way of natural law (*dharmatā*) at the time of cosmic dissolution. At that time, all beings belonging to the lower stages produce that dhyāna, because the activity of all dharmas has become fully manifest. Furthermore, for how long will this True Dharma (*saddharma*) remain, in which such varieties of dharmas are discerned? The True Dharma of the Teacher is twofold, consisting of scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*). (39ab)
In this regard, the *āgama* consists of the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, while the *adhigama* consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment; thus, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is twofold.
Its preservers are those who teach it and those who practice it. (39cd)

For those who uphold and proclaim the scripture (*āgama*) are its preservers, while those who practice it are the preservers of realization (*adhigama*). Therefore, it should be understood that as long as these [preservers] remain, so long does the True Dharma (*saddharma*) endure; however, they say that its duration is one thousand years. This refers to realization; others say that for the scripture, it lasts for a much longer time.
Regarding this Abhidharma taught here in this treatise: is this the very Abhidharma of the treatise that was taught?
For the most part, this Abhidharma has been related by me as established according to the system of the Kaśmīra Vaibhāṣikas.
Whatever has been poorly grasped here is our own fault; regarding the principles of the True Dharma, the Sages are the authority.

(40) [p.460] For this Abhidharma has been explained by us according to the system established by the Vaibhāṣikas of Kaśmīra. Whatever we have poorly grasped herein is our transgression. However, regarding the principles of the True Dharma, the Buddhas themselves and the sons of the Buddha are the authority.
When the Teacher, the eye of the world, has closed his eyes, and when the witnesses for the most part have passed away...
This teaching has been thrown into confusion by bad logicians who have not perceived the truth and are unrestrained. //41//

Now that the Self-Existent One has attained supreme peace, and the upholders of the Self-Existent One’s burden of the teaching have likewise passed away, this world is left without a protector; today it is roamed at will by unrestrained doctrines that destroy the spiritual community. (42)
Thus, knowing that the Sage’s teaching has its life-breath reaching the throat, and that this is the time of strength yet the world is defiled, those who desire liberation must not be negligent. (43)
Thus concludes the eighth chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled "Exposition of the Meditative Attainments."
Chapter IX [p.461] Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Chapter 9
Homage to the Buddha.

Is it, then, that there is no liberation elsewhere? No, there is not. What is the reason? Because they are settled in a false view of a self (*vitathātmadṛṣṭi*). For they do not determine the designation of a self (*ātmaprajñapti*) as being merely the continuum of the aggregates (*skandhasantāna*). What then? They conceptualize the self as a distinct substantial entity (*dravyāntara*), and all afflictions (*kleśa*) originate from this grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*). How, moreover, is it known that this designation "self" applies only to the continuum of the aggregates and not to some other designatable object? Because of the absence of both direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*).

For those phenomena that exist, their perception occurs through direct observation when there is no obstruction, such as in the case of the six sense objects and the mind. There is also inference, such as in the case of the five sense faculties. In this regard, the inference is as follows: when a cause is present, the absence of another necessary cause is seen to result in the absence of the effect, whereas its presence results in the presence of the effect, just as in the case of a sprout.

Furthermore, even when the object has come into range and the causal mental attention (*manaskāra*) is present, the non-occurrence of the apprehension of the object is observed in those who are blind or deaf, whereas its occurrence is observed in those who are not blind or deaf. Therefore, in that case as well, the absence and presence of another cause are determined; and since that other cause is the sense faculty (*indriya*), this is an inference. Since such [an inference] does not exist for the self (*ātman*), there is no self.

As for the fact that the Vātsīputrīyas maintain that the *pudgala* exists, this must first be examined: do they maintain that it exists substantially (*dravyataḥ*) or as a designation (*prajñaptitaḥ*)?

And what is this "substantial existence," and what is "designation"? If it is a distinct entity like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, then it exists substantially; in that case, because its intrinsic nature would be distinct [from the aggregates], it must be declared to be other than the aggregates, just as the aggregates are distinct from one another.

And its cause must be stated: either it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), in which case there follows the consequence of [accepting] the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and its lack of purpose. Or, if [it exists] by way of designation (*prajñapti*), we too say the same. For it does not exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*), nor does it exist by way of designation. What then? The person (*pudgala*) is designated in dependence upon the internal, appropriated, and present aggregates (*skandha*). This is blind speech with an unclarified meaning; we do not understand it. What is this "in dependence upon" (*upādāya*)?

If this meaning is that the person is characterized by the aggregates, then the designation "person" would apply to those very aggregates themselves—just as, depending upon form and so forth, the designation "milk" applies to those very things. Or, if this meaning is "in dependence upon the aggregates," then because the aggregates are the cause for the designation of the person, the same fault remains. It is not designated in that way. How, then? Just as fire is dependent upon fuel. And how is fire designated in dependence upon fuel?

For fire is not designated without fuel, nor can fire be designated as something other than fuel, nor as something non-other. If it were other, the fuel would be cold; if it were non-other, that which is burned would itself be the burner. In the same way, a person (*pudgala*) is not designated without the aggregates (*skandhas*); nor can it be asserted as other than the aggregates, because that would entail the consequence of eternalism; nor can it be asserted as non-other, because that would entail the consequence of nihilism.

Come now, tell me: what is fuel and what is fire? Then we shall understand how fire is designated in dependence upon fuel. What is to be said here? Fuel is that which is to be burned, and fire is the burner. This is precisely what must be explained here: what is that which is to be burned, and who is the burner? For in the world, wood and such that are not yet ablaze are called fuel and that which is to be burned; that which is ablaze is called fire and the burner.

That which is luminous, hot, and intense—by that very [fire] it is ignited and burned, because it brings about a transformation in the continuum. And both of these consist of eight substances; moreover, fire arises in dependence upon fuel, just as curd arises in dependence upon milk, or vinegar in dependence upon honey. Therefore, it is said that [fire] exists "having taken up" the fuel. Furthermore, fire is other than the fuel because they exist at different times.

And if the person (pudgala) were thus produced in dependence upon the aggregates (skandhas), it would follow that it is both distinct from them and impermanent. Furthermore, in the case of wood or the like being set ablaze, that which is heat is fire, while the three co-nascent primary elements (bhūtas) are held to be the fuel; even in these two cases, their distinctness is established due to the difference in their characteristics (lakṣaṇa).

However, the meaning of "in dependence upon" (*upādāya*) must be explained. How is it that fire is designated "in dependence upon" that fuel? For that [fuel] is neither the cause of the fire, nor is it the cause of its designation; rather, fire itself is the cause of its own designation. If the meaning of "in dependence upon" were the sense of a support (*āśraya*) or the sense of coexistence (*sahabhāva*), then the aggregates (*skandha*) would likewise become the supports or coexistent factors of the person (*pudgala*). Thus, their distinctness (*anyatva*) would be clearly asserted. Furthermore, in the absence of those [aggregates], the non-existence of the person would follow, just as there is no fire in the absence of fuel.

As for that which was said: "If fire were other than fuel, then the fuel would be non-hot, because its intrinsic nature would be different [from fire]. Or, if it possesses heat, then even though it is other than fire whose nature is heat, it is established as hot through its connection with heat. Thus, there is no fault in their being other. Furthermore, if all that—namely, the burning wood and so forth—is intended to be both the fuel and the fire;

Furthermore, the meaning of "depending on those" must be explained. It follows that the person (*pudgala*) is nothing other than the aggregates (*skandhas*), and thus their non-difference becomes unavoidable. Therefore, this [position] is not established: namely, that "just as fire is designated depending on fuel, so the person is designated depending on the aggregates. Moreover, if this [person] were not to be described as distinct from the aggregates, then it would follow that one could not say: "The objects of knowledge are fivefold: past, future, present, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the inexpressible (*avaktavya*). Thus, it would be impossible to speak of the inexpressible.

Indeed, it cannot be said that this [person] is a fifth category distinct from the past and so forth, nor can it be said that it is not a fifth category. Furthermore, when a person (*pudgala*) is designated, is it designated by apprehending the aggregates (*skandha*), or rather the person itself? If it is by apprehending the aggregates, then the designation of a person would apply to the aggregates alone, since the person is not apprehended. If, on the other hand, it is by apprehending the person, how can there be a designation of the person "in dependence upon" the aggregates? For in that case, the person itself would be the basis of dependence for that designation.

Now, if it is thought that the person (pudgala) is perceived when the aggregates (skandhas) exist, and therefore its designation is said to be based upon the aggregates, then in the same way, since form (rūpa) is also perceived when the eye, mental attention, and light exist, its designation must likewise be said to be based upon them. Furthermore, as in the case of form, the distinctness of the person [from the aggregates] would be evident.

This must first be addressed: by which of the six consciousnesses is the person (pudgala) to be cognized? It is said: by all six. How so? If one perceives a person in dependence upon forms that are cognizable by the eye-consciousness, then the person should be said to be cognizable by the eye-consciousness; yet it should not be said whether they are the forms themselves or not.

In the same way, up to: if one discerns a person (pudgala) in dependence upon mental objects (dharmas) cognizable by the mind, that person should be said to be "cognizable by the mind," but it should not be said whether they are "the same as" or "different from" those mental objects. If that were so, then [the person] would be equivalent to milk and the like. For if one discerns milk or water in dependence upon visible forms (rūpa) cognizable by the eye, then that milk or water should be said to be "cognizable by the eye," but it should not be said whether they are "the same as" or "different from" those visible forms.

In the same way, that which is cognizable by the nose, tongue, and body should be stated; however, it should not be stated whether they are tangible objects or not, lest there be the undesirable consequence of milk and water being [erroneously] categorized as fourfold. Therefore, just as milk or water is designated based on the totality of visible forms and so forth, it is established that the person (*pudgala*) is likewise designated based on the aggregates (*skandhas*).

As for what is said—that one discerns a person (pudgala) in dependence upon forms cognizable by the eye—what is the meaning of this statement? Does it mean that forms are the cause for the perception of the person, or rather, that while perceiving forms, one perceives the person? If forms are the cause for the perception of the person, then he [the person] must not be said to be other than them.

In that case, form (*rūpa*) also should not be said to be something other than light, the eye, and mental attention, because these are the causes for its perception. Now, when perceiving forms, does one perceive the person (*pudgala*) by means of that very same perception, or by means of another? If it is by means of that very same perception, then the person must either have a nature non-different from form, or the designation "person" applies to form itself. How is it understood that "this is form" and "this is the person"?

If it is not determined in this way, how can it be asserted that "form exists" and "the person (pudgala) also exists"? For its existence is asserted on the basis of perception. This should be stated for everything up to the mental factors (dharmas). Alternatively, because they are perceived at different times, the person would follow as being other than form—just as yellow is other than blue, or one moment is other than another moment. This should be stated for everything up to the mental factors.

Now, just as in the case of form (*rūpa*) and the person (*pudgala*), the identity or difference between their respective perceptions (*upalabdhi*) is also inexpressible. If that is so, then it follows that even regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), [the relationship] would be inexpressible; thus, there is a contradiction with your own tenet. Furthermore, if this [person] exists but cannot be said to be either "form" or "not form," then why did the Blessed One say: "Form is not-self, up to consciousness is not-self"?

By which visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) is this person (*pudgala*) apprehended? Does that [consciousness] arise in dependence upon visible forms (*rūpa*), or rather upon the person, or both? If it arises in dependence upon visible forms, it will not be capable of cognizing the person, just as [visual consciousness] cannot cognize sound and so forth. For whatever object arises in dependence upon within the visual cognitions, that alone is its objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*). If, on the other hand, it arises in dependence upon the person, or upon both, this contradicts the Sūtra.

For it is determined in the Sūtra that the arising of consciousness occurs in dependence upon a duality. Thus it is said: "O Bhikṣu, the eye is the cause and visible forms are the condition for the arising of visual consciousness. For what reason? Whatever visual consciousness there is, O Bhikṣu, all of that arises in dependence upon the eye and visible forms. In this way, it follows that the person (*pudgala*) is impermanent, because of the statement in the Sūtra: "Whatever causes and whatever conditions there are for the arising of consciousness, they too are impermanent. Furthermore, if the person is not its object (*ālambana*), then it cannot be cognized by that consciousness.

Furthermore, if it is asserted that the person (pudgala) is cognizable by the six consciousnesses, then because it is cognizable by auditory consciousness, it follows that it is other than visible form, just like sound; and because it is cognizable by visual consciousness, it follows that it is other than sound, just like visible form. The same logic should be applied to the others as well. Moreover, this scriptural passage would be contradicted: "O Brahmin, these five faculties have different ranges and different objects; each experiences its own respective range and object."
