"One faculty does not experience the range and object of another; namely, the eye-faculty, the ear-faculty, the nose-faculty, the tongue-faculty, and the body-faculty. It is the mind that experiences the range and object of these five faculties, and the mind is their refuge. Furthermore, the person (*pudgala*) is not an object. If it is not an object, then it is not something to be cognized (*vijñeya*). If this were so, it would follow that the mind-faculty (*manaindriya*) is also non-deviant [in its relation to its objects].

It is stated in the *Ṣaṭprāṇakopama* (The Simile of the Six Living Beings): “These six faculties have different ranges and different objects; each desires its own respective range and object. In that context, it was not said by taking the sense-faculty itself as the faculty. This is because it is impossible for the five [physical] faculties to desire seeing and so forth, nor for their corresponding consciousnesses. Therefore, it is spoken of here by taking the mental-consciousness-faculty (*manovijñānendriya*), which is produced through the predominance of those [five], as the faculty.

Furthermore, that mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) which is produced solely through the predominance of the mind does not at all desire the objects of the other [senses]; therefore, this fault does not apply. And it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, I shall teach you the Dharma-discourse on 'all that is to be directly known' (*sarvābhijñeya*. Having said this, he spoke of what is to be directly known by the eye: forms, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact; and also whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises internally conditioned by that eye-contact.

"Or, up to: conditioned by mental contact. This is called "the discourse on the Dharma concerning all that is to be directly known and fully understood. Therefore, it is determined that only this much is to be directly known and to be accepted, and not a *pudgala*. Consequently, it [the *pudgala*] is also not an object of consciousness (*vijñeya*), because wisdom (*prajñā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have the same objective domain. Furthermore, those who maintain the existence of a *pudgala*, seeing with the eye, fall into a basis for false views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*), thinking: "We see the *pudgala," or "we see the self by means of what is not-self."

And this has been definitively established by the Blessed One in the Sūtra: "The designation 'person' (pudgala) applies only to the aggregates," as stated in the *Mānuṣyaka-sūtra*. "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises; the meeting of these three is contact; born together with contact are feeling, perception, and volition. These four formless aggregates and the eye-faculty, which is form—this much is called 'humanity'."

In this regard, there are these designations: "sentient being," "man," "human," "mortal," "nourisher," "person," "individual," "living soul," and "creature. In this regard, there is this claim: "I see forms with the eye. In this regard, there is this conventional usage: "That venerable one has such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such an experience of pleasure and pain, such a long life, such a duration, and such a limit to his lifespan."

For thus, monks, this is merely a designation, this is merely a conventional expression: "All these phenomena are impermanent and conditioned," and "they are dependently originated. And the Blessed One has stated that a sutra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is the refuge. Therefore, it is not to be further examined. And thus it was said: "O Brahmin, 'everything exists' refers only to the twelve sense-bases (*āyatana*). If this person (*pudgala*) is neither an āyatana nor [included in] them, it is established that he does not exist.

Then, since it is a sense-field (*āyatana*), it is not inexpressible. For regarding them as well, it is said: "To whatever extent there is the eye, to whatever extent there are forms—in detail, to that extent, O monk, the Tathāgata designates everything and all designations.

And it is said in the *Bimbisāra-sūtra*: "O monks, the foolish, unlearned worldling, following after mere designation, thinks 'self, self,' yet herein there is neither self nor anything belonging to a self; it is this suffering that, when arising, arises," and so forth. Also, by the Arhatī Śailā, addressing Māra, it was said: [p.466]
"Do you think there is such a thing as a 'being'?
This is merely a view held by you, Māra;
this heap of conditioned formations is empty."
For no sentient being exists here.
For just as the designation "chariot" is used based on a collection of parts,
so too [the designation "person" is used] by depending upon the aggregates (skandhas).
Conventionally, it is called a "sentient being."
Thus it is said; and in the *Kṣudraka Āgama* as well, it is stated concerning the Brahmin Bādari:
"Listen, O Bādari, to the Dharma that releases all knots."
How the mind becomes defiled, and how the mind becomes purified.
For the self itself does not exist for the self; it is conceptualized through perversion.
There is no sentient being or self here.
But these phenomena are accompanied by causes.
There are exactly twelve links of existence— the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements—
having reflected upon all of these.
A person is not apprehended.
Behold the internal as empty; behold the external as empty;
even that [agent] is not to be found.

"He who cultivates emptiness"—thus it has been said: "There are five disadvantages in the apprehension of a self: there arises the view of a self and the view of a sentient being; one becomes indistinguishable from the non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika); one has entered upon a wrong path; one's mind does not enter into, does not find clarity in, does not abide in, and is not liberated by emptiness; and the noble dharmas do not become purified for him. Yet they do not accept this passage as authoritative. What is the reason?

"This is not recited in our school (nikāya). But is their school alone the authority, or is the word of the Buddha (buddhavacana) the authority? If their school alone is the authority, then the Buddha is not their teacher, nor are they followers of the Son of the Śākyas (śākyaputrīya). If, on the other hand, the word of the Buddha is the authority, why is this text not authoritative? [They reply: "Because, it is said, this is not the word of the Buddha. For what reason? "Because it is not recited in our school."

This is an injustice. What is the injustice here? For when a text is transmitted in all other schools (nikāya) and does not contradict the Sūtras or the nature of reality (dharmatā), to claim that it is not the word of the Buddha simply because we do not recite it is mere recklessness. Furthermore, do they even possess this Sūtra which states: "All phenomena are without self"? [p.467]

It might be thought: "The person (*pudgala*) is neither said to be a phenomenon (*dharma*), nor is it other than a phenomenon. If that were so, then it would not be established as cognizable by the mental consciousness (*manovijñeya*), because of the restriction: "The arising of consciousness occurs in dependence upon a dyad. Furthermore, it is analyzed here as follows: "'The notion of a self in what is not-self is a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), a perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). This perversion is [the notion] of a self in what is not-self, but not [the notion] of a self in a self."

Furthermore, the self is not the aggregates, the sense-bases, or the elements. As for what was previously stated—that it "should not be said whether [the self] is the forms or not"—that has now been refuted. And it is said in another Sūtra: "O monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins regard anything as the self, they all regard these very five aggregates of clinging as such. Therefore, every instance of grasping at a self is directed toward what is not-self.

Thus it has been said: "Whoever, in various ways, have recollected, did recollect, do recollect, or will recollect their former dwellings—all of them [recollected] these very five aggregates of clinging. If this is so, why was it said: "I possessed form in past time"? This is shown in order to demonstrate that they recollected in such various ways.

If, however, one were to perceive a person (pudgala) as possessing form, there would be the undesirable consequence of being dragged into the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi). In this case, the mere absence of such a scriptural reading would be the only refuge. Therefore, the person exists as a conceptual designation (prajñaptisat), like a heap or a stream.

If this were so, then it would follow that the Buddha is not omniscient; for there is no mind (*citta*) or mental factor (*caitta*) that could know everything, because they are momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Rather, it is the person (*pudgala*) who would know. In that case, since you admit that the person does not perish when the mind perishes, you have effectively admitted its permanence (*nityatva*). Furthermore, we do not declare the Buddha to be omniscient because of the simultaneous presence of knowledge regarding all things; rather, we do so by virtue of his capacity.

For that continuum which is called "Buddha" possesses this capacity: that by the mere utterance of [a word], non-erroneous knowledge arises regarding whatever is intended. And it has been said in this regard:
"Because of its capacity through the continuum, just as fire is considered to be all-consuming."
Likewise, he must be accepted as omniscient because of his knowing everything simultaneously.
How is this understood? From the mention of the past and so forth.
Those who were the perfectly awakened ones of the past,
those Buddhas who are yet to come,
and he who is the perfectly awakened one at present—
"The destroyer of the sorrow of many. [p.

468] Furthermore, you maintain that only the aggregates (*skandha*) belong to the three time periods, not the person (*pudgala*). If the aggregates themselves are the person, why did he say this: "O monks, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the bearer of the burden"? Why would this not have been said? For it is not logical that the burden itself should be the bearer of the burden. What is the reason? Because it is not observed to be so. Nor is it logical that it be "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*). What is the reason?

For it is not seen in this way; moreover, it would follow that the taking up of the burden (*bhārādāna*) would not be included within the aggregates (*skandha*). It was for this very purpose that the Blessed One designated the bearer of the burden (*bhārahāra*): "That venerable one of such a name, who has such a lifespan and such a limit to his life"—this was said so that he might be understood in this manner, and not otherwise, as being either eternal or indescribable.

Furthermore, it is the aggregates themselves that lead to the affliction of the aggregates, the former being the cause of the latter's impairment; thus they were spoken of by making a distinction between the burden and the bearer of the burden, for the meaning of "burden" is indeed affliction.

The person (*pudgala*) certainly exists, because it has been said: "To say 'there is no spontaneously born being' is a false view. Who, indeed, says: "There is no spontaneously born being"? We reply that the Blessed One has analyzed the existence of a being exactly as it is in the *Mānuṣyaka-sūtra*. Therefore, for one who denies the continuum of aggregates designated as a "spontaneously born being" in another world, this is the false view: "There is no spontaneously born being," because the aggregates themselves are what are spontaneously born.

Now, if this false view (mithyādṛṣṭi) were one that negates the person (pudgala), by what means would it be abandoned? For it is not logical that it should be abandoned either by vision (darśana) or by cultivation (bhāvanā). This is because the person is included within sentient beings (sattva). If you argue that [the person is not the aggregates] because of the scriptural statement, "One person arises in the world," and thus it is not the aggregates, we say no. This is because the designation "one" is applied even to a collection, as in the cases of "one sesame seed," "one grain of rice," or the singular expression used for "one heap."

Or rather, the person (*pudgala*) should be said to be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because you admit that it possesses the quality of having an origin. Yet, it does not originate in the same manner as the aggregates (*skandha*), which come into being as something previously non-existent. How then? It originates through the appropriation of other aggregates. Just as one says, "a sacrificer is born" or "a grammarian is born," because of the appropriation of knowledge; or "a monk is born" or "a wandering ascetic is born," because of the appropriation of a mark (*liṅga*); or "an old man is born" or "a sick man is born," because of the appropriation of a different state. [This is] not so.

For it has been rejected by the Blessed One in the *Sūtra* on Ultimate Emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*): "Thus, monks, there is action and there is its maturation, but no agent is found who casts off these aggregates and joins with other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharma-saṃketa*). And in the *Phālguna Sūtra*, it is said: "I do not say, Phālguna, that one 'appropriates'. Therefore, there is no appropriator of the aggregates, nor any caster-off.

Furthermore, whom do you take to be the sick person regarding whom you, as a ritualist (*yājñika*), form this conviction? If you cite the *pudgala* as the example, that is unestablished (*asiddha*). If you mean the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), no; for they arise as something entirely new at every moment. If you mean the body, it is the same for that too. Moreover, just as with the terms "body," "knowledge," and "mark" (*liṅga*), it would follow that the aggregates (*skandha*) and the *pudgala* are distinct entities. For the aged body is indeed one thing, and the diseased body another. Indeed, the Sāṃkhya theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) has already been refuted. Therefore, these are not valid examples.

And if the prior arising of the aggregates is not admitted for the person, yet it is held that he is other than them and permanent, then he is clearly demonstrated to be distinct from them. By saying "the five aggregates are one person," how is their difference not stated? How, for instance, is it that the four elements are four while matter is one, and yet matter is not other than the elements? This fault applies only to a particular position. In which position? In the position that holds there are only the elements (*bhūtamātrika*).

Nevertheless, just as it is accepted that form (*rūpa*) is merely the elements (*bhūta*), so too it must be accepted that the person (*pudgala*) is merely the aggregates (*skandha*). If the person is merely the aggregates, why did the Blessed One not provide a categorical answer to the question, "Is that life-principle (*jīva*) the same as the body, or is it different? It was because he took into account the intention of the questioner. For the latter asked with reference to a single substantial life-principle, an internal active agent; since such a thing does not exist in any way, how could its identity or difference be explained? It would be like asking whether the hair of a tortoise is hard or soft.

And this very text was already established by the predecessors. For the Elder Nāgasena was approached by King Kaliṅga, who said: "Venerable sir, I would like to question you; for śramaṇas are often talkative. If I were to ask something, please answer that very thing. Having been told, "Ask," he questioned him: "Is the soul the same as the body, or is the soul one thing and the body another? The Elder replied, "This has not been declared. He said:

"But did not the Venerable One previously cause me to take a vow that nothing else should be explained? Why is this other thing now being said, namely, that the mango tree itself does not exist? He replied: "How can I explain the sourness or sweetness of the fruits of a tree that does not exist? In the same way, Great King, that very *jīva* does not exist; how then could I explain its being either different from or non-different from the body?"

Why did the Blessed One also not say that it simply does not exist? It was out of consideration for the intention of the questioner. For he might have understood non-existence even of that continuum of aggregates which is designated as a "living being," and thus would have fallen into a wrong view due to his ignorance of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Furthermore, he was incapable of receiving that teaching. From this, too, it is determined that this is so.

As the Blessed One said: "Ānanda, if, when asked a question by the wanderer Vatsagotra, I were to answer that 'the self exists,' would it not be improper for me to say that all phenomena are without self? And Ānanda, if, when asked a question by the wanderer Vatsagotra, I were to answer that 'the self does not exist,' would not the wanderer Vatsagotra—who was already confused—fall into even greater confusion, thinking: 'I had a self before, but now it no longer exists'?"
"‘The self exists,’ Ānanda, leads to eternalism; ‘the self does not exist,’ Ānanda, leads to nihilism,” and so forth. And it is said here:
“Having regard for the piercing of the fangs of [wrong] views, and for the loss of [wholesome] actions.”
The Victors teach the Dharma like a tigress carrying away her cub.
For one who has accepted the existence of a self would be pierced by the fangs of [wrong] views,
resulting in the destruction of the ship of virtue.
"One would act without having attained conventional reality.
Furthermore, it says:
"Because of its non-existence, the Blessed One [speaks of] the living being (*jīva*)."
He did not speak of it as being either identical to or different from [the aggregates];
nor did he say that it does not exist,
lest even the conventional designation should be non-existent.
For in that continuum of aggregates where there is the existence of the fruits of good and evil,
that which is called "the living being" would not exist there.
Because of the teaching on the existence of the living being (*jīva*).
The aggregates are mere designations; he did not even say "there is a living being.
One who is unfit is incapable of awakening to emptiness.
At that time, such a person [exists].
For indeed, when asked whether the self exists or does not exist, he remained silent;
this was out of consideration for the disposition of the questioner.
But when it exists, why do you not say "it exists"?

The non-explanation of such matters as whether the world is eternal also depends upon the intention of the questioner. For if "the world" were intended to mean the self (*ātman*), then since that does not exist, a fourfold explanation would be improper. Alternatively, if "the world" refers to the entirety of saṃsāra, even for that, [an explanation] would be improper. If the world were eternal, no one could attain final nirvāṇa (*parinirvāṇa*). If it were non-eternal, the annihilation of all would follow. If it were both, it would necessarily follow that some would attain final nirvāṇa while others would not.

If it were neither [of the two], one would attain neither final nirvāṇa nor non-final nirvāṇa. Therefore, because final nirvāṇa depends upon the Path, no definitive determination is made in any of the four ways, just as in the case of the sparrow of the Nirgrantha disciple. For this very reason, the tetralemma regarding whether "the world is finite" is not explained; for this tetralemma has the same meaning.

For instance, after the wanderer Muktika had asked the fourfold set of questions, he asked again: "Does the entire world depart by means of this path, or only a portion of the world? The Elder Ānanda said: "Muktika, you have asked the Blessed One this very same question at the very beginning; now you ask it again in this different manner," and so on for everything.

The tetralemma, "Does the Tathāgata exist after death? and so forth, was not answered by the Buddha out of consideration for the intention of the questioner; for he had asked the question by identifying the Tathāgata with the liberated self.

But the proponent of the *pudgala* must be questioned: for what reason does the Blessed One declare that a living *pudgala* exists, yet does not declare it after death? [Otherwise] there would be the consequence of the fault of eternalism (*śāśvata-doṣa*). If so, why then does he declare: "Maitreya, you will become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha in a future age"? And why does he declare the rebirth of a deceased disciple who has passed away, saying: "So-and-so has been reborn in such-and-such a place"?

For even in this way, the consequence of eternalism follows. Furthermore, if the Blessed One, having previously seen the person, does not see him again after he has attained parinirvāṇa and thus does not provide an answer due to ignorance, then either the Teacher’s omniscience would be undermined, or one must admit that such a person does not exist at all. On the other hand, if he does see him, then even if it is not stated, it is established that he exists and is eternal. Now, it might be argued that one should not say whether he sees him or not.

If that is so, then this too should be made gradually inexpressible: whether the Blessed One is omniscient or not, or whether he exists or not. [The opponent argues: "The person (pudgala) certainly exists, because it is stated that 'I have no self' is a basis for views (*dṛṣṭisthāna*) from the standpoint of truth and stability; likewise, 'it exists' is also stated to be a basis for views. Therefore, this is not a proving argument. The Abhidharmikas reply: "Both of these, however, are subsumed under the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), specifically the views of eternalism and nihilism. And that alone is logical."
"Ānanda, to say 'the self exists' leads to eternalism; to say 'the self does not exist' leads to annihilationism," according to the statement in the Vātsya-sūtra.

If, then, the *pudgala* does not exist, who is it that transmigrates? For it is not logical to say that "transmigration itself transmigrates. And yet, the Blessed One said: "Of sentient beings hindered by ignorance, who run on and transmigrate. [p. 472] Now, how does the *pudgala* transmigrate? By abandoning one set of aggregates (*skandha*) and taking up another. This is the successive position.

Just as it is said that momentary fire "transmigrates" by way of its continuity (*saṃtati*), so too the collection of aggregates (*skandhasamudāya*) designated as a "sentient being" is said to "transmigrate" through the grasping of craving (*tṛṣṇopādāna*). If this is merely the aggregates, why did the Blessed One say, "At that time, on that occasion, I myself was the teacher named Sunetra"? Why would he not have said so? Because the aggregates are different [from one lifetime to the next]. What then is a "person" (*pudgala*)? That very same person would be eternal (*śāśvata*).

Therefore, by saying "I am that very person," he demonstrates the continuity of a single stream, just as one says, "That same fire has come burning along. Furthermore, if a self existed, the Tathāgatas would certainly perceive it clearly. And for those who perceive it, the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) and attachment to a self (*ātmasneha*) would become even firmer. Moreover, because of the statement in the Sūtra, "When there is a self, there is what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*)," their grasping at a self would operate even more intensely toward the aggregates (*skandhas*). This would be the view of a real body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

And when the view of "mine" exists, there is attachment to what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-sneha*). Thus, for those whose bonds have been strengthened by attachment to self and what belongs to the self, liberation would become even more remote. Now, if it is thought that attachment does not actually operate toward a self, then what kind of logic is this, that attachment arises through the mental conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of a self in what is not-self, yet it does not arise toward the self itself?

Therefore, this tumor of views has arisen within this teaching: namely, the grasping at a person by some, and the grasping at the non-existence of everything by others; and for those non-Buddhist teachers who conceive of a self as a distinct substance, the fault of the impossibility of liberation remains unshakable.

If, then, there is no self whatsoever, how does the recollection or recognition of an object experienced long ago occur within momentary states of mind? [It occurs] from a particular state of mind (cittaviśeṣa) that follows upon the mental impression (saṃjñānvaya) of the object of memory. From what kind of particular state of mind does memory immediately follow? [It follows] from one that possesses attention toward that object, a similar mental impression, and associated perceptions, and whose power has not been impaired by factors such as a change in the physical basis, grief, or distraction.

For even such a particular state of mind (*cittaviśeṣa*) that does not possess that same continuity is not capable of producing that memory; nor is a different kind of state, even if it possesses that continuity, capable of producing that memory. However, it is only when both conditions are met—that there is continuity and the state is of the same kind—is it capable; thus memory occurs, because no such capacity is observed in other cases. [Objection: How then can one mind remember what was seen by another? For if that were so, the mind of Yajñadatta would remember what was seen by the mind of Devadatta. [Reply: No, because there is no connection.

For there is no connection between those two, because they lack the relationship of cause and effect, unlike two [moments] belonging to a single continuum. Nor do we say that one mind remembers what was seen by another; rather, a different mind of recollection arises from the mind of seeing through the transformation of the continuum, as has been explained. What fault is there in this being so? Furthermore, recognition arises precisely from memory. If the self does not exist, who is it that remembers? What is the meaning of "remembers"? It means that one grasps the object by means of memory.

What is this apprehension other than recollection? Who, then, performs the recollection? That which performs it has been explained: it is a particular state of mind that serves as the cause of recollection. As for the expression "Caitra remembers," since that recollection arises from the continuum designated as "Caitra," one says "Caitra remembers" upon seeing it occurring from that continuum. If there is no self, to whom does this recollection belong? What is the purpose of this genitive case? It is used in the sense of ownership. For example, who is the owner of what? Just as Caitra is the owner of the cow.

How is he her owner? For it is dependent upon him that her employment for carrying, milking, and so forth occurs. And where, moreover, is the memory to be employed such that one searches for its owner in this way? It is to be employed toward the object to be remembered. For what purpose is it to be employed? For the sake of remembering. Oh, how well-spoken are the words of those who have grown up in comfort! For it is that very memory which is to be employed for that purpose. And how is it to be employed? Is it by way of production, or by way of sending forth?

Because memory and movement are impossible [in that way], [the mind] exists by way of production. In that case, it follows that the cause alone is the master and the fruit alone is the property; for the cause has sovereignty over the fruit, and by virtue of the fruit, the cause possesses it. For that very cause which is the cause of memory, this [memory] belongs to it alone.

Furthermore, that continuum of the collection of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) designated as "Caitra," which is grasped as a single unit and called the "owner" of what is termed "the cow," is so called by taking into account its causal role in the production of modifications in another location; however, there is certainly no single entity named Caitra, nor is there any such thing as a cow. Therefore, even in that case, the status of being an owner does not exist apart from the state of being a cause. This same principle should be stated regarding such questions as "Who knows? and "Whose is the cognition?
The specific distinction here is that the causes are, as appropriate, the sense faculty, the object, and mental attention (*manaskāra*).

As for the one who says: "Because existence depends upon an existent being, for every state of being depends upon a subject that exists; just as in the case of 'Devadatta goes,' the action of going is a state of being that depends upon the goer, Devadatta, so too consciousness is a state of being. Therefore, there must be one who cognizes. To him it should be said: "Who is this Devadatta? If it is the self (*ātman*), that is precisely what remains to be proven. If, however, it is the conventional person (*vyavahārapuruṣa*)," [then it is merely a designation].

Even that [Devadatta] is not a single entity; rather, those very conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) bear such a name. In this regard, it is said that Devadatta goes or that he cognizes. And how does Devadatta go? Conditioned phenomena are indeed momentary, yet they possess an undifferentiated continuum. Fools, through their grasping at a single sentient being as a solid mass, are convinced that "Devadatta" exists. As these phenomena become the cause for their own continuum to arise in another location, they are said to "Devadatta goes. Furthermore, that arising in another location is what constitutes "going."

Just as the words "going" and "one who goes" are applied to a continuum of flames or sounds, so too, when those very [moments] become the cause of consciousness, it is said that "Devadatta knows. Even the Noble Ones speak in this way using those conventional designations for the sake of communication.

If that is so, what does consciousness do in the Sūtra statement, "consciousness cognizes"? It does nothing at all. Just as it is said that an effect conforms to its cause—because it acquires its own being through similarity even while doing nothing—so too consciousness is said to "cognize," because it acquires its own being through similarity even while doing nothing. What, then, is this similarity? It is the possession of that [object's] aspect (*tadākāratā*).

For this very reason, although it arises from the sense faculty, it is said that consciousness cognizes the object, not the sense faculty. Alternatively, here too there is no fault in the statement "consciousness cognizes," because the continuum of consciousness serves as the cause for the arising of [subsequent] consciousness; for the term denoting an agent is applied to the cause, just as one says, "the bell rings. Furthermore, just as it is said that "the lamp goes," so too is it said that "consciousness cognizes. And how does the lamp go? The term "lamp" is used metaphorically for the continuum of flames.

Just as one is said to "go to that place" when arising in other locations, so too consciousness is metaphorically designated as a "continuum" (*saṃtāna*) of mental states; when it arises with respect to another object, it is said to "cognize that object. Furthermore, just as in the expressions "matter is born" or "matter persists," the agent of becoming is not distinct from the act of becoming itself, so it would be for consciousness as well.

If consciousness arises from consciousness and not from a self, why does it not always arise as exactly the same, nor according to a fixed sequence like a sprout, a stalk, and a leaf? This is because change while persisting (*sthityanyathātva*) is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). For this is the very nature of the conditioned: that there must necessarily be a transformation within the continuum.

Otherwise, for those who are absorbed in meditative concentration at will, since there would be no distinction from the first moment when similar body and mind arise, there could be no self-emergence even later. For the sequence of moments of consciousness is indeed fixed; because it arises only from that specific [preceding] state from which it ought to arise. Even though they possess an identical aspect, some are capable of producing [a subsequent state], due to the distinction of their lineage (*gotra*).

For example, if immediately after a woman’s mind there arises a mind that reviles her body, or a mind directed toward her husband, son, and so forth, and subsequently, through the transformation of the continuum, a woman’s mind arises again, it is capable of producing either that mind which reviles her body or that mind directed toward her husband, son, and so forth, because it belongs to that same lineage (*gotra*); otherwise, it would not be capable.

Furthermore, when by way of alternation various kinds of thoughts arise from a female thought, that very same [female] thought arises again more frequently or more immediately because its cultivation is stronger, except for specific external bodily conditions at that time. Why does that same stronger cultivation not always bear fruit? Because change of state (*sthityanyathātva*) is a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), and that change of state is conducive to the arising of the fruit of another cultivation.

For this is merely a brief indication regarding all the modes of mind; however, the Buddhas possess mastery in knowing the uninterrupted causal sequence. Thus they have said: "The causes for every single aspect, even of a single eye on a peacock's feather, cannot be known by those who are not omniscient; for that knowledge is the power of the Omniscient One."
Thus [it is said].
This is even more so for the various types of formless minds.

However, this objection clearly applies to that particular non-Buddhist who believes that the arising of the mind originates from a self: "Why does it not always arise as exactly the same, and why does it not follow a fixed sequence like a sprout, a stalk, and a leaf? If he should reply, "Because it depends on specific conjunctions with the mind," we say no, because the conjunction with anything else is unestablished.

Furthermore, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is defined as "the attainment of what was previously unattained by two conjoined things that are limited," it follows that the self (*ātman*) must be limited. Consequently, because the mind (*manas*) moves, it would follow that the self either moves or becomes devoid of passion (*virāga*). If you argue that it is a conjunction with a specific location (*pradeśa*), we say no; for it is impossible for that very [self] to possess such a location. Or, even if such a conjunction were granted, how could there be a distinction in conjunction when the mind is eternal and undifferentiated? If you claim it depends on a distinction in cognition (*buddhi*), [we reply:]...

That very point is challenged: how is there a particularity of cognition? If it is argued that it arises from the contact of the self and the mind depending on a particularity of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), then let it arise from the mind alone, since it depends on a particularity of mental impressions. Indeed, no capacity whatsoever is perceived in the self, just as the "phuḥ svāhā" of a quack doctor is not effective in accomplishing the action of a medicine. If it is argued that their contact occurs only when the self exists, that is mere words. If it is argued that the self is their substratum (*āśraya*), then in what way is one the substratum of the other?

For it is not logical that those [mental states] are supported by it in the manner of a painting or a jujube fruit, nor is it logical that it is their support in the manner of a wall or a bowl; because of the faults of resistance and conjunction, it cannot be a support in that way. How then? If you say "just as the earth is for odors and so forth," we are thoroughly satisfied! For this very point is what convinces us that there is no self: just as the earth is not something other than the odors and so forth. For who can distinguish an earth that is other than the odors and so forth?

The designation "the odors and so forth of the earth" is for the purpose of specification; it is so that those very things called odors and so forth may be understood as such, and not others. This is like the designation of a wooden statue as a "body. Furthermore, even though [cognition] depends on specific mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), why does there not arise simultaneously the production of all cognitions? For that which is strongest obstructs the others. Why, then, does that very strongest one not always bear fruit? Let the principle that applies here belong to mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*); the self (*ātman*), however, is postulated needlessly.

If it is argued that a self must necessarily be admitted because memory and so forth belong to the category of qualities (*guṇapadārtha*), and because a quality must necessarily reside in a substance (*dravya*) by implication, and because those [qualities] cannot have anything else as their substratum—[we reply: No. For it is not established that these [memory and so forth] belong to the category of qualities. According to us, everything that exists is a substance, because of the scriptural statement: "The six substances are the fruits of the ascetic life" (*ṣaḍ dravyāṇi śrāmaṇyaphalāni*). Nor is it established that these [memory and so forth] reside in a substance; for the meaning of "substratum" has already been examined. Therefore, that [argument] is merely something arbitrary.

If the self does not exist, for what purpose is the undertaking of action? It is for the purpose of thinking, "May I be happy; may I not be miserable. What is this thing called "I" which is the object of this ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)? Its object is the aggregates (*skandhas*). How is this known? Because of the affection felt toward them, and because of their grammatical coreferentiality with cognitions such as "fair-complexioned" and so forth.

"I am fair," "I see," "I am stout," "I am thin," "I am old," "I am young"—this word "I" is observed to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) with such cognitions as "fairness" and so forth. Yet these modes [of appearance] are not observed to belong to the self (*ātman*). Therefore, it is understood that this [sense of "I"] refers to the aggregates (*skandhas*). Even though the body is merely a benefactor to the self, there is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of the self upon it, just as one says, "He who is this [person] is the very same as I," or "This is my servant. While such metaphorical designation of the self occurs even toward a benefactor, the actual sense of "I" (*ahaṃkāra*) does not.

If the body is the objective support (*ālambana*), why does [the notion of "I"] not also have another's body as its objective support? Because of the lack of connection. For this sense of "I" arises only with respect to that very body or mind with which it has a connection, and not elsewhere; this is due to such habitual practice throughout beginningless *saṃsāra*. And what is this connection? It is the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). If there is no self (*ātman*), to whom does this sense of "I" belong? This brings us back once again to the question: "For what purpose is this genitive case used?"

"...up to: 'This belongs to that very cause which is its own. And what is this other cause? It is the faulty mind, which has been permeated by previous notions of "I" and has one's own continuum as its object. If there is no self, who is it that is happy or suffering? [It is] that basis upon which pleasure or pain has arisen, just as one says, "the tree is in flower" or "the forest is bearing fruit. But what is the basis for these two? The six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). This has been stated according to how it is established.

If the self does not exist, who is the agent of these actions, and who is the experiencer of their fruits? What is the meaning of the term "agent"? An agent is one who acts; an experiencer is one who enjoys. These are merely synonyms; they do not denote a distinct entity. Grammarians define the characteristic of an agent as "one who is independent. Yet, independence is observed in some cases regarding certain effects, as seen in the world in the case of Devadatta’s bathing, sitting, walking, and so forth.

Furthermore, who is this "you" (bhavān) that you cite as Devadatta? If it is the self (*ātman*), then that very thing is what remains to be proven. If, on the other hand, it is the five aggregates (*pañcaskandhaka*), then that itself is the agent (*kartṛ*). This action (*karman*) is of three kinds: bodily, vocal, and mental action. Regarding bodily action first: the activity of the body is dependent upon the mind; the activity of the mind with respect to the body is likewise dependent upon its own causes; and for those [causes] as well, it is the same. Thus, there is no independence (*svātantrya*) for anything whatsoever. For all phenomena (*bhāva*) proceed in dependence upon conditions (*pratyaya*).

Furthermore, since it is admitted that the self (*ātman*), being independent, is not a cause, its autonomy is not established. Therefore, no agent characterized in such a manner is perceived. That which is the primary cause of something is called its "agent. And no causality whatsoever is observed in the case of the self; therefore, even in this sense, it is not logical for it to be an agent.

For desire is born from mindfulness; discursive thought is born from desire; from discursive thought comes effort; from effort comes wind; and from that, action. What does the self do here? Furthermore, what is this "enjoyment" of the fruit for which the self is postulated as the enjoyer while performing [action]? If it is argued that it is "perception," there is no capacity for perception in the self, because that has been refuted in the case of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

If the self does not exist, why is the accumulation of merit and demerit—which is based on a sentient being—not absent? Because sensation and so forth are not accidental. And the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are the support for those [sensation, etc.], not the self; how this is so has already been explained.

If there is no self (*ātman*), how can a fruit arise in the future from a karma that has perished? And even if a self exists, how can a fruit arise in the future from a karma that has perished? [The answer is: from merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) which are based upon it. This formulation of speech—asking "What is based on what?"—has already been answered. Therefore, let it be that the fruit arises from merit and demerit precisely without being based on anything else. However, we do not say that the fruit arises in the future from a karma that has perished. What then?

"Because of a specific transformation in the continuum of that [seed], like a seed and its fruit. Just as it is said that a fruit arises from a seed, yet it does not arise from a seed that has already perished, nor does it arise immediately after it. What then? It arises from a specific transformation in its continuum, produced through the sequence of sprout, stalk, leaf, and so forth, culminating in the flower. Furthermore, why is that which is produced from the flower called the "fruit of that seed"? Because the capacity for that [fruit] was deposited by it in the final flower.

For if it were not preceded by that [action], it would not be capable of producing such a fruit. Thus it is said that the fruit arises from the action; yet it does not arise from an action that has already perished, nor does it arise immediately after it. What then? It arises from a specific transformation within the continuity of that [action].

What, then, is the continuum (*saṃtati*), what is transformation (*pariṇāma*), and what is the specific transformation (*viśeṣa*)? That which is the production of successive moments of consciousness preceded by karma is the continuum; its arising in a different state is transformation. Furthermore, that [moment] which is immediately capable of producing a fruit is the "specific transformation," because it is distinguished as the final transformation. For example, the death-consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna*) [is the cause] of rebirth. Even though there are three kinds of karma as antecedents, the capacity produced by that karma which is weighty, proximate, or habitual is manifested, and not that of another. And it is said:
Whatever karma is heavy, whatever is proximate, whatever has been frequently practiced, and whatever was performed previously— in the cycle of existence, each preceding one ripens before the next.

In this regard, the capacity to yield a ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*), which was deposited by the ripening cause (*vipākahetu*), ceases once it has given its ripened fruit. However, the capacity to yield a flow-on fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), which was deposited by the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), ceases in the case of afflicted states upon the arising of their antidote; in the case of non-afflicted states, it ceases when one attains final nirvana due to the absolute cessation of the mental continuum. Now, why does another ripened fruit not arise from a ripened fruit, just as another fruit arises from the fruit of a seed? First of all, everything is not necessarily identical to the illustrative example.

Even in that case, however, another fruit does not arise directly from the fruit itself. What then? It arises from a specific transformation produced by a specific state of softening. For that particular mode of the primary elements (*bhūta*) which brings about the sprout is its seed, and nothing else. Nevertheless, the preceding continuum is also designated as the "seed" either by way of a future name or because of its similarity [to the actual seed].

Likewise here too, if from that maturation (*vipāka*) there arises—due to specific conditions such as hearing the true or false Dharma—a wholesome-with-outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*) transformation of the mind, then from that [transformation] another transformation arises, and not otherwise; this is the same [as the previous case]. Alternatively, this should be understood in the following way:

Just as from a *mātuluṅga* flower dyed with lac juice, a red filament arises in the fruit, produced by a specific transformation within the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma-viśeṣa*), and yet no further [filament] arises from that one; so too, from a maturation (*vipāka*) born of karma, no further maturation arises. This has been shown according to its gross features, as it is accessible to our intellect. However, that "continuums perfumed by various karmas distinguished by manifold potencies reach such a state and produce such a fruit" is the domain of the Buddhas alone. As it has indeed been said:
No one other than a Buddha can know, in every respect and with certainty, that karma, its cultivation, the attainment of its activity, and the resulting fruit.
Thus, having heard this nature of the Dharma of the Buddhas, which is purified by well-established causes and paths,
[one should avoid] those who are blind, whose conduct is characterized by various false views.
Having cast aside the views of the non-Buddhists, those who are not blind proceed [to liberation].

For one with dull vision does not perceive this selflessness— even when it is laid open— though it proceeds directly toward the city of Nirvana, shines with the rays of the Tathāgata’s words, and has been traversed by thousands of noble ones.
Thus, this has been taught as merely a mere indication for those of great intelligence,
like the site of a wound where poison spreads by its own power. The *Pudgalakośa*, the commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa*, is hereby completed.
This is the work of the venerable teacher Vasubandhu.
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has explained their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

This is the religious gift of the venerable Śrī Lāmāvāka, a scholar from the Northern Region (Uttarāpatha) and a bearer of the burden of the entire teaching of the Tathāgata according to the most excellent Mahāyāna. Whatever merit is herein... [and so forth]. May there be auspiciousness!
